The tale is pure range adventure: quick talk, hard rides, and a hero who settles rows with nerve and a gun. Note for readers: the hosted text here stops mid-sentence in an early saloon scene, so the full trail is told in the chapter list more than in the pages that follow. The opening still gives the flavor of Hendryx's cattle country.
16982-bunny-rabbit-s-diary:
Mary Frances Blaisdell wrote this 1915 school edition of Bunny Rabbit's Diary, issued by Little, Brown in Boston with pictures by George F. Kerr. Contents run from Bunny's diary and Billy's slide, through a Christmas tree, Bobtail's kite, April Fool's Day, Mrs. Duck's secret, a swimming lesson, a clover patch, moving day, a summer shower, Sammy's flying machine, a cabbage patch, a white rabbit, a teddy bear, and Bobby's party.

Blaisdell writes short, gentle tales for young children, with Bunny talking to Mrs. Duck in the frontispiece. Each tale stands alone, full of farm and home fun. Young readers get a sweet, old-style animal book for early reading, and grown readers get a sample of 1915 school books at their most charming.
17001-an-elementary-course-in-synthetic-:
Derrick Norman Lehmer's course teaches projective geometry without coordinates, by pure reasoning about points, lines, and planes. It starts with one-to-one matching between sets, the same idea that sits behind counting and naming things. Later chapters build up the main theorems step by step, with problems and a full index.

The style is spare and exact, made for students who want proof, not pictures alone. Lehmer keeps each step short and shows why it matters before he moves on. Readers with basic geometry will find a clear, old-school path into a subject that still underpins much of modern math and design.
17066-tangled-trails-a-western-detective:
William Macleod Raine wrote this 1921 western detective story, issued by Grosset and Dunlap in New York, third impression March 1922. Chapters move from no altruist and Wild Rose taking the dust into a championship and cousins meeting. Lights out, foul play, and a fire escape follow. A story in the News, Kirby asking a direct question, and a coroner's inquest appear. That's the man, a glove and its hand, and a lady with violet perfume lead to Dry Valley. A discovery, a brass bed, and a detective getting two surprises close the tale.

Raine mixes western action with detective work, as Kirby cuts trail through cousins, suspects, and a tangled murder. The tale moves fast, with inquests, conferences, and a finger of suspicion pointing anew. Readers who like western mysteries will find a brisk, plot-rich novel, full of range, romance, and a detective who earns his answers.
1723-cow-country:
Bud is a ranch boy with more ambition than sense, and this western follows him from a trail herd to the day he must prove himself a man. Chapters track his roping, his warnings to older hands, his coin-flip with fate, and the woman he meets when the work turns serious.

Bower writes the cow country from the saddle: horses, ropes, dust, and the small codes by which a crew judges a newcomer. The novel's charm is Bud himself, young and headstrong, learning that courage counts for little without judgment. It reads as a coming-of-age story dressed in chaps and spurs.
17249-added-upon-a-story:
Nephi Anderson's Added Upon, first copyrighted in 1898 and here in its ninth edition, tells the Latter-day Saint plan of life in story form. Its preface asks the great questions: what am I, whence came I, what is this life for, and what is my destiny? The tale then traces the scheme of things from a distant past toward a future point, in brief, suggestive scenes.

Anderson writes to justify and praise the ways of God as taught by his faith, with a story meant to light the eye of faith. Details stay light where revelation is spare, leaving readers to fill the garden in their minds. Latter-day Saint readers and students of Mormon fiction will find a classic, earnest outline of the plan.
17268-ontario-teachers-manuals-history:
Ontario's 1915 Teachers' Manual for history, authorized by the Minister of Education, guides teachers of public and separate schools. Chapters cover aims and stages of study, general methods, correlation of subjects, and special topics such as current events, local material, and civics. Illustrative lessons run from Form I Bible stories, like Moses and Joseph, to Form IV work, with devices and a bibliography.

The manual stresses telling stories well and having pupils retell them, joining history, literature, and composition. Its tone is practical and Canadian, made for classroom use. Teachers and historians of education will find a clear record of how Ontario taught history to children a century ago.
1730-michael-brother-of-jerry:
Michael is an Irish terrier whose brother Jerry starred in London's earlier dog story, and his own life runs through training rings, performances, and beatings. The foreword states London's aim plainly: he came to dislike trained-animal shows because curiosity led him behind the glitter to the beatings that made the tricks possible.

Michael's story is told from the dog's side of the bargain — loyalty, hunger, and the defence of his meat against all comers. And it builds into an attack on the whole business of breaking animals for applause. Readers who know The Call of the Wild will recognize London's method, and his anger here is aimed at men, not at beasts.
17364-types-of-weltschmerz-in-german-poe:
Wilhelm Alfred Braun's 1905 Columbia study treats Weltschmerz, world pain, in German poetry through close readings of three types. Chapters cover Holderlin, Lenau, and Heine, after an introduction that sets the term's range since Werther. Calvin Thomas, in a note, praises Braun's choice to analyze conspicuous types rather than write an exhaustive history.

Braun weighs each poet's life, feelings, body and mind, and theory of existence, joining psychology with philosophy. His prose is scholarly yet clear, with a bibliography for further work. Students of German letters will find a concise, classic study of sorrow, longing, and the lyric mind in the nineteenth century.
17386-the-leading-facts-of-english-histo:
D. H. Montgomery wrote this school history of England for the Leading Facts of History series. Ginn and Company published it in Boston, New York, Chicago, and London in a revised edition, with copyrights from 1887 to 1912. Montgomery takes his motto from Stubbs: nothing in the past is dead to the man who would learn how the present came to be what it is. He dedicates the book to the memory of his friend J. J. M.

The volume carries the story of England from early times through its kings, parliaments, and empire, in the clear, orderly style of a classroom text. Readers get a solid late Victorian and Edwardian survey, once widely used in American schools. It still serves as a readable outline of English history for newcomers.
17507-everybody-s-lonesome-a-true-fairy-:
Clara E. Laughlin, author of The Lady in Gray, published this fairy story in 1910 with Fleming H. Revell Company, with pictures by A. I. Keller. It is dedicated to Mabel Talliaferro, called the faery child. The chapters move from disappointment in life and waiting for one's own. They pass through finding a first fairy and being kind to a tired man, to a party, a lion of the evening, and candle-light time.

Later chapters teach being brave and sweet, telling the secret to mother, and a meeting with the old world and the king. Readers get a gentle, moral fairy tale for children, where kindness counts as magic. Laughlin's tale suits young readers who like their wonder mixed with homely feeling.
17510-when-the-yule-log-burns-a-christma:
Leona Dalrymple, author of Uncle Noah's Christmas Party, published this Christmas story in New York in November 1916 with Robert M. McBride and Company. The book is built in two parts, each around a yule log. Part one lights a log in chapters called Kindlings, Wishing Sparks, By the Fire, and Embers. Part two lights the new log with embers of the old.

Chapters called The Fire Again, It Blazes Higher, The Log at Dawn, and The Log at Twilight carry the second half. Readers get a fireside Christmas tale, where the burning log frames stories, wishes, and family feeling. The book suits readers who like old-fashioned holiday fiction, warm, simple, and meant to be read aloud in winter.
17743-rosemary-a-christmas-story:
C. N. and A. M. Williamson wrote Rosemary as a Christmas story in 1906, with pictures by William Hatherell. The tale opens on a terrace where a girl in white meets a rose girl at a casino, and it moves through dogs, fathers, and a child's long search.

Rosemary hunts for a father, meets fairy fathers who must vanish, and finds a white shape at the door. The Williamsons mix light romance with a child's clear-eyed hope, and the Christmas setting warms the whole tale. It is a sweet, old-fashioned holiday story, made to be read aloud by the fire.
17804-if-you-re-going-to-live-in-the-cou:
Thomas H. Ormsbee and Richmond Huntley wrote this guide for readers thinking of living in the country, published in New York in 1937 by Thomas Y. Crowell Company, with decorations by Frank Lieberman. Chapters open with why live in the country and selecting the location. Shopping for property and calling in an architect follow.

Building versus remodelling, looking an old house in the mouth, and new sites for old houses carry the practical advice on. Readers get a Depression-era handbook for moving out of town, sensible and encouraging. The book suits readers of country houses, restoration, and American domestic life.
17890-when-wilderness-was-king-a-tale-of:
Randall Parrish wrote When Wilderness Was King in 1904, a tale of the Illinois country printed by A. L. Burt in New York. The book ran through seven editions in two years, a mark of how well readers liked Parrish's frontier tales.

Chapters run from a message from the West to Captain Wells of Fort Wayne, a lane of peril, Old Fort Dearborn, and a contest of wits. A young man, two men and a maid, and a circle in the sand drive the plot through forest and fort. It is a rousing old tale of the Illinois frontier, full of action, honor, and young love.
17938-contrary-mary:
Temple Bailey wrote Contrary Mary in 1914, put out in New York by Grosset and Dunlap, with pictures by Charles S. Corson. The book ran through seven printings in its first year, a mark of Bailey's wide appeal.

Mary, a contrary young woman, meets silken ladies on one stair and a lonely wayfarer on another, and the tale winds through rose-leaves, old slippers, and a rented gentleman's library. Bailey writes bright, modern romance with a light, comic touch. It is a cheerful, old-style love story, best for readers who like a heroine with a will of her own.
17943-the-observations-of-henry:
Jerome K. Jerome wrote The Observations of Henry in 1901, printed in Bristol by Arrowsmith. Jerome, famed for Three Men in a Boat, here lets Henry the waiter, now Henri, tell his tales, heard in the long dining room of the Riffel Alp Hotel.

Henry begins in a Mile End Road coffee shop, where a boy named Kipper sells papers and earns mugs of coffee and scraps. Tales of ghosts, guests, and hotel life follow, told in Henry's own backward, muddled order, tidied by Jerome. The book is light, comic, and humane, a set of waiter tales full of London life and wry wit.
18053-spanish-life-in-town-and-country:
L. Higgin wrote Spanish Life in Town and Country, part of the Our European Neighbours series edited by William Harbutt Dawson. The series set French, German, Russian, Dutch, Swiss, and Spanish life side by side, for English readers who wished to know their neighbors.

Chapters run from land and people to types and traits, national character, Spanish society, and modern Madrid. Higgin writes with a traveler's ease and a student's care. The book gives a warm, period portrait of Spain at the turn of the century, best read now as a window on how the English once saw their southern neighbor.
18127-the-beginner-s-american-history:
D. H. Montgomery wrote The Beginner's American History in 1893, printed in Boston by Ginn and Company, as an introduction to his larger Leading Facts of American History. Montgomery vows the small book is not a cut-down, but a new work for pupils just starting the subject.

Chapters run from Columbus and the Cabots to Balboa, Raleigh, John Smith, Hudson, Standish, Penn, Franklin, Washington, and Boone. Montgomery picks only tales he deems sound, with pictures by C. S. King. The book is a plain, old school history, best read now as a window on how American children once learned their past.
18276-essays-in-literature-and-history:
James Anthony Froude published this set of essays on literature and history with J. M. Dent at London in 1906. The pieces first appeared in reviews of the 1850s and 1860s: the Westminster Review, Fraser's Magazine, the Eclectic Review, and The Leader. Froude, known for his histories, here writes as a critic, judging poets, saints, monks, and philosophers.

Contents include Arnold's poems, words about Oxford, England's forgotten worthies, the Book of Job, the lives of the saints, and the dissolution of the monasteries. Later essays treat the philosophy of Christianity, a plea for free discussion of theological difficulties, Spinoza, Reynard the Fox, and a commonplace book of Richard Hilles. Readers get Victorian criticism at its boldest: learned, partisan, and eager to judge the past by present lights.
1845-zuleika-dobson-or-an-oxford-love-st:
Zuleika arrives at Oxford, a music-hall performer, and every undergraduate in the university falls into despair over her. The note to the 1922 edition recalls Beerbohm in Italy when the book first appeared. He was surprised to hear friends speak of Zu-like-a, a name he hardly recognized as his own.

The comedy turns on love as epidemic: young men, told they cannot have Zuleika, choose drowning instead. One hero, troubled that he can swim, walks to the river anyway. Beerbohm writes the satire with perfect manners and a straight face, and the novel remains the classic Oxford fantasy, witty, cruel, and impossible to forget.
18489-a-court-of-inquiry:
Grace S. Richmond wrote this novel, published by A. L. Burt in New York by arrangement with Doubleday, Page, with copyrights from 1901 to 1916. Richmond, author of Red Pepper Burns and Mrs. Red Pepper, builds her story round a private court of inquiry into the condition of friends.

The contents name the women by flowers in part one: Althea, Camellia, Dahlia, Rhodora, Azalea, and Hepatica. Each is then paired with a man: a professor, a judge, a cashier, a promoter, a preacher, and a philosopher. Part three follows sixteen miles to Boswell's, honour, and a word of honour, as the court weighs love and character.
18521-an-expository-outline-of-the-vesti:
Printed at London in 1846, this short work sums up and judges the Vestiges of the Natural History of Creation, a then-famous anonymous book on how the world and life developed. It first ran as a review in the Atlas newspaper in 1845, then was reprinted on its own after readers kept asking for it. The outline follows the author's facts and chain of reasoning step by step.

It then weighs the replies of critics such as Sedgwick, Whewell, and Bosanquet, and adds a notice of the author's sequel, Explanations. The closing pages judge where the case stands and what it means for faith and morals. The tract is a useful guide to one of the great science debates before Darwin.
18569-voltaire-s-philosophical-dictionar:
Voltaire's Philosophical Dictionary, here in a New York Carlton House edition, gathers his sharp entries in alphabetical order for dipping into rather than straight reading. The preface says the book is made for readers who think for themselves, extending and testing each germ of thought. Entries run from adultery, atheism, and authority through liberty, luxury, and marriage to reason, religion, superstition, tolerance, and tyranny.

Voltaire takes aim at priests, kings, and common prejudices with wit and irony, praising reason and tolerance. Short pieces on Joan of Arc, Cromwell, and the man in the iron mask add history to the argument. The book stands as a compact entry to Enlightenment thought.
18618-stories-of-later-american-history:
Wilbur F. Gordy, former schools chief of Springfield, Massachusetts, published this school history at New York in 1915 with Scribner's, maps and pictures included. Its chapters run from Patrick Henry and Samuel Adams through the war near Boston. They continue with Washington in the Revolution and heroes of the South, then Daniel Boone, John Paul Jones, and George Rogers Clark.

Later chapters cover the new republic, its growth, internal improvements, three great statesmen, the Civil War, and four great industries. Pictures range from pioneers on the overland route to Paul Revere's ride and winter at Valley Forge. The book is a clear, story-led history for young readers.
1864-hero-tales-from-american-history:
Henry Cabot Lodge and Theodore Roosevelt join forces in this book of hero tales. The tales are chosen to show Americans — in the editors' phrase, nurtured in freedom and well born — doing glorious deeds in public and private life. Mad Anthony Wayne, hard-fighting general of the Revolution, leads the parade, and Gouverneur Morris writes from Paris in August 1792 with Horace on his lips.

The tales run from the Revolution through the Civil War, with each hero given a short, stirring chapter. Written before Roosevelt's presidency, the book is a deliberate work of civic teaching. It reads as a window into how two future statesmen wanted young Americans to remember their past.
18685-lectures-on-modern-history:
Lord Acton's Cambridge lectures on modern history open with his inaugural address of June 1895. He argues that modern history has no neat beginning or end, since the fortunes of peoples weave on without a break.

History made and history still making, he adds, cannot be pulled apart. Politics, he says, grow vulgar without history, while history fades into mere letters when it forgets practical politics. The lectures press two demands on the student: certainty before abundance, since common report copies reality badly, and detachment from the passions of one's own day. The result is a guide to reading the past as a practical record of truths tested by trial, not as a store of tales.
1872-the-red-house-mystery:
A country house, a guest found dead, and a host who has vanished. That is the setup Milne offers, with an apology for adding one more detective story to the shelf. Milne then supplies one, set in a country house where a guest is found dead and the host has vanished.

Antony Gillingham, an amateur detective on holiday, teams with Bill Beverley to work the case, and Milne plays fair with clues, timetables, and secret passages. The novel is a model of the golden-age puzzle, witty and civilized, and it shows the Winnie-the-Pooh author in a different, sharper mood.
1888-the-bittermeads-mystery:
E. R. Punshon's Bittermeads Mystery opens with a lone passenger, a fight in the woods, and a coincidence that pulls an ordinary man into a conspiracy. A woman weeps, a woman and a man meet. A discovery in an attic raises the stakes, until Dunn, following Deede Dawson into a dark attic, is appalled by the man's rashness.

Punshon writes the thriller of his day with energy, and the novel moves from woods to house to captivity and capture without pausing for breath. The mystery's pull is its villain, a man whose boldness frightens even his own accomplice, and a hero who must outthink rather than outfight him.
18880-the-new-york-times-current-history:
The February 1915 issue of The New York Times Current History gathers writing on the European War then in its first winter. It opens with portraits of the Prince of Wales in war kit and Field Marshal Paul von Hindenburg, commander of German armies in the East. An appeal by Russian authors, artists, and actors speaks for a country at war.

Inside are reports, documents, and commentary collected while the war was still young and its shape unclear. The magazine aimed to give American readers a monthly record of events abroad, in the participants' own words where possible. Readers get a contemporary source for 1914 and 1915, valuable for its immediacy and for what it shows about American views of the war before the United States entered it.
18939-andy-at-yale-or-the-great-quadrang:
Roy Eliot Stokes published this school story in 1914, following a boy named Andy from his home town to Yale University. Early chapters show horseplay, friendships, and trouble at school, then the move to campus life in New Haven. Once at Yale, Andy faces new rivals, football on the gridiron, and a circle of friends that includes Link.

At the heart of the book is a campus mystery: money goes missing, then a watch, and suspicion falls in turn on different boys. Andy must clear his name and work out who is really to blame. Readers get a cheerful college tale of sport, loyalty, and detection, written for young readers who liked school and campus stories.
19049-the-builders-a-story-and-study-of-:
Joseph Fort Newton's 1914 study The Builders offers both a story and an interpretation of Freemasonry, tracing the craft's history, symbolism, and spiritual meaning. Newton presents Masonry as one expression of a timeless human quest, in which seekers use symbol and ritual to approach truths that direct statement cannot convey.

The book moves from ancient building guilds and their lore through the development of speculative Masonry, reading its symbols, degrees, and traditions as a drama of moral and spiritual growth. A candidate's raising, remembered by Newton as a significant day, opens a meditation on how ritual shapes character. Written from a Christian perspective that finds the lost word in the life of Christ. The work remains a classic statement of Masonry as a living tradition of brotherhood, symbolism, and the search for meaning.
19129-the-she-boss-a-western-story:
Arthur Preston Hankins wrote this 1922 western, The She Boss, about Bear Valley and a drone named Hiram. Uncle Sebastian urges Hiram, who has dreamed of being poet, officer, and everything he reads about, to leave the backwoods for San Francisco with one hundred dollars. Imagination, his uncle says, is wasted where he lives.

Hiram must meet the stage at Wharton's store, deed property before a notary, and face a world beyond the woods. A woman boss, a fire, and a rival fill later chapters. Readers get a western tale of a dreamer pushed from idleness toward work, love, and a life of his own.
19139-the-buccaneers-in-the-west-indies-:
C. H. Haring wrote this 1910 history of buccaneers in the West Indies in the seventeenth century, with ten maps and pictures. It opens with Spain's colonial system and its trade rules, then follows freebooters, the conquest of Jamaica, Tortuga, Porto Bello, and Panama. Appendices, a bibliography, and an index close the book.

Haring shows how Spain's drive to hoard silver and tax trade starved its own industry and pushed merchants to smuggle with foreign help. From that failure rose the buccaneer world. Readers get a scholarly, clear history of piracy, empire, and trade in the Caribbean.
19168-studies-in-forensic-psychiatry:
This 1916 volume of Studies in Forensic Psychiatry examines minds in conflict with the law. It treats criminal acts, mental illness, and the courts, with case material on soldiers, prisoners, and offenders whose acts raise questions of responsibility. The work belongs to early American forensic science.

Chapters weigh how doctors judge sanity, feigned illness, and the line between crime and disease, while notes correct terms from German and French sources. The tone is clinical and careful. Readers get a serious study of law and mind, valuable for the history of psychiatry and criminal justice.
19272-the-early-bird-a-business-man-s-lo:
George Randolph Chester wrote this 1910 novel, The Early Bird, a business man's love story. Arthur William Brown drew its pictures. Mr. Turner, a very busy young man, plunges into deals. He meets Miss Josephine's father. He tangles with maraschino chocolates, dances, pianola training, and Westlake investments. Business and courtship mix throughout.

Turner meets young Princeman of the paper mills and weighs tariff effects. He offsets trip costs with introductions. Then he meets Miss Hastings, a thin young woman with piercing black eyes. Her claw-like hand puzzles him. Readers get a brisk business romance of ambition, humour, and love.
19341-a-maker-of-history:
E. Phillips Oppenheim wrote this novel of intrigue and high society, published in the early nineteen hundreds. A chance accident draws a young Englishman into a circle of lords, diplomats, and watchers, where a secret paper or a careless word can shift the fate of nations. Lord Runton and his friends anchor the plot.

The story moves between country houses and London rooms, with romance and spying kept in close step. Oppenheim's gift was pace: short scenes, sharp talk, and a new turn at each chapter's end, all in service of a hero learning how history is sometimes made in private rooms.
19343-the-making-of-mary:
Jean Forsyth wrote this novel about a girl named Mary, published in the late eighteen hundreds. The story opens in a deserted farmhouse in western Michigan, where a sturdy, unloved child finds a new chance at life. Her path leads her, step by step, toward schooling, church, and people willing to call her their own.

A young rector, Mr. Armstrong, helps her see that joining the church means gaining a family of faith, a thought Mary greets with joy. The novel's heart is that longing: an orphan's wish, in her own word, for folks of her own.
19421-the-french-revolution-a-short-hist:
R. M. Johnston, an assistant professor of history at Harvard, wrote this short history of the French Revolution, brought out by a New York house in the early nineteen hundreds. It moves from Voltaire and the old regime through the storming of old powers to the Tribunal, with Danton, Carrier, and Fouquier-Tinville among its grim actors.

Johnston stresses how organized crowds, national guards, and provincial troops such as the Marseillais battalion pushed events faster than any single leader planned. The book remains a clear, compact guide for readers meeting the Revolution for the first time.
1969-catherine-a-story:
William Makepeace Thackeray's Catherine, a story, retells the life of Catherine Hayes, a notorious murderess of the eighteenth century, as a warning against the sentimental criminal romance. Thackeray writes the tale in a deliberately plain style, refusing to make his heroine glamorous or her crimes romantic.

The novel follows Catherine from servant girl to thief to murderer, with Thackeray pausing to argue that crime fiction should show crime as it is, not as readers wish it to be. The book is an early work, sharp and moralizing, and it shows Thackeray already arguing with the popular fiction of his day.
19743-the-outdoor-chums-at-cabin-point-o:
Captain Quincy Allen wrote this boys' camp tale, published in Cleveland in the mid nineteen teens. The Outdoor Chums head to Cabin Point, take possession of camp, and work like beavers, until a call for help, a chained door, and a flashlight trap pull them into mystery.

A golden cup lies at the heart of it, with trespassers, storms, warnings, and an accusation before the mystery is solved. The book mixes camp sport with detective fun, in the easy style boys loved in the series. The home of the osprey and a foraging party add camp detail before trespassers enter the big timber.
19771-henrietta-temple-a-love-story:
Benjamin Disraeli wrote Henrietta Temple as a love story, published in 1837. Its background reaches back to Tudor risings under Henry the Eighth. A Lord Tewkesbury in the tale was beheaded after a failed rebellion. His estates were forfeited and his blood attainted. A younger branch of the family turned Protestant and married into Walsingham's line. Old disgrace shadows the lovers' world.

Disraeli, later prime minister, began as a fashionable novelist. Henrietta Temple is his most direct love story. It draws on his own early passion, lightly disguised. Politics stays at the edges; feeling takes the center. Readers meet the romantic before the statesman formed. The novel helps explain Disraeli's lifelong taste for drama.
19925-at-the-sign-of-the-barber-s-pole-s:
William Andrews wrote At the Sign of the Barber's Pole as studies in hirsute history. Old shop signs have mostly been swept away, he notes. The pawnbroker's three brass balls survive, and so does the barber's pole. Round those relics Andrews builds his chapters. Beards, shaving, and barbers' customs across centuries fill them. The tone is antiquarian and amused throughout.

Andrews collected curious history by profession and delight. Hair makes a surprisingly rich thread through social life. Kings, priests, and soldiers all legislated the chin. The barber was once surgeon as well as shaver. Andrews records that double trade in detail. His book is a small classic of trade folklore.
1996-the-divine-comedy-volume-2-purgator:
Dante Alighieri carries his great poem onward in this middle volume, translated by Charles Eliot Norton, as Dante climbs the mountain of Purgatory with Virgil at his side. Souls who delayed repentance wait here, cleansed step by step. Norton, an American scholar of Dante, aimed for a faithful prose version that students could follow canto by canto.

Canto by canto, Dante meets Manfred, Belacqua, Sordello, and the princes in the valley, hearing their stories and learning the order of the afterlife. Norton keeps the sense clear and steady, making this a sound English door into Dante's second realm. Purgatory, the middle realm, suits readers who find Hell too grim and Paradise too remote, since hope grows here.
20105-the-land-we-live-in-the-story-of-o:
Henry Mann published The Land We Live In in 1896, the story of the United States told for general readers. For the Battle of New Orleans, Mann draws on a rare source. Vincent Nolte wrote Fifty Years in Both Hemispheres, printed in Hamburg in 1853. Nolte owned the cotton that Jackson seized before that battle.

Nolte also served as a volunteer in the fight itself. Mann treats him as a strong voice on what truly happened there. The book moves through the nation's growth in a clear, brisk line. Readers get American history with an eye for firsthand tales and odd details.
2018-the-library:
Andrew Lang published this 1881 guide for people who love books and want to build a sound private library. With a chapter by Austin Dobson on modern English illustrated books, it covers old manuscripts, early printing, and the pleasures of collecting. Lang, a Scottish critic and folklorist, wrote for the growing class of readers who bought books for home shelves.

Lang writes about bookstalls, book thieves, bindings, and the care of volumes, mixing practical advice with stories from his own shelves. The result still reads as a friendly handbook for readers who value books as objects as well as texts. His advice still helps collectors, since he treats a library as a living room companion, not a museum piece.
20258-hunter-s-marjory:
Hunter's Marjory is a story for girls, set in woods and country homes. Marjory's dog begins to whine softly as her own mood shifts. Suddenly the whines turn to growls deep in his throat. He shakes free of her arms and stares into the wood beyond.

A dog's alarm in such tales often warns of danger close at hand. Marjory must face whatever waits among the trees with nerve. Girls' stories of the era prize courage, kindness, and quick thought. Readers get a wholesome tale where a girl and her dog stand together.
20297-ten-american-girls-from-history:
Kate Dickinson Sweetser published Ten American Girls from History in 1917. One tale opens with warriors marching in single file through forest settlements. They lead a captive white man to Powhatan for judgment and sentence. Crowds of onlookers hurry in along the wood trails to see him.

That captive is Captain John Smith, in the famed Pocahontas story. Sweetser retells such moments through the eyes of ten real girls. Each girl stands at a turning point in early American history. Young readers get biography, adventure, and patriotism in short, vivid lives.
20357-jerry:
Jean Webster published Jerry in 1907, a light novel of Americans in Italy. Jerry jokes that a letter is indeed a love-letter, since Gustavo asks. In fact, his sister writes that they arrive tonight by train. They will pull out for Riva by the first boat tomorrow.

Lake Garda's Riva gives the tale its sunny Italian stage. Webster, famed for Daddy-Long-Legs, writes with wit and warm economy. Jerry's banter hides a growing love he teases others about freely. Readers get a bright, brief romance in Webster's clear, charming style.
20384-david-lannarck-midget-an-adventure:
David Lannarck, Midget is an adventure story about a circus performer of very small stature. David leaves the show world behind him. He becomes friends with big, rangy Sam Welborn, and the circus midget decides to make his home in the wide open spaces of the West.

The friendship between the tiny performer and the big ranchman drives the tale. David must prove himself in a land built for larger men. The story mixes humour, loyalty, and outdoor adventure, and it gives young readers a hero who wins by grit and good sense rather than size.
20436-sunshine-factory:
Pansy, the pen name of Isabella Alden, wrote Sunshine Factory as a story for children about making cheer at home. Its young characters learn to bring light into dull days. A kind grown-up, Uncle Jack, shows them how play can be made from almost nothing.

Uncle Jack teaches a girl to cut holes in paper for a mask. He shows her how to cut a whole family of paper dolls, and pretty things for Willie. Then he takes a tea tray and rolls a marble round it. The book's lessons ride on such small, warm scenes.
20516-christmas-a-story:
Zona Gale's Christmas: A Story is set in Old Trail Town, the small town she made famous in her fiction. The town watches a quiet wonder in one woman's garden. There she has a great patch of purple violets blooming out of season.

All Old Trail Town takes account of its neighbors' flowers, of the migratory birds, and of eclipses. So the whole town comes to see the wonder of violets at Christmas. Gale builds her tale of giving around that bloom, in the plain, tender style that won her a wide and loyal readership.
20548-the-secret-of-the-storm-country:
Grace Miller White's The Secret of the Storm Country, published in 1916, continues the story she began in Tess of the Storm Country. The scene is the squatter country along Cayuga Lake in New York. It opens in the lazy warmth of a May afternoon.

That spring follows Orn Skinner's release from Auburn Prison. Three men lounge on the shore in front of Satisfied Longman's shack, with the lake waters at their feet. Old wrongs and a hidden secret hang over the settlement. White's tale mixes romance and hardship among the fisher folk of the lake.
2056-the-life-of-william-carey-shoemaker:
George Smith tells the life of William Carey, the Northamptonshire shoemaker who became a Baptist missionary in India and a pioneer of modern missions. Carey sailed in 1793 and spent forty years in Bengal. Smith, a biographer of missionaries, wrote Carey's life from letters and from Indian records.

Smith draws on the promise of Carey's colleague Joshua Marshman to write the life, and on Carey's own letters. The book follows translation, printing, schools, and reform, and it presents Carey as a working man turned scholar and servant. Carey's work in translation gave India the Bible in Bengali and other tongues, a labour of decades.
20584-you-should-worry-says-john-henry:
George V. Hobart's You Should Worry, Says John Henry, published in 1914, collects the slang monologues of his comic hero John Henry. John Henry is a cheerful New York sport with an opinion on everything. Dance crazes, schemes, and city types all pass through his talk.

We are not a couple of patsies with the pumps, he protests. We can learn enough in two lessons to make good in this boob community. He vows to start a tango craze that will put life and ginger in the whole outfit. Hobart's John Henry books caught the street slang of their decade exactly.
20620-rosemary:
Rosemary is a novel for girls about three sisters in a quiet house, watched closely in the opening scene. Sunlight picks out their hair one by one. One head glows a deep red, and another turns to a fairy web of spun yellow silk. The light searches out a faint copper tint in the dark locks of the third.

The girls sit motionless, their faces turned toward the stairs, as silent as everything else in that silent house. From that held breath, the story opens into the sisters' home life, work, and hopes. Rosemary herself carries the book's warmth, in the domestic series fiction of its day.
20756-rabbi-and-priest-a-story:
Milton Goldsmith published Rabbi and Priest in 1891, a tale of Russian Jewish life. The preface owns that names and dates are not strictly exact. Still, it follows Mendel Winenki from boyhood to old age with care.

Through Mendel, readers see the faith, pain, and pride of a scorned people. A rabbi and a priest stand for two worlds that clash and meet. Goldsmith aimed to win fair thought for Russian Jews in hard times. The book mixes story with plea, a common shape for fiction that hoped to soften real hate in its readers.
20782-triplanetary:
Two patrol ships vanish without a word in Triplanetary, and a captain draws the grim lesson. At three losses, he says, it would get to be a habit. Detector screens and new arms guard his own ship, yet clear ether feels like a trap.

E. E. Smith opens his Lensman saga with space war on a vast scale. Alien foes, bold fleets, and secret plans span ages of hidden strife. Smith's tales set the mold for grand space opera in the pulp age. Readers who like vast stakes and swift action will find this first book a brisk start.
20805-lloyd-george-the-man-and-his-story:
A Welsh countryside boy found no path up, so he moved to Manchester to teach. There his son David was born on January 17, 1863. That boy, Lloyd George, would rise to lead Britain in war and peace.

The Man and His Story, from 1917, traces that climb while it still unfolded. Village roots, law, Parliament, and reform mark the stages of the tale. Lloyd George pushed pensions, insurance, and bold budgets before the war. When this life came out, he had just taken the top post. Readers get a wartime portrait of a leader at his peak.
20848-an-elementary-study-of-chemistry:
A full list of the elements waits in the appendix of An Elementary Study of Chemistry. Stars mark the common ones a pupil must know well. A third of the whole list, the book says, suffices for sound basic grasp.

William McPherson and William Henderson built this text for first courses in the science. Atoms, gases, metals, and acids proceed in clear, tested order. Lab work and plain talk share the pages. The book shows how American colleges taught chemistry then. It stays firm on facts and keen on experiment throughout.
20912-the-daffodil-mystery:
Thornton Lyne lounges at his desk, too sure of his own genius to heed a warning look. Edgar Wallace opens The Daffodil Mystery on that sober grey-eyed gaze. Lyne's wealth and pride set him square in a killer's path.

Wallace, king of the fast thriller, spins murder, blackmail, and London low life here. Daffodils left with the dead give the case its odd name. Short chapters and sharp twists keep the pages turning at speed. The book shows why Wallace ruled crime fiction in his day: no fuss, no pause, just plot wound tight as wire.
20967-a-guide-to-peterborough-cathedral-:
Peada, son of Penda of Mercia, founded the monastery of Medeshamstede in 655, this guide recounts. The Saxon chronicler counts 5,850 winters from the world's birth to that reign. A Guide to Peterborough Cathedral opens its brief history at that deep root.

From Saxon minster to Norman giant, the cathedral's growth fills the guide's pages. Tombs, chapels, carved bosses, and buried queens mark the guided walk. Katharine of Aragon and Mary, Queen of Scots both once lay here. Small guides like this taught Victorian visitors to read a great church stone by stone, saint by saint.
20992-tom-dick-and-harry:
Cold sweat, shaking limbs, and hair on end wake the teller of Tom, Dick and Harry. He sits bolt upright at midnight, chin on knees, in a grip of fright. Talbot Baines Reed opens his school tale on that raw, comic scare.

Three boys whose names became a phrase for any lads at all star here. Reed's school world of dorms, games, and scrapes fills the tale with life. He wrote scores of such tales for The Boy's Own Paper and kin. This one shows his warm, brisk touch, with fear and fun in near equal parts from the first dark page.
20996-an-epoch-in-history:
Four hundred ninety-nine trained teachers sailed from San Francisco to school a new land. P. H. Eley calls that sailing An Epoch in History in his 1904 book. Their task: plant free public schools through the whole Philippine Islands.

The Thomasites, as those teachers were named, reached Manila in 1901 aboard the Thomas. Eley, himself of that band, tells of schools raised from bare rooms. Language, custom, and war's wreckage made the work vast and slow. His book keeps a proud, dated view of America's school crusade in its new Pacific colony.
21070-a-middy-of-the-slave-squadron-a-we:
One of the last books Harry Collingwood wrote, this West African story puts a young midshipman aboard His Majesty's corvette Psyche. First Lieutenant Perry mops his brow in the heat as the ship works against the slave trade. The squadron patrolled the coast to intercept slave ships.

Collingwood was a naval architect in real life, and his handling of sea terms is exact throughout. Orders, skylights, and night watches are rendered by a man who knew ships from the drawing board. The tale gives young readers patrol duty, danger, and discipline on the West African station, told in his late, practised style.
21095-she-and-i-volume-1-a-love-story-a-:
John Conroy Hutcheson is known for sea stories. But this early novel stays in a dull London suburb just after the middle of the nineteenth century. Its hero spots a pretty young woman in church and falls in love at once. His first problem is simply getting an introduction.

He manages that, but the girl's mother looks hard at money: the hero is not well off, while richer suitors are less likeable. Church parties and outings move the courtship along until the wooing seems to succeed. Hutcheson fills chapters with poems and foreign quotes, in a style quite unlike his later nautical books.
21096-she-and-i-volume-2-a-love-story-a-:
Volume Two of John Conroy Hutcheson's love story keeps the same cast as the first. The vicar and Miss Pimpernell, Lady Dasher and her daughters, curate Mawley, and Min Clyde all return. The hero, Lorton, loves Min, the girl with the striking grey eyes. Their affair now deepens toward its outcome.

Hutcheson opens with a dream of Min and quotes Shakespeare on dreams before plunging back into visits, doubts, and jealousy. French, German, Italian, Latin, and even Greek quotes dot the pages, as in Volume One. The two volumes together form a full Victorian courtship, told as a life history.
21102-tom-and-some-other-girls-a-public-:
Rhoda Chester has been taught at home by governesses while her brothers went out into the world. When her German governess leaves to marry, her father decides Rhoda should try boarding school at last. Her mother dislikes the idea, but Rhoda herself is keen to go.

Mrs George de Horne Vaizey sends Rhoda among Tom and the other girls of the title, where she enjoys school and does well. Then an important exam looms, and Rhoda overworks until her brain fails her in the exam hall. The story treats ambition, health, and friendship among schoolgirls of the period with unusual sympathy.
21107-on-board-the-esmeralda-martin-leig:
Martin Leigh loses his naval officer father in Africa and then his mother. He is left to an uncle's household, where Aunt Matilda makes his life miserable. John Conroy Hutcheson sends the orphan to a cheap boarding school whose fine prospectus hides grim reality. Martin bears it for years, helped by his friend Tom.

After a Guy Fawkes prank brings expulsion, the boys run away and stow aboard a small coaster. Its captain beats them worse than their headmaster had. Martin's log then follows him to kindness, to sea aboard the Esmeralda, through fire and wreck off South America, and home again.
21118-etheldreda-the-ready-a-school-stor:
The Saxon family's Christmas holidays start with parties and pleasure in Mrs George de Horne Vaizey's school story, then a shadow falls without warning. Mr Saxon hides in his study looking old and worn. Mrs Saxon smiles a twisted smile and sends for the governess, Miss Bruce, in haste.

The parents slip away to their country house on some worrying errand, leaving the household in suspense. Etheldreda, the ready and capable girl of the title, stands at the centre of the family as trouble unfolds. Vaizey mixes schoolgirl life with a household mystery, keeping the tone warm even when the parents' secret hangs over everything.
21123-english-literature-and-society-in-:
Leslie Stephen delivered these Ford Lectures at Oxford in 1903, though illness kept him from reading them himself. His nephew Herbert Fisher read them aloud in his place, and Stephen published them in London in 1904. The lectures ask how social conditions shaped English writing in the eighteenth century.

Stephen argues that literature grows from the life of its age: its readers, publishers, coffee houses, and class habits. The book is divided into five chapters from the six lecture sections. Written in Stephen's clear, dry style, it became a lasting short study of the age of Pope, Johnson, and the rising reading public.
21210-thomas-davis-selections-from-his-p:
Thomas Davis, the young poet of Ireland's Nation newspaper, died at thirty in 1845, and this selection gathers his prose and poetry in one volume. T. W. Rolleston introduces the book for the Library of Irish Literature series. It opens with Davis's study defending the Irish Parliament of James II.

Articles from The Nation and other papers follow, on history, literature, and politics, then a selection of the poems and ballads. Rolleston aimed to give everything of lasting value Davis wrote in prose, plus his best verse. Davis helped invent a cultural nationalism for Ireland, and this volume shows both the arguments and the songs that carried it.
21233-all-s-well-or-alice-s-victory:
Emily Sarah Holt set this novel in the Weald of Kent in 1556, in the first heat of the Reformation. A local family has turned Protestant in private while still seeming Catholic in public. Their priest hears confessions, learns their secret, and carries it to the Bishop.

One young woman of the family, Alice, is strongest in the new faith. She is taken before the Bishop, jailed on straw with only bread and water, and badly treated. Her prison is improved only because she is to be burned alive. Holt wrote many such tales of Protestant sufferers, and Alice's victory is one of faith under sentence of death.
21254-in-africa-hunting-adventures-in-th:
John T. McCutcheon, cartoonist of the Chicago Tribune, traded his drawing board for a rifle. He took an African hunting trip and published this account in 1910. He calls it merely the record of a delightful trip along the Equator. There the roar of the lion and the crack of the rifle still ruled. His own photographs and cartoons illustrate it.

McCutcheon had wanted since boyhood to hunt lions and elephants, unsure whether he would rather be an Indian fighter. In Africa he lives in what he calls a story-book atmosphere of thrilling adventures. The book is dedicated to adventurous souls who resent the beaten path.
21264-the-four-pools-mystery:
Jean Webster, who later wrote Daddy-Long-Legs, published this mystery with the Century Company in 1908. The narrator arrives at Four-Pools Plantation in Virginia, where a ha'nt is said to walk and a robbery stays unsolved. Terry Patten, a New York newspaper man, is on the story's track from the first chapter.

Cat-Eye Mose creates sensations, a detective is sent for and sent back, and an inquest follows a tragedy in a cave near Luray. False clues pile up before Terry searches the abandoned cabins and finds the bonds. Polly's confession and proposal close a mystery mixed with romance and Virginia local colour.
21411-holborn-and-bloomsbury:
Holborn and Bloomsbury, by Sir Walter Besant and G. E. Mitton, forms one part of the Fascination of London set. The booklet came out in 1903, after Besant's death, from his great survey of the city. Its aim was to save the history held in London's streets.

The authors walk two districts rich in old inns, courts, and homes of writers. Staple Inn, at Holborn Bars, stands at the front as a famed survivor. Street by street, the book ties places to the folk who lived and worked there. Local readers and students of London both find much to keep here.
21431-mary-powell-deborah-s-diary:
Anne Manning joins two linked tales in Mary Powell and Deborah's Diary, reissued by Dent in 1908. Mary Powell was the wife of John Milton, and her home at Forest Hill still drew visits long after. The last scraps of the house were pulled down in 1854.

Manning tells of Milton's spring, the walnut trees, and the church on the hill near Mary's home. The tales wear the dress and speech of the seventeenth century with care. A warm portrait of Mary, drawn from an old praise of a fair milkmaid, opens the book. It suits readers who love quiet, well-kept historical tales.
21465-hurricane-hurry:
Hurricane Hurry is a long historical novel by W. H. G. Kingston, set around the year 1780. The printed book ran to some four hundred and seventy pages of small type. Its hero bears the odd name Hurry, though the text twice slips and calls him Poynder.

Kingston writes ship and storm with his usual fine touch. By the ninth chapter Hurry has fallen for a young American lady. Her father is a colonel serving on the Rebel side in the war. Love and war thus pull the hero in two ways at once. Sea fights, divided loyalties, and family secrets fill the tale.
21623-usury:
Calvin Elliott attacks interest on money in Usury, a scriptural, ethical, and economic view, copyrighted in 1902. The Anti-Usury League of Millersburg, Ohio, published the book. Elliott begs readers to follow his argument in its set order, as it grew in his own mind.

Chapters move from a definition of usury to the law of Moses. David and Solomon, Jeremiah and Ezekiel, and Nehemiah's reform come in turn. The teachings of the Master and the parables of the talents and pounds get close reading. Elliott builds a full biblical case against lending at interest, step by step.
21649-a-cluster-of-grapes-a-book-of-twen:
Galloway Kyle gathers new verse in A Cluster of Grapes, a book of twentieth-century poetry issued in 1914. His title comes from Sidney's praise of poetry, a cluster given at a vineyard's gate. Kyle refuses to sort his poets into schools or isms.

No group, he insists, is set above another in the gathering. The aim is a taste that makes the reader long to pass further. Poems stand as examples of the present century's art, each under its own author's rights. The slim book serves as a period tasting of British verse on the edge of the Great War.
21663-aunt-mary:
Mrs Perring, who wrote The Story of a Mouse, tells a children's tale in Aunt Mary, issued in 1881. A pretty suburban villa opens the tale, with new neighbours to judge. Mr Maitland and his two sweet children promise pleasant society for the street.

Routledge of London and New York published the book, with a picture of Aunt Mary at the front. Perring's tales of cats, castles, and cottages had already won young readers. Kindness, home manners, and small trials shape the story's world. The book is a fair sample of the gentle, moral tale Victorian children were given to read at home.
21685-the-cockatoo-s-story:
Mrs George Cupples lets a white cockatoo tell his own tale in The Cockatoo's Story, issued in 1881. The bird owns he is ashamed of himself and brought his troubles on his own head. Twelve pictures, from a greedy dog onward, fill the book.

Mrs Polly, a small gray parrot across the room, walks her perch fast and ruffles her feathers. She calls the cockatoo sulky and ungrateful, and offers to peck him well. The boy who owns them, she insists, means only kindness. Chat between caged birds carries a gentle lesson for young readers, in Cupples's known style.
21687-the-youngest-girl-in-the-fifth-a-s:
Angela Brazil promotes Gwen in The Youngest Girl in the Fifth, a school story drawn by Stanley Davis. Gwen protests she has done nothing, under looks fit for a criminal and a martyr. Miss Roscoe's word has moved her up a form, youngest in the Fifth.

Chapters promise a false step, trouble in the Fifth, and a casting vote. Gwen keeps Christmas, turns henwife, meets a storm, and learns first aid. A gymkhana, a tennis tournament, and the Senior Oxford exams crown the year. Gwen to the rescue is the last chapter's promise, in Brazil's bright, loyal school world.
21748-black-ivory:
Black ivory was the traders' grim name for enslaved people, and this Ballantyne novel confronts the East African slave trade head-on. A wreck casts two heroes ashore on the east coast of Africa. There, Arab and Portuguese traders still run their trade despite British patrol ships. The castaways meet a slaver almost where they land.

Rescued by a warship that takes a slaver's dhow, they reach Zanzibar and push inland with fresh funds. What they find in the interior fills most of the book. Ballantyne meant the tale to open young eyes to a trade still alive in his day. It is one of his most earnest books, adventure carrying a real charge of outrage.
21751-the-middy-and-the-moors-an-algerin:
Piracy and slavery on the North African coast drive this Algerine tale by R. M. Ballantyne. A middy, a young naval officer in training, falls into the hands of Moorish captors in the world of Algiers. Ballantyne researched Algiers and deep-sea diving for the book, as the notes to this edition record. The Barbary coast was famed in his day for corsairs and Christian captives.

The tale follows the young sailor through capture, hardship, and the strange life of the city that holds him. Escape and rescue hang over every chapter. Ballantyne writes it as a boy's adventure with a serious core. It asks what slavery meant in a foreign land, and what courage freedom took.
21891-the-brand-of-silence-a-detective-s:
Fog in New York harbor opens The Brand of Silence, a 1919 detective story by Harrington Strong, issued by Street and Smith's Chelsea House. The tramp steamer Manatee wallows in from a three-day fight with the ocean, rusty and lurching like a drunk. Aboard her come a girl, some discourtesies, and the first threads of the mystery. A man called Murk stands near the center of it.

Chapters promise battered keys, liars, a moment of violence, and a startling story before the truth comes out. Strong writes in the pulp manner: short chapters, sharp turns, and a campaign planned like a battle. Kate Gilbert's part and a trip up the river deepen the plot. It is a brisk period mystery, built to be read at one sitting.
21913-the-talking-leaves-an-indian-story:
Two girls on a mountain watch a crowd of men stoop and hunt in the grass in William O. Stoddard's The Talking Leaves, an Indian story of 1882. Rita leans over her pony's neck, her long hair falling, while Ni-ha-be sits still in her silver-mounted saddle. The air is so clear among the snow-capped ranges that far things seem close. The men below have found something in the grass, and hunt for more.

Talking leaves is the girls' world name for written pages, and paper drives the mystery. Stoddard wrote many tales of the frontier for young readers. His West mixes scouts, native peoples, and lost parties in bright mountain light. The two heroines, alike in size and unlike in all else, carry the tale's wonder.
21944-the-pleasant-street-partnership-a-:
A shop run as a neighborhood partnership anchors Mary F. Leonard's The Pleasant Street Partnership, a story published in 1903. The Terrace where the tale sits is rather far downtown, with the busy city closing in on commonplace houses, schools, and noisy car lines. A wave of improvement starts the chapters. Chapters follow the naming of the shop, an alien arrival, and Miss Wilbur's place in the scheme.

Leonard writes of loyalty, spools of twist, and the adventures of a birthday cake with a neighbor's eye. Charlotte, to whom the book is offered, presides over its affections. Frank T. Merrill drew the small boy surveying the partners with great composure. It is a cozy American neighborhood story, where trade and friendship share one counter.
21953-aurelian-or-rome-in-the-third-cent:
Rome under the Emperor Aurelian is rebuilt in letters in William Ware's Aurelian, a historical novel first issued in 1838. The tale is told as letters of Lucius M. Piso from Rome to Fausta, daughter of Gracchus, at Palmyra. It follows Ware's Zenobia, and was first named Probus before foreign editions settled on the better title. This fifth edition of 1874 gathers both volumes in one.

Zenobia's Palmyra and Aurelian's campaigns stand behind the letters. Ware, a Unitarian minister, loved the early Church's world and stocked his fiction with its debates. Pagan Rome and rising Christianity meet in his pages. The novel was among the earliest American works of Roman historical fiction, and readers abroad reprinted it for decades.
21964-the-short-story:
Nine master tales teach the short story form in this 1916 school anthology edited by W. Patterson Atkinson of Lincoln High School, Jersey City. Atkinson opens with a history: mankind has always loved tales, from the storyteller at the cave mouth onward. His contents run from Irving's Rip Van Winkle through Poe's Gold Bug and Purloined Letter to Hawthorne's Birthmark. Bret Harte's Outcasts of Poker Flat and Stevenson's Markheim follow.

Kipling's Wee Willie Winkie closes the set, with notes and a bibliography behind it. Portraits of the authors face their tales. Atkinson defines the form, traces its growth, and sorts its kinds before letting the masters speak. Generations of American schoolchildren met the short story here first, in a book built to be taught from and loved.
21969-the-outcry:
Old pictures in a great house stir modern greed in Henry James's last completed novel, The Outcry, published in 1911. Banks the servant reports that no stranger has yet arrived at Dedborough Place. Lady Sandgate crosses the hall, a folded telegram pink in her hand, to meet Lord John. Around them the house breathes two hushed centuries of stored treasure: portraits, cabinets, and tapestries of high distinction.

The outcry of the title is the public noise raised when national treasures are sold to foreign buyers. James turns an art sale into a comedy of manners and morals. Love and money tug at the same canvas. Written first as a play, the novel moves in scenes of brilliant talk. It is late James at his most theatrical.
22002-a-simple-story:
Elizabeth Inchbald wrote A Simple Story, first printed in 1791 and reprinted many times after. Inchbald had spent thirteen years on the stage despite a speech impediment. In her preface she admits the book was written through weariness, not inspiration. The story centres on Miss Milner, a lively young ward, and her grave guardian Dorriforth.

Miss Milner falls in love with the man meant to guide and correct her. Pride, temper, and rash acts wreck what might have been a happy match. Years later the tale turns to her daughter, who must face a cold house and a bitter father. Readers still value the book for its sharp scenes and its honest picture of feeling ruled by pride.
22057-kid-wolf-of-texas-a-western-story:
Ward M. Stevens published Kid Wolf of Texas, a western story, in 1930. His hero rides into view whistling a Texas tune. Kid Wolf is a lean young rider in fringed buckskin touched with bright Southwest colours. His California stock saddle is decorated with silver conchas, and he sits his horse like part of the animal.

Stevens wrote for the cheap western trade, where a hero's look told readers what to expect. Fast riding, gunplay, and a code of honour drive such tales. Kid Wolf's adventures belong to the pulp years, when westerns filled newsstands every week. The book is a plain sample of that hard-riding popular fiction.
22064-tess-of-the-storm-country:
Grace Miller White published Tess of the Storm Country in 1909, and it became her best-known novel. Tessibel Skinner is a squatter's daughter living by Cayuga Lake near Ithaca. The squatter law let her people keep land once they raised a hut on it. But the authorities kept tightening the game laws until the fishermen dared only draw their nets by night, though the fish were their food.

Tess fights for her father, her baby charge, and her people's right to live. A rich man's son and a young minister cross her rough world. White's melodrama was filmed again and again, once with Mary Pickford. It still defines the storm-country squatters for most readers.
22173-the-grell-mystery:
Frank Froest, a former Scotland Yard superintendent, wrote The Grell Mystery in 1913. Froest knew police work from the inside, and his fiction shows it. Robert Grell, the victim at the story's centre, was a daring explorer famous on two continents. His friend Fairfield, a writer on travel and peoples, matches him in fame.

Grell's murder sets detectives hunting through London clubs and beyond. Froest builds his case from clues, timetables, and patient inquiry rather than genius flashes. The book appeared just before the Great War, in detective fiction's golden dawn. It remains a solid specimen of the police novel written by a real policeman.
22179-old-rail-fence-corners-the-a-b-c-s:
Old Rail Fence Corners calls itself the A.B.C.'s of Minnesota history. Lucy Leavenworth Wilder Morris started the project, gathering tales from the state's old settlers. A book committee of pioneer women edited and issued it, copyrighted in 1914. The incidents are advertised as authentic, gleaned from the old settlers themselves.

Old-timers argue in its pages over roads, claims, Indians, and winters. One growls that anyone who travelled the old mud roads would be glad they are gone. Such talk is the book's treasure: first-hand memory of territorial Minnesota. Committees like this one saved pioneer recollection across America before the witnesses died.
22219-the-flight-of-pony-baker-a-boy-s-t:
William Dean Howells, the dean of American letters, wrote The Flight of Pony Baker as a boy's town story. It follows his memoir A Boy's Town, drawn from his Ohio childhood. Pony Baker is a small boy in a river town who dreams of running away. All the fellows gather round to ask what he is going to do now.

Howells turns the runaway plot into gentle comedy about boyhood fears and glories. The town, its gangs, its circuses, and its terrors are drawn from real memory. Nothing very terrible happens, and that is the point. Few American writers wrote about boys with Howells's honesty, and this small book shows why his town stories were loved.
22225-mary-louise-in-the-country:
Edith Van Dyne, the pen name behind the Aunt Jane's Nieces books, wrote Mary Louise in the Country in 1916. Van Dyne was in fact L. Frank Baum, the creator of Oz, writing girls' books under another name. Mary Louise arrives at a country station that disappoints her. After a sumptuous train, she finds only a shed-like structure, open on all sides, serving as the station house.

The Kenton place, the folks across the river, and village quarrels fill her summer. Mary Louise becomes a peacemaker, as one chapter title admits. A red-headed mystery and calls for help enliven the quiet. The book shows Baum's gift for girls' series fiction in a realistic, small-town key.
22243-dwell-deep-or-hilda-thorn-s-life-s:
Dwell Deep; or, Hilda Thorn's Life Story is a religious novel told in the first person. Hilda grows up in an English boarding school until she is nineteen. Then she goes to an old cousin in London. For three years she lives a quiet, uneventful life in a dull square, seeing little society beyond elderly ladies and a few clergymen.

From that narrow world the novel draws its drama of faith and feeling. Hesba Stretton, who wrote under initials and moved millions with Jessica's First Prayer, shaped such tales of tested piety. Hilda's inner life, not incident, carries the book. It is a fair specimen of the evangelical novel at its most inward and domestic.
2231-all-roads-lead-to-calvary:
Jerome K. Jerome's 1919 novel opens with a young woman journalist stepping into an old London church to gather copy on its history. Joan, ambitious and modern, finds herself drawn from newspaper work into deeper questions of faith, duty, and the lives of women around her. London's churches, streets, and drawing rooms frame her search.

The book follows Joan as work, friendship, and belief pull her in new directions, and as the war's shadow touches everyone she knows. Jerome writes with warmth and plain good sense about a woman making her own way. Readers get a thoughtful, humane story of a modern heroine finding what she truly stands for.
22310-in-the-border-country:
In the Border Country was published in 1908, with no author named in the record. The passage preserved in the catalog is a tense, pleading talk between two people. One voice begs the other not to risk something grave.

The speaker gives his word that her present state of mind makes the risk wrong. Yet he insists she could change both her mind and her conditions. If she would only say she could, he would risk anything himself. That push and pull gives the work its emotional charge. Readers meet a story built on persuasion, doubt, and a choice that will not wait.
22408-chatterbox-stories-of-natural-hist:
Chatterbox Stories of Natural History packs short animal tales into one children's volume. Its contents promise a singular habit of the woodcock first. The skylark, the story of a seal, and the king of the mountains follow.

Cunning wood-pigeons get a story of their own here. Rats carrying eggs up stairs earn another curious entry. A heron attacked by a hawk makes a third dramatic scene. A battle between a fox and a swan closes the list shown. Each tale takes one striking animal act as its hook. Young readers learned natural history as a string of wonders, not as dry classroom facts.
22463-chivalry:
James Branch Cabell wrote Chivalry, a book of tales published in 1909. Cabell set his stories in a bleak, florid age of knights. His preface asks readers to interpret his makeshift widely.

In that age, he says, chivalry named a world-wide code. It was rarely a matter of personal trait alone. All estimable people lived and died by that code's terms. Cabell's tales play within those rules with sly, elegant irony. He later built a famous cycle around such medieval romance. These early stories already show his polished, teasing style. Readers get knights, ladies, and honor handled by a writer who loved and mocked them together.
22571-frank-merriwell-s-bravery:
Frank Merriwell's Bravery, issued by Street and Smith in 1903, continues Frank's western tour. Readers of former books know Frank does not travel alone. Professor Scotch, his guardian, tours with him on this trip.

Barney Mulloy, Frank's old schoolmate from Fardale, also travels along. The professor and Barney did not want to stop at Oklahoma. They went on ahead, leaving Frank to catch up later. Left behind, Frank faces the adventure that tests his bravery alone. Merriwell stories made a formula of pluck, sportsmanship, and rescue. This volume gives that formula a western stage and separations. Boys read Frank as the model of what they should be.
22790-the-accomplisht-cook-or-the-art-my:
Robert May wrote The Accomplisht Cook, or The Art and Mystery of Cookery, the great English cookbook of the seventeenth century, first published in 1660. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. May, trained in France and servant to noble households, set down the cookery of the age in some five hundred recipes.

One section promises all manner of carbonadoes of flesh or fowl. It adds all manner of fried meats, collops, and eggs. It ends with the finest way of making pancakes, fritters, and tansies. Banquets, pies, and preserved fruits fill the rest. May writes for professionals, assuming a kitchen brigade and a lord's table. Food historians treat the book as the fullest record of English cooking before the Civil War's world vanished.
22794-the-shellback-s-progress-in-the-ni:
Thomas Runciman wrote The Shellback's Progress in the Nineteenth Century, a sailor's account of life in the merchant sailing fleet as steam closed in. The catalog record gives no year. A shellback is an old sailor, one who has crossed the line, and Runciman writes as one, watching his world of canvas give way.

The sample shows the old order at anchor. A large fleet waits at anchor: sailing brigs, barques, and schooners, all hoping for a favorable wind and spring tides. Only then can they put to sea without risking their keels on the Bar. The vessels had waited loaded for several weeks. Many were bound to the Baltic. Such waits governed a shellback's life. The book records the seaman's nineteenth century from the deck up, in the years when sail still earned its keep.
22836-town-versus-country:
William's steadiness anchors Town Versus Country, a village tale by Mary Russell Mitford. Talk in the excerpt praises the young man warmly. Young men all take their foolish turns, one speaker allows. William, though, shows unusual steadiness for his years. His master thinks so well of him that he now serves as foreman in the business.

Mitford sets that country-bred character against the pull and glitter of town life. Work, courtship, and family pride all test where a young man belongs. Her method is patient and close, built from talk at cottage doors and in workshops. The story asks an old question in a local accent. Which life makes the better man, the town's or the village's? Mitford lets her people answer.
22906-a-war-time-wooing-a-story:
Captain Charles King's A War-Time Wooing, published in 1888, opens on news of victory. Authentic word has come at last. Word arrives that Lee has abandoned the field and withdrawn beyond the Potomac. Union supporters everywhere exhale at last. Newsboys yell through crowded streets while evening trains are besieged by buyers hungry for lists of the killed and wounded.

Against that backdrop of war's end, King builds a courtship. He wrote from inside the army world he depicts, and his officers and their families carry conviction. Wooing under wartime rules, with honor and absence pressing on both sides, gives the romance its shape. Readers get a period love story framed by the Civil War's closing campaigns.
22994-the-frontier-in-american-history:
Frederick Jackson Turner builds The Frontier in American History, published in 1920, around a census bulletin. The Census of 1890 declared that the unsettled area had been so broken into by isolated settlement that a frontier line could hardly be said to exist. From those dry words Turner drew his famous thesis on American development.

The essays gathered here argue that the frontier shaped American democracy, energy, and individualism. Land at the edge, he held, remade Europeans into Americans. Later historians have argued with Turner for a century, and the argument itself proves the book's force. Anyone studying how Americans explain themselves must pass through these pages. The prose is measured, the claim enormous, the influence unmatched.
23186-the-handbook-to-english-heraldry:
The Handbook to English Heraldry is a guide to coats of arms and the rules behind them. In the editor's notes, the editor admits to changing unclear wording so the true, intended meaning stands out. Points that rest on deduction, and so on opinion, are treated with more care.

On those points, the book keeps Mr. Boutell's own views, even where the editor does not fully share them. That candour tells readers what kind of handbook this is: a working reference that sorts firm rules of heraldry from one expert's judgement, and says plainly which is which.
23187-mistress-margery:
Mistress Margery is a work of historical fiction set at Lovell Tower in the spring of 1395. Sunlight falls on the tower's battlements and window frames. Inside, though it is barely seven in the morning, the house is already full of bustle and noise.

Dame Lovell oversees her serving women as they get dinner ready. The early hour and the scale of the work show a great household run on strict routine. Readers are placed inside medieval domestic life, where a lady's standing rests on order, food, and the smooth running of her hall.
23288-little-mary:
Sabina Cecil wrote this picture book of Little Mary, printed in London in the early eighteen hundreds and sold for sixpence. It opens at evening, as the sun sets and a shepherd drives his master's sheep to the fold with his good dog.

Mary, the shepherd's young mistress, watches farm life in simple scenes, each with a picture and a short text. The book was made for little children learning to read through pictures of country days. Short texts and pictures suit children just learning to read farm life. Mary passes through a park one day where she first sees deer, then jumps and plays on its lawns and shrubberies.
23293-primitive-psycho-therapy-and-quack:
Robert Means Lawrence, a Boston physician, wrote this study of primitive psycho-therapy and quackery, published in Boston and New York. It traces how faith, suggestion, and ritual healed the sick long before modern medicine, and how quacks copied those arts.

Notes on prescriptions, measures, and Greek terms show a scholar's care, while tales of cures keep the pages lively. Lawrence, author of a book on the horseshoe's magic, writes a fair, curious history of healing by mind and belief. Lawrence writes fairly about faith healing, neither scorning nor praising it blindly. The blue-glass mania chapter claims blue glass strains out red rays said to harm eruptive diseases.
23323-stephen-grattan-s-faith-a-canadian:
Margaret M. Robertson set this short Canadian tale among three families whose lives are bent by drink. Stephen Grattan, a young builder, marries Alice Lambton and hopes to leave his old temptation behind, while his neighbours watch to see which way he will go.

The story moves between households in hard times. One father drinks away work and pay as a harsh winter closes in. A family is scarred by a house fire, and a mother has known the same grief. Through weddings, work, and sudden harm, Robertson presses a plain moral case that drink ruins homes, and that faith and steady conduct can still pull a man back.
23324-surly-tim-a-lancashire-story:
Frances Hodgson Burnett wrote this Lancashire story, published in the late eighteen seventies. Tim, a workman called surly by his mates, defends himself to a visitor: what seems crustiness may be something else, and hearsay should not be trusted.

The narrator studies Tim's bent face and finds it neither bad nor sulky, despite its heavy lines. Burnett's tale, told in Lancashire speech, asks readers to look past a rough manner to the man beneath. Burnett writes in Lancashire speech, so Tim's defense sounds true to life. A sick little chap opens his eyes as sun crosses the room, crying Daddy and catching at floating sunshine.
23382-crown-and-sceptre-a-west-country-s:
George Manville Fenn set this West Country tale in the Devon valleys near the sea, where two families, the Markhams of the Hall and the Forresters of the Manor, live as friends. Their teenage sons, Scarlett Markham and Fred Forrester, find secret passages, chambers, shafts, and wells in the old house.

Then the English Civil War breaks over them, with Roundheads for Parliament and Cavaliers for the King, and the Markham household takes the King's side. Loyalty, hiding places, and divided friends drive the action, with pictures by J. Nash adding to the period feel. Fenn keeps the tension high, so young readers get both a stirring war tale and a vivid look at a divided countryside.
23383-archibald-hughson-an-arctic-story:
W. H. G. Kingston wrote this Arctic tale of Archibald Hughson, a Shetland teenager whose father is dead and whose mother is unwell. Longing for the sea, Archy stows away with the help of a seaman aboard the whaler Kate, bound for Greenland waters rich in whales.

The kind captain takes the stowaway in, but Archy hides aboard a whale boat as well, and the boat is stove in, spilling its crew onto the ice. Rescue by the Laplander ends in fresh ruin, as ice besets and breaks that ship too, and a long walk over ice brings some survivors back to the Kate. Kingston fills the tale with whaling, ice, and pluck, making it a stirring read for young lovers of the far north.
23475-the-works-of-lord-byron-vol-5-poet:
This fifth volume of Byron's works gathers his poetry with the full scholarly apparatus of the Coleridge edition, including copious footnotes. Numbered notes give facts, bracketed notes are the editor's, and lettered notes track variant readings, so readers can see how texts changed.

The volume's later poems and regular dramas, from Cain and Werner to Sardanapalus, The Two Foscari, The Age of Bronze, and The Island, get a thoughtful hearing. Byron believed posterity would weigh these dramas afresh, and the editor asks whether works once admired by Goethe, Lamartine, and Scott can still grip a modern reader. Students of Romantic verse will value the texts, notes, and variants as a serious door into Byron's later art.
23489-godfrey-morgan-a-californian-myste:
Jules Verne wrote this Californian mystery of Godfrey Morgan, in an author's copyright edition from Sampson Low, Marston. The tale opens with a chance to buy an island in the Pacific, and with William W. Kolderup of San Francisco at loggerheads with J. R. Taskinar of Stockton.

Godfrey, Phina Hollaney, and T. Artelett, otherwise Tartlet, prepare to sail, and Godfrey's talk with Phina over piano music gives way to island adventure, a new personage, and a ship Kolderup was wise to insure. Verne mixes business rivalry, love, and Robinson Crusoe echoes with his usual inventive zest. Readers who like a mystery with a Pacific island at its heart will enjoy Godfrey's trials, which test a young man far from California comforts.
23623-the-white-lady-of-hazelwood-a-tale:
Emily Sarah Holt set this tale at the end of the fourteenth century, in her usual medieval manner, with quaint words and phrases that have since dropped from the tongue. The old speech, the book's editor notes, sometimes lights up how modern words and spellings arose, a pleasure for language lovers.

Life runs fairly evenly, without too many of the murders noble families then practised. The heroine, the White Lady, Countess of Montfort, fought bravely to restore her son to power, only to be ignored by him for years until her death.
