A mercer tempting customers with rich cloths gives a favourite scene. Holt writes a moving, period rich tale of a mother's fight, a son's neglect, and a lady in white who endures both.
23647-shining-ferry:
Arthur Thomas Quiller-Couch, writing as Q, published this novel in 1905 about the Rosewarne family and their Cornish estate of Hall. John Rosewarne runs the family business from his counting-house, dealing in barrel-staves for the fishery trade. His heirs, stewards, and servants carry the estate's fortunes forward and its quarrels with them.

Across three books the story moves from a father's pilgrimage and penance to the arrival of Hester, disputes over the ferry crossing, a love letter, a rescue, and a homecoming. It is a patient family saga about duty, inheritance, and the small community bound together by one stretch of water.
23650-ten-boys-from-history:
Kate Dickinson Sweetser gathered ten boys from history into this illustrated 1910 volume, each chapter telling how a famous man spent his youth. Stephen and Nicholas, the boy crusaders, share one chapter. The rest belong to Peter of Haarlem, who saved his country; David the shepherd boy; Louis XVII, the boy king who never reigned; and Edward the Black Prince, the boy warrior.

Later chapters meet Tad Lincoln in the White House, Samuel Morse before the telegraph, David Farragut as a midshipman on the Essex, and Mozart as a boy musician. Sweetser, who also wrote Ten Boys from Dickens, writes for young readers: short, lively lives that show greatness beginning in ordinary boyhood courage and work.
23869-little-mr-thimblefinger-and-his-qu:
Joel Chandler Harris published Little Mr. Thimblefinger and His Queer Country in 1895, with pictures by Oliver Herford. Harris explains in a note that his stories fall into three kinds. Some were gathered from Black storytellers but left out of Uncle Remus, because he was not sure they were Negro stories.

Another group draws on Middle Georgia folklore with roots most likely in England, while the rest sprang purely from Harris's own imagination. All were written amid daily work on a morning newspaper, which accounts for their crude setting. Mr. Rabbit falls kerthump on the frontispiece, and the queer country that follows mixes folklore, fancy, and Harris's own invention.
2398-the-renaissance-studies-in-art-and-:
Walter Pater's Renaissance: Studies in Art and Poetry changed how English readers saw the Italian Renaissance, treating Botticelli, Leonardo, and Michelangelo as figures of sensuous, fleeting beauty. Pater's essays argue for art experienced intensely, in the moment, and his famous conclusion urges readers to burn with a hard, gemlike flame. The prose itself is the argument.

The book influenced Wilde, the aesthetes, and generations of critics, for better and worse. Its subjectivity shocked Victorian moralists. Students of art and literature still read Pater for his style and his daring. Pater's conclusion was condemned by Oxford moralists and cut from later editions.
23987-the-torch-bearer-a-camp-fire-girls:
I. T. Thurston's The Torch Bearer is a Camp Fire Girls' story, published when Thurston was already known for The Bishop's Shadow and The Scout Master of Troop 5. The publisher's note presents it as another conspicuous success in stories of girl life. The author knew how to win the hearts of girls as well as boys.

Thurston's earlier books followed city boys on hikes, in camp, on exploring trips, and in hunts for hidden treasure. The Torch Bearer turns the same gift for true-to-life young character toward the Camp Fire Girls, with their torch, their council fire, and their code. For readers of girls' camp stories, it is a period piece of earnest outdoor fellowship.
23989-caleb-in-the-country:
Jacob Abbott published Caleb in the Country at Halifax in 1852, subtitled A Story for Children. Abbott, author of The Child at Home, wrote it in the family of the Rollo Books, aiming at useful and instructive reading for young children.

His prefatory notice states the aim plainly: not so directly to communicate knowledge as to develop moral and intellectual powers. Habits of discrimination and correct reasoning, and sound principles of moral conduct, matter more than facts alone. Caleb's country life gives Abbott's lessons a farmyard setting, where a child's choices and mistakes can be talked over and learned from.
24103-cousin-henry:
Anthony Trollope wrote this novel, first run in papers in the spring of 1879 and published in book form that October. It opens at Llanfeare on the Carmarthenshire coast, where old Squire Indefer and his niece Isabel Brodrick argue over conscience and duty. When the squire dies, the search for his will, its reading, and a libel action stir the whole household.

At the center stands Cousin Henry, the heir whose dreams, second attempts, and trips to Carmarthen and Hereford drive the plot toward doubt and exposure. Trollope keeps the focus on wills, family claims, and moral choice. Readers get a compact Victorian tale of inheritance, conscience, and a family put to the test.
24105-for-the-master-s-sake-a-story-of-t:
Emily Sarah Holt set this historical novel in London in the middle of the sixteenth century. It is set in the reign of the Catholic Queen Mary, shortly before her marriage to Philip of Spain. Protestant bishops were replaced by Catholic ones, and Bonner, Bishop of London, moved harshly against the least signs of Protestant belief. Ordinary Londoners had to work out what they were supposed to think and do.

Holt tells the tale through invented citizens. Only John Laurence and Agnes Stone are drawn from real life. She writes as a firm Protestant urging young readers to choose their faith with courage. The book asks whether its people will follow the Master even at great cost. Readers get a plain, earnest story of conscience under persecution.
24177-the-right-knock-a-story:
Helen Van-Anderson wrote this metaphysical story, published in a thirteenth edition in New York with copyright in 1889. Its preface notes that, though fine food abounds on the table of metaphysical thought, no metaphysical story had yet pictured everyday life seeking, and finding, satisfaction. Van-Anderson sets out to supply that picture.

Chapters follow Mrs. Hayden, girls at home, a fire and a retrospect, old doubts, a new hope, Mrs. Pearl's lecture, the true foundation, questionings, the spiritual birth, the power of thought, and practical application, ending with found at last, after three years. Readers get a story of inner search, told through household life and plain talk.
24196-victory:
Lester del Rey wrote this science fiction story for Astounding Science Fiction in August 1955, with pictures by Rogers. Captain Duke O'Neill shaves his heavy black beard aboard a battered flagship. He hears men singing for the first time in a long while, even old Teroini, who lies without legs or arms on his pad. Burke Thompson hobbles past to shout the news: they are home, and Meloa is in sight.

Fourteen years of war have passed, five since O'Neill last saw Ronda on leave, and of a fleet of eight hundred only three ships limp home. They have won, yet O'Neill grimaces at the thought of Earth resting in unearned safety. Readers get a bitter victory tale, where homecoming and loss arrive together.
24370-mercenary:
Mack Reynolds wrote this science fiction story, with pictures by Birmingham, about war as a trade in a caste society. Every status-quo caste society, the blurb notes, leaves two roads to rise above caste, the priest and the warrior. In a society of television and tranquilizers, the warrior takes a strange new meaning. Joseph Mauser spots a recruiting line in Kingston for Vacuum Tube Transport, where Baron Haer hires for a fracas with Continental Hovercraft.

Haer watches pennies, a bad sign to an old pro of the Category Military, who trusts instinct to avoid losing sides. Low-Lowers and Mid-Lowers sign for a snappy uniform and stock shares, but Mauser weighs budgets, and Continental, heavy with capital, can hire Stonewall Cogswell himself as tactician. Yet the die is cast: to climb a caste level, or two at once, Mauser must take risks. Readers get a mercenary's gamble.
24578-mary-louise-solves-a-mystery:
Edith Van Dyne, author of the Aunt Jane's Nieces series, wrote this girls' mystery, published at Chicago in 1917 with a frontispiece by Anna B. Mueller. Mary Louise, a sensible and kind-hearted girl detective, takes up a puzzle involving a doctor and patient, a mother and daughter, and a girl named Alora.

Chapters follow Alora's father, her new life, and a studio, as Mary Louise pieces together clues the grown-ups miss. Van Dyne's tale mixes friendship, family secrets, and gentle suspense. Young readers get a wholesome detective story, in the style that made Mary Louise a favourite of her age.
24602-through-veld-and-forest-an-african:
Harry Collingwood wrote this African story of Edward Laurence, an eighteen-year-old farm boy in early nineteenth-century South Africa. Sent off on a shopping trip of several days, Edward returns to find his farm attacked, his father and mother dead, and all the stock taken away.

At a neighbouring farm the same ruin waits, except that twelve-year-old Nell has been taken away alive. Edward, left with little money, since his father spent profits on breeding stock, sets out to find her. Collingwood's tale mixes veld travel, danger, and rescue into a stirring boys' adventure of old South Africa.
24632-the-fifth-form-at-saint-dominic-s-:
Talbot Baines Reed wrote this famous school story of the fifth form at St. Dominic's, a boys' boarding school. It opens with little Steevie, not quite eleven, entering the school, where his older brother already studies. Readers learn the school at the same time as Steevie does.

Steevie becomes fag to Loman, an older boy, and refuses his fag work, for which he is soundly beaten. Later Loman falls into debt to Cripps, an unsuitable public-house owner, and the debt drives the plot. Reed's tale mixes schoolboy humour, loyalty, and danger into a classic of the genre.
24725-stories-from-english-history:
Hilda T. Skae wrote these stories from English history, published at London and New York in 1907 with pictures by Frank Dadd. She dedicated the book to her nephew Charles Vaughan, and to Charlie and all other little boys and girls who love stories, as she believes most grown people do too.

Her frontispiece shows Caradoc betrayed to the Romans, and her stories run through English history in tale form, from ancient Britons to later kings. Skae writes for children, with clear narrative and lively pictures. Young readers get a friendly first history of England, told story by story.
24742-mary-mary:
James Stephens published Mary, Mary in New York in 1912. Its heroine, Mary Makebelieve, lives with her mother in a single cramped room at the top of a dingy Dublin house. The novel follows Mary through poverty, small jobs, and daydreams, as she tries to keep her spirits up while money runs short and work calls each morning.

Stephens writes with humor and warmth, turning shabby rooms, cockroaches, and a trip to the butcher into scenes full of life. Mary herself is sharp, funny, and stubborn, and her voice carries the book. Readers who like character-driven novels will enjoy this portrait of a poor Dublin girl who refuses to be beaten down.
24931-elements-of-agricultural-chemistry:
Thomas Anderson, professor of chemistry at Glasgow and chemist to the Highland and Agricultural Society of Scotland, published his Elements of Agricultural Chemistry in Edinburgh in 1860. The book offers farmers a short, plain outline of the science, avoiding needless technical terms.

Anderson enlarges on soils, manures, and the rules for applying them, since those bear most on daily farm work. Figures make the lessons concrete: a Mid-Lothian wheat soil holds only seventy pounds of water-soluble potash per acre, while a hay crop carries off thirty-eight and turnips two hundred. The book remains a clear guide to Victorian farm science.
24964-handbook-of-embroidery:
L. Higgin's handbook, edited by Lady Marian Alford for the Royal School of Art-Needlework and published in London in 1880, teaches embroidery as both craft and art. It covers stitches, materials, and framing, moving from the plainest groundwork to the finishing that turns needlework into a picture for the wall. Designs by Morris and Fairfax Wade show the standard the school set for its pupils.

The volume's showpiece is its list of one hundred named lace stitches, each described for the worker at the frame. That care for names and method makes the book a working manual rather than a pattern album. Modern stitchers still find it useful, and historians of design value it as a record of Victorian needlework at its most serious.
24979-a-source-book-for-ancient-church-h:
Joseph Cullen Ayer Jr.'s source book, published by Charles Scribner's Sons in 1913, gathers documents for ancient church history from the Apostolic Age to the close of the Conciliar Period. The first division covers the church under the heathen empire to A.D. 324, opening with the Apostolic Age: the Neronian persecution, the deaths of Peter and Paul, the death of John, and persecution under Domitian. Later periods follow the post-apostolic church and its critical second century.

Gnostics and other sects receive full treatment, with Basilides, Valentinus, and Marcion among the systems examined. One vivid passage tells of Mani, who at twelve received a revelation from the King of the Paradise of Light through the angel Eltawan, the Companion. Urged to continence, he began his public work at twenty-four. The volume serves students who want the sources themselves, arranged for study.
25004-a-confederate-girl-s-diary:
Sarah Morgan Dawson's diary, published by Houghton Mifflin in 1913, with an introduction by Warrington Dawson, records a Confederate girl's war in a Louisiana family. The volume is dedicated to those who endured and forgave, and its illustrations show Miriam Morgan, James Morris Morgan, a facsimile diary page, and the family's Baton Rouge home on Church Street. Her brother Philip, a judge who disapproved of secession like their father, declared for the Union and stayed in New Orleans after the Federals took the city.

The diary's entries catch war's odd intimacies. Wagons coming from the sugar-house prompt Sarah, Phillie, and Lilly to snatch up five bottles of gin and run out to give them to passing soldiers. A rough old sailor receives hers with thanks, while an officer warns that Yankee cavalry are after them and they must fight in the corn. The book is vivid, personal, and unsparing.
25026-bristol-bells-a-story-of-the-eight:
Emma Marshall's 1892 story of the eighteenth century, published by Seeley of London, draws on the life of Thomas Chatterton, the boy poet of Bristol. Marshall notes that incidents from Chatterton's pathetic life and tragic death come chiefly from Masson's essay and Chatterton Dix's biography, while Bristol citizens from his sad history appear beside wholly imaginary characters. Chapter titles trace longing for flight, an elegy, the songs of Rowley the priest, and the final blow.

Among the imaginary household, Bryda the maid draws notice: Mr. Lambert warns his mother to look sharp, for the fellows will be at her heels, and Henderson's bright nephew Jack already counts among her beaux. Her mother calls her quiet as a mouse, a bit too quiet, but maker of the best pastry ever tasted. Bryda walks sedately beside Mrs. Lambert, carrying prayer book and Bible, while her mistress leans on a gold headed cane.
25100-the-story-of-commodore-john-barry:
Martin I. J. Griffin's Story of Commodore John Barry, published in Philadelphia in 1908, celebrates the Irish-born officer called the father of the American navy. Griffin, historian of the Friendly Sons of St. Patrick, argues that Barry's early, steady service and his training of younger officers earned the title.

Barry commanded the Lexington under the Continental Marine Committee, fought through the Revolutionary War at sea, and sat on courts-martial that shaped the young navy's discipline. Griffin writes with open admiration, but the career he traces, from merchant sailor to commodore, is well documented and central to American naval origins.
2516-redgauntlet-a-tale-of-the-eighteent:
Walter Scott sets this tale in Scotland in the years after the Jacobite rising of 1745, when loyalty to the exiled Stuarts still burned among Highland families. Two young friends, Darsie Latimer and Alan Fairford, are pulled apart when Darsie is seized by his uncle, Hugh Redgauntlet, a fierce Jacobite plotting a fresh rising.

The novel follows their efforts to escape, reunite, and untangle a family past tied to the old cause. Scott mixes courtroom wit, border chases, and scenes of Highland pride with a sober view of a lost cause. Readers get both a fast adventure and a portrait of Scotland caught between loyalty to a fallen prince and life under a new order.
25165-the-candy-country:
Louisa M. Alcott's Candy Country, published in Boston in 1885, is a children's book that opens with a girl named Lily and a red sun umbrella. On a windy day by a bridge, Lily clutches the umbrella as a gale lifts her away like a thistledown, bound for strange places.

Later tales in the volume follow boys roughing it in the bush, camping by trout brooks and pine forests, and hunting blackberries among ferns. Alcott, author of Little Women, writes with warmth and humor about children's wishes, scrapes, and outdoor freedom. The book suits young readers who like fancy mixed with country life.
25275-margaret-of-anjou-makers-of-histor:
Jacob Abbott's Margaret of Anjou, in the Makers of History series, tells the stormy life of the queen of Henry VI. The Harper edition of 1902 reprints a text first entered in 1861, with engravings including a bridal procession.

Margaret, of continental birth, became queen of England and lived through the Wars of the Roses, as the houses of York and Lancaster fought for the crown. Abbott traces her courtship, wedding, and reception in England, then her adventures in a violent age. The book also sketches the manners and customs of chivalry, in peace and war.
25277-the-right-of-american-slavery:
T. W. Hoit's Right of American Slavery, published in St. Louis in 1860, is a pro-slavery pamphlet issued on the eve of the Civil War. Its Southern and Western edition claims 500,000 copies printed, and its preface warns that section fights section, churches split, and treason stalks at noonday.

Hoit defends slavery as right and attacks emancipationists with sweeping, often wild arguments, even demanding they adopt or denounce cannibalism on ancient authority. Modern readers will find the pamphlet repellent, but it documents the extreme rhetoric with which slavery's defenders met the crisis of 1860.
25333-the-great-k-a-robbery:
Paul Leicester Ford's Great K. & A. Robbery, published in 1897, began as a tale read aloud to fellow travelers on overland specials 218 and 97. Ford dedicates it to his traveling companions and, more particularly, to Miss George Barker Gibbs, who asked for a souvenir copy.

The story follows a party on a special train, the holding-up of Overland No. 3, a night's work on the alkali plains, and queer road agents. A trip to the Grand Canyon and happenings down Hance's Trail follow, with a stage ride past Flagstaff and a silent meal for Miss Cullen. Ford writes light adventure with a traveler's eye.
25351-xerxes-makers-of-history:
Jacob Abbott's Xerxes, in the Makers of History series, tells the life of the Persian king for school readers. The Harper edition of 1902 reprints a text first entered in 1850, with engravings including Artabanus and the ghost.

Abbott's preface argues against mere compends of history, where pupils memorize names and dates without ideas. He prefers single lives that hold attention, and Xerxes gives him war, counsel, and character. Artemisia of Caria, regent for her child son, commands five ships and more, proving one of the fleet's ablest leaders. Abbott writes for pupils, not scholars, and keeps his story moving.
25356-aunt-madge-s-story:
Sophie May's Aunt Madge's Story, published in Boston in 1874, is the third volume of Little Prudy's Flyaway Series. Aunt Madge gathers Horace, Prudy, Dotty, and Flyaway for a story, warning that she cannot recall her life in right order and must tell it as it comes.

Chapters recall Totty-Wax, a lady child, a blue parasol, Lize Jane, a party, a patchwork school, and a lie-girl. School scenes feature Miss Rubie, whose little boy Zed must swallow dreadful medicines, including dry senna with raisins at recess. May writes with the warmth that made her children's books beloved.
25413-blue-ridge-country:
Jean Thomas writes the folkways of the Blue Ridge mountains in prose and verse. Her opening poems make the hills a church, with red-bud, dogwood, and wild grape as its furnishings. She then turns to mountain people, their speech, their music, and their long feuds. Elliott County men face Rowan County men across old killings and threats.

The feud chapters name the clans and their politics, with Democrats on one side and Republicans on the other. A sheriff's election, a bystander's killing, and vows of revenge keep the counties tense. Published in 1942 in the American Folkways series edited by Erskine Caldwell, the book treats mountain life as a living culture, not a curiosity.
25469-pretty-tales-for-the-nursery:
The Religious Tract Society published this book of short moral tales for nursery readers. Fanny's Birthday opens it: five-year-old Fanny receives a pretty new book from her papa and resolves to learn to read well. She scolds her cat Puss for sleeping on the rug, since idleness may do for a cat but would make a girl a dunce. Her mother's warning shapes the tale: a girl must learn many things before she becomes a woman.

Other tales teach obedience through small mishaps. Mary loses her little tin can at the pond and must drink from a teacup ever after, a lesson to mind her mother. In Mamma's Doll, Ellen weeps when baby throws her doll down and breaks its nose, and her mother comforts her with a story. The tales speak in dialogue a child can follow.
25476-golden-deeds-stories-from-history:
This Blackie picture book retells famous deeds of courage for little folk. Horatius keeps the bridge against Lars Porsena's army while Romans hew it down behind him, trusting two companions to hold the narrow path. William Tell, Catherine Douglas, and Casabianca follow, with Handel the great musician and the story of Columbus. Each tale fits a page or two, with pictures for young readers.

Later stories give Antonio Canova, whose butter lion led to fame, a marquisate from the Pope, and a pension of 3000 scudi that he gave to poor brother artists. Damon and Pythias show friendship under Dionysius of Syracuse, who sentenced Pythias to death. Charlemagne and the charcoal-burner closes the set with a king among common folk.
25527-australia-the-dairy-country:
Australia's Department of External Affairs publishes this 1915 guide to invite dairy farmers to settle in Australia. It argues that a young country with much land suited to dairying will reward settlers, and that settlers will in turn advance the country.

Contents cover breeds of cattle in use, butter exported, cheese making, condensed milk, clearing land, conditions of selection, and co-operative dairying, beside bacon curing and bee farming. The booklet mixes practical farming advice with a plain invitation: come, take up land, and build a dairy living. It was printed in Melbourne under the minister's authority.
25551-six-girls-a-home-story:
Fannie Belle Irving writes this 1882 home story for girls, illustrated by F. T. Merrill and published in Boston by Dana Estes. Six girls, their families, and visitors fill chapters that move from under the trees and around the fire to a stranger, a little black trunk, and a missing Ernestine.

A foundation that brought Kat to grief, what Olive heard, and Mr. Congreve surprising himself and everybody else mark the plot's turns. Later chapters visit the opera, Congreve Hall, and coming home, closing with a sad story and my lady. Irving keeps the tone domestic, warm, and gently moral.
25720-a-lecture-on-the-study-of-history:
Lord Acton delivers this lecture on the study of history at Cambridge on 11 June 1895. He served as Regius Professor of Modern History. Macmillan published the lecture, with a first edition in October 1895 and reprints to 1911. Acton opens by looking back to his own student days at Edinburgh before mid century.

He had wished fervently to come to Cambridge University, and the lecture weighs how history should be studied, written, and judged. Acton, a scholar of vast learning, urges students to seek truth without party or nation, and to treat the past as a moral as well as a factual record.
25848-william-the-conqueror-makers-of-hi:
Jacob Abbott tells the life of William the Conqueror for young readers in his Makers of History series. The book follows William from his youth in Normandy through his accession, his hard reign at home, and his great gamble across the Channel. Chapters take in the invasion plans, the crossing, the fight for England, and Prince Robert's revolt against his father.

Abbott's preface says the series picks names known to all, whose lives give useful knowledge and not mere pastime. Harold's stay with William, the pair sharing tent and table on a raid into Brittany, shows the Norman duke's charm and craft before the crowning clash. Maps and engravings, from Normandy's coast to Cook-like portraits of the age, help the young reader track the tale.
25937-studies-in-literature-and-history:
Sir Alfred C. Lyall gathers essays on books and history in this 1915 volume from John Murray. Contents range from novels of adventure and manners and nineteenth century letter writing to Thackeray, the Anglo Indian novelist, heroic poetry, Byron, the English utilitarians, and Swinburne's poetry. Frontiers ancient and modern and a memoir of Sir Spencer Walpole close the set.

Lyall writes as a critic with a statesman's eye. On the utilitarians he notes their wish to reshape institutions toward everyone's greater happiness, checked by a dislike of handing the state autocratic powers. Tories, he says, woke to the need for government to do more for the people, yet feared radical reform. The essays give a wide, humane view of letters and power.
260-an-introduction-to-the-study-of-robe:
Hiram Corson, professor of English at Cornell, wrote this guide for readers daunted by Browning. An Introduction to the Study of Robert Browning's Poetry, third edition from 1886 in a 1910 printing, opens with a map of Greek terms for the poems' classical allusions. Corson calls Browning the subtlest assertor of the soul in song.

Chapters explain Browning's dramatic monologues, his obscurity, and his faith in human growth. Corson pairs close reading with biography and philosophy. The guide suits students meeting Pippa Passes or Rabbi Ben Ezra. It remains a patient companion to a hard poet.
26063-a-coin-of-edward-vii-a-detective-s:
Fergus Hume's detective tale turns on a coin of Edward VII and a tangle of mistaken identity. Giles, Morley, and Mrs. Benker each read the same man differently, and the likeness between a scamp and his brother drives the confusion. A summer-house hiding place recalls an older burglary at Mother Meddlers, where Black Bill gave himself away.

The story opens at a Christmas tree and moves through talk, spying, and cramp in a cupboard toward the truth about Franklin and his brother. Hume hides the real criminal behind the likeness, letting each witness correct the last. Romance runs beside the mystery, in the pattern of his earlier novels.
26094-hebrew-heroes-a-tale-founded-on-je:
A. L. O. E., the pen name of Charlotte Maria Tucker, sets this tale in the Jewish revolt against Syrian rule. Chapters follow faithful families under a tyrant king, a midnight burial, Hadassah's quest, the death of Mattathias, and the battles at Emmaus and Bethsura, closing with the Feast of Dedication.

Court scenes at Antioch show Pollux, once the king's favored companion, envied by Lysimachus as royal favor shifts. The story keeps close to the Maccabean struggle: hiding, flight, prison, trial, and a final return, told as a tale of faith held under persecution.
2615-discourses-on-satire-and-on-epic-po:
John Dryden wrote these two discourses late in life, and the 1888 Cassell edition presents them as his maturer thought, beyond even his famous Essay of Dramatic Poesy. Dryden weighs what satire can do, how it bites without mere abuse, and what an epic poem demands of its hero and its age.

He draws on Horace, Juvenal, Virgil, and Homer, judging ancients and moderns with a critic's confidence. The prose is clear, learned, and full of good sense about craft. The discourses still serve as an introduction to Dryden the critic, and to the rules that shaped Augustan verse.
26232-sunny-boy-in-the-country:
Ramy Allison White's 1920 children's book sends Sunny Boy from town to Brookside for a country stay. Contents list a mended drum, packing a trunk, a train ride, and adventures that begin on arrival. Later chapters bring fishing, a hay slide, apple pies, more mischief, another hunt, and Sunny's good luck.

Sunny drums to catch Harriet's notice, hides a clock in a trunk corner, and learns to skate with help from a railing. Pictures show boxes of goodies, a baby rabbit placed in his hands, and a tumble into a flour barrel. The book offers gentle, funny tales of a small boy's summer, full of pets, chores, and scrapes.
26275-homer-s-odyssey-a-commentary:
Denton J. Snider's commentary on Homer's Odyssey, issued by the Sigma Publishing Company in Chicago and St. Louis, reads the poem as a work that maps its own design. Snider contrasts it with the Iliad, which opens with a bare invocation to the Muse and leaps into action. The Odyssey, he says, begins with a general introduction that sets out its structure, proof of a poet grown conscious of his art.

His table divides the first twelve books into the Telemachiad and the Ulyssiad, with Ogygia, Phaeacia, and Fableland inside. The second twelve form the Ithakeiad, split into preparation and execution, then wrong, punishment, and reconciliation. The book guides readers through Ulysses' tears at Troy tales and his long road home.
26311-choice-cookery:
Catherine Owen's Choice Cookery, issued by Harper and Brothers in 1889, gathers chapters first written for Harper's Bazar. Its preface says the book is not for households counting every penny, but for those who can spend a dollar on luxury materials yet not four or five on a caterer. Many families, Owen notes, wish to give little dinners but fear anything beyond daily fare.

Owen thanks Mrs. Clarke of the South Kensington School of Cookery and Madame de Salis for help. Recipes show the range: cutlets simmered in vinegar and stock, served with grated tongue and parsley, and quails a la Lucullus, a costly dish eased by saving chicken livers. The book teaches hostesses to attempt fine cooking step by step.
26331-a-child-s-primer-of-natural-histor:
Oliver Herford's Child's Primer of Natural History, issued by Charles Scribner's Sons in 1899 with pictures by the author, teaches animals in funny verse. Each poem breaks its words into syllables, so children learn to read as they laugh. A seal dines with care on fish, ice water, and fresh air, lest his fur lose its fine Broadway finish.

A giraffe stands so tall his head tops the spire, and he must breakfast early since his food travels far down his throat. A yak neglects his haystack hair, living far from anywhere. The primer runs through whale, leopard, sloth, elephant, geese, ant, wolf, ostrich, hippo, platypus, chimpanzee, mole, rhinoceros, penguin, cat, dog, and chameleon.
26390-the-two-great-retreats-of-history:
Edited by D. H. M. for school use and published by Ginn and Company in 1889, this volume pairs two famous marches home from disaster. The first selection gives George Grote's account of the Retreat of the Ten Thousand Greeks, drawn from his History of Greece and based on Xenophon. The second abridges Count Ségur's narrative of Napoleon's retreat from Russia.

Each selection carries an introduction, notes, and maps. Grote's chapters follow the Greeks after the death of Cyrus, through Tissaphernes' treachery, Xenophon's dream, the Karduchian mountains, and bitter cold in Armenia, to the first sight of the Black Sea. The book then traces the army onward to Byzantium, setting ancient endurance beside modern catastrophe.
26396-no-clue-a-mystery-story:
James Hay Jr.'s 1920 mystery opens with Catherine Brace staring at a grey envelope leaning against her mantel clock, an object she regards with mingled satisfaction and defiance. The forceful, high-shouldered woman impresses herself on all around her, and the envelope sets off a chain of inquiry. A woman on the lawn, an unexpected witness, and an interview with Mrs. Brace draw the sheriff into the case.

Chapters follow Hastings, retained to investigate, through Sloane's hostility, a man who runs away, and the breaking down of Webster under strain. Motives surface, a bribe is offered, and a pursuit closes the hunt for the whole truth. Hay, author of The Winning Clue and The Melwood Mystery, keeps the puzzle turning until the final denial meets ample evidence.
26426-nagualism-a-study-in-native-americ:
Daniel G. Brinton, professor of American archaeology and linguistics at the University of Pennsylvania, read this study before the American Philosophical Society on January 5, 1894. It examines nagualism, the belief in a personal guardian spirit and in practitioners credited with transformation and hidden knowledge, across Mexico and Central America. Brinton traces the word nagual and its Aztec form naualli through early sources.

Chapters treat sacred intoxicants such as peyotl and ololiuhqui, the tonal and the birth-sign system of the Nahuas, and a sodality of master magicians. Later sections follow the Mixe, Zapotec, and Mixtec peoples, nagualism in Chiapas as described by Bishop Nuñez de la Vega, and revolt in Guatemala led by Maria Candelaria. Brinton presents these beliefs as folk-lore and history, not as verified powers.
26538-madge-morton-s-victory:
Amy D. V. Chalmers's 1914 girls' novel, published by Saalfield, follows Madge Morton after commencement day at Miss Tolliver's school. Madge, chosen valedictorian though Phyllis Alden is the most popular girl in class, hates the honor and clings to her chum's graduation gown. The story then moves to Cape May, where Madge and the girls holiday under Mrs. Curtis's eye.

Tania, a princess and a problem, joins the party, with a mischievous mermaid, Captain Jules the deep-sea diver, and the wreck of the Water Witch. A fairy godmother's wish, wicked genii, a bow of scarlet ribbon, and a race for life carry the adventure to its victory over fate. Madge, little captain of the Merry Maid, ends the book starting on a journey.
26628-the-mirror-of-taste-and-dramatic-c:
This February 1810 number is the second issue of the first volume of The Mirror of Taste, and Dramatic Censor, an early American periodical on the stage. Its main historical piece continues a history of the stage. It traces the rise of drama in Greece from its origins in worship to Thespis and Aeschylus, called the father of the tragic art. Early Chinese, Roman, Spanish, French, and English stages get brief notice along the way.

A biographical sketch of Mrs. Warren and dramatic criticism fill the rest, judging actors such as Mr. M'Kenzie in pathetic and powerful speeches. The issue shows a young republic taking theatre seriously, weighing acting, poetry, and taste in print. Readers get both a primer on Greek tragedy and a snapshot of what American playgoers applauded in 1810.
26734-charles-i-makers-of-history:
Jacob Abbott published this life of Charles the First with Harper and Brothers at New York and London in 1901, entered in 1848 and copyrighted in 1876, with engravings. It is part of Abbott's Makers of History series, written expressly for young American readers aged fifteen to twenty-five. Abbott argues they need leading events told for their own ideas and situation, not merely republished from older accounts.

Chapters run from childhood and youth through the expedition into Spain, accession to the throne, and Buckingham. They continue through the king and his prerogative and Archbishop Laud to the Earl of Strafford. The downfall of Strafford and Laud, civil war, captivity, and trial and death close the book. Engravings show the Tower of London, Queen Henrietta Maria, Windsor Castle, the Escurial, Lambeth Palace, Westminster Hall, and Carisbrooke Castle.
26752-the-way-to-geometry: Peter Ramus wrote The Way to Geometry, translated by William Bedwell. It was meant as necessary and useful for astronomers, engineers, geographers, and architects. Land-measurers, carpenters, seamen, painters, and carvers were also named. The hosted text contains only this title page and a submitter's note: because the book depends heavily on diagrams and illustrations, no text version was prepared.
26785-modern-british-poetry:
Louis Untermeyer edited this 1920 anthology for Harcourt, Brace and Company, gathering recent British verse under one cover. Its permissions pages name the houses that let him reprint, from Macmillan and John Lane to Knopf and the Poetry Bookshop. The poets represented run from Rudyard Kipling and Thomas Hardy to Siegfried Sassoon, Walter de la Mare, and James Joyce. War poems sit beside lyrics, ballads, and Georgian verse.

John McCrae's title poem from In Flanders Fields appears by permission of Putnam's Sons, and D. H. Lawrence, Robert Graves, G. K. Chesterton, and Rupert Brooke all have work here. The volume reads as a snapshot of British poetry at the close of the Great War years, chosen by an editor who had already made a companion American collection.
26842-the-sense-of-beauty-being-the-outl:
George Santayana published this theory of beauty with Charles Scribner's Sons in 1896, in four parts. The first treats beauty as a matter of value. It argues that preference is at bottom irrational. Aesthetic pleasure differs from moral and physical pleasure not by being disinterested or universal, but by being objectified, felt as a quality of the thing seen. The second part surveys the materials of beauty, from love and social feeling to sound and color.

The third part takes up form, with chapters on symmetry, types, landscape, and the place of utility in nature and art. The fourth treats expression, including the sublime, the comic, and wit. Symmetry, Santayana argues, helps us grasp a thing by marking it off from others, and that clarity itself is part of the pleasure it gives.
26925-the-bradys-beyond-their-depth-or-t:
Number 95 of the Secret Service weekly, dated November 16, 1900, sends Old King Brady and Young King Brady into the Great Swamp mystery. The father-and-son detective pair, heroes of Frank Tousey's five-cent weeklies, chase desperadoes through a case that leaves them, as the title warns, beyond their depth.

The story moves in short, breathless chapters, with surprise appearances, angry suspects, and the Bradys' steady plain talk cutting through bluster. As a dime novel it offers pure period pulp: quick action, clear villains, and two detectives who always arrive at the right moment.
26936-the-gallery:
Rog Phillips's science-fiction short story finds Arthur in the middle of a doctorate thesis when a telegram from Aunt Matilda breaks his concentration. The message is terse: come at once, she is in terrible trouble, and do not phone.

Arthur leaves his work for Sumac, a small Wisconsin town, where his aunt lives among dustless bric-a-brac and Spode china. There he finds that the aunt who needed him desperately no longer seems to want him, and a strange power behind a lens follows him wherever he goes.
26939-richard-i-makers-of-history:
Jacob Abbott wrote this life of Richard I for his Makers of History series, published by Harper and Brothers, entered in 1857 and copyrighted in 1885. A preface pledges strict historic truth. The narratives are history itself, not tales founded on history, without embellishment. Nothing is stated, even in minute detail, without what was deemed good historical authority. Engravings include a map, preaching the crusades, portraits of Henry II and Richard, and the battering-ram, ballista, and catapulta.

Twenty-two chapters run from King Richard's mother, Eleanor of Aquitaine, and his early life through Fair Rosamond, accession, coronation, and preparations for the crusade. They follow the embarkation, Richard at Messina, Berengaria, and the Cyprus campaign. They follow the voyage and fall of Acre, through reverses, the Old Man of the Mountains, the battle of Jaffa, and the truce. They end with departure from Palestine, captivity, and return to England.
2695-jeff-briggs-s-love-story:
Bret Harte sets this love story at Eldridge's Crossing, where rain and wind batter stately pines and hysterical willows alike. Jeff Briggs, a rough camp man, falls for a woman far above his station, and his courtship must survive gossip, rivals, and his own pride.

Harte writes the tumult of weather as a mirror of feeling, and the comedy of camp manners with warmth. Jeff's honesty wins out over polish, in the author's favorite moral. The story charms as a frontier romance, short, funny, and tender at its core. Rain, wind, and camp gossip frame the courtship.
26955-advanced-chemistry:
Jack G. Huekels's humorous science-fiction story stars Professor Carbonic. He has spent fifteen years in the same laboratory with the same servant, Mag Nesia, analyzing dead rats a neighborhood boy brings for twenty-five cents each. His latest mix of zinc oxide, copper sulphate, and sal ammoniac promises, like its predecessors, to be abandoned.

The comedy comes from the professor's grand aims, his shortcuts with time and language, and a servant who answers in a tone like citrate. Short, sly, and full of chemical jokes, the tale treats the mad scientist as a fussy householder whose great discovery keeps slipping past him.
27173-an-account-of-the-expedition-to-ca:
An Account of the Expedition to Carthagena, with explanatory notes and observations, third edition of 1743, tells of the British attack on the Spanish port. Readers are pointed to the plan of city and harbour in the London Magazine for April 1740 for a clearer idea of the action.

The pamphlet describes Carthagena and its suburb Himani, irregular in figure but well fortified with bastions, lakes, and morasses, and a harbour too shoal for ships to do execution with their guns. Cannon, bomb-ketches, and dispositions fill the account, with a Sallust motto on blame shifted to business.
27209-the-la-chance-mine-mystery:
S. Carleton's The La Chance Mine Mystery, published by Little, Brown in March 1920, opens with its narrator coming home as the wolves howl. Chapters follow a dream and Dudley's girl, Dudley's mine and Dudley's gold, and the man in the dark, along the Caraquet road and the corduroy road to Skunk's Misery.

The frontispiece shows a drive for all it was worth, with the girl beside the narrator shooting and hitting. Thompson's cards, four dead men, Tatiana Paulina Valenka, high explosive, and Lac Tremblant fill a northern mystery of mines, wolves, and murder.
27223-eyebright-a-story:
Susan Coolidge's Eyebright, copyright 1879 and published by Roberts Brothers in 1894, follows a capable girl through changes at home and abroad. Early chapters introduce Lady Jane and Lord Guildford, Mr. Joyce, a day with the Shakers, and how the black dog had his day.

Eyebright, trusted to wash up after breakfast on Mondays and Tuesdays, works carefully until a bad day leaves wet rings on shelves and soap in the teapot spout. Later chapters bring Causey Island, being shut up in the oven, a storm on the coast, and a transplanting, in Coolidge's kind, observant style.
27224-the-writing-of-the-short-story:
Lewis Worthington Smith's The Writing of the Short Story, published by Heath in 1902 for Drake University, teaches story craft to college classes. Smith's suggestions for teachers start with the three stories in Three Hundred Dollars for their simplicity, then move to The Bonnie Brier Bush and Bret Harte.

Mrs. Phelps Ward's Loveliness shows how a simple theme grows dramatically interesting, and students mark stories with symbols and discuss principles. One-third of class time goes to short themes, and each member hands in a complete original story at the term's end.
27240-pyrrhus-makers-of-history:
Jacob Abbott's Pyrrhus, in the Makers of History series from Harper, tells the ancient king's life for young readers. Abbott warns that heroes before regular records began leave accounts where romance and history have no clear line, and tales of Cyrus, Darius, Xerxes, Romulus, and Pyrrhus are more or less fabulous.

Modern scholars have disentangled much false from true, yet the tales, told for twenty or thirty centuries, mingle with the literature and poetry of every civilized nation. Chapters follow the reconquest of Macedon, Sparta, and Pyrrhus's last campaign, viewing the Roman encampment in the frontispiece.
2728-hunter-quatermain-s-story:
H. Rider Haggard frames this hunting story as a tale heard at Sir Henry Curtis's hospitable Yorkshire house. Sir Henry, as everybody knows, is one of the most hospitable men on earth, and over his hospitality the narrator hears the story he now transcribes.

Hunter Quatermain's tale runs through African bush, dangerous game, and narrow escapes, told in the hunter's plain voice. Haggard writes with the authority of a man who loved the veld. The story charms as a fireside yarn, short, vivid, and full of the Africa of his imagination.
2736-the-champdoce-mystery:
Emile Gaboriau wrote this mystery as a sequel to Caught in the Net, opening with a ducal monomaniac. A traveler from Poitiers to London takes the stage coach to Saumur, and the polite clerk warns him to take his seat punctually, a small detail that soon matters.

The Champdoce family, its madness, its marriages, and its crimes tangle across France, with detectives picking up the thread. Gaboriau, a father of the detective novel, writes with method and suspense. The book rewards readers who like a long, knotty plot unwound with patience.
27430-the-critical-period-of-american-hi:
John Fiske wrote this political history of the United States from 1783 to 1789, published by Houghton, Mifflin in Boston and New York in 1888. The book holds the substance of lectures Fiske gave in Boston's Old South Meeting-House in December 1884, at Washington University in St. Louis in May 1885, and at New York's University Club in March 1886.

Fiske calls the period critical because the new nation, free of Britain, still had to invent a working government. He quotes Jay telling Washington in June 1786 that he was more uneasy than during the war. Grouping facts to show their causal sequence, Fiske carries the story to the adoption of the Federal Constitution. The book remains a classic account of the Confederation years.
27482-domestic-life-in-virginia-in-the-s:
Annie Lash Jester, a member of the Virginia Historical Society, wrote this booklet on domestic life in Virginia in the seventeenth century. It appeared at Williamsburg in 1957 as number 17 in the Jamestown 350th Anniversary Historical Booklets. Part one is called Laying the Hearthstones, and it begins with the first homes.

The Laydon marriage probably took place in Jamestown's rough little stockade church. That stockade held the settlers' first houses, with a guardhouse and a storehouse. Jester builds a picture of home life from such beginnings. Readers get a compact, well-grounded introduction to Virginia's earliest households.
27551-hannibal-makers-of-history:
Jacob Abbott wrote this life of Hannibal in his Makers of History series, in a Harper edition of 1901, entered in 1849 and copyrighted in 1876. Abbott follows the Carthaginian general from the First Punic War through his most famous campaigns.

Chapters cover Hannibal at Saguntum, the opening of the Second Punic War, the passage of the Rhone, and the crossing of the Alps. They go on to the Apennines, the dictator Fabius, the battle of Cannae, and Scipio, ending with Hannibal a fugitive and exile and the destruction of Carthage. Engravings show elephants crossing the Rhone and Hannibal on the Alps.
27577-the-works-of-lord-byron-vol-7-poet:
This seventh volume of the new, revised, and enlarged edition of the works of Lord Byron, edited by Ernest Hartley Coleridge, gathers jeux d'esprit and minor poems from 1798 to 1824. Each piece carries notes on its first publication.

Early entries include an epigram on an old lady with curious notions about the soul, an epitaph on John Adams of Southwell, and a version of Ossian's address to the sun. Lines written aboard the Lisbon packet, a translation of the nurse's dole in Euripides' Medea, and an ode to the framers of the Frame Bill follow. The volume shows Byron in brief, playful, and occasional verse, not only in his great poems.
27633-to-mars-via-the-moon-an-astronomic:
Mark Wicks wrote this astronomical story, To Mars via the Moon, with illustrations, published by Seeley and Company in London in 1911 and printed at the Ballantyne Press in Edinburgh. Wicks dedicates it to Professor Percival Lowell of the Flagstaff observatory, whose researches taught the world so much of Mars.

Its epigraph, from Sir Edwin Arnold, says astronomy will in time be humanity's chief educator and emancipator. A frontispiece drawn by Wicks shows the air-ship's view over Sirapion's canals and city. Canals stretch in line after line, as far as the eye can reach, across the country the voyagers had been so anxious to see. The book joins astronomy and adventure.
2764-the-mahatma-and-the-hare-a-dream-st:
H. Rider Haggard wrote this dream story of a mahatma and a hare, opening with a good hare found in the field. Hounds press her, the hunt arrives at a cliff edge, and the hare's fate becomes a parable of life, death, and mercy.

The great white road, the shooting, the coursing, and the coming of the red faced man carry the dream through hunting fields to a judgment beyond them. Haggard writes with mystical earnestness, pleading for kindness to hunted things. The story stands as his most unusual plea, short, strange, and moving.
27692-romulus-makers-of-history:
Jacob Abbott's Romulus, part of his Makers of History series for young readers, tells the legendary founding of Rome. First entered for copyright in 1852 and reissued by Harper and Brothers, it is illustrated with engravings and maps.

Abbott begins with Cadmus and the story of Aeneas, then follows Rhea Silvia, the twin brothers, the founding of the city, and the Sabine war. Written in clear, short chapters, the book mixes myth with history as nineteenth-century readers understood it, aiming to teach as well as entertain. Abbott opens with Cadmus, credited in legend with bringing letters to Greece, before reaching Rome's own founders.
27798-the-silver-lining-a-guernsey-story:
John Roussel published this Guernsey story in 1894, following a boy and girl through disobedience, boarding school, deceptions, and love, toward reconciliation and domestic happiness. The chapter titles map the moral arc: failure, dark days, shadow and sunshine, and success after success.

Set on the island of Guernsey, with mackerel boats at Cobo and island households, the novel belongs to the Victorian tradition of moral fiction for family reading. Its pleasures are local color, steady character growth, and a happy ending earned through repentance. The opening scene shows mackerel boats setting sail from Cobo on a calm June afternoon.
27802-darius-the-great-makers-of-history:
Jacob Abbott's Darius the Great, part of his Makers of History series, was entered for copyright in 1850 and reissued by Harper and Brothers in 1904 with engravings. The preface explains Abbott's method: calm, simple, impartial narration, following scripture's example of condemning sins without pharisaical wrath against sinners.

Chapters follow Cambyses, Smerdis the Magian, the accession of Darius, the provinces, and the reconnoitering of Greece. Written for young readers, the book presents the Persian king's reign as history with moral instruction, and it shows Abbott's influential blend of narrative and character teaching.
27853-how-the-flag-became-old-glory:
Emma Look Scott wrote this 1915 book for young readers on how the flag became Old Glory, published by Macmillan with illustrations by A. C. Valentine. It tells the flag's story through poems and episodes from American history.

Chapters run from Lexington and Bunker Hill through Yorktown, the Star-Spangled Banner, and the Civil War battles of Shiloh, Fredericksburg, and Gettysburg, to Santiago. The book was meant to teach patriotism through narrative, giving children heroes, battles, and verses attached to the flag. The opening poem cries hats off to bugles, drums, and a flash of color beneath the sky.
27869-a-theodicy-or-vindication-of-the-d:
Albert Taylor Bledsoe, professor of mathematics and astronomy at the University of Mississippi, published this theodicy in New York in 1854, vindicating the divine glory. The introduction weighs whether a theodicy is possible at all.

Bledsoe also reviews Plato, Leibnitz, Calvin, Luther, Hobbes, Locke, Hume, Kant, and Edwards on liberty and necessity, then argues at length that moral evil is consistent with God's holiness. The book is a major American work of philosophical theology, written with the confidence of a mathematician addressing the deepest moral question. The book argues from reason.
27948-progress-and-history:
F. S. Marvin arranged and edited Progress and History, essays published by Humphrey Milford at Oxford University Press in 1919, in a third impression. Contributors include R. R. Marett on prehistoric times, F. Melian Stawell on Hellenism, A. J. Carlyle on the Middle Ages, and Baron von Hügel on religion.

Later essays cover moral progress, government, industry, art, science, and philosophy, closing with progress as an ideal of action. Marvin opens by noting how a philosopher friend defined progress as increase of knowledge, while he urged increase of power, setting the debate the volume explores.
27954-handbook-of-the-new-york-public-li:
The New York Public Library published this handbook in 1916, chiefly as a guide to its Central Building, with a frontispiece of the building itself. Contents walk readers floor by floor, from exterior and sculpture through entrances, elevators, and the exhibition room to reading rooms and divisions.

Later sections cover circulation, branches, traveling libraries, work with children, and lectures, with a historical sketch from the Astor and Lenox libraries and the Tilden Trust to consolidation and Carnegie branches. The handbook preserves the great library at its opening height, as both an institution and a public building.
2799-eben-holden-a-tale-of-the-north-cou:
Irving Bacheller wrote this tale of the north country, opening with hardy wood choppers coming west out of Vermont early in the last century. They founded homes in the Adirondack wilderness, clearing rough acres with axe and charcoal pit.

Eben Holden, a kind, shrewd hired man, guides a boy through years of toil in a rigorous climate, toward learning and manhood. Bacheller writes with warmth about frontier endurance and neighborly grace. The novel became a beloved American bestseller, and a portrait of a vanishing pioneer age. Bacheller's Vermont woods smell of pine and charcoal smoke.
27990-theo-a-sprightly-love-story:
Frances Hodgson Burnett wrote Theo, a sprightly love story, published by Hurst and Company after an 1877 copyright by T. B. Peterson and Brothers. The publisher's praise calls Burnett one of the most charming American writers, with a crisp and breezy freshness rarely found in contemporary fiction.

Theo belongs with Kathleen, Pretty Polly Pemberton, and Lindsay's Luck among Burnett's early novelettes, lively, cheerful love stories in which shadow is small beside sunlight. The tale shows Burnett before The Secret Garden, writing bright romances that first won her public. The publisher adds that no sprightlier novel than Theo could be desired, and no sweeter romance than Kathleen exists in print.
28164-the-big-bow-mystery:
I. Zangwill's The Big Bow Mystery, copyrighted in 1895, is a murder story set in London's East End. A man is found dead in a locked room in Bow, and no one can see how the killer entered or left. Zangwill, writing four years later in his introduction, calls it sensational yet full of humour and character.

The tale gives the reader all the clues, and Zangwill insists a fair mystery must let the reader solve it, or at least feel the answer is just. Comic neighbours crowd around the grim centre. The book remains a classic locked-room puzzle, praised for wit as well as plot.
28167-a-modern-mercenary:
The Prichards wrote A Modern Mercenary in 1902, copyright 1899, as a romance of a frontier soldier of fortune. Rallywood, a lieutenant of frontier cavalry, serves in the small state of Maasau, where guards, castles, and diplomacy tangle with love. Chapters follow Count Simon of Sagan, Anthony Unziar, and a question of two moralities.

Love in two shades, a court-martial, and an arrest test Rallywood's honour and his orders. The Prichards, writing as the Herons, keep the action brisk and the setting Ruritanian. Readers of adventure romance will enjoy its swords, castles, and divided loyalties.
28247-a-popular-history-of-astronomy-dur:
Agnes M. Clerke wrote A Popular History of Astronomy During the Nineteenth Century, London, 1908, fourth edition, first published in 1885. Clerke traces astronomy from Herschel's founding of sidereal work through the century's rapid advance, with pictures of Jupiter, Saturn, and the great nebula in Orion. Her earlier books treated astrophysics and the system of stars.

Chapters cover the first half of the century, then later progress, in clear prose for general readers. Clerke explains discoveries, instruments, and ideas without heavy mathematics. The book remains a classic popular history, written by a woman at the height of Victorian astronomy.
28269-art-in-needlework-a-book-about-emb:
Lewis F. Day and Mary Buckle wrote Art in Needlework in 1900 as a textbook of ornamental design on embroidery. Day, author of Windows and Alphabets, and Buckle look at embroidery from its practical side, not neglecting the artistic, since its use is to be beautiful. They argue against treating needlework as mere time-killing for women, calling it at best an art.

The book explains the craft: its stitches, its methods, and its uses, with samplers and diagrams. B. T. Batsford published it in London. It suits students, needleworkers, and designers who want embroidery taken seriously as craft.
28277-my-first-battle-a-sergeant-s-story:
Adam Mickiewicz wrote My First Battle, a Sergeant's Story, as a Polish soldier's memoir of his first fight. The sergeant, a light artilleryman, confesses he loved war only in his first week, and tasted Attila's delight in slaughter only once. He compares a first battle to first love: hopes, illusions, terror, and crazed joy in a single hour, with keepsakes for life.

The battle, an episode of a famous war, won a great victory and Europe's admiration, though later defeats and triumphs are now half forgotten. Mickiewicz writes with passion and irony. The memoir offers a vivid, personal view of war's first shock.
28283-mary-queen-of-scots-makers-of-hist:
Jacob Abbott wrote Mary Queen of Scots in 1904 for the Makers of History series, first entered in 1848. Abbott explains that he tells Mary's story expressly for young Americans aged fifteen to twenty-five, who need the leading events of Old World history in terms they can grasp. Engravings, including Dumbarton Castle on the Clyde, illustrate the volume.

The narrative follows Mary from birth and queenship through marriage, murder, imprisonment, and death, with care for character and motive. Abbott's tone is plain and instructive, not partisan. The book remains a clear school life of a queen whose fate still stirs readers.
28305-a-likely-story:
W. D. Howells wrote A Likely Story in 1894 as a farce in Harper's Black and White Series, priced at fifty cents. Howells, in a short, illustrated comedy, turns a likely tale into a stage joke, with the most exciting part pictured at the front. Harper and Brothers published the farce, alongside his Five O'Clock Tea and The Mouse-Trap in the same series.

Howells, America's leading realist, writes farce with the same clear eye for manners as his novels. The play suits readers of light comedy and students of Howells's lighter side. It offers a brief, witty sample of American stage humour in the 1890s.
28400-an-obscure-apostle-a-dramatic-stor:
Eliza Orzeszko's An Obscure Apostle, translated from the Polish by C. S. de Soissons and published in London in 1899, brings a leading Polish novelist to English readers. The translator's introduction calls Orzeszko the Polish George Sand and notes that Henryk Sienkiewicz still gave her the sceptre as a novelist.

The novel's own introduction declares education the best apostle of universal brotherhood, polishing roughness without and cutting overgrowth within. That theme drives the dramatic story that follows, set among Polish people whose lives are shaped by hardship, faith, and the hope of national renewal. The book offers English readers a window on Polish literature long little known abroad.
28433-richard-ii-makers-of-history:
Jacob Abbott's Richard II, in his Makers of History series, tells the story of the medieval king for young readers, with engravings. The volume takes up English history at the death of Richard I. It carries the tale to the deposition and death of Richard II, presenting the manners, customs, and military life of a chivalrous age.

Chapters follow Richard's predecessors, the Black Prince, the battle of Poitiers, Richard's childhood, accession, and coronation, and the code of chivalry itself. Wat Tyler's insurrection, Good Queen Anne, and the little queen follow, ending with deposition and death. Abbott writes clearly for students, pairing narrative with maps, castles, and portraits.
28445-madame-roland-makers-of-history:
John S. C. Abbott's Madame Roland, in his Makers of History series, tells the life of the French Revolution's most famous woman writer and salon hostess. Abbott's preface calls her memoirs a spur to high intellectual culture and heroic endurance, even in the dungeon's gloom.

Chapters follow Jane Maria Phlippon from childhood and youth through maidenhood, marriage, and the ministry of her husband Roland. Later chapters cover Madame Roland and the Jacobins, the last struggle of the Girondists, her arrest, prison life, and trial and execution. Engravings show her in prison and at the scaffold, closing a tragic revolutionary life.
28546-a-history-of-england-principally-i:
Leopold von Ranke's History of England, Principally in the Seventeenth Century, Volume I, brings a great German historian to English history. Ranke, writing about a nation not his own by birth, argues that no period matters more than the religious and political wars of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.

He follows England's part in freeing Europe from the western hierarchy, and the monarchy's balancing act between reform and old institutions. Ranke admits that a foreigner cannot write a nation's history in full detail, but aims at the epochs that shaped mankind. The volume is a landmark of scholarly history, resting on thorough research yet written to attract general readers.
28561-richard-iii-makers-of-history:
Jacob Abbott's Richard III, in his Makers of History series, calls its subject Richard the Usurper, and argues that hereditary sovereignty made him reckless, unscrupulous, and cruel. Abbott doubts Richard was born depraved, but holds that pride, ambition, and a desperate love of power, instilled from childhood, bore their fruits.

Chapters follow Richard's mother and father, his childhood, the accession of his elder brother Edward IV, Warwick the King-maker, and the downfalls of York and Lancaster. Later chapters cover Richard's marriage, his time as lord protector, his proclamation and coronation, the fate of the princes, and the field of Bosworth. Engravings illustrate castles, battles, and portraits.
28574-connie-morgan-in-the-fur-country:
James B. Hendryx's Connie Morgan in the Fur Country, copyrighted in 1921, sends its young hero into the Canadian north. The story opens in a little cabin, where Waseche Bill lays aside his week-old newspaper and listens to the wind. The first chapter asks a trapper's question: dog, or wolf?

Later chapters follow 'Merican Joe, a plague flag glowing in the sky, and the trap line. They go on to the trail of the carcajou, a caribou hunt, hooch-runners, the passing of Black Moran, and fox traps, with a man in a cave near the end. A frontispiece shows a great grey wolf-pack leader at a doorway. Hendryx writes brisk northern adventure for boys.
286-laddie-a-true-blue-story:
Little Sister tells the story of her brother Laddie, who loved and asked no questions. Gene Stratton-Porter's Laddie, a true blue story, follows the Stanton family through school days, weddings, and a mystery at the Pryor house. The Princess from the house of mystery draws Laddie on.

Chapters cover an angel boy, a wedding gown, Shropshire sheep, and keeping Christmas the family way. Mr. and Mrs. Stanton face life shoulder to shoulder, and the Pryor mystery resolves in faith. Stratton-Porter dedicates the book to her brother. It remains a warm family classic.
28743-miss-ashton-s-new-pupil-a-school-g:
Mrs. S. S. Robbins wrote this 1892 school story about Marion, the new pupil at Miss Ashton's Montrose Academy, a school for the higher education of young ladies. The chapters follow Marion entering school, settling to work, joining and leaving clubs, facing school cliques, and choosing a profession. A November snowstorm, a sleigh ride, detectives at work, diphtheria, and Christmas in the academy fill the school year.

Miss Ashton guides her girls with Friday-night talks and firm advice, while Gladys, Kate Underwood, and Cousin Abijah add friendship and friction. Robbins writes in the earnest, improving style of girls' school fiction of the 1890s, valuing repentance, honesty, and women's work. The book offers a period picture of academy life, from tableaux to commencement.
28776-stuyvesant-a-franconia-story:
Jacob Abbott wrote this Franconia story about Stuyvesant, entered for copyright in 1853 and reissued by Harper and Brothers in 1904. Abbott's preface argues that a boy's character forms more by sympathy and example than by formal precepts. A father who feeds a robin in spring teaches kindness, while a father who reaches for a gun teaches a wish to kill.

The story applies that lesson through the boys at the mill and the daily life of the Franconia hills. Abbott, a famous writer for the young, keeps his moral teaching inside scenes rather than sermons. Readers get a gentle nineteenth-century tale of character formation, written for families who wanted their children's books to shape conduct as well as entertain.
28849-smugglers-reef-a-rick-brant-scienc:
John Blaine wrote this 1950 Rick Brant science-adventure story about smuggling on a reef. Rick, Scotty, and the Brant family open the book debating what adventure means, on the front porch at Spindrift Island, before a night assignment sends them into trouble. Chapters bring Cap'n Mike, the redheaded Kelsos, a warning, a mysterious phone call, and the ship Albatross.

Later chapters follow a search for a clue, an old tower, a night watch, a capture, and a hearing, ending with a fight at Creek House. Blaine mixes sea mystery with science and detective work, in the brisk style of the series. Young readers get a fast coastal adventure, with maps, boats, and a smuggling plot that keeps its secrets until the end.
28983-how-girls-can-help-their-country:
Juliette Low adapted this 1917 handbook, How Girls Can Help Their Country, from Agnes Baden-Powell and Sir Robert Baden-Powell's scout handbook, for the Girl Scouts of America. The book's contents run through history, how to begin, laws, and self-improvement, to membership, grades, enrollment, and badges. Later parts treat games, camping, scoutcraft, stars, and gardening, with sanitation, health, home life, first aid, and patriotism.

Copies sold for thirty cents postpaid from Girl Scout headquarters at 527 Fifth Avenue, New York. A long list of patronesses, from New York, Washington, and Boston society, fronts the book. Readers get the founding handbook of American Girl Scouting, practical, patriotic, and aimed at girls ready to learn outdoor skills and useful service.
29028-louisiana-lou-a-western-story:
William West Winter wrote this 1922 western story, Louisiana Lou, published by Chelsea House in New York. The book opens at Ike Brandon's ranch at Twin Forks, as a new century begins and the old order yields to the new. The desert still stretches south to the Esmeralda Mountains and north, unpopulated and unmarked, as if change had barely begun.

Chapters follow a general demoted, Morgan La Fee, a sporting proposition, and a marriage of convenience, through prison bars and a getaway to the secret of the lost mine. A frontispiece shows a trail across a cañon busy with moving men and beasts. Readers get a rousing western of ranches, mines, and vengeance, in the popular style of the 1920s, ending at the vale of Avalon.
29084-the-cook-and-housekeeper-s-complet:
Mrs. Mary Eaton wrote this dictionary, The Cook and Housekeeper's Complete and Universal Dictionary, published at Bungay by J. and R. Childs in 1822 and 1823. The work gives a system of modern cookery in all its branches, adapted to private families, with original and valuable information on baking, brewing, carving, cleaning, collaring, and curing. It also covers bees, the dairy, poultry, family medicine, and gardening.

Further entries treat home-made wines, pickling, potting, preserving, and rules of health, with every other subject of domestic economy. Engravings embellish the volume, and a portrait of Mrs. Eaton fronts it. Readers get a fat early nineteenth-century household bible, useful for cookery history and for the daily work of a well-run house.
29107-queen-elizabeth-makers-of-history:
Jacob Abbott wrote this life of Queen Elizabeth for his Makers of History series, published by Harper and Brothers with engravings. Abbott promises history without embellishment, drawn strictly from annals written when the events happened. The chapters run from Elizabeth's mother and her childhood as a princess through Lady Jane Grey and the Spanish match.

Later chapters cover Elizabeth in the Tower, her accession, the war in Scotland, her lovers, her personal character, the Spanish Armada, and the Earl of Essex. Readers get a nineteenth-century biography written for young readers, clear and brisk, that still serves as a readable first life of England's long-reigning queen.
29166-the-flying-mercury:
Eleanor M. Ingram published this motoring novel in Indianapolis in 1910, with illustrations by Edmund Frederick. It opens at night on Long Island, where a young woman standing in the glare of two cars' searchlights flags down a passing motorist. The driver, braking hard, calls across to ask if she signaled, and the meeting sets the story in motion.

Ingram dedicated the book to her two brothers, her motor instructors, and the motor car itself drives the plot: speed, roads, breakdowns, and chance meetings. Readers get an early automobile-age adventure, written when driving was still new enough to feel daring, and told with the fresh excitement of the open road.
29190-the-great-dome-on-mercury:
Arthur L. Zagat published this story in Astounding Stories in April 1932. Darl Thomas, stationed on Mercury, mops sweat from his bronzed face at a paper-strewn desk and curses the directors of the ITA, who demand quarterly reports on fuel consumption per man-hour. He wishes they could spend one Earth-month sweating on Mercury themselves.

Thomas soon finds himself trapped in the great dome, defending Earth's Mercury station from a Martian bird-man and his pygmy henchmen. Zagat pits paperwork and heat against a siege. Readers get a hot, breathless pulp adventure about an isolated outpost, an alien attacker, and a clerk turned defender.
29241-little-masterpieces-of-science-inv:
George Iles edited this science anthology, published by Doubleday, Page and Company in 1902. The volume gathers short masterpieces on invention and discovery, written by the inventors and scientists themselves or by close observers. Benjamin Franklin opens with lightning identified with electricity, kite, spark, and lightning rod.

Later pieces cover Michael Faraday preparing the way for the dynamo and motor, Joseph Henry and the electric telegraph, Alexander Graham Bell and the telephone, and George Stephenson's work. Count Rumford writes on heat and motion. Readers get the heroic age of electrical science in short, readable pieces, chosen to show how great inventions were first explained.
2930-criticisms-on-the-origin-of-species:
Thomas Henry Huxley published these criticisms of the Origin of Species in the Natural History Review in 1864, reviewing foreign commentaries on Darwin's work. He notes that Sir Charles Lyell had drawn a parallel between the development of species and that of languages. The German philologist Schleicher had independently published a pamphlet supporting similar views. The notice in the Reader for February 27 praised Schleicher's argument.

Huxley weighs genetic classification against other kinds, asking whether a genetic relation might underlie even the classification of minerals. The inorganic world, he notes, has had its metamorphoses and a long development out of a nebular blast. The essay shows Victorian science debating Darwin across national and disciplinary lines.
29368-patrick-henry:
Moses Coit Tyler's life of Patrick Henry, in the American Statesmen series from Houghton Mifflin, traces the Virginia orator from his early years to his role in the fight for American independence. Tyler revised the book with care, drawing on newly printed letters and speeches of Henry and George Mason. Chapters follow Henry as lawyer, debater, and leader in the First Continental Congress.

The narrative pauses over the great questions of the day: was Henry learned or merely loud, and how did a backcountry lawyer become a voice of revolt? Tyler answers with documents, close reading, and steady judgment. Readers seeking a classic, source-based life of a founder will find a full, sober portrait of Henry the man and the speaker.
29407-the-valley-of-silent-men-a-story-o:
James Oliver Curwood's novel of the Three River Country opens before the railroad, when Athabasca Landing stood as the doorway to the Athabasca, the Slave, and the Mackenzie rivers. The frontispiece shows a girl's revolver spitting smoke and flame, a fitting emblem for a North of romance, tragedy, and hard travel. Curwood, author of The River's End, writes of a land still reached by trail, roughly 150 miles north of Edmonton.

The valley of the title holds silence, danger, and a code of loyalty among trappers, traders, and Mounted men. Love and law clash in a country where the old trail still rules. Readers of northern adventure will find a sturdy, atmospheric tale from the classic age of Canadian wilderness fiction.
29494-king-philip-makers-of-history:
John S. C. Abbott's King Philip, in the Makers of History series from Harper and Brothers, tells the story of the Wampanoag leader whose war with New England settlers shook the colonies. First entered for copyright in 1857, the 1901 printing adds engravings and a preface that laments how few busy readers know the trials of their forefathers in settling New England. Abbott writes for general readers, not scholars, with clear narrative and moral color.

The book follows Philip from Plymouth Bay to the clash that bears his name, stressing courage, grievance, and loss on both sides. Its nineteenth-century view now reads as dated in places, yet vivid. Readers of American history will find a popular, old-style life of a Native leader cast by Abbott as a tragic maker of history.
29513-opinion-of-the-supreme-court-of-th:
Chief Justice John Marshall delivered this opinion of the Supreme Court at the January term of 1832, in the case of Samuel A. Worcester against the State of Georgia. Printed in Washington in 1852 from authenticated copies, with a statement of the case drawn from the Court's own records, it records a landmark clash over Georgia law and Cherokee rights. A writ of error had called up the record from the Superior Court of Gwinnett County.

Marshall's opinion weighs state power against federal treaties and the standing of Native nations under American law. The case became a touchstone in debates over sovereignty, removal, and the limits of state courts. Students of constitutional history will find a primary text whose reasoning still echoes in law and in Native rights cases today.
29547-the-preface-to-aristotle-s-art-of-:
A. Dacier's preface to Aristotle's Art of Poetry, first printed in 1705, was reissued in 1959 by the Augustan Reprint Society as publication number 76, from the William Andrews Clark Memorial Library. Dacier, writing for French readers of his day, sets out Aristotle's doctrine of poetry before the text itself. His notes treat katharsis, or purging, with care.

Dacier argues that Aristotelian katharsis aims not to expel passions from the soul, but to moderate excess passions and to harden the audience against them. The preface thus frames tragedy as moral training. Students of poetics and classical reception will find a key early modern guide to Aristotle's art.
29566-the-centurion-s-story:
David James Burrell's Centurion's Story, printed by the American Tract Society of New York with copyrights in 1892 and 1911, speaks in the voice of an old Roman soldier. Burdened by fourscore years, he recalls an April day in the year 783 A.U.C., half a century past, when he stood with his hundred on guard at the Castle of Antonia in Jerusalem. Ordered to take charge of an execution, he chose twelve men hardened to bloody deeds.

The tale that follows is the Passion seen through a soldier's eyes: hurry and excitement at the Praetorium, a Roman court refusing a religious charge, and a prisoner turned over to Rome. Readers of religious fiction will find a moving, first-person retelling of the central story of the faith.
29568-charge-it-keeping-up-with-harry:
Irving Bacheller's Charge It, or Keeping Up With Harry, printed by Harper and Brothers in 1912, tells of fashionable extravagance and the efforts to restrain it. Its hero is the Honorable Socrates Potter, the genial friend of Lizzie, who watches Harry Swift pass swiftly from one stage of his career to the next. Later chapters force Harry to abandon swamp fiction and like follies, and to study the geography and natives of a land unknown.
