Bacheller writes a comedy of spending, status, and sense, in which keeping up proves a costly game. Potter's genial wisdom steadies the tale. Readers of American comic fiction will enjoy a light, moral satire on the age of charge accounts and social climbing.
29602-the-coyote-a-western-story:
James Roberts's 1925 western was printed by Chelsea House of New York. It opens on a land of red rocks, saffron slopes, green pines and firs, buck brush, and white cliffs, all clean-cut in brilliant sun for miles. Its chapters run from rewards offered and a boy and a girl through the law, a capture, and the real low-down. Where to hide, two queer moves, and caught in the cellar follow. Freedom behind bars and a man and his horse close the tale.

Roberts writes a western of pursuit, disguise, and rough justice, where the coyote of the title stands for cunning itself. The hero must outthink law and outlaw alike. Readers of western fiction will find a brisk, colorful novel from the pulp era's height.
29603-henry-iv-makers-of-history:
John S. C. Abbott's Henry IV, in the Makers of History series from Harper and Brothers, follows the first Bourbon king of France from Navarre to the throne. First entered for copyright in 1856, the 1904 printing adds engravings and a preface calling history our Heaven-appointed instructor and guide for the future. Its chapter heads run from Catharine de Foix and Ferdinand and Isabella through the dismemberment of Navarre, plans for revenge, and Henry's marriage to Margaret.

Abbott writes for general readers, with clear narrative and moral color, tracing how Henry survived war, faith, and faction to rule. The book's nineteenth-century view now reads as dated, yet vivid. Readers of French history will find a popular, old-style life of a king remembered for courage and clemency.
29637-introduction-to-the-study-of-histo:
Ch. V. Langlois and Ch. Seignobos of the Sorbonne wrote this introduction to the study of history, translated by G. G. Berry with a preface by F. York Powell, and printed in New York in 1904 by Henry Holt. Its preface recommends the book as useful and well written, praising pages on evidence that aid anyone seeking truth about any series of facts. To the historian, the book insists, history is not merely a pretty but difficult branch of literature.

Langlois and Seignobos teach method: how to weigh sources, judge testimony, and build knowledge rather than praise or condemn. Caesar, they note, is not theirs to acquit or blame, but to understand. Students of history will find a classic manual of method, still clear after a century.
29644-the-island-mystery:
G. A. Birmingham, author of Gossamer, General John Regan, and Spanish Gold, set this 1918 novel on a mysterious island, printed by George H. Doran Company of New York. Its narrator notes with irony the efficiency of press censorship: in three years, only one reference to the island appeared in any newspaper. The tale that follows blunders, secrets, and island intrigue.

Birmingham writes with his usual light, ironic touch, mixing comedy with wartime mystery. The island itself, half-hidden by silence, becomes a character. Readers of Irish and wartime fiction will enjoy a clever, amusing novel where what is not said matters as much as what is.
29660-three-years-in-the-federal-cavalry:
Willard Glazier, author of The Capture, the Prison-Pen and the Escape, wrote Three Years in the Federal Cavalry, printed in 1870 by R. H. Ferguson and Company of New York. Dedicated to Major-General Henry E. Davies, Jr., whose star burned brightest where battle raged, it opens with the war for the Union: enthusiasm of the North, Washington threatened, and Bull Run with its lessons.

Glazier enlists under Captain Buel in the Harris Light Cavalry and follows Scott and the cavalry through three years of war. The book mixes memoir with campaign narrative. Readers of Civil War history will find a soldier's full, earnest account of cavalry service from first enthusiasm to hard experience.
29670-against-odds-a-detective-story:
Lawrence L. Lynch, writing as E. Murdoch Van Deventer, published this detective tale in 1894. It opens in Chicago, where a man who has lost his cash to sharpers tells his tale of woe and sets a hunt in motion. From there the trail leads through disguise, false clues, and a cast of confidence men, with a king of that trade and a foe named Delbras at the far end of it.

Carl Masters and other hands join the chase, which runs from city streets to the Columbian Guard and a string of close calls. Lynch keeps the plot moving from one snare to the next, and the charm lies in the slang, the bluffs, and the slow unmasking of who is playing whom. The final chapters close the net on the men who ran the game.
29699-hetty-s-strange-history:
Helen Jackson, writing as H. H., is best known for Ramona, and this novel carries a copyright date of 1877. The Boston edition here is dated 1886. Two opening verses set its theme: love is not proved by swift words or costly gifts that all men see. It is proved, the verses say, by giving one's own life up in the daily groove of common days.

Hetty's tale follows that hard measure of love through a life that the title calls strange. Jackson writes in a plain, earnest voice, with feeling held close rather than spread wide. The book suits readers of her other domestic tales, who like a heroine tested less by grand deeds than by steady, daily faithfulness.
29743-the-missionary:
George Griffith, author of The Angel of the Revolution, published The Missionary in London in 1902. A prologue, twenty-five chapters, and an epilogue make up the book. The prologue opens on two lads and a golden-haired girl named Eny. One lad calls her his sweetheart, the other vows to have her, and a swinging open-hand blow across the cheek settles nothing.

From that childhood quarrel the novel follows its title figure through a grown man's course. Griffith writes in the brisk, romantic style of his popular romances, with love, rivalry, and duty in the foreground. The book suits readers who like a long, colorful tale where a boy's first fight foreshadows a man's larger trials.
29966-slaves-of-mercury:
Nat Schachner wrote this complete novelette for Astounding Stories in September 1932. Back toward a smiling Earth, rising fast to greet his craft, Hilary Grendon guides his battered and time-worn space flier, the Vagabond. His hands tremble at the controls, and only long practice saves him from a smash. He can scarcely believe he is home, after the unhuman glittering cylinders of Saturn and the harsh red angularities of Mars.

Earth's warm sunlight, soft green grass, and slender birches seem heaven itself to him, and the carefree skeptic of old is now a Fundamentalist. A sidenote warns that Hilary returns to find alien diskoids in Earth's stratosphere, with out-world lords patrolling her cities. A blinding beam shearing through Peabody's middle fronts the tale. Schachner builds a grim homecoming in which Earth itself is no longer free.
30113-the-one-way-trail-a-story-of-the-c:
Ridgwell Cullum sets a cattle-country novel on a trail that runs one way, with no turnings, bypaths, or turning back. A gentleman ranker, a shooting match, and a stay in Barnriff open the story, before Jim proposes and the action moves to the red, dancing devil. Eve and Will, a chicken killing, the boys of the village, a woman's care, and an evil night follow in turn, as life on the range tests each figure.

George W. Jacobs published the Philadelphia volume in 1911, and its epigraph calls the one-way trail the trail of life, full of pitfalls that make men curse, yet good to walk. Two cattle brands appear as pictures in print, a double star and a diamond, marked as such in the text. Cullum, author of The Watchers of the Plains, writes the range in brisk, popular style.
30155-relativity-the-special-and-general:
Albert Einstein explains relativity in a book written in 1916, here in the authorized translation by Robert W. Lawson, revised in 1924. Part 1, the special theory, begins with the physical meaning of geometrical propositions, systems of coordinates, and space and time in classical mechanics. It then sets out the Galileian system, the principle of relativity in its restricted sense, and the old rule for adding velocities.

Later chapters face the clash between light propagation and relativity, the idea of time in physics, the relativity of simultaneity and of distance, and the Lorentz transformation. Measuring rods and clocks in motion close the opening movement, before the general theory extends the argument. Einstein writes for readers willing to follow careful reasoning, not for specialists alone, and Lawson's translation keeps the exposition clear.
30167-royal-children-of-english-history:
E. Nesbit tells English history through its royal children, with pictures by Frances Brundage and M. Bowley, for Raphael Tuck and Sons of London, Paris, and New York. Alfred the Great learning to read fronts the book. Chapters follow Prince Arthur, Henry the Third, the first Prince of Wales, Edward the Black Prince, and Henry the Fifth and the baby king. Black and white drawings and letterpress were printed in England.

Nesbit opens by confessing that, very little, she hated history learned from a horrid little outlines book of kings' names and battle dates. History, she tells young readers, is a story of real live people in England long ago, where mothers loved children and fathers worked for them. The book suits children who want kings and princes as people, not as lists to memorize.
30215-intarsia-and-marquetry:
F. Hamilton Jackson, examiner to the Board of Education in principles of ornament, explains intarsia and marquetry in a Sands and Company handbook from London in 1903. Pictures from photographs and from drawings and tracings by the author support the text, and companion volumes in the series treat mural painting and mosaic and marble inlay. Historical notes open with antiquity, then Italy in medieval and Renaissance times, cloistered intarsiatori and their pupils, and Germany, Holland, England, and France.

Later sections give the process of manufacture, the limitations and capabilities of the art, and workshop receipts for the craftsman. Plates show border patterns, a chair back from Sant' Ambrogio in Milan, and a door of the Sala del Papa in Siena. Figure intarsia from the Florence cathedral sacristy includes the prophets Amos and Hosea and the Annunciation. The book suits designers and makers who want history with practice.
30313-the-preacher-of-cedar-mountain-a-t:
Ernest Thompson Seton tells The Preacher of Cedar Mountain, a tale of the open country. Doubleday, Page and Company at Garden City, New York, published it in 1917, with a frontispiece by Clarence Rowe. An illustration poses the choice: you must choose between us, is it Belle or Blazing Star? Book one, The Child of the Stable Yard, follows little Jim Hartigan from the home land of his boyhood through the strains mingled in him.

How he lost his father, the atmosphere of his early days, his tutors, losing everything, and a lesson carry Jim toward book two. The Conversion brings college, escape to Cedar Mountain, a new force in his life, Belle Boyd, a sermon, the lure of the saddle, and Pat Bylow's sprees. Book three, The Horse Preacher, gives Blazing Star, Red Rover, the secret of Yellowbank Canyon, and the start and finish of a race.
30387-mark-mason-s-victory:
Horatio Alger tells a rags-to-respectability tale in Mark Mason's Victory, in a post-1900 edition that drops seven chapters between chapter thirty-one and the close found in the 1899 version. Contents open with two strangers from Syracuse, where Mark lived, an unexpected call, a night at Daly's, and Mark as a hero.

Later chapters follow the Evening Globe, the great Mr. Bunsby, a scene in Mrs. Mack's room, an adventure in a Fifth Avenue stage, and an important commission. Alger's formula holds: a hardworking boy meets chance, temptation, and kind helpers, then earns his victory by honesty and pluck. The novel offers a classic American success story for young readers.
30401-the-flying-stingaree-a-rick-brant-:
John Blaine tells The Flying Stingaree, a Rick Brant science-adventure story published by Grosset and Dunlap in New York in 1963. It is dedicated to his sons Chris and Derek, who watched stingarees from the sun deck of the houseboat Spindrift. A riddle opens the book: what sting-ray shape flies over Chesapeake Bay? Rick Brant and Don Scott meet it while sheltering from a storm, anchored in a Maryland cove aboard Spindrift.

Their sighting is not unique, and one such thing stands suspected of kidnaping a man. Eastern Shore residents take the objects for flying saucers, but ridicule has silenced their reports. Scientific curiosity drives Rick and Scotty to investigate in full, with encouragement from Steve Ames, a young government intelligence agent with a summer cottage near the cove.
30496-fire-mountain-a-thrilling-sea-stor:
Norman Springer writes Fire Mountain, a thrilling sea story published in New York in 1923 by G. Howard Watt, following his earlier Blood Ship. Twenty-three chapters move from the mission and the weeping boatswain to the happy hunchback, the black cruiser, Wild Bob Carew, and a prisoner.

Later scenes add the mate of the brig Cohasset, talk around the cabin table, a mountain in a smoky sea, and the whaleman's log. A code, a passage, Fire Mountain itself, fog, and a lazaret follow. Three gentlemen converse, two men meet a maid, and an elephant's head, the edge of an abyss, and a treasure cave close the list. Springer pairs sea adventure with mystery and treasure.
30600-the-pines-of-lory:
J. A. Mitchell writes The Pines of Lory, published in New York in 1901 by the Life Publishing Company, with decorations by Albert D. Blashfield. Mitchell, author of Amos Judd, That First Affair, and Gloria Victis, dedicates the book to all lovers of lovers and lovers of out-of-door things and milder forms of folly.

An illustration quotes Byron on pleasure in the pathless wood and rapture on the lonely shore, while another shows a place that is no gardener's cottage. Mitchell sets a romance among pines, woods, and open air, where love and folly meet in a gentle, old-fashioned tale. The novel suits readers who enjoy nature, courtship, and a light, affectionate tone.
30624-alexander-the-great-makers-of-hist:
Jacob Abbott writes Alexander the Great in the Makers of History series, with engravings, published in New York and London by Harper and Brothers. Entered for copyright in 1849 and copyrighted in 1876, the volume opens with a preface on lives that attract wide attention.

Such lives, Abbott notes, have been written in many ways by a multitude of authors, and readers sometimes wonder why another life is needed. His answer lies in method: a clear, school-ready narrative for young readers. Alexander the Great traces the Macedonian conqueror from youth to empire in Abbott's direct, moralizing style.
30664-callista-a-tale-of-the-third-centu:
John Henry Cardinal Newman writes Callista, a tale of the third century, in a new impression published in London, New York, and Bombay in 1904 by Longmans, Green. Newman dedicates the book to Henry William Wilberforce, who knew him long and loved him well, and who will recognize the author in his work.

An epigraph in verse urges love of God alone, warning that hearts twined with mortal beings still dwell apart, and that the deepest soul remains single. An advertisement calls the tale a simple fiction, set in the early church's age of trial. Newman blends romance, faith, and history into a story of conversion and steadfast belief.
30675-presbyterian-worship-its-spirit-me:
Robert Johnston, a doctor of divinity, wrote this 1901 study of worship in the Presbyterian churches, with a warm introduction by John Campbell of Presbyterian College, Montreal. Johnston's core claim, as Campbell states it, is that the church must first guard the spiritual side of worship and set aside what gets in its way. His method is history, not bare rule or taste.

The book traces how Presbyterian worship grew and changed, weighing scriptural precedent, Christian principle, order, beauty, and the needs of mission fields and mixed congregations. It argues for a broad but principled view, with room for honest difference and charity toward other minds. Readers who study church life, liturgy, or Canadian church history will find a fair, learned survey from inside the tradition it describes.
30707-cyrus-the-great-makers-of-history:
Jacob Abbott writes Cyrus the Great in the Makers of History series, with engravings, published in New York and London by Harper and Brothers. Entered for copyright in 1850 and copyrighted in 1878, the volume includes a map of the Persian Empire.

Abbott states a special object for the series: to adapt each volume for use as a school textbook. A general compend of history, he argues, serves well if it arrives at the right stage of education. Cyrus the Great offers young readers a clear life of the Persian king, from rise to empire, in Abbott's plain, instructive style.
30809-aunt-charlotte-s-stories-of-greek-:
Charlotte M. Yonge, author of The Heir of Redclyffe, wrote this little history for young children, in a London edition marked eighth thousand. Yonge says she tried to trace Greek history so a child could follow it, and she would start a child's reading with England, then pass to Greece and Rome. She begins with a few Greek myths, which she calls needful for grasping both history and art.

The book moves from myth to the course of Greek life in simple order, with names given in their usual reading. Yonge links Greek events to scripture history and to the march of time, so young readers gain a sense of the ancient world before they start classical study. It is a gentle, old-fashioned school book, clear in tone and made for reading aloud at home or in class.
30822-campaign-of-battery-d-first-rhode-:
Ezra K. Parker, late first lieutenant of Battery E, First Rhode Island Light Artillery, wrote this campaign history for the Rhode Island Soldiers and Sailors Historical Society, published at Providence in 1913. It is seventh series, number six, in the society's personal narratives of the War of the Rebellion. Its subject is Battery D, First Rhode Island Light Artillery, in Kentucky and East Tennessee.

In March 1863, General A. E. Burnside, relieved at his own request of the Army of the Potomac, took the Department of the Ohio, and the Ninth Army Corps was detailed for service there. Battery D, under Captain William W. Buckley and attached to the Ninth Corps, moved with it from Virginia to Kentucky. Parker gives a soldier's account of march, camp, and fight, valuable for readers of Rhode Island and Civil War history.
30875-maria-antoinette-makers-of-history:
John S. C. Abbott wrote this life of Maria Antoinette for his Makers of History series, published by Harper and Brothers in New York and London in a 1901 printing, entered in 1849. Abbott says in his preface that he aimed for a faithful narrative of facts and, as far as possible, the soul of history. He calls her story a mournful tragedy seldom matched on earth, yet full of instruction for future ages.

Chapters trace parentage and childhood, bridal days, Maria Antoinette enthroned, the diamond necklace affair, and the mob at Versailles, among later scenes of revolution and fall. Abbott argues that intelligence and moral worth alone can ground national prosperity or domestic happiness, but he lets the simple story carry its own moral. Readers get a vivid, old-fashioned life of a queen caught in revolution.
30955-the-princess-idleways-a-fairy-stor:
Mrs. W. J. Hays wrote this fairy story, published by Harper and Brothers in New York and London in 1879, with pictures. Its frontispiece shows a speaker saying, I have brought my little daughter to you, my friend. The heroine is the Princess Idleways, and the first chapter warns the reader not to suppose she was a great, grand woman.

She was only a little young lovely girl named Laura, of high birth, whose father, grandfather, and great-grandfather, with all the fine lady grandmothers, never had to labor for themselves or others. Like beautiful roses grown more beautiful by planting, transplanting, and shielding from hot sun and sharp wind, Laura was bright and bewitching as any rosebud. She had a few sharp thorns which could prick. She lived in a great castle high in the mountains, looking out on hills, eagles, and foaming cascades. It is a Victorian fairy tale.
31007-the-girls-and-i-a-veracious-histor:
Mrs Molesworth's 1892 children's book is told by Jack, a boy growing up with his younger sisters Serena and Maud, and it calls itself a veracious, or truthful, history of their doings. Twelve chapters carry the three through a lost diamond ornament, a dancing class, a town crier's errand, a farm stay at Mossmoor, and a string of small mischiefs and alarms.

The charm lies in Jack's plain first-person voice and in the way everyday childhood plans keep tipping into mild adventure. Young readers meet a household where sisters argue, scheme, and look out for one another. The book still reads as a warm, clear picture of Victorian family life seen from a child's height.
31033-james-vi-and-the-gowrie-mystery:
Andrew Lang's 1902 inquiry takes up the Gowrie mystery: the killing of the Ruthven brothers and the tangled stories told about it afterward. Seventeen chapters weigh the king's own narrative against the Ruthven vindication and test the theory of an accidental brawl. They follow later clues through Logan of Restalrig, the notary Sprot, and a set of letters said to be forged.

Lang sifts depositions, pamphlets, and the casket letters with a detective's patience, asking what each witness had to gain and where the accounts break down. The book remains a model of historical detective work, and a clear guide to a Scottish puzzle that has divided readers for three centuries.
31049-bugle-blasts-read-before-the-ohio-:
William E. Crane, late captain of the 4th Ohio Volunteer Cavalry, read this paper before the Ohio Commandery of the Military Order of the Loyal Legion on November 5, 1884. Speaking as a man who held only a modest place in the Union army, Crane argues as follows. The small incidents seen by single soldiers, like battered bullets picked up on old battlefields, help complete the grand story of the war.

The address mixes modesty, comradeship, and pride in the Ohio men who made chapters of history, and it looks ahead to grandchildren pointing at their ancestors' deeds. As a document, it shows how Civil War veterans told their war to one another in the 1880s, valuing the small link as much as the great battle.
31165-the-church-handy-dictionary:
Published in New York by James Pott and Company in 1890 and dedicated by permission to Christopher Wordsworth, Bishop of Lincoln, The Church Handy Dictionary is a compact Anglican reference book. Its preface admits the work is mainly a compilation, with articles on controverted subjects setting out the views of the best authorities rather than the compiler's own. It speaks from a distinctly Anglican standpoint.

Additions and corrections touch altar cloths and the Sarum colors of red and white, heresy, miracles, and the real presence, quoting Bishop Harold Browne and Jeremy Taylor on the Supper. For clergy and lay readers, the little book offered quick, orthodox answers to the questions churchgoers actually asked.
31171-1931-a-glance-at-the-twentieth-cen:
In Hartshorne's 1881 volume, the twentieth century arrives as a fictional diary dated 1931, kept by an idle man of means positioned to watch events closely. Its author warns readers not to hold him responsible for the diary's views, since his purpose is to show what will probably occur, not what ought to occur.

The entries for January 1931 picture sympathy for an ex-queen of England in enforced retirement, a seventy-first Congress meeting at St. Louis, and a Texas member's motion to admit Mexico as the fifty-second state, with Central America to follow as three territories. Wrong in detail and charming in spirit, the book is an early exercise in forecasting the future.
31222-the-homicidal-diary:
Earl Peirce Jr.'s story, printed in Weird Tales in October 1937, is told by the lifelong friend of Jason Carse, a brilliant criminologist turned weekly murderer. The narrator writes in the interests of justice, psychiatry, and demonology, citing the newspaper record and the official report of the alienists who examined Carse at his trial.

Carse, once a law-school roommate who rose to the pinnacle of his field, roamed the streets one night each week to commit decapitation murders, and he was hanged until dead. The narrator insists the case turns on evil and dark lore unseen since the Inquisition, leaving readers to judge whether madness, crime, or something stranger drove his friend.
31232-history-of-morgan-s-cavalry:
Basil W. Duke's 1867 history of Morgan's Cavalry, published in Cincinnati and entered in 1866 by Mrs. Henrietta Morgan, tells the Confederate raiders' four-year career from just after the war's outbreak. Dedicated to the women of Kentucky and of the South whose kindness eased the men's hardships, the book aims at a correct and graphic record. It tells the warfare John Hunt Morgan made famous.

Duke admits the book is less complete than he wished, since the very activity of the service kept his men from preserving records. Limited space forced him to pass over many brave deeds. Even so, it remains the insider's history of one of the Civil War's most celebrated cavalry commands.
31252-the-red-moccasins-a-story:
Morrison Heady's 1901 story, printed in Louisville by the Courier-Journal Job Printing Company, follows Sprigg, a boy of about twelve in green Kentucky in the days when great-grandfathers were children themselves. The narrator muses that Sprigg is an odd name for a hero, wishing he could christen the boy Jack, the fitting name for a juvenile novel's hero. The will at the story's end proves Sprigg real enough in law.

Sprigg is of a wild and runaway turn, the kind of boy who seeks ice on a summer day at risk of drowning. Heady offers him as a warning example to dissatisfied youngsters tempted to leave home. Warm, digressive, and old-fashioned, the tale is Kentucky storytelling in the classic boys'-book manner.
31283-english-critical-essays-nineteenth:
Edmund D. Jones's selection of English Critical Essays of the nineteenth century, published in Oxford's World's Classics and first issued in 1916, gathers the century's great statements on poetry and criticism. Wordsworth opens on poetry and poetic diction in 1800, Coleridge follows on Wordsworth's theory and metrical composition, and Blake on the Canterbury Pilgrims. Lamb follows on Shakespeare's tragedies for the stage, and Shelley with his Defence of Poetry.

Later essays include Hazlitt's first acquaintance with poets, Keble on sacred poetry, Newman on poetry and Aristotle's Poetics, and Carlyle on the hero as poet. They go on to Leigh Hunt on what poetry is, Arnold on the choice of subjects, Ruskin on the pathetic fallacy, and Mill's thoughts on poetry. The volume is an essential anthology for anyone tracing how English criticism learned to talk about poems.
31373-solaris-farm-a-story-of-the-twenti:
Milan C. Edson's 1900 book, published by the author in Washington, D. C., is a story of the twentieth century built around a farm of the future. Edson offers the book to farm sons and daughters across the Republic, on the ground that farm folk make up most of its workforce. For him, farming underlies all industrial and commercial success, so farm boys and girls ought to rise as the country's leading thinkers and leaders.

Against that hope he sets land monopoly and the small farm's inability to afford the latest machinery, threatening land-owning farmers with extinction and reduction to dependent farm labor. Meanwhile isolated life and severe toil depress their minds. Solaris Farm proposes the changes its author believed would save the independent farmer, making it a utopian tract as much as a novel.
31383-the-industrial-canal-and-inner-har:
Thomas Ewing Dabney's The Industrial Canal and Inner Harbor of New Orleans was published by the Board of Commissioners of the Port of New Orleans in May 1921. It gives the history, description, and economic aspects of a giant facility built to encourage industrial expansion and develop commerce. A foreword opens with a meditation on the mind of man, frail yet able to move mountains. It points to New Orleans as proof: a canal dredged through buried forests 18,000 years old, an underground river created, and a lock built that was thought impossible.

Dabney traces the need for the canal, recognized for a century, through endorsement by New Orleans and construction to operation. The book serves as both civic history and commercial argument, showing how a port city remade its geography for trade. Readers of Louisiana or engineering history will find a detailed, boosterish, and informative account.
3147-a-summer-in-a-canyon-a-california-s:
Kate Douglas Wiggin sends a party into a California canyon for the summer in this 1914 story. Preparation and departure lead to the journey itself, then to life in the canyon, where the heir apparent loses himself. Rhyme and reason, a forest of Arden, and good news follow, with Queen Elsie paying a visit to the court.

The book is a holiday tale, full of children, talk, and outdoor play. Wiggin, beloved for Rebecca of Sunnybrook Farm, writes the canyon as a place where young people invent their own kingdom. Readers get sunshine, scrapes, and a gentle moral: a summer lived outdoors teaches more than a summer spent indoors.
31495-the-wailing-octopus-a-rick-brant-s:
John Blaine's The Wailing Octopus, a Rick Brant science-adventure story, was published by Grosset and Dunlap of New York in 1956. Its contents run from destination Clipper Cay and the scuba slip, through the shadow, visitors by night, the warning, and the deadly tank. They continue to the derelict, the fancy frogmen, and the wreck of the Maiden Hand. An illustration shows Scotty jerking off an enemy frogman's face plate with his spear.

Rick Brant and his friends face undersea adventure, with diving, salvage, and enemies in frogmen's gear. Blaine writes the science-adventure series for boys with a steady mix of gadgetry and action. Readers who enjoy juvenile adventure will find a fast-moving undersea tale, where the wailing octopus of the title is only the strangest part of the mystery.
31584-history-of-the-seventh-ohio-volunt:
Captain R. C. Rankin's history of the Seventh Ohio Volunteer Cavalry was printed at Ripley, Ohio, by J. C. Newcomb in 1881. Rankin writes that the honor of writing it was conferred on him, though he calls himself no historian and not even a letter writer. He warns that he must rely almost wholly on memory, because the regiment's notes and papers were captured.

The regiment was raised on an order from the War Department, under which Governor Todd of Ohio would raise one regiment. Rankin's account traces the organization of the Seventh Ohio and its service in the Civil War. It was written by a captain who served with it and who knew how much good service the regiment had done.
31589-the-blue-ghost-mystery-a-rick-bran:
John Blaine's Rick Brant science-adventure story The Blue Ghost Mystery was published by Grosset and Dunlap in 1960. Its twelve chapters open with a spooky invitation, then death at Costin's Creek, the blue ghost itself, and the old mine. Night alarm and the dark pit follow, with the Frostola man and a plan of attack.

The later chapters bring the splitting atoms, an assist from Janig, the ghost's reappearance, and the dead water. Blaine's tale mixes ghost-story atmosphere with boy inventors' science, as Rick and his friends chase a haunting that proves to have a rational, mechanical explanation behind its spooky face.
31678-in-the-border-country:
In the Border Country pairs twenty-five pictures in colour by James Orrock with historical notes by W. S. Crockett. It belongs to a series of popular books on art edited by W. Shaw Sparrow, and it treats the border country between England and Scotland as a place of history and of beauty together. Orrock's pictures carry the landscape, and Crockett's notes carry its past.

The book moves through a region shaped by raids, castles, and ballads, and it presents its hills, valleys, and old strongholds as scenery with stories attached. For readers who know the border by name, it gives the country itself, in colour and in history, page by page.
3180-a-double-barrelled-detective-story:
Mark Twain sets this detective tale in Virginia in 1880. It opens with a wedding joining a good-looking young man short of money to a wealthy young woman. Instant love rushes them into a quick marriage that the girl's widowed father fiercely opposes. Jacob Fuller, the bridegroom, is twenty-six, from an old but unconsidered family that had come down in the world.

From that domestic quarrel Twain builds a story of revenge and detection, turning the methods of the famous fictional detectives inside out. Clues are followed with great solemnity to absurd ends. Twain's late, darker comedy is on full show: a solemn inquiry collapsing under its own machinery.
31813-checkers-a-hard-luck-story:
Henry M. Blossom Jr.'s novel Checkers, a hard-luck story copyrighted in 1896 and issued here in the 1899 printing, opens on Derby Day in Chicago. Its narrator, a Boston man new to racing, drives out Michigan Avenue with his sporting friend Murray Jameson among coaches, cabs, and crowds of every description.

The story follows the gambler Checkers and Pert, whose weak and irregular heart action a doctor examines, warning against violent exercise, excitement, stimulants, and drugs. Readers get a sporting-life novel that turns from the races to a tender question: how a reckless man learns to guard the woman he loves.
31844-the-unconstitutionality-of-slavery:
Lysander Spooner's 1845 book The Unconstitutionality of Slavery, published at Boston by Bela Marsh, argues that slavery was never lawful under the American Constitution. Spooner begins by defining law itself, asking what law judicial tribunals are morally bound to declare and sustain under all circumstances.

Thirteen chapters then work through written constitutions, colonial charters and statutes, the Declaration of Independence, the state constitutions of 1789, and the Articles of Confederation. They end with the Constitution itself and the claim that children of slaves are born free. Readers get a rigorous abolitionist legal argument, still cited for its close reading of constitutional text.
31903-anarchism-a-criticism-and-history-:
E. V. Zenker's Anarchism, a criticism and history of the anarchist theory, published by G. P. Putnam's Sons in 1897, opens by faulting earlier writers on the subject. Laveleye, he says, does not even know of Proudhon and takes Bakunin as the only representative of anarchism. Garin, author of a big book called The Anarchists, knows no anarchist author except some youthful writings of Proudhon.

Zenker argues that such ignorance mingles socialism, nihilism, and anarchism in wild confusion and even identifies anarchism with collectivism. Readers get a late nineteenth-century scholarly history that tries to separate anarchist theory from its caricatures and to judge it on its own writers.
31919-blooms-of-the-berry:
Madison J. Cawein's 1887 poetry book Blooms of the Berry was published at Louisville by John P. Morton and Company. It opens with a proem in which wine-warm winds lead the poet through green sonorous woods of belated spring. The fields are strewn, wild and white with starry bloom, like a milky way dashed into billowy foam.

The poet, bewildered as one roused from heavy dreams, offers not grander flowers but these berry-blooms, evanescent as their dew. Later poems include By Wold and Wood and The Hollow, where swallows dart beneath empty vaults of blue. Readers get an early Cawein collection, lush with Kentucky woods and fields.
31949-the-bartlett-mystery:
Louis Tracy's 1919 novel The Bartlett Mystery was published by Edward J. Clode. It is the story of love and crime filed with the New York Detective Bureau under the name Yacht Mystery. It involves almost no yachts and is a mystery no longer. It concerns the troubles of pretty Winifred Bartlett and her true lover, the alert, well-groomed Rex Carshaw, far more than the portly millionaire owner of the Sans Souci.

The story begins on October 5, 1913, when traffic in Fifth Avenue is interrupted near Forty-second Street, and the diary of James Steingall, chief of the Bureau, opens. Readers get an Edwardian detective romance of New York, yachts, and a nine days' wonder that hundreds of thousands followed.
32030-selections-from-ancient-irish-poet:
Kuno Meyer's selections from ancient Irish poetry, published in London by Constable and Company in 1911, gather early Irish verse in English translation. Meyer dedicated the book to Edmund Knowles Muspratt, described as an enlightened and generous patron of Celtic studies at the University of Liverpool. The collection is arranged by theme, so readers can move from myth to prayer to nature to love without needing to know the original Irish.

The myth and saga group includes The Isles of the Happy, the sea-god's address to Bran, and Deirdre's farewell to Scotland and her lament. Religious poetry offers The Deer's Cry, Patrick's blessing on Munster, and the hermit's song. Nature poems sing of summer come and gone, the sea, and winter, while love poetry gives the song of Crede and the tale of Liadin and Curithir. It is a compact doorway into a literature most readers meet only in fragments.
32038-the-flaming-mountain-a-rick-brant-:
John Blaine's 1962 Rick Brant science-adventure story The Flaming Mountain was published by Grosset and Dunlap. It opens on San Luz, a little island near South America's coast, where rock melts like butter on a hot stove. Dan Scott and his pal Rick Brant fly out to the resort island to meet Rick's father, who heads the Spindrift Scientific Foundation. They find a seemingly inactive volcano about to explode. It could blow San Luz off the map.

A small town at the volcano's foot faces the immediate threat, and Rick and Scotty first build a scale model of the island for the Foundation's staff. Readers get a boys' adventure of science, volcanoes, and a race against eruption.
32047-josephine-makers-of-history:
John S. C. Abbott's Josephine, in the Makers of History series, tells the life of Napoleon's wife for young readers. The Harper and Brothers edition of 1904 carries an 1879 copyright in the name of Susan Abbott Mead, with the work first entered in 1851. Abbott's preface places Josephine beside Marie Antoinette and Madame Roland as leading heroines of the French Revolution. Each, he says, displayed traits worthy of imitation.

Abbott's framing gives the book its shape: Marie Antoinette saw the Revolution begin, Madame Roland saw its harsh middle, and Josephine watched it fade. The history of their lives, he argues, records the most interesting events of that fearful tragedy. Young ladies especially, Abbott writes, will be ennobled by contemplating the fortitude and grandeur of spirit these women showed. Readers get a nineteenth-century biography, moral in aim and dramatic in subject.
32059-the-pirates-of-shan-a-rick-brant-s:
John Blaine's 1958 Rick Brant science-adventure story The Pirates of Shan was published by Grosset and Dunlap. It opens with Rick Brant stating grimly that they had better do something, and fast, as he throws a stone far out over the Atlantic's green waters. Don Scott, nicknamed Scotty, soothes him that his father is just as worried, perhaps more, because he feels responsible.

Two staff scientists of the Spindrift Scientific Foundation, headquartered on Spindrift Island off the New Jersey coast, have mysteriously disappeared, and Rick's restlessness is augmented by fear for their safety. Its twenty chapters run from the missing scientists and the Hindu merchant through Bagobo country, the man in the red fez, and the dancing pirates to a plan of attack. Readers get a boys' adventure of pirates, jungles, and missing scientists.
32078-love-story:
Irving E. Cox, Junior's short story, printed in If Worlds of Science Fiction in April 1956, imagines a compound where everything serves the whims of women. Its tagline explains the premise: popular clichés, pretty romances, and advertising catchwords have become realities, and the compound keeps its men enslaved. George, the hero, knows what he has to do, though the story leaves his plan to unfold.

The opening shows the routine of that servitude. A duty bell rings, and George clatters down from his cubicle above the garage. His mother's chartreuse Cadillac convertible purrs to a stop in the drive. Mother and son mouth a formula of words, with deception now a part of George's character. Readers get a satire on romance, advertising, and domestic power, turned inside out as science fiction.
32091-down-adown-derry:
Walter de la Mare's book of fairy poems, published in New York by Henry Holt and Company in 1922, gathers verse about fairies, witches, and the unseen folk of field and house. Dorothy P. Lathrop supplied the illustrations. Its contents divide the poems into groups, opening with fairies and moving on to witches and witchcraft, with further sections beyond. The titles promise small, eerie, and playful pieces rather than long narrative poems.

Among the fairy poems are The Fairies Dancing, Dream-Song, The Double, The Horn, The Changeling, Lob Lie by the Fire, and the title poem, Down-Adown-Derry. The witchcraft group includes The Hare, I Saw Three Witches, The Isle of Lone, Sunk Lyonesse, and Sleeping Beauty. Readers get de la Mare's gift for quiet strangeness: short lyrics where a household, a wood, or a winter night may hide a watching presence.
32146-fugitive-poetry:
N. P. Willis's Fugitive Poetry, published in Boston by Peirce and Williams in 1829, gathers verse that had first appeared in scattered places. Its title page carries an epigraph from Washington Irving, stating the author's hope for his writing. Irving's words run: if he can rub out one wrinkle from the brow of care, he will not have written entirely in vain. The same hope covers beguiling a heavy heart of sorrow for a moment.

Willis's aim, as the epigraph frames it, is gentler than grandeur: to prompt a benevolent view of human nature, and to leave readers in better humour with their fellow beings and themselves. The book was entered for copyright in September 1829, in the fifty-fourth year of American independence. Readers get an early American poetry collection, modest in ambition and warm in intent.
32200-sowing-and-sewing-a-sexagesima-sto:
Charlotte M. Yonge's Sowing and Sewing, a Sexagesima story published in New York by E. P. Dutton and Company, links needlework to the parable of the sower. Yonge's preface notes that readers may see allusions to a sacred parable underlying the little story, and hopes they will not think its application irreverent. Sexagesima, the Sunday before Lent, gives the tale its church calendar frame.

Its chapters run from The Sermon and The Sunday School through The Working Party, Teacher Amy, and The Trousseau to Stitch, Stitch, Stitch, Wandering Eyes, and Amy's Visits. The story opens with four girls in a pleasant cottage room, three of them Miss Lee's apprentices, in a room built out at the back of a baker's shop. Readers get a gentle Victorian tale of sewing girls, a teacher, and a reckoning over which seed shall prosper.
32269-the-caves-of-fear-a-rick-brant-sci:
John Blaine's The Caves of Fear, a Rick Brant science-adventure story published by Grosset and Dunlap in New York in 1951, sends Rick's crew from Spindrift to Hong Kong. Its twenty chapters run from Changes at Spindrift and The Cipher Message through Heavy Water and Project X. They continue to Hong Kong, The Golden Mouse, and The Junk with Purple Sails. Long Shadow, The Trail to Korse Lenken, and The Ambush at Llhan Huang lead to The Goatskin Water Bag, The Buddhist Monk, and The Black Buddha.

An illustration shows a floor section swinging upward at the base of the Black Buddha. Hammer and saw disturb Spindrift Island, while Rick Brant struggles with the noise. The Caves of Fear, The Labyrinth, and The Lake of Darkness follow, with hostages, dark glasses, Canton Charlie's, and a home flight. Readers get an adventure of ciphers, heavy water, and caves.
32270-the-golden-skull-a-rick-brant-scie:
John Blaine's The Golden Skull, a Rick Brant science-adventure story published by Grosset and Dunlap in New York in 1954, sends its heroes to the Philippines. Its twenty chapters run from The Head-Hunter and Manila After Dark through The Gods of Banaue, Inside the Walls, and Manotok the Mighty to Igorot Country, The Bontoc Road, and Ifugao Country. Ambush, Warriors Three, and The Ifugao Village lead to The Peaceful Profession, Sign of the Dragon, and Under the Dragon's Claws.

An illustration shows the Ifugaos, faces distorted with hatred and fury, in pursuit. The story opens aboard the freighter Asiatic Dream, in tropical heat that penetrates steel and flaking paint. Readers get a boys' science-adventure of head-hunters, mountain roads, flying spears, and a sky wagon, ending with a surprise package.
3230-the-counterpane-fairy:
Katharine Pyle wrote and illustrated this children's fantasy, published by Dutton in New York in 1898. The contents promise a princess of the golden castle, owls and a gamblesome elf, and two children named Starlein and Silverling. A magic circus, the edge of the polar sea, and a ruby ring follow, with rainbow children and Harriett's dream.

Down the rat-hole and the counterpane fairy herself close the journey. The book is a bedtime voyage: a sick child's quilt becomes a landscape, and each square opens a new wonder. Pyle's pictures match her prose, gentle and fanciful. Young readers get a classic of the nursery fantasy kind, where the smallest room can hold a whole world.
32363-ten-girls-from-history:
Kate Dickinson Sweetser's book, published in New York in 1912, tells the lives of ten girls from history for young readers. Its subjects are Jeanne d'Arc, Maid of France; Victoria, girl queen of England; Sally Wister of the American Revolution; Cofachiqui, an Indian princess of historic legend; and Jenny Lind, the Swedish Nightingale. Eliza Lucas, girl planter of the fifteenth century, also appears.

Later lives cover Lady Jane Grey, the Nine Days Queen; Gentle Annie, daughter of the regiment; Madeleine de Verchères, heroine of Castle Dangerous; and Adrienne de Lafayette, a young patriot's wife. Sweetser, author of Ten Boys from History and Ten Girls from Dickens, writes each life as a short, stirring story of courage, duty, and growth.
32370-secret-diplomatic-history-of-the-e:
Karl Marx's volume on secret diplomacy, edited by Eleanor Marx Aveling and Edward Aveling, examines how great powers used hidden deals, treaties, and back-channel talks to pursue their aims. Its front matter pairs the title subject with letters written from 1853 to 1856 on the Eastern Question and the Crimean War, showing Marx applying the same lens to a later crisis. The editors present the material as a sustained critique of official explanations for war and alliance.

Marx stresses detail, motive, and interest over ceremony, tracing how governments said one thing in public while arranging another in private. Readers get a sharp, argumentative account of diplomacy as power politics, written with the energy and scorn for small-minded statecraft that contemporary reviewers noted. The book remains a useful source for the history of diplomatic double-dealing.
32375-shan-folk-lore-stories-from-the-hi:
William C. Griggs's collection gathers Shan folk lore from the hill and water country, dedicated to J. N. Cushing, principal of the American Baptist College in Rangoon and translator of the Bible into Shan. Its stories include A Laung Khit, How Boh Han Me Got His Title, The Two Chinamen, and The Story of the Princess Nang Kam Ung. Animal tales follow, such as How the Hare Deceived the Tiger and The Story of the Tortoise.

Other tales tell how the world was created, how the king of Pagan caught a thief, and how a sparrow raised a wonderful brood. Griggs opens with a pious woman of Lai Hka who gives rice to priests each morning and joins children washing pagodas at the river. The book preserves Shan story, humour, and belief for readers interested in Burma, folklore, and missionary-era collecting.
32422-three-prize-essays-on-american-sla:
Three Prize Essays on American Slavery, published in Boston in 1857 under the motto The Truth in Love, gathers essays offered for a one-hundred-dollar premium. A benevolent donor, with friends North and South and knowledge of all sections of the nation, feared for national institutions and wanted Christian men harmonised by kind yet faithful truth on slavery. Nearly fifty writers answered the call, and a committee chose the winners.

The volume presents the prize essays as arguments meant to sway Christians across the country in a time of peril. Readers get abolition-era reasoning at its most earnest, with moral, legal, and religious appeals side by side. The book remains a valuable primary source for the slavery debate on the eve of civil war.
3243-glengarry-school-days-a-story-of-ea:
Ralph Connor returns to Glengarry County in this story of early school days. A spelling match opens the book, followed by the deepole, the examination, and the new master. A crisis, one that ruleth well his own house, and Foxy with his partner follow, leading to Hughie's emancipation and a bear hunt.

John Craven's method, a downfall, and rounds of fighting close the schoolroom drama. Connor, who knew Glengarry's Scottish settlers well, writes their children with affection and without sentimentality. Learning, loyalty, and fists decide the schoolhouse world, where the settlement's center was a classroom.
32477-the-future-of-english-poetry:
Edmund Gosse's pamphlet, number twenty-five of the English Association and dated June 1913, asks what English poetry may become. Gosse, speaking to an audience used to speakers of recognised authority, calls his subject chimerical, vague, and founded on conjecture, unlike themes distinct in definition or consecrated by tradition. He opens with a French epigraph from Henri de Régnier on a rose horse opening golden wings toward day and night.

Gosse, a critic and man of letters, weighs new movements, changing taste, and the place of poetry in modern life, without pretending to prophecy. The pamphlet, supplied to full members of the association for a shilling extra, suits readers interested in Edwardian literary debate. It remains a short, thoughtful survey of poetry at a moment when old forms and new voices competed.
32490-hernando-cortez-makers-of-history:
John S. C. Abbott's life of Hernando Cortez, in the Makers of History series and published in New York and London in 1901, tells the conquest of Mexico for young readers. Abbott calls Cortez's career among the wildest and most adventurous in fact or fiction, yet insists its prominent events are well authenticated. A small part of the volume first appeared in Harper's Magazine as an article on the conquest.

Chapters follow the discovery of Mexico, Cortez's early life, the voyage to Mexico, the founding of a colony, the subjugation of the Tlascalans, and the march to Mexico. Later chapters cover the invaded metropolis, the Battle of the Dismal Night, and the besieged capital. Abbott writes vividly, leaving moral inferences, as he puts it, obvious enough to need no pointing out.
32500-discussion-on-american-slavery:
Discussion on American Slavery records a public debate between George Thompson, agent of the British and Foreign Society for the Abolition of Slavery Throughout the World, and the Reverend Robert J. Breckinridge, delegate from the Presbyterian General Assembly to the Congregational Union of England and Wales. The discussion took place in Dr. Wardlaw's Chapel, Glasgow, Scotland, on the evenings of June 13, 14, 15, 16, and 17, 1836, with an appendix.

Originally published in 1836 by Isaac Knapp of Boston, the volume was reprinted in 1969 by Negro Universities Press. It opens with Breckinridge's letter accepting Thompson's challenge, sparked by a passage in Thompson's letter to the London Patriot. Readers get a verbatim-feeling record of abolitionist argument, with American slavery, ministry, and national character at issue. It remains a primary source for transatlantic abolition.
32524-a-fourth-form-friendship-a-school-:
Angela Brazil's A Fourth Form Friendship follows Aldred and Mabel Farrington through a school term shaped by sketches, a model cottage, domestic economy lessons, and theatricals. Out-of-bounds adventures, an awkward predicament, false colours, Chinese lanterns, a frosty January, and a new teacher test their friendship. Visits, alarms, and a river outing carry the girls toward loss and gain.

Illustrated by Frank E. Wiles, the story stays close to classroom routine, dormitory talk, and the small crises of school life. Brazil writes for girls about loyalty, fairness, and growing steadier under pressure, using incident and humor rather than grand adventure to show how a friendship survives misunderstanding and change.
32568-a-frontier-mystery:
Bertram Mitford's Frontier Mystery opens with insults shouted in clear, sonorous Zulu across a river flowing between high, tree-shaded banks. Two parties of about a dozen young men each, lithe and straight, armed with assegais, knobsticks, and small hide shields, trade names such as white dogs, calves, pups, and sweepings. Outwardly they look alike, sprung from the same stock, yet one party lives on the Natal side and the other serves the king across the river.

Come over and fight, the king's warriors challenge, waving shields, while the river laughs and bubbles between them. Mitford, writing from the South African frontier, builds a story of divided kin, chiefly power, and the border itself as a line of danger. The novel offers Victorian adventure fiction rooted in Zulu country, with its language, weapons, and rivalries at the fore.
32644-essays-on-the-materialistic-concep:
Antonio Labriola, professor at the University of Rome, explains historical materialism in two essays, translated by Charles H. Kerr. The first honors the Communist Manifesto, the second sets out the doctrine itself. A preface by Georges Sorel calls the book a landmark beside Marx and Engels.

Labriola argues that history is best read through the growth of material life, work, and institutions, not through abstract ideas alone. He answers critics who tore the doctrine to tatters, and he denies that it offers a neat formula for how much labor is robbed. The book aims to clarify socialist thought for readers new to it.
32703-the-making-of-a-country-parish-a-s:
Harlow S. Mills tells how a scattered Michigan farming district became one larger parish, published by the Missionary Education Movement in 1914. The story centers on Benzonia, with chapels and preaching points at Beulah, Eden, Champion Hill, Platt Lake, and North Crystal, each with its own services, Sunday school, and societies.

Mills shows the minister walking farm lanes, sitting on plow beams, and sharing family meals, so that he meets people as friend rather than stranger. Social gatherings, literary meetings, and wholesome recreation join worship in the plan, answering the isolation of country life and binding separate settlements into a single parish community.
32706-triplanetary:
E. E. Smith, known as Doc Smith, opens the Lensman series with a universe-wide war hidden behind human history. Two ancient powers, the Arisians and the Eddorians, clash across galaxies, and the fall of Atlantis, the fall of Rome, and later wars are moves in their game.

Three books carry the tale: Dawn, The World War, and Triplanetary proper. Readers meet space pirates, a planetoid base, a super-ship, and the strange Nevians. At last one man learns the truth behind the chessboard and must face his part in the final struggle for the universe.
32736-the-bible-story:
This complete set, published by the King-Richardson Company in 1917, gathers six volumes for homes and schools. A guide volume, How to Use the Bible Story, organizes the other five: the Golden Book, Hero Tales, Tales of Old Judea, Life of Jesus, and Songs of the Ages.

Six parts lead the reader on: the child and the Bible, character and living, the land of the Bible, the Bible in literature, the Bible and the teacher, and a pronouncing dictionary. Mothers' questions, art, geography, and review lessons help children meet Bible heroes as friends and learn the stories well.
32742-the-auto-boys-mystery:
James A. Braden sends Phil Way, Billy Worth, Dave MacLester, and Paul Jones camping on Opal Lake, far in the northern woods. An abandoned clubhouse on a nearby point draws their eyes, with smoke, strange sounds, and voices where no one should live.

Paul slips inside and escapes through a cellar window, learning of a satchel of twenty thousand dollars stolen three years before. The Longknives Club's treasurer, a man called Murky, a cheerful stranger named Chip Slider, and unpaid foreman Nels Anderson all circle the prize. The boys must solve the theft before the thieves do.
32782-success-story:
Robert Turner tells the life of Jeff McKinney, in this story illustrated by Kelly Freas. It opens on December 8, 1952, at two-thirty in the morning, with blinding light pressing on tightly squinched eyes and big smooth hands dragging a small struggler toward it.

At three Jeff tips a pot of scalding water onto himself and hovers between life and death for weeks. A wealthy man pays for plastic surgery, yet Jeff keeps a strange hue and a frozen, mask-like smile. At eight he watches his father killed by a speeding truck that takes a taxi door half a block. Poverty, reading, and his mother's promise that good times will come shape a strange boy into his success.
32825-the-goddess-of-atvatabar-being-the:
William R. Bradshaw sends a polar expedition through an Arctic chasm into an interior world, in a New York volume from J. F. Douthitt dated 1892. Fifty-nine chapters carry the explorers from a polar catastrophe to a combined marriage and coronation. They learn Atvatabarese, march in triumph to Kioram, and reach Calnogor, throne of the gods.

At the center stands Lyone, supreme goddess, whose worship, confession, and arrest drive the later chapters. The explorers meet twin-souls, the mystery of Egyplosis, and the temple of Harikar. Their terrorite guns give them an edge over gunpowder batteries, yet one harbor battle pits them against a hundred vessels. In the end Lexington and Lyone are hailed king and queen of Atvatabar.
32867-mopsa-the-fairy:
Jean Ingelow tells of Jack and the fairy Mopsa, published in Boston by Little, Brown and Company in 1919 in an author's edition. The book is dedicated to her little cousin Jane Hollway. Sixteen chapters run from Above the Clouds to Mopsa learning her letters and running away from Old Mother Fate.

Jack, a boy in a buttercup meadow with his nurse and baby sister, climbs into the hollow of an old hawthorn tree. Inside he finds a nest of white wool and moss, larger than a goldfinch's nest three times over, and voices calling his name. His fairy adventures follow: a slave woman bought with a shilling, a queen, and an apple woman. Beyond the mountains lies a land whose people are the gentlest and kindest.
32900-rats-in-the-belfry:
John York Cabot tells of a contractor hired to build a dream castle, in a story from Amazing Stories of January 1943. The narrator, Kermit, sizes up George B. Stoddard at once: baldish, fortiesh, bespectacled, and a combination grouser and eccentric. Stoddard and his wife bring plans they have shaped over years of decision.

The house mixes every architectural nightmare known to man, and Kermit looks at the sheets a little sickly. Stoddard is ready to pay for the extra special work, so Kermit takes the job. Then come the rats, stranger than any ordinary infestation, and a belfry that will not stay built. By the end Kermit is lending a hand at tearing down, while neighbors grow certain that both men are crazy.
32925-the-king-s-assegai-a-matabili-stor:
Bertram Mitford's Matabili story opens with an old Zulu, Untuswa, refusing gold for his broad spear. Even a wagon loaded with shining gold pieces, he tells the white stranger who calls him Nkose, would not coax the assegai from his hands. The stranger, sorry to have made the offer, senses at once that the weapon carries a price longer than money, and the old man's faint, satirical smile says he knows it too.

The spear becomes the key to a tale of kings, warriors, and a kingdom under pressure, told from the frontier where Zulu and Matabili histories meet. Mitford lets the weapon's story unfold through memory and conflict, giving the assegai the weight of a life and a people. It is a period adventure, rich in custom and battle, and the opening refusal still hooks a reader at once.
32955-the-children-of-westminster-abbey-:
Rose G. Kingsley's 1886 book tells English history through the children buried or remembered in Westminster Abbey. Each chapter takes a young life and the age around it. The span runs from the building of the Abbey and the conquest of Wales to Edward the Fifth and his brother, Edward the Sixth, and the Stuart princes. Illustrations from rare old prints give faces to names that might otherwise stay dry in a textbook.

Kingsley wrote for young readers, but she does not soften the hard parts of the story: early deaths, disputed thrones, and wars that cut short promising lives. By tying each child to a place visitors can still walk through, she makes centuries of history feel near and human. It is a gentle, well-planned introduction to England's past, built chapter by chapter around its youngest figures.
32984-an-essay-on-the-trial-by-jury:
Lysander Spooner's Essay on the Trial by Jury, published in Boston and Cleveland in 1852, argues that the common law trial by jury is a people's guard against unjust law. Spooner claims that no legislation in conflict with the common law has validity. He presses that claim so far as to assert his English copyright on common law principles alone, forbidding any reprint without his consent. The volume gives evidence of what the common law jury really is.

The essay's core argument is that jurors may judge law as well as fact, and that a jury drawn from the people stands between the citizen and the state. Spooner's prose is dense and legal, but his position has echoed in later debates about jury nullification and civil liberty. For students of American law and radical thought, the essay remains a sharp, uncompromising statement of a distinctive theory.
33007-edelweiss-a-story:
Berthold Auerbach's Edelweiss opens on a sunny mountain slope where a house stands as a sign of happiness won through long and painful struggle. It was translated by Ellen Frothingham and published by Henry Holt in 1874. Its young housewife, fair of face but white-haired as snow, calls her children in from their noise. An old woman in the garden wipes away tears and a young fellow with a knapsack prepares to set out on a journey.

The story that follows explains how that household passed through the valley of the shadow of death and rose to new life. Auerbach, known for On the Heights and The Villa on the Rhine, writes village life with warmth and moral seriousness, letting work, family, and faith carry the plot. It is a gentle German tale of suffering faced and happiness earned, in a translation that keeps its plain, heartfelt tone.
3310-a-forgotten-empire-vijayanagar-a-co:
Robert Sewell recovers a lost Hindu empire in this contribution to the history of India. Vijayanagar, the city of victory on the Tungabhadra, ruled much of southern India for over two centuries, then fell to ruin. Sewell gathers its chronicles, inscriptions, and travelers' tales into a single narrative, giving a forgotten power back its story.

The book follows kings, temples, and wars, with Portuguese visitors as witnesses to the capital's splendor. Its title states its claim: an empire forgotten by Europe, but central to India's past. Readers interested in Indian history beyond the Mughals will find here a whole world: a Hindu state at its height, told from its own records and from strangers' eyes.
33193-satan-absolved-a-victorian-mystery:
Wilfrid Scawen Blunt's Satan Absolved, a Victorian mystery published in London and New York in 1899 with a frontispiece after George Frederick Watts, opens in the antechamber of Heaven. There, Satan walks alone among angels conversing in groups. Satan, calling himself the heresiarch, waits on the Lord's good pleasure, pacing halls among the orthodox, unfallen sons of God. Satan finds Heaven's sandalwood floors, old-world furniture, incense, and scent of holiness intoxicating, haunting, and hurtful.

Blunt's dramatic poem asks whether Satan would rather be God's liveried servant in Heaven than reign outside it, and the mystery that follows turns on judgment, mercy, and rebellion. Dedicated by permission to Herbert Spencer, the poem blends theology with Victorian doubt. It remains a striking, strange work, part closet drama and part theological argument, for readers interested in how the age reimagined its oldest rebel.
33211-an-artilleryman-s-diary:
Jenkin Lloyd Jones's Artilleryman's Diary, published by the Wisconsin History Commission in February 1914 in twenty-five hundred copies, records a private of the Sixth Wisconsin Battery in the Civil War. Its contents run from first impressions, through up and down the Mississippi and Yazoo and encircling Vicksburg, to the siege of Vicksburg, a well-earned rest, and work again. The commission notes that opinions or errors of fact in its publications were not corrected, and that the author alone is responsible for his statements.

Jones writes as a gunner, not a general, describing river travel, siege work, and camp life in the plain terms of a diary kept close to events. The volume gives readers the Vicksburg campaign from the ranks, with its hardships, humor, and boredom intact. For Civil War historians, it remains a valuable primary source, short, direct, and grounded in a battery's daily round.
33263-the-third-class-at-miss-kaye-s-a-s:
Angela Brazil's school story follows the third class at Miss Kaye's, a girls' school full of lessons, friendships, and scrapes. Brazil, praised for writing schoolgirl tales that other schoolgirls loved to read, sets her story among girls who learn, quarrel, and make up in the familiar rhythms of term time. The book belongs to a series that included The Girls of St. Cyprian's and The Youngest Girl in the Fifth.

The tale's charm lies in its true-to-life school detail: classes, games, and the small dramas of dormitory life. Brazil writes with warmth and humor, catching the voices of girls on the edge of growing up. For readers who enjoy classic school stories, The Third Class at Miss Kaye's offers a lively, kind-hearted term with a class worth knowing.
33270-just-gerry:
Christine Chaundler's school story follows Geraldine, known as Gerry, at Wakehurst Priory, a girls' school full of dormitory life, hockey, and form-room scrapes. Published in London in 1920, the chapters move from cubicle thirteen and an introduction to the school's ways. A caricature and its fallout, a German lesson, and a mouse that causes much stir follow. Gerry makes friends, faces the head girl, and learns the school's unwritten rules.

Chaundler, known for other Fourth Form tales, writes with warmth and humor for young readers. The book's charm lies in its everyday school detail: lessons, matches, breaks in the clouds, and great decisions made by girls on the edge of growing up. It is a lively, kind-hearted school story in the classic English tradition.
33300-mary:
Björnstjerne Björnson's novel Mary, translated from the Norwegian by Mary Morison, appears here as volume thirteen of his novels, edited by Edmund Gosse. The story follows Mary Krog, a young woman whose life and choices form the heart of the tale. Björnson, a leading voice of Norwegian letters, writes with plain force about love, duty, and the bonds of family in a rural world.

The novel's strength lies in its character study, as Mary's hopes meet the limits set by kin, custom, and her own heart. Morison's translation keeps the clear, direct tone of the original. For readers new to Björnson, Mary offers a good entry point: a short, humane story of a woman finding her way in a changing Norway.
33337-astronomical-discovery:
Herbert Hall Turner's Astronomical Discovery, published in London in 1904, traces how the planets and stars yielded their secrets to patient observers. Turner, Savilian Professor of Astronomy at Oxford, opens with Uranus and moves through the great finds of modern astronomy, with plates to guide the eye. The book is inscribed to Edward Emerson Barnard.

Turner's gift is to tell discovery as a human story, full of false starts, keen eyes, and sudden insight. His chapters suit general readers who love the night sky, as well as students of science history. For all who wonder how we learned what we know of the heavens, Astronomical Discovery offers a clear, engaging tour of a great age of stargazing.
33383-penny-nichols-and-the-knob-hill-my:
Joan Clark's Penny Nichols and the Knob Hill Mystery, copyrighted in 1939, opens with a cottage at Knob Hill, a stranger helped, and a queer old man. Its chapters move from inside information and a night visitor to an attic door, Penny's discovery, a toy lantern clue, and a search of the loft, with aid from Michigan friends. Clark writes for young readers who love a fast, girl-centered mystery.

Penny herself, sharp and brave, drives the tale, with clues that reward close attention. The book's pace is brisk, its setting vivid, and its villains suitably sly. For fans of series mysteries, the Knob Hill tale offers a lively, old-fashioned adventure, where a girl detective outwits grown-up crooks and saves the day.
33387-the-fortunes-of-philippa-a-school-:
Angela Brazil's Fortunes of Philippa follows a schoolgirl through a term of ups and downs. It is told in the author's familiar, lively style. Brazil, author of The Luckiest Girl in the School and The Jolliest Term on Record, sets the story among girls who learn, play, and grow together. A frontispiece shows friends rubbing moss from words carved in stone. The tale's heroine, Philippa, faces fortune's turns with pluck.

The book's charm lies in its true school detail and its warm, comic voice, catching the talk and trials of girls together. Its scenes of friendship, rivalry, and fun carry readers through the term. For fans of classic school stories, The Fortunes of Philippa offers a bright, old-fashioned tale of a girl finding her place.
33390-bosom-friends-a-seaside-story:
Angela Brazil's Bosom Friends, a seaside story, follows two girls whose friendship grows by the sea. Its chapters move from fellow travelers and a letter from Mrs. Stewart to a meeting on the sands, the Sea Urchins' Club, a hot friendship, and days on the cliffs. Later scenes bring the Stormy Petrel, cross-purposes, Silversands Tower, and wild maidenhair, all in a coastal setting.

The tale's charm lies in its seaside detail and its warm portrait of a close friendship, tested by misunderstandings and mended by loyalty. Brazil writes with humor and heart for young readers. For fans of school and holiday stories, Bosom Friends offers a sunny, old-fashioned tale of two girls, a shore, and a friendship that lasts.
33393-avery:
Elizabeth Stuart Phelps's Avery, published in 1902 and copyrighted in 1901, first appeared as a serial in Harper's Magazine under the title His Wife. Its first part opens with a mother who cannot lift her child Pink, and a plea to Molly to amuse the baby somehow, a domestic scene that sets the novel's intimate tone. Phelps, a noted American novelist, writes of marriage, motherhood, and duty.

The novel's strength lies in its close, humane portrait of a wife and mother, whose daily trials carry moral weight. Its prose is plain and feeling, suited to readers who love domestic fiction with a serious heart. For fans of Phelps, Avery offers a tender, thoughtful story of a woman's life, told with the author's usual moral clarity.
33439-a-reading-book-in-irish-history:
P. W. Joyce's Reading Book in Irish History gathers the story of Ireland in a form made for school and home reading. Joyce, one of the commissioners for the ancient laws of Ireland, writes with a scholar's care and a teacher's clarity, moving through Ireland's past in short, readable chapters. His book aims to give young readers a true sense of their country's story.

The volume's value lies in its plain, well-ordered narrative, free of jargon yet rich in fact. Its tone is patriotic but fair, suited to classrooms and families alike. For readers who want an introduction to Irish history, Joyce's reading book remains a clear, engaging guide, written by a man who knew the sources well.
33487-barbarossa-an-historical-novel-of-:
Conrad Von Bolanden's Barbarossa, an historical novel of the twelfth century, published in Philadelphia in 1867, tells of the emperor Frederick Barbarossa in a tale of medieval power and faith. Bolanden writes of a world of kings, popes, and knights, where an emperor's will shapes nations and souls. The book was entered for copyright by its publisher, Eugene Cummisky.

The novel's appeal lies in its sweeping, romantic view of the Middle Ages, with battles, courts, and moral trials. Its tone is earnest and Catholic, reflecting its author's faith and age. For readers who enjoy historical romance of the old school, Barbarossa offers a grand, if dated, portrait of a legendary emperor.
33569-kastle-krags-a-story-of-mystery:
Absalom Martin sets a mystery in the slow river country of central Florida. The Ochakee River rises in a nameless lake on the central ridge. It drifts through live oak and cypress forest toward the coast, a landscape of dark water, moss-draped trees, alligators, manatees, and abundant waterfowl. Naturalists from northern universities treasure the region, and its remoteness makes it a fitting place for secrets.

Into that setting Martin brings a story of hidden dealings and danger around a place called Kastle Krags. The novel uses the river's stillness and the forest's close cover to build suspense, as characters move between isolated settlements and wild waterways. It is an early twentieth-century American mystery rooted firmly in Florida geography.
33599-a-rose-of-a-hundred-leaves-a-love-:
Amelia E. Barr tells a love story set in the north of England in this 1891 novel. The narrator retells the oldest and newest story in the world, the story of invincible love, through Aspatria Anneys. Aspatria was born at Seat-Ambar, an old house in Allerdale sheltered by Skiddaw and looking across the Solway toward the Vale of the Deadly Nightshade. There villagers still knew the medical value of belladonna taught by Furness monks.

Seven chapters follow Aspatria through brother Will, her mother's sake, youth, and love's lordship at Sandy-Side, to the rose of a hundred leaves itself. Barr writes with warmth about Cumbrian landscape, family loyalty, and a love that survives hardship. Readers of Victorian regional romance will enjoy its landscape detail and its earnest, old-fashioned feeling.
33635-the-great-discovery:
Norman Maclean writes a wartime meditation on faith, patriotism, and prayer in this 1915 Glasgow volume, opening with a proclamation by King George V on Belgium and France. The narrator, a parish minister, tries to set down while it is fresh an incredible thing that has happened in his parish. People long living on the surface of things have come face to face with life's greatest realities.

Six chapters take up the great discovery itself, the revival of patriotism, the shadow of the cross, the power of prayer, victory, and the cities of the plain. Maclean moves from hillside gardens and town offices to spiritual awakening under the pressure of war. The book suits readers interested in Scottish religious writing and in how the First World War reshaped ordinary congregations.
33658-a-history-of-english-poetry:
Thomas Warton's History of English Poetry gains an unpublished continuation in this scholarly reprint, edited with an introduction by Rodney M. Baine for the Augustan Reprint Society in 1953. The volume prints material that nineteenth-century editions presented misleadingly, as if eight sheets had been prepared from manuscripts left at Warton's death. Baine shows instead that those sheets were certainly printed before Warton died, probably in the early 1780s.

The edition therefore corrects the record of how Warton's pioneering history of English verse was composed and circulated. Notes trace the text's sources, including Joseph Warton's essay on Pope and Milton's poems as edited by Thomas Warton. Literary historians will value the volume for its careful textual detective work and for what it reveals about eighteenth-century scholarship.
33663-the-origin-and-development-of-the-:
Max Planck sketches the origin and development of the quantum theory in his Nobel Prize address, delivered before the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences at Stockholm on June 2, 1920. It was translated by H. T. Clarke and L. Silberstein for Oxford's Clarendon Press in 1922. Planck sets out to outline the history of the theory's origin and to give a brief account of its development and its influence on the physics of the present day.

Looking back twenty years, he recalls when the conception of the physical quantum of action first began to disentangle itself from experimental facts. He also recalls the long, tortuous road that led to its disclosure. Quoting Goethe that man errs so long as he strives, Planck reflects on how striking facts occasionally prove an investigator has moved nearer his goal. The address remains a first-person classic of modern physics.
33695-x-y-z-a-detective-story:
Anna Katharine Green, author of The Leavenworth Case, writes a detective story told by a detective in this 1883 volume. The narrator explains that a detective chasing one crime sometimes stumbles on the clue to another, rarely in a more unexpected manner than here. Washington officials had been baffled by counterfeiters flooding western Massachusetts with spurious Treasury notes, when notice arrived of suspicious letters addressed daily to the simple initials X. Y. Z. at Brandon, Massachusetts.

Sent north to investigate in the middle of June 1881, the detective steps from the cars at Brandon into a pretty village street lined with maples sparkling in noonday sun. From that bright opening, Green builds a mystery of letters, rendezvous, and counterfeit money. The novel shows why Green became a founder of American detective fiction: careful plotting, a professional narrator, and a puzzle that deepens with every clue.
33814-the-mystery-of-evelin-delorme-a-hy:
Albert Bigelow Paine published this tale of hypnotism in Boston in 1894. While writing it, Paine met Dr. Herbert L. Flint, a known hypnotist, and Flint gave him pages from an unpublished memoir that supplied a missing link in the plot.
