The novel builds its mystery around Evelin Delorme and the strange power that seems to govern her.

Paine mixes a first-person account with the doctor's memoir, so the reader hears the case from two sides. Questions of will, trance, and hidden knowledge drive the story forward. The book is a period piece of popular science fiction, curious about a science that then fascinated the public.
33879-the-romance-of-the-canoness-a-life:
Paul Heyse wrote this German novel in 1887, in J. M. Percival's English version. Its German title names a Stiftsdame, a woman who lived in a religious house in common with others yet took no monastic vows. The tale opens in June 1864, when a visitor travels to Brandenburg to stay with a friend from his youth.

The visitor's walk through a small town sets the scene for the life story that follows. Noble families could secure a place in such a house for a daughter, and she lost that place if she married. Through that rule and the quiet town around it, the novel weighs duty, love, and the narrow choices open to a woman of rank.
33990-the-red-cross-girls-with-pershing-:
Margaret Vandercook wrote this girls' war tale, published at Philadelphia in 1919 by the John C. Winston Company. The Red Cross girls serve with the American Army in France, in a bright winter near the middle of November, with frost and light snow in the air. A late recruit, a move toward Germany, and a stay in Luxemburg open the story.

Later chapters follow a journey to Coblenz, New Year's Eve there, a walk along the river bank, Major James Hersey, and a rainbow bridge. Vandercook, author of the Ranch Girls series, writes warmly for girls. The book offers a cheerful tale of service after victory.
34057-when-bear-cat-went-dry:
Charles Neville Buck wrote this mountain novel, published in New York in 1918 by W. J. Watt and Company, with pictures by George W. Gage. Buck, author of The Call of the Cumberlands and The Code of the Mountains, opens with an old mountaineer on a porch. His brogans rest on rattling boards, and his eyes search a wooded mountainside like hawk and ferret.

His loud whoop skitters across a rocky creek bed where Little Slippery feeds Big Slippery ten miles below, and echoes break on the Old Wilderness Ridges as he bellows for Turner. Buck writes of mountain folk in their own speech and humor. The novel offers a Kentucky tale of a town turned dry.
34070-the-american-nations-vol-i-or-outl:
Constantine S. Rafinesque published this first volume on the nations of the Americas at Philadelphia in 1836. The American Nations, or Outlines of a National History, treats ancient and modern nations of North and South America. A prospectus promised the work in twelve numbers, sold quarterly at five dollars in advance for six numbers.

Volume one holds an introduction, a general view, an account of materials, and a treatment of cataclysms. Rafinesque, a bold and wide-ranging naturalist and historian, writes with his own system in view. The book remains a curious early attempt at a full history of the Americas.
34086-the-ifs-of-history:
Joseph Edgar Chamberlin wrote this book of counterfactual history, published at Philadelphia in 1907. Each chapter asks what if a single turn had gone otherwise. What if Themistocles had not beaten Aristides, or the Moors had won at Tours? What if Ethelred had not married the Norman Emma, or Columbus had kept a straight course westward?

Later chapters ask more such questions. What if Elizabeth had left a child, or the Armada had sailed on time? What if Champlain had tarried at Plymouth Bay, or young George Washington had become a British midshipman? Chamberlin writes with wit and learning. The book invites readers to weigh how much hangs on one choice.
3419-rebecca-mary:
Annie Hamilton Donnell writes a gentle story for children about a small girl named Rebecca Mary. The book is built from short episodes with names such as The Dream, The Cookbook Diary, and The Bereavement, each following Rebecca Mary through a day or a small crisis. In one scene she counts her stitches aloud, waiting with grave care for the hundred and first.

The charm lies in the child's point of view. A doll, a cookbook, a lost article, or a family sorrow all matter greatly at her scale, and Donnell treats them with respect rather than mockery. Young readers will recognize the mix of pride, worry, and wonder in growing up, while older readers will enjoy a quiet, old fashioned tale of home life.
34245-the-khedive-s-country:
The Khedive's Country is a book on Egypt and its farming by George Manville Fenn. The text opens without a title page, in mid-argument about the oldest trade of man. The Khedive was the ruler of Egypt, and his country is the subject throughout.

Fenn begins with the tilling of the soil. Man was a gardener first, he says, hunting only while his crops grew. Fighting, wild beasts, and bitter lessons with roots and fungi filled his early days. The love of a garden is inborn in most children still. From that start the book turns to Egypt. Its fields, waters, and crops are the theme. England's own hard season, and the call of new lands overseas, stand in the first pages as the push that sends men's eyes to such a country.
34493-draw-swords-in-the-horse-artillery:
In the Horse Artillery, the boys' tale Draw Swords was written by George Manville Fenn. Forty-three chapters of camp and fight fill the long contents list. A young horse gunner and his chum Wyatt stand at its heart. Early chapters test the boy's pluck and put him through his paces. A black horse called Black Bob and a hot temper stir trouble.

India is the ground of the tale once the troop sails for service. A royal dinner party and first action come in the mid chapters. Sergeant Stubbs, a smell of oil, and a night attack raise the stakes. A jewel theft, a search, and a dismissal darken the plot line. The Wazir works harm in secret till a confession clears the air. Dick sees much, and Wyatt runs a foe through to save a life.
34557-happiness-in-purgatory:
Happiness in Purgatory is a theological essay printed in The Catholic World in April 1897. That journal was a monthly of literature and science. The essay argues that purgatory fits reason and common sense. If it did not exist, it would have to be created, it says. Travellers at a trip's end want rest and clean clothes. Souls, the writer holds, feel the same need. Earth leaves its mud and dust on them.

Gerontius, from Newman's poem, is called as a witness. He cried to his angel to be taken away. Even a blessed soul could not face heaven travel-stained. The heavenly banquet needs a change of garment, the essay urges. Dust, rust, and moth must be wiped away first. The piece defends a doctrine oft attacked in print. It writes for Catholic readers in a calm, reasoned tone.
34615-alaska-the-great-country:
Alaska, the Great Country, by Ella Higginson, was published by Macmillan in 1908. Higginson wrote Mariella of Out-West and When the Birds Go North Again. A photograph of Alexander Baranoff, by Merrill of Sitka, stands in the front. The book was reprinted twice within two years of its first appearance.

Russian America, gold rushes, salmon, and scenery fill such a survey of the territory. Higginson writes for readers who knew Alaska mainly as a far cold purchase. Towns, missions, mines, and native peoples pass in review through her chapters. A woman of the Pacific Northwest speaks for the great country in this account. Booster pride and travel wonder mix in the picture of 1908 Alaska.
34628-i-thou-and-the-other-one-a-love-st:
I, Thou, and the Other One is a love story by Amelia Barr, issued at New York in 1898. Its contents open with a chapter on the Athelings, then introduce Cecil and Edgar. The lord of Exham and the dawn of love follow. A lost ring and a hard question, will she choose evil or good, mark the rising trouble.

A foolish virgin, trouble coming unsummoned, and life going the old, old way fill the middle chapters. The shadow of sorrow stretches out before a chapter called not yet, and one at the worst. The heroine stands as lady of Exham Hall at last, and the tale closes after twenty golden years. Barr was a prolific writer of romances of English and American life, and this is a fair sample of her art.
34664-the-mynns-mystery:
The Mynns' Mystery is a novel by George Manville Fenn, in an edition issued at Montreal and dated 1889. Its first chapter is called A Rough Suitor. It opens in mid scene, with a man gripping a young woman and mocking her struggles. Be quiet, he tells her; what a silly little fluttering dove it is, ruffling its plumes and reddening its face.

He kisses her against her frightened looks, again and again, crying that he loves her and knows she loves him. It is not true, she answers; let me go. She would have screamed the house down, she says, but will not alarm his uncle. Fenn wrote scores of such tales of love, money, and hidden wrong, and this opening plants his knot at once: a forced courtship inside a house of secrets.
34729-how-to-prosper-in-boll-weevil-terr:
How to Prosper in Boll Weevil Territory, by Alford, was issued in Chicago by the farm extension arm of the International Harvester Company. A front quote from Holden, head of that arm, warns that a one-crop system will impoverish any country and its people. A photo shows a good stalk of cotton.

The preface says the book gives facts on farming where the boll weevil has spread, with stress on cotton growing in infested districts. Its author farmed cotton all his life in Mississippi, Louisiana, and Texas, then spent years studying the weevil as a demonstration agent. Varied crops and work spread over the whole year are the core cure urged on southern farmers.
34777-a-lame-dog-s-diary:
Macnaughtan wrote this diary novel, printed by Nelson in 1908. Nelson houses in London, Edinburgh, and New York issued the book. A frontispiece shows a woman ask Hugo why he hid truth. Chapter one opens on keen curiosity and a baffling village mystery.

Friends to tea meet at each house to reach sound conclusions. Callers chat by the narrator sofa in the afternoons for news. Each lady claims she is in the secret but may not speak. The two Miss Traceys plan to build a new house, Fairview. Furniture rode in state on a van for all the village to see.
34805-betty-s-battles-an-everyday-story:
Betty's Battles is a tale for the young by S. L. M., the author of Jabez the Unlucky. It is billed as an everyday story. The book came out from the Salvationist Publishing house in London, with pictures by Gertrude M. Bradley. A note by Florence E. Booth, dated November 1907, stands at the front.

The first chapter is a parting: Good-bye, Grannie. Then comes Home Again, and a third chapter in which the battles begin. Betty's birthday forms the fourth chapter in the list as shown. The front picture shows Betty in tears at the thought of a parting she dreads. The tale is a story of a girl's home life and its small wars, told for young readers of its day.
34920-silver-pitchers-and-independence-a:
Silver Pitchers: and Independence, subtitled A Centennial Love Story, is a book of tales by Louisa Alcott, the author of Little Women. Roberts Brothers of Boston published the collection in 1888, under a copyright of 1876. The title story was written for the American centennial year.

The contents mix story and sketch: Anna's Whim, Transcendental Wild Oats, The Romance of a Summer Day, My Rococo Watch, By the River, Letty's Tramp, and Scarlet Stockings. Silver Pitchers itself opens with three friends by a fire, talking things over. Portia speaks in her most dignified tone about showing displeasure in a proper manner. Pauline would cut the offenders dead for a year, while Priscilla thinks they might make such a thing impossible to repeat. Alcott's lighter fiction shows the same household world as her famous novels.
34931-the-woman-of-mystery:
The Woman of Mystery is a novel by Maurice Leblanc, published in New York by the Macaulay Company in 1916. Leblanc is named on the title page as the author of the Arsène Lupin books. The contents map a tale of crime and war. A murder and a locked room open the plot. A call to arms and a letter from Élisabeth follow. Paul, the hero, sees things at Ornequin that drive the tale on. A diary, a ferryman's house, and a Major Hermann fill the mid chapters.

The scene at the start is the Lorraine frontier, near Corvigny. Paul tells Élisabeth of an event from his childhood that scarred his life. The town stands fifteen miles from the border, in the Liseron valley. War hangs over the love tale from the first pages. The book mixes the detective form with the spy tale of its war years.
34937-tieck-s-essay-on-the-boydell-shaks:
Tiecks Essay on the Boydell Shakspere Gallery is a study by George Henry Danton, out in nineteen twelve. It is the third of a set of tracts on the German tongue and lore. The book is given to the name of a late friend of that school. Tiecks blast at the Boydell set of plates was his first work of print note.

That blast dealt with the great bard and with art, the two loves of his life. A print man had hired the best hands of the day to paint scenes from all the plays. Near one hundred oils were made at a cost past a vast sum, to stand in a hall built for them as a shrine to the bard. War and the mans death in want broke the plan, and the works were sold off.
34947-the-house-of-strange-secrets-a-det:
The House of Strange Secrets, by Eric Bayly, is a detective story printed in New York in 1899. Dutton held the copyright of that year. The contents alone map a thicket of linked mysteries across thirty-five chapters.

A strange affair on a lonely moor opens the tale, then a man disappears. Padded footprints, a haunted barn, and a silent house follow in order. Selene tells her story, and a major trusts a message to an odd delivery. The horrors of Durley Dene and a figure in the moonlight darken the middle. Potter works out a solution, yet a confession still astounds. A man from Dartmoor, a disputed piece of writing, and the fate of an eavesdropper fill the later chapters. The squire's long story, in four parts, unlocks the house at last.
34988-the-professor-s-mystery:
Wells Hastings and Brian Hooker wrote a novel of a school man's dark hint. Hanson Booth drew its plates. The book's rights date to 1911 in this copy. No good comes of half grasps, a front plate's key warns in full. Things Turned Upside Down leads the list of parts with a bang.

The Meadow of Illusion and a night scare fill the front parts. A slight at morn and a sea side pause mark the next steps. A come back to the main theme stands at part six in the list. A ban with costs and a wild road to town build the mid arc. A home brought bind and press talk crowd the late parts. A man hunt makes the teller's own place hot.
35139-manual-for-noncommissioned-officer:
Manual for Noncommissioned Officers and Privates of Cavalry is a War Department handbook issued at Washington in 1917. It was also to be used by mounted engineer companies for cavalry teaching and training. Extra copies sold for fifty cents from the Superintendent of Documents. The order of the Secretary of War, signed by the Acting Chief of Staff, puts the manual forth for the guidance of all concerned.

The first chapter treats military discipline and courtesy. Its sections cover the oath of enlistment, obedience, loyalty, discipline, and saluting. The oath printed in the book binds the soldier to bear true faith to the United States and to obey the President and his officers. The manual set the daily standard for horse soldiers entering the Great War.
35276-canterbury:
Canon Danks described and Haslehurst pictured this portrait of Canterbury for Blackie in London and Glasgow. A frontispiece shows the Canterbury weavers, and the list of plates reads like a walk. Nicholas at Harbledown, Canterbury from the Stour and the Greyfriars' House come early in the views.

Mercery Lane, the cathedral from Christ Church Gate and Fordwich follow in the list. Martin's church, Westgate and the gateway of Augustine's Abbey fill out the set. Danks says his text is neither a guidebook nor a history, though it may serve as enough of both, and calls the book a keepsake of famous scenes.
35277-the-childerbridge-mystery:
Guy Boothby wrote a mystery tale set round a place called Childerbridge. The book came out in London in 1902. Boothby wrote Doctor Nikola and A Millionaire's Love Story. Its first man, William Standerton, bears the look of success. Bold eyes, a square chin, and a high brow mark him at first sight.

Standerton is the son of a hard-worked country doctor. Fate set him to leave his home ground for a wider field. Wealth and will lift him, but a dark case waits ahead. The Childerbridge riddle pulls him in from that bright start. Crime tale fans get Boothby's smooth, swift pace. Each part ends with a fresh hook.
35287-awd-isaac-the-steeple-chase-and-ot:
John Castillo wrote Awd Isaac, The Steeple Chase, and Other Poems, with a Glossary of the Yorkshire Dialect, issued at Whitby in 1843 by Horne and Richardson. Dialect is kept as printed throughout. An index to the poems sits at the back. A front note disowns two stock kinds of preface.

Castillo says he offers nothing new in matter or in tongue. He also scorns the plea that friends forced a shy author to print. Most pieces were writ years past at wide gaps, he says. The lead poem gives the book its name, Awd Isaac. Verse in Yorkshire speech, with a word list to aid plain readers, fills the volume. Local life, sport, and humor in dialect are its charm.
35337-miss-theodora-a-west-end-story:
Miss Theodora, a West End story by Helen Leah Reed, was published in Boston in 1898. Chapter heads and a front plate come from drawings by Florence Pearl England, the heads after photographs. The tale opens with Boston seen two ways: the tourist's narrow streets and graveyards, and the Back Bay dweller's pride in new avenues.

Reed says neither view knows the real Boston, the old West End, with its tree-lined streets sloping from Beacon Hill toward the river. She bids the reader pause on Mount Vernon Street at dusk and note the Gothic arch of trees over old brick houses. Halfway down a quiet street stands the house of Miss Theodora, whose true name, a famed jurist's, she will not tell.
35358-a-song-of-a-single-note-a-love-sto:
Amelia Barr wrote A Song of a Single Note, a love story printed in New York in 1902. Barr had written The Bow of Orange Ribbon and The Maid of Maiden Lane. She gives the novel to her friend Doctor Stephen Decatur Harrison, an American who loves his country right or wrong and always believes she is right. Contents open with Red or Blue Ribbons, then The Fair and the Brave. Life in the captive city follows.

The title song has the fourth chapter, then love's sweet dream and an intercepted message. The price of Harry's life, the help of Jacob Cohen, and the turn of the tide fill the middle. Maria goes to London, the question of marriage is faced, and love and victory close the tale. A prologue in verse weaves love and glory, homely toil and martial show.
35389-why-marry:
Jesse Lynch Williams wrote a comedy in three acts, first out in book form in 1914 and staged in New York in 1917. The scene is a weekend at a country house, from Saturday noon to Sunday night. Jean has been raised to wed and do naught else, while Helen wants to wed no one at all.

Ernest, a man of science, holds no faith in wedlock or in divorce, yet makes a great find in the course of the play. A judge uncle reads the young with care, and a churchman cousin holds hard against divorce. Talk, wit, and clash of views on love drive the house party tale.
35394-the-bridling-of-pegasus-prose-pape:
Alfred Austin bridles verse in The Bridling of Pegasus, prose papers on poetry. Austin was poet laureate. Macmillan first published the book in 1910; this copy is a 1967 reprint. A note gives the title's root: when Bellerophon, mounted on Pegasus, set forth to kill the Chimera, Minerva gave him a golden bridle. With it he could curb and guide his winged steed. Hence the name.

A letter to Sir Alfred Lyall opens the volume. Even in the most accredited organs of opinion, Austin charges, the rules of literary criticism are often ignored in the notice of some work in the very same number. The result can only be to create confusion in the public mind. In this volume, he pledges, no such clash will be found. The papers were written across the last thirty years. His canon: no verse which is unmusical or obscure can be regarded as poetry.
35504-miss-maitland-private-secretary:
Miss Maitland, Private Secretary is a mystery novel by Geraldine Bonner. Appleton of New York and London issued the book in nineteen nineteen. Keller drew the pictures, from moonlit Suzanne to the night pike ride. The tale first ran in part in Curtis papers in eighteen eighteen and nineteen.

Chapters mix Miss Maitland letters with Molly story told in turn. A cigar band clue, robbery in high places, and detectives enter early. A man who would not tell and signed Clansmen letters deepen the case. Suzanne finds a friend, and cards go on the table near the end. Night on the Cresson Pike brings the counter plot to its crisis.
35516-the-man-without-a-memory:
The Man Without a Memory, by Arthur Marchmont, was published in 1919. Ward and Lock issued it in London, Melbourne, and Toronto. Marchmont's earlier adventure novels fill a front list. Thirty chapters make the book. Chapter one is called How I Lost My Memory. The narrator and Dick Gunter fly a fighting machine over the German lines. Two enemy machines come out to drive them off. The pair feign fear, then swing round and fire. One foe falls nose first, and the second soon follows. A third machine, unseen in the excitement, swoops from the clouds.

Later heads promise spies, a bread riot, and a poison charge. Rosa and Nessa share the love interest. Berlin names fill the list: Baron von Gratzen, Von Erstein, and the Tiergarten. A hue and cry and a hairsbreadth escape lead to the end.
35538-the-squatter-and-the-don-a-novel-d:
C Loyal published a novel at San Francisco in 1885 describing contemporary occurrences in California. Chapter one has Squatter Darrell reviewing the past. The Don's view of the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo follows. Pre empting under the law and efforts to right the wrong come next. The Don in his broad acres anchors the middle.

A dog named Milord becomes an important factor, the contents joke. The journey runs from Alameda to San Diego. C Loyal was the pen name of María Amparo Ruiz de Burton. Her novel attacks the land laws that stripped Californio rancheros. It is among the first Mexican American novels in English.
35583-two-years-among-the-savages-of-new:
Two Years Among the Savages of New Guinea is a travel account by W D Pitcairn. Ward and Downey published it in London in 1891, with a map of the author's route. Pitcairn was a fellow of the Royal Geographical Society. He dedicates the book to Oscar Soelberg, his companion in New Guinea. His preface, dated from the Vicarage at Eccles in June 1890, answers a literary friend.

The friend called New Guinea thrashed out and overdone, without having been there. Pitcairn answers that the writers, not the country, are thrashed out. An introduction treats North Queensland first. Cooktown, the Palmer goldfield, and the tin fields appear there. The New Guinea chapters sail in the schooner Spitfire. They pass the wreck of the Papua and ride out a dead calm. Government policy, the death of Sir Peter Scratchley, and the discovery of gold follow. Native customs fill a long chapter.
35692-the-history-of-company-a-second-il:
The History of Company A, Second Illinois Cavalry is a Civil War unit history by Samuel Fletcher, a member of the company, written with Fletcher. The authors dedicate it to the memory of the men who fought in Company A. A portrait of Major John Hotaling fronts the book. The first chapter treats the causes of the war, naming slavery as the national issue, and the conditions just before the outbreak.

The second chapter covers organization and departure. It prints a flag presentation and speeches. The company was mustered at Camp Butler and served at Fort Massac, Cairo, and Bird's Point. Later chapters follow the embarkation from Paducah and the capture of Fort Henry. The reconnaissance and investment of Fort Donelson come next, with the gunboat attack, the sortie, and the surrender by Buckner that made Grant's name.
35833-the-black-star-a-detective-story:
The Black Star, by Johnston McCulley, is a detective novel of a master crook. Chelsea House issued it at New York in 1921 with a Wittmack frontispiece. Roger Verbeck wakes at midnight as sleet and snow lash the city outside. Chapter one, an aided escape, sets the Black Star gang in motion first.

Thirty six chapters chase the gang through pits, nets, and charity balls in turn. Muggs, the small sidekick, guards, acts, and takes tricks through the tale. Identical orders, a voice on the wire, and a bank job fill the middle. Police tips, launches, and custody scenes keep the pace at full run. How it ended promises the unmasking readers of McCulley expected.
35863-the-pocahontas-john-smith-story:
Pocahontas Wight Edmunds retells a famed rescue in The Pocahontas John Smith Story, printed at Richmond, Virginia, with copyright in 1956. James Bailey edits the book for the Dietz Press. The catalog year of 1918 is wrong; the title pages give 1956.

Edmunds opens by saying Smith was well worth rescue, for the sake of the land if not her own. Yet he was no model lad, she adds. She tells of his school at Louth and his youth in the lush fields of Lincolnshire. His father George Smith, a tenant farmer, died young and left good beds and pewter. His widow wed again too fast to suit her son.
35966-loveliness-a-story:
Loveliness is a story by Elizabeth Stuart Phelps. It came out in 1899, with pictures by Sarah S Stilwell. A line from Browning stands at the front as a blessing.

The tale opens on Loveliness at rest on a soft cushion. The cushion is worked with cherry coloured puppies on pearl satin. A maid moves through the early scenes of the house. Love for a small, gentle creature sits at the heart of the book. The tone is tender, and the story asks how kindness to beasts shapes the folk who show it. Sarah S Stilwell's plates show the pet at home and at rest.
35974-corianton-a-nephite-story:
Corianton is a Nephite tale by Roberts, first out in parts in eighteen eighty nine. It ran in the Contributor sheet to a warm crowd in that year. This book form bears a right claim of nineteen two from Roberts. Calls to other work kept him from more tale craft in that line. A stage form by Bean made the tale name known more wide in late years.

Dawn sun gilds the towers of Zarahemla as the tale first part opens. Seven horse men ride worn from a night trek by hill Manti foot. Two ride front, two rear, and three ride flank to flank mid way. The mid man is bound, his horse held by hide straps at each side. Bold calm scorn marks that bound man past his dull guards.
36015-little-miss-peggy-only-a-nursery-s:
Mrs Molesworth's Little Miss Peggy, only a nursery story, was published in London in 1887 by Macmillan, with pictures by Walter Crane. She gives the book to the memory of a dear young friend who suggested its name. The frontispiece shows a lady asking two little girls what is the matter.

The chapters keep to a nursery's round: a breakfast party, the white spot on the hill, and the children at the back. The little red shoes get a chapter, and the shoes-lady returns near the end. The pictures fill in the household: Peggy settled on the hearth-rug with the baby on her lap, a baby drumming with a spoon, and a rolling umbrella loose on the pavement.
36135-the-spawn-of-ixion-or-the-biter-bi:
A verse allegory printed at the Forge of Vulcan in 1846. Its subject is Ixion, the mythic ingrate of Greek story. The poem retells his crimes in rough couplets. Ixion murdered his wife's aged father, casting him into burning fire. Every circle shunned the outcast for that deed. Jupiter in pity raised him to heaven anyway.

At the gods' own tables the guest repaid kindness with lust. He tried to steal Juno's heart and Jupiter's bed. A cloud shaped like Juno received him instead. From that union the monstrous Centaur sprang. Jupiter hurled Ixion down to an eternal wheel in hell. His vile offspring, the poem warns, stays behind among men. The title calls that offspring the biter bit.
3635-mother-a-story:
Kathleen Norris writes a novel about family life centered on a schoolteacher named Margaret. The book opens at the end of a school week. Little girls downstairs in the playroom plan holidays over cold lunches, while Margaret looks out at gray rain and feels sick of it all. She has spent her days among small girls who sulk, cry over lost lunch baskets, and catch colds with no handkerchiefs.

Norris follows Margaret from the schoolroom into home life, where mothers, daughters, and daily work shape the story. The novel praises the patience and love that hold a family together through small trials. Readers who enjoy early twentieth century domestic fiction will find a gentle, warm tale of a woman learning what motherhood means.
36354-problems-in-greek-history:
Problems in Greek History is a set of essays by Mahaffy of Dublin. Mahaffy was fellow and tutor of Trinity College, Dublin, in his day. Macmillan of London and New York brought the book out in 1892. He had writ Prolegomena to Ancient History and Social Life in Greece. The first chapter treats our earlier historians of Greece as its theme.

Definite and indefinite problems open the argument of that first essay. Examples from theology, metaphysics, and literature set up the case made. Greek history holds special claims above Rome and the Jews, he argues. Greek influences in our religion add weight to those claims, he holds. Materials for the study grow year by year in his account here. Universal histories, Gillies, and the French Revolution's effect get weighed. Mitford wrote a Tory history of Greece and stirred his foes.
3659-the-rosary:
Florence Barclay writes a romance centered on a rosary and the people it passes among. The chapters open with the entrance of a duchess, introduce the Honourable Jane, and follow a surprise packet, Jane's volunteering, confidences, and the lifting of a veil. Garth finds his rosary, then added pearls, then a cross, while a house party, a doctor's prescription, and a revelation move the plot.

Barclay, famous for sentimental romance, writes about love, faith, and sacrifice in an English country house world. The rosary beads become a symbol of prayer and of a promise kept. The novel suits readers who enjoy early twentieth century romance with a religious thread and a tender, old fashioned heroine.
36685-national-rhymes-of-the-nursery:
National Rhymes of the Nursery gathers the old songs of the English nursery, with an introduction by George Saintsbury and drawings by Gordon Browne. The London firm of Wells, Gardner, Darton and Co issued it from Paternoster Buildings. Ride a cock horse fronts the book as its emblem.

Saintsbury opens with Peacock's novel Melincourt, where the great folk of nursery tale hang in one grand picture: Margery Daw, Jack and Jill, Jack Horner with his pie. He notes that since the Brothers Grimm made folklore a study, nursery songs draw grave scholars as well as children. The rhymes that follow are the stock of the English home, kept in print for a new set of readers.
36773-oxford-lectures-on-poetry:
Oxford Lectures on Poetry is a book of talks on the art of verse. Bradley wrote the talks. He once held the chair of verse at Oxford. He was a fellow of a great hall of that school. The first print came in the spring of nineteen hundred and nine.

The book is sworn to the Oxford friends of the hand. Those friends span forty years of his life. A quote stands past the sworn leaf. It tells of friends who shake hands past a vast gulf. A note says the new print is the same in its bones. A few points of fine sense are made more clear. The keen words of the hand's own kin helped that work. The talks hold the ripe thought of a life spent on verse.
36776-inventions-in-the-century:
William H Doolittle surveys Inventions in the Century, a volume of the Nineteenth Century Series edited by Justin McCarthy, from the Linscott Publishing Company in 1903. Doolittle was an expert and patent solicitor, once an examiner in the Patent Office and assistant commissioner of patents at Washington. The first chapter draws his line: inventions are useful contrivances of man, discoveries new things found in nature.

Galileo's telescope and Newton's gravitation open the account, and the Egyptian crooked stick stands as precursor of the modern plough. A second chapter turns to agriculture and its implements. Patent law gets its due as invention's great spur.
37182-colorado-the-bright-romance-of-ame:
Colorado: The Bright Romance of American History, printed at Denver in 1911, is Grable's popular history of the state, with paintings by Allen True. The book is dedicated to the pioneers of Colorado. Its preface takes Emerson's thought that all true history is biography. Men, the author holds, are the very pages of history.

Chapters run from Coronado and the old Spanish country through Pike, Major Long and the lost period of the trappers. Kit Carson and Fremont stride through the middle. Gold brings its lustre, and men of vision close the tale. Illustrations show Estes Park, a Zuni village and the clean-up of a placer claim, all in a warm, heroic tone.
37211-castles-and-chateaux-of-old-tourai:
Castles and Chateaux of Old Touraine and the Loire Country is a travel book by Francis Miltoun. L C Page and Company published it in Boston in 1906. Blanche McManus painted the illustrations on the spot. The publisher's list prices the square octavo at $3.00, profusely illustrated. A peasant girl of Touraine fronts the volume.

Miltoun's introduction, headed By Way of Introduction, disowns the conventional tour. The book grew from leisurely wanderings along the Loire and its tributaries. The conventional round had already been done, Baedeker in hand. Angers and Nantes had been tasted on earlier journeys. Note-books and the artist's portfolio overflowed before this trip began. More note-books, crayons, and sketch-books followed Mark Twain's advice. The Renaissance chateaux of the Loire, Miltoun says, appeal to strangers beyond any similar buildings anywhere. His pages wander among them at walking pace.
37224-popular-books-on-natural-science-f:
Popular Books on Natural Science is a household science book by Bernstein. Schmidt of New York published it; the copyright dates to 1869. Its title promises practical use in every home, for readers of all classes. The contents list its range on the title page. The weight of the earth, velocity, and nutrition stand there. Light and distance, astronomy, and meteorology follow.

The food proper for man closes the announced list. A Latin motto from Cicero heads the treatise. It praises man's drive to seek and investigate truth. A transcriber's note flags an error in one calculation, left as printed. That note concerns the speed of electricity through a wire circuit. The book belongs to a wave of cheap science for the common reader. Bernstein wrote for households, not for specialists.
37288-virginia-architecture-in-the-seven:
Virginia Architecture in the Seventeenth Century is a short study of old homes. Henry Forman, an architect and scholar, wrote and drew it. It came out in Williamsburg in 1957 for a big feast year. The year marked three and a half centuries since Jamestown was founded.

Forman had lived on the road to Jamestown and had kin there. His kin lines ran back to the first folk on the James River. He starts with the wood homes of the folk found on the land. Those homes were frail and are lost, he tells the reader. The book then turns to the homes the new folk built in brick and wood. Drawings and shots by his own hand show the work throughout.
37510-by-trench-and-trail-in-song-and-st:
Angus Mackay, who wrote as Oscar Dhu, gathered his songs and tales in By Trench and Trail in Song and Story, issued in 1918. Mackay had written of a Canadian outlaw and of the first settlers, and his songs were sung by camp fires from British Columbia to Maine. Some, he says, were fired at the foe in France like shot.

The front note tells how fans wrote from all over the land to beg extra copies of songs long out of print. So he put the most asked for verse in one book, with art. War songs, trail songs, and tales of the north woods fill the pages. The tone is rough, fond, and proud of the men who marched and worked the wilds.
37681-the-teaching-of-geometry:
The Teaching of Geometry, by David Eugene Smith, was copyrighted in 1911 and published by Ginn in Boston, New York, Chicago, and London. Twenty-one chapters run from questions now at issue and why geometry is studied, through a history of geometry and its teaching, to Euclid and efforts at improving Euclid. Later chapters treat the textbook, the conduct of a class, axioms, definitions, and how to attack the exercises.

Book-by-book chapters then lead through the leading propositions of Euclid's first eight books. Chapter one opens with a caution: it is commonly said that the new century is an age of unusual advance in the school. Smith doubts the future historian will agree, or rank the leaders of his generation as high as those gone by. Smith wrote as the dean of American mathematics teachers, reform-minded but wary of fashion.
37803-rocky-mountain-boys-or-camping-in-:
Rocky Mountain Boys, or Camping in the Big Game Country, is a boys' adventure by St George Rathborne. Donohue published it at Chicago. The contents run from comrades of the trail through a first taste of venison to hunting the bighorn. A wakeful night, out for a grizzly, and the terror of the Rockies fill the later chapters.

Tom and Felix, the heroes, tramp toward a dugout camp in the foothills, guided by a chart from old Sol Ten Eyck. Felix hopes to sight it within half an hour, for his pack is getting heavy. Besides modern repeating rifles, the lads carry ditty bags, hunting knives, and snowshoes strapped to their packs. They mean to stay in the foothills a long while, ready for deep snow. This one mixes wolf packs, honey thieves, and big game into a winter in the mountains.
3784-the-sheridan-road-mystery:
Paul and Mabel Thorne set this Chicago mystery on a still October night. Policeman Murphy, on his two o'clock round, finds Sheridan Road deserted save for a belated taxi's red tail light. A shot soon draws Detective Sergeant Morgan into a case that runs through an apartment across the hall, a cable from London, a stolen suitcase, and a last letter. The contents list promises a trail that grows clearer, then darker, with a kidnapping and a closed country house.

Morgan and his men pick over peculiar facts in the Atwood apartment while Mr Marsh's part in the affair shifts under their eyes. The Thornes keep the plot moving at a brisk clip, with a night call and a fallen pine among the later turns. Readers who like fair play detective tales will find a tidy puzzle with Chicago streets as its stage.
37893-oxford-and-her-colleges-a-view-fro:
Goldwin Smith wrote Oxford and Her Colleges, a short history seen from the Radcliffe Library. Macmillan issued the book in New York and London in eighteen hundred ninety five. Photos of the old town and its halls fill the pages. Smith wrote the sketch with American guests in mind, he says.

Mount to the Radcliffe roof for the book’s first wide view. Spires and gardens spread below in fair summer light, he hopes. The Isis and the Cherwell bound the low gravel spit of town. Boat races stir the one stream, while lilies crowd the other. Smith once dug the school’s own archives for a royal review. New lives of the school and its halls fed his work since. Reform had joined Oxford back to the whole land, he holds. American eyes might now turn there as to German schools of fame.
37926-as-gold-in-the-furnace-a-college-s:
As Gold in the Furnace, a college story, by the Reverend John E Copus, was printed by Benziger Brothers in New York, Cincinnati, and Chicago in 1910. The book is a sequel to Shadows Lifted. Copus had written Harry Russell and Tom Losely, Boy, each at eighty five cents.

A plate line says it was hard, a sore trial, to give up his dream of years. Chapters open with Roy surprises his friends, the motive, and the conditions. Roy and Garrett follow. The text has the hero tell his friends once for all that he cannot go in for baseball next spring. He cannot even play the few games still left this fall. A dream of sport thus meets a hard call of conscience at a Catholic college. School tale fans get faith tested like gold in a furnace.
37997-the-american-reformed-cattle-docto:
G H Dadd wrote a guide that lets each farmer serve as his own cattle doctor. Phillips, Sampson, and Company issued the book at Boston in 1851. Dadd was a veterinary practitioner and wrote on the horse as well. A West Highland ox fronts the illustrated work.

Dadd holds that cures must aid nature, not crush it with knife and poison. Parts treat feeding, barns, milking, breeding, and cheese and butter making. More parts cover the gut, lungs, blood, and a long list of cattle ills. Locked jaw and lung fever get full care in a book built for farm shelves.
38062-in-mr-knox-s-country:
In Mister Knox's Country is a book of Irish sketches by Somerville and Martin Ross. Longmans, Green published it in London and New York in 1915. The authors also wrote Some Experiences of an Irish Resident Magistrate. Eight illustrations by Somerville accompany the tales. The contents list eleven pieces in all. The Aussolas Martin Cat opens the volume. The Finger of Mrs Knox and The Friend of Her Youth follow.

Other pieces treat a pony, a major, and a country doctor. The Bosom of the McRorys and The Shooting of Shinroe close the list. The first sketch opens with a fourteen mile drive. Flurry Knox and the narrator ride to a tryst together. The frontispiece warns of hounds pointing toward a cliff. Readers get hunting, neighbours, and horse country comedy in Ireland. The Knox circle anchors the tales throughout.
38093-the-christian-religion-an-enquiry:
The Christian Religion, An Enquiry, is a freethought tract by R G Ingersoll, the famed American orator against orthodox faith. The opening attacks how England teaches the poor, granting them new schooling but clogging it with old error, it argues. Fallen nations are said to show that mass ignorance is a fatal flaw. Ingersoll writes as counsel for reason in a public trial of belief.

The enquiry presses Christian claims against evidence, history, and morals in Ingersoll's courtroom manner. Its distress, he says, is that teachers counsel for the poor a creed their own culture has outgrown. Readers get a short, sharp sample of the lectures that packed halls across America in his lifetime.
38141-john-dewey-s-logical-theory:
John Dewey's Logical Theory is a thesis by Delton Thomas Howard. The work stands as number eleven in the Cornell Studies in Philosophy. Howard gave it to Cornell's graduate school for his doctor's degree. Longmans, Green printed the book in New York in the year 1919. Nine chapters trace Dewey's thought from first stands to later growth.

Two essays in Mind from 1886 hold Dewey's earliest standpoint, Howard notes. Those pieces tie to the Psychology Dewey put out that same year. Chapters move through moral theory, functional mind study, and evolution's role. The Studies in Logical Theory get a chapter, then a fighting period. Later developments and Howard's own conclusions close the survey of the man. He calls the mind-first standpoint bold for its day and hour. British empiricism stood or fell by that same standpoint, he adds.
38169-the-heath-hover-mystery:
Bertram Mitford wrote this mystery of Heath Hover and its haunted house. Ward, Lock printed the edition dated 1911 with Drestier plates. Chapter one, The Door in the Corner, opens at midnight stroke. John Mervyn sits in his accustomed armchair and looks about.

Dark red paper and low black beams gloom the medium room. A bright fire fails to dispel a sense of shadowy evil. No one had lived in the house for years, even rent free. Winter wind moans and rafters crack in the midnight solitude there. He sat in full knowledge that the house stood empty for years past alone.
38301-illustrated-catalogue-of-cotton-ma:
An illustrated catalogue of cotton machinery was issued in nineteen hundred and nine by the Howard and Bullough American Machine Company. The firm's plant stood at Pawtucket, Rhode Island, with offices in Boston and Atlanta. C E Riley served as treasurer.

The catalogue covers opening, picking, carding, drawing, roving, and spinning machines. Twisting, winding, warping, and slashing gear follow. Ring spinning frames get a long section, with tables of lengths and output. Gearing diagrams, twist tables, and yarn numbering tables aid mill men. Floor spaces and speeds are given for each machine. The makers say users asked them to gather facts once spread across circulars.
38373-liberty-in-the-nineteenth-century:
Frederic May Holland wrote Liberty in the Nineteenth Century, issued in eighteen ninety nine. Chapter one treats Napoleon and his work. France had been freed by the Revolution from many ghosts of kingly, feudal, and priestly privileges, Holland opens. But she was still the prey of the most deadly of vampires, military glory, he says. The followers of this fatal guide found a ruler after their own hearts in Napoleon, he adds.

In eighteen oh four the conqueror became Emperor, Holland notes. Thus was established an enlightened despotism, as some metaphysicians suppose the best government, he says with irony. The autocrat gave political equality such authority that it has continued supreme in France, he grants. Her sons are still equals before the law and owners of the land they till, he adds. Later chapters trace liberty in England, America, and Europe. History readers get a liberal survey of a century.
38486-rule-of-the-monk-or-rome-in-the-ni:
Rule of the Monk, or Rome in the Nineteenth Century, is a novel by Giuseppe Garibaldi. This English version dates to 1870. An introduction speaks first, though Garibaldi gave none. Caesar wrote no preface to his Commentaries, the editor notes. Garibaldi likewise let his tale speak for itself. The translators warn that his vivid native style loses much in English. The manuscript was in the general's own hand. He wrote it as a solace in heavy hours at Varignano.

There the King of Italy held him prisoner, the editor charges. That king owed the gift of the Two Sicilies to Garibaldi's sword. Verse at the front answers that stone walls do not make a prison. The novel turns a soldier's captivity into a story against monkish rule in Rome.
38577-the-blue-lights-a-detective-story:
The Blue Lights is a detective story by Arnold Fredericks, printed at New York. Grosset and Dunlap issued it, with copyright in 1915 held by Watt and Company. Will Grefe drew the illustrations. Fredericks also wrote The Ivory Snuff Box. A front note gives the hook: a hasty look at a sailing list shows a woman that Richard is not on board.

The tale opens as a mud-spattered touring car plows north from Washington. A stout, keen-eyed man named Hodgman springs out at a gateway and asks for Richard Duvall. His business is most important, he says, and he means to persuade Duvall to go with him. Grace Duvall approaches the house in a blue linen dress as the car arrives.
38679-miranda-of-the-balcony-a-story:
Miranda of the Balcony, by Mason, was published in 1899. Macmillan issued the story in New York and London. Twenty four chapters carry long, playful titles. A short-sighted taxidermist from Tangier opens the tale. His discovery upon Rosevear sets the plot moving. Charnock, the hero, is presented as a spectator. A woman's face in a mirror troubles chapter three. Charnock and Miranda meet in the fourth chapter. They improve their acquaintance in a balcony in the fifth. The mystery of the Tarifa's cargo is explained midway. A blind man makes use of a dark night. Major Wilbraham tells how he won his majority.

Charnock wanders in Morocco near the end. A walnut-wood door and a tombstone turn late chapters. A mist in the Channel ends the book as it began.
38681-practical-basketry:
Practical Basketry is a craft guide by Anna Gill, a school teacher. The author taught a class for frail children in Philadelphia schools. Her own drawings show the work of the hands in the book. The book bears a rights line of the year nineteen sixteen.

First parts list tools and stuff, then teach the base weaves step by step. Mats, rims, and small baskets form the first set of class models. Baskets with split bases form the next set in the course of work. Reed, rush, and willow pass through plain rules a child can hold. The guide served class rooms that trained hand skill with eye skill.
38703-the-black-moth-a-romance-of-the-xv:
Georgette Heyer wrote this romance of the eighteenth century, her first novel in shape and manner. A prologue opens on Hugh Tracy Clare Belmanoir, Duke of Andover, at his writing desk. He sits clad in black and silver, with raven hair unpowdered and diamonds on his fingers and in his cravat.

No rouge touches his face, and a patch sits beneath his right eye by design. His narrow, heavy-lidded eyes are green under slanting black brows. Twenty-nine chapters and an epilogue follow this striking figure into a world of duels, disguise and love in Georgian dress.
38874-browning-and-his-century:
Helen Archibald Clarke wrote on Browning and the age that made him. Her book came out in New York in 1912. She wrote Browning's Italy and Browning's England in past works. A plate shows the bard at twenty-three in London of 1835. She gave the book to the Boston Browning Society in full.

That gift marks the bard's birth feast: 1812 to 1912 in round years. The fight of mind and soul leads her list of parts. The age's end and hopes of peace fill the next long span. State drifts of the age take their due in the list as well. Verse and its age are weighed as one life in her scheme. Bard fans get a rich guide.
38907-transcendentalism-in-new-england-a:
Transcendentalism in New England, a history by Octavius Brooks Frothingham, appeared in 1876. Putnam published it at New York in that centennial year. Beginnings in Germany opens the contents at page one of the work. A second chapter treats Kant, Jacobi, and Fichte in the German line.

Theology and literature, with Schleiermacher, Goethe, and Richter, fill the third chapter. France follows, with Cousin, Constant, and Jouffroy in the fourth head of the list. England comes next through Coleridge, Carlyle, and Wordsworth in the survey. Transcendentalism in New England itself forms the sixth chapter of the history. Practical tendencies of the movement close the plan of the book. Emerson and Parker get their movement history from a friendly hand here.
38973-lace-its-origin-and-history:
Samuel L Goldenberg wrote on the origin and history of lace for trade readers. Brentano's issued the book in New York, with rights from 1904. A plate shows Barbara Uttmann, dated 1561, near the front. Goldenberg calls his work a nosegay of culled flowers, after Montaigne.

His aim is a practical guide for men whose tie to lace is trade, he writes. Five centuries of comedy and tragedy cling to the craft all the same. Chalets, convents, and weary fingers fill the human side of the tale. Lace sellers gain a handy survey of their goods' long, storied past.
39028-servian-popular-poetry:
John Bowring translated Servian Popular Poetry, printed for the author in London and sold by Baldwin, Cradock, and Joy in eighteen twenty seven. The original title is in Serbian letters. Bowring dedicated the book to Dr Stephen Vuk Karadžić in verse. My friend, it is thou who hast ushered these gems into day, the dedication sings. It is my pride and privilege now to honour thy toils, it says.

We knew that the sun light shone fair on thy Servia, Bowring writes. We knew it was a clime of mountains and streams, where the air was fragrant, he says. But we knew not the spirit sublime of music, pathos, and song that dwelt there, he admits. It had dwelt in the Morava long, he adds. Poetry readers get the first English window on Serbian folk song.
39408-the-grateful-dead-the-history-of-a:
The Grateful Dead: The History of a Folk Story is a work of folklore study by Gordon Hall Gerould of Princeton. It was published for the Folk-Lore Society in London in 1908, as the sixtieth of its publications. The introduction sets out the riddle of the field. Why do the same tales turn up in land after land? Theories are plenty, Gerould says. What the field needs is close study of single themes. Collectors have now gathered treasures enough for such work.

The theme here is the grateful dead man. A traveller pays the debts of a corpse so it may be buried. The dead man's ghost or a stranger then repays the kindness. Gerould sorts the tales by their joins with other themes. A full bibliography opens the study. The book is a model of the theme-and-variation method in folk tale science.
39479-the-independence-day-horror-at-kil:
Asenath Coolidge wrote this tale of a Fourth of July horror, published at Watertown, New York in 1905. Cassius Coolidge, her kinsman of poker-dog fame, illustrated the story for the press. She dedicates it to her grandmother, a descendant of John and Mary Carver of the Mayflower.

That grandmother's faith would not countenance war or its vain-glorious celebrations, the dedication says. The Carvers came to escape persecution for such beliefs, she recalls with pride there. Fireworks and cannon crackers made the old Fourth a day of wounds and fires, and reformers like Coolidge told horror tales to win a safe and sane holiday.
39528-mohave-pottery:
Mohave Pottery, by Kroeber and Michael Harner, is an anthropological study from California. It leads volume sixteen of the Anthropological Records of that state university press. The volume spans the years 1955 to 1961 in its publication run. A reprint by Kraus at Millwood, New York, followed in 1976 for libraries.

The Mohave people of the Colorado river and their clay ware form the subject. Forms, paints, and uses of pots in daily and ritual life fill such a study. Two papers by Cook on native population stand in the same volume contents. One treats the San Joaquin valley, the other the north coast of California. Alameda and Contra Costa counties get a third population study in the set. West coast native life in number and craft is the shared ground here.
39626-an-alphabet-of-history:
Wilbur D Nesbit wrote the words and Ellsworth Young the pictures for An Alphabet of History. Paul Elder and Company published it at San Francisco in 1905. A quatrain promises the plan: who frets about the mystery enshrouding history will find it made plain as A, B, C. Alexander the Great takes the letter A. He was a victim of fate, the verse says, who sighed there was naught to delight him.

He had chased all the armies and wasted all the lands, and clamored for more. The Gordian knot, cut in two, sat labeled in his palace. The cause of his woe was the lack of war correspondents to cable his scraps. No kodak clicked for him, and no dime magazine printed his articles. Brutus, back in the time of Rome sublime, takes the letter B.
39629-irma-in-italy-a-travel-story:
Irma in Italy is a travel tale for young readers by Helen Leah Reed, put out at Boston in the early nineteen hundreds. She was known for a set of girl books and for a tale of a famed exiles young neighbor. The book holds prints from photos and from the pen of an artist.

Its parts trace a full trip in good order. The start, the west isles, and the road to the main land come first. Then come a stop at a great rock fort, a first step on shore, and Naples with its bay towns. Caves, dead cities dug from ash, and Rome fill the mid run. The shape is a girls tour told as a tale, with sights, tales of the past, and the feel of each place.
39631-the-runaways-a-new-and-original-st:
Nat Gould wrote The Runaways, billed as a new and original story, and a London house issued it with an appreciation of the author at its front. That tribute calls Gould's novels of the Turf the work by which multitudes knew him. A picture after G. Heath Robinson stands with the title.

The appreciation tells the reader what to expect. Gould had written a hundred odd books, and their sales ran into a score of millions. He wrote to please and not to puzzle, the tribute says, to give pleasure and not to educate, and his reward was the gratitude of lovers of clean, healthy fiction. His main theme was the King of Sports, horse racing. A tale called The Runaways from such a hand promises stables, courses, and the men who live by the thoroughbred. Racing readers get Gould in his home country.
39741-in-my-nursery:
Laura Richards's In My Nursery was printed at Boston by Little, Brown, under a copyright of 1890 held by Roberts Brothers. Richards, who had written The Joyous Story of Toto, gives the book to her mother, Julia Ward Howe. The gift is made in verse, thanking her mother's silver singing for the music of her own childhood.

The contents are a nursery's shelf of short pieces: The Baby's Future, Baby's Hand, The First Tooth, and Johnny's By-Low Song. A ballad of the fairy spoon, a song of the little winds, and good-night songs follow. The Owl and the Eel and the Warming-pan stands among the nonsense pieces, and Little John Bottlejohn and Jemima Brown among the character verses.
39892-scottish-loch-scenery:
Thomas A Croal wrote the notes for Scottish Loch Scenery, a set of coloured plates from drawings by A F Lydon, issued at London in 1882 by John Walker and Company. Twenty six scenes fill the contents. Lochmaben leads the set. Loch Doon, the Grey Mare's Tail, and St Mary's Loch follow.

Duddingston Loch, Linlithgow Loch, and Corra Linn sit in the lowland part. Loch Leven, Loch Lomond, and Loch Katrine mark the middle. Loch Tay, Loch Awe, Loch Ness, and Loch Coruisk close the highland run. Falls at Inversnaid, Foyers, and Garravalt break the loch list. Croal opens with Lochmaben, an ancient burgh near Lockerbie. Its folk are called the king's kindly tenants, he notes. Bruce's men won land rights there under the Crown.
39900-the-slipper-point-mystery:
Augusta Huiell Seaman wrote a girls' mystery copyrighted in 1919, drawn by C M Relyea. A girl sits on the prow of a beached rowboat at Carter's Landing, digging her bare toes in the sand. The Manituck River shore holds dozens of boats and canoes for hire. A pavilion above sells candy, ice cream, and soda water.

Chapters move from an encounter to Slipper Point itself. A first clue, a place called Roundtree's, and a hidden space behind a cedar plank follow. One picture shows a girl gasping that a hidden place is a room. Doris forms a new theory. The real buried treasure is promised near the end.
40013-the-master-of-warlock-a-virginia-w:
The Master of Warlock is a Virginia war novel by George Cary Eggleston, author of Dorothy South. Lothrop Publishing Company of Boston issued it in January 1903, with pictures by Williams. Eggleston dedicated the book to his wife of thirty-four years. He says her character, in its several phases, stands behind every heroine he ever wrote.

The tale opens with a break in a bridge and the bringing up of Agatha. Chapters move through Jessamine and Honeysuckle, a farewell at the gate, and a red feather. War chapters bring action at Warlock, escort duty, canister fire, and a brush at the front. Agatha's venture and her wonder-story carry the home side of the war.
40132-a-report-on-washington-territory:
A Report on Washington Territory is a survey by Ruffner, published in New York in 1889 by the Seattle, Lake Shore and Eastern Railway. The railway issued the illustrated report to draw settlers and capital to the territory it served. An early plate shows the upper Snoqualmie Falls, a hundred and twenty feet high.

Ruffner's preface lays out six chapters. The first gives his itinerary, the places visited and the dates. The second is a general account of the territory: its history, its location, and its great Pacific market. Under that head he piles up facts meant to surprise readers who have not studied the commercial advantages of Puget Sound. Topography, climate, soils and natural vegetation follow. Later chapters describe the beds of coal and iron ore, granite, limestone and marble, and the ores of precious and base metals found across the territory.
40151-constance-sherwood-an-autobiograph:
Lady Georgiana Fullerton wrote this tale as the life story of a woman of the fifteen hundreds. Constance Sherwood first ran in parts in The Catholic World, and was gathered here whole. Its teller speaks as Constance herself, in old faith and old grief.

I had not thought to write the story of my life, she begins. The wishes of those with right to command her pressed the pen into her hand. Trials and strange comforts have tossed her on an uneasy sea, the world. They have taught her a deep sense of the goodness of God. His ways are not as our ways, she quotes, nor his thoughts like ours. From that text her whole life, set in a torn church age, unfolds.
40309-the-art-of-amusing-being-a-collect:
Frank Bellew wrote The Art of Amusing, issued at New York by Carleton at two dollars with near one hundred and fifty pictures. The full title calls it a set of graceful arts, merry games, and odd tricks. A front ad pairs it with books on talk and on good society manners. The three were sold as a set for five dollars.

Bellew aims to amuse all and to help all amuse the rest. Private plays, tableaux, and charades get full space. Parlor and family fun of all kinds fills the book. Ads call the set fresh, sound, and good humored, not dry rules. The Art of Conversation and The Habits of Good Society are its mates. The book suits hosts who need games and tricks for a night at home.
40336-the-agrarian-problem-in-the-sixtee:
Richard Tawney wrote this study of English farming life in the sixteenth century, first published at London in 1912. A New York reprint in the Burt Franklin Research and Source Works series followed, with six maps. He dedicated it to William Temple and Albert Mansbridge, president and secretary of the Workers' Educational Association.

Part one treats the small landholder, setting out the classes of landholders, the freeholders, and the customary tenants. It then turns to the variety of peasant conditions and the joining of small holdings into larger ones. Part two follows the transition to farming for profit, with the growth of the large leasehold farm and enclosure carried out by manorial lords. The struggle for the commons and the removing of landmarks close Tawney's account of how the old rural order gave way.
40416-the-rest-hollow-mystery:
The Rest Hollow Mystery is a mystery novel by Rebecca Porter, issued at New York in 1922. Porter dedicates it to her brother in a playful page. He is that ideal reader of mystery stories, she writes, with the eagerness to pursue and the faith to believe. He also has the kindness to guess wrong, she adds. The tale then opens on a man who cannot remember his own accident.

Kenwick himself had no memory of it, the first lines say. But he knew there must have been one. His clothes were full of burrs, his hat badly crushed, and one leg throbbed hard when he woke. He dragged himself into a clearing and looked about him. It was one of those narrow, wooded mountain ravines the West calls a canyon. Bleak, wintry, hostile slopes rose behind.
40434-the-place-of-dragons-a-mystery:
William Le Queux wrote a mystery tale whose part names hide as much as they tell. Le Queux wrote In White Raiment and The Room of Secrets. A problem leads, and a part of sheer amaze comes next. Light from mist and a heap of asks fill the first parts. A shadow falls, and the riddle stands past all sense.

Two men, a night watch, and a clue thread the mid tale. The case of the seventeenth and a girl named Lola stand out. A strange tale told and a free word made turn the plot. Jules slips each net as the hunt runs on. Crime fans get Le Queux's thick fog.
40484-black-star-s-campaign-a-detective-:
Black Star's Campaign is a detective novel by Johnston McCulley, author of Black Star, published by Chelsea House of New York in 1919. Street and Smith held the copyright. Its thirty-two chapters open with News for the Sheriff and A Shock for the City. The New Headquarters, Over the Telephone, and Trailed set the master criminal moving.

Inside the Museum and Missing Masterpieces show his game: the theft of art. Muggs, his henchman, sees his man, meets disaster, gives a tip, and takes a chance. Verbeck investigates while Sheriff Kowen works the county side. On the Roof, A Tense Moment, Caught in the Net, and An Empty Net pace the pursuit. The Letter concludes. A passage preserved in the copy gives the sheriff's visitor. My dear Miss Blanchard, Kowen said, glancing at the card handed him, and for once forgetting his usual gruff manner.
40537-the-history-of-chivalry:
The History of Chivalry is G P R James's study of knighthood and the crusades. Harper and Brothers published it in New York. James had written the novels De l'Orme, Darnley, and Richelieu. His preface pleads the difficulty of compression. Extensive matter had to fit one volume, the most the public would read. He wrote, he says, because other authors' errors gave false impressions.

James promises that no point, however minute, lacks authority. Marginal references tie each statement to its writer. The preface then grades those authorities for inquiring readers. William of Tyre stands beyond doubt the most illustrious crusade historian. Born in Palestine and raised to its archbishopric, he tutored a king. He served on embassies and chancellored the kingdom of Jerusalem. Albert of Aix and Fulcher of Chartres were present at the events they describe.
4060-the-renaissance-studies-in-art-and-:
Walter Pater's Renaissance studies follow the soul's steps from love of a physical object to love of unseen beauty. His thoughts, however little their positive value, connect to springs of deep and passionate feeling beneath them, and his analogies lift the reader upward.

Essays on Botticelli, Leonardo, Michelangelo, and others made Pater famous for the claim that art should be judged by the quality of its moments. The prose glows with a vehemence that recalls poetry itself. Readers who like art history written as literature will find a landmark book of Victorian criticism.
40654-a-system-of-midwifery:
Edward Rigby, physician to the General Lying-In Hospital and lecturer on midwifery at St Bartholomew's Hospital, wrote this system of midwifery. The hosted copy fronts the text with the publisher's ads for other medical books. Those ads puff Dunglison's New Remedies and his dictionary of medical science, both from the same Philadelphia house.

Rigby's own work is a full course on the art of childbirth for students and practitioners of his day. It stands in the line of hospital teaching, from a man who both lectured and attended at a lying-in hospital. The ads around it map the trade in medical books of the time, when American houses reprinted and sold British and home works side by side.
40665-studies-in-logical-theory:
John Dewey and his Chicago colleagues test a new theory of logic in a volume issued by the University of Chicago Press in 1903. It stands as volume eleven of the Decennial Publications, second series.

Dewey's own four chapters open the book. They treat thought and its subject-matter from four sides: the thing itself, its antecedents, its datum, its content and object. His premise runs plain: reflective thought comes after something, out of something, and for the sake of something. Helen Bradford Thompson takes up Bosanquet's theory of judgment. Simon Fraser McLennan traces typical stages in the growth of judgment. Myron Lucius Ashley weighs the nature of hypothesis. Later chapters treat image and idea, and the logic of the pre-Socratic Greeks. The volume marks pragmatism's first full muster.
40710-a-summer-s-outing-and-the-old-man-:
A Summers Outing and the Old Mans Story is a travel book by Carter Harrison. The Chicago mayor wrote it from letters sent home on a tour west. Those letters first ran in a Chicago daily paper to warm praise. The book form came out in Chicago in the year eighteen ninety one.

Letters tour Wisconsin, Minnesota, the Bad Lands, and the Yellowstone park in turn. Geysers and steam vents earn the park the name of a wonder land. A run on to Alaska caps the route of the summer trip. The old mans tale is bound in as extra fare for idle hours. The author says the small book will cost little and serve would be tourists well.
40723-the-battle-of-life-a-love-story:
The Battle of Life is a Christmas book by Charles Dickens, published by Bradbury and Evans in 1846. Its subtitle calls it, simply, a love story. Dickens inscribed it cordially to his English friends in Switzerland. Maclise, Doyle, Stanfield, and Leech drew the illustrations between them.

The tale opens upon an ancient battlefield in stalwart England. Once, on a long summer day, a fierce fight was waged there. Wild flowers filled their cups with blood instead of dew that day. Insects were stained anew by the dying men as they crawled. The moon rose at last over a plain of upturned faces. Against that ground of old violence the love story sets its figures. Snitchey and Craggs, a pair of lawyers, appear in the picture list. A parting breakfast, a secret interview, and a night of return follow.
40727-pictures-of-southern-life-social-p:
Pictures of Southern Life, Social, Political, and Military, gathers letters by William Howard Russell. Russell was a special correspondent, and the letters were written for a London newspaper. The New York edition is dated eighteen sixty one. A first full letter is dated from Charleston, April thirty, eighteen sixty one. A note says an earlier letter only described Fort Sumter after its siege.

Nothing I could say can match one forced fact, Russell begins. He has spent days among the gentlemen of the state, he writes. He visited their plantations and conversed freely with them. From all quarters the same voice reached his ears, he says. There is no discord in the note, he adds. Their admiration for monarchy on the English model is one theme he reports. Privileged classes and a landed aristocracy win their praise, he writes.
40834-the-under-secretary:
A political tale opens at two o'clock in the morning in sleeping London here. Big Ben had boomed its solemn note over the city as chapter one begins. A patient constable at Westminster Bridge stamped his feet for the last time, the narrator says, and was relieved with the password 'All right' in the night.

Smart broughams still stood in New Palace Yard while the Commons sat late, the chapter goes on. A ray of electricity streamed from the tower of Stephen's, showing the House still at work. Great men and secret errands move through a silent metropolis that the narrator calls the throbbing heart of an empire.
40847-a-short-history-of-h-m-s-victory:
A Short History of H M S Victory was gathered from various sources and put together by Captain W J L Wharton of the Royal Navy. Griffin and Company printed it at Portsmouth in 1884. The book was sold for the benefit of the Seamen and Marines Orphan School and Female Orphan Home.

A line from Shakespeare heads the title, whose life was England glory. Plates show the Victory in battle and the Salvador del Mundo striking to her at St Vincent. Wharton opens by saying every Englishman knows the Victory bore Lord Nelson flag. On board her he took his death wound in the moment of triumph off Cape Trafalgar. Yet few know her many famed services across long years before that sad, glad climax. Ship fans get Nelson flagship whole life.
40865-paris-and-the-social-revolution-a-:
Sanborn studied the revolutionary elements in the various classes of Parisian society for this book, published by Small, Maynard at Boston in 1905 with drawings by Trowbridge. It is reverently inscribed to the proletariat of America. Byron and Whitman supply the mottoes: of no party, he will offend all parties; he has no mockings or arguments, he witnesses and waits. The first chapter asks what the anarchist wants.

Jean Grave's exposition of anarchist doctrine stands for the creed: the free individual in free humanity, freedom of the soil first, then of knowledge and art. Kropotkine, Reclus, and Grave are its contemporary voices. Later chapters follow the propaganda by word of mouth and in print: the groups and their federations, the soup conferences, the singing of revolutionary chansons in the street. Sanborn, an American who had lived inside the Paris movement, reports it as an anthropologist of his own adopted tribe.
40892-the-pyrotechnist-s-treasury:
Fireworks fill this trade treasure of the Victorian stage and garden party. The Pyrotechnist's Treasury stands among the Secret Out books, sold in cloth with rich plates. Its head pages list its shelf mates, the whole fun trade of its day.

Art of Amusing leads the list, with Bellew's graceful arts, games, tricks, and puzzles. Hanky-Panky gathers easy tricks and hard ones, white magic and sleight of hand. The Magician's Own Book teaches cups and balls, eggs, hats, and cloths from real practice. Magic No Mystery works cards, dice, and balls. The fireworks book itself gives the trade's recipes and builds: rockets, wheels, and set pieces for the night shows of the age.
40975-life-in-a-railway-factory:
Alfred Williams, who wrote A Wiltshire Village, here tells the life of a great railway works from inside. Duckworth first printed Life in a Railway Factory in London in 1915. Williams gave the book to his friend Alfred Zimmern.

Labour unrest opens the tale, a sore theme of those years. Then the shops in turn: stamping, the coalies, the rolling mills, and the scrap waggons. Shunters, watchmen, carriage finishers, and painters fill the next walk. The old canal, ash-wheelers, bricklayers, and the wheel shed follow. Few books show heavy works life so close: the noise, the risk at the rolls, and the pride of the men.
40995-the-zeppelin-destroyer-being-some-:
The Zeppelin Destroyer, subtitled Some Chapters of Secret History, is a war novel by William Le Queux. It was published in London by Hodder and Stoughton in a nineteen sixteen edition. Chapter one opens in a work shed of an aeroplane factory at Hendon. Two young airmen talk over cigarettes after testing their monoplanes that morning.

The narrator, Claude Munro, is twenty five and the son of a London doctor. He nearly died the day before in a wind pocket eight thousand feet up. His friend Teddy Ashton watched from the lawn and feared the worst fall. Claude turned to wireless study after a short spell reading for the bar. Both men learned to fly at Brooklands before the war broke out. The talk turns on the secret work of bringing down German airships.
41111-the-wonder-book-of-knowledge-the-m:
The Wonder Book of Knowledge is a big reference book for young readers, compiled and edited by Henry Chase Hill with the help of experts from each industry. It was published at Philadelphia by the John C Winston Company. Seven hundred and eighty photographs and drawings fill its pages. Its sub-titles promise the marvels of modern industry and invention. The stories of common things are told in its pages too. The processes of nature are set out beside them, all in simple terms.

The book opens in the world of making and moving things. How colours print, how goods are made, and how power is won all find their place. Each trade speaks through a man who knows it at first hand. The aim is to answer the questions a keen boy or girl asks of the world at work.
41122-rayton-a-backwoods-mystery:
Rayton, a backwoods mystery novel by Theodore Goodridge Roberts, was first issued in 1910 and reprinted in Boston in 1912. Samson's Mill Settlement had prided itself on its respectability for fifteen years. Then Reginald Baynes Rayton arrived, full of good humour, and shook the place up. The story opens with a poker game among five men of the settlement and their guest.

Chapters follow Jim Harley's old story, a trapper's confession, Doctor Nash's suspicions, and young Marsh's misfortune. Rayton confesses, red crosses appear again, and Captain Wigmore suggests an amazing thing. The tale runs through fear forgotten and recalled, a charge, and what its chapter list calls the chosen instrument of fate. It closes with the death of the curse and a chapter named In the Way of Happiness. The book is illustrated by John Goss.
41130-the-stolen-statesman-being-the-sto:
The Stolen Statesman, being the Story of a Hushed Up Mystery, is a novel by William Le Queux published in London by Skeffington and Son. Its first chapter concerns Sheila Monkton, and the tale centers on her father. Reginald Monkton is a Right Honourable statesman of fifty-odd years, lightly worn by twenty years of political strife.

Monkton had been a Bencher of the Inner Temple and Quain Professor of Law at University College, London. He sat in Parliament for North-West Manchester, then East Huntingdon, then the Govan Division of Glasgow, and rose to Colonial Secretary. Le Queux was the era's master of the political mystery, and a statesman of this rank, wrapped in a hushed-up affair, is exactly his ground.
41140-bible-atlas-a-manual-of-biblical-g:
Jesse L Hurlbut wrote the Bible Atlas, a manual of Bible lands and Bible history in a revised form. Rand, McNally and Company issued the book in Chicago. It was made for teachers, students, and Sunday school classes. Maps, plans, charts, and views of key towns fill its pages.

An opening essay by John H Vincent stresses how far the Bible world sits from modern life. Dress, food, and travel all differed from place to place in that old world. The atlas then ties each map to the tales and kings named in the text. Charts help a class review what it has learned. The book suits readers who want the land clear before they read the story.
41185-the-voice-from-the-void-the-great-:
The Voice from the Void, subtitled The Great Wireless Mystery, is a novel by William Le Queux. Cassell and Company published it in London, New York, Toronto, and Melbourne. The first chapter, Concerns a Stranger, opens in a Norman church after evening service. The Reverend Norton Homfray, the white-haired rector, stands shaken in the vestry. He is certain he has seen Gordon Gray.

Gray sat in the last pew during the sermon. Homfray cannot forget that face, he says, among a million. Yet Gray was reported dead at the Waldorf-Astoria in New York eighteen months ago. The rector wonders why the man has come to Little Farncombe. Homfray is a Balliol man and a theological scholar, popular in his parish. His wife died four years before the story opens. His son Roderick is twenty-six. Le Queux builds the mystery from this impossible return.
41209-venice-and-its-story:
Okey wrote this history of Venice, first issued in 1903 and revised in 1910. Drawings by Nelly Erichsen and co-artists enrich the book. A Bellini portrait of Doge Loredan stands near the front. The tale starts with the founding of the city at Rialto.
