Chapters trace Saint Mark cult, sea growth, and wars with Genoa. Enrico Dandolo and the capture of Constantinople get a full part. Later parts treat the Council of Ten and mainland conquests. The Turkish threat and trade decline close the long arc of the city story. Three editions came out within seven years of the first.
41404-mostly-mary:
Mostly Mary, by the writer who signs as Clementia, is a tale of a little girl and her house. Matre printed it at Chicago in 1921. Clementia had written Uncle Frank's Mary and The Quest of Mary Selwyn before it.

The book is given to four little rancheros: Patricia, George, Edward, and Eleanor. A plate shows Mary entering the sitting-room loaded down. Her white kitten, a rubber doll, a ball, and a teddy bear fill her arms. Fifteen chapters run from a surprise to a firelight close. A visit to Maryvale, Mary's plan, and the first Friday come. A little cross, a shadow falling, and the rustle of angels' wings darken the middle. Precious last hours and Sister Julia close the tale. It opens with her father hunting his Goldilocks in the playroom.
41525-the-house-opposite-a-mystery:
The House Opposite, by Elizabeth Kent, is a mystery novel told by a doctor. Putnam issued it at New York and London, rights in 1902, reprinted 1903. On a scorching August night in 1899 the narrator cannot sleep at home. He takes rug and pipe to the roof for air and stars above.

Lights burn late in the Rosemere apartment house across the street that night. Through his neighbour windows he is drawn into a case of death. A coroner inquest and unwilling witnesses fill the early chapters in turn. Atkins at home, a missing hat, and a hysterical patient deepen the puzzle. The truth of the whole matter closes eighteen chapters.
41538-the-progress-of-invention-in-the-n:
The Progress of Invention in the Nineteenth Century is a survey by Edward Byrn, published by Munn and Company at the Scientific American office in New York in 1900. The frontispiece shows steam and electricity in the great power station of the Metropolitan Street Railway. Archimedes' boast, give me where to stand and I will move the earth, stands as motto.

Byrn apologises in his preface for a single writer's ambition. His authority, he explains, is the patent record, which carries the government's responsibility for dates and the inventor's oath for subject matter. He avoids disputed claims between rival inventors and pleads lack of space for his omissions. A quarter century spent in the high tide of the arts and sciences, with friends in and about the Patent Office, is his credential. The book is the century of invention surveyed at its close, by the patent profession's own house historian.
41615-tuffy-todd-s-adventure-a-true-stor:
Tuffy Todd's Adventure is a tale in verse by Samuel Doggerel of Philadelphia, printed in 1886 for private circulation. The title page calls it a true story. An opening note says the event took place that summer in a quiet part of the Catskill Mountains. The rhymes were written for the guests at Todd's Hillside Home. They first saw print in a sheet called the Dry Brook Evening Mail.

The poem tells of a little white house dog, fat and round as a mole. His soft brown eyes are bright, and his temper is mild as a child's. Yet he guards the yard with force. Strangers who climb the hill meet his loudest bark, and tramps must flee or face him. He lives for his master, Orrin Todd, and owns a host of friends. The light verse keeps the tone of a house party joke.
41617-a-complete-guide-to-heraldry:
Arthur Charles Fox Davies wrote A Complete Guide to Heraldry, issued in London by T C and E C Jack in nineteen oh nine. Fox Davies was a barrister of Lincoln Inn, author of The Art of Heraldry and editor of Armorial Families. Nine plates in colour and nearly eight hundred other designs aid the text. Graham Johnston, herald painter to the Lyon Court, drew most. Thirty chapters and more fill the guide.

An introduction leads into the origin of armory and the status of a coat of arms in Great Britain. The heralds and officers of arms, heraldic brasses, and parts of an achievement follow. The shield, tinctures, and rules of blazon fill the core. Ordinaries, the lion, beasts, monsters, birds, and fish follow in turn. Helmets, crests, crowns, mantling, supporters, and mottoes close the survey. Genealogists get the standard English heraldry manual.
41643-the-theory-and-practice-of-archery:
The Theory and Practice of Archery is a manual by Horace Ford, revised by Butt for this new edition. Longmans, Green published it in London in 1887. Ford had been champion archer of England from 1850 to 1859, and again in 1867. Butt served many years as secretary of the Royal Toxophilite Society.

Ford's work first appeared as articles in the Field newspaper. It became a book in 1856, and a second edition followed in 1859. That edition had long been out of print when this one was planned. No other guide, the preface says, could teach a young archer his art. The publisher bought the copyright from Ford's representatives for the purpose. Butt then rewrote the book thoroughly, bringing it up to present knowledge. Obsolete matter was cut rather than reprinted for bulk's sake.
41668-rustic-carpentry:
Rustic Carpentry is a hand book of work in rough wood for the yard. Paul Hasluck shaped it from pieces in his craft print Work. It came out in London and three more towns in 1907. Cuts and plans crowd its pages for the hand at the bench.

The pieces tell how to make yard goods in the rough bark style. Seats, gates, and sheds in that style are the stock of such a book. The preface says the book is made for use at the bench each day. Those who want more lore on a point are sent to a past book. Hasluck was known for a long run of such craft hand books. The style of the work suits a cot yard or a wild nook of a park.
41703-women-in-modern-industry:
B L Hutchins wrote this study of women's work, published in London in 1915, with a chapter by J J Mallon. The front pages set out grim texts: Chrysostom calling woman a necessary evil, and the Statute of Labourers of 1563, which let justices imprison an unmarried woman who refused assigned service.

In her preface Hutchins explains the book was finished before the summer of 1914, and that she chose not to rewrite it for the war, leaving the earlier chapters as they stood. She had already co-written a history of factory legislation. Readers get a sober, documented account of women's wages and conditions on the eve of great change.
41790-quintus-oakes-a-detective-story:
Quintus Oakes, a detective story by Charles Ross Jackson, was printed in New York in 1904. Jackson also wrote The Third Degree. The narrator, Rodney Stone, is an attorney who leaves his rooms one stifling summer evening to stroll along Broadway in search of a roof garden.

Smoke from a third story window draws a crowd, and a girl of ten appears at a sill, trapped by the fire filling her room. A tall man in the crowd speaks calm to her as engines shriek in the distance. The contents then promise Oakes at home, a letter, a murder, and an inquest, followed by a mansion, a cellar, a night walk, a witness, and a man's confession.
41870-gold-and-incense-a-west-country-st:
Mark Guy Pearse wrote Gold and Incense, a West Country story, printed in London. The copy shown is the forty-seventh thousand. Pearse gives the book to Sidney Hill of Langford House, Somerset. A note with the giving says the story is perfectly true. The first chapter opens on its heroine: to think it is Jennifer Petch of whom I am going to tell, little Jennifer.

How she would laugh if she only knew of it, that shrill, silvery laugh of hers. It was her great gift. Jennifer was wise in laughing, the teller says: knowing how to laugh and when. The village itself would wonder almost as much as Jennifer. Village people do not see much in what they see always. Sam Petch was the tallest and straightest of the village lads. Phyllis and Chloe stand in the opening pages as well.
41989-the-starling-a-scottish-story:
Norman Macleod tells a Scottish tale in The Starling, a Scottish story, printed in London and Glasgow. Blackie and Son made the book, with branches in India and Canada. A plate shows a cry of the tale: here he is, take him and finish him. A life note of the author fronts the volume.

Norman Macleod was born in 1812 at Campbeltown, the note says, where his father was parish minister. He entered the University of Glasgow in 1827, and in 1837 became a licensed minister of the Church of Scotland. He served parishes at Loudoun and Dalkeith, then the Barony parish in Glasgow till his death in 1872. He was chaplain to Queen Victoria, and edited the journal Good Words from its start. His books include The Gold Thread, The Old Lieutenant and his Son, and Highland Parish life recalled. The Starling itself dates to 1867, the note records.
42010-the-barrel-mystery:
Barrel Mystery is a detective memoir by William Flynn, a Secret Service chief. Flynn headed the United States Secret Service and wrote The Eagle's Eye. McCann published the book in New York with rights in 1919. Contents open with The Barrel Murder at page one in bold capitals. What was the motive for the murder forms the second chapter.

Organized terrorism, counterfeit bills, and a greenhorn's story follow in order. Don Pasquale, a Black Hand skirmisher, fills the sixth chapter there. The plant of the counterfeiters and the society behind them ensue. A knock at the door at 2 in the morning raises suspense. Flynn recounts his war on the Black Hand and the counterfeiters.
4207-aesthetic-poetry:
An essay on aesthetic poetry weighs songs of morning and dawn, where terrors known in all their forms give way to strange tenderness. The crown of one English poet's book is an appreciation of dawn, praying for one prayer between closed lips and one thought among the stars.

Summer night wanes, morning light slips faint and gray between aspen leaves and cloud bars waiting patiently. The essay favors beauty, mood, and the music of verse over moral argument. Readers who enjoy criticism of poetry will find a short, lyrical study of dawn as a muse.
42181-poetry:
Thomas Oldham wrote this book of poems, printed in London in 1840. Bailey of Cornhill sold it, with Black of Edinburgh and Cumming of Dublin. Oldham opens with a vow: if he ever soils the lyre for pay, let him be cast out. Let him lose the poet's name for good.

In his preface he says verse was his pastime for many years. Friends urged him to print, and a father's fondness for the work of his own brain won out. He grants that the times are poor for books of verse and that sellers report weak demand. Still, he holds that true poetry, well made, will never lack readers for long.
42287-the-girl-from-the-big-horn-country:
Mary Ellen Chase wrote this novel for girls, printed by the Page Company of Boston in 1916. R Farrington Elwell drew the plates. Five impressions ran between January and August of that year, a sign of its pull. Chase gives the book to the memory of her father, who, she writes, perhaps knows, and is glad.

Virginia leaves her Big Horn country for school in the East. Chapters trace her last night at home, the journey, and Vermont as she sees it. St Helen's and the Hermitage, rules of decorum, and the disciplining of Miss Van Rensaelar fill her school days. A Thanksgiving oration by Lucile Du Bose and a band of vigilantes mark the turns. A western girl's manners meet eastern polish.
4231-the-malady-of-the-century:
A novel of Berlin in 1871, The Malady of the Century, opens on a hot summer day, June 16. Sun streams down on Unter den Linden, and life gathers in a restless throng. The bustle differs from eleven months before, with joyful excitement in the air, in children's laughter and girls' talk.

Beneath the celebration, the novel probes a generation's spiritual sickness, the malady that gives the book its name. Set just after the Franco-Prussian War, it follows young Berliners seeking meaning after victory. Readers who enjoy European novels of ideas will find a serious, atmospheric work.
42333-the-cleverdale-mystery-or-the-mach:
A political novel by W A Wilkins, published at New York in 1882. Fords, Howard and Hulbert issued the book. Wilkins edited the Whitehall Times in upstate New York. His preface states his aims plainly. He hopes to inform some readers and mirror others. The warp is reality, the woof fiction, the colouring domestic.

The dramatis personae list a state senator called the Boss. Darius Hamblin rules a political machine with loyal lieutenants. A bolting assemblyman, a wily country politician, and purchasable hangers-on surround him. George Alden, a bank officer, plays the hero. Lake George opens the tale in beauty, then schemers gather. Caucuses, conventions, a burning factory, and a secret marriage follow. The epilogue explains the machine and its wheels.
42398-historic-adventures-tales-from-ame:
Historic Adventures is a book of American history tales for young readers by Rupert Holland, printed at Philadelphia in 1913. Holland also wrote Historic Boyhoods and Historic Girlhoods. A front plate shows cannon shooting tongues of smoke from their great black throats. The book is dedicated to Robert Jenks.

Fourteen tales fill the contents. The lost children and the great journey of Lewis and Clark open the set. The conspiracy of Aaron Burr, the Barbary pirates, and the fate of Lovejoy's printing press follow. Marcus Whitman saving Oregon, the Mormons settling Utah, and the golden days of forty-nine carry the westward story. A pig that almost caused a war, John Brown at Harper's Ferry, the story of Alaska, and the sinking of the Merrimac close it. Each tale is a small drama told straight.
4249-in-the-sweet-dry-and-dry:
Christopher Morley and Bart Haley wrote this comic novel in Philadelphia in 1919, on the eve of Prohibition, and dedicated it to G. K. Chesterton. Its chapters promise a mystery of the unexpected julep, a house on Caraway Street, gooseberry bombs, the treachery of Miss Chuff, and a band of pilgrims calling themselves the Decanterbury Pilgrims.

The foreword warns readers not to draw conclusions about the authors' own habits from the story, which follows drinkers, schemers, and reformers through an election and a mock war over alcohol. It is a light satire of the dry age, written while the law was still about to arrive, and it keeps its jokes close to the politics of the moment.
42629-the-violoncello-and-its-history:
Wasielewski wrote a history of the cello and its playing, turned into English by Isobella Stigand for Novello in 1894. A portrait of Robert Lindley stands at the front. In his preface, dated at Sondershausen in December 1888, the author explains his plan. He has set a history of the viola da gamba before that of the cello.

The gamba, he holds, must be taken as the forerunner of the later instrument. He drew on the great musical word books of his day and on the lives of musicians by Fétis. A Saxon court director lent him a vast store of old and new cello music. By that means he found his way through the growth of music written for the instrument. Music samples and pictures fill the book. It remains a sober, full account of how the cello rose from its elder kin.
42652-scott-greenwood-catalogue-of-speci:
Scott, Greenwood and Company listed their trade books for makers in a January 1905 list. The list is a catalogue, not a tale or a text book. It names books by expert hands for mills, schools, and shops. A subject index in A-to-Z order leads the list. Each line gives a book's theme and page in the list.

Themes run from farm chemics to dyes, clays, and coal dust fire. Paint, scent, bone goods, and book binding all find a place. Weaving, spinning, and color match fill a large share. Works on damp walls and build terms serve the build trades. Buyers in 1905 could scan the whole stock at a glance.
42665-satan-s-diary:
Satan's Diary, by Leonid Andreyev in an authorized translation with a preface by Herman Bernstein, was published in New York in 1920 by Boni and Liveright. The diary opens on January 18, aboard the ship Atlantic. Satan writes that this is exactly the tenth day since he became human and began this earthly life. His loneliness is very great.

He has no need of friends, he says, but he must speak of himself, and he has no one to speak to. Thoughts alone will not serve; they clear only when set in words, laid in a row like soldiers or telephone poles. Andreyev's Satan finds human logic slow, hard, and repulsive, and glimpses the asylum door. The novel is a dark satire on a Europe Andreyev saw as ripe for the devil.
42769-the-new-york-book-of-poetry:
The New-York Book of Poetry, published by George Dearborn in 1837, gathers verse by state natives. Dearborn kept his shop at 38 Gold Street in New York City. A Latin motto on smoke of one own land heads the title page. An advertisement at the front states the chief object of the collection.

It was made to give a local home and a name to fugitive pieces, the note says. Such verses had run only in newspapers and periodicals before this gathering. Specimens of New York poets whose works were already in books join the set. That choice gives the volume completeness in the eyes of its maker. The whole book was planned and printed in a rush of weeks, the note confesses.
42862-king-of-ranleigh-a-school-story:
Captain F S Brereton wrote a school story with pictures by Ernest Prater. S W Partridge and Company issued King of Ranleigh from the Old Bailey in London. Brereton had written The Hero of Panama and The Great Aeroplane. Twenty-one chapters run from plots at home to the crown of the school.

Clive Darrell cracks nuts with a small anvil as the tale opens, pockets bulging. Hugh and Bert Seymour, brothers near his age, share his schemes. A booby trap, a ruined tower, burglars, and a great row crowd the terms. Boys of the time got a brisk tale of loyalty, pluck, and school honor.
42936-engraving-its-origin-processes-and:
Le Vicomte Henri Delaborde wrote Engraving, Its Origin, Processes, and History, rendered into English by R A M Stevenson. Cassell and Company in London, Paris, New York, and Melbourne issued the book in eighteen eighty six. The book stands in The Fine Art Library, edited by John C L Sparkes of the National Art Training School. William Walker added a chapter on English engraving.

An editorial note says Delaborde gave English engraving too little care in the French work. Walker account of the British school and his table of engravers mend that gap. Chapter one treats early engraving in relief, wood cutting, and printing with movable type. Chapter two treats playing cards and the dot manner. Later chapters treat Florentine goldsmith nielli and painter engravers of the fifteenth century. Art students get a clear, learned tour of print craft.
42955-standard-paper-bag-cookery:
Emma Paddock Telford wrote this book of cookery in bags of paper, printed in 1912. A note for the man who set the text warns of a quirk in its parts. The word at the front and the first word are named as the first part in the list, but in the text they bear no count. The count of parts starts with the part that asks what this cookery is. Two parts on cakes share one count as well.

A note with the text adds a warn of a grave kind. The book was made long past, when the rules of safe work were far free than they are now. Its ways are not to be tried at home, or in any place at all, the note says.
43074-mary-queen-of-scots-in-history:
Campbell wrote Mary Queen of Scots in History, printed at Montreal in nineteen three, a short life meant for busy readers. In his preface, dated at Halifax in February, nineteen two, Campbell says much has been written on Mary, but few lives in English are both brief and sound. He aims to give facts and arguments on the disputed points of her story. The tale opens on the Scotland of her birth.

Campbell tells how Ralph Sadler saw the baby queen at Linlithgow and called her a fair and goodly child. Parts follow her youth in France, her rule in Scotland, and her marriages. The tragedy of Kirk o' Field, her captivity, and her flight lead to her years as a prisoner of Elizabeth. A last part weighs the proof against her and the sentence of death.
43198-samuel-boyd-of-catchpole-square-a-:
Farjeon wrote this mystery of Samuel Boyd of Catchpole Square in London. Hutchinson and the New Amsterdam house printed it in 1899. Contents open with Abel Death at work and a trap set. A lady of fashion pays Samuel Boyd a visit soon after.

Silence, police men, and a flight through Deadman Court build suspense. Dick Remington reviews his past service to Boyd in long chapters. A lady handkerchief picked up in the dark square gives a clue. The chamber of death and a bursting cloud close the long chain. Hutchinson issued the book at London in 1899.
4326-the-expansion-of-europe-the-culmina:
Ramsay Muir, professor of modern history at the University of Manchester, wrote this survey of Europe's expansion. He treats that expansion as the culmination of modern history. In his preface he states a twofold purpose. He wants to explain how world politics and imperial rivalries now touch every life.

He also wants to give general readers a brief, clear summary of how that came about. Muir traces the greater states of western civilization as they spread trade, settlement, and empire across the globe. The second edition keeps the argument compact and readable. It serves as an introduction to imperial history, written before the First World War reshaped those rivalries.
43422-a-syllabus-of-hispanic-american-hi:
A Syllabus of Hispanic-American History is a course guide for schools. Pierson, a teacher of the past at a state school, drew it up. The guide came out in its third form at a set low price. It was made for a one year course on the lands of the south.

A line from Clay at the front states the stake of the States there. Clay held that no choice in the realm's far plans weighed more. The guide picks and drops facts to fit the span of the course. A keen hand can grow each part to a full study of its own from it. The canal through the isthmus fed the day's keen will to learn, it says. The isle sea lands and their weight in talk grew with the canal. The guide maps the past of the south realm in brief heads.
43477-bell-s-cathedrals-the-cathedral-ch:
The Cathedral Church of Lincoln is a guide book by Kendrick, first out in eighteen ninety-eight. It is one of a set of such books on the great churches of England. The set aims to give guests sound and well drawn guides at a low price. Each book blends lore deep past the student yet plain past the plain guest.

The front note lists the wells of fact for the set, from shire past books to rolls of state. For this book the chief well was the work of a late church man of the house, with four more named hands. The book gives the past and form of the church cloth and a list of its bishops past all time. Past forty plates show the church and its parts.
43645-a-present-for-infants-or-pictures-:
A Present for Infants, or Pictures for the Nursery, a picture book for small children, was printed at London for Darton, Harvey, and Darton in 1819. It sold at one shilling plain or eighteen pence coloured. Numbered plates carry the whole book, each with a short piece in prose or verse. The pieces teach care, kindness, and steady habits.

The first plate shows a little girl with a pitcher and warns her not to fall in the water when she fetches it. A sheep and lambs piece follows in verse, spoken to a child named Fanny. A market man cries his turnips, cabbages, and codlins in the third. A milk maid and her quiet cow fill the fourth. The fifth warns a boy riding full speed for Brighton to mind his reins.
4383-maria-chapdelaine-a-tale-of-the-lak:
Louis Hemon wrote this tale of the Lake Saint John country in Quebec, translated by W. H. Blake and published in New York in 1921. Its contents run from Peribonka and home in the clearing through Francois passing by, wild land, and the vows, to the stuff of dreams and a meager reaping. Maria Chapdelaine stands at the center.

The novel follows a farm family clearing land at the edge of the forest, through seasons, courtships, and losses. Hemon's prose is plain and unsentimental, and Maria's choice between suitors becomes a choice about the land itself. The book became a classic of French Canada, and a portrait of a people holding to soil and faith.
4395-in-wicklow-and-west-kerry:
John M. Synge gathered these Irish sketches in 1912, reworking articles from the Shanachie and the Manchester Guardian. The Wicklow pieces treat the vagrants of Wicklow, the oppression of the hills, life on the road, and the people of the glens. A Wicklow fair, a landlord's garden, and Glencree complete the first part.

The West Kerry pieces continue Synge's walking tour of the west, listening to speech and watching work. Synge writes as a listener rather than a judge, letting island and hillside voices carry the book. The volume pairs naturally with his Aran Islands, as a record of rural Ireland before its old ways faded.
44039-hymns-of-the-early-church-being-tr:
Hymns of the Early Church is a set of Latin hymn turns by John Brownlie. McCrie wrote the past front talk and life notes for the book. A Nisbet house of London brought it out in eighteen ninety six. Hymns stand in the rank of the church year in its scheme. Sunday and week day hymns open the set in its first rank.

Advent, Yule, and star feast hymns fill the next scheme ranks. Cross week hymns of the banner king and the sweet tongue stand mid set. Easter, rise day, and ghost feast hymns crowd the glad ranks. Saint day, supper, death, and heaven hymns close the year scheme. Latin name lists head each rank for those who seek the first forms.
44112-argentina-legend-and-history:
Argentina: Legend and History is a Spanish reader edited by Garibaldi Laguardia and Cincinato Laguardia. The brothers taught at the United States Naval Academy. Sanborn published it in 1919 for the Hispanic Series, edited by Fitz-Gerald of the University of Illinois.

José de San Martín fronts the volume in portrait, and the Argentine anthem opens the readings. Vicente Fidel López writes on the Argentine gaucho, and Sarmiento on originality and characters. Sarmiento's pieces sketch the tracker, the guide, the bad gaucho, and the singer. Bunge retells legends of the forest country, Santos Vega, and Lucía Miranda. A story by Manuela Gorriti recalls the dictatorship of Juan Manuel Rosas. An introduction and biographical notes prepare readers for the selections.
44270-mars-and-its-mystery:
Edward S Morse wrote on Mars and the riddle of its canals, issued at Boston in 1906. Little, Brown, and Company held the rights that year. Morse gave the book to Percival Lowell, whose globe of Mars fronts the work. A quote from Simon Newcomb grants that life may exist on Mars.

Sixteen chapters weigh vast space, other worlds, and the marks men draw on Mars. Morse tests views of Schiaparelli, Lowell, and other watchers with care. Air, water, and watering works get their own close parts. Readers of the time gain a fair guide to a hot debate on life beyond Earth.
44330-valerius-a-roman-story:
Valerius is a Roman story issued in Blackwood's Standard Novels in a new edition from Edinburgh and London. Its narrator, after threescore years in a remote province of the empire, tells his friends at length the story of his youthful journey to Rome.

He remembers, he says, the minutest particulars of that sojourn far more clearly than events of a few months ago. Rome was then recovering, imperfectly, from the flagitious tyranny of the last of the Flavii. His father had come to Britain with his legion and married a lady of native blood before Agricola first arrived. The father won distinction in Agricola's wars under Vespasian and Titus, but retired to his wife's lands when Domitian's jealousy recalled the general.
44398-poems-on-slavery:
Poems on Slavery is a small volume of verse by Henry Wadsworth Longfellow, printed at Cambridge in 1842. John Owen published this second edition. Eight poems make up the contents. A piece addressed to William Channing opens the book. Longfellow wrote most of them at sea in late October. A note explains that Channing had died before the poet heard of it.

The address stays as written, a testimony of admiration. The Slave's Dream is the best known of the set. The Slave in the Dismal Swamp and The Slave Singing at Midnight follow. The Quadroon Girl and The Warning close the volume. A motto from Massinger contrasts freed horses with slaves denied any end. The poems made Longfellow's abolitionist voice public in his own name.
44684-the-pilgrims-way-from-winchester-t:
Julia Cartwright's The Pilgrims' Way from Winchester to Canterbury was published by Dutton in New York in 1911, with drawings by Hallam Murray. Chaucer's lines stand on the title page, of the folk from every shire's end of England who wend to Canterbury to seek the holy blissful martyr. Fourteen chapters walk the road in stages, and a note on the binding explains the Canterbury bell and lead badges pictured on the cover.

The stages are the contents: Winchester to Alton, Alton to Compton, then Shalford, Albury, Shere, Reigate, Chevening, Otford, Wrotham, Hollingbourne, Lenham, Charing, and Harbledown to Canterbury. The Martyr's Shrine closes the walk. Coloured plates show Winchester Cathedral, Chawton House, Ightham Mote, and Aylesford Bridge. Half-tones add Loseley, the hospital at Guildford, and Mercery Lane, and a line block shows the doorway Becket passed through on his way to vespers.
44754-a-manual-for-teaching-biblical-his:
A Manual for Teaching Biblical History is a handbook for Jewish school teachers by Eugene Kohn, rabbi of a Baltimore congregation. It was published in New York by the United Synagogue of America in 1917. The book is inscribed to the memory of Solomon Schechter.

The opening note states the need. Jewish writing on teaching, it says, is still in its infancy. Textbooks for children exist, but guides for the teacher are few and new. Many teachers, above all those with no training school behind them, fall back on books by Christian authors. Those books give the facts, but not the Jewish point of view. Schechter's saying is quoted: we cannot have our love letters written for us. The manual aims to give teachers both method and loyalty to their own tradition.
44761-the-way-to-abolish-slavery:
Charles Stearns published his plan for ending slavery in Boston in 1849, at his own cost. In his opening pages he says he writes for no party and for no anti-slavery society. Eighteen years of preaching, he holds, have shown the evil plainly. What is still needed is a cure that works.

Stearns calls slavery a disease that lives only on help from outside itself. Priests, men in office, and traders in slaves, he argues, keep it alive with their support. Draw that support away and the system falls by its own rot. He asks readers to test all things and hold fast to what is good. The tract is fierce in tone and short in compass, a bold call from the years just before the Civil War.
44773-a-likely-story:
William De Morgan wrote this tale, printed at London in 1911. It is sent forth to the man of science who asks. The list of parts gives the flavour of the first part in a run of heads. A good deal is made of a box of matches. A wed pair is met, whom any man would deem cross, to hear them talk. The wife finds the keep of the house hard, and her man is no help at all.

Still, the pair go to a show of art. The maid Sairah just wipes soft across a tacky print with a cloth, and Mr. Aiken speaks wild words. A fair girl in fine dress and her man of war come into the tale, and Mrs. Aiken is prim with them. She speaks a word of mystic sense on the young maid.
44787-a-vindication-of-the-presbyteriall:
A Vindication of the Presbyteriall Government and Ministry is a church tract of the bounds of London. The church men and elders of those bounds met in a joint meet on the second day of the eleventh month of sixteen forty nine and put it out. It was print at London in sixteen fifty. With it stands a call to all church men, elders, and folk of those bounds, both those who join with the band and those who break from it.

Its points in chief are laid out in a list of twelve. Church rule is by the right of God, and the civil sword is not its spring. The rule by elders is by that same right, and the path of the lone flock way is shown full of ills. The rule elder is by the right of God as well.
44792-buffon-s-natural-history-volume-01:
Buffon's Natural History, volume one, is the first of ten volumes translated from the French. Symonds sold this edition in London in 1797. It is known as Barr's Buffon from its translator editor. Its title promises a theory of the earth and a history of man. The brute creation, vegetables, and minerals are also promised. Notes by the translator accompany the French text. The contents of this volume begin with the Theory of the Earth. Articles on the formation of the planets follow it.

Other articles weigh the systems of Whiston, Burnet, and Woodward. Geography, strata, and shells found inland are treated in turn. The inequalities of the earth's surface and rivers close the list. Fossil shells far from the sea argued the earth had a history. Buffon's theory made that history a subject of natural science. The volume opens a classic of Enlightenment natural history.
44908-the-law-of-civilization-and-decay-:
Brooks Adams wrote The Law of Civilization and Decay. The Macmillan Company issued the essay in 1896. Twelve chapters carry its sweep of history. The Romans open the argument. The Middle Age follows at chapter two. Two crusade chapters come next in line.

The fall of Constantinople fills chapter five. The suppression of the Temple knights follows. England's break with Rome and the closed convents take two chapters. The eviction of the yeomen shows change at home. Spain and India pair in chapter ten. Modern centralization and a conclusion close the book. Adams reads Rome's first farmers as land men of martial type. Dense farm folk held some twelve acres a family, he says. A bold theory of wealth and power drives this bleak view of nations rising and rotting.
45092-the-post-office-of-india-and-its-s:
The Post Office of India and Its Story, by Geoffrey Clarke, was published in London in 1921. Clarke served in the Indian Civil Service. Sixteen plates show officers, vans, and post office buildings. A front plate groups senior officers of the year 1884. Clarke thanks two assistant directors general for help with set chapters. The chapter on stamps rests on a standard work from Stanley Gibbons.

Chapters trace the post from its origin through early and later rules. Parcel post, the railway mail service, money orders, and savings banks each get a chapter. Later parts treat the Indian postman, native states, and the sea post office. War service in 1857 and in the Great War is covered. Tables in the appendix run to 1918.
45102-salvador-of-the-twentieth-century:
Percy Martin wrote a full survey of Salvador for Edward Arnold of London and Longmans of New York in 1911. A map and forty eight pictures go with the text. Martin had written in the same way on Mexico and Peru. His contents open with the finding of the land, its scenery, and its volcanoes.

Later chapters treat the frame of rule, the courts, prisons, police, and schools. One chapter gives short lives of the president, Araujo, of the past president Figueroa, and of the cabinet. Money fills the next part, with the foreign debt and the budget for 1910-11. Wars with Honduras and Nicaragua take up the middle of the book. Martin writes as a friend of the small republic, keen to show its gains in roads, posts, and trade to British and American readers.
45125-the-story-of-slavery:
Story of Slavery is a school sketch of American slavery by Booker Washington, copyrighted in 1913. Owen of Dansville and Hall and McCreary of Chicago issued it jointly for schools. Washington, president of Tuskegee Institute and author of Up From Slavery, wrote the sketch. A biographical sketch of Washington by Emmett Scott fronts the small book.

Scott notes Washington was himself born a slave, about 1858, near Hales Ford, Virginia. The region was then a flourishing tobacco country, now almost deserted, he writes. The story of the author life begins where the story of slavery leaves off. Black schoolchildren gained their history from a man who had lived its end.
45233-history-of-the-twelfth-west-virgin:
History of the Twelfth West Virginia Volunteer Infantry, by William Hewitt, was published by the Twelfth West Virginia Infantry Association for the regiment's survivors and the families of its fallen. Hewitt had served as a first lieutenant, and Colonel Curtis stands in the portraits beside him. The book tells the part the Twelfth took in the War of the Rebellion, from 1861 to 1865.

Chapters follow the regiment from its raising in West Virginia to Clarksburg, Winchester, and the Shenandoah Valley. The battle of Winchester and the retreat, service under Milroy, Sigel, and Hunter, the battle of New Market, and the Lynchburg campaign all get their telling. Lists of killed and wounded, captures, jokes, and camp tales fill the pages between the marches. Such regimental histories, written by the men themselves, kept a unit's war from being lost.
45277-studies-in-folk-song-and-popular-p:
Studies in Folk Song and Popular Poetry is a set of essays on the songs of the folk, by Williams. A word at its front by a famed sage of lore stands with the text. It came out at London in the mid eighteen nineties.

Its first piece takes the sea song of the Rio Grande. No man old to call to mind the grand sight of a full rig ship, it says, is like to have lost that sight. Her white sails drop from the yards and swell to the fresh wind. A cloud of bright cloth stands in the sun. The ship takes on a strong, fair life in their pull, and foam curls at her bow in her rush.
45336-paris-and-its-story:
T Okey wrote Paris and Its Story, with illustrations by Katherine Kimball and O F M Ward, issued in London by J M Dent and Company in nineteen oh four. Macmillan in New York issued the American edition. A long quote from Montaigne heads the book. Montaigne says Paris has ever had his heart from his infancy. A Rue St Antoine view faces the title page.

Okey traces Paris from early times through kings, wars, and revolutions to the modern streets. Churches, palaces, bridges, and quarters fill the tale with names and dates. Montaigne words frame the love of the city. Paris is great in people and in the felicity of her situation, he says. He calls it the glory of France and a noble ornament of the world. Travellers and history lovers get a warm, learned city story.
45602-buffon-s-natural-history-volume-02:
Volume two of the ten volume English Buffon, printed in London in 1797, carries on a wide survey of nature taken from the French. Its first and longest part gives proof for a theory of the earth. Short pieces, called articles, treat seas and lakes, tides, winds, and storms in turn.

Later articles turn to volcanoes and earthquakes, new islands, caves, rain, marshes, and land that has changed into sea. The volume then starts a history of animals. Chapters there compare animals with plants, and treat food, growth, and how young are born. Notes by the translator run through the text. Readers get an early, orderly attempt to explain the whole face of the earth in one scheme.
45604-the-lives-of-the-saints-volume-02-:
Baring-Gould wrote these lives of the saints in sixteen volumes, of which this is the second. February is its month, with a frontispiece of the repose in Egypt after Cranach. Dancing angels attend the flight in that picture, the caption at the front explains.

The painter points by a robbed nest to the massacre of the innocents, it adds. This new edition is revised with an introduction and added lives of English martyrs, the title states. Cornish and Welsh saints join the calendar, with a full index promised to the entire work, in the standard Victorian lives of the saints.
45639-buffon-s-natural-history-volume-03:
Buffon, the great French student of nature, stands behind this third volume of his Natural History. The English version, with notes by its translator, came out in London in 1807. The full work runs to ten volumes, under the name Barr's Buffon.

The title page maps the whole: a theory of the earth, a history of man, of beasts, and of plants and stones. This volume turns to the history of animals. Long chapters treat how life is bred, with trials and tests set out in full. Buffon weighs his own sightings against those of Leeuwenhoek, the Dutch lens man. Thoughts on the trials close the part of the list shown here.
45645-japan-from-the-japanese-government:
Japan, in the History of Nations series, was published in New York by Collier under copyrights of 1907, 1910, and 1913. The copy at hand is the Ghent Edition, volume seven of the series. Henry Cabot Lodge stands as editor-in-chief, and the Japan volume is drawn from the Japanese government history, edited with supplementary chapters by Asakawa, instructor in Japanese civilization at Yale University.

Plates at the front face the reader with the late war in Manchuria: the Japanese and Russian commanders on the Liaotung Peninsula, drawn by Koekkoek from photographs. Generals Nodzu, Kuroki, Nogi, and Oku stand for Japan, Marshal Oyama over them as victor at Liao-yang, Sha-ho, and Mukden. Kuropatkin and his successor Lignievitch stand for Russia. The associate editors named run from Sayce at Oxford to Mommsen at Berlin.
45674-prison-poetry:
McKnight's Prison Poetry was copyrighted in 1896 and signed from the Ohio Penitentiary at Columbus. A verse on the title page asks readers to cast a look at the book and think of the writer in his cell. The preface explains that fellow prisoners helped fill the pages. Donated verses are credited by the donor's name or serial number. Some had already appeared in the prison paper, the News, which reached few readers outside the walls.

McKnight's motto is exchange: let free readers share the prisoners' solitary musings and noblest resolutions. Men are not devoid of principle, he insists, because they are cast, some justly and others unjustly, into prison. A dedication poem sends the little volume forth to its fate. Many of the verses were meant to reappear in the appendix of his work on crime and criminals.
45683-the-wonder-child-an-australian-sto:
Ethel Turner's The Wonder-Child, an Australian story, was published in London in 1901 by the Religious Tract Society, in its fifth impression, with illustrations by Gordon Browne. Turner, who also wrote as Mrs Curlewis, had written Seven Little Australians and The Camp at Wandinong before it. A passage from Robert Browning on making life fair heads the book, and a frontispiece shows Hermie.

Chapter one, Two Worlds, walks the schoolchildren of Wilgandra to the paddock where their horses graze. Peter Small, the butcher's son, jabs at Bartie Cameron for having no present for the teacher. Bartie, whose boots are burst and whose father holds a mortgage over sheep, answers airily that mortgages make the sheep grow. The contents run on through Dunks' selection, thirty thousand a year, an atheist, a squatter patriot, and a crossing of the veldt.
45729-buffon-s-natural-history-volume-04:
Buffon's Natural History, in the Barr edition of 1807, runs to ten volumes translated from the French. Volume four, printed in London, belongs to the general history of man. Buffon, the great French naturalist, set out to describe the earth, mankind, animals, vegetables, and minerals in one vast work.

This volume continues the account of infancy, then treats puberty and gives a description of man. Old age and death follow. Chapters on the sense of seeing, the sense of hearing, and the senses in general come next. The volume closes with the varieties of the human species, Buffon's attempt to explain how one stock of mankind spread and changed across climates. His flowing style made natural history popular reading across Europe.
45730-buffon-s-natural-history-volume-05:
Buffon's Natural History, in the Barr's Buffon set of ten volumes, is a work from the French with notes by the translator. Volume five was printed in London in 1807 and sold by Symonds of Paternoster Row. The set as a whole treats the theory of the earth, man, beasts, plants, and stones.

This volume opens the History of the Brute Creation with a long part on the nature of animals. Buffon sets out to compare their build, mark their likeness to man, and sort out their differences. A second part turns to tame beasts kept by man. The horse fills the most room, then the ass and the ox. Sheep, goats, swine, and the dog close the volume, each with plates.
45731-buffon-s-natural-history-volume-06:
Buffon Natural History, volume six of ten, treats beasts in English dress. Barr Buffon was sold by Symonds of London in eighteen o seven. The set holds a theory of the earth, a history of man, and brute creation. Vegetables and minerals share the great French naturalist plan as well.

Volume six opens with domestic animals, the cat standing first among them. Wild animals follow: the stag, fallow deer, roebuck, hare, and rabbit in turn. Meat eating animals fill chapter four, from wolf and fox to badger and otter. Martin, polecat, ferret, weasel, ermine, and squirrel follow in close order. Rat, mouse, hedgehog, mole, and bat close the beast catalogue here.
45821-buffon-s-natural-history-volume-08:
Volume eight of Buffon's Natural History, in the Barr edition of 1807 translated from the French, treats animals in careful, ordered essays. The contents open with the camel and the dromedary, then move through the buffalo, zebu, sheep, zebra, and hippopotamus.

Later essays cover the elk, giraffe, llama, sloths, porcupine, hamster, jerboa, and many more, each with engraved plates. The opening essay explains that camel and dromedary are two races of one species, told apart by two humps against one. Cross-bred offspring, it says, are stronger than either parent. Readers get the great French naturalist's menagerie, one animal at a time.
45858-lucian-s-true-history:
Lucians True History is an old Greek tale of wild travel in new English. Francis Hickes turned the text, and three artists drew its plates. Charles Whibley wrote the lead in for this fine press print. The book came out in London in the year nineteen two.

Lucian sails past the known world to the moon and the deep sea. Vast spiders, a war of turnips, and a feast of fish crowd the route. A whales vast mouth gives the crew a strange inn for a time. Dream isles, sage groves, and isle maids of vines mark the far road home. The tale mocks tall travel tales and stands as the first of its kind.
45868-buffon-s-natural-history-volume-10:
Volume ten closes Barr Buffon Natural History, Englished from the French. Symonds sold the set in London, this volume in 1807. It follows a theory of earth and histories of man and beasts. Translator notes run with the text through the ten volumes.

Contents open with the degeneration of animals across kinds and lands. Deer with solid branched horns form a separate family, Buffon argues. Light, heat, fire, air, water, and earth get long essays. Trials on heat in minerals and burning mirrors follow in turn. General views of nature close the tenth and final volume of the set.
46013-famous-american-belles-of-the-nine:
Virginia Tatnall Peacock sketches society queens in Famous American Belles of the Nineteenth Century, printed at Philadelphia and London in 1901. Lippincott made the book, with copyright in 1900. A portrait of Emily Marshall, painted by Chester Harding, fronts the volume. Peacock gives the book to her dear mother.

Short lives run from Marcia Burns to Adele Cutts. Theodosia Burr and Elizabeth Patterson, who wed Jerome Bonaparte, stand early in the line. The Caton sisters share a chapter. Margaret O'Neill, Cora Livingston, and Emily Marshall fill the mid run. Octavia Walton, Jessie Benton, who wed Fremont, Sallie Ward, and Harriet Lane keep the parade of beauty and fame. Portraits dress each life.
46020-the-gayton-scholarship-a-school-st:
Herbert Hayens wrote this school story for Nelson, published in 1904. Dick Boden opens it, bringing wild flowers for his chum's invalid sister Susie. Dick is the school pickle and the school darling at once: round-faced, curly-haired, honest as the day. The art teacher once painted him as an angel, and the Deanery boys dubbed him the Angel for it. His chum Jim Hartland is a sailor's son and one of the head boys.

The talk is of the Gayton Scholarship, which pays fees and books to sixteen. Jim will be a candidate for certain, and Perce Braithwaite another. The contents darken the playground: news of the Morning Star, an examination, missing money, and the question, is Jim a thief? An amateur detective and a fresh start close the tale. Hayens mixes the exam room with the mystery in the approved school-story way.
46064-the-deep-lake-mystery:
Carolyn Wells wrote Deep Lake Mystery, a tale of crime put out in New York with rights from 1928. Wells had told a long shelf of such tales, of crypts, of keys, and of lost girls. She gives this book to her dear friend Lucy C Joyce. A first part takes its name from a famed poem of a dome of bliss.

The teller looks back on a life calm in long spans, with thrills in spots. The great thrill of that life, he says, came at the sight of a dead man. That man was Sampson Tracy, found by the lake of the tale. Parts bear names like The Girl in the Canoe and The Lady of the Lake. A nail, a watch in a jug of water, and a court of inquiry speed the hunt.
46077-the-judgment-books-a-story:
Benson wrote The Judgment Books, a story, printed in New York in 1895. Benson had written Dodo. A plate shows a figure cut and stabbed in fifty places. The first chapter opens on a terrace to the south of Penalva Forest. It basks in early September sunshine. Even the bees from two hives beneath the laurel bushes seem drowsy at their work.

Eight steps lead down to a lawn with a tennis court. Below the lawn the ground slopes to a fence along brown rocks. Over them the still water of the Fal estuary creeps up at high tide. The woods climb steeply from near the water's edge to a broad Cornish moor, purple and gold with gorse and heather. In a corner of the lawn, on a wicker sofa in the shade, lies Jack Armitage. His thoughts, just now, run only on tea-time.
46104-the-girl-in-industry:
Collier's investigation of the girl in industry was published by Bell at London in 1918, with a foreword and introduction by Hutchins, author of Women in Modern Industry. Stanley Hall's words on adolescence stand at the front: the stage of life most inviting study and in most crying need of service. Collier's charge is that the law guards the child worker and then forgets her. Restrictions on hours and conditions for young persons differ but slightly from those for adult women.

The evidence, Collier argues, points the other way. Children often grow despite hardship, while adolescence is easily retarded by unfavourable surroundings. Witnesses before the Physical Deterioration Committee in 1904 stressed the falling off in physique when girls of fourteen to eighteen pass from school to work. The first part of the book investigates; the second recommends. Tables close a wartime study written while girl labour filled the factories.
46153-the-notting-hill-mystery:
The Notting Hill Mystery is a detective novel by Charles Felix, first printed in the magazine Once a Week from November 1862 to January 1863. An editorial note introduces the papers of the case. It asks readers to attend closely to names and dates to follow the compiler's view. The evidence, it warns, is circumstantial.

The compiler believes he has found a new species of crime. The tale unfolds as an insurance investigator's dossier of letters, statements, and reports. A baron, his wife, and a strange poisoning in Notting Hill stand at its centre. The book is among the earliest full detective novels in English, built from documents rather than narration.
46274-oxford-and-its-story:
Cecil Headlam wrote Oxford and Its Story, first printed in 1904 and here in a second, cheaper edition from London in 1912. Herbert Railton drew twenty-four lithographs and other pictures, tinted by Fanny Railton. Oxford Castle fronts the book. Headlam had written books on Nuremberg and Chartres before this one.

The contents start with St Frideswide and the cathedral, then the mound, the castle, and some churches. The origin of the university and the coming of the friars follow. A long chapter treats the medieval student, and later ones take Oxford through the Reformation and its martyrs. Elizabeth, Bodley, and Laud share a chapter, and the royalist capital and Jacobite Oxford close the tale.
46344-eighty-fourth-regiment-pennsylvani:
Captain Thomas Merchant's address marks the placing of a monument to the Eighty-fourth Regiment, Pennsylvania Volunteers, on the Gettysburg battlefield in 1889. Pennsylvania had voted money in 1887 for a tablet or monument for each of its commands at Gettysburg. A regimental committee chose the design and the words cut in stone. One hundred and forty-six comrades came back for the dedication day.

The pamphlet prints the whole ceremony: the opening words, the chaplain's prayer and letters from men who could not come. General Carr, who had led the brigade holding the 84th, spoke as well. The survivors asked for print so the day would not be lost.
4636-a-tramp-through-the-bret-harte-coun:
Thomas Dykes Beasley, author of The Coming of Portola, wrote A Tramp Through the Bret Harte Country, with a foreword by Charles A. Murdock. A verse from Dickens in Camp stands at its head, with pines, a slowly drifting moon, a singing river, and dim Sierras lifting minarets of snow. Chapters begin with reminiscences of Bret Harte, Plain Language from Truthful James, and the glamour of old mining towns, before the tramp itself begins.

The route runs from Stockton to Angel's Camp, Tuttletown and the Sage of Jackass Hill, and Tuolumne to Placerville. Charm of Sonora, San Andreas, and Mokelumne Hill follow, with Bradley and the Cary House, ruins of Coloma, and James W. Marshall and his pathetic end. Auburn to Nevada City, Grass Valley to Smartsville, and Smartsville to Marysville close the walk. Readers get a literary walking tour of gold country, full of Harte lore and pioneer memory.
46433-a-handbook-of-pictorial-history:
Henry Donald wrote and drew this handbook of history in pictures for students and teachers. It holds 680 plates from first-hand and old sources. Donald also made the Britannic Historical Geography and sets of history plates for schools.

The title page lists its fields: building, arms and armour, old finds, dress, and customs. Shipping, heraldry, and the church join the roll. Notes and short articles on each theme stand with the plates. Such a book lets a class see the past, not just read of it. A teacher of 1900 could show a Norman helm, a Tudor gown, and a man-of-war side by side, each drawn from true sources.
4653-god-s-good-man-a-simple-love-story:
Marie Corelli calls God's Good Man a simple love story, dedicating it to the living original of the Reverend John Walden and his wife. Her epigraph quotes the New Testament: there was a man sent from God whose name was John. The book opens in May-time in England, after a long, hard winter whose last frost has melted from broad, low-lying fields, and whose young corn now sprouts thick and tender green.

Buds nipped by cruel cold, biting east winds, and stormy northern caprices have played havoc with woodland blossoms. Into that English spring comes a tale of a good clergyman, love, and duty, told in Corelli's warm, earnest manner. Readers get a popular Edwardian romance of faith and feeling, with country detail and a moral heart, for readers who like a story that wears its goodness openly.
46729-the-history-of-yiddish-literature-:
Leo Wiener, who taught Slavic tongues at Harvard, wrote a history of Yiddish letters in the nineteenth century, issued in New York in 1899. He gave the book to his mother. Early parts set out the Judeo German tongue itself, then the folk lore and folk songs of its speakers.

Later parts trace verse before the 1880s, then the new verse in Russia and in America after that line. Prose men get three runs of parts, from the early years through the age of Abramowitsch to the age of Spektor, Rabinowitsch, and Perez. The Jewish theatre and other forms close the survey. A reader of samples at the end gives short texts in Yiddish with English heads.
46947-the-lives-of-the-saints-volume-01-:
Rev S Baring Gould wrote The Lives of the Saints, here volume one of sixteen, for January, in a new edition issued in London by John C Nimmo in MDCCCXCVII. Over four hundred engravings illustrate the set. The new edition adds lives of English martyrs and Cornish and Welsh saints. Baring Gould preface to the first edition of eighteen seventy two opens the work.

The undertaking difficulty few can have any idea, he says. Saints lived in every century for eighteen hundred years, he notes. Their acts are interwoven with the profane history of almost every nation, he adds. Records are sometimes fragmentary, sometimes mere hints, and some are forgeries, he grants. January saints follow day by day, from the Circumcision onward. Church readers get the great Victorian saints calendar.
46967-isabella-orsini-a-historical-novel:
Guerrazzi wrote this Italian historical novel, Englished by Luigi Monti of Harvard. The book came out in New York in 1859 with Rudd and Carleton. Its scene is Italy in the fifteenth century, as the title states. A drawn portrait of Isabella Orsini fronts the volume.

Chapter heads run Guilt, Love, and a knight named Lionardo Salviati. Homicide, jealousy, and a confession drive the dark plot onward. Death closes the named chain of chapters in stark, grave terms. The tale blends passion and crime in a rich old Italian frame. The knight Lionardo Salviati stands near the heart of the plot.
47002-the-usurper-an-episode-in-japanese:
The Usurper is a historical novel by Judith Gautier, translated from the French by Abby Langdon Alger. Roberts Brothers published it at Boston in 1884. Its subtitle calls it an episode in Japanese history. The contents list thirty one chapters. The Lemon Grove opens the tale, and Nagato's Wound follows. Feasts, castles, tea houses, and hawking parties fill the middle chapters. The Usurper himself is named at the mid point of the book.

The story is dated to the year 1615 in its head note. It opens at night in the bright city of Osaka. Sentinels call to one another on the ramparts in the dark. The palace and gardens of the Shogun loom over the city. A star fades above that dark mass as dawn nears. Later chapters bring battles and a funeral pile. The novel dresses Japanese court intrigue for Western readers of its day.
47032-baudelaire-his-prose-and-poetry:
Smith edited this set of Baudelaire prose and poetry in English dress. Boni and Liveright printed the book in New York in 1919. A Swinburne poem, Ave Atque Vale, opens the volume in tribute. A study of Baudelaire life and art by Sturm follows it.

Prose poems come from Arthur Symons, Shipley, and Sturm in turn. Titles range from Windows and Crowds to Be Drunken and Solitude. The Flowers of Evil close the book in Sturm English form. Dance of Death, The Beacons, and Spleen stand among its famed pieces. Smith edited the volume for Boni and Liveright.
4707-the-valley-of-silent-men-a-story-of:
James Oliver Curwood sets The Valley of Silent Men in the Three River country, opening at Athabasca Landing before the railroad bit its way through the wilderness. That landing, still called Iskwatam, the door, opens to the lower Athabasca, the Slave, and the Mackenzie. Its history, Curwood says, runs through more than a hundred and forty years of romance, tragedy, and adventure, about a hundred and fifty miles north of Edmonton by the old trail.

Beyond that door the wilderness still howls as it always has, and the story follows men and women caught in its silence, law, and violence. A frontispiece shows a girl's revolver spitting smoke and flame, a sign of the action to come. Readers get a northern adventure of pursuit and justice, with rivers, forests, and remote settlements, in Curwood's fast, vivid style.
47098-all-sorts-and-conditions-of-men-an:
All Sorts and Conditions of Men is a novel by Walter Besant and James Rice. Its subtitle calls it an impossible story, a hint at its bold social scheme. A preface tells that the ten year partnership of Besant and Rice was ended by death. Besant writes that nothing short of death would have closed their joint work.

The book is offered to the memory of Rice in a brief dedication page. Their tales of London life had won a wide public in their joint years. An heiress scheme to lift the poor of the East End drives this famous tale. Social hope and city poverty stand at the heart of the story told.
47206-nineteen-centuries-of-drink-in-eng:
Nineteen Centuries of Drink in England is a history by Richard Valpy French, rector of Llanmartin. The hosted copy is the second edition, enlarged and revised. It was issued from a temperance depot at London. French also wrote a history of toasting, his title page notes. Part of the book first ran in a London weekly journal.

The introduction sets out the aim of the work. It seeks the part drink has played in the life of the English people, each man and the nation. It asks what beverages have been in use and what customs went with them. Drinking vessels in vogue are treated too. Efforts to control or ban strong drink, by church or state, form another thread. The tie between the drink traffic and the revenue is also traced.
47245-battles-of-english-history:
Battles of English History is a military history by Hereford George of Oxford. George was a fellow of New College in that university city. Methuen published the book in London in the year 1895. A first map outlines England and Wales for the campaigns ahead. Contents open with an introductory chapter, then Hastings at page nine.

The Barons' War follows as the third chapter of the battle list. Norman conquest, civil wars, and later fields fill the march of chapters. George writes for students who need causes clear and ground plain. Maps and crisp narrative carry each fight from Hastings onward in time. School and college readers of 1895 learned England by her battles.
47371-first-lessons-in-the-maori-languag:
First Lessons in the Maori Language is a small tongue guide by Williams. A Trubner house of London brought it out in eighteen sixty two. Its full name adds a short word list at the book end in full. Williams grants it is no full tract on the tongue in strict form. Plain hints on speech part use fill its small space by plan.

Snags that meet new hands first are its chief aim to clear out. Choice of points was no light task, he grants in the front words. Tongue speech can not be learned from books alone, he warns at end. Talk with the folk who use that tongue is the true school, he holds. Maunsell word craft book will pay deep study, he adds as a guide.
47476-poems-of-american-history:
Poems of American History is an anthology collected and edited by Burton Egbert Stevenson, published by Houghton Mifflin. Copyrights of 1908 and 1922 cover the collection. It opens with America, Samuel Francis Smith's hymn beginning My country, 'tis of thee. The copyright notice lists the poets and publishers whose work fills the volume, all rights reserved by their holders.

From the Century Company come Richard Watson Gilder's poems, including At the President's Grave, Charleston, and The White City. Robert Underwood Johnson contributes Dewey at Manila. Silas Weir Mitchell gives Herndon, How the Cumberland Went Down, Kearsarge, Lincoln, and The Song of the Flags. Stevenson's plan is to let the nation's verse tell the nation's story, battle by battle and hero by hero. Such anthologies stood in schoolrooms and parlours as the family record of American memory in verse.
47586-everyday-objects-or-picturesque-as:
Everyday Objects; or, Picturesque Aspects of Natural History is a popular science book edited and enlarged by Davenport Adams. William Nimmo published it in London and Edinburgh in 1876, with numerous illustrations. Adams had earlier made a companion volume called The Circle of the Year.

In his preface Adams explains the design. The earlier book drew on the first series of a popular French work, Les Saisons, by Hoefer, and this one follows the second series. He omitted much, revised more, and added considerably at many points. His standpoint, he says, is popular rather than scientific. He does not aim to lay the foundations of any science. Instead he shows how much wonder lies in familiar things around us. A line from Milton stands on the title page: to know what lies about us in daily life is the prime wisdom.
47663-mr-oseba-s-last-discovery:
George Bell, who signs himself Colonel Bell and seven years United States consul at Sydney, Australia, wrote this book, printed by the New Zealand Times Company at Wellington in 1904. He dedicates what he calls these erratic pages to the people of New Zealand, the most advanced community among men.

Bell explains in a note that he came to New Zealand in early 1903 on a lecture tour. He heard the colony called submerged with socialism, and set out to inquire who started the town and for what purpose. He studied the literature, mingled with the people, and sat through parliamentary sittings taking notes. What others derided as socialism he found to be a series of cooperative measures, promising not nerveless socialism but the sturdiest democracy civilization had produced. An individualist himself, he measured the colony against his long study of Anglo-Saxon history.
47673-the-pinos-altos-story:
The Pinos Altos Story, by Dorothy Watson, was first printed in July 1960 at Silver City, New Mexico, and reprinted through 1970. Watson tells the past of Pinos Altos, the oldest Anglo settlement in Grant County. The small town stands in the southwestern part of the state.

The town lies across the Continental Divide at just over 7000 feet, between the Diablo Range and the Pinos Altos Mountains. Bear Creek starts in those mountains, splits the town, and joins the Gila River twenty miles off. Tall pines once covered the site. Parts of the book treat early history, the 1880s and 1890s, schools, churches, and mines. Family tales and a look at the town today close it. Local past fans get a mining town whole life in short form.
47823-jewellery:
Jewellery is a survey of the goldsmith's art by Clifford Smith, issued in the Connoisseur's Library in 1908. The New York issue is from Putnam's Sons and the London issue from Methuen. Plates open the book, starting with pendent jewels of enamelled gold from the fifteen hundreds.

The chapters run in time order across the whole field. Egypt and Phoenicia come first, then Greek, Etruscan, and Roman work. Byzantine, Celtic, and Anglo-Saxon pieces follow. The middle ages get a long block of chapters. They treat the lore of precious stones, head ornaments, necklaces, pendants, rosaries, brooches, rings, and belts. The survey closes with the Renaissance, starting in Italy. The book suits readers who collect, as well as those who study craft and dress.
4789-black-caesar-s-clan-a-florida-myste:
Albert Payson Terhune wrote Black Caesar's Clan as a Florida mystery story, dedicated to John E. Pickett. Its contents run from The Hidden Path and The Man in the Dark, through The Mocking Bird and The Stranger from Nowhere, to Traps and Trapper and In the Day of Battle. Secrets, The Siege, The Figure in White, and The Ghost Tree follow.

The foreword begins not with a villain but with a wiggling, brainless, slimy atom, the coral worm, and trillions of its kind. Living and dying on the sea bottom, successive generations piled higher on skeletons and lifework of those before. At last a coral reef rose in uncharted waters tall enough to smash a wooden ship's keel. Above the waves it nosed its way, greyish white, until a mangrove bud floated a hundred miles to touch it. Readers get a mystery rooted in a Florida island's strange birth.
47989-the-yellow-phantom-a-judy-bolton-m:
The Yellow Phantom is a Judy Bolton mystery by Margaret Sutton, held under a 1933 copyright and printed in New York by Grosset and Dunlap. A plate shows Judy glancing at Jasper Crosby, who watches her like a cat. The book stands sixth in the Judy Bolton list.

Early chapters open with a mysterious telegram and a discovery by Irene. A daring scheme is tried, then put to the test. A new yellow gown stands in the heads, which hints at the phantom of the title. The series list at the front runs from The Vanishing Shadow to The Trail of the Green Doll. Girl readers of the 1930s got a bright, brave sleuth in Judy, with clues, risk, and friends at her side.
48133-the-secret-victory:
Secret Victory is a novel by Stephen McKenna, third of The Sensationalists. Doran of New York issued the trilogy close in nineteen twenty two. Lady Lilith and The Education of Eric Lane form parts one and two. McKenna gives this volume to Alexander Teixeira de Mattos with gratitude.

A dedicatory letter thanks him for reading all three volumes in manuscript. Friendship long, intimate, and unmatched is the bond McKenna celebrates there. Shortcomings in the tale are McKenna own, he acquits his friend of blame. Sonia, Sonia Married, and Midas and Son stand in his other works list. Ninety Six Hours Leave and The Sixth Sense complete the Doran shelf.
48144-the-mystery-of-the-iron-box-a-ken-:
Bruce Campbell wrote a mystery for boys in the Ken Holt series, and Grosset and Dunlap copyrighted it in 1952. The tale opens in the great hall of an airport. Crowds press to the windows that face the landing field. A slender young man in a gray flannel suit and tan trench coat finds the crush too thick and heads outside.

His mate towers over him, with shoulders that hint at great strength. The chapters that follow are brisk and ominous. They bring a cold draft, a fire, a scrap of film, and a booby trap. A package changes hands, and some ounces go missing. Deep waters, a catapult, and a robbery by the waves fill the later pages. The iron box of the title comes back near the end, and the tale closes with front page news.
48196-zoo-logy-the-science-of-animal-lif:
Zoology: The Science of Animal Life, by Ernest Ingersoll, is volume twelve of the Popular Science Library issued by Collier in 1922. The series ran to sixteen volumes. Ingersoll's volume opens with a reflection on how early man pondered the nature and origin of life. It then sets out to stock the globe with life in orderly chapters.

The contents move from how the globe was stocked with life to the sea as a vast aquarium. A chapter of foundations follows, then the humblest animals, the sponges. From such beginnings the book works upward through the animal kingdom for the general reader. The series editor was Garrett Serviss, and the volume is illustrated. It aims to give lay readers a clear, connected account of animal life and its order, in the plain style of the popular science of its day.
48233-lincoln-s-love-story:
Eleanor Atkinson wrote a tale of the love of Abraham Lincoln for Ann Rutledge. The book came out in New York in 1909. Atkinson also wrote The Boyhood of Lincoln. Jay Hambidge drew the pictures. The tale first ran in the Ladies' Home Journal in 1908. There it bore the name of Ann Rutledge in its title.

Lincoln is shown as a young man in love and in grief. A line in the front plate has him dread her lone in a storm. The short book treats a famed, sad part of his youth. It stays close to the tale as folk have told it. Readers get a soft, grave glimpse of young Lincoln.
48245-mr-punch-s-irish-humour-in-picture:
Editors of the Punch Library of Humour gathered Irish jokes from Punch magazine, from its start in 1841 onward. Hammerton edited the set. This volume holds one hundred fifty four pictures by famed Punch artists. Charles Keene, Phil May, and George du Maurier are among the hands at work.

One front joke shows a man with his coat buttoned on a warm day to hide the shirt he does not own. The editors leave out the bitter jokes on Fenians and Home Rule, they say. What stays is stage Irish wit, priest and peasant tales, and bulls and blunders in speech. The book shows how London laughed at Ireland, for good and ill, across sixty years.
48319-lincoln-and-the-sleeping-sentinel-:
Lincoln and the Sleeping Sentinel tells the true story of a famed pardon. Chittenden, register of the treasury from 1861, tells the tale himself. Harper and Brothers published it in New York in January 1909. Chittenden also wrote Recollections of President Lincoln and His Administration. Portraits of Lincoln, one from a Howard Pyle painting, front the book.

Lincoln in 1857, from a photograph, appears among the illustrations. The tale turns on a young sentry who slept at his post on duty. By the usual account, Lincoln spared the boy from a death sentence. Chittenden claims the true version, told by a man who was there. Readers fond of Lincoln lore get a short, pointed anecdote in full.
48454-inventors-at-work-with-chapters-on:
George Iles, who wrote Flame, Electricity and the Camera, made this book on the men who invent. Doubleday, Page printed Inventors at Work at New York in 1907, thick with plates. A portrait of Alexander Graham Bell heads the list of plates.

Iles gave the book to his friend Josephus Larned of Buffalo. Form opens the study, with a neat point: a joist is stiffer than a plank of the same stuff. The girder grows from the joist, and rail tracks are girders in their turn. Such plain steps link workshop craft to great finds. Chapters on how finds are made stand beside tales of the men who made them.
48511-vikram-and-the-vampire-or-tales-of:
Vikram and the Vampire, or tales of Hindu devilry, is a set of Indian wonder tales adapted by Richard Burton, printed at London. Its front picture shows a pair returning in silence over three hours. Burton calls the book tales of Hindu devilry on his title page, in the bold manner of his time. The frame is famous in Indian story.

King Vikram, sent to fetch a corpse haunted by a vampire spirit, must carry it in silence. The spirit tells tale after tale on the road, each ending in a riddle the king cannot help answering. Each answer breaks the silence, and the corpse flies back to its tree. Burton, the great traveller and linguist, Englished the cycle from its Sanskrit line. His version carried the tales to readers across the English speaking world.
48621-light-fingered-gentry:
Light Fingered Gentry is a novel by David Graham Phillips, published at New York in nineteen oh seven. The hosted title page credits other works by the author, such as The Second Generation. A portrait of Neva is set as the frontispiece. The chapter list runs to more than thirty items.

Chapter heads sketch a tale of family, love, and social rise. They move from a matrimonial mistake and a feast that ends in a fiasco to Neva at school and in her studio. Names such as Armstrong, Hugo, Boris, and the Fosdick family recur through the list. A riddle is solved by Neva, a proposal is made, and a duel follows lunch. The tale roots give a clear map of its cast.
48767-the-quest-of-glory:
The Quest of Glory, a novel by Marjorie Bowen, author of The Viper of Milan, was first published by Methuen in London in 1912. A French epigraph from Vauvenargues heads it, on the natural authority glory gives over hearts. The book is built in three parts: the quest joyful, the quest sorrowful, and the quest triumphant.

The joyful part opens at Prague in 1742, in the chapel of Saint Wenceslas, and names Carola Koklinska, a blunder of Cardinal Fleury, and the retreat from Prague. The sorrowful part moves to Paris: a walled garden, a pavilion at Versailles, despair, a painter, Voltaire, the Louvre, and a convent. The triumphant part promises a father, a return to life, a betrothed, and a conflict. Bowen's other listed works include I Will Maintain, Defender of the Faith, and God and the King.
48860-the-brown-owl-a-fairy-story:
The Brown Owl is a fairy story by Ford Hueffer, printed at New York in 1892 as volume one of The Children's Library. Madox Brown, the artist, drew its two pictures, and this copy is a third edition. The tale opens long before Egypt rose to power, or Rome or Greece were heard of, in a vast and mighty kingdom.

Its king, Intafernes, has reigned nine hundred and ninety-nine and a half years, kept on the throne by magic. In his land the people split into magicians, who call themselves Aristocrats, and the rest. The king is the greatest magician of all, save that his chancellor, Merrymineral, comes near him. A beautiful daughter completes the court of this wry, learned fairy tale.
48882-the-mystery-of-the-ravenspurs-a-ro:
The Mystery of the Ravenspurs is a novel by Fred White, published in New York by Ogilvie and copyrighted in 1911, with illustrations by Takacs. Its subtitle calls it a romance and detective story of Thibet and England. A frontispiece shows a dark Eastern face inside a circle, its awful eyes filled with agony, rage, and pain.

Chapter one, The Shadow of a Fear, sets the scene at a granite castle above the North Sea. The castle has housed the Ravenspurs for five hundred years, its moat, drawbridge, and portcullis intact. The family is rich, with a chronicle of brave and bloody deeds behind it, yet a shadow hangs over the house. No Ravenspur ever shrank from a tangible danger, but this fear turns the stoutest heart to water and makes strong men start at their shadows.
48910-a-digit-of-the-moon-a-hindoo-love-:
Bain translated A Digit of the Moon, a Hindoo love story, from a manuscript. Methuen at London put out this ninth edition in November 1911. The book first appeared from another house in 1898, the list says. Editions ran in 1901, 1902, 1904, 1906, and 1909 in turn. Bain gives the book to his wife on the dedication page.

A preface to the second edition explains a stanza on its fly-leaf. In Hindoo mythology, a beautiful woman, the moon, and the sea dissolve together. Those three ideas merge, Bain writes there. The stanza calls the lady an incarnation of the nectar-dropping moon. Come down from heaven to lighten our darkness, it begs her. In a literal prose version, the reverberation is lost, he owns. The echo of the sea undertones the word he renders, he adds. Bain gives an Indian tale in a poet's English dress.
49081-reube-dare-s-shad-boat-a-tale-of-t:
Charles Roberts wrote Reube Dare's Shad Boat, in 1895. A tale of the tide country is its second title. Hunt and Eaton at New York put out the boy's book. The Dido Goes Adrift opens the contents of the tale. The Red Bull and the Chase of the Dido follow in it.

A cave and a prison house follow. A hacked shad net fills the middle list. The boat's first fishing trip comes later. Foiling the sharks stands late in it. A shot from the rocks closes the contents in drama. She's adrift, he shouted in one pictured moment of it. It was coin, all coin, another picture's caption exclaims. A dozen shad showed their shining silvery sides in a third. Roberts gives the Bay of Fundy tides a boy's crew.
49112-national-apostasy-considered-in-a-:
