National Apostasy is a sermon by John Keble, preached in Saint Mary's, Oxford, before His Majesty's judges of assize on Sunday, July 14, 1833. Keble was a fellow of Oriel College and professor of poetry in the university. The sermon was printed at Oxford by Parker in the same year. An advertisement added for the press explains the occasion.

Keble's charge is against the legislature itself. For a state legislature to dispose of the church's own order was, in the sermon's terms, national apostasy. The sermon is famous beyond its pages: it is counted the opening act of the Oxford Movement, the campaign to renew the Church of England's catholic doctrine. The pamphlet preserves the text as Keble published it, with his own angry preface written after the act had passed.
49177-india-under-ripon-a-private-diary:
India Under Ripon is a private diary by Wilfrid Scawen Blunt, printed in London in 1909. It continues his Secret History of the English Occupation of Egypt. The book records India as he found it in the years of Lord Ripon's viceroyalty. Blunt says he might well have called it The Awakening of India.

The chapters trace a tour: Ceylon, Madras, Hyderabad, Calcutta, Patna and Lucknow, then Delhi and Rajputana. They take in the Nizam's installation at Hyderabad and a Mohammedan university. Later chapters step back to judge: an apology for failure, the agricultural danger, race hatred, and the Mohammedan question. The book closes on the future of self-government for India. Letters from Sir William Hunter and Major Claude Clerk fill the appendices. It is an insider's diary with a rebel's edge.
4918-the-lilac-sunbonnet-a-love-story:
Ralph Peden rests under a thorn bush above the Grannoch water in Galloway, and this love story follows the young man through heather, lochs, and parish life. His father's friend Allan Welsh, minister of the Marrow kirk at Dullarg, questions him closely about his soul's health and his life among the pious folk of the great city.

The novel weaves romance with Scottish religious life, as Ralph finds love amid preaching, grasshoppers, and bees drunk on heather scent. The catalog record names no author, so the story stands on its own pastoral charm. Readers get a gentle tale of faith and feeling in a countryside rendered with affectionate detail.
49304-days-before-history:
Days Before History, by Hall, with illustrations by Randall, was printed by Harrap in London. A first edition of November 1906 was followed by a second, revised, enlarged, and newly illustrated, in September 1908. Its preface to the new edition sets honest limits: in a book of this kind nothing more will be expected than an outline sketch of some phases of prehistoric life in Britain.

The known facts are few, Hall admits, and habits differed between tribes and places. But the learned agree on various conclusions, and from those, with comparisons to primitive life in modern times, a picture can be built that stays within reasonable conjecture. Some licence is confessed: a man of the newer stone age is made to hear traditions of the old stone weapon makers and still witness the first bronze weapons arrive.
49356-hero-tales-from-history:
Smith Burnham, head of history at the Western State Normal School in Kalamazoo, wrote hero tales from history, copyrighted in 1922 and written for young readers. A picture of Benjamin Franklin's printing office opens the book. Moses is presented as the greatest law giver and the meekest man. David the giant killer king follows.

Homer, Socrates, and Alexander the boy who conquered the world fill the ancient part. Middle age heroes include Charlemagne crowned at Christmas and Joan of Arc. Shakespeare, Cromwell, Napoleon, and Nelson lead the old world section. Discoverers close the book: Columbus, Magellan, Cortes, De Soto, Drake, Raleigh, Hudson, and La Salle.
49445-mechanics-the-science-of-machinery:
Russell Bond's Mechanics: The Science of Machinery forms volume five of the Popular Science Library, published in New York by Collier in 1922. Bond had been managing editor of the Scientific American. Garrett Serviss edited the sixteen-volume set, and the frontispiece shows a drop forge: a fourteen-ton hydraulic press at work on an immense steel plate.

Twenty-four chapters survey the machine world. Tool-making animals and the anatomy of a machine come first, then machines for making machines, and counting seconds. Rivers are put to work, liquid levers and gears explained, and power drawn from heat. One chapter asks what happens when coal and oil are exhausted. The invasion of the sea and of the sky, help for the farmer, cloth, paper, printing machinery, and engines of destruction follow.
49468-arabella-stuart-a-romance-from-eng:
James wrote this romance from English history, printed at London by Simpkin, Marshall, and Company in 1849 as volume nineteen of his collected works, revised and corrected by the author. The volume opens with a long French preface on the novel as a form, quoting Madame de Stael on fiction's power over morals.

James dedicated the tale to Rear-Admiral Sir George Seymour, and in his letter he makes a striking admission about its making. The public, he writes, may judge this one of the most interesting tales he has written, yet he can take little credit for it. All the principal events are so strictly historical that little was left to the author but to tell them as agreeably as he could. Forty-six chapters carry the story of Arabella Stuart, the lady whose royal blood made her a danger to the crown.
49671-honest-wullie-and-effie-patterson-:
Honest Wullie is a Scottish tale by Lydia Rouse, published by the American Tract Society in 1884. The society issued the book at New York from Nassau Street, copyrighted that year. Rouse is named as author of Sandy Faith and Jim Bentley Resolve. Contents list the chapters of Wullie life and of Effie Patterson story beside it.

Wullie and Rab, The New Home, and Daft Jamie open the tale in order of the chapters. Death in the Cup, A Year of Gloom, and A Clear Sunset follow in the list. Home Life, The First Vacation, Belle, and Archie and Belle carry the shown contents on in the book. Rouse writes in the Scots of the village for an American tract audience. Hers is a temperance and faith tale in dialect. The drink of the death in the cup chapter is the enemy that the clear sunset answers.
49790-scottish-poetry-of-the-sixteenth-c:
Scottish Poetry of the Sixteenth Century is a volume in the Abbotsford Series of the Scottish Poets, edited by George Eyre-Todd. William Hodge and Company published it at Glasgow in 1892. The poets gathered are Sir David Lyndsay, John Bellenden, King James the Fifth, Sir Richard Maitland, Alexander Scot and Alexander Montgomerie.

An editor's note explains the volume's plan. Many fine editions, Eyre-Todd complains, make old language harder with the old long s, Anglo-Saxon letter forms, blackletter type and irritating punctuation. Such obstacles, with scarcity and cost, explain the popular neglect of a noble heritage. This series keeps the text intact but improves its readability, with a running gloss to help modern readers. Contents lists Lyndsay's works first, from The Dreme to the Papyngo poems.
49860-the-smuggler-of-king-s-cove-or-the:
The Smuggler of Kings Cove, or the Old Chapel Mystery, is a novel by Sylvanus Cobb the younger. The tale first bore a rights claim in the year eighteen ninety six. Its scene is a wild stretch of the coast of England. A bay and a hid cove shape the ground of the plot.

Eighteen chapters run through wrecks, crags, crypts, and shocks in fast order. A new lord, a dead mans reef, and a ghost in a monks chapel mark the turns. A broke hand leads to a find in a secret crypt below ground. Murder bids and castle panic raise the stakes near the close. A girls reveal near the end ties the loose threads of the tale.
49869-the-ways-of-a-worker-of-a-century-:
Ways of a Worker of a Century Ago draws on the diary of Joseph Lye. Fred Gannon built the small book from a talk and a shoe shop gift. Newcomb and Gauss of Salem printed it in nineteen eighteen. Henry Tapley gave the Lye shop to the Essex Institute.

Joseph Lye was a Lynn shoemaker born in seventeen ninety two in Massachusetts. He was one of nine sons of a shoemaker and Revolution soldier. His diary shows him as church clerk, fire club clerk, and juryman. He trained in the militia, sat with sick neighbours, and worked many trades. Shoemaking, painting, fishing, and small boat sailing all fill his busy days.
50038-the-story-of-hungary:
The Story of Hungary, published in 1886, is Arminius Vámbéry's volume in the Story of the Nations series, sold at a dollar fifty. Vámbéry taught at the University of Buda-Pesth and worked with Louis Heilprin on the book. He wrote it to make English and American readers know his native land. He chose story over deep history on purpose.

The narrative covers nearly a thousand years of Hungarian life. Vámbéry picks the salient events, the strong personalities and the thrilling episodes. A frontispiece shows the sally from the fortress of Szigetvár. He calls it the first story of Hungary written in English, and writes as a Hungarian man of letters for foreign friends.
50066-war-services-of-the-62nd-west-ridi:
Colonel Anderson wrote War Services of the 62nd West Riding Divisional Artillery, put out by Heffer at Cambridge in 1920. Anderson led the guns of the division from 1916 to 1919. A preface by Braithwaite, a lieutenant general, opens the book. It is given to the memory of fallen comrades, with a verse by Mary Byron. The tale starts on December 23, 1916, when the division was told to sail for France.

From Havre the guns were railed to Wavans, near Auxi-le-Chateau, in January 1917. Chapters trace trench war, Cambrai, the great German push, and a turn with the Fifth French Army. A final triumph and a last phase close the tale. Lists of officers and of honors fill the appendices. Gunners and kin get a clear record of their war.
50139-a-practical-treatise-on-the-manufa:
A Practical Treatise on the Manufacture of Perfumery is a trade manual by Doctor C Deite and several expert helpers. It was translated from the German by William T Brannt and published in Philadelphia in eighteen ninety two. Twenty eight engravings illustrate the book. Its title promises directions for making all kinds of perfumes.

Sachet powders, fumigating materials, tooth pastes, and cosmetics are all covered beside perfumes. A full account of volatile oils, balsams, resins, and other scent substances follows. Fruit ethers and their making are included, with tests of purity for the goods. The book served working makers who needed recipes, materials science, and checks in one volume.
50174-on-english-poetry:
A book of reflections by Robert Graves, published at New York in 1922. Alfred A Knopf issued the volume that May. Its subtitle calls it an irregular approach to poetry's psychology. The evidence, Graves admits, is mainly subjective. He dedicates the book to T E Lawrence and W H R Rivers. Both gave him valuable critical help.

A frank note disarms argument in advance. Critics may blow his fortress to pieces, Graves says. His garrison has withdrawn without a shot. The sections stand alone or gain force by neighbourliness. They grew from problems in his last two poetry volumes. Fairies and Fusileers and The Pier-Glass were those books. Graves had lately survived the Great War's trenches. His notebook argues that poetry yokes irreconcilable things together.
50476-the-three-miss-kings-an-australian:
Ada Cambridge's The Three Miss Kings, an Australian story, was published in New York in 1891 by Appleton. Cambridge had written My Guardian before it. Fifty-two chapters carry the tale, and the first is called A Distant View.

On the second of January, 1880, three sisters newly left orphans sit on a grassy cliff above a wide bay of the Southern Ocean. Each has an income of exactly one hundred pounds a year, and they take counsel on how to use their freedom. No sign of human life is in sight but a fishing boat's far sail. The contents then promise a departure, a Paul, a first invitation, triumph and slighting, and Patty's choice of a career.
50548-a-beginner-s-history:
William Mace, once a professor of history at Syracuse University, wrote a first history book for young children. Homer Colby drew its pictures and Jacques Reich drew portraits. The book came out in Chicago and New York in 1909, with later printings for years after. A map shows the United States and its outlying possessions.

Mace says the stuff of history lies all round the child in things and deeds he sees each day. Teachers should use the tales to show that life is a steady struggle against hard odds. Great men in the book stand as models of grit and work. Short tales, big pictures, and plain words make the nation's past fit for a first school reader.
50604-the-phantom-friend-a-judy-bolton-m:
The Phantom Friend is a Judy Bolton mystery by Margaret Sutton. Grosset and Dunlap put the book out in New York in 1959. It stands late in the long run of Judy Bolton tales listed first. The Vanishing Shadow and The Haunted Attic head that series roll. The book is given to Alice Thorne, the writer's editor and friend.

Chapter heads run from an empty chair to a name on a calendar. Clarissa Valentine, a tour group, and strange questions open the case. A witch's curse and a night of terror raise the chill factor. Judy starts the tale on skates at Radio City in a cold wind. Irene Meredith begs her to come in from the biting cold. A film that will not be shown again hints at the core secret.
50640-elements-of-surgery:
Elements of Surgery, by Robert Liston, surgeon to the North London Hospital, came out at Philadelphia in 1842. The American issue follows the second London edition of his work. Samuel Gross added copious notes and additions for American readers. Gross was professor of surgery at the Louisville Medical Institute.

The book carries numerous engravings of operations and instruments. Liston was famed for the swiftness of his knife in the years before ether. Gross, the great American surgeon, vouches for the text with his notes. Agents sold the volume from New York to Charleston and Louisville. Surgical students learned their craft from such heavy folios. The pair of names makes this a landmark of the art before anaesthesia.
50810-patience-worth-a-psychic-mystery:
Casper Yost, a St Louis newsman, wrote this account of a strange ouija board case. Holt printed Patience Worth: A Psychic Mystery at New York in February 1916. Two women of St Louis sat with a board on a July night in 1913, and the tale begins.

The board had been a mere toy for months, its pointer spelling scant sense. Then came Patience Worth, a voice that claimed a past age and spoke in poems and tales. Yost maps the case in order: the coming, the kind of the messages, and the speaker's self. Her poetry and prose fill two long parts. Talks, views on faith, and thoughts on death close the study of a case that puzzled America.
50961-the-slipper-point-mystery:
Augusta Huiell Seaman wrote The Slipper Point Mystery, dated nineteen nineteen and issued at New York in nineteen twenty-one. C M Relyea drew the pictures. Seaman had written The Girl Next Door and The Sapphire Signet.

The tale opens at Carter's Landing, on the Manituck River, where pleasure boats are hired. A girl sits on a beached rowboat, digging her bare toes in the sand. A pavilion there serves picnics, candy, and dancing to violin and piano. Chapters bring a first clue, a panel behind cedar, and word from the past. The real buried treasure, not the expected kind, ends the riddle. A front picture shows a hidden room found.
51224-billy-in-bunbury:
Billy in Bunbury is a children's cookbook issued by the Royal Baking Powder Company in 1925. It was printed at the Price Baking Powder factory in Chicago. Colour illustrations throughout show the town of Bunbury, its people, and recipes.

Verses present Bunbury as a tasteful town beside a syrup sea. Sponge cake fish and waffle whales disport themselves in its waters. Its streets are good to eat, made of finest marble cake. Recipes follow the verses, all calling for Price's baking powder. Cocoa raisin muffins mix flour, cocoa, raisins, and cinnamon, baking twenty minutes. The batch makes sixteen muffins. Muffin surprises hide a date, currant jelly, or candied cherry inside. The whole is a piece of brand advertising in story form.
51246-great-disasters-and-horrors-in-the:
A H Godbey wrote Great Disasters and Horrors in the World's History. The Royal Publishing Company issued it at Saint Louis. One hundred fifty engravings fill the book. Its copyright dates to 1890. The Louisville tornado heads its list of woes. Floods in the South join that storm.

The Charleston earthquake and Johnstown flood stand named. A storm on Samoa's coast joins the sea tales. Great floods in China, Holland, and Japan fill pages. Laws of the storms and quakes get their own treatment. Tales of heroism and narrow escapes crowd the text. Dire scenes of agony fill it as well, the title boasts. Methods of prediction close the whole. The preface denies any wish to feed morbid taste. A door-to-door disaster book shows what scared and thrilled plain readers in the flood-haunted 1890s.
51421-man-in-a-quandary:
Man in a Quandary, by L J Stecher Jr, appeared in Galaxy magazine in July 1958. The story takes the form of a letter to Miss Dix VI. The writer signs himself Alfred the Magnificent. His full name, he says, is Alfred Vanderform. He reports that he was born in the year 2352. He was reared, he adds, at the Harvard Creche.

Alfred lays out a personal problem for an advice columnist of a future century. He uses the polite forms of a lonely-hearts letter. The humour rests on the gap between the old-fashioned letter and the strange world behind it. In that world a creche at Harvard raises children. A Miss Dix the Sixth still answers letters there. Stecher keeps the piece short. The odd details of Alfred's life do the work of building his world.
51538-brazilian-gold-mine-mystery:
Andy Adams wrote Brazilian Gold Mine Mystery for boys. Grosset and Dunlap issued it at New York in 1960. Biff Brewster stars in the mystery line. Twenty chapters carry the tale. Up the Amazon opens the action. Mr Stannart speaks low at Idlewild Airport there.

Guard this letter as you would your life, he says. The sealed letter goes to Biff's father in Brazil. Thomas Brewster works as chief field engineer there. The Ajax Mining Corporation employs them both. Gregg Stannart heads that company from New York. The Hotel Jacares at Manaus is the address. The Clutching Hand and The Hidden Boathouse follow. Shrunken heads and head-hunters fill the middle. The River of Death and El Dorado come late. The Man of Gold stands at chapter seventeen. Jungle gold and a father's peril gave the Biff Brewster line one of its richest treks.
5155-c-sar-s-column-a-story-of-the-twent:
Ignatius Donnelly's dystopian novel, published in 1890 under the pen name Edmund Boisgilbert, imagines America a century ahead. A wealthy oligarchy rules it, while workers starve in an underworld beneath a great city. Its narrator reaches the city, meets Estella Washington, and is drawn into a secret brotherhood plotting revolt.

Donnelly, better known for his comet theories, wrote one of the earliest American dystopias, complete with airships, poisoned knives, and a sermon on the ruined world. The book's warning about concentrated wealth and class war struck a nerve in the 1890s. It remains an early landmark of science fiction as social protest.
51681-amateur-in-chancery:
Amateur in Chancery, a science fiction tale by George Smith, ran in Galaxy in October 1961. The creature from Venus, the blurb warns, did not know right from left, and life and death hung in the balance. Paul Wallach, director of Project Tunnel, comes into the narrator's office looking distraught. The tunnel car, he reports, is working. That is the trouble.

Holly Carter drew the short straw and rode the tunnel to Venus. She made it, but she cannot be brought back. Fumes in the Venus air, Wallach says, struck her nerves, stopped her breath, and then her heart. She is not yet dead, and modern medicine could revive her if she returns within fifteen or twenty minutes, though some brain harm may follow. Smith builds a taut rescue puzzle.
51712-a-trace-of-memory:
Trace of Memory is a science fiction novel by Keith Laumer. Rights pages date the book to 1963, with a serial run in 1962. A short form ran in Amazing in July, August, and September 1962. Tor later reprinted it in New York as a paperback in 1984. A note stresses that all persons and events in it are fictional.

The tale opens in flight, with a voice urging a fast escape. An alarm may already have sounded as the two men run at dawn. Laumer's hero faces lost years and a past he cannot recall at first. Alien tech and cold war style pursuit drive his search for truth. Fans of brisk sixties science fiction find his stamp on each page.
51739-the-romance-of-the-london-director:
The Romance of the London Directory is a book on names by Charles Bardsley. The Hand and Heart offices published it in London in 1899. Bardsley was vicar of Ulverston and the author of English Surnames. An old church register verse, on the Book of Life, stands as epigraph.

The chapters began as articles in the magazine called The Fireside. Its editor proposed printing them together, to the author's surprise. Half were written with some degree of care, Bardsley confesses. The rest were indited amid the press of heavy ministerial labours. Yet he stands by the accuracy of their contents throughout. Diligent checking, not fine writing, is the credit he claims. Readers had written asking about their own names and others' besides.
51755-hawaiian-sea-hunt-mystery:
Andy Adams sends Biff Brewster to Hawaii in Hawaiian Sea Hunt Mystery, a Biff Brewster Mystery Adventure from Grosset and Dunlap in 1960. The contents move from Peril in Paradise and a disturbing call through worried twins, a police call, and a mysterious message. Wharf rats, a bomb, a storm, and men missing raise the stakes.

Later chapters promise a dangerous dive, exploring the depths, a dawn attack, and a human fish. The tale opens at the Royal Poinciana Hotel on Waikiki Beach, where a man hides behind a coconut palm in the garden, watching the porch and losing patience.
5182-the-old-english-baron-a-gothic-stor:
Clara Reeve's Gothic novel, written as a reply to Horace Walpole's Castle of Otranto. It tells of a young man raised in obscurity who proves to be the rightful heir of a barony. Ghosts, a haunted castle, and a long-hidden crime drive the story, as the hero's true birth is revealed and justice returns to the house.

Reeve aimed to join the romance of old tales with the realism of the modern novel, keeping the supernatural within bounds of belief. The book became a founding work of Gothic fiction, and it offers readers a gentler. It is a more moral ghost story than Walpole's, with a plot that turns on inheritance, honour, and proof.
51829-the-old-chelsea-bun-house-a-tale-o:
The author of Mary Powell wrote this tale of the old Chelsea bun-house, published in London in 1855. Its narrator is one of the bun-house family, remembering the great who once came there to eat and be seen.

The first chapter mourns Lady Betty Spadille, once a toast, now fallen into the autumn of life with no resources but green tea and brag. The narrator recalls her arriving in a peach-coloured sacque and red-heeled shoes, beaux fluttering round her, lacqueys bearing a hamper of French wine. She brought her own strawberries, as if the bun-house's were not good enough. Readers get an eighteenth-century world recalled with affection and gentle spite.
51856-the-kiss-and-its-history:
The Kiss and Its History, by Christopher Nyrop, is a learned treatise on kissing. Harvey translated it from the Danish for Sands of London in 1901. Nyrop taught Romance philology at the University of Copenhagen in Denmark then. Two Danish editions and three translations had already spread the book abroad.

A Dante scene of Paolo and his lover opens the preface on kiss power. Poet quotes in many tongues form a striking feature of the work. Harvey marks his own verse renderings with his initials in the text. Dorat song on the doux mystères du baiser fronts the treatise in French. Custom, law, and love lore of the kiss fill its pages.
5198-the-library:
George Crabbe's poem The Library argues that books console a troubled mind by replacing its own distress with a lighter kind. Its argument moves through the arrangement of a library, from ancient chained folios to pamphlets and numbers. Its classes run through divinity, controversy, medicine, law, history, drama, and romance.

Crabbe reflects on sceptical authors, the friends of religion who do more harm than its foes. He also reflects on the hopes of an author to be known in distant times. The poem ends with the genius of the place answering the poet's doubts. It offers readers a thoughtful, verse-length meditation on reading itself.
51986-two-women-or-one-from-the-mss-of-d:
Henry Harland wrote Two Women or One, from the manuscripts of Dr Leonard Benary, issued in New York in eighteen ninety. A dedication in verse, dated January eighteen ninety, links the author wagon to a star. Chapter one is The First Night. Benary tells his own tale. He is a physician and surgeon, retired from practice, in the American city of Adironda.

My name is Leonard Benary, a foreign sounding name, though I am a pure blooded Englishman, he opens. He was born in Devonshire on July twenty first, eighteen eighteen. He craves indulgence for his ungraceful style and his provincialisms, he says. He has lived in Adironda for nearly half a century. His tale begins on the night of Friday, June thirteenth, eighteen eighty four. A singular story follows, he promises, better ill told than not told. Novel readers get a mystery of identity in two women.
52091-an-essay-on-the-foundations-of-geo:
An Essay on the Foundations of Geometry is a work by Bertrand Russell, printed at Cambridge in 1897. Russell was a Fellow of Trinity College, and the book grew from a thesis he gave at the college in 1895. Parts were also read as talks at Johns Hopkins and at Bryn Mawr College in America.

Russell asks what must hold for space and shape to be known at all. He thanks Professor Klein, whose talks on geometry outside Euclid's lines guide the first chapter. The book sorts past work into three ages and tests each claim by logic. It is an early work by a thinker who would reshape how the West argues.
52223-the-campaigns-of-the-124th-regimen:
The Campaigns of the 124th Regiment, Ohio Volunteer Infantry is a regimental history by Lewis of Medina, Ohio, printed by the Werner Company of Akron. Portraits of the regiment's commanders stand in front: Colonel Oliver Payne, Lieutenant Colonel James Pickands and Major James Hampson. A roster and roll of honor close the volume.

Lewis dedicates the book to all the noble men of the regiment, living, and to the memory of the dead. They counted as nothing, he writes, all sorrows, dangers, marches, battles, wounds and death, so that their common country might not perish. The narrative runs from Cleveland to Manchester in Tennessee, then to the Chattanooga campaign and Chickamauga. The siege of Chattanooga, Lookout Mountain and the storming of Missionary Ridge follow. The Atlanta campaign and the march back to Nashville end the story, before the company rosters name every man.
52345-the-scott-country:
The Scott Country, described by John Geddie and painted by E W Haslehust, was published by Blackie and Son of London and Glasgow. It belongs to the Beautiful Scotland series, beside Loch Lomond, Edinburgh, and the Shores of Fife. A plate of Newark Tower stands at the front. The book walks the border country that Sir Walter Scott made famous.

Geddie asks where and what the Scott Country is. Edinburgh, Scott's birthplace and his own romantic town, claims a share. The plates answer in views: Kelso Bridge, Smailholm Tower, Roxburgh Castle, Dryburgh Abbey, Melrose Abbey, and Abbotsford, Scott's own house. Traquair House, Ashestiel, and Neidpath Castle follow. Lasswade, Roslin, and the Pentlands ring the ground where the Master of Romance lived and wrote.
52391-outlines-of-ecclesiastical-history:
A church history textbook by Elder B H Roberts, in its third edition. Salt Lake City published it in 1902. Roberts also wrote the Life of John Taylor and Missouri Persecutions. He dedicates the work to the Seventies of his church. That body carries the duty of preaching and defending truth worldwide. A prefatory word explains the book's structure to students.

Four parts divide the argument. Part one covers the church's establishment under Messiah and his apostles. Part two treats the apostasy that followed persecution and false teachers. Part three recasts the Reformation as a revolution, not a restoration. It cleared ground without rebuilding primitive Christianity, Roberts argues. Part four presents the restoration through Joseph Smith's revelations. Numbered paragraphs and bold topics suit classroom lessons.
52413-the-black-death-in-the-fourteenth-:
Black Death in the Fourteenth Century is a history from the German of Hecker. Babington rendered it into English for Schloss of London in eighteen thirty three. Hecker taught at Frederick William University at Berlin and held learned posts. Chapters treat general observations, the disease itself, and its causes and spread.

Mortality figures fill chapter four, and moral effects fill chapter five next. Physicians of the plague age get a chapter of their own in six. An appendix prints the ancient song of the Flagellants from those years. The trial of Jews accused of poisoning wells stands in the appendix too. Counsel against the sweating sickness closes the grim documentary add on.
52523-indian-palmistry:
Dale wrote a small book on Indian palmistry, issued in London, New York, and Madras in 1895 by the Theosophical Publishing Society. A plate of the reference hand fronts the work. The preface gives the Greek roots of the art's old name: cheir for the hand, and manteia for foretelling.

Dale notes that sages read the mark on the Buddha's foot at his birth, which shows the art was old in India by his day. She grants that palmistry fell out of use in the West, in part from the nonsense of late writers. Her plan is to set out the best of the old Western masters and of the East, in the plain speech used by working palm readers.
52581-fountains-abbey-the-story-of-a-med:
Fountains Abbey, the story of a medieval monastery by George Hodges, dean of a theology school at Cambridge in Massachusetts, was printed in London in 1904. Hodges inscribes the book to his wife as the fruit of a golden summer, in a note dated September 1903. A Turner drawing of the abbey fronts the volume.

Chapter one traces the Cistercian order from Citeaux and Saint Bernard to a band of discontented monks who left Saint Mary's at York. Fountains was founded in 1132, endured a starving time, then grew rich and planted daughter houses such as Kirkstall and Meaux. Chapter two follows the buildings abbot by abbot. The ruin's beauty and the monks' rule share the stage.
52632-the-third-officer-a-present-day-pi:
Percy F Westerman wrote The Third Officer, A Present Day Pirate Story, with pictures by E S Hodgson for Blackie and Son. Westerman lists a long shelf of sea and air tales at the front. Rivals of the Reef, Captain Starlight, and The Wireless Officer are among them. The tale opens on the steamship Donibristle.

Hilda Vivian enters in the second chapter. A cry of heave to or I will sink you comes next. Capture, life under hatches, and a man named Ramon Porfirio follow. A compound, a first day on an island, and a fight build the middle. The book is a brisk sea yarn for boys, in the style Westerman made his own. Risk at sea drives each turn.
5270-the-film-mystery:
Arthur B. Reeve's Film Mystery brings Professor Craig Kennedy into the world of moving pictures. A camera crime, a tiny scratch, and a fatal script open the case. Chapters follow tangled motives, white-light shadows, chemical research, and an antivenin, as Kennedy and his friend Jameson investigate among actors and studios.

Enid Faye, Lawrence Millard, Emery Phelps, and Marilyn Loring are among the film people caught in the mystery. Jameson himself becomes a detective before the banquet scene closes the case. The novel offers a lively early look at Hollywood, where science meets show business and every clue may be a performance.
52700-happy-island-a-new-uncle-william-s:
Jennette Lee wrote a warm tale of Uncle William and his small island home. The book came out in New York in 1911. It is a new tale in a loved set of books. The first scene finds Uncle William bent over a map.

Andy comes in with lobsters while Juno the cat sleeps near by. Talk, plans, and small chores fill the calm days that follow. Lee writes in a plain voice with soft wit and ease. Readers who like kind folk and sea air will feel at home here.
52778-the-gases-of-the-atmosphere-the-hi:
William Ramsay, a chemistry teacher in London, traced how men found the gases of air. The book came out in 1896 with Macmillan, with portraits. Ramsay starts with Boyle, Mayow, and Hales and their early tests. He shows how a few facts sparked bold new guesses.

Later chapters tell of Black and his fixed air work. Priestley and Scheele found a pure air that fed flame well. Lavoisier then broke the old phlogiston view for good. The book reads as a clear tale of science in the making, told with names, dates, and tests that any keen reader can follow.
52809-the-banner-boy-scouts-mystery:
George Warren sets scouts sleuthing in the Banner Boy Scouts Mystery, published in Cleveland and New York in 1937. The World Syndicate Publishing Company made the book. Twenty nine chapters of boy detective work fill it, from Lost to Mystery Solved.

A fire heads the early run, then Paul looks into the matter. Detectives, a suspicious individual, the spy, and the robbery build the case. Who is Mr Grey, the boys ask in a chapter of that name. Stumped, a hunch, and a bump on the head vary the pace. Captured and escape raise the stakes in the late run. Convincing the police and a battle follow. The mystery of the white card gets two chapters near the end. Chapter one opens at a family dinner table, with Ken Armstrong racing downstairs to his place.
52848-space-nomads-meteorites-in-sky-fie:
Lincoln LaPaz and Jean LaPaz wrote a book on stones that fall from the sky. The book came out in New York in 1961. Its title calls such stones space nomads. A front photo shows a fireball caught by chance in 1923. That shot was made while a man took a view of a far star cloud.

Parts tell of falls in Siberian woods and in wheat land at home. Lost giants, false craters, and wise or rash finders fill the mid part. The last parts ask what meteors are and what use their study has. Clear maps, marks, and tools guide the hunt. Sky fans get a full, plain guide.
53021-torquemada-and-the-spanish-inquisi:
Torquemada and the Spanish Inquisition is a history by Rafael Sabatini, the famed writer of romances. A portrait of Frey Tomas de Torquemada, from a painting ascribed to Miguel Zittoz, stands at the front. A Spanish line from Bernaldez heads the book: the fire is lit, and it will burn till the dry wood fails.

The Pall Mall Gazette, quoted at the front, calls the book not only a graphic and gripping account of the Inquisition but a serious gift to the writing on the subject. Sabatini had also written a life of Cesare Borgia, and he brings a novelist's pace to grim record. The history holds the reader, the same notice says, until the last page is turned.
5308-the-paradise-mystery:
Fletcher's Paradise Mystery opens at the Close of Wrychester. American tourists halt in wonder before a thirteenth-century cathedral set on a great green sward, fringed by elms and beeches, its spire piercing skies where rooks circle and call. The novel's first chapter is called Only the Guardian, and the cathedral close holds its secret.

Fletcher, a master of the English detective story, builds a mystery around an ancient church, its guardian, and a hidden past. Readers will find a classic puzzle of place, with cathedral atmosphere, local characters. The solution turns on what the Close has long concealed.
53145-the-great-taxicab-robbery-a-true-d:
James H. Collins wrote this true tale of a great theft, printed in 1912. It was made from the files of the case and from the tales of men who had a hand in it. Those goods were given by the Police Department of New York. A cut at the front shows Rhinelander Waldo, the head of that force in those days. The book is sent forth with a word on the good fruit of a wise rule of the force in that town.

The theft at its heart was of a cab for hire, a new kind of crime in a new age of the street. A force that keeps good files, and that can put a case in the hands of the press in full, is the hero of the book as much as any one man.
53148-ballads-of-bravery:
George Baker edited Ballads of Bravery, an anthology of heroic verse published in Boston by Lee and Shepard in 1877. Forty full-page illustrations dress the volume. The poems were chosen for school and home reading, and the contents list reads like a roll of honor.

Curfew Must Not Ring To-Night opens the book, the famous tale of a girl in the bell tower. Leigh Hunt gives The Glove and the Lions, and Tennyson The Beggar Maid and Sir Galahad. Calvert sings Bunker Hill, and a Lexington ballad follows it. Browning's Hervé Riel brings the French pilot who saved the fleet. Shakespeare lends Othello's story of his life, and Scott the meeting of Marmion and Douglas. The Loss of the Hornet and Man the Life-Boat turn to the sea. Elocution teachers and schoolboys got their recitation pieces here: courage in verse, ready to declaim.
53210-canterbury:
Canterbury is a guide to the city and its cathedral, written by W Teignmouth Shore. W Biscombe Gardner painted the pictures. The London edition was published in April nineteen oh seven. A view of the north side of the cathedral serves as frontispiece. Contents run from a first view and the story of the cathedral to pilgrims, shrines, and a roundabout of the town.

A list of pictures names Christ Church Gate and the south side of the cathedral. The tomb of Edward the Black Prince and a Norman staircase appear among them. The opening view stands on the summit of the cathedral's great tower. From there, the text says, much of the history of England lies spread beneath the reader's feet.
53314-america-a-history:
Robert Mackenzie wrote America, a History, for Nelson and Sons, who published it at London, Edinburgh, and New York in 1882. The work stands in three parts: the United States, the Dominion of Canada, and South America.

The American part runs from discovery and colonization through Virginia, New England, witchcraft, and slavery, to Washington, Franklin, and the Revolution. Bunker Hill, Saratoga, the surrender of André, and the close of the war lead on to a second war with Britain. Later books treat King Cotton, Missouri, Texas, the war with Mexico, California, Kansas, and the Underground Railway. John Brown, secession, Bull Run, and Gettysburg carry the story toward its end. Mackenzie wrote in a terse, rapid style, and his histories were praised as guides as much as records.
53349-our-cavalry:
Our Cavalry is a military text book by Major-General Rimington. Macmillan published it in London in 1912 with eight diagrams. It belongs to a series of military text books. Other volumes in that series treat field artillery and the Russo-Japanese War. Rimington's subject is the mounted arm of the British service. The contents open with an introductory chapter. That chapter begins with cavalry in past ages. The title promises a survey of what cavalry is and does.

The book appeared two years before the Great War changed mounted warfare. Machine guns and trenches would soon test its lessons. For its first readers it was a professional's handbook. Students of the late horse era find doctrine here in plain form.
53368-don-t-marry:
Don't Marry is a book of plain advice on how, when, and whom to marry, issued by Ogilvie of Rose Street, New York. Its counsel comes as a long list of warnings, each one a short rule to live by. The book is split into three parts: the main rules, then romantic marriages, then unromantic ones.

The rules warn against wedding for beauty alone or for money, and against drunkards, spendthrifts, misers, and coquettes. Readers are told not to elope, not to marry too young or too old, and not to dally about proposing. Other rules guard the other side: do not spurn a man for his poverty, and do not marry without love.
53447-the-fishing-industry:
The Fishing Industry is a trade volume in Pitman Common Commodities series. Each book in that series sold at three shillings net, crown octavo, illustrated. Sister volumes treat tea, coffee, sugar, oils, wheat, rubber, and coal alike. Shipbuilder adverts from Aberdeen and Hull brokers front this fishing volume richly.

Hall, Russell of Aberdeen built steam trawlers for North Sea and Iceland work. Massey of Hull sold and valued trawlers as Admiralty contractors in the trade. The series aimed to give each great British industry one plain handbook. Cotton, silk, wool, linen, tobacco, and leather stand in the same list. Glass, by Marson, is the sister volume in the set.
53448-the-silver-ring-mystery:
Helen Wells flies a mystery in The Silver Ring Mystery, a Vicki Barr Flight Stewardess story from Grosset and Dunlap, copyrighted in 1960. A front list places it last among the Vicki Barr books, after Silver Wings for Vicki and The Clue of the Gold Coin. Wells thanks American Airlines stewardess supervisors for help with the facts.

The contents begin aboard the Electra, where Vicki meets the Bryants and hears the story of Lucy. A puzzling discovery, the girl in the portrait, and a chapter asking which Lucy follow. Secrets at midnight, a signal, an escape, and the silver rings close the case.
53458-the-chemistry-of-cookery:
The Chemistry of Cookery, a popular science book by W Mattieu Williams, explains what heat and water do to food. The front of the book is filled with praise from the press. The Spectator calls it an attempt to explain the rationale of the familiar work of the kitchen. Knowledge, the Westminster Review, and the Athenaeum praise its clearness and its facts drawn straight from real life.

The Scotsman notes the book is meant chiefly for cooks of the middle and upper classes, while the review in Food says it reads like a novel. Williams takes each process of the kitchen in turn and asks its why and wherefore. The first chapter treats the boiling of water itself. From that simple start he builds the chemistry of roasting, baking, and brewing for readers with no laboratory at hand.
53475-the-end-of-the-middle-ages-essays-:
Mary Robinson, named on her title page also as Madame James Darmesteter, published this volume of essays and questions in history with Fisher Unwin at London in 1889. She dedicated it to her friend and master Symonds, who had stood at her side through ten years of study. They had talked the book over in his study at Davos two years before.

In the dedication she recalls how they hunted through the innumerable pages of Litta and Muratori for the secret of the French claim to Milan, and found many better things instead. The great figures of the past rose before her and stayed alive, yet the beautiful chronicles were not always precise about what was done, and when, and why. So she turned to manuscripts, and the essays in this book grew out of that exacting search.
53580-the-princess-tarakanova-a-dark-cha:
Danilevski writes a pretender's tale in The Princess Tarakanova, a dark chapter of Russian history, printed in New York and London. Macmillan and Sonnenschein issue the book, with four portraits. Mouchanoff renders it from the Russian. A portrait of the princess fronts it, with verses on her guilt and shame.

Two parts divide the story. Part one is the diary of a lieutenant. Tempest tossed, my imprisonment, and important news open his record. I see the princess, my interview with the princess, and the princess asks me to assist her build trust. I convey a letter and I deliver a letter follow. Is the count a traitor, the departure from Rome, and the marriage deepen the snare. Treachery and remorse close the part. Part two, named for a fortress ravelin, brings Ekaterina at Moscow and the princess at Saint Petersburg. Orloff and the princess circle each other there.
53616-the-jesus-problem-a-restatement-of:
The Jesus Problem is J M Robertson's restatement of the myth theory, issued for the Rationalist Press Association by Watts and Company of London in 1917. Robertson had argued the case at length in Christianity and Mythology and Pagan Christs; here he compresses it. The theory holds that the gospel Jesus is a myth built on older ritual, not a life remembered.

The central myth is dissected first: the sacrificial rite, the mock-king ritual, the cross, the suffering messiah, the rock tomb, and the resurrection. Roots follow, in prototypes and the mystery-drama. The evolution of the cult takes up the silence of Josephus and the myth of the twelve apostles. Organization, economics, and early book-making come next: the Didache, the Apocalypse, the epistles, then gospel-making itself. Appendices translate the Teaching of the Twelve Apostles and treat the myth of Simon Magus.
53639-last-words-on-evolution-a-popular-:
Ernst Haeckel, professor at Jena, summed up his lifelong case for evolution in Last Words on Evolution. Joseph McCabe translated the popular retrospect from the second edition, and Owen published it at London in 1906. Three chapters frame the fight: the controversy about creation, the struggle over the human genealogical tree, and the controversy over the soul, covering immortality and God. Three plates show the vertebrate family tree, the skeletons of five anthropoid apes, and the embryos of three mammals.

An appendix of tables gives the ages of the earth, the grouping of the primates, and man's family tree in two halves. A postscript answers the Jesuit opposition Haeckel faced. The plate explanation argues that fossils, anatomy, and embryology together prove all vertebrates descend from one stem, rising from lancelet-like forms through fishes and amphibians to apes and man.
537-tales-of-terror-and-mystery:
Arthur Conan Doyle gathers twelve tales of dread and detection in this volume, split into terror and mystery. The Horror of the Heights sends a pilot into a sky full of unseen beasts. The Leather Funnel and the New Catacomb chill with old crimes, while the Brazilian Cat stalks a lone man.

Doyle writes with brisk, eerie craft, mixing science with the uncanny. Mystery tales track a lost train, a beetle hunter, and a japanned box. Each tale closes with a twist that reframes all before it. The book shows Doyle beyond Sherlock Holmes, as a master of short, sharp shocks for readers who like a cold shiver.
53739-the-duty-of-american-women-to-thei:
The Duty of American Women to Their Country was published by Harper and Brothers at New York in 1845. No author is named on the title page. The argument opens with a truism: intelligence and virtue are indispensable to a democratic government where the people hold all power. America, the writer warns, is in peril for want of both. To make the danger vivid, the tract first shows France in the Reign of Terror. There an extravagant king, a selfish aristocracy, and an exacting priesthood ground the people down.

The same dangers, the writer argues, hang over the United States. A people without education cannot know what will secure their safety, nor do what they know to be right. Women's duty follows from the diagnosis: the intelligence and virtue of the republic must be built at home and in school.
53812-the-book-of-clever-beasts-studies-:
Myrtle Reed wrote The Book of Clever Beasts, studies in unnatural history, with pictures by Peter Newell. G P Putnam's Sons published it at New York and London in 1904. Reed dedicated the book to lovers of truth everywhere. Her earlier books, Lavender and Old Lace among them, are listed at the front. The frontispiece shows animals made to gallop around an imaginary ring.

Eight tales fill the book: Little Upsidaisi, Jagg the Skootaway Goat, and Snoof. Kitchi-Kitchi, Jim Crow, and Hoop-La follow. Jenny Ragtail and Hoot-Mon close the set, with an appendix behind them. One picture shows a beast using a crotch as a crutch under its wing. Another shows Hoop-La rocking with laughter, hands on her sides. Reed gathered her beasts from the nature books of recent years, Burroughs among them, and retold their feats as comedy.
53904-slavery:
Slavery, a pamphlet by Baker, was printed at Philadelphia in 1860, on the eve of the Civil War. It opens with John Brown's recent attempt to raise an insurrection at Harper's Ferry. That desperate act, Baker says, was the natural result of a twenty years' war waged in the free states against the institutions of the South.

He calls the abolition cause a reform based on no sound principle, fruitful only in bitter words and sectional hate. Many lives were lost, he notes, and an old man led out to suffer the law's last penalty. Baker hopes the scene will open the nation's eyes to the gulf at whose brink it stands. The pamphlet defends the southern system and attacks its critics. It stands as a period piece of pro slavery argument in the crisis year, useful now chiefly as evidence of how the defence was made.
54053-the-laird-of-norlaw-a-scottish-sto:
The Laird of Norlaw is a Scots tale by the hand of Margaret Maitland. A Harper house of New York brought it out in eighteen fifty nine. The house of Norlaw stands on a low hill slope by the three Eildons. A small old town of the Waverley tales lies not far from its seat. Corn grows on the hill sides while a small stream winds to the Tweed.

The low house is two floors in front and one at back by the slope. Its yard lies all at back where the ground is snug from wind. At its right hand stands the old keep of Norlaw, gaunt and bare. Square, grim, and pierced high like a jail, it foils the calm house. The Livingstones were knights when the Border was a wild home land.
54144-the-new-forest-its-history-and-its:
The New Forest: Its History and Its Scenery, by John Wise, with 63 illustrations drawn by Walter Crane and engraved by Linton, and two maps. Smith, Elder and Company published it in London in 1867. Twenty two chapters and four appendices survey the forest whole.

Scenery and early history open the book. Calshot Castle, Beaulieu Abbey, Brockenhurst, and Lyndhurst follow by district. Minstead and Rufus's Stone, the valley of the Avon, and Christchurch come next. The gipsy and the West Saxon, folk lore and the speech of the forest, and the barrows are treated. Roman and Romano-British potteries, parish registers, geology, botany, and the birds close the chapters. The appendices give a glossary of local words, and lists of the flowering plants, the birds, and the moths and butterflies. The Avon chapters pass Fordingbridge, Breamore, and Ringwood.
54219-a-little-english-gallery:
A Little English Gallery is a set of biographical studies by Louise Imogen Guiney, printed at New York by Harper and Brothers in 1894. Guiney dedicated the book to Edmund Gosse, calling it a friendly trespass on his fields. The studies were written at irregular intervals, from sheer interest in their subjects. Portions had appeared in The Atlantic Monthly, Macmillan's, The Catholic World and Poet-Lore.

The gallery opens with Lady Danvers, who lived from 1561 to 1627. Henry Vaughan, the Welsh poet of 1621 to 1695, follows. Then comes George Farquhar, the playwright of 1677 to 1707. Topham Beauclerk and Bennet Langton, the wits of Doctor Johnson's circle, share a study. Her aim, she says, was to make these sketches approximately lifelike. The book is literary portraiture of minor figures, done from fresh material at first hand.
5424-icelandic-primer-with-grammar-notes:
Henry Sweet wrote this Icelandic Primer as a short, easy introduction to the study of Icelandic, in a second edition dated 1895. The preface explains that students in England had long wanted such a book. The larger Icelandic Reader by Vigfusson and Powell was valuable, but it left room for an elementary primer, and its editors raised no objection to Sweet undertaking one.

The primer supplies grammar, notes, and a glossary, giving beginners the tools to read Old Icelandic texts. Sweet writes for students, not specialists, keeping the path into the language as clear as possible. Readers get a compact, practical textbook that still serves as a first step into medieval Icelandic literature.
54405-motor-tours-in-the-west-country:
Motor Tours in the West Country is a guide for the new car tourist. Stawell wrote it as part of a set of such tour books. The set was bound in red cloth and rich in shots of the road. Past books in the set took Wales and the broad shire of York.

The press praised her fine sense of the road in those books. They praised her chat on books and men met on the way. They held the set to be of use and a joy to read at once. This book does the same work for the west of England. It tells the driver what is worth a stop on each tour. Maps and shots back the words through the whole of the book. It is a guide from the first age of the car on tour.
54475-discoveries-and-inventions-of-the-:
Robert Routledge, a science examiner for the University of London, wrote a popular account of the discoveries and inventions of the nineteenth century. A thirteenth edition, revised and partly rewritten, appeared in 1900 with four hundred fifty six illustrations. A verse from Emerson heads the title page. Its lines speak of galvanic wire and strong shouldered steam.

Routledge argues the century stands apart from all before it in ideas and material gains. Railways and steam navigation changed travel and trade most, he says. Both rest on the steam engine, so that claims first notice. Iron and steel making, work of the century's second half, underpin much of the advance described.
54575-redcoat-captain-a-story-of-that-co:
Redcoat Captain is a story of That Country by Alfred Ollivant, author of Bob, Son of Battle, published in 1907 with illuminations by Graham Robertson. Ollivant writes a deliberate nonsense tale in fairy-tale cadences. Its hero is Tiny, a very tall captain of redcoats, and its heroine is Baby, whose real name is Mabel.

Tiny comes to the Fort on the Hill, a round wall with a barrack square, a cannon peeping out to keep Them down, and an elephant named Goliath in the stable. A door painted OGRE turns out to mean the Officers' Grub of the Royal Elephants. There Tiny announces to the shining, bulging General that he is going to marry Baby, and asks how long he must stop in this hole and about taking a house. The book is a jeu d'esprit, barrack-room absurdity told as solemnly as a saga.
54623-the-common-objects-of-the-country:
Wood wrote The Common Objects of the Country, in its sixteenth edition from Routledge at London in 1897. Coleman drew the many plates for the book. Wood had written on the sea-shore, feathered friends, and a full natural history before this work. His preface promises short and simple accounts of things found in the fields. Hard science words are shunned, and Latin names are given only where no plain name can be found.

The book was part of a line of country books from the same house. Kindred works treat sea-shore finds, moths, beetles, birds' eggs, and wild flowers. Wood writes for walkers who wish to name what they meet on a lane or heath. Each find gets a clear note, in words a child can grasp. The book turns a country walk into a small school of nature.
54660-the-disagreeable-woman-a-social-my:
Julian Starr wrote The Disagreeable Woman, a tale billed as a social puzzle, put out in New York in 1895. A line from Fletcher heads the book, on acts as our good or ill shades. Starr says the thought for the book came from a famed tale of ships that pass in the night. If there are such men, he asks, are there not such women too?

The parts trace a puzzle that grows deep, step by step. A Professor Poppendorf gives a talk, then falls in love in his turn. A talk with the woman at the heart of the tale shifts her light. A Count Penelli, a shop, a house of rooms, and a poor sick man all play a part. A rich sick man and a speech from a throne add turns. The close brings a shock find and a gleam of hope.
54673-sir-harry-a-love-story:
Sir Harry, subtitled A Love Story, is a novel by Archibald Marshall, published in New York by Dodd, Mead and Company in 1919. The contents promise twenty-nine chapters: Royd Castle, Lady Brent, the moor, and chapters named for Viola and Wilbraham. Marshall's earlier novels are listed on the title pages, a shelf of country-house fiction.

The story opens with the Reverend David Grant, newly appointed vicar of Royd, who is a novelist as well as a priest. Unable to bring his wife Ethel, who is near childbirth, he tours Royd Castle alone. The couple have been married thirteen years and have long dreamed of the ideal country parsonage, saving his royalties to make the home they want. The opening sets a gentle tone of married affection and village expectation.
54695-the-new-england-country:
The New England Country is a picture book of rural New England with text and illustrations by Clifton Johnson. Lee and Shepard of Boston published it in 1897; Johnson held the copyright of 1892. Its four parts move in time. Old Times on a New England Farm comes first, then The New England of To-Day, New England as the Traveller Sees It, and Camping Among the New England Hills.

The illustrations crowd the list of plates: an old fireplace, a foot-stove, the churn, a loom, flax-wheels, gourds and piggins, and a country stage coach in winter. A frontispiece marks January, and the plates follow the months. A passage preserved in the copy gives Johnson's theme. About old times, he writes, there always hovers a peculiar charm, and a dreamland atmosphere overhangs them. The present seems full of hard, dry facts as we battle through it.
54878-a-source-book-of-english-social-hi:
A Source Book of English Social History gathers the raw records of how English people lived, from Saxon times to the seventeen hundreds. Monckton Jones, a lecturer in history at Homerton College, Cambridge, compiled it. Methuen published it at London, first in 1922. Chapters run from the Saxon village and manorial systems through the gilds.

Medieval life and explorations, thirteenth century London, and fifteenth century life follow. Exploration and extracts from the sixteenth, seventeenth, and eighteenth centuries close the book. The first chapter prints the laws of Ethelbert, dated to the year 600, three years after Augustine came to Kent. In them, the notes say, law that had been oral custom was first written down and made lasting. Money payment for wrongs appears already, if not always in coin. Such source books let students read the past in its own words, rather than in a textbook's summary.
54971-the-s-p-mystery:
Harriet Pyne Grove wrote The SP Mystery, a girls book put out at Akron in 1930. The tale starts when Jean Gordon rushes home from school on a sharp, cold day. She begs her mother for the attic room as a club room. That small ask sets the whole plot in motion.

Jean and her friends form a club whose short name gives the book its title. Shamrocks, night prowlers, and a witch theme party fill the first half. The girls then hold an attic party and plan a grand surprise. A lone girl named Greta joins their world, and camp life brings more small trials. The last parts bare the secret and show what the club name means.
55102-the-wooden-hand-a-detective-story:
The Wooden Hand is a detective story by Fergus Hume. The author had fame from a cab crime tale that sold in vast runs. This print was made for sale in India and the crown lands past seas. The book came out in London in the year nineteen five.

Misery Castle leads, then a young love dream and a wastrel son in turn. A strange loss, a warn note, and a court probe of death fill first turns. A hid pack, a lords name, and a next wife raise the threads of the case. A lad plays sleuth while a kind friend stands by in the pinch. Gems and a last plain tale wind the skein to its close.
55140-a-house-in-bloomsbury:
A House in Bloomsbury is a novel of London home life by Mrs Oliphant. Rights for the book date to the year eighteen ninety four. A New York print of the work bears the year nineteen hundred and one. The tale opens in the rooms of a man and his girl Dora.

Dora asks leave to go up stairs to sit with a lone young wife. Her father has heard the name but kept scant hold of the facts. The young pair live above, and the wife waits long hours for her man. Kind calls and small talk draw the two house holds into one web. Oliphant traces class, rent, and lone hearts in a great town house.
55189-the-summit-house-mystery-or-the-ea:
L Dougall wrote this novel, printed by Funk and Wagnalls of New York and London in 1905. Dougall had written Beggars All, The Madonna of a Day, and The Zeit-Geist. The publishers' note opens with a creed: the story's the thing. It grants that art, style, and character count, yet holds that most readers put story first.

The note asks why the two kinds of fiction should not blend, wedding the art of George Eliot to the thrill of Anthony Hope and Conan Doyle. Dougall, it claims, does just that here. The tale is no plain detective story, though hiding and seeking drive it. Nor is it a love story, though love of a high order feeds the mystery at its heart. A summit house holds the secret.
55243-the-puzzle-in-the-pond-a-judy-bolt:
Margaret Sutton wrote The Puzzle in the Pond, A Judy Bolton Mystery, issued at New York by Grosset and Dunlap in 1963. Front pages list the Judy Bolton series in full, from The Vanishing Shadow to The Secret Quest. Sutton gives the book to past, present, and future students in her creative writing classes. A front print shows Judy's fingers close on a small round object.

A stolen typewriter leads the chapters. Help for Holly and a rude shopkeeper follow. A mysterious truck and another green car build the puzzle. A woods road and a beaver dam set the middle scenes. An impossible discovery and more puzzles press the plot. A boy named Danny enters at chapter ten. Judy works the clues to the pond puzzle in the Bolton style for young mystery fans.
55309-the-crimson-cryptogram-a-detective:
The Crimson Cryptogram, a detective story by Fergus Hume, author of The Mystery of a Hansom Cab, was published in New York in 1902. Twenty-six chapters run from A Midnight Surprise and The Writing in Blood to The Truth and A Confession. An open verdict, a red pocket-book, a blind girl, and a solicitor at bay fill the middle heads.

The tale opens with a speech on poverty. Naked poverty can be borne, the speaker says. Genteel pauperism is worse: a middle-class lie kept up at the cost of constant worry. That, he holds, is the true misery of life. Ellis tells Cass his modest wishes: a good practice, a fair income, a home, and a wife to love him. Fate blocks all four. Hume builds a blood-written puzzle in his famed brisk style.
55310-the-lone-inn-a-mystery:
Fergus Hume wrote The Lone Inn, a mystery, printed in New York, copyright 1894 and 1895. The first chapter is the adventure at the inn. If there is anything in warnings felt beforehand, he was well warned by his first glimpse of the inn. Its huge bulk of gables, sloping roofs, and lean chimneys hunched blackly against the sky.

All day he had walked under blue sky between green hedgerows, whistling. Faced in the dusk by so grim a scene, he felt qualmish. Ragged clouds hung over a sullen western red, and salt marshes spread round in their bleak waste. Some fate drove his unwilling feet to that unwelcoming door. A handsome woman opened it while his hand was still raised. She was not a lady, yet above the common sort. He asks for a bed for the night.
55343-ambassador-morgenthau-s-story:
Ambassador Morgenthau's Story is the memoir of Henry Morgenthau, American ambassador at Constantinople from 1913 to 1916, published by Doubleday, Page of New York in 1919. The book is dedicated to Woodrow Wilson. Its dedication declares that the rights of small nations shall be respected and such crimes as it describes shall never darken history again.

The chapters trace German power inside the Ottoman Empire. Ambassador Wangenheim, the Kaiser's personal representative, opposes the sale of American warships to Greece. Germany mobilizes the Turkish army. The German warships Goeben and Breslau are smuggled through the Dardanelles. Morgenthau watched an empire become Germany's instrument from inside its capital. His story remains a firsthand source on how the Ottoman Empire entered the First World War and what followed for its peoples.
55376-the-piccadilly-puzzle-a-mysterious:
The Piccadilly Puzzle is a mystery novel by Fergus Hume. White of London issued it in 1889. Hume had won fame with The Mystery of a Hansom Cab. A foggy night opens this tale. Music sounds from a lit house in Park Lane at two in the morning. The Countess of Kerstoke is giving a late ball. Inside, lamps, flowers, and gay dresses shine. Outside, thick yellow fog chills the street.

Dowker the detective enters by chapter three. A Saint John's Wood household and Piccadilly rooms follow. A missing link and a family history deepen the plot. Myles Desmond finds friends and thinks hard. What Dowker discovered is saved for near the end. Hume's puzzles fed the first great boom in detective tales.
55439-peeps-at-heraldry:
Peeps at Heraldry, by Phoebe Allen, is a first book on coats of arms for young readers. Adam and Charles Black published it in London in nineteen twelve. Eight full page colour plates and many line drawings fill its pages. The frontispiece shows a herald in the tabard once worn over mail armour.

Twelve short chapters build the subject from the shield outward in plain steps. Form, points, and colours of the shield come before its divisions are explained. Blazoning, the art of describing arms in set words, follows in its turn. Common and animal charges fill three chapters of the little book. Quartering, marshalling, pennons, banners, and standards close the course of talks. Five full coats, from the duke of Leinster to Sir William Herschel, are worked through.
55541-a-treatise-on-the-origin-progress-:
A Treatise on Dry Rot in Timber, by Thomas Allen Britton, takes up the origin, progress, prevention, and cure of that decay. A sketch at the front shows dry rot fungus on a basement joist at Greenwich. The end of that joist crumbled into fine red powder at a touch. Colours of the fungi are listed as white, yellow, green, purple, and red.

Britton adds remarks on saving wood from sea worms, beetles, and ants. Builders, ship men, and house owners all feared the rot he studies. A floor can look sound while its joists turn to dust beneath. His treatise teaches how to spot, stop, and prevent the spread. The book is a practical classic of Victorian building care.
55546-the-progress-of-the-century:
Harper and Brothers issued The Progress of the Century in nineteen hundred one, a survey of the past hundred years. Seventeen famed men wrote its chapters. Alfred Russel Wallace leads off on the growth of life forms. William Ramsay takes up the stuff of matter.

Flinders Petrie covers old digs and lost towns. Norman Lockyer writes on the stars. William Osler and W W Keen split health and surgery in two. Elihu Thomson treats the new force of electric power. Alfred Mahan writes on war ships at sea. Andrew Lang takes up books and poems. James Gibbons and Goldwin Smith close on faith and free thought. Few one volume sets range so wide with such names.
55658-the-horse-in-history:
The Horse in History is a study by Basil Tozer, first issued at London in 1908, with twenty five illustrations. A print by Durer, the knight with death and the devil, faces the title. Tozer had written practical hints on riding to hounds. His opening note takes a wide view of his subject and a sober one.

The horse, he writes, helped on the progress of the world almost from the age of the wild herds of the drift. Now, with the dawn of the twentieth century and the sudden coming of horseless traffic, its reign is over. Board of Agriculture figures prove the fall in part, he says. Yet he hopes horses will be with us still for many years. The book looks back over the whole reign as it closes.
55708-death-the-knight-and-the-lady-a-gh:
Death the Knight and the Lady is a ghost story by Stacpoole. John Lane, at the Bodley Head in London and New York, published it in 1897. The front matter carries warm reviews of the author's earlier tale, Pierrot. Critics there praise his poetic mystery and delicate fancy.

A ballad of Arras stands before the prologue as a threshold piece. The narrator then describes himself and introduces one James Wilder. A sound that recalls his past sets the haunting in motion. Chapters promise a dimly-painted face and a little black book. A ballade of the falcon and a black horse and a white deepen the pattern. An old oak chest waits among the later chapter titles. The tale belongs to the 1890s taste for romance touched with the supernatural.
55717-in-the-days-of-queen-mary:
In the Days of Queen Mary is a historical tale by Edward Crake, rector of Jevington. It was published at London by the Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge. Crake also wrote Henri Duquesne and When the Puritans Were in Power. The book is illustrated by Stacey and is dedicated to the Duke of Devonshire. Seventeen chapters tell the tale.

The chapters name the road: Chiddingly Place, The Apparitor, The Pursuivant, Thames Pirates, Gray's Inn and The Star Chamber. Then come The Arrest of Ralph, The Verdict, The Dawn of Hope and Whitehall. The story opens on Midsummer Day, a day of unbroken sunshine, on a broad terrace in Sussex. Two Sussex boys lie on the turf while the rooks caw in the great rookery. It was written for young readers, in the line of the society's improving historical tales.
55719-the-social-secretary:
David Graham Phillips tells a society tale as a young woman's diary in a novel issued by Grosset and Dunlap at New York. Copyright rests with the Bobbs-Merrill Company in 1905. Clarence F Underwood drew the pictures.

The diary opens on November 29. At half-past one exactly, the writer begins her career. Mrs Carteret calls for her ten minutes late. Jim watches from the drawing-room window with her. He has proposed more than twenty times in three years. His army pull keeps him safe at Washington, a colonel at thirty-five. She admires his self-restraint. Yet she could not bear a husband who worshipped her. For four months she has tried hard to love him, as her affairs grow desperate. Phillips wrote hard novels of money and ambition in the new century.
55800-mosaic-of-new-mexico-s-scenery-roc:
Paige W. Christiansen and Frank E. Kottlowski set in order this guide to the rocks of New Mexico, printed in 1972. It is the eighth book in a set of trips through the rock past of the state. The set runs from Santa Fe and Taos to Silver City, Roswell, and the high plains of the north-east. The front of this book shows Redondo Peak, seen from Jemez Canyon.

A photo in the book shows Whitewater Canyon near Glenwood. The name of the book gives its plan: a tile work of scenes, rocks, and tale. It was put out by the Bureau of Mines and Mineral Resources of the state. Such guides lead the man in a car from sight to sight, and tell him what the stones at each stop say of the deep past.
55854-letters-from-the-raven-corresponde:
Letters from the Raven is the correspondence of Lafcadio Hearn with Henry Watkin. Bronner edited it with introduction and critical comment for Brentano's. The New York edition came out in the year 1907 there. A dedication to three sweethearts, Marian, May, and Motherkin, fronts it. Contents add Letters to a Lady and Letters of Ozias Midwinter.

The editor opens on Hearn's books about Japan as delicate interpretation. Their English is a delight to read, he says in praise. Calm, serenity, and self poise mark that writer at first sight. He seems a stone Buddha by the Japanese highways in stillness. Yet these letters show the humor and gaiety his Japan books hide.
55956-the-lost-parchment-a-detective-sto:
The Lost Parchment, a detective story by Fergus Hume, author of The Mystery of a Hansom Cab, was copyrighted in 1914 by Dillingham of New York. Chapter one, Schoolfellows, reunites two Rugby chums in a garden glowing in hot July sunshine.

Hendle is a squire who entered into his snug little kingdom at fifteen, twelve years ago, and enjoys an income of four thousand a year. Carrington, his visitor, lost his father, was left without a sixpence, and qualified for the Bar on next to nothing. The contents promise the machinery of a mystery: a vicar, lovers, a revelation, and counsel's opinion. A nine days wonder, a search on the track, a confession, and circumstantial evidence follow. A trap and a final surprise close the list.
56083-de-soto-coronado-cabrillo-explorer:
David Lavender retraces three entradas in De Soto, Coronado, Cabrillo: Explorers of the Northern Mystery, Handbook 144 of the National Park Service, issued in Washington in 1992. The book's own note argues that American history begins not with Jamestown or Plymouth but with Spanish exploration from Florida to California in the sixteenth century.

Chapters on the ways of the conquerors, the wanderers, and the seafarers carry the three expeditions, their meetings with native peoples, and the results, good and ill. A guide to sites follows: De Soto National Memorial, Coronado National Memorial, Pecos, and Cabrillo National Monument.
56105-the-dickens-country:
Frederic G Kitton wrote this guide to the places of Dickens's life, in the Pilgrimage Series printed by Adam and Charles Black of London. First issued in 1905, it was reprinted in 1911. Kitton had written Charles Dickens by Pen and Pencil and Dickens and His Illustrators. Forty-eight full-page plates, mostly photographs by T W Tyrrell, fill the book. A new photograph of Dickens in 1857 fronts it.

Chapters start at Portsmouth and Chatham, then take boyhood and youth in London. The London and suburban homes follow, street by street: Bayham Street in Camden Town, Lant Street in the Borough, the blacking warehouse. The west country, southern England, East Anglia, the north, and the midlands round out the map of a life.
56154-the-man-from-bar-20-a-story-of-the:
The Man from Bar 20, a story of the cow country by Clarence Mulford, author of Bar 20 and Hopalong Cassidy, was copyrighted in 1918. A frontispiece by Frank Schoonover shows a man's head rising into a leveled gun. Twenty-three chapters run from A Stranger Comes to Hastings through moonlight scouting, councils of war, and a night skirmish, to All but the Cows.

Chapter one sends a horseman slowly out of a draw and up a lava-covered ridge. He is singing The Cowboy's Lament, to the disgust of his horse. The horse arches its back and stops the song in the twenty-ninth verse. Dearly beloved, the rider grins. Mulford writes in the Bar 20 line: range craft, dry humor, and gun work, with identity itself in question from the second chapter on.
56176-guild-court-a-london-story:
George MacDonald wrote Guild Court, a London story, issued in New York by Routledge and Sons in 1883. The publisher's list at the front gathers his writings, from Annals of a Quiet Neighborhood and Phantastes to Sir Gibbie and Malcolm. A wood engraving shows a girl fallen into a dreamy study of the fire.

The first chapter is called The Walk to the Counting-House. On a grand November morning, one of those rare days that dawn two or three times a year, a young man walks from Highbury into the City of London. The tale that follows stays with city work, city rooms, and the people of a small court. MacDonald, better known for fairy romance, here grounds his gift in offices and lodgings. Readers get a Victorian London novel of business life and quiet hearts.
56250-santa-claus-message-a-christmas-st:
Tregaskis wrote a Christmas story dated 1921 that opens in Twenty-foot, a near empty mining camp in Australia. Old gold workings scar the wide valley, and felled trees and poor farms mark the land. A school, a store, and a small church still serve the few folk who stay.

Two men still dig for gold in the camp, with thin luck and hard terms. Hampton, who lives with his wife and family up the gully, has had a dry winter and poor wash dirt. With funds gone and rain far off near the end of December, want hangs over the camp as the feast draws near.
56349-goodbird-the-indian-his-story:
Goodbird the Indian tells his own life story to Gilbert L Wilson. Fleming H Revell issued the book in nineteen hundred fourteen. It stands in a home mission study course for young readers. Frederick N Wilson drew the plates for the plain, true tale.

Edward Goodbird was born on a sand bar of the Missouri shore. Ice ran in the stream as his folk crossed in bull boats there. Seven years had passed since Long Hair fell in his last fight. The Hidatsa and Mandan once held five towns at Knife River’s mouth. Birth, childhood, and the gods fill the tale’s first three parts. School days under the white man’s rule take the next long span. Buffalo hunts and farming mark the old life’s proud employ. The White Man’s Way, last part, weighs what the change has cost.
56356-the-scarlet-bat-a-detective-story:
Scarlet Bat is a detective story by Fergus Hume, the hansom cab author. White of London issued the novel in nineteen o five. Hume also wrote The Golden Idol, Madam Midas, and The Indian Bangle. Twenty six chapters run from Sowing the Wind to A Wedding Present.

An inquest, a scrap of paper, and a queer mark build the case. A two hundred pounds reward and Cupid bargain lighten the dark plot. A sealed letter, a strange will, and a Quaker lady enter midway. Frank story, what Mildred knew, and Miss Cork explains turn the screw. Chapter one opens with a street quarrel and a man felled flat.
56412-seventeen-years-in-paris-a-chaplai:
Noyes wrote Seventeen Years in Paris, a chaplain's story, printed by Baines and Scarsbrook at London in 1910. Noyes had been honorary chaplain to the British embassy and head of the Embassy Church in the Rue d'Aguesseau. The book is given to the British and American colonies in Paris. With them he spent what he calls happy years, from 1891 to 1907. His predecessor, Gill, had warned him not to stay past seven years in the post.

Noyes stayed near seventeen, at the call of many friends who asked for this account. He warns that it is no guide to Paris life or to the beauties of the town. A chaplain's days there were full, strenuous, and full of surprise work. Sight-seeing had to wait, week by week, he says. The book gives church work abroad in plain, warm strokes.
56426-the-mummy-a-tale-of-the-twenty-sec:
Jane Webb, in print as Loudon, wakes a dead king in The Mummy, a tale of the twenty second century, printed in London in 1827. Colburn made the book, first in three volumes. A Samuel tag fronts it: why hast thou disquieted me, to bring me up. Thirty two chapters carry the tale.
