Her first word is frank about the hunt for a hero. She had long wished to write a novel, she says, but could not bear anything common place. Heroes are so much alike, so dull, so fully brothers of one race, she holds. Sauntering down a shady lane one fine June evening, she resolved she must have something new. Something quite out of the beaten path was her need, and a mummy serves the turn.
56479-hymn-stories-of-the-twentieth-cent:
Hymn Stories of the Twentieth Century is a book of hymn anecdotes by William Hart, printed at Boston by the Wilde Company with copyright of 1948. Bishop Ledden wrote the foreword. Hart dedicates the book to the churches he served as pastor. The stories are grouped in chapters by the occasions they fit.

Let's Sing opens the collection, with the Marine Band, a chaplain's wife's song and a popular processional hymn. Morning Melodies and Sunset Songs follow, the latter with singing soldiers and a hymn discussion at Oyster Bay. Hymns of Comfort gathers God's angels in charge, singing Welshmen at Oxford and songs of a sorrowing nation. Songs of Childhood and Youth closes the visible contents, with the Scouts and Jesus Bids Us Shine. The book is a pastor's treasury of illustrations, proving hymns by the lives they touched.
56494-ecclesiastical-vestments-their-dev:
Ecclesiastical Vestments, Their Development and History is a study of church dress by Macalister. He was a master of arts. It came out as part of a set of books on old lore. Two fellows of the guild for such study shaped that set. A note tells how the print form was set from page scans.

Slant text is shown by set signs in the copy. Greek words stand in plain marks as well. A front print shows a brass plate of a church man of old. The study traces how the robes of church rites grew from age to age. It tells their first forms, their cloth and hue. It tells their signs, and the laws that fixed their use in time.
56544-monsieur-henri-a-foot-note-to-fren:
Louise Imogen Guiney wrote Monsieur Henri, a foot-note to French history, published by Harper and Brothers in New York in 1892. Guiney dedicated the book to an old teacher of her childhood, with thanks for six studious years. Her subject is Henri de La Rochejaquelein, whose portrait fronts the volume. He was the young hero of the war in La Vendée, where royalist peasants rose against the French Revolution.

Guiney quotes a republican officer on that war. It was no commonplace war of ambition or policy, he wrote, but one rooted in soil and conscience, fought for family and fatherland in an impassioned, Homeric way. Guiney looked into the war narrowly, thinking of it by day and dreaming of it by night. Her short book gives English readers the Vendée through its most beloved commander, killed at twenty-one.
56563-her-sailor-a-love-story:
Her Sailor, a love story by Marshall Saunders, bears a copyright of 1899. This New York edition came out in 1901. Saunders had won young readers with Beautiful Joe, and she gives this first story of hers to her mother at Halifax, Nova Scotia.

A note from the publishers says her first printed work came out in England in 1889 as My Spanish Sailor. In this book she keeps the plot but adds new scenes and shifts the time and place a little. The chapters open with the unexpected, then a schoolma'am who is a wife but never a mother. Rubicon Meadows are left behind as the pair take to the sea. Later parts treat a girl's will, a rebuff for Adonis, and words weighed with reason.
56709-texas-in-the-civil-war-a-re-sume-h:
Allan Ashcraft, who taught history at the Agricultural and Mechanical College of Texas, wrote this short history of his state in the Civil War. The Texas Civil War Centennial Commission issued it at Austin in January 1962. Its title calls the book a résumé, a summing up.

The commission's roll heads the book: Walter Long of Austin in the chair, with men and women from Abilene to Tyler. The state set up the body to mark a hundred years since the war. Ashcraft, a trained hand, gives the plain tale in brief: Texas men, Texas fronts, and the home state through four hard years. Schools and readers of 1962 got a clear, short guide.
56728-a-modern-purgatory:
Carlo De Fornaro tells of his trial in A Modern Purgatory. Kennerley printed the book in New York in 1917. A Wilson line fronts it, on poor men and justice odds. The trial is on its second day as the account opens.

The case against him is legally perfect, his defence near none. Strong unseen political forces hem him in on all sides. He rates his chance of escape as a snowball in Hades. His accuser, a Mexican congressman, blushes under sharp questions in court. His other book, Carranza and Mexico, stands named beside this one on the title page.
5676-a-double-story:
George MacDonald opens a fairy tale in a country where nothing behaves as expected. Rain may turn to hail without warning. Milk may sour overnight, and a baby may wake sweet-tempered or cross for no clear reason. The tale is told in short numbered chapters, and its odd rules set the tone at once, as if the world itself were testing the people who live in it. Young readers are invited to watch how small choices play out under strange laws.

The story rewards patience, since its wonders unfold slowly and its lessons arrive through events rather than lectures. MacDonald mixes homely detail with outright magic, so a walk, a meal, or a meeting can turn surprising. Children and adults who enjoy old-fashioned wonder tales will find a gentle, curious book that treats goodness and folly as real forces in its invented land.
56776-practical-hand-book-of-gas-oil-and:
John Rathbun, a consulting gas engineer and editor of Ignition, wrote this practical handbook on gas, oil, and steam engines, published at Chicago in 1916. It covers stationary, marine, and traction engines, farm and automobile engines, and locomotives, in plain terms for the men who run and repair them. Early chapters treat heat and power, the values of fuels from gasoline to producer gas, and the working cycles of two-stroke and four-stroke engines.

Later chapters take up indicator diagrams, ignition systems, carburetors, and lubrication, with the troubles of each and how to cure them. Pictures range from a Curtiss aero motor to marine Diesels. The book aims to be comprehensive and simple at once, a bench companion for the age when the gas engine was remaking farm, road, and sea.
56780-the-hemlock-avenue-mystery:
Hemlock Avenue Mystery is a detective novel by Roman Doubleday of Boston. Doubleday was a pen name for Lily Augusta Long, a note explains. Little, Brown published it with rights held in 1907 and 1908. Drawings by Charles Grunwald illustrate the case from its first chapter. A front plate shows half a dozen men breaking up a sudden fight.

Young Lyon, a reporter for the Waynscott News, haunts the court house daily. He gathers his daily tale of items there for the paper's columns. Lyon alone knew exactly how the quarrel between Lawrence and Fullerton began. Later events gave that quarrel an unexpected weight in the case. A small town feud turns to mystery and to murder here.
56787-7-to-12-a-detective-story:
Seven to Twelve is a detective story by Anna Katharine Green, published by G P Putnam's Sons in eighteen eighty-seven. Green had already made her name with The Leavenworth Case, and the tale is told by a young detective in a New York station house.

The story opens with a call for a detective to a second-story window entrance at the East Seventy-third Street house of Mr Winchester, a banker. The superintendent sees the note was written by Winchester himself, and the plea asks that it be kept quiet and that the discreetest man be sent. The superintendent takes the case in hand himself. The point is sharpened when word arrives that the window-climbing gang was caught that night, so whatever happened at the banker's house is something else.
56894-nancy-brandon-s-mystery:
Nancy Brandon's Mystery, a girls novel by Lillian Garis, was copyrighted in 1925 by the Milton Bradley Company and issued by Whitman Publishing of Racine, Wisconsin. Garis also wrote the earlier book Nancy Brandon. The contents promise incident at every turn.

Chapters bring an incidental explosion, a fall in the woods, and a strange rescue. Nancy and her friends are marooned at nightfall, follow a spy, and face mysterious happenings. A small brown bag and a party cape of blue figure in the plot. The opening shows Nancy packing with her mother, who sails for Europe on business. Nancy stays home, saving her own trip for later, and the mystery grows from her summer circle.
56924-german-influence-on-british-cavalr:
German Influence on British Cavalry is a military study by Erskine Childers. Edward Arnold published it in London in 1911. Childers also wrote War and the Arme Blanche and The Riddle of the Sands. The contents open with the German model of cavalry. A German book, Cavalry in Future Wars, is examined there. Sir John French on the arme blanche gets a chapter. The British theory of the arme blanche follows it. Cavalry in Combat treats instruction from history and general principles.

Tactics against the various arms fill the fifth chapter. The purely cavalry fight and the charge upon infantry are weighed. The dismounted attack by cavalry is treated as well. The fight of the independent cavalry compares German and British views. Reconnaissance and the rifle's rule over tactics close the heads. Childers argues the lance and sword were giving way to the rifle.
5695-jim-cummings-or-the-great-adams-exp:
Frank Pinkerton's dime novel dramatizes the great Adams Express robbery through the career of Jim Cummings and his gang. It opens in a back room in Chicago, where three men sit around a pine table behind drawn curtains, closed shutters, and a nailed blanket, plotting with a forged letter. From that secret council the story moves to detectives, hideouts, and a robber's retreat, as chapter titles promise.

Readers get fast, plain melodrama in the classic detective-story mold: conspirators plan, lawmen close in, and each chapter ends with a fresh danger. The book preserves the flavor of late nineteenth-century popular fiction, where crime and pursuit matter more than fine psychology. It suits readers curious about early American crime tales and the cheap, thrilling books that carried them.
56960-the-midnight-guest-a-detective-sto:
The Midnight Guest is a detective novel by Fred White. The book came out in New York in the year nineteen hundred and seven. White had won note with past tales of crime and secret plots. Chapter heads in the list promise a mark, a face, and a voice in the dark.

A long run of chapters tracks a cast led by Vera Rayne and a man named Dallas. Finds, strong steps, and tales told late raise the heat of the case. Names of men shift as one Valdo shows in a fresh light near the end. The worth of a name forms one late turn in the hunt for truth. Old wrongs after many years drive the close of the long case.
57118-the-padre-island-story:
The Padre Island Story is a popular history of the Texas barrier island by Loraine Daly and Pat Reumert. The Naylor Company of San Antonio published it, with a copyright of 1962. This copy is the fourth printing. The Library of Congress card number is 62-13061. The authors thank the Fish and Wildlife Service and the Texas Game and Fish Commission for photographs.

The contents promise a lusty past. Chapters treat the glittering graveyard, the tropical ladyfinger, and airy wanderers. Matadors and promenaders share a chapter with the fun calendar. Playfolk and sportsmen close the book, before Padre's promise. The introduction hopes readers feel the island's primitive, swashbuckling history. Savages, cavaliers, pirates, soldiers, and pioneers roamed there once. Now causeways cross Laguna Madre to the mainland. A national seashore park, the authors note, was being considered for the island's centre.
57158-the-puppet-show-of-memory:
The Puppet Show of Memory is a book of recollections by Maurice Baring, published by Little, Brown of Boston in 1922. Baring opens by refusing the usual regret over diaries never kept. Memory, he says, is the greatest of artists, cutting the unessential and choosing what is worth keeping. His first memory is a Christmas tree of 1876 at Shoreham in Kent.

Twenty-four chapters run from the nursery and the schoolroom to Eton and out into the world. Germany, Italy, Cambridge, Oxford, Paris, and Copenhagen follow in turn. A chapter on Sarah Bernhardt reworks his National Review article on her. Russia and Manchuria take up the middle of the book, with battles, the beginning of the revolution, and travel in Russia. Constantinople and the Balkan War of 1912 bring the travels toward their close.
57236-thieves-wit-an-everyday-detective-:
Thieves Wit, an everyday detective story by Hulbert Footner, was held under a 1918 copyright and printed in New York. Footner tells the tale in the voice of the detective himself. The man calls this his first case and tells it with a thrill.

He says the case was not one he sought, but one that fell to him by chance, like most good things in life. He warns that he is no hero of romance with superhuman keenness. He is a plain fellow who plugs away, falls down, and gets tricked by crooks at times. He had once been a clerk in a railway freight office, with a father who had no faith in his dreams. Readers get crime work shown as daily grind, not magic.
57311-the-heart-of-a-mystery:
Speight wrote this mystery novel for Fenno of New York, who printed it in 1896. The Heart of a Mystery takes its name from Hamlet: pluck out the heart of my mystery. A prologue, then the story proper, frames the hunt.

The Pengarvons of Broome stand in the prologue's close. Hazeldine changes his notes for gold to open the story. Ephraim Judd cuts his hand, and a discovery follows. One chapter asks outright who did it. An inquest, an anxious week, and a verdict crowd the middle. The trial comes at chapter thirteen. Exit Miss Letitia and a revelation lead to the old story retold. Speight was a tireless hand at the sensation tale, and this shows his full kit.
57340-coffee-and-chicory:
Simmonds wrote a full book on coffee and chicory as trade crops. The book came out in London in 1864. A plate shows a branch of the coffee plant in bloom and fruit. Simmonds wrote a word book of trade goods as well. His front note says a fresh work on coffee was long sought.

Sources of the bean had much changed in late years, he notes. How the crops grow and are made fit for sale fills it. What is in each, and how men mix in cheap stuff, stand clear. Plain tests show false goods to buyer and shop man alike. Grower and user share the worth of his facts. Plates aid each step.
57457-the-book-of-husbandry:
The Book of Husbandry is a Tudor farming manual, reprinted from the edition of 1534 printed by Berthelet and edited by Walter Skeat in 1882. Skeat collated the text throughout with a curious edition of 1598. The reprint keeps the spelling variations and inconsistencies of the originals.

Line numbering from the 1534 text is retained in this edition. Skeat's notes and sidenotes stand in modern English around the old text. The introduction takes up the question of who wrote the book, a point of chief interest for its readers. Farming books of this age taught planting, grafting, and stock keeping to gentlemen and husbandmen. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
57460-the-genetic-and-the-operative-evid:
Genetic and the Operative Evidence Relating to Secondary Sexual Characters is a research work by Morgan. The Carnegie Institution of Washington published it in 1919 as its publication number 285. Contents divide the work into parts, opening with an introduction at page five. Castration of Sebrights, a breed of bantam fowl, is the first experiment of the book.

A male Sebright that did not become cock feathered after castration is reported in the contents. The Sebright cock wears hen plumage, and Morgan asks what the glands contribute to that dress. His operations and crosses weigh the parts of inheritance and of internal secretion in sex characters. Morgan, the founder of the fruit fly school of genetics, here works with fowls on a border question. The paper is a document of genetics in its first decades, when the gene and the hormone were rival keys to the same lock.
57472-fanny-burney-and-her-friends-selec:
Fanny Burney and Her Friends, edited by Seeley, was issued in a new edition by Seeley and Company of London in 1895. Seeley, once a fellow of Trinity College, Cambridge, had written on Horace Walpole before. The book picks choice passages from Burney's diary and other writings, and sorts her life by chapters.

The first chapter runs from her birth and parentage through her father's early life and the family's friends. David Garrick walks in, and Samuel Crisp, the family adviser whose own tragedy failed. Burney's backward childhood, her mother's death, and her neglected schooling are set beside her taste for scribbling. The making of Evelina and her father's History of Music close the chapter's long map.
57816-jet-plane-mystery:
Roy J Snell wrote Jet Plane Mystery, a war tale for young readers first held in 1944 and printed at Chicago in 1946. Ensign Jack Steel flies a scout plane from a large carrier in the mid Pacific. The tale runs to twenty eight chapters. Jack is known to his mates as Jackknife Johnny.

Jack whittles and thinks on deck while he waits for dawn flights. He had hoped for a dive bomber but learned to love scout work. Strange sounds, a wrecked plane, night fights, and a secret book build the plot. A jet plane sits at the heart of the tale. The last chapters bring air fights and the jet plane's last battle.
57917-the-boy-s-hakluyt-english-voyages-:
The Boy's Hakluyt retells the English voyages of adventure and discovery for young readers, edited from Richard Hakluyt's great collection by Edwin Bacon. Scribner's published the book in 1910 in its series of boys' classics. Bacon's preface quotes praise of Hakluyt as the saviour of the records of England's explorers by land and sea.

The contents move from the beginnings of America through Hakluyt the man and his Principal Navigations. Then come the voyages themselves: the Cabots, the quest for the Northwest Passage, the Northeast Passage, and the opening of Russia by the Muscovy Company. Bacon argues that Hakluyt's quaint language is no hard nut for the American boy, since such rich meat is within. The book is a gateway abridgment, turning a vast Elizabethan archive into a schoolboy's shelf of heroes.
57925-master-simon-s-garden-a-story:
Cornelia Meigs wrote Master Simon's Garden for Macmillan of New York in 1916. The story stands in two parts, named for Margeret and for Stephen, and its illustrations show the garden folk of a colonial village.

It opens after a long, hard winter, when old Goody Parsons climbs to Master Simon with an empty basket and a sorrowful face. She goes home smiling, the basket piled high from his garden, with loaves and honey added by his wife, and his little daughter Margeret walking beside her. Chapters ahead promise a tale of witches, a storm breaking, a firebrand lit, a prisoner of war, and Quaker ladies. At the centre stands the garden itself, and the generous man whose door no hungry visitor left unsatisfied.
58173-the-great-invasion-of-1813-14-or-a:
The writing pair Erckmann and Chatrian wrote The Great Invasion of 1813-14, also called After Leipzig. Ward, Lock and Company published the English edition in London. The pair had already written Waterloo, The Conscript, and The Blockade. Their subject is the entry of the allied armies into Alsace and Lorraine after Napoleon's defeat at Leipzig, the battle of the nations, and the march on Paris.

An old huntsman, Frantz du Hengst, tells the story. The narrator takes readers to Charmes, a village in the Vosges along the river Sarre. Thirty small houses stand there with mossy roofs, beehives closed with wisps of straw, and gardens divided by hedgerows. Winter is near and the honeysuckle has withered. From this quiet ground the tale watches invasion come home to ordinary French villages, in the plain spoken manner that made the pair's war stories popular across Europe.
58179-the-purpose-of-history:
The Purpose of History, by Woodbridge, was published at New York in 1916. Columbia University Press issued the three lectures in July of that year. They were delivered at the University of North Carolina on the McNair Foundation. A note at the front states what the lectures try to settle.

They express certain conclusions about history reached by their author over years. Study of the history of philosophy led him toward those views of the past. Reflection on Bergson, Dewey, and Santayana helped form them, he grants there. What history is for, and why men write it at all, is his question. Deans and teachers of philosophy in that age argued such points in lecture form.
58213-the-rosary:
Rosary is a Catholic devotion book on the prayer of the beads. The book carries a nineteen fifteen imprimatur from Archbishop Hanna of San Francisco. A Dominican censor, Arthur McMahon, gave the nihil obstat for its printing. Its name means a crown of roses, the first page explains.

The rose, fairest of flowers, gives the devotion its beautiful name here. The garland decks the brow of Mary, Queen of Heaven, in prayer. Leo the Thirteenth urged the Rosary on the Church above all prayers. The devotion was revealed to Saint Dominic by the Virgin, the book says. He was charged to preach it through the whole wide world.
5828-in-the-pecos-country:
In the Pecos Country opens in the valley of the Rio Pecos, where hardy New Englanders attempt a settlement years ago under a leader like a sort of Don Quixote. The leader travels hundreds of miles, passing richer land, balmier climate, and places protected by law, for the sake of locating where he chooses. Chapters warn, confer, and send Fred on guard, before facing Lone Wolf and the coming Apaches.

The book gives a classic frontier adventure of warning, attack, trees, capture, and escape, told in brisk chapters. Fred's trials among Apaches, old enemies, and hot quarters test a young hero's nerve. The book suits readers of vintage western adventure, while modern readers should note its period portrayal of Native peoples as part of its dated frontier viewpoint.
58314-slavery-in-history:
Slavery in History is a historical survey by Adam Gurowski, published at New York in 1860. Burdick issued it, and Gurowski dedicates it to a friend at Geneseo. Twenty one chapters march through the peoples of the ancient and medieval worlds. Egyptians, Phoenicians, and Carthaginians open the procession. Hebrews, Assyrians, Medes, and Persians follow in order. Greeks and two classes of Roman slavery take long chapters.

Christianity, its churches and creeds, gets a chapter of reckoning. Gauls, Germans, Franks, and Britons carry the story north. The Slavs close the survey, their very name tied to slavery in his telling. The introduction attacks the new American creed of slavery as a positive good. That faith, Gurowski writes, now shadows the whole national life.
58330-the-dune-country:
Earl Reed, author of The Voices of the Dunes and a practical treatise on etching, wrote The Dune Country. John Lane published it at New York in 1916, with sixty illustrations by the author. Fourteen chapters walk the sand hills along Lake Michigan: the gulls and terns, the turtles, and the crows. A cast of local characters follows, with names like Old Sipes, Happy Cal, Catfish John, and Doc Looney. Later chapters go into the back country, meet Judge Cassius Blossom, and follow the winding river to the Red Arrow.

The opening chapter explains the dunes themselves: post-glacial hills still moving east and southeast under the lake winds. Fixed dunes hold their shape under scraggly growth, while wandering dunes bury whole forests and later give back the dead trunks. Reed writes as a resident observer, mixing natural history with the talk and habits of the shore people.
58388-colored-branches-of-the-louisville:
A pamphlet printed at Louisville in 1915 describes the colored branches of the Louisville Free Public Library, with pictures of the buildings and figures on cost, equipment, and use. It marks the tenth anniversary of the opening of the first free public library in America exclusively for colored readers. A motto urges: when you see a book, think of the public library. A summary of work follows the title pages.

Louisville's Western Colored Branch opened in 1905 under Thomas Fountain Blue. Its success made it a model for segregated library service in the South. The pamphlet argues the branches' value in print. It preserves rare detail on an early black library institution.
58413-the-billiard-room-mystery:
Brian Flynn wrote a detective novel first published in the United States in October 1929. Bathurst as an aid to memory opens the contents, then in the billiard room and Bathurst and the bed clothes. Under the billiard room window and the methods of Inspector Baddeley follow. Lieutenant Barker attempts to remember, and Lady Considine complicates matters.

Bathurst has a memory for faces, calls upon the postmistress, and walks into a parlor in turn. What was found on the spider, Major Hornby and the Venetian dagger, and Bathurst potting the red fill the middle. Mary consults Bathurst, the inquest is held, and Baddeley puts his cards on the table. An authentic history of the case can harm nobody, the narrator owns. A country house death and a cool amateur sleuth drive the tale.
58431-orville-college-a-story:
Orville College is a story by Mrs. Henry Wood, the author of East Lynne and The Channings. This copyright edition came out at Leipzig in 1861 from Bernhard Tauchnitz, with the right of translation reserved. The contents set out a school tale. The first chapter is In the Plantation, and the second The New Boy.

Hard and Obstinate as Nails stands third in the list, then Sir Simon Orville's Offered Reward. Mother Butter's Lodgings and Mr. Gall Abroad stand next. Mr. Lamb Improves His Mind in Private, A Loss, and Christmas Day stand there too. A Man in a Blaze, Only the Heat, and In the Shop in Oxford Street carry the list on. If the Boys Had But Seen, Over the Water, Dick's Bath, and The Duel stand later in the list shown.
58530-english-wayfaring-life-in-the-midd:
English Wayfaring Life in the Middle Ages is a study of fourteenth-century travel by J J Jusserand. Lucy Toulmin Smith translated it from the French. T Fisher Unwin published it in London. The first edition appeared in 1889, and impressions ran to a second edition by 1920. English knights travelling in August 1399, from a Harleian manuscript, front the book.

Jusserand opens with a problem of evidence. We know Egypt by her tombs and Rome by Pompeii, he writes. The middle ages of ordinary men left no such deposits. Poets cannot be trusted alone for everyday life; they embellish and transform. The records of old England are the remedy. Thousands of documents had lately been printed or analysed. From such records Jusserand rebuilds the roads of Chaucer's century. Wayfarers and pilgrims people his pages. The result is social history drawn from accounts and court rolls rather than from romances.
58626-north-woods-manhunt-a-sugar-creek-:
Paul Hutchens wrote North Woods Manhunt, a Sugar Creek Gang story for boys. Scripture Press issued the book at Wheaton, Illinois, in nineteen hundred forty eight. The gang camps in the Chippewa forest of northern Minnesota. Paul Bunyan country frames their wild week in the pines.

A Saint Paul girl, Marie Ostberg, has been seized for ransom there. The boys freed her by night and caught her captor in a grave yard. Now they dig in an old icehouse for the hid ransom cash. Stuffed pike from the sawdust hold thousands sewed in their skins. Little Jim’s gunny sack grows fat with the fish and the cash. Then an outboard motor roars straight for their shore in haste. Fast clear thought must save the gang and the gold they found.
587-danny-s-own-story:
Don Marquis lets Danny, a foundling boy without a last name, tell his own tale in this comic novel. Danny begins life in a basket on Hank Walters's steps, where a drunken kick and a wife's sharp eye decide his fate. From hearsay and memory, Danny recounts farms, villages, and the grown-ups who raised, scolded, and loved him.

Marquis writes in Danny's warm, misspelled dialect, full of humor and heart. The boy's lack of a name becomes a running joke and a quiet ache. The book charms as a tall-tale memoir of rural America, where a nobody child talks his way into a place of his own.
58702-the-cricket-of-abel-hirst-and-shre:
Benson and Miles edited this cricket study of three famed players. Dutton printed it in New York in 1903 with thirty four photos. The photos, by Mason and Basebe, show stances from behind for study. Editors say beginners fail to profit from watching experts at play.

Players lack training to observe with later trial in mind, they write. Fast action flashes by too quick to catch and realize plainly. Photo notes train the eye to feet, stances, and changes first. The aim is self teaching from models, not one fixed method.
58733-spatial-delivery:
Randall Garrett wrote this science fiction story for Worlds of If, where it ran in October 1954. The head note sets the hook in a few lines: women on space station duty should not get pregnant, but there is a first time for everything. Garrett turns that first time into the whole tale.

Space Station One circles Earth once every two hours, 1075 miles up. In its hospital ward, Lieutenant Alice Britton lies in labor, the first woman to give birth off the planet. Major Banes, the doctor, waits for the station to swing within radio range of White Sands so he can call for help. Readers get a tight, warm story about a birth that makes history.
58751-the-friendly-five-a-story:
Mary Hungerford wrote The Friendly Five, a story of school life published in New York in 1891. She dedicated it to a young friend in New Haven as a token of warm regard. The contents show a school year in thirty-four chapters. A Mr Bellamy's offer opens the tale, and Katie's room, a rainy day, and leaves from a diary carry the early terms.

A girl named Mary Ann Stubbs enters in the fifth chapter and receives a charge to keep. A mean act, a committee buying ribbons, and dressing dolls fill the middle. Later chapters bring a letter in cipher, a chase to catch a train, and Elfie gone. An exciting night in Troy precedes the close, where Marion is happy and a prize awarded. Hungerford wrote wholesome fiction for girls, turning on friendship among schoolfellows tested by secrets and small wrongs.
5876-ten-englishmen-of-the-nineteenth-ce:
James Richard Joy presents Ten Englishmen of the Nineteenth Century in 1902, dedicating the work to his daughter Helen with a father's love. His preface states the object plainly: to set forth with as much clearness as possible the more important facts in the history of England in the nineteenth century. He chooses to do this through the medium of ten lives, letting biography carry history.

This introduces a century through its leading men, with each life illustrating politics, industry, reform, or letters. The method favors narrative over abstract survey, so a general reader can follow change through character. The book suits students of Victorian England, biography lovers, and anyone wanting a readable introduction to a century of transformation.
58939-the-dolphin-in-history:
The Dolphin in History gathers two papers delivered by Ashley Montagu and John Lilly at a symposium at the Clark Library on October 13, 1962. The William Andrews Clark Memorial Library of the University of California at Los Angeles printed them in 1963. A photograph of the Dionysos cup by Exekias, from about 540 before Christ, fronts the book.

In his foreword, O'Malley notes the new scientific interest in the dolphin's intelligence and friendliness toward man. Montagu argues that the ancients understood the dolphin well, and that this knowledge was nearly lost to the sophisticated western world. Lilly then adds his own astonishing observations of dolphin behavior, drawn from his studies.
58992-modern-american-poetry:
Modern American Poetry, edited by Louis Untermeyer, appears here in a revised and enlarged edition. Harcourt and Brace printed it at New York, with copyrights of 1919 and 1921. Untermeyer had written The New Era in American Poetry. Emily Dickinson opens the gathering, with Chartless and The Railway Train. Thomas Bailey Aldrich and John Hay follow. Bret Harte gives Plain Language from Truthful James. Joaquin Miller crosses the plains in verse.

Sidney Lanier sings of the Chattahoochee and the marshes of Glynn. James Whitcomb Riley and Eugene Field bring dialect and childhood. Edwin Markham's Man with the Hoe stands among the best known pieces. Charlotte Gilman, Louise Guiney, and Bliss Carman widen the roll. The anthology maps American verse from Dickinson's day to the editor's own.
58996-the-story-of-coventry:
Mary Dormer Harris wrote The Story of Coventry, with illustrations by Albert Chanler, issued in London by J M Dent and Sons in nineteen eleven. Harris gave the book to her mother, from Leamington in August nineteen eleven. A first essay treats the three spires and Coventry. Sixteen chapters follow. Chapter one is Leofric and Godiva. A Henry the Sixth portrait heads the book.

The Benedictine Monastery, The Chester Lordship, and Beginnings of Municipal Government follow. Prior Half and Earl Half, and The Seigniory of the Prior and Queen Isabella, fill the feudal chapters. The Corporation and the Guilds and The Mayor, Bailiffs, and Community treat town rule. Coventry and the Kingdom of England, The Red and White Rose, and the last struggle of York and Lancaster follow. The Lammas Lands, the craft companies, and daily life close the book. Local readers get a full medieval town history.
59084-a-modern-legionary:
Modern Legionary is a memoir novel by John Patrick Le Poer of the Legion. Methuen of London issued it in the Colonial Library in nineteen o four. The narrator lands in Paris in the early eighteen eighties with few francs. He tells in chapter one how a schoolboy flight brought him there.

Two and a half years of boarding school routine had wearied the Irish boy. Masters never tried to teach, and boys never tried to learn there. At sixteen he skipped the return to school and set out via Dublin. A day in London, then Paris, with vague hopes and vaguer misgivings followed. The Legion path of a runaway schoolboy opens from that Paris morning.
59093-the-great-sieges-of-history:
William Robson wrote tales of the great sieges of history, with pictures by John Gilbert. The book came out in London and New York in 1856 and reached a fourth thousand fast. Robson had written a life of Richelieu. His preface says late wars prove the age of peace has not yet come.

Science, trade, and art have softened life, he grants, yet ambition and passion still drive men to fight. Against that truth he sets siege after siege. Walled towns, long hunger, bold assaults, and last reliefs fill the tales. The assault on the Malakoff fronts the book. Readers of military history get drama drawn from real sieges across the ages.
59099-the-eureka-springs-story:
The Eureka Springs Story is a local history of the Arkansas spa town by Otto Ernest Rayburn. The text here is the Diamond Jubilee edition of 1954, with drawings by Gloria Morgan Bailey. Rayburn dedicated the book to Sam A. Leath, who served Eureka Springs as guide and historian for over half a century.

The first chapter weighs legends of the magic healing springs. Rayburn warns that tales of Indian visits are badly mixed, and that some were cooked up by white writers. He holds that sound legends come from the Indians themselves, well documented. The famous tale tells of a chief whose sick or blinded daughter was healed by bathing in the waters.
59170-tea-its-mystery-and-history:
Tea, Its Mystery and History is a treatise on tea by Samuel Day. A front note in Chinese, with its turn in English, leads the small book. That note came from the scribe of a Chinese school mission in Europe. The book came out in London in the year eighteen seventy eight.

A plate shows the leaf in hand script of that same guest scribe. Parts trace the plant from its myth birth to the trade of the age. The gift page sends the work to all lovers of pure tea leaves. A shilling bought the neat guide to the worlds famed drink. Grow, pick, and brew lore fills its short and keen pages.
59288-french-painting-of-the-19th-centur:
Grose Evans's French Painting of the 19th Century in the National Gallery of Art was published at Washington under a copyright of 1959, and revised in 1967. Evans was the Gallery's curator of extension services. The cover shows Renoir's A Girl with a Watering Can, dated 1876, from the Chester Dale Collection.

The opening essay calls the century's story an exciting one, colored by personal rivalries and revolutions in taste. Academic painters, it says, bitterly opposed every young artist with a new style, and originality came only at a painter's own peril. Jacques-Louis David leads off: a Paris tradesman's son who rose in the Revolution, failed four times at the Prix de Rome, and in 1774 reached Italy. There, ancient statues turned him against the gay, trivial style of the old court art.
59324-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
Index of the Project Gutenberg Works of Lucy Maud Montgomery, compiled by David Widger, is a finding list for the novels and stories of the Canadian author. Montgomery wrote the Anne books, loved by generations of readers. The index prints the table of contents of each of her works in electronic text. A reader can trace any chapter of any volume at a glance.

Anne of Green Gables heads the list, with its thirty eight chapters from Mrs Rachel Lynde's surprise to the reaper whose name is death. Anne of Avonlea and Anne of the Island follow. The Golden Road, Anne's House of Dreams, and the two Chronicles of Avonlea stand beside them. Rilla of Ingleside, Kilmeny of the Orchard, The Story Girl, and Rainbow Valley complete the novels. Six bundles of short stories, sorted by year from 1896 to 1922, close the index.
59336-a-new-system-of-sword-exercise-for:
A New System of Sword Exercise for Infantry is a drill manual by Richard Burton, printed in London by Clowes in 1876. Burton, the explorer and linguist, had written a system of bayonet exercise in 1853. He dedicates the work, by permission, to the Duke of Cambridge, commander-in-chief of the army, who had encouraged the attempt.

The contents run in order of teaching. Introductory remarks come first. Then preparatory instruction without the sword, and with the sword. The manchette, or forearm play, follows, with a conclusion and an appendix note on sabre handles. Burton held that the British infantry's sword teaching was clumsy and out of date, and he drew on fencing schools abroad for a better method. The manual is a soldier-scholar's try at reform, from a man who knew blades as few Englishmen did.
59343-the-s-s-glory:
The S S Glory is a sea novel by Frederick Niven, the author of Justice of the Peace. It was published in London by William Heinemann in 1915, with pictures by Fred Holmes. The frontispiece shows the Glory sliding into the fog off Newfoundland.

The tale opens on a wharf at Montreal. A band of hard cases waits by the sheds of the Saint Lawrence Shipping and Transport Company. They hope for a job on the cattle ships. A man with a mouth organ plays while they shuffle and watch the barrier. The pictures promise a rival cattle ship, a fight along a line of men, and the dark hold below decks. The novel follows the rough life of the men who worked the Atlantic cattle trade.
59358-all-about-your-canary:
All About Your Canary is a bird care booklet published by the French Company of Rochester, New York, copyrighted in 1951. The firm sold packaged bird seed, and its head, George French, had raised caged birds for years as a hobby. Letters from owners flooded in, and in 1925 he wrote the first French bird book under the pen name Bird.

An opening history runs from the Canary Isles to the Crystal Palace. Wild green finches from the Canary and Madeira islands charmed sailors, who carried them to Europe as prized song birds. Breeders shaped many types: the German Roller, the crested Lancashire Coppy, the Yorkshire, and the Norwich. A 1948 London show drew a record 5430 birds.
59454-in-the-vine-country:
E. Œ. Somerville and Martin Ross wrote this book of the land of the vine. The pair had made a past book of a trip through Connemara in a cart of a maid of charge. F. H. Townsend drew the cuts, from the draws of Somerville in the field. The pages first stood in a sheet for ladies. The first part opens not with vines but with the hunt: it was the pair's first day out with the young hounds.

All had gone ill from the start of that day, the tale owns. They had set out late, for the ticks of the clock twixt five and six in the dawn are few and close, more so than at any other hour.
59470-laboratory:
Jerome Bixby wrote a tale that ran in Worlds of If in December 1955. Trying to keep a supercolossal laboratory invisible when two curious aliens are poking around can try even the most brilliant of minds, the blurb warns. Gop's thoughts had the tint of abject apology: they're landing, Master. Pud looked up from the tiny thig field he was shaping in his tentacles.

Of course they are, he thought snapped, you practically invited them down. If you'd only kept a few eyes on the detector instead of day dreaming, he scolds. I was observing the magnificent skill with which you shaped the thig, Gop answers. A scientist isn't supposed to suppose, Pud thunders. Thirty of his eyes glowered up at the alien spaceship, ninety miles above the laboratory world.
59566-jamestown-virginia-the-townsite-an:
Jamestown, Virginia, the Townsite and Its Story is a park handbook by Charles Hatch. The National Park Service issued it as Historical Handbook number two. The Government Printing Office printed it at Washington in 1949. A revised form came out in the year 1957 for park visitors. The book sold for twenty-five cents from the Superintendent of Documents.

Part of Jamestown Island lies in Colonial National Historical Park here. The Association for the Preservation of Virginia Antiquities holds the rest. A joint agreement since 1940 gives the island one unified program. Contents run from the study of Jamestown to a guide to the area. The colonial parkway and how to reach Jamestown fill later pages. Suggested readings and notes about your visit close the handbook out. The seal of His Majesty's Council of Virginia stands pictured inside.
59617-when-wilderness-was-king-a-tale-of:
When Wilderness Was King, a tale of the Illinois country by Randall Parrish, came out at Chicago in 1904 and ran to three editions that year. Six full color plates and more art fill the book. Its verse motto shows the picket flag of Fort Dearborn above a marching line.

Thirty-six chapters move from a message from the West to a call of duty. The tale names Captain Wells of Fort Wayne, old Fort Dearborn, and a camp of chiefs in council. Dark names mark the turn, from The Last Night at Dearborn to The Day of Doom. A rescue at the stake and a shore fight close the book. Readers get a fierce frontier tale of fort, forest, and war.
59637-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
Index of the Project Gutenberg Works of Henry is a finding list compiled by David Widger. Henry is named in full as William Sydney Porter on its title page. Contents list the volumes of his works held by the project in a row. The Four Million, The Voice of the City, and The Trimmed Lamp stand first.

Options, Whirligigs, Roads of Destiny, and Heart of the West follow in the list. The Gentle Grafter, Strictly Business, Waifs and Strays, and Cabbages and Kings complete the shown contents. The Four Million list opens with Tobin Palm, The Gift of the Magi, and A Cosmopolite in a Cafe. Widger indexes were the road maps of the early Gutenberg library. This one lets a reader find any story of Henry among his dozen volumes in the collection at a glance.
5970-lovey-mary:
Alice Hegan Rice presents Lovey Mary as a bundle of contradictions, from hands and feet meant for a big girl to high ideals that seem too large for her. The book belongs to the Cabbage Patch world of Mrs. Wiggs, and its chapters run from a cactus plant and a runaway couple to a hazy household and a denominational garden.

Neighborly advice, Labor Day, a timely visit, and a Christmas play fill the middle of the tale, with Mr. Stubbins and a pumpkin pie among the homely details. Rice writes with warmth about poor folk who keep their pluck. The cactus blooms at the end, a small emblem of care rewarded.
5972-a-fascinating-traitor-an-anglo-indi:
Richard Henry Savage follows Major Alan Hawke from a low hour at Geneva, where he feeds swans around Rousseau's Island and weighs ending his troubles. The tale then reaches back to Delhi, a veiled rosebud, a diplomatic tiffin, and a mysterious bungalow where safety has a price.

Three books carry Hawke through a devil-for-luck middle act and Prince Djiddin's visit to England, with cliffs at Jersey, a council at Granville, and a French fishing boat. Savage mixes Anglo-Indian service, court intrigue, and adventure. The traitor of the title moves between loyalties, and every alliance looks double-edged.
59818-the-markenmore-mystery:
The Markenmore Mystery is a detective novel by Fletcher, master of plot in the praise of the press. A Boston paper quote in the front calls his plotting sound and his English a vital tool. His stories entertain by manner and style as well as by puzzle, that notice holds. A list of his mystery tales fills the front pages of the volume.

The Middle Temple Murder of 1918 leads that roll of earlier successes. The Paradise Mystery, Dead Men Money, and The Orange Yellow Diamond follow in the list. Titles run on through 1922 and 1923 in a flood of steady output. Markenmore takes its place in that line as a full length country house style mystery. Readers who liked his earlier cases get the same tight craft here.
59893-the-charing-cross-mystery:
Fletcher wrote The Charing Cross Mystery, a London detective novel issued by Herbert Jenkins; this is the sixth printing. The story opens late at night with Hetherwick, a young barrister set on criminal practice, catching the last train east by a fraction of a second. His first-class smoking car stands empty until St James's Park, where two men get in and sit opposite him.

Hetherwick, who loves to size up strangers, studies the elder man: burly, silver-haired, erect as a drill-yard veteran, with a cane headed like a crown. The contents show where the ride leads: a portrait to identify, a potential fortune, a diamond necklace, samples of ink, a medicine bottle, and a mysterious visitor. Later chapters run through Lady Riversreade, torn labels, a telegram chase, and a respectable solicitor. Readers get a brisk puzzle in Fletcher's practiced hand, built clue by clue.
60231-virginia-dare-a-romance-of-the-six:
Virginia Dare is a historical romance published by Thomas Whittaker in New York in 1892. Its subtitle calls it a romance of the sixteenth century. The author signs with initials only and had written tales of Easter-tide. A dedication thanks a rector at Saratoga Springs. The preface reminds readers of the schoolbook history behind the tale. Governor White sailed for England from Roanoke in August 1587. He left behind his daughter and her newborn child.

War with Spain kept White from returning at once. After three years he found Roanoke Island deserted. A palisade stood as if there had been a fight. No cross marked distress, as he had directed. Instead, the word Croatoan was carved on trees at the site. The romance builds on that famous lost colony mystery. Its frontispiece shows a man turning to escape an arrow.
60268-covered-with-mud-and-glory:
Georges Lafond's Covered with Mud and Glory is his Ma Mitrailleuse in Edwin Gile Rich's translation. Small, Maynard published it at Boston in 1918, with a preface by Maurice Barres of the French Academy. Lafond served as sergeant-major of territorial hussars and intelligence officer with machine gun sections of the French Colonial Infantry. The book is a machine gun company in action, dedicated to his comrades of the second company who fell at the Somme in July 1916 and on the Aisne in April 1917.

A tribute by Georges Clemenceau opens the volume, watching the blue-uniformed poilus march, generously covered with mud, from one battlefield to another with no thought but keeping on. Lafond calls his pages a modest share of the huge narrative the anonymous epics of every day would make. The frontispiece caption has Sergeant Lace crying that a man is hit, and indeed he is hit.
60272-tales-of-a-cruel-country:
Tales of a Cruel Country is a story collection by Gerald Cumberland, author of Set Down in Malice, published by Brentano's of New York in 1919. It carries an epigraph from De Quincey on everlasting farewells, and a dedication to Frederick Noel Byron.

Twenty-two tales are listed, among them The Two Lovers, The Baths Murder, The Dreamer, and When the Green Roses Came. Others are Trench Madness, Loot, The Man Who Gave His Soul, and The Deaf-Mute of Kilindir. Two stories follow a woman named Katya, and one takes Paul of Tarsus for its subject. The opening tale shows Stephanie Miniati in bed, summoning her lover Orosdi in imagination. His black eyes burn in her brain, and his hands are about her throat in what the story calls love-cruelty.
60289-science-primers-introductory:
Science Primers: Introductory is a school book by Professor Thomas Huxley, printed at Toronto in 1881. Its first part treats nature and science. Sections ask what sensations and things are, what causes and effects are, and what explanation means. Huxley holds that nothing happens by accident and that there is no such thing as chance.

Laws of nature, he teaches, are not causes, and knowledge of nature is the guide of practical conduct. Science is the knowledge of the laws of nature got by observation, experiment, and reasoning. The second part takes up material objects, beginning with water. A tumbling cup of water is weighed, measured, and pressed to show what matter is. A body floating in water, the primer teaches, displaces its own weight of water. The little book was made to ground children in the method of science before its facts.
60324-the-young-enchanted-a-romantic-sto:
Hugh Walpole's The Young Enchanted, a romantic story, came out from Grosset & Dunlap by arrangement with the Doubleday-Doran house, under a Doran copyright of 1921. Walpole gives the book to his friend Lauritz Melchior, and through him to all his friends in Denmark. A motto from Walt Whitman stands at the front.

Four books divide the tale: Two Days, High Summer, First Brush with the Enemy, and Knight Errant. Chapter one, The Scarlet Feather, opens on young Henry Trenchard one spring afternoon in 1920, standing at the edge of Piccadilly Circus by Swan and Edgar's, where the omnibuses then stopped. Millie and Peter stand close to him in the contents, with Duncombe, a death in the Trenchard family, and a rescue near the end.
60368-the-heir-a-love-story:
The Heir is a volume of long stories by Sackville-West, issued in New York in 1922. The title piece is styled a love story. Four shorter pieces follow it in the contents. Their names are The Christmas Party, Patience, Her Son, and The Parrot. The Heir opens on the death of an old lady. Miss Chase, aged eighty-four, lies dead a full day. Her heir and a lawyer move about the darkened room.

A delay over the coffin vexes the funeral plans. Telegrams must change the day from Thursday to Friday. The nephew chafes at lost work in Wolverhampton. Such small frictions open the tale's true theme. An inheritance is set to change a man's whole life. Sackville-West had already written Heritage. Country houses and their heirs were her home ground.
60408-elizabeth-empress-of-austria-and-q:
Elizabeth, Empress of Austria and Queen of Hungary, is a biography for young people, translated from the German of Carl Küchler by George Upton. McClurg and Company of Chicago published it in 1909 in the Life Stories for Young People series, with four illustrations.

In his preface the translator calls Elizabeth's story one of the saddest in the history of royalty. It recalls, he says, the life of Marie Antoinette: both lives were sorrowful, and both ended tragically, one by an assassin and the other on the guillotine. Elizabeth will not be remembered as a sovereign, he argues, since throne and court life disgusted her. She remains the beautiful, sorrowful daughter of the Wittelsbachs: a scholar and linguist, a good musician, and a passionate lover of woods and mountains.
60434-learning-theory:
James McConnell wrote this science fiction story for Worlds of If in December 1957. Its blurb calls the plot one of destiny's weird tricks, a cosmic joke and a witch that could make a nightmare seem tame. The narrator writes because he presumes that He wants him to write.

Paper and pencil have been left handy, the narrator reasons, so writing must be intended. He capitalizes He as the only thing to do, whether he is dead in hell or merely a captive. One moment he walked in woods near his suburban home; the next he woke naked in a small, featureless room.
60524-the-pageant-of-british-history:
Pageant of British History is a picture history described by J Edward Parrott. Great artists supplied the pictures, the title page boasts. Names listed run from Turner and Watts to Millais and Ford Madox Brown. The London, Edinburgh, Dublin, and New York edition is dated nineteen oh eight. A motto from Augustine Birrell heads the book: history is a pageant, and not a philosophy.

The foreword bids the reader watch the procession wind across the greensward. King and queen, statesman and priest, warrior and merchant file past in its telling. Poet and man of law, shipman and others follow in the train. A humble chronicler begs leave to recall their stories as they pass, the foreword says. Heroisms, trials, glories, and shames will all be told of them.
6059-confession-or-the-blind-heart-a-dom:
Gilmore Simms opens Confession, or The Blind Heart, with an epigraph from Goethe's Faust. It asks who dares bestow the infant his true name, and what we can know of the heart and mind of man. The few who felt and knew, and blindly gave their knowledge to the multitude, fell, crucified or burnt.

Simms answers that the pains and penalties of folly are not necessarily death today, though the present has penalties of its own. A domestic story follows, about secrets kept or spilled and hearts that cannot hold their fullness in. The novel treats confession as both relief and risk.
60662-the-beginnings-of-poetry:
Francis B. Gummere wrote this study of the birth of verse, first put out in 1901. He taught the tongue of England at Haverford College. A fresh print came out in 1908. A line from Chaucer's Canterbury Tales stands at its front: I have no text of it, the line says, but I shall find it in a kind of gloss. The list of parts shows the way of the first part: the aim of the book and its method.

That method is the tale of times past set side by side with like cases. The aids of the new science are named, and their bounds are set as well. The proof that verse can give is the theme that the part works out.
60729-slater-s-1859-shropshire-directory:
Slater's Shropshire Directory is a county directory and gazetteer from 1859. Isaac Slater printed and published it at Manchester. The volume opens with a full account of the shire. Trade lists for its towns follow in the directory proper. David Price transcribed this copy for the digital edition.

The county essay fixes the boundaries first. Cheshire bounds Shropshire on the north. Staffordshire lies east, Wales west. The shire runs forty-five miles from north to south. Its area is given as 1,341 square miles. The name Salop defies sure derivation, Slater admits. The Celtic Cornavii held the land first. Their chief town became the Roman station of Viroconium. Shrewsbury's early history fills the next pages.
60733-the-silverton-story:
The Silverton Story is a local history of Silverton, Colorado, written by Mary Ann Olsen and copyrighted in 1962. The Project Gutenberg text was printed by Beaber Printing in Cortez, Colorado. The author thanks local people for facts and pictures. One of them is a former publisher of the Silverton Standard.

The book opens with the town's setting high in the San Juan Mountains. Silverton sits in a valley over nine thousand feet up. Four peaks rise above the tree line around it. Olsen tells how the town took its name from miners boasting of silver by the ton. It was first called Baker's Park, after Charles Baker. Baker led a party of prospectors into the country in 1860 or 1861. The first pages trace that hard early journey and the traces the party left behind.
60926-captains-of-harley-a-school-story:
Captains of Harley is a school story by Hylton Cleaver, printed at London in 1921 by Humphrey Milford of Oxford University Press. Brock drew the pictures, one showing a boy who hit the boards and lay still. Cleaver wrote other Harley tales, among them Brother o' Mine and The Harley First Eleven, and this book runs to twenty-three chapters.

The chapter heads open with The Boy in the Corner and The Great Game, then move through mistakes and breakers ahead. A rising star, a cabinet meeting, and the thumb-screw follow, before the tale turns to yesterday's captain and the cup of bitterness. Cleaver writes the boarding school world of games, honour, and quiet feuds, with the day of reckoning saved for the close.
61081-cinderella-story:
Cinderella Story is a science fiction tale by Allen Kim Lang. It appeared in Worlds of If in May 1961. Orison McCall applies for a job at the William Howard Taft National Bank and Trust Company. The First Vice-President, Mr Wanji, is no public picture of a banker. He wears hound's-tooth checks, a scarlet vest, and furry green earmuffs. The elevator operators wear earmuffs too.

Wanji speaks in the slang of a much later decade. He offers Orison, in his words, a cee-and-a-half a week. A Franklin and a Grant, he explains, make the sum. Floors above the fifth, he warns, are Iron Curtain Country to staff. The tiny office on five holds a desk, a telephone, and a microphone. Lang plays the Cinderella plot inside a bank that is phony, in the blurb's words, as a three-dollar bill.
61119-dangerous-quarry:
Jim Harmon's story, printed in Worlds of If in March 1962, puts a computer on the trail of insurance fraud. Madison adjusts claims for Manhattan-Universal Insurance. His boss, Thad McCain, beams over the new Actuarvac, an automatic brain that reads claim cards and clears the honest ones. The machine, McCain says, will keep Madison from flying off on wild-goose chases. Then, as a demonstration, he feeds it one plain claim.

The Actuarvac rings its bell and spits the card back with a new notation: investigate the Ozark village of Granite City. Madison protests that a whole town cannot be filing false claims. McCain only tells him to circle up the wagon train and see how the Indians fall. The teaser above the title gives the joke: one little village could not have a monopoly on all the bad breaks in the world. They did, though.
61147-the-day-of-glory:
Dorothy Canfield wrote of France at war in a book printed in New York in 1919. Canfield had written The Bent Twig and Understood Betsy. Six pieces fill the book. The first, On the Edge, follows Jeanne, a French mother whose life rises and falls with the daily mail from the front.

Jeanne feeds six hungry children and gives most of her own share away. At night she dreams that her husband Andre lies wounded and calls to her. Other pieces tell of a woman doctor at the front, of Lourdes, and of a day of glory. Canfield shows French home life under war strain with warmth and close detail.
61185-common-sense-papers-on-cookery:
Payne's Common-Sense Papers on Cookery, issued by Cassell, Petter and Galpin, first appeared as papers in Cassell's Magazine. The preface disclaims any complete cookery book. Instead, recipes are given at greater length than ordinary cookery books allow, and mingled with anecdote for entertainment. The book is meant more for the drawing room than for the kitchen. Its target is the middle-class mistress whose helplessness, Payne holds, makes helpless servants.

Twenty papers run from the uses and abuses of a frying pan to food for invalids. Kitchen economy, a cold leg of mutton, breakfast dishes, and how to give a nice little dinner fill the early papers. Salads, picnic dainties, cooling drinks, game and gravy, and Christmas dinners follow. The opening paper begins with the cry of young housekeepers about Mary Ann the maid.
61234-common-sense-country:
L S Bevington wrote Common-Sense Country, a Liberty pamphlet. James Tochatti printed it at the Liberty Press, Chiswick. One penny was its price in the line. The Liberty journal of anarchist communism stands behind it. That paper ran monthly at the same penny price. Its writers list fronts the pamphlet in pride.

Louise Michel and Kropotkin stand in that list. Malatesta, Reclus, and William Morris join it. G B Shaw and Bevington herself stand there too. Sister pamphlets crowd the press list as well. Malatesta writes on parliamentary politics there. Reclus writes on the ideal and youth. Voltairine de Cleyre defends Emma Goldman in one. The Why I Ams gather creeds in two series. Shaw tells why he is a social democrat there. A penny anarchist press list shows the 1890s movement arguing every road to freedom at a working man's price.
61402-sand-dunes-story:
Sand Dunes Story is a small guide booklet by Donna Bessken about the sand dunes of Death Valley. A map at the front names the landmarks round about: mountains, hills, wells, a cornfield of the devil, and a canyon. The welcome page asks what each visitor sees when looking across the dunes. Piles of lifeless sand, a giant sandbox, the booklet asks.

Each of us sees the dunes in a different way, it answers. The booklet promises to share the story of the dunes with the reader. It answers questions about the origin, makeup, and shaping of the sand hills. Plants come next, and signs of the animals that make their home there. All the features treated lie near the edge of the dunes, needing only curiosity, and water against the heat.
61593-arabic-thought-and-its-place-in-hi: Arabic Thought stands in Trubner Oriental Series, sold at a uniform price in green cloth. Front pages list the set, from Alberuni India to lives of the Buddha. Works on Hindu thought, Chinese Buddhism, and Indian poetry fill the list. The series aimed to bring Eastern learning to English readers in sound form.
61624-the-fall-of-ulysses-an-elephant-st:
Charles Dwight Willard tells a tall tale in The Fall of Ulysses, an elephant story from George H Doran of New York in 1912, with pictures by Frank Ver Beck. A plate gives the scheme away: the narrator began a systematic and determined effort to teach Ulysses to read and write. The book is framed as a confession.

The narrator owns the blame for the calamity that overtook his elephant, a real Asiatic animal, no metaphor, and calls himself the creature's Frankenstein. He bought Ulysses through Jerry Rhahob, a half breed trainer in Madras who knew elephants best. Comic rue fills the telling.
61643-the-book-of-topiary:
Charles Curtis and Gibson wrote The Book of Topiary, number eighteen of the Handbooks of Practical Gardening, edited by Harry Roberts and printed in London and New York in 1904. Curtis was assistant editor of the Gardeners' Magazine and had served at Kew. Gibson was head gardener at Levens Hall. A view in Levens gardens fronts the book. A saying of Shirley Hibberd heads the title, on pitying the man who sneers at a well cut peacock.

Contents open with an introduction, then topiary itself and its early history. The golden age of topiary, the crusade against it, and Addison and Pope follow. The revival of the art comes next. The making of a topiary garden and the care of old trees fill the working chapters. The training of young trees and the general care of such a garden close the book. Plates show boats, pyramids, and peacocks.
61662-the-people-of-palestine-an-enlarge:
The People of Palestine, by Elihu Grant, is an enlarged edition of his Peasantry of Palestine, printed in Philadelphia and London by Lippincott, with rights held from 1907 and 1921. Grant taught biblical literature at Haverford College. A photo shows a Siloam woman with her infant on her back and produce on her head.

The book stands as a companion to The Orient in Bible Times, in a series on Bible lands and peoples. Its parts treat the seasons, wet and dry, the rainfall, and the effect of weather on health and food. Flora, wild animals, birds, and the look of cities follow. Grant lived among the villagers and set down their work, dress, food, and feasts. Bible readers get the land of the text as its folk lived it in his day.
61672-handbook-for-light-artillery:
Handbook for Light Artillery, by Dyer, first lieutenant of the Fourth Artillery, appeared in 1896. Wiley published it at New York, with Chapman and Hall at London. A preface states the aim of the work for its first readers. The author sought to place in compact form all data of service on the subject.

Officers of the Regular Army and the National Guard form the audience he names. He held strictly to army regulations, drill rules, and official reports in the text. What came from other sources was chosen with care from the best authorities. He makes no claim to originality in the work, the preface grants at once. Foreign service handbooks of the same kind gave him his model for the book. Guns, horses, drill, and field craft fill such a pocket manual.
61829-peggy-from-kerry:
Mrs L T Meade wrote a girls' novel in 1912 about Peggy, a girl from Kerry in Ireland. Early chapters take her from home on a journey to Preston Manor. Chapters promise adventures at a farm, a lost and found Peggy, and life with school companions. A bequest, a hockey field mishap, and a contest all lie ahead.

Mrs Wyndham of Preston Manor is kind to poor neighbours but somewhat worldly. Peggy must fit into a new house and a new school. Later chapters bring trouble, flight, and a chance to make things right. Meade writes a brisk school and home story with an Irish heroine.
61904-world-of-mockery:
World of Mockery is a science fiction tale by Sam Moskowitz of Ganymede. The story ran in Planet Stories for Summer nineteen forty one. John Hall walks on Ganymede with a thousand weird beings beside him. One man voice rings in a world of shrieking echoes there.

Hall wipes blood from his mouth and frees himself from wreckage. His helmet was shocked open, and thin bitter air rushed in on him. He had run out of fuel on his way to Vesta city unwisely. A kicked rock sails thirty feet in the weak pull of Ganymede. Then a dozen stones rise and fall in slow mockery of his kick.
61940-a-sermon-thou-shalt-not-commit-adu:
A Sermon is a church talk on the seventh law of the old book of faith. That law is set at its head in the words of the book: thou shalt not break the wed bond. The host text is made from a copy with no date, bound with the sheets of a church man. A note at the front thanks the keep ers of that copy for its use. No name for its hand stands in the host text.

No thing is more grave than faith, the talk starts. And this law, which God him self has taught us, no thing is less grave thought on. Faith teaches us our charge to our make, to our next folk, and to our selves, it says. It shows us the way to flee woe to come and woe at hand.
62044-billy-and-hans-my-squirrel-friends:
William James Stillman wrote Billy and Hans, My Squirrel Friends, a true history first printed in the Century Magazine in February 1897. This reprint, issued at Portland, Maine in 1914, follows the revised edition of 1907. Stillman was a journalist and a lover of animals, a friend of Lowell, Longfellow, and Charles Eliot Norton.

The story begins at Laufenburg, a town at the edge of the Black Forest, where a farmer's boy brings him a young squirrel for sale. The creature is a dark grey variant of the European squirrel, with black tail and ears. At first it only drank milk and slept, and Stillman was unsure it was not a dormouse. The book follows his two pet squirrels with the patience of a naturalist and the affection of a friend.
62189-louisiana-prehistory:
The State of Louisiana sums up its deep past in a public booklet on the first peoples of the region. The Archaeological Survey and Antiquities Commission issued it at Baton Rouge. It first printed in June 1982, then again with changes in April 1987.

The text opens about 10,000 B C, when man first entered the region. Group after group settled there in the ages since. Each left signs of its presence in the ground. The booklet belongs to the commission's Anthropological Study series. Its cover shows a hunter with an atlatl, the old spear-thrower. State law charged the office with sharing such knowledge with the public. The printing cost is stated on the page, as state rules demand. It serves schools, landowners, and diggers alike.
62199-the-thought-men-of-mercury:
The Thought-Men of Mercury is a science fiction story by Winterbotham. It ran in Planet Stories in the fall of 1942. Two men, Cappy Upjohn and Terry Hall, must escape a no man's land on Mercury. Their captors can read minds, so even forming a plan is peril. The scene is neither night nor day but a twilight strip. Mercury's habitable band runs twenty miles wide between roast and freeze.

Giant ferns flash with phosphorescence under a green corona light. Cappy, veteran of Venus and of a prior Mercury trip, mocks Terry's fear. Terry's jaw sets as they pick through the ferns. Then a ghostly face peers through an opening in the plants. It looks more ape than man, yet less than human. Terry claws for the strange rifle slung on his shoulder. Escape and mind reading drive the tale from there.
62276-historical-and-descriptive-guide-t:
Williams's Historical and Descriptive Guide through Shrewsbury, in a new and revised edition, was printed and published by Drayton Brothers of Shrewsbury in 1881. The prefatory note is modest: no pretensions to a full history or a complete handbook. The guide is a sketch of the town's historical associations, with a directory just full enough to lead residents or visitors to the principal places of interest.

The opening chapter takes up the associations as a boast. Proud Salopians, it asks, have we not reasons for pride. Shrewsbury has found homes and hiding-places for kings, kept a mint, and seen the British Parliament held within its walls. Charters came from kings' hands, and loans went back without security. Charles the First raised an army here and laid his head in a house on the Wyle Cop. And Falstaff, by his own account, fought one long hour by Shrewsbury clock.
62309-the-old-man-s-story:
Old Man Story is a farthing book for children from Dean of London. Dean and Son issued it in their Illustrated Farthing Books cheap line. An old man called Uncle John lives in the village of C in the tale. Children love his stories and sit on the grass at his feet.

On Wednesday afternoons he tells what he did when he was a boy. This story tells how young John loved playing with gunpowder in secret. His odd half pence were saved to buy powder and make fireworks with. His mother would never have allowed the dangerous play if she had known. A visiting gentleman gave him money for a good little book instead.
626-the-love-of-books-the-philobiblon-of:
Richard de Bury praises books and book lovers in this medieval treatise, here in E. C. Thomas's translation. De Bury, bishop of Durham and tutor to Edward III, collected books across England and Avignon, where he met Petrarch. His Philobiblon argues that books hold hidden treasure, to be taken up, kissed, and thanked for, as Thomas à Kempis urged.

A preface traces de Bury's rise from Bury St. Edmunds to chancellor of England. The treatise mixes lore, complaint against book neglect, and joy in reading. It endures as a classic hymn to libraries, where a bishop's love of books still speaks to any reader.
62824-when-the-sea-gives-up-its-dead-a-t:
Mrs George Corbett wrote this detective tale, printed by the Tower Publishing Company of London in 1894. Corbett had written Adventures of a Lady Detective, New Amazonia, and Secrets of a Private Enquiry Office. The Diamond Robbery opens the tale, with a man cursing a bus upset that will make him two minutes late on slippery streets.

Miss Annie Cory, the confidential lady detective, takes the case. A suspicious death, a mysterious disappearance, and evil tidings follow. A balloon adventure, an accommodating postman, and a wily siren fill the middle. Sergeant-Major Twiley gets a surprise, and the cry of ware assassin marks the climax. Annie's return and a last chapter called Jubilate close the hunt.
62927-the-jugglers-a-story:
Molly Elliot Seawell wrote a story of France in the days of Louis the Fourteenth. The Macmillan Company issued The Jugglers in New York in October 1911. A front plate shows an actress with the line, think what it is to act when one feels it. Six chapters run from Diane the dreamer to the day of glory.

The lazy blue river and brown plains of Picardy open the tale in autumn hush. Herons stand one-legged in a marsh, grave and still. The Marquis Egmont of the Holy Angels and a bridal veil stir the plot. Readers gain a romantic tale of players, pride, and a flood.
63044-a-girl-of-the-plains-country:
A Girl of the Plains Country is a novel by Alice MacGowan, published in New York by Frederick Stokes in 1924. MacGowan had written Judith of the Cumberlands before it. The tale is set in the ranch country of the plains, and its thirty-two chapters follow a girl growing up among cattle and horses.

The contents sketch the world she enters. An arrival opens the book, then an affair of the heart, a firing squad, and a doll. A Christmas valentine, stockings and shoes, and a carriage mark the child's world. Then the range takes over: a roping match, a fugitive, a boy on the train, and a trail herd of twenty-seven hundred cattle. Hilda and the flying brands, a blue roan horse, and a dance at a ranch house fill the later chapters. The book closes with a telegram and an arrival.
63056-home-canning-of-meat-and-poultry:
Home Canning of Meat and Poultry is Home and Garden Bulletin number 106 of the Department of Agriculture. Washington issued it in February 1966 and revised it slightly in October 1972. It sold for 15 cents from the Government Printing Office, and the Consumer and Food Economics Institute of the Agricultural Research Service prepared the text.

The bulletin warns at the start that meat and poultry canned at home have to be processed in a pressure canner, in glass jars or tin cans. Its contents run from getting ready and choosing equipment through packing, sealing, and processing times. Yield tables, cooling, checking seals, labeling, and storing follow. A spoilage section stands before the recipes: cut-up and ground meat, sausage, corned beef, heart and tongue, and then poultry. A question and answer section closes the book. Home canners got the federal rules in plain order.
6311-a-knight-of-the-nineteenth-century:
Edward P. Roe, in the third volume of his works, dedicates this novel to his honoured father and opens with verse on knighthood within. He best deserves a knightly crest, the poem says, who slays the evils that infest his soul, for the world bows low to knightly deeds and stays cold to pleading. The chapters that follow test that claim in modern dress, through icebergs, passion's clamour, birds of prey, and a victim.

Haldane is arrested, meets a memorable company, and sits as a knight in jail, while Mr. Arnot's system works badly and wounded pride drives him at odds with the world. A paper poniard, a sorry knight, and God's angel mark later chapters, as public opinion is made and a man who hated himself learns to face consequences. Roe writes a moral romance of the nineteenth century, where chivalry means mastering one's own evils first.
63156-boys-of-the-central-a-high-school-:
Boys of the Central, a high-school story by Thurston, author of Ruth Prentice, was copyrighted in Boston in 1896. Nineteen chapters move from an algebra class to commencement. Heads name Hamlin, Clark, Crawford, Henderson, and Freeman, a competitive drill, a hunt for a thief, a snowball fight, and an election for captain of a company.

The tale opens in section D, where Reed explains a problem with his usual speed and care. The teacher stops him and calls on Crawford, who stumbles and owns he does not know where Reed left off. Inattention earns him a failure, and pale Freeman, in the seat in front, takes up the proof, then halts as color floods his face. Thurston writes school life as a field of honor, study, and sport.
63302-cousin-mary:
Cousin Mary, a novel by Oliphant in its third edition from Partridge of London, opens on the Prescotts of Horton, a county family fallen from greatness. Their fall dates from the rising of the Fifteen, when the Prescott of the day joined the Jacobite attempt and barely kept his life.

The squire keeps the ancestral house on modest means and shelters the scattered younger kin. Around Mary the chapters build a domestic story of a curate, a disclosure, alarms, a midnight visitor, a sick room, and a restoration. Oliphant fills the tale with the quiet pressures of a proud but reduced household, where standing in the county still matters more than money. It is characteristic work from one of the most productive novelists of the Victorian years.
63318-some-experiments-concerning-mercur:
Boerhaave, professor of physick at Leyden, wrote a set of trials on mercury that the Royal Society received from his Latin. Roberts of London printed the English version in 1734, at the price of one shilling. The book opens with a defense of the old alchemists. Trial and test, Boerhaave holds, are the only sure road to knowledge of bodies and their powers.

He grants that the hermetic writers hid their great secret in dark words. Yet he warns that it is rash to scorn what skilled men of an art declare can be done. No men, he says, have worked matter through so many modes of enquiry as the alchemists. Geber stands as his proof of their plain dealing in what they had truly found. The essay is a plea for fair trial over scorn, from one of the great doctors of his age.
63446-the-silver-domino-or-side-whispers:
The Silver Domino, or Side Whispers, Social and Literary, is a book of satire. Its maker hides his name, and the press of the day praised the mask. The Daily Chronicle hailed its sharp way with words and phrases. The Star found itself in an up-to-date literary satire by surprise. The Times of London called its sallies candid at great men's cost.

A parody of Olive Schreiner won praise as fierce and fine from reviewers. The World said the writer has his knife into a great many people. News of the World owned to chuckling hugely over the thrusts. Politics, letters, and journalism all take their thwackings in the pages.
