A literary creed in the book takes free aim at the Saturday Review. The mask let the writer strike where a named man could not.
63462-over-there-with-the-marines-at-cha:
Capt George H Ralphson wrote Over There with the Marines at Chateau Thierry, issued by M A Donohue and Company in Chicago and New York in nineteen nineteen. Ralphson had written mate books on the Doughboys at St Mihiel and the Canadians at Vimy Ridge. Phil and Tim are the young heroes. More than thirty chapters carry the tale from camp to fight and flight.

Early chapters show four kilos on hobnails, digging in, gas masks, and a machine gun barrage. The foe then charges, and woods fighting and aid from the air follow. Phil is taken and held in a barbed wire prison, then plots escape by tunnel. Later chapters bring overheard plots, a fight in a cellar, and flight to hiding. Boys of the age got a fast, brave tale of the Great War just past.
63528-a-class-book-of-old-testament-hist: A Class Book of Old Testament History is a school textbook of the Bible’s first great narrative, made for classroom use. Its text keeps the older spellings of its period, as the notes to this edition warn. Genesis, Exodus, and the kings of Israel give such a book its march. Class books of this kind broke the story into lessons with questions. Victorian and Edwardian schools taught the Old Testament from volumes of this stamp.
63551-verena-in-the-midst-a-kind-of-a-st:
Lucas wrote Verena in the Midst, subtitled a kind of a story, published by Doran in New York in 1920. He was a prolific essayist and editor, author of The Vermilion Box and the Wanderer travel books, and biographer of Charles Lamb. The book is dedicated to Frances and Sidney Colvin.

A note to the reader explains the form. The letters in the book were selected from a correspondence that passed during 1919, with the last letter a little later. Richard Haven is one of the writers whose letters appear. Through the letters, Verena stands in the midst of a circle of friends, seen in their own words. Lucas builds the tale gently, out of talk, travel, and affection, in his usual easy manner.
63581-the-age-of-science-a-newspaper-of-:
The Age of Science is a book in the form of a newspaper of the twentieth century, written under the name Merlin Nostradamus. It was printed at London by Ward, Lock and Tyler. Verses from Tennyson's Two Voices front it. The paper announces, as its great news, the greatest discovery ever achieved by man: the new Prospective Telegraph.

By this wonderful invention, the editors say, the obstacle of Time is conquered as fully as the Electric Telegraph conquered Space. Future years, and even future centuries, will answer to our call as promptly as the uttermost parts of the earth now do. The force at work is not electric, magnetic or galvanic. It is the Psychic Force, whose laws a new and greater Wheatstone has found out and put to use.
63582-oliver-s-bride-a-true-story:
Oliver's Bride, billed as a true story, is a novel by Mrs Oliphant. The Standard Library Company published it in London from Clerkenwell Road. Oliphant had written The Chronicles of Carlingford. The first chapter opens as Oliver and Grace promise themselves to each other. Their friends have known for weeks what was coming. Oliver is pale with the discovery that she loves him.

He will not let her take him without a confession. He has not been always what he ought to have been, he says. The best man alive might call himself undeserving, but he means more. He is not worthy, he insists, to touch her hand. Grace stops his lips: all that has been is done with, for both of them. She hints that she too might have a confession. He seizes her, crying that she must never name herself in such a comparison.
63687-the-geisha-memory:
Winston Marks wrote The Geisha Memory, a tale in a planet magazine of 1954. It opens with a song in the hearts of the celibates of Mars. Peter Duncan lies strapped and drugged on a bucket-couch. He is one of eighty passengers on the Mars-bound vessel. He is miserably and continuously sick on the passage out.

The sickness is a shifting instability in three dimensions, the tale says. The ship veers and corrects to avoid meteorites by radar control. The other passengers suffer as much as he does, it owns. They at least have a substantial reason for being here, he thinks. They supply energy-starved Earth with fissionable stuff from Mars. The single ship is the only link between the two planets. A public relations man named Peter Duncan rides that link, the notices say. Marks gives a pulp tale of Mars, memory, and longing.
6385-simple-italian-cookery:
Antonia Isola writes Simple Italian Cookery as a practical book, from soups and macaroni to rice, sauces, eggs, fish, vegetables, meats, salads, and desserts, with an index. Beef soup stock opens the soups. Round of beef, bones, carrots, potatoes, onion, tomato, and parsley are boiled slowly in two quarts of water, skimmed, salted, and finished with sherry after two hours. That stock forms the basis of all soups that follow.

Richer stock adds a turkey leg and chopped beef, meat jelly takes gelatine before straining, and a dark colour comes from a few drops of caramel, as the sample shows. A later recipe fries ham and onion golden in butter, adds uncooked rice, bouillon, nutmeg, and Parmesan for a risotto like dish. Isola writes plainly for home cooks, with quantities, times, and reasons, so that Italian food can be made without a restaurant kitchen.
63870-a-southern-woman-s-story:
Phoebe Yates Pember wrote this tale of her life in the wartime South, and Carleton printed it at New York in 1879. Pember had served in a Southern hospital through the Civil War. A verse on fate heads the book: it is well we cannot see what the end will be.

Pember writes as a woman of the South who saw the war from inside its wards. Her story, famed since its first run, mixes pride, grief, and dry wit. The verse she chose sets her tone: each launch on life's waters is hid from us at the start. Readers who want the war's home face, told by a sharp and brave hand, find it here in full.
63877-never-fire-first-a-canadian-northw:
Never Fire First is a Canadian Northwest Mounted story by James French Dorrance, printed at New York by the Macaulay Company in 1924. Dorrance was co-author of Get Your Man and Glory Rides the Range. Charles Durant drew the frontispiece. The slogan is the title: never fire first.

Twenty-seven chapters tell the hunt. He has overslept, and a Mountie in close pursuit of a murder suspect should not slip. The chapters run through the Eskimo way, a cryptic messenger, living targets, the scarlet special and the closed creek. La Marr had enlisted dreaming of gay uniformed details in Montreal or Quebec, not an Arctic assignment. His fear is what his superior, Staff Sergeant Russell Seymour, will think if the news leaks. The novel is northern adventure in the Mounted Police tradition.
63962-ashes-cenere-a-sardinian-story:
Grazia Deledda wrote a Sardinian story called Ashes, or Cenere in Italian. Helen Hester Colvill turned it into English for John Lane in London and New York. Roman numerals on the title page give the year as MCMVIII. Two parts of eight and nine chapters shape the tale.

Oli, fifteen and bright eyed, slips out on Midsummer Eve to mark flowers of St John. She wears a red skirt and stiff brocade, with scarlet ribbons in hand. Herbs picked at dawn will serve for charms and cures, the custom holds. Wild Sardinian spring, kin duty, and young love fill a rich, grave tale.
6406-the-monastery:
Walter Scott, after Ivanhoe, chooses for his next scene the celebrated ruins of Melrose, near his own home, though he cannot recall the reason or caprice that dictated the change. The Monastery, in the Abbotsford edition of the Waverley Novels, complete in twelve volumes, opens with an 1830 introduction weighing that choice. Halbert Glendinning invoking the White Lady fronts the book.

A ruffian asks a sub prior what gold he would get for couching a lance, and what for levelling it at a heretic. The church answers with spiritual censures before Saint Peter's sword. A primate, the tale hints, recommends a little strangling and burning in aid of both. Scott writes border romance at Reformation's edge, where monastery, lady of the lake, and reforming sword contend for Scotland's soul.
6410-once-aboard-the-lugger-the-history-:
A. S. M. Hutchinson begins with excursions in a garden, where Mr. Christopher Marrapit dozes in a chair on the lawn, his darling cat Rose of Sharon asleep on his lap, and Mrs. Major, his companion, sits stiffly beside him, a masterly woman. The narrator warns that meeting strangers goes better with some knowledge of the first person met. At Paltley Hill, neighbourhood chatter fails to supply that knowledge.

Book One follows George, Book Two his Mary, through melancholy, hospitals, and life itself, with a heroine's arrivals. George, promising himself all night to say four words, at last says them: Mary, I love you. She laughs her clear, unique pipe of mirth, and he protests he is not foolish. Hutchinson writes a long, playful courtship, where a lugger voyage frames a love that laughs at itself.
6412-nature-s-serial-story:
E. P. Roe, in the first volume of his works, tells Nature's Serial Story as a tale of a house and its people, with Mr. and Mrs. Clifford from life. A hard brain worker, tired and losing zest, finds renewal in love of nature, Roe says in his preface. No one deeply interested in her manifestations can wholly lose life's savour. The house itself, built nearly half a century ago, has grown homelike with years, grey as its venerable owner, set back among elms and maples.

Late December shows the old homestead sharp in white landscape, sober hue matching dark tree boles. Under the mistletoe, buds blackened under the microscope tell a spring story. Webb cuts peach buds and finds eight of nine killed by nature's thinning, saving summer labour and promising larger fruit. Roe writes seasons as serial chapters, where a house, a garden, and a marriage mature together.
64142-final-glory:
Henry Hasse wrote this science fiction tale, first printed in Planet Stories in the spring of 1947. A headnote sketches the setting: the Sun was dying, and with it the system. Earth was a cold stone. Survivors huddled on a cheerless Mercury, waiting numbly. The tale itself opens far away, at the forward port of a great ship, where N'Zik stands forlorn and weary.

N'Zik balances his frail, bulbous body on four of his eight limbs, working an etheroscope with the rest. Ahead lies a system with a dull reddish Sun and darksome planets, and it is not for them. Bitterness floods him: in all the galaxy, here was the one Sun that held planets, and that Sun was dying. Shi-Zik comes to stand beside him. Only she and N'Zik are left of all the thousands who sailed. She points to the inner planets and hopes for warmth.
64260-lyra-celtica-an-anthology-of-repre:
Lyra Celtica is a book of Celtic poetry gathered from many tongues and ages. The first edition came out in 1896, and this second edition, revised and enlarged, was printed at Edinburgh in 1924. Sharp and Matthay edited the poems, and William Sharp wrote the intro and notes.

The poems span ancient Irish, Alban, Gaelic, Breton, and Welsh verse, plus modern Scots and Irish work. The first part holds the oldest Irish and Scottish songs. The Mystery of Amergin and the Song of Fionn lead off. Cuchullin in his chariot, Deirdre's lament, and the Lament of Queen Maev follow. The Rune of Saint Patrick and songs of Columcille show the church's hand in the verse. Cornish pieces come next in the plan.
6431-the-law-of-the-land-of-miss-lady-wh:
Emerson Hough's 1904 novel opens with Miss Lady dancing alone before a great mirror in an old plantation house, sweet, strong, and full of grace, like a bird in all her motions. Feet scarce touching the floor, skirt held like wings between dainty fingers, she swims through air, darting, nodding, beckoning, and courtesying to something only she sees. The mirror gives her back line for line, flush for flush.

John Eddring, gentleman of the South, reads the deeper meaning of the law of the land that involves Miss Lady in mystery, while Colonel Blount, Mrs. Eddring, and a mother at a hotel shape the social world around her. Hough writes a southern romance of a girl, a dance, and a secret, where law means custom, honour, and the unseen ties that bind a household. The dance is the novel's emblem, light, free, and watched.
64468-birds-of-song-and-story:
Elizabeth and Joseph Grinnell wrote this book of birds of song and story. Mumford printed it at Chicago in 1901 with many plates. A fox sparrow fronts the volume, poems of birds open it. Contents start with singers and their songs as first survey.

Our comrade the robin, the mocking bird, and cat bird follow. Hermit thrush, grosbeaks, orioles, and a canary life come next. Sparrows, the summer yellowbird, bluebird, and tanagers fill the middle. Meadow lark, skylark, bobolink, and nesting time close the bird tales. The romance of ornithology and an index close the Grinnell bird book for young readers.
64559-the-magic-cameo-a-love-story:
The Magic Cameo is a love tale by Mrs Georgie Sheldon. The full title adds that its form is a love story in plain words. A New York house sold her books in cloth at sixty cents a copy. A next tale in the line is named in the ads as its kin book.

Long ad lists in the front name a shelf of her past tales for fans. Wives by fate, church yard vows, and lost heirs crowd that broad list. A cameo with some strange power or past steers the love plot here. Hearts won and lost mark the stock turns of her famed mode. The tale fed the vast shelf of cheap love tales of its day.
64570-dutch-etchers-of-the-seventeenth-c:
Dutch Etchers of the Seventeenth Century is an art history by Laurence Binyon, of the Department of Prints and Drawings at the British Museum. Seeley and Company published it in London in 1895, with Macmillan in New York. Plates and text figures reproduce the etchings Binyon discusses.

Paul Potter's Two Plough Horses forms the frontispiece. Other plates show a wife spinning by Ostade, a sea piece by Backhuysen, and an ox and sheep by Van de Velde. The text figures are thick with Ostade's peasant scenes: the spectacle seller, the game of backgammon, the humpbacked fiddler, and peasants saying grace. Hercules Seghers and Rembrandt appear with a Tobias and the Angel and a Flight into Egypt, and Everdingen brings Norwegian landscapes. Binyon opens with Adam Bartsch, whose great catalogue of engravers put the Dutch masters first.
6463-a-handbook-of-ethical-theory:
George Stuart Fullerton writes A Handbook of Ethical Theory for students of ethics in universities and outside them, seeking clearer insight into moral maxims we hold with more or less confidence. Reflection and serious effort are needed, he argues in his preface, and in a field of so many differences of opinion, clearness and breadth of view are eminently desirable. The book asks first whether any accepted content of ethics exists.

Codes of communities follow, justice, veracity, and the common good, then codes of moralists, Epicurean and Stoic, Plato, Aristotle, and the Church. Ethical method, materials, and aim as science come next, with man's nature and environment, impulse, desire, will, and intention. A mid passage notes that a child, and many adults, live as parasites on society, their ends chosen by others. Fullerton writes ethics as a student's map, careful and plain.
64631-let-the-ants-try:
Let the Ants Try is a tale by James MacCreigh from Planet Stories magazine. The tale ran in the Winter 1949 issue of that pulp sheet. Doctor Salva Gordy looks at the radioactive smear that was Detroit. Then he looks down at a boiling anthill and thinks, why not. Gordy survived the Three-Hour War though his city did not survive.

He was bound for Washington with blueprints when the bombs struck home. His wife died in the city with no trace of her body found. His children at summer camp caught the wind and died within a month. One blessed week with them stands as his year's whole companionship. He came back to Detroit when the radioactivity had died down. The Emergency Administration laughed at his wish to buy a house there. Pink, hairless mice fed unmolested in his filthy kitchen later.
648-wild-wales-its-people-language-and-s:
George Borrow walks Wales in this travel book, first published in 1862 and reprinted in a definitive 1907 edition. Borrow, who loved the Welsh tongue, praises Wales as a picturesque country deserving more notice, and quotes Taliesin's prophecy that the Welsh shall keep their language even if they lose their land. Plates show Llangollen, Snowdon, and the Devil's Bridge.

Borrow writes with keen, personal prose, meeting folk, hearing speech, and tracing his route on a map. The book mixes scenery, history, and talk in one long walk. It endures as a classic Welsh travelogue, where a wanderer finds a nation's soul in its hills and words.
64833-the-mesa-verde-story:
Mesa Verde National Park in southwest Colorado sent out this small book on its museum's diorama set. The Mesa Verde Story comes on a mail sheet from the park itself. Petroglyphs, the rock marks of the old folk, head the page.

Diorama one shows early man in North America at a hunt of twelve thousand years past. Near Folsom, New Mexico, diggers in 1926 to 1928 found the bones of thirty bison of a lost kind. Nineteen spear points of a strange make lay with them. The beasts had come to a water hole to drink or wallow, and men killed them there. Such small models taught park guests how the first Americans lived.
64934-the-castlecourt-diamond-mystery:
Geraldine Bonner wrote The Castlecourt Diamond Case as a chain of sworn statements. Funk and Wagnalls issued the book in New York and London in nineteen hundred six. Harrie F Stoner drew its front plate of a grasp at a case. Bonner had written Hard Pan and The Pioneers before this.

Six voices tell how the Castlecourt diamonds were stolen in London. Sophy Jeffers, the marchioness’s maid, speaks first and last here. She had served Lady Castlecourt two years when the theft struck. Burridge’s Hotel housed the family for the town season then. Lilly Bingham, known to police as Laura the Lady, speaks next. A box firm chief from Ohio adds his odd sworn tale. Gilsey, a hired detective on the case, gives his full account. The marchioness herself closes the chain of claims and clues.
6494-mr-world-and-miss-church-member-a-t:
Rev. W. S. Harris casts modern faith as a tale of two figures, Mr. World and Miss Church-Member, set against the rush of a new century. His preface notes the flood of new books each week, most soon lost, and hopes his own volume will find real use rather than an early grave. Friends and critics read the draft and urged small changes along the way.

Through twenty-five chapters, the allegory pits worldly pull against church life, testing what a believer does when fashion, gain, and ease call loud. Harris writes plainly, with scenes meant to be read as lessons rather than as mere fun. The aim is plain: to help a reader see daily choices in a sharper moral light.
65243-prints-a-brief-review-of-their-tec:
Emil Richter wrote a brief book on prints, their arts, and their past. The book came out in Boston and New York in 1914. A plate shows a Herodotus print from Venice in 1494. Part one tells how prints are made, step by step. Bank notes and magazine plates show the art in daily use.

Wood cut, wood carve, and line carve are the first three ways. Dry point, mezzotint, etch work, and stone print come next. Press kinds and their use close the first part. Part two runs the past of prints from old to new. Art fans get a clear, short map of a wide field.
65247-a-class-book-of-new-testament-hist:
G F Maclear wrote a class book of New Testament history for school use, as a sequel to his Old Testament volume. It takes up the story where that book ends. The narrative runs through to the close of Paul's second imprisonment at Rome. The preface frames it as part of a series of elementary theological class books.

Maclear wrote for pupils who need a clear, ordered account. Chapters follow the life of Christ and the spread of the early church in sequence. Maps, notes, and an index support classroom work in this edition. The book reflects the plain, factual style of Victorian school texts on the Bible.
65336-the-personal-relation-in-industry:
The Personal Relation in Industry gathers addresses by John Rockefeller the younger. Boni and Liveright of New York brought the book out in 1923. A second printing followed in January 1924, a month after the first. The speeches stand much as he delivered them on many occasions. Six chapters run from cooperation in industry to the people of Colorado.

Labour and capital as partners fills the second chapter of the set. Representation in industry and words to employees follow in due order. An appendix gives plans for employee representation and joint committees. District conferences and the settling of disputes stand spelled out there. The soundest policy keeps employee welfare in mind beside profits, he holds. Industrial relations are at bottom human relations, the book insists throughout. Leaders owe it to do all they can for that human side.
65345-under-three-flags-a-story-of-myste:
Under Three Flags, a Story of Mystery, was published in 1896. Rand and McNally issued it at Chicago and New York. Two authors share the title page: Taylor and Thoits. The tale won third prize in a Chicago Record contest. Out of 816 competing stories, the paper's judges placed it third. Chapter one opens on a Vermont hillside in late spring. A young man lies in a grassy nook with a girl beside him. He is not tired of life, he says, only of his dull way of living.

Their valley is a split in the mountains, he complains. The same story runs day after day, world without end. His wild ambition: to rule a savage tribe in far New Zealand. The girl teases that he does not know what he wants.
65445-deep-waters-or-a-strange-story:
Deep Waters, or A Strange Story, is a novel by the Reverend R H Crozier, published at St Louis by the Publishing House of Farris, Smith and Company. Crozier had written Fiery Trials, Araphel, Cave of Hegobar, Confederate Spy, and Bloody Junto before it. The title page takes its motto from the hymn line about being called to go through the deep waters.

The chapters trace a young graduate through a great change and a mysterious voice into the Civil War. Manassas and After the Battle bring the fighting home, and a dangerous mission, a prison stay, and a Confederate marriage follow. Peace does not end the trials: a drunkard, a crime, a second prison, and a trial close the list. Crozier wrote religious novels of the South in which faith is tested by war, temptation, and the law.
65463-the-end-how-the-great-war-was-stop:
The title page calls it a novelistic vagary. Eleven chapters make the book. They run from Saint Choiseul and Gabrielle to The War, The Invasion, The Repulse, God's Hand and The End.

The tale opens at Saint Choiseul, a pretty village on a hillside in France. Its narrow streets are lined with prim poplars stiff as soldiers. The houses are simple things of one or two stories, built of limestone blocks weathered into brown blotches and white strips. They rise amid beds of flowers, and in the sunshine they gather tints of gaiety. From the road below, the Eiffel Tower can be seen far off. Into this quiet place come Gabrielle, her seance, and her visitation. The book is a wartime fancy of peace, set in a loved corner of France.
65500-essentials-of-music-theory-element:
Carl E Gardner sets out the first steps of music theory in a short textbook issued in New York in 1912. Gardner also wrote on music composition, and aims this volume at busy teachers and pupils. He notes that skill practice eats so much time that theory books are often skipped.

Inside, chapters treat rhythm and note values, then the building of major and minor scales. Gardner urges teachers to press the structure of scales rather than drill keys by rote. Intervals and chord building follow, with inversions and seventh chords, then a short account of sound and a course of ear training. The book also serves as groundwork for harmony, composition, and music appreciation classes.
65504-the-indians-in-wisconsin-s-history:
The Indians in Wisconsin's History is a handbook by John Douglass of the Milwaukee Public Museum. Douglass served in the museum's history division. He died in 1951, soon after finishing the manuscript. The museum printed the book in 1954. It is number six in a popular science handbook series. The first chapter treats Wisconsin before white men came.

The text paints the old wilderness of forest and prairie. Caribou, moose, elk, and buffalo then ranged the state. The Indians lived by hunting and gathering, the book says. Most groups also grew corn, squash, and beans. The reader is asked to step back some 350 years. A camp scene shows women raising a wigwam cover. The handbook aimed at schools and general readers. It sums the state's first peoples in plain terms.
65619-cerise-a-tale-of-the-last-century:
Cerise, a tale of the last century, is a novel by G J Whyte-Melville, author of Market Harborough and Katerfelto. G P Jacomb-Hood drew the illustrations. The story is set in the France of the Grand Monarque. In the gardens of Versailles, as everywhere within the freezing influence of that king, nature herself accepts the chain of order and courtly etiquette.

The chapters open with a daisy-chain and the family of the Montmirails. An abbe, a Jesuit's task, and the Grey Musketeers carry the court intrigue forward. Later chapters bring a masked ball, the raising of the devil, and a quiet supper. Pressed men, dirty weather, and a port welcome follow. Whyte-Melville, famed for hunting novels and tales of the turf, here writes of the old French court. His Cerise mixes romance, plotting, and the sea service of the age.
65707-the-crime-of-caste-in-our-country:
Benjamin R Davenport wrote The Crime of Caste in Our Country, issued in Philadelphia by the Keystone Publishing Company in eighteen ninety three. The copyright of eighteen ninety two is held by Joseph W Morton. Subtitles promise that Americans enforce equality and permit no sham aristocracy of wealth. Bullets in eighteen sixty one and ballots in eighteen ninety two frame the plea. A plate of Abraham Lincoln heads the book.

Davenport gave the book to all citizens who hold that patriotism, honesty, virtue, and merit alone make inequality in mankind. He attacks arrogance and presumption in the possessors of wealth. Caste, he notes, comes from a Portuguese word for race, from the class system of India under Brahmin rule. Records for three thousand years, he says, were searched for examples. Populist readers got a fierce blast at wealth and foreign mannerisms.
6572-haste-and-waste-or-the-young-pilot-:
Oliver Optic, the pen name of William Taylor Adams, tells a boys' tale set on Lake Champlain, where a young pilot learns that haste brings waste. Adams, a Boston teacher for twenty years, knew boy life at close hand, and his books were loved for being both fun and clean. His life note, set at the front, traces his work from 1850 to his death in 1897.

The young pilot must steer with care, judge wind and water, and own his faults when speed tempts him past sense. Optic keeps the lessons inside the action, so the moral never halts the fun. Haste and Waste is a brisk, old-style adventure for young readers, with lake air and honest work on every page.
65727-the-most-horrible-story:
John W Jakes wrote The Most Horrible Story, a short tale of dread. It ran in Imagination Stories of Science and Fantasy in January nineteen hundred fifty two. The title page dares the reader to face a tale too strong to bear. Thompson, the hero, walks into a plain room he has never seen.

An old man with a clipped beard sits at a gray desk in the room. A candle burns there but never shrinks. The man signs Thompson into the Horror Book Club. He takes his name and birth date for the files. Thompson asks for famed tales such as Dracula. The old man laughs at such mild fare. What the club lends, he hints, is real horror.
65811-the-phone-booth-mystery:
The Phone Booth Mystery is a detective novel by John Ironside, printed at New York by Henry Holt in 1924. Ironside also wrote The Red Symbol. The book sold well enough to need a second printing within two months. Its first chapter presents Lady Rawson.

The second chapter cries murder most foul. A taxicab, a belated bridegroom, and a return follow, with a numbered clue and a cigarette case. Grace learns the news, halcyon days give way to dark hours, and Austin forms a theory. A girl at a grave, a Chinese room, and what Giulia saw build the last act. Sir Robert Rawson speaks in the sample pages with hearty thanks to a man clearing his papers. The novel is a neat period whodunit of the drawing-room school.
65886-special-delivery:
Special Delivery, a science fiction story by Kris Neville, first appeared in the magazine Imagination in January 1952. Its premise is stated at the head. Parr came to Earth as the advance guard for an invasion. His mission was to see that every person received a package being mailed to them.

The story opens as shell fire meets a silver listening post crossing a moonlit desert. A radar-controlled gun brings it down, and on the Advanceship above, one of the Knougs blows it up so no fragments can be found. The newspapers and the government give the usual explanations. Three days later the Advanceship moves east, seeding advance men toward strategic centres in North America, namely towns with big post offices. Neville builds the invasion out of the mail itself.
65918-guide-to-the-bayeux-tapestry:
Birrell guides readers in a Guide to the Bayeux Tapestry, from the Department of Textiles of the Victoria and Albert Museum. The Stationery Office printed it in London in 1921, first in October 1914. The price is one shilling, and Harold Enthroned fronts the book.

A first note owns that the tapestry itself is not in the museum. Two full size copies earn the guide its place, it says. One is a hand colored photograph set on the wall of gallery 79. One is a photograph on rollers, kept for students in the Students' Room. Museum guests get a cheap, expert key to the great cloth and its tale.
66011-devils-tower-national-monument-a-h:
Devils Tower National Monument: A History is a booklet by Ray H Mattison, a National Park Service historian. The Devils Tower Natural History Association published it. First printed in the Annals of Wyoming in 1956, it was revised in March 1973.

The year 1956 marked fifty years since the monument was set aside. It was the first national monument, created under the new Antiquities Act. The tower rises some 1,200 feet above the Belle Fourche River in Wyoming. Indians called it Mateo Tepee, meaning Grizzly Bear Lodge. Mattison retells the Kiowa legend of its making. Seven little girls fled from bears onto a low rock. The rock heard their prayer and rose, pushing them into the sky. The bears' claws scratched the tower's fluted sides. The girls remain in the sky as the seven stars of the Pleiades.
66025-the-lady-poverty-a-xiii-century-al:
The Lady Poverty, a thirteenth-century allegory, was turned into English and shaped by Montgomery Carmichael and printed by John Murray at London in 1901. Its Latin name runs Sacrum Commercium, the holy trade of Saint Francis with the Lady Poverty. Giotto's plate of the saint's espousals to her fronts the book. Father Cuthbert adds a last word on what gospel poverty means in the soul.

The tale walks Francis on his search: two old men point the road, and he finds the Lady on a mountain with his first mates. She speaks of the apostles, of peace as her foe, and of greed in its false masks. She took the names of good sense and care, and called sloth to her aid. Faith fans get a grave, sweet dream of the poor Christ life.
6605-unconscious-memory:
Samuel Butler, known for Erewhon and The Way of All Flesh, argues in this 1910 work that memory lives in the body, not just in the mind. A new introduction by Marcus Hartog frames the book, which Butler first set out as a paper with no claim to new tests or finds. Critics of his day, he notes, wished to block such bold ideas.

Butler holds that habit, instinct, and growth in living things show a kind of recall passed down through life itself. His prose is sharp, combative, and full of wit, taking on the science of his time head-on. Unconscious Memory is a daring, odd book, best read as a thinker's challenge to how we view life and learning.
66215-hidden-country:
Hidden Country is a north roam tale by Henry Oyen of The Snow Burner fame. Gardner Pitt, its tale voice, sits at a desk on a May morn at start. He scans the East River from a high floor with dread of the day work. Age thirty, school trained, sound, and keen, he calls his own life a fail. His post is mail trade pen work at twenty five a week in coin terms.

His chief verdict is that Pitt has no punch and sits deep in a rut. George Chanler, an old school mate now rich and idle, wires a bid then. Pitt is to ride as writ hand on his north trip from Seattle. The yacht Wanderer is fit out there for that sail in the note. Light task, a warm months break, and rich terms seal his yes.
66353-the-american-national-red-cross-bu:
The American National Red Cross issued its first Bulletin in January nineteen hundred and six, from Washington. The group had been chartered by Congress on January fifth, nineteen hundred and five. Its office stood in the Colorado Building, in room eight hundred and twenty-six.

The Central Committee hails branches formed in sixteen states, the District of Columbia, and the Philippine Islands. The preface says the nation lags behind others in this great work of mercy. Under its new charter and the eye of the national government, the Red Cross aims to show humane aims beside trade aims. It asks readers to join branches and to form new ones where none exist.
66356-forest-trees-and-forest-scenery:
Frederick Schwarz wrote this tour of American forests for the Grafton Press of New York in 1901. A river scene in Florida heads the book as its front plate. Plates of oak leaves, maple sprays, and pines run through the text.

Forest Trees opens the work: the broadleaf trees first, then the cone-bearers. Forest adornment, the look of woods in their dress, takes the next part. How American forests spread across the land follows. The character of the broadleaf woods and of the cone woods gets a part each. Europe's planted forests close the book, for contrast with the wild growth of home. A book for walkers who want names for what they love.
66363-a-soldier-s-diary:
Ralph Scott kept this Soldier's Diary of the Great War, published by Collins of London in 1923. General Frederick Maurice supplies the introduction. Maurice quotes Lord Robert Cecil: the history books give a false picture of war, and only the men who fought can give the true one.

The things that matter, Maurice writes, are the misery, suffering, and endurance, the filth and horror that form the greater part even of a triumph. Scott gives his own reason in an entry for October 6: the only way to stop war is to tell these facts in the school history books. Out with the rot about gallant charges and blushing damsels scattering roses, he writes. Readers get a ranker's war, set down day by day, with an argument for teaching it raw.
66454-the-liberry:
The Liberry is a novel by Ian Hay, printed at Boston and New York in 1924. Kleber Hall drew the frontispiece. Copyrights of 1922, 1923, and 1924 stand on its page, the first held by the Curtis Publishing Company. The tale opens at a fourpenny box outside a second-hand bookshop in High Street.

There the narrator, a doctor, first meets Baxter. The old man handles the dirty, dog-eared books with loving care. He never snatches one up or throws it down. He blows off the dust, straightens the warped cover, and smooths the pages before reading. Baxter tells the doctor that a book is a human thing. A dilapidated book is a patient, and he likes to repair its broken back.
6674-umbrellas-and-their-history:
William Sangster asks how a busy, practical people like the English, exposed to a fickle sky, could ever have lived without the umbrella. His motto, a shield against rain, sets the tone for a history that runs from ancient times to England, then to the parachute, umbrella stories, and the umbrella's rebirth. The opening chapter teases the reader with disbelief.

Sangster treats a humble object with wit and learning, showing how a rain shield became a mark of fashion and sense. His prose is light, yet full of fact. Umbrellas and Their History is a delightful, odd little book, perfect for readers who love the stories behind daily things.
66754-david-vallory:
David Vallory is a novel by Francis Lynde, published by Scribner in New York in 1919. Arthur Becher drew the frontispiece for the volume. The book is inscribed to Thomas Frank Gailor, bishop of Tennessee, as bishop, adviser, and friend of the author. A list of earlier books by Lynde stands at its front.

Chapter titles sketch a tale of work and honour in the American South. The first chapters are In the Green Tree, The Deluge, Eben Grillage, and An Honorable Discharge. A chapter named Gloriana then brings in the heroine of the tale in her turn. The frontispiece note shows Vallory pleased to find the heroine versed in the details of his world. The sample text in the catalogue shows a homecoming to a Florida coast town, with familiar things looking jarred after a distant assignment.
66869-the-origins-of-art-a-psychological:
The Origins of Art is a psychological and sociological inquiry by Yrjo Hirn. Hirn lectured on aesthetic and modern literature at the University of Finland at Helsingfors. Macmillan published the book in London and New York in 1900. Twenty-one chapters run from the problem stated and the art-impulse through the enjoyment of pain and social expression. The deduction of art-forms, and art and work, art and war, and art and magic, follow.

Chapter one notes that Baumgarten, a hundred and fifty years before, had to apologize for his Aesthetica. A theory of the liberal arts and beautiful thinking seemed too low and sensuous a field for philosophy. Hirn faces no such shame: he asks where art comes from, in feeling, society, sex, and labor. Lists of authorities and two indexes close a learned, wide-ranging study of why men make things beautiful.
66910-wesley-s-designated-successor-the-:
Tyerman's Wesley's Designated Successor, issued in New York in 1883, gives the life, letters, and literary labours of John William Fletcher, vicar of Madeley in Shropshire. Fletcher, born Jean Guillaume de la Flechere, was the man Wesley marked out to follow him.

The preface piles up praise: Southey called Fletcher a man of rare talents and rarer virtue. Isaac Taylor called him a saint, and Robert Hall called him a seraph burning with divine love. Tyerman notes the earlier lives by Wesley in 1786, Benson in 1804, and Cox in 1822, and finds them all wanting. His book argues Fletcher's place as the ablest defender of Methodism and one of the most pious men of his church.
66921-the-boy-scouts-victory:
The Boy Scouts' Victory is a war tale for boys by George Durston, printed at Akron, Ohio, with copyright in 1921. Twelve chapters run from The Call of Home to Greater Things. Along the way come a struggle in the sea, a letter home, and a bit of romance. The front picture shows boys sending a message quickly and well.

The tale opens at a military school after reveille, where three boys walk to the mess hall deep in thought. Nickell-Wheelerson, the tall one, means to go home to England. His father and second brother are in the field. His oldest brother was shot in the trenches in France two months before. At nineteen, with his allowance hoarded for second cabin fare, he holds he has a right to go.
67017-first-notions-of-logic-preparatory:
Augustus De Morgan wrote a short first book on logic for geometry students. The book came out in London in 1839. De Morgan taught mathematics at University College, London. A Bacon line heads it on the false praise of man's mind. He says the tract holds just what new Euclid men lack.

He grants it is not the whole of logic for all ends. He has long rued how logic is left untaught, he writes. Clear terms, true splits, and sound proof steps fill the tract. Each rule is tied to the geometry work it must serve. It was to hang at the end of his book on sums. Math men get a keen, brief first step.
67133-waheenee-an-indian-girl-s-story:
Waheenee tells her own life story to Gilbert L Wilson, a field worker for a New York museum. Wilson wrote the tale down, and Frederick N Wilson drew the pictures. The book came out in 1921.

Waheenee recalls her youth as a Hidatsa girl in an earth lodge camp. She tells of winter camp, games, dogs and the work girls learn to do. Later chapters cover berry picking, the corn husking and a buffalo hunt. Her marriage and her child close the arc. A short word list and notes help young readers, and a supplement tells how to make a camp. Her voice stays plain and direct, which gives the tale its strength.
67223-the-strangest-things-in-the-world-:
Thomas R Henry wrote a book about extraordinary workings of nature, copyrighted in 1958 in Washington. A first chapter is titled The Invisible Underground Jungle. Henry says a gram of soil the size of a grain of sand may hold as many as twenty five million invisible plants and animals. A thousand such grains would make a marble.

This population is made chiefly of single celled organisms: bacteria, molds, yeasts, and protozoa. Thousands of species have been identified, yet most soil life remains unknown. Hunter and hunted struggle without pause in that jungle. Thread like white worms, up to a fifth of an inch long, are its giants. Henry writes as a science reporter for general readers.
67255-the-story-of-zephyr-a-christmas-st:
Jeanie Oliver Smith wrote The Story of Zephyr, a Christmas story, at New York in 1917. She also wrote under the name Temple Oliver, the title notes. Chapter one is called Edwy's Wish, and opens at a lake camp. Father, may I have an English setter for my Christmas present, Edwy asks. He speaks low, for a club president has come to say good-bye.

One branch of the campers breaks up for city schools. The stranger sits on the broad veranda, his dog at his heels. Bruno knows his little friend Edwy well, the tale says. The boy strokes the dog's ears and speaks gentle words to him. The dog lays his head on crossed paws, one eye alert for his master. A dog gets terribly homesick if left with servants, Edwy urges. Smith gives a boy, a dog, and a Christmas wish.
6756-little-memoirs-of-the-nineteenth-ce:
George Paston sketches minor celebrities of the nineteenth century, chosen to show literary and artistic life in its first half. He picks subjects not lately overwhelmed by small biographers, and adds two foreigners, on the theory that a stranger's verdict matches that of later posterity. A German princeling and a gilded American democrat lead the outsiders.

Each memoir is short, vivid, and full of telling detail, from salons to studios. Paston's tone is urbane and amused. Little Memoirs of the Nineteenth Century is a delightful gallery of half-forgotten figures, for lovers of literary gossip and history.
6763-aristotle-on-the-art-of-poetry:
Aristotle's Art of Poetry, in Ingram Bywater's translation with a preface by Gilbert Murray, opens with Plato's attack on poetry in the Republic. Plato calls poetry a false siren, an imitator of shadows, and an ally of the low and weak in the soul. Yet he ends with a touch of compunction. He invites poet-lovers to defend her in plain prose.

Aristotle takes up that defense, showing poetry as both sweet and helpful to society and to human life. Bywater's Oxford text keeps the argument crisp. On the Art of Poetry is a short, essential work on tragedy, imitation, and why stories matter.
67661-gallipoli-diary:
Major John Graham Gillam wrote a Gallipoli Diary, first issued in London by George Allen and Unwin in nineteen eighteen. Gillam held the Distinguished Service Order. A preface and an intro on the climate at the Dardanelles head the book. Entries run from a prologue in March nineteen fifteen to an epilogue after January nineteen sixteen. Photos show Cape Helles, Suvla Bay, and the gangway of the River Clyde.

Day by day Gillam records the landing of April twenty fifth and the long fight that followed. He shows troops pouring from the grounded River Clyde at V Beach. Bathing off Gully Beach, divisional headquarters, and taken Turkish trenches appear in plates. August, September, and the wet late months fill long entries of strain and loss. Readers get a staff level diary of a famed, sad campaign, told as it happened.
67677-rainbow-landing-an-adventure-story:
Rainbow Landing, a novel by Frank Lillie Pollock, came out from Chelsea House in New York in 1926. Its hero, Lockwood, rides a slow stern wheel boat up the Alabama River from Mobile toward Selma. The river trade is in decay, with poor freight and few riders, and the night trip sets a tense mood for what lies ahead.

Twenty parts move through oil claims at Pascagoula, poker games, a pay car, plots and counter plots, fog, and deep water. Woods riders, warnings, and open war raise the stakes chapter by chapter. The book mixes river lore with a fast tale of greed, land, and risk in the rural South.
67678-the-glacier-gate-an-adventure-stor:
Frank Lillie Pollock wrote The Glacier Gate, an adventure story published by Chelsea House at New York in 1926. Doctor Rupert Lang, a rising Boston surgeon under thirty, loses his future in a few weeks: a poisoned scratch leaves stiffness in his right hand, ruin to a surgeon's craft. Then the Automotive Fuel Company collapses, and its promoter Arthur Rockett vanishes with the liquid assets. Lang talks of burying himself in a country practice in the piney woods, while Eva Morrison protests.

The chapter list promises the turn: False Colors, Wrecked, Yuma Oil, Green Stones, and Unexplained Disappearances. The trail runs south to a castaway, a camp of the dead, imprisonment in snow, and the glacier's heart. The closing titles, In His Own Net, The Knife, and Tronador Light, point to a reckoning with the vanished promoter. Pollock opens at the Bayview Hotel near Mobile, over tea.
67735-the-north-shore-mystery:
The North Shore Mystery is a crime tale by Henry Fletcher, put out at London in the late eighteen nineties. Its parts open with the crime, then turn to the woes of a young grad of a London college. A house wife, a board house and its guests, and a police man who makes his name fill the next run.

A woman is bound for trial, and the tale looks back to a great town of the past. Two lovers, two mates who set up in trade, a gold bar, and a big horse race build the mid plot. The trial, a river of the colony, the weights for a famed cup, and a jockey of deep faith lead to the night ere the race and the race itself.
67881-hilda-strafford-a-california-story:
Beatrice Harraden, author of Ships That Pass in the Night, wrote Hilda Strafford, a California story published in New York by Dodd, Mead in 1897. Eric Pape drew the illustrations. Twelve chapters carry the tale from Hilda's coming to a farewell to California.

The first chapter asks its question: would it smile to her? The day has come, and Robert Strafford looks around the isolated spot he chose for his ranch. Terrible misgivings seize him. Scores of times he has tried to see the country through her eyes. The chapter titles trace what follows: Hilda comes, growing regrets, a storm, and a stretch down by the river. A stricken man, passion and loyalty, and the farewell close the book. Harraden sets an English bride's test in the California hills.
67894-victorian-poetry:
Victorian Poetry is a short survey by John Drinkwater, printed at New York in 1924. It stands in Doran's Modern Readers' Bookshelf, a line of brief, fresh appraisals for modern readers. The line aimed to free history, letters, and science from stiff and forbidding learning, and to stir keen readers anew.

Drinkwater opens by noting that the split of poetry into periods is artificial, yet not without use. Seen close, he says, the poets of one age often show little likeness to each other. His survey gives general readers a clear, short path through the verse of the Victorian age, written by a poet in his own right.
67936-working-life-of-women-in-the-seven:
Working Life of Women in the Seventeenth Century, by Alice Clark, was published in 1919. Routledge issued it at London, with Dutton at New York, in that year. Clark was a Shaw research student of the London School of Economics. The book stands as number fifty six in that school study series.

An introduction opens the contents of the monograph at page one. Clark asks how women earned their living before factory industry remade work. Farm, shop, trade, and home production by women fill her evidence in the chapters. Capitalism pushed women out of trades they once shared, her famed argument holds. Wives and daughters in family industry stand at the centre of her picture. A landmark of women economic history grew from this quiet study.
68005-qrm-interplanetary:
QRM Interplanetary is a science fiction tale by George Smith. It ran in Astounding Science Fiction in October of the year 1942. Kolliker drew the illustrations for the magazine printing of the tale. A handbook quote defines QRM as interference made by man, not nature. Static of natural source bears the twin code QRN in that book.

Korvus the Magnificent, Nilamo of Yoralen, picks up a telephone in his palace. He asks to talk to Wilneda at a hotel in Detroit on Earth. The operator regrets that talk is barred by a fifteen minute lag. Interplanetary Communications will not permit audio across that vast gap. Teletype messages are welcome instead, she tells the baffled ruler.
68022-nick-carter-stories-no-145-june-19:
Nick Carter Stories number one hundred forty five, dated June nineteen fifteen, is a weekly pulp fiction issue from Street and Smith of New York. It was edited by Chickering Carter, the head notes. The copy price was five cents, and back numbers could be had by mail on the terms listed.

Its story, An Unsolved Mystery, is billed as Nick Carter's government case. The first chapter is called A Secret Conference. It opens at a railway station, where an old gentleman passes two men as if they were strangers. He jostles past them without a glance. No watcher in the crowd would have seen a link between them, the tale says, a set up that points to a hidden plot.
6805-the-mill-mystery:
Anna Katharine Green, author of The Leavenworth Case, opens The Mill Mystery with an alarm, a fearful question, and a girl named Ada. The Pollards, doubts and queries, a flower from their conservatory, and an unexpected discovery follow, with Rhoda Colwell and a secret under the mill floor. Dwight and Guy Pollard, correspondence, gossip, and a green envelope deepen the puzzle.

A last request, a fatal delay, an old mill, a vat, a cypher, and a final confrontation lead to the truth. Green, a pioneer of detective fiction, keeps the plot tight and the clues fair. The Mill Mystery is a classic, gripping whodunit from the queen of early American mystery.
68054-columbus-and-other-heroes-of-ameri:
D'Anvers tells young readers of Columbus and Other Heroes of American Discovery. A plate of Christopher Columbus fronts the book. Notes by the maker of this text own that spelling was not yet fixed in the book's day. Words shift in form from page to page, and those shifts are left as they stand.

The title sets the scope: the heroes who found and mapped the new world for Europe. Columbus leads, as the plate and the first place in the title show. Tales of bold sails, strange coasts, and hard first landings suit the school and home trade of the day. History fans of a young age get brisk lives with a full index at the back.
68144-thoughts-upon-slavery:
Thoughts Upon Slavery, by John Wesley, reached its fifth edition at London in 1792, sold for two pence at the Methodist houses. Wesley starts with a plain mark: by slavery he means house service owed to a master. Its marks are grim. Work is owed for life, freed by the master's word alone. The lash falls at his will, and no goods are the slave's own. Sale comes like a cow or horse, and the chain passes from parent to child.

He traces the thing from the first ages through Jews, Greeks, and Romans. It waned as Christ's faith spread in Europe, then rose again when America and the coasts of Africa were found. In 1508 the Portuguese sold the first Africans to Spanish planters. Faith readers get a founder's stern brief against the trade in men.
68157-manual-of-the-apiary:
Manual of the Apiary, by Cook, professor of insect science at the Michigan State Agricultural College, is a handbook of bee keeping. The fourth edition, revised, enlarged, and mostly rewritten, was printed at Chicago in 1879. Cook dedicates it to the Reverend Langstroth, inventor of the movable frame hive. He calls Langstroth the Huber of America and the greatest master of bee science in the world.

In his preface Cook asks why another treatise is needed, with Langstroth, Quinby, King, Bevan, and Hunter already in print. Each has done fine service, he grants, and each has its own striking merits. Yet none combines all the qualities wanted in a popular manual, he holds. He promises science for students and clear practice for workers, with a full index to keep the two apart. The manual helped spread the frame hive system that remade American bee keeping.
68242-a-commentary:
John Galsworthy's A Commentary was published in New York by Charles Scribner's Sons. The front leaves carry a long list of his works, novels, stories, and plays, with the Forsyte Saga among them. A note of thanks records where the sketches first appeared: Justice in the Albany Review, Power in the New Age, and all the rest in The Nation of London.

Nineteen pieces follow the title essay, each named for its theme. The Lost Dog comes first, then Demos, Old Age, The Careful Man, Fear, Fashion, Sport, and Money. Progress, Holiday, Facts, Power, The House of Silence, Order, The Mother, Comfort, A Child, Justice, and Hope complete the set. The title piece opens on an old man whose calling in life was to warn the public against the dangers of the steam-roller, a small red flag in his remaining hand.
6841-mosaics-of-grecian-history:
Marcius Willson and Robert Pierpont Willson aim, in Mosaics of Grecian History, to give a trustworthy and interesting history of Greece in moderate compass. Standard histories, they note, are seldom read by the people at large, while school manuals, mere outlines of larger works, fare no better. The outline system, they argue, inverts the natural order of learning and turns study into drudgery for the young.

Their mosaic method instead builds history from vivid pieces, anecdotes, and scenes, so beginners can grasp the whole. The book suits general readers and schools alike. Mosaics of Grecian History is a lively, old-style primer, made to make Greece live for new readers.
68469-french-life-in-town-and-country:
Hannah Lynch describes French life in town and country in a volume issued at New York and London in 1902. The book belongs to an Our European Neighbours series edited by William Harbutt Dawson. Companion volumes treat German, Russian, Dutch, and Swiss life on the same plan.

Chapters open with rural and provincial life, then turn to Paris and its ways. Social pastimes, the army, schooling, national bodies, home life, peasants and artisans, the press, salons, and organized charity follow. Lynch opens with a sharp contrast, Paris as a boiling political furnace set against slow, humdrum days in the provinces. Pictures of peasants, deputies, and seaside services back the text. Readers get an Irish writer's brisk survey of France at the turn of the century.
68504-down-the-line-with-john-henry:
Hugh McHugh wrote Down the Line with John Henry, published by Dillingham in New York in 1901. McHugh had already made John Henry known in an earlier book of the same name. The hero narrates his own adventures in the slang of the day, illustrated by McKee Barclay.

The sketches take John Henry to the races, among traveling salesmen, into Bohemia, and up against a hotel clerk. He rides in a benzine buggy, attends a musicale, and plays golf. In the first piece he rushes his girl Clara Jane to the race track, posing as a wise boy who knows every horse. He owns he is a dub on the dope, but love makes him brag. The book belongs to the John Henry craze of slang humor that swept American papers around 1900.
68569-the-wyvern-mystery:
The Wyvern Mystery is a novel by Le Fanu, published at London in 1889. Ward and Downey issued it with illustrations. Le Fanu had written Uncle Silas and Guy Deverell before it. More than fifty chapters carry the tale. Alice Maybell is introduced first, in the vale of Carwell. The Grange, its old squire, and the terrace garden follow. The squire's eldest son comes home early in the story.

An omen hangs over Carwell Grange from the twelfth chapter. Letters, inspections, and warnings thicken the middle. Mildred Tarnley tells a warning story; an abduction follows later. Pursuit, twilight, and darkness build toward the end. Bertha Velderkaust and the heir of the Fairfields close the contents. Le Fanu's late novel keeps his gothic manner: old houses, family secrets, dread.
6907-from-wealth-to-poverty-or-the-trick:
Austin Potter, a minister, wrote this story of the drink curse from two motives he states plainly. He hated the rum traffic, which had brought hardship and suffering on himself and those dear to him. He also sought to expose the tricks by which the liquor party made the Dunkin Act fail, so as to bring that law into disrepute. He dedicates the book to the friends of prohibition the world over.

An Othello line on drink turning a sensible man first to a fool and then to a beast stands at the head of the tale. The story follows a fall from wealth to poverty, showing how drink and the trade behind it wreck a home. Potter writes as a preacher and a reformer, aiming to warn as much as to move.
69149-the-woman-of-mystery:
The Woman of Mystery is a novel by Georges Ohnet, author of The Ironmaster, translated by Fred Rothwell and published by Chatto and Windus of London in a new edition of 1904. The story is told in three parts. It opens in Paris, in the study of the Minister of War in the Rue Saint-Dominique. The minister walks to and fro in furious fashion, twisting his moustache, which seemed even redder than usual.

He fingers his eyeglass in a manner promising anything but a cordial welcome. A profound silence reigns around him, broken only by birds in the garden. At last he marches to the mantelpiece and presses an electric bell. Has Colonel Vallenot returned, he exclaims, in fierce tones. A passage preserved in the copy draws out the wait.
69234-the-long-road-of-woman-s-memory:
Addams was already known for Twenty Years at Hull House. The book is inscribed to her friend Mary Wilmarth of Chicago. It holds an opening essay and five chapters, each on a power of memory in women's lives. Two chapters turn on the story of the Devil Baby at Hull House.

The first chapters show old women's memories reshaping the past and then acting back on life. Later chapters show memory breaking with set custom, binding up the world of industry, and standing against war. A last chapter gives a case from the writer's own life. Addams argues that the old, looking back down the long road, can change their hard experiences into something of worth. Memory, in her hands, is a social force and not just a private store.
69312-the-naiad-a-ghost-story:
The Naiad is a ghost story by George Sand, Englished by Katherine Berry Di Zéréga and printed by the press of William R Jenkins in New York. Her copyright in the translation dates to 1892. The translator read the tale in French with delight years before and turned it into English so others could share the pleasure. She dedicated the book to her only daughter, the late Lady Frankland, whose sudden death had broken off the work.

The narrator is a young lawyer of twenty-two, sent by his father on a delicate mission in May 1788. His errand takes him to the château of Ionis, a dozen leagues off between Angers and Saumur, where Madame d'Ionis waits. Chapters move from The Three Loaves through The Apparition and The Law Suit to The Naiad and The Duel.
69389-the-arctic-regions-and-the-norther:
Arctic Regions and the Northern Whale Fishery is a sea book by Captain Scoresby. The Religious Tract Society of London issued this cheap edition for readers. Its pages abridge Scoresby's first volume on the Arctic from 1820. That work came out at Edinburgh in a costlier form then. The hydrographical survey chapter of the Greenland Sea stands omitted here.

Some matter also comes from his papers in the Edinburgh Philosophical Journal. A plate of Spitzbergen fronts the abridged narrative for young readers. Contents open on the old question of a sea passage north. Atlantic and Pacific communication by polar seas drives that first chapter. Ice, whales, Greenland seas, and hard winters fill Scoresby's record.
69481-austria-hungary:
Mitton wrote this portrait of Austria-Hungary for Adam and Charles Black of London in 1915, while the empire stood at war. It carries 32 full-page pictures in color, and a view of Aggstein in the Wachau serves as frontispiece. Sister volumes on England, France, Italy, and Switzerland are named at the front.

Sixteen chapters cross the dual monarchy. The first sets out the two-crown state, and the next tells the making of modern Austria and the place of the Emperor. Hungary and its people follow, then the Austrian Danube from Vienna down past Budapest. Later chapters tour Bohemia, the Tyrol and its heroes, the mountain passes, and the Dolomites. The book ends in Transylvania and Galicia. The color plates show Schönbrunn, Prague, Magyar shepherds, and paprika sellers. British readers got the enemy empire drawn as a land and a people.
69501-at-the-fall-of-montreal-or-a-soldi:
Edward Stratemeyer's Colonial Series holds a soldier boy tale of the fall of Montreal, sold cloth bound and illustrated at a dollar twenty five. The series also lists With Washington in the West, Marching on Niagara, and On the Trail of Pontiac. Stratemeyer's Old Glory and Pan American shelves crowd the front pages of his books. The tale itself belongs to the French and Indian War's last campaign.

A weapon rings out and a red man leaps in the pictured scene. Boys of the colonies march with the armies that close on Montreal, the last French stronghold in Canada. Woods fighting, scouts, and sieges fill such tales. Stratemeyer wrote for boys by the hundreds of volumes, and this one gives them the war's end on the Saint Lawrence. Duty and pluck win the day.
69638-nineteen-hundred-a-forecast-and-a-:
Nineteen Hundred, subtitled A Forecast and a Story, is a novel by Marianne Farningham, published in London in eighteen ninety two. In her preface the author calls the work a little dream of what may be in the near future. Part of that dream, she says, has already come true. The force behind the change is applied Christianity at work in England.

She holds that the hope of England lies in her young people. The book is addressed to fathers and mothers who see each child as a treasure. Chapter titles trace Sundays in town and country, a wedding, and signs of the times. Later chapters move to a new order, a city of homes, and a happy exodus. The tale ends by asking whether it was all a dream.
69685-just-sweethearts-a-christmas-love-:
Just Sweethearts is a Christmas love story by Harry Stillwell Edwards. It came out in Macon, Georgia, from the J. W. Burke Company, with a copyright date of 1920. Edwards was the author of Two Runaways, His Defense, and Eneas Africanus. The first chapter opens on a street corner in the South at Christmas time.

A young man stands in the sun of one of those fine days that come with Christmas in the South. A light cane rests across his shoulders, his gloved hands on it, and his eyes rove with keen interest. A half smile is on his dark face. It is writ all over him, the tale says, that he has no calls to meet and no tasks to do. He is in the moving scene by chance, and not of its cast.
70046-a-guide-to-plymouth-and-its-histor:
Guide to Plymouth and Its History is a 1938 town guide compiled by Helen Briggs and Rose Briggs. Raymond Dreher supplied the pictures for the Pilgrim Society printing of the work. Its matter comes from tablets, monuments, and statues raised to honour the Pilgrims. Prose and verse from memorial days add to the record the sisters gathered.

A foreword praises how Plymouth guards the places tied to her forefathers with loyal care. Stones across the town bear witness to the honour paid that small band. Church, state, and nation all share in that public act of memory. Readers get a walking companion to the shrines of the first settlement.
70048-the-great-skene-mystery:
Bernard Capes wrote this mystery novel, first published by Methuen in 1907 and told largely in the first person. A prologue, Mother Carey's chicken, opens in a Clapham fog forty-five years before.

The fog packs White Square, a thieves' stronghold sacred from the police, where Mother Carey is the most respectable unit. The contents then turn autobiographical: I come of age, the lodge in the Caddle, and a young lady's chastening in two phases. Morgiana, the writing on the wall, and the letter in the book follow. Lady Skene kneels to the narrator; a body is found in a cave; the great Skene case closes the hunt. Readers get a Dickensian London mystery, fog first and detection after.
70226-carpentry:
Carpentry, by Ira Samuel Griffith, is a trade textbook from the University of Missouri. Griffith chaired the manual arts department, and the Manual Arts Press of Peoria issued his book. Copyright came in 1916, and this copy is the fourth edition of 1919.

Numbered sections walk a house up from the ground, in work order. Foundations come first: laying out, grade line, digging, footings, and forms for concrete walls. Waterproofing and basement frames close that chapter. The main frame follows, with sills, girders, bridging, trimmers, headers, and joists. Openings in the framework end the frame chapter. Two chapters then master the roof: the square-cornered building first, then any polygon. Common, hip, valley, and jack rafters each get their cuts and lengths figured. Plumb cut, seat cut, cheek cut, and backing are treated cut by cut.
70300-legendary-romantic-tales-of-indian:
Hobart Caunter wrote these legendary and romantic tales of Indian history. Warne printed the book in London and New York in its Prize Library. A front plate shows Jehangire going to visit Mher-ul-Nissa in state. Past sets treated England, France, Spain, and Italy in like form.

Publishers reissue the tales in one compact volume for a new age. The tales confine their scope to the Mahomedan conquests in India. Preface says those records hold events of signal, stirring interest aplenty. They show human action ends alike under all climes and change.
7036-the-poorhouse-waif-and-his-divine-t:
Isabel Byrum tells the true story of a poorhouse waif and his divine teacher, opening with a deserted child scarcely a month old. A Crabbe verse at the head holds that the fondest and best are most tried, troubled, and distressed. A woman leaves the infant where hands are already more than full, and the contents trace life in the almshouse, from bad to worse, finding friends, and suffering for others faults.

A strange visitor, mysteries unfolding, and the discovery of God follow, with a witch's home, a contrast, and a search for light. Revelations on eternity, prayer, tobacco, and God's word lead through camp meetings to a call to service and a church found. The waif's journey from desertion to faith forms the book's arc.
70414-training-infantry:
Colonel John Morrison of the infantry wrote Training Infantry, a handbook printed at Fort Leavenworth, Kansas, in 1914. Its twelve chapters set out what foot troops must learn and how officers should teach it. Early parts treat the chief and the wished-for skills and the winning of fire mastery. Later parts cover battle, guards, patrols, marches, the National Guard, reviews, and the raising of a new regiment.

The first chapter holds that talk of a good plain soldier who knows no theory is nonsense, since no man can practice what he does not know. A young commander needs the chief rules of his arm's use, above all with the guns, and long practice in putting them to work. It shows how the United States Army trained its foot troops on the eve of the Great War.
70453-clerk-maxwell-s-electromagnetic-th:
Hendrik Lorentz delivered this lecture on Clerk Maxwell's electromagnetic theory as the Rede Lecture for 1923. Cambridge University Press printed it that year. Lorentz chose his subject with a date in mind. Maxwell's Treatise on Electricity and Magnetism had appeared exactly fifty years before, in 1873. That work raised Maxwell to the first rank of investigators.

Lorentz explains what Maxwell proved. Electric and magnetic actions pass through a medium rather than acting at a distance. The theory reached its crown in showing that light itself is an electromagnetic event. Before Maxwell, the field held confusion and rival theories, with the laws of Ampère and Grassmann and the guesses of Weber, Riemann, and Clausius in competition. Lorentz uses the lecture to show how Maxwell's ideas swept that tangle aside and simplified the whole science.
70501-moon-of-memory:
Bryce Walton's Moon of Memory ran in Future, combined with Science Fiction Stories, in November 1950. Barstac crosses a red Martian plain toward a resort building, meaning to steal one of its sports rockets and reach Deimos, or die trying.

The law of the New System will not let the police kill him: criminals are taken alive with superson guns and turned into zombies for life in a mine three miles underground. Barstac shoots his way toward the rockets instead, trusting his heat gun and ready to turn it on himself. A note on the story adds that a girl helped him escape, and that her reason is the twist. Walton packs pursuit, gunfire, and dread into a short space.
70587-terry:
James Hilton's Terry was first published in 1927 by Thornton Butterworth of London. Hilton had written The Passionate Year and The Dawn of Reckoning before it. A note at the front states that the tale is fiction and its people drawn from the writer's fancy.

The narrator first meets Terry outside the Tube station at Hampstead, having marked him on the train: a shabby overcoat over a dress suit. Both men are bound for the End House and Severn's dinner party, so they walk together. Terry is tall, fair, and good-looking in a restrained way, yet looks grimly ahead as if life were a tremendous ordeal. I hate dinner parties, he bursts out, shy and vehement at once.
70730-a-history-of-england-principally-i:
A History of England, Principally in the Seventeenth Century, volume two, is the English edition of Leopold von Ranke's great history. The Clarendon Press at Oxford published it in 1875. Ranke, the German founder of modern historical method, wrote England's crisis century from the archives of Europe.

This volume opens with book six, on government in England without the Parliament and the troubles in Scotland. Chapters treat the peace with France and Spain and England's share in the Thirty Years' War. Then comes the heart of the matter: taxes levied without a grant of Parliament, Charles the First's relations with Catholicism, and the state of opinion in the Church of England. Ranke reads the road to civil war as a European story, in which England's kings, churches, and parliaments move among the great powers.
70842-the-champlain-tercentenary:
The Champlain Tercentenary, the final report of the New York Lake Champlain Tercentenary Commission, was prepared by its secretary, Henry Wayland Hill. J B Lyon Company of Albany printed it in 1913. The commission reported to the legislature of New York on April 10 of that year. The celebrations had marked three hundred years since Samuel Champlain sailed the lake that bears his name.

The report gives the origins of the commission and the story of the great festival of 1909. It then turns to the permanent memorials. A bust called La France, the work of Rodin, was unveiled, and a French delegation was entertained in 1913. A new lighthouse at Crown Point, appropriations, and the care of the monuments fill the later pages. Photographs and prints record the events.
70996-the-d-arblay-mystery:
The D'Arblay Mystery is a detective novel by Austin Freeman, creator of the scientific investigator Thorndyke. Its contents promise a case opened by a pool in a wood. A conference with Thorndyke follows in the second chapter. The narrator is a young doctor looking back across twenty years.

He tells how one day suddenly plunged him into a strange drama. He was twenty-five then, with a brand-new medical diploma in his pocket. A holiday walk through Highgate, sketch-book in hand, began the business. Chapters bring an inspector's discovery and the death of Simon Bendelow. Marion D'Arblay is seen at home, then placed in peril as the net tightens. A haunted man, a dramatic discovery, and a narrow escape crowd the middle. Thorndyke disentangles the threads in the final chapter, as his method requires.
71030-the-spokesman-s-secretary:
Upton Sinclair's The Spokesman's Secretary, the letters of Mame to Mom, was published by Sinclair himself at Pasadena, California, under a copyright of 1926. Eighteen letters make the book, each headed by what Mame does in it: joining the higher-ups, going behind the scenes, ringing the bell, guessing a riddle.

Mame writes home as a manicurist suddenly cast, as she puts it, for little Cinderella in the big political show. Letter one sets her at her table in the parlor when a quiet, well-kept gentleman in his forties picks her out of the line of girls. Later letters have her putting on the glad rags, missing half a dinner twice, going on strike, and losing her lover.
71078-her-country:
Mary Raymond Shipman Andrews wrote this short novel, issued by Charles Scribner's Sons in New York in 1918. It sold for fifty cents, like her brief tales Old Glory and The Perfect Tribute. The story opens on a June Sunday in a sunny garden at the edge of a city, behind hedges a hundred years in the growing. A girl in a white frock walks the path with a basket and shears, praising the roses on the lattice wall.

Two men watch her and trade views on her looks and her youth. The talk turns to Honor, the garden, and what can be sent to McIvor. Andrews writes with a light hand, and the tale keeps the warm, home-front mood of her war-time work.
71091-father-duffy-s-story:
Francis P Duffy wrote Father Duffy's Story in 1919. George H Doran Company issued it at New York. Duffy served as chaplain to the 165th Infantry. His men were the Fighting Sixty-Ninth of old fame. Joyce Kilmer wrote a history sketch at the back. The book honors the unit's dead.

Chapters move from training at home to camps abroad. The Luneville and Baccarat sectors come next. The Champagne defense and the Ourcq battle fill the middle. Saint Mihiel and the Argonne close the fighting. Duffy thanks officers, clerks, and map makers by name. A chaplain's warm, funny, and sad record shows war as the men near him lived and died it.
71231-bible-history-and-brief-outline-of:
Bible History and Brief Outline of Church History is a school text by Volrath Vogt. Vogt had been principal of the Cathedral School at Christiania in Norway. Brun turned the revised edition into English from the Norwegian. Augsburg Publishing House of Minneapolis issued it, with copyright in 1919.

The book teaches the Bible story as a chain of numbered lessons. The Old Testament part opens with creation, Adam and Eve, and the fall. Cain and Abel, the flood, and the tower of Babel follow in order. Abraham's journeys and trials fill a long run of the early chapters. Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph carry the story down into Egypt. Moses leads the lessons of the exodus and the wilderness wandering. A brief outline of church history stands behind the Bible narrative as the second half.
71395-a-guide-to-modern-cookery:
A Guide to Modern Cookery is the great cookbook of Auguste Escoffier, in its English form. Press opinions quoted in the front matter call it one of the most important cookery books of its century. One paper says it should rank as a standard and be placed in the hands of all who train as high class cookery teachers. Another calls it a culinary education in itself.

Escoffier's book begins at the beginning and explains principles, that notice adds. Sauces, stocks, and the full order of French haute cuisine are set out as a system a working cook can follow. Hotel kitchens across the world took it as their bible. The press pages alone show the fame it arrived with.
714-the-bobbsey-twins-in-the-country:
Laura Lee Hope sent the Bobbsey twins, Bert, Nan, Freddie, and Flossie, from town to Meadow Brook for a country summer. An invitation starts the trip, and a train ride with their dog Snoop brings them to farm life. They pick peas, tend small gardens, and join a Fourth of July picnic.

Country fun turns to mild peril when a runaway, a circus, and a flood stir up the town. The twins help neighbours, find a well's secret, and end the stay with a camp for fresh-air children. The tale is gentle, wholesome, and full of small tasks done well, just the kind of summer story young readers loved.
71431-the-life-of-st-patrick-and-his-pla:
Bury wrote The Life of St Patrick and His Place in History, printed at London in nineteen five. Bury held the chair of modern history at Cambridge and was a fellow of King's College. His book opens with the spread of the Christian faith past the bounds of the Roman Empire. It then turns to Patrick's youth, his capture, and his escape.

Later parts place Patrick in Gaul and Britain, at Lerins and Auxerre, and note the mission of Palladius to Ireland in four thirty-one. Bury sets out the state of Ireland, Patrick's work in Meath and Connaught, and the founding of Armagh in four forty-four. A last part weighs Patrick's own writings, the Confession and the letter against Coroticus, and his death in four sixty-one. Long notes list the old sources.
71511-the-london-pleasure-gardens-of-the:
The London Pleasure Gardens of the Eighteenth Century is a history by Warwick Wroth of the British Museum. His brother Arthur Edgar Wroth assisted him. Macmillan published the book in 1896 with sixty two illustrations. Pepys supplies the motto: cheap, pleasant evenings with music and fine company. The introduction surveys the gardens as a class. Chapters then take them district by district.

The Clerkenwell and central group opens the survey. Islington Spa, called the New Tunbridge Wells, heads the list. Sadler's Wells and Bagnigge Wells get full chapters. Lesser spots like Merlin's Cave and the Mulberry Garden fill out the group. Each entry traces the garden's rise, its shows, and its fall.
