The book preserves a lost world of outdoor tea, music, and fireworks. Londoners of the 1700s took their leisure in these grounds.
71575-the-hand-book-of-artillery:
Captain Joseph Roberts of the Fourth Regiment of Artillery wrote The Hand-Book of Artillery, printed at Richmond in eighteen sixty-one by Ritchie and Dunnavant. The hosted text opens with proceedings instead of a preface. A committee of the Artillery School staff at Fort Monroe reports on the book, which their commanding officer had referred to them as a proposed textbook for the school.

The committee notes the handbook's method. Under each subject head, except the last, the work teaches by questions and answers. Some of that material came from Burns' Questions and Answers on Artillery. Yet Roberts changed it so far, the committee judges, that his book fairly counts as an original compilation. The report prints the contents by which the school weighed his claim.
71609-andersonville-diary:
John L Ransom kept the Andersonville Diary in the worst prison of the Civil War. He printed the book at Auburn, New York, in eighteen hundred eighty one. Ransom had served as first sergeant in the Ninth Michigan Cavalry. His diary had first run in a Michigan newspaper years before.

Mothers, wives, and sisters of the dead hold his gift leaf. A List of the Dead stands with the diary in this full form. Name, company, regiment, death date, and grave number fill its rows. Dorence Atwater and Clara Barton stand behind that grave roll’s truth. Deaths from March eighteen hundred sixty four to April of the next year crowd it. The diary itself was a mind’s shield in a place of dread, he writes. Death would have been a glad release to thousands in that pen. Misprints of the first print stand mended in this careful form.
71663-the-life-and-works-of-sir-charles-:
Alfred Barry writes his father's life in The Life and Works of Sir Charles Barry, printed in London in 1867. Murray made the book. Barry, principal of Cheltenham College, sets out his materials and his method in a preface. A portrait and signature of the architect front the volume.

For the tale, he says, he found no lack of sound materials. His father's life as a builder is written in outline in his own work journals, he notes. Its great periods left their record in public papers of undoubted weight. Some of those papers are quoted in full at the back of the book. Others are summed up, with a note of where they stand. Where no paper could be seen, he fell back on his own memory and on the word of eye witnesses.
7181-the-bushman-life-in-a-new-country:
Edward Wilson Landor's Bushman speaks for Britain's far colonies at a time when, he argues, they were too remote for sympathy and too weak for respect. The public and the government, he writes, obeyed the need to mind colonial welfare with reluctance, as if long neglect were a right. Yet the weakness of childhood was passing, and the colonies were growing into strength.

Landor sets that claim beside scenes of new-country life, kangaroo hunting among them, so that argument and experience stand side by side. His preface asks readers at home to take colonial wants seriously, not as distant news but as part of the empire's own business. The book mixes plea and picture in the voice of a man who knew the ground.
71922-essays-in-american-history:
Essays in American History collects four essays by Henry Ferguson, professor of history and political science at Trinity College, Hartford. Pott printed the book in New York in 1894. The essays treat the Quakers in New England, the witches, Sir Edmund Andros, and the Loyalists.

Ferguson's preface argues that early American history was long written in a glow of patriotism that praised the settlers and hid their shadows. Something, he says, can now be said for Andros, who fought the separatist spirit New England mistook for liberty itself. Something can even be said for the Loyalists, driven from homes they loved by devotion to their principles. The war of secession, he adds, taught Americans to understand loyalty from the inside.
71975-a-mediaeval-burglary:
A Mediaeval Burglary is a lecture by TF Tout, professor of mediaeval and church history at the University of Manchester, given at the John Rylands Library on January 20, 1915. It was reprinted from the library's Bulletin in October 1915 and published at Manchester in 1916.

Tout explains that he did not find his burglary by hunting the annals of crime. The case turned up while he was studying the workings of the king's Wardrobe, the office that handled the king's money and goods on the move. From the dry records of that department he pieced together a break-in of the middle ages, with its losses, its suspects, and its pursuit. The lecture shows how much life a skilled historian can draw from account books and writs. Tout held the Bishop Fraser chair at Manchester.
72288-biological-analogies-in-history:
Theodore Roosevelt gave the Romanes Lecture at Oxford in 1910. Biological Analogies in History was his theme. Oxford University Press issued the speech that year. He spoke on June seventh before the university. An American feels the charm of Oxford's past, he opens. Its fame lives in minds across the seas, he says.

Men of English stock hold no stronger tie to it, he adds. His own people had dwelt eight years in America. Eight generations, he means, of mixed blood. Holland, Huguenot, Scots, and Irish veins run in him. The ethnic mix of America keeps shifting, he notes. New stock grows more like the old mixed kind. Respect among English-speaking peoples grows with time, he claims. A former president used biology's lens to read nations, races, and the slow drift of peoples.
72306-tea-its-history-and-mystery:
Tea, Its History and Mystery, by Joseph Walsh, author of a companion book on coffee, was copyrighted in 1892 and printed by Coates at Philadelphia. Walsh aimed at utility, not originality. Entering the tea trade, he had found dealers almost wholly ignorant of the article they were commissioned to sell, and inquiries for a book containing all about tea set him compiling.

The material grew over more than twenty years of intervals and revisions. Ten chapters cover the early history of tea, its spread across the globe, and its botany. Cultivation and preparation, classification and description, and adulteration and its detection follow. Testing, blending, and preparing take a long chapter, and the book closes on world production and on tea culture as a probable American industry.
72333-mr-belloc-objects-to-the-outline-o:
Belloc Objects to the Outline of History is a book of controversy by Wells, published by Doran at New York in 1926, with portraits. Wells opens by calling himself the least fighting-minded of men, long silent under invented opinions pinned on him by others. Now, in his sixtieth year, he finds himself drawn into a strong dispute with Hilaire Belloc over his own Outline of History.

Belloc had followed the Outline part by part in journals at London, St. Paul, and Cape Town, charging errors and answering them. Wells here takes up his arts of controversy, then states the theory of natural selection. A chapter treats Belloc as a specimen critic of that theory. His ventures among the sub-men, and the question of fixity or progress, close the reply.
72411-the-glories-of-mary:
The Glories of Mary, turned from the Italian of Alphonsus Liguori, founder of the Congregation of the Most Holy Redeemer, reached America in a second edition at New York in eighteen fifty-two. The preface calls it the first complete rendering of the work into English. Archbishop John of New York approved the translation in January of that year. A protest by the author submits all he wrote to the judgment of the church.

The book expounds the Salve Regina line by line. Mary is hailed as queen of mercy, as mother of sinners who repent, and as our life and sweetness. Sections tell how she wins pardon for sins, helps her servants hold fast, and makes death sweet to them. Prayers and petitions to Jesus and Mary frame the teaching.
725-men-of-invention-and-industry:
Samuel Smiles profiled men who built modern industry with little schooling but great skill and grit. Phineas Pett laid the roots of English shipbuilding, and Francis Pettit Smith brought the screw propeller into practical use. Other chapters follow engineers, makers, and workers whose hands shaped ships, machines, and trade.

Smiles argues that such men, ignorant of letters yet rich in wisdom, freed nations by deeds rather than words. Each life is told as a lesson in patience, thrift, and steady work. The book is a Victorian hymn to self-help through craft, and it still offers vivid portraits of the age when Britain's workshops remade the world.
72609-elmer-gantry:
Sinclair Lewis wrote this novel, copyrighted by Harcourt, Brace in New York in 1927. Lewis dedicates it to Mencken with profound admiration on the dedication page. A note warns that no character in the book is the portrait of any actual person.

Elmer Gantry was drunk, the first chapter begins in a Missouri saloon. He was eloquently drunk, lovingly and pugnaciously drunk, Lewis writes of his hero. Gantry leans on the bar of the Old Home Sample Room in Cato that night. He asks the bartender to join him in 'The Good Old Summer Time,' before a tale unfolds of a preacher who sells faith like goods.
72614-the-missionary:
J F Bone wrote The Missionary, a science fiction tale printed in Amazing Stories in October nineteen sixty. Emsh drew the pictures. A hard saying heads the tale, about promises made to the Father of Evil.

The narrator lies with a broken leg in a cast that itches past bearing. His forced companion is Wolverton, a man he loathes more the longer they talk. Wolverton, lean and yellow-eyed, speaks with a voice like a skilled preacher's. For near two weeks that voice has pounded and pierced the captive hearer. Bone hints that men, crowded on a worn world, strike out in pairs for new ones.
72658-the-principles-and-practice-of-mod:
Principles and Practice of Modern Surgery is a medical textbook by Roswell Park of Buffalo. Lea Brothers and Company published the work at Philadelphia and New York. Park was professor of surgery in the medical department of the University of Buffalo. He had been president of the American Surgical Association and of the Medical Society of the State of New York.

The book carries 722 engravings and sixty full page plates in colours and monochrome for its teaching. Park was surgeon to the Buffalo General Hospital, as the title page states for the reader.  The volume is a monument of American surgery at its confident height, when antisepsis and new operations had remade the craft. Students and practitioners bought such books as working tools, and Park name carried weight on both sides of the Atlantic in his generation.
72722-loveday-s-history:
Loveday's History is a tale of many changes by Lucy Ellen Guernsey. Shaw published the new edition in London. The story belongs to a series called the Stanton-Corbet Chronicles. Its year is 1529. Guernsey had earlier written The Foster-Sisters and Winifred.

Loveday narrates her own story from old age. She lived as a little maid with her kinswoman Lady Peckham in Somerset. Thunder gathered over the religious houses in her childhood. The cardinal had put down some thirty small convents. Their revenues endowed his college at Oxford. Loveday herself was destined for one of those houses. She was an orphan without provision, kept by charity. The suppression of her convent changed her whole course.
72771-the-sea-mystery:
The Sea Mystery is a detective novel by Freeman Wills Crofts. Inspector French, his regular detective, handles the case. Twenty chapters are listed in the contents. Morgan meets tragedy in the first of them. The Burry Inlet, on the south coast of Wales, sets the scene. Morgan sits fishing in his boat's sternsheets on an autumn evening. His son Evan rows lazily over the still water.

The inlet at full tide spreads ten miles into the land. Carmarthen lies north and the Gower Peninsula south of it. Experimental detection and a change of venue follow French's arrival. The despatch of a crate becomes a chapter of its own. Dartmoor, a night watchman, and a duplicator mark the middle. Blackmail precedes certainty at last, the contents promise. Danger, Hampstead Heath, and the bitterness of death close the case.
72817-warships-and-their-story:
Fletcher wrote a broad history of warships, printed in London in 1911. The book has a color front plate and eighty full page plates. Fletcher had also written on steamships. His tale starts with war craft in ancient Egypt and runs to the great ships of his own day.

Chapters cover war canoes in far lands, the coming of guns on ships, and the shift to steam. Later parts deal with iron armor, broadside and turret ships, and ships in real fights. Guns, shot, and armor get a chapter of their own. A last chapter looks at the warships of the new century and the types still to come.
7284-the-chosen-people-a-compendium-of-s:
The author of The Heir of Redclyffe wrote this compendium of sacred and church history for schoolchildren. It opens with Hebrews on God speaking through prophets and, in these last days, through his Son. Verse follows on altars that blazed and died, on silence torn with song, and on a revolving sphere where no desert now hides from heaven's light and order.

The book traces the chosen people from old covenant to church, in short lessons suited to young readers. Its tone is devout and didactic, joining Bible story to church history in one clear line. Schoolchildren meet sacred history as a single unfolding tale, told with reverence and simplicity.
72849-a-private-chivalry:
A Private Chivalry, a novel by Francis Lynde, was printed by Appleton at New York in 1900, as number 291 of the Town and Country Library. Its motto, from Sir Philip Sidney, praises brave acts that stayed small and famed by none. The tale opens at dusk at the Jessica works, a mine high above the town of Silverette. Piano notes float up the slope to two men on the porch of the assayer's hut.

One hears in them his free school days; the other rises, lights a cigar, and says he must go down to do what he has set his hand to. His mate sees no need, but the need is there. Heads cite verse at each turn: a wreck, the migrants, a blow in the dark. West fans get mine, oath, and quiet grit.
72883-the-layton-court-mystery:
Anthony Berkeley wrote this detective novel around his investigator Sheringham, and he opens with a letter to his father explaining his method. A detective, Berkeley holds, should behave as he might in real life, far removed from a sphinx, and he should make a mistake or two occasionally. Every scrap of evidence is set down as it is discovered, so the reader has exactly the detective's data.

Twenty-eight chapters follow, from Eight o'Clock in the Morning and An Interrupted Breakfast through The Vase That Wasn't and Dirty Work at the Ash Pit. Sheringham investigates a footprint, lectures on Neo-Platonism, and amuses an ancient rustic. The contents warn that his first solution will be refused by the mystery itself. One chapter is called The Mystery Finally Refuses to Accept Sheringham's Solution, and Grierson tries his hand before Sheringham hits the mark.
72927-the-victory:
The Victory is a novel by Molly Elliott Seawell, published by D Appleton and Company of New York in nineteen six. Seawell had written The Sprightly Romance of Marsac. Her setting is Harrowby, an old manor house in lowland Virginia on a broad river. The Tremaines have held it since a discontented gentleman fled England after Monmouth's rebellion.

The story opens at the bright Christmas of eighteen sixty. Angela Vaughn becomes Neville Tremaine's wife by page one hundred fourteen. Chapters named the Point of Honor, the Quaking of the Earth, and Spartans All carry the family into war. The iron hand of war and circumstance, the tongue of calumny, and the hegira follow. Dust and ashes precede the close of love and life and the aftermath. Seawell writes the Civil War as a Virginia house divided against itself.
72971-a-dead-man-s-diary:
A Dead Man's Diary, written after his decease, was published by Ward, Lock and Company in 1890. G T Bettany wrote the preface. A verse from the Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam heads the title, in Fitzgerald's translation. The soul, sent through the invisible for word of the afterlife, returns answering that it is itself heaven and hell. Bettany's preface surveys the literature of the state after death.

Such books have erred, he says, by too great detail. Swedenborg made the next world just like this one, with cities, books, and merchandise. Letters from Hell drew semblances of men repeating their earthly acts in despair. Archdeacon Farrar had gathered the divines' horrors on the future of the wicked. No one, Bettany holds, has said the last word on the subject. Portions of the diary had already appeared in serial form.
72986-the-cheyne-mystery:
The Cheyne Mystery is a detective novel by Freeman Wills Crofts. Its first chapter is the episode in the Plymouth Hotel. The narrator begins by quoting the King in Alice: begin at the beginning, go on till you come to the end, then stop. In practice, he finds, it is hard to live up to that rule.

Where is the beginning of Maxwell Cheyne's adventure? Carried back far enough it might reach Noah, or even Adam. The strange episode at the Edgecombe Hotel in Plymouth started the extraordinary series of events he calls the Cheyne mystery. The contents promise a burglary, the launch Enid, and a question of a peerage. An amateur sleuth works before Inspector French takes charge at chapter thirteen. The clue of the clay-marked shoe and the torn hotel bill follow. Crofts builds his puzzle in his patient, timetable manner.
73027-percival-s-picture-gallery:
Percival Picture Gallery, by A L O E, was printed in London by Morgan and Scott, at the office of The Christian in Paternoster Buildings. A L O E, the pen name of Charlotte Maria Tucker, wrote Pearls of Wisdom from the Parables and The Young Pilgrim. A plate shows a Persian, an Afghan, and an old Sikh hearing holy words.

In her preface the writer hopes the small volume may wake thoughts of a churchly kind in some minds. Some of its ideas came to her in a chamber of sickness, once thought to be her chamber of death. The thoughts were pleasant and soothing to her, and she prays they may soothe fellow pilgrims too. Chapters treat the passage through the Red Sea, King David vision, and the night after the crucifixion. Church readers get short sacred tales.
73102-the-shore-road-mystery:
The Shore Road Mystery is a Hardy Boys novel by Franklin Dixon, printed at New York with copyright in 1928. Walter Rogers drew the pictures. Grosset and Dunlap issued it after The Tower Treasure and The House on the Cliff. Twenty-three chapters run from Stolen Cars to The Mystery Solved.

Frank Hardy calls it a mystery how the autos disappeared. Two cars vanished last week, two the week before, and one the week before that. Martin's car was brand new when it went. The three boys ride their motorcycles along the Shore Road by Barmet Bay. Every one of the five stolen cars vanished along that shore. No thief was seen at either end of the road.
73623-the-war-myth-in-united-states-hist:
Hamlin, of Atlantic Christian College, wrote this pacifist history, copyrighted by the Vanguard Press in 1927. Dole supplies an introduction, and the book reached a fifth printing at New York. Hamlin dedicates it to his brother Askew, a life of promise cut short in early manhood.

Patriotism and peace opens the contents, then each American war gets a chapter. The Revolution, 1812, Mexico, the Civil War, Spain and the World War follow in order. For the republic's first 135 years the treasury spent about $66,000,000,000 in all, Hamlin writes, and about $56,000,000,000 of that went to warfare in his accounting of the myth.
73840-cho-cho-and-the-health-fairy:
Cho-Cho and the Health Fairy tells a tale for children about how good habits guard health. In the story, the Witch Ignorance creeps to the lovely garden of Fairy Health with cruel eyes. She throws a yellow ball onto the roof, and fire spreads until the fairy's house burns beyond all help.

As Health weeps in her garden, a bird in a green bush tells her the house can rise again by the hands of children alone. Each child who learns to eat the right food adds a brick. Fresh air sleep adds a shingle, and happy play adds colored glass to the windows. The bird, whose name is Education, flies with his brother Rumor to tell teachers far and near. Children learn the lesson as a story, and the fairy's house grows whole again.
73856-molly-s-treachery:
Molly's Treachery is a dime novel by Mrs Alex McVeigh Miller, issued as Number Sixty-Two of the Hart Series. George Munro copyrighted it in 1886; the Arthur Westbrook Company of Cleveland reprinted it. Forty-six chapters carry the tale. It opens with a letter dated at Ferndale, Greenbrier County, West Virginia, on June 20, 1878.

Dear sister and Aunt Lucy, the letter begs, oh, please do let me come home. Ferndale is horrid, the lonesomest old hole the writer ever saw. There has not been a caller since she came. She has not seen a man for two weeks except the gardener and the old black coach driver. That, she adds, is all the better, since her clothes are shabby. Miller was a queen of the story papers, and this is her machinery in full: a country exile, a treachery, and love forcing its way back.
74197-reuben-stone-s-discovery:
Reuben Stone's Discovery, or The Young Miller of Torrent Bend, is a boys' novel by Edward Stratemeyer, copyrighted in 1895 and revised in 1900. It is the second volume of the Ship and Shore series. Reuben, a young miller, is left in charge of his father's mill property while his father goes west to seek a better field for business.

Stratemeyer's preface tells the plot in advance. Many things happen in the father's absence, and Reuben is fed several stories about his parent and the property that cause him great uneasiness. Growing suspicious that all is not right, he sets out on a tour of investigation that places him in more than one position of peril. He tells his own story, and his triumph at the end is fairly earned. The book sits in the author's vast output of series fiction for boys, between war stories and biographies of presidents.
74245-a-hausa-botanical-vocabulary:
John M Dalziel, of the West African Medical Staff, compiled a word list of Hausa plant names. T Fisher Unwin issued it at London in 1916. Each entry pairs the Hausa word with Latin names and plain notes.

The cotton entry shows the book's depth. Abduga covers the local kinds of the cotton plant, with their district names. Dalziel then gives words for the seed, for cotton crushed free of seed, and for carded cotton. Thread for warp and weft each has its own term. Even the coarse cloth goddo gets a note, with its loom and fringe. Such lists served doctors, traders, and farm officers in Northern Nigeria. They still serve students of Hausa speech and of African plant use.
74257-kanamori-s-life-story:
Paul Kanamori tells his own life story, published by the Sunday School Times Company at Philadelphia in 1921. How the higher criticism wrecked a Japanese Christian, and how he came back, the subtitle promises. The servant sent opens the contents, and the servant disobedient follows in the story's own framing.

The servant restored, the servant reaping and sowing in the evening close the contents list. Kanamori opens in 1852, when Perry's expedition reached Japan with four ships and 560 men. That treaty opened the hermit nation, he writes, and his own path from samurai schools to the pulpit follows the new Japan he dates from Perry.
74300-a-lady-of-the-last-century:
John Doran wrote A Lady of the Last Century, a life of Mrs Elizabeth Montagu, published at Boston by Francis A Niccolls and Company in an edition limited to one thousand copies. A photogravure shows Garrick and his wife, after Hogarth. Doran gave the bit of mosaic to Andreas J G Holtz of Twyford Abbey. Long contents heads tell the tale. Chapter one treats her birth and parentage as Miss Robinson.

Early training and Mrs Makin system of female education open the life. School at Tottenham High Cross and the Duchess of Portland circle follow. La Petite Fidget at Bath and Tunbridge Wells brings the girl into society. Garrick Richard the Third and offers of marriage close the chapter. Chapter two treats Edward Montagu, the wedding tour, and life at Allerthorpe. Later chapters make her queen of the blue stockings. Biography lovers get a gay eighteenth century life.
74400-a-mediterranean-mystery:
A Mediterranean Mystery is an adventure novel by Fred E Wynne, published by Duffield and Company of New York in 1923. The narrator is a quiet, ordered man who hates telegrams. His servant Bates brings one that changes everything.

His ne'er-do-well brother Edmund is coming to dinner, after two years of silence. Bates lights up at the name and fetches the 1847 port. The chapters then run far from that dining room. A bishop proposes a toast, and the narrator sails in the Astarte. A plan is made to save Jakoub. Camels, a khamsin sandstorm, and the dope trade follow. Captain Welfare explains, promises, and signals. Blackmail enters, and Jakoub is no more seen. Wynne writes a clubman's mystery, where a settled life is pulled into smuggling and danger around the Mediterranean.
74523-a-church-dictionary:
Walter Farquhar Hook wrote A Church Dictionary, shown here in a seventh edition at London in 1854. Hook was Vicar of Leeds. The book first came out as monthly tracts for his parish folk. Those tracts sought to set out church truths and terms in clear words.

Each tract drew a large sale of four thousand a month. Hook then grew the plan into a book of wide use. Each new edition added more heads. The seventh adds more than one hundred new heads. Short essays treat faith terms and church ways that folk had got wrong. Hook cites his sources for each claim. The book was meant for home study as much as for clergy.
74534-a-companion-to-mr-wells-s-outline-:
A Companion to the Outline of History is a work of answer and fight by Belloc, aimed at the famed world tale of his rival Wells. It came out at San Francisco in the late nineteen twenties, though printed in Britain. Its gift word makes it out to the authors brother in law in a wine town of California.

Its parts take the rival book point by point. First come the making of the world, the fall of man, and the place of God. Then the start of faith, the rank of priests, and the use of an east faith as a stick to beat the church. The birth of Christ, the start of the church, Islam, the dark ages, and the break of the west church close the run.
74630-in-the-stranger-people-s-country:
Charles Egbert Craddock wrote In the Stranger People’s Country, a novel of the Great Smoky Mountains. Harper and Brothers issued the book in New York in eighteen hundred ninety one. Stone graves of a small lost folk open its pages. Who they were, none can say, the tale begins.

Some call them a dwarf race, gone from the earth long since. Some say Aztec children, buried apart for a hid cause. Plain sense lays the graves to Cherokee infants instead. The hills keep their hush round the rise where they sleep. Near mountaineers start and turn shy at a plain question. Stephen Yates tells how a valley man asked him once. His deer laden horse and worn hounds crowd his cabin door. A pale young woman hears all from the rickety porch.
74644-a-land-girl-s-love-story:
Berta Ruck's A Land-Girl's Love Story came from Dodd, Mead of New York in 1919, with pictures by Caswell. Ruck dedicates the novel to all the girls she met in farm, field, and forest during the war, wishing them luck, life, and love.

Joan tells the story, starting from a letter that betrays her: the young man she loves has sailed for Salonika without a goodbye. She joins the Land Army, and chapters follow the first night in camp, a milking lesson, the girls' letter-bag, hay harvest, and the Land Army tests. Colonel Fielding talks of love, the harvest of 1918 is gathered, and a postscript ends with a victory dance. The novel catches women's farm work in wartime from inside.
74672-heath-s-french-and-english-diction:
James Boielle revised and enlarged the Heath French and English Dictionary for the Heath firm of Boston, New York, and Chicago. The book carries a 1903 copyright and was made with help from Payen-Payne, a French examiner at London. Boielle spent four and a half years on the work. A live tongue gains new words and new senses each day, so the book had to grow too. Thousands of new words, set phrases, and proverbs went in.

Two hundred columns of fresh print joined the book, and chapter and verse were given in many cases. For the French to English side, Boielle followed the small Littre close. The work serves students, teachers, and traders who need both tongues at hand. It is a tool built for daily use, not a mere list of words.
74739-a-military-dictionary:
William Duane's A Military Dictionary was printed and published by the author at 98 Market Street, Philadelphia, in 1810. Duane, late lieutenant colonel in the army of the United States and author of the American Military Library, shapes the book for the military institutions of the United States. Two mottoes stand on the title page, from Saxe on discipline and from Jomini, dated 1808, on the tactics of Frederic.

The title promises the whole art in pocket form. The dictionary explains the systems of discipline for infantry, artillery, and cavalry, and the principles of fortification. It takes in the Pocket Gunner, the military regulations of the United States, and the weights, measures, and monies of all nations. The technical terms of war in French close the list. A copyright entry, made August 10, 1810, follows.
74741-horse-hoeing-husbandry:
Horse-Hoeing Husbandry, an essay on the principles of vegetation and tillage by Jethro Tull of Shalborne in Berkshire, reached a fourth edition in London in 1762. Tull promises a new method of culture that will raise the produce of land while lessening the usual expense. Cuts show the instruments used in the work. A new preface by the editors speaks to all concerned in agriculture.

The editors note that the essay has been out for years, and the world has formed some judgment of it. Any reader who weighs Tull's principles, they say, can judge how far his theory agrees with nature. Yet too few, they add, have made trials enough to know its worth. The book is the classic statement of drill sowing and horse hoeing between rows.
74755-a-story-teller-s-story:
Sherwood Anderson published A Story Teller's Story in New York in 1924, a memoir in four books with an epilogue. Anderson, author of Winesburg, Ohio and Poor White, dedicated the book to Alfred Stieglitz, whom he called more than a father to puzzled children of the arts. 

Anderson begins with his mid-American boyhood, insisting that in the towns of his youth there was no poverty of the kind he later saw in great industrial cities. His own family was poor in a different way. His father, a ruined dandy from the South, kept a harness-repair shop, then took to painting houses and barns while calling himself a sign-writer. The boy drove the horse on sign-painting trips while his father picked fences with a general's care. Readers get the raw material of Anderson's fiction, told as the growth of a writer's mind.
74869-staffordshire-pottery-and-its-hist:
Josiah Wedgwood wrote a history of the Staffordshire pottery trade, a district bound to one craft as no other in the land. First chapters show potting as a farm side craft that grew as coal and iron grew near it. Elers and art, salt glaze ware, and the start of the factory mark the early rise.

Wedgwood and cream colour, Spode and blue printing, and steam power and strikes fill the next span. Tiles and china from Minton close the tale, with modern men and methods at the end. Prints show old ware, works, maps of Burslem and Hanley, and the great master potters of the trade.
74875-profitable-poultry:
Tegetmeier, a famed hand at poultry, wrote this guide to keeping fowls at a profit. Darton printed this new, greatly enlarged edition in London in 1854. Harrison Weir, the great animal artist, drew the plates. A Black Spanish fowl heads the book.

Their management in health and disease is the title's plain plan. Tegetmeier thanks the public for buying a large first run so fast. Fellow amateurs gave him hints and help, he owns. Reviewers praised the book's sound common sense, he says, in place of the gross nonsense of cheap poultry books before it. Fraser's Magazine gave it a long, kind review in December 1853, a mark of its standing.
75070-larry-dexter-and-the-bank-mystery:
Raymond Sperry wrote Larry Dexter and the Bank Mystery, or Exciting Days in Wall Street. The Garden City Publishing Company issued this edition in 1926; the copyright line reads 1912. Sperry's other Larry Dexter books, at the big flood and with the missing millionaire, are named on the title page.

The first chapter is called A Big Robbery, and it opens at a subway entrance. A man in a frantic hurry brushes past young Larry Dexter, nearly knocking him off his feet, and runs for his train. The newsboy Jim, from whom Larry buys his morning papers, laughs at the rush. Larry is the star reporter of the New York Leader, an afternoon journal, and he reads the day's news on his trip downtown before his duties begin. A bank mystery waits along his beat. Boy readers got newspaper work and crime detection in one hero.
7517-sanctuary:
Edith Wharton's short novel opens with a young woman's undivided happiness, a feeling youth seldom allows itself. Kate Orme has yielded herself to happiness since her engagement to Denis Peyton two months before, letting it soak into every faculty like spring rain into a germinating meadow. She watches from the slopes above a lake as Denis approaches by the short cut from the Peyton place, her smile prolonged by the impossibility of her joy.

Wharton builds the novella around what that happiness must face: the past, the family, and the moral choices that test a marriage before it begins. Sanctuary, in Wharton's sense, is both a refuge and a question: what shelter can love offer against knowledge? The book is a concentrated Wharton, all her themes of society, conscience, and consequence in brief compass.
752-a-young-girl-s-diary:
An anonymous girl of the upper middle class kept this diary from age eleven to fourteen and a half. It reached print with a prefatory letter from Sigmund Freud, dated 27 April 1915. Freud called the diary a gem, praising its frank view of a young mind. Eden and Cedar Paul made the English translation.

The diary runs in four parts, one for each year, closing with a short conclusion. It records school, friends, family, first crushes, and the small dramas of growing up, in a voice that is candid and unguarded. The book matters as a rare, direct record of girlhood, and as a text that early psychoanalysis prized for what it shows of the mind at work.
75222-the-draycott-murder-mystery:
Molly Thynne wrote this murder mystery, first published by Hutchinson in 1928. Wind swept down the crooked main street of the village of Keys as chapter one opens. Fortunate folk by warm firesides drew their chairs closer against the March gale, the first page says.

All month it had rained almost without ceasing over the north of England, she writes. Lanes knee-deep in mud dried with miraculous swiftness in the icy wind that followed. Into such a village, sealed by weather and gossip, a murder at Draycott brings a detective's questions, in Thynne's neat golden-age manner of clues and country houses.
75487-deeds-of-heroism-and-bravery:
Rupert Hughes gathered this book of heroes and personal daring, edited by Barron and published by Harper in 1920. The Great War had just ended, and its stories fill the first and longest part: field and trench ordeals. Marines, Foreign Legion men, tank crews, and medical corpsmen tell what happened in short, named pieces. One survived, says a title. Not dead but fighting, says another.

The second part honors women who dared, with Edith Cavell, the martyr heroine, at its head. Adventure in the air follows: the Lafayette Escadrille, the aces, and the Red Battle Flyer. Sea and sub-sea stories close the march, from torpedoed ships to a rescue extraordinary, with Alan Seeger's rendezvous poem among them. Hughes writes in the brisk magazine manner of his day. The book is a memorial in anecdotes, meant to keep the war's brave deeds in common memory.
75531-ladies-dress-shoes-of-the-nineteen:
Ladies' Dress Shoes of the Nineteenth Century pictures sixty three shoes worn by ladies of that age. Watson Greig of Glencarse gathered and described the shoes. Douglas published the book at Edinburgh in 1900. Greig had written an earlier work on old fashioned shoes.

Each shoe, Greig writes, was chosen to show the range and change of fashion. Any shoemaker, he adds, could copy them from the plates. The frontispiece shows a bedroom slipper in green velvet. Its arms are worked in silk and metal thread, with a white silk frill. Later plates set plain black satin beside pointed, trefoil trimmed shoes. Heel height, toe shape, and trimming mark the decades. The book is a small museum of the Victorian foot.
75663-porridge-poetry:
Hugh Lofting wrote Porridge Poetry, cooked, ornamented, and served up by himself, issued by Frederick A Stokes Company in New York in nineteen twenty four. Lofting draws and writes in a free, comic hand for children. The Porridge Poet speaks first in his own person. He says his inspiration is in the ice box and his rhymes come from the spice box.

The poet owns that his verse is free and easy, with a flavour at times slightly cheesy. He makes macaronics from peelings off spring philharmonics, he jokes, and turns out comic songs like summer salads. One recipe takes a pint of vermicelli, pounds it to jelly, and adds a pinch of grammar. Sifted syntax, tin tacks, and eggstravaganza make a lovely stanza, he claims. Children get nonsense cookery in rhyme, with bright plates.
75922-the-amazing-adventures-of-letitia-:
The Amazing Adventures of Letitia Carberry is a comic novel by Mary Roberts Rinehart, author of The Circular Staircase. Bobbs-Merrill published it at Indianapolis in 1911, with pictures by Howard Chandler Christy. The narrator opens by owning that the story is Tish's, though Tish lies laid up and cannot write it. Three friends keep the record while the affair is fresh.

Tish, a member of the Ladies' Committee, takes a firm hand at a hospital gone astray. A scream outside her room at night starts the trouble. The narrator adds that Tish's nurse slept so soundly that Tish learned to throw the clock to wake her. The tale mixes hospital doings with Rinehart's brisk humor.
75967-dr-mabuse-master-of-mystery:
Dr Mabuse, Master of Mystery, is a novel by Norbert Jacques, here in the authorized English version by Lilian A Clare. It was first published in this form in London in 1923.

A note from the translator explains the hero's odd office. Wenk is a German state prosecutor who, unlike any English official, hunts his man in person, even in disguise. The novel opens at a gaming table, where a distinguished stranger lays down twenty thousand marks. His scarf pin, a single white pearl, draws every eye. Behind such scenes moves Dr Mabuse, the master criminal of postwar Germany. The translator also warns readers that the sums staked in the story, in the money of the day, run to millions.
76040-a-house-with-a-history:
A pamphlet printed at New York in 1882 tells the biography of Colonel Roger Morris's mansion, one of the oldest residences on Manhattan Island. Forfeited to the state, the house became a source of profit to the Astors, its headline says. It still stands to tell its story. The writer calls it a treat to see a house different from its neighbors.

New York houses, he complains, are cast in one brownstone mould: front, steps, railing, and area alike. A few houses escape that mould, and this is one. The Morris house served Washington as headquarters in 1776. The pamphlet preserves its tale for a changing city.
76056-women-in-american-history:
Grace Humphrey wrote these lives of women in American history. Bobbs-Merrill printed the book at Indianapolis, copyright 1919. Pocahontas opens the fifteen lives in chapter one place. Anne Hutchinson, Betsy Ross, and Mary Lindley Murray follow next.

Molly Pitcher, Martha Washington, Jemima Johnson, and Sacajawea come on. Dolly Madison, Lucretia Mott, and Harriet Beecher Stowe fill middle. Julia Ward Howe, Mary Livermore, Barbara Fritchie, and Clara Barton close. Pocahontas chapter opens in a James River long house scene. An epilogue, a bibliography, and an index close the women lives volume at its end.
76195-the-mulfuza-t-timu-ry:
Charles Stewart translated The Mulfuzat Timury, the autobiographical memoirs of the Moghul Emperor Timur. Murray and other London houses sold the book in 1830, for the Oriental Translation Committee. Timur wrote in the Jagtay Turky tongue, and Abu Talib Hussyny turned the work into Persian. Stewart, who had taught Oriental languages at the East India Company college, made the English form. A map of Transoxania and its neighboring provinces fronts the book.

Stewart gives the book to Colonel Davy, whose father earned thanks for this work. That father had procured and first brought to Europe a true copy of the memoirs. He had also translated the Institutes of Timur with skill and persistence. The memoirs give a great conqueror's own tale of his reign, wars, and rule. Readers get Timur in his own voice, by way of two translations.
76339-the-roman-hat-mystery:
The Roman Hat Mystery, a problem in deduction by Ellery Queen, was published by Frederick A Stokes Company of New York in 1929. It went through four printings in its first two months. Professor Alexander Goettler, chief toxicologist of the city of New York, is thanked for his help with the tale. The book opens where a mystery should: in a theatre, with a corpse.

The first chapter introduces a theatre audience and a corpse together. One Queen works while another Queen watches, for the case belongs both to Inspector Queen of the police and to his son Ellery. A parson comes to grief, and the district attorney turns biographer. The dead man's top hats begin to assume proportions, as chapter ten puts it. An interlude midway halts the tale and speaks straight to the reader, in the fair play manner the Queens made famous.
76401-a-survey-of-modernist-poetry:
Laura Riding and Robert Graves wrote this survey of the new poetry together, word by word. Heinemann printed it in London in 1927. The pair take up a live gripe of their day: plain readers found the new verse hard, and said so.

The plain reader's rights open the book, then form and subject in the new mode. Shakespeare and Cummings meet in a study of spelling and stops. Why the new verse fails to please, dead movements, and the making of a poem fill the middle. Verse and the life of nations, range, and humour close the main line. A final chapter, reworked by both hands, ends the survey.
76434-a-brief-history-of-the-tenth-michi:
Brief History of the Tenth Michigan Cavalry was written by General Trowbridge. Trowbridge, late colonel of the regiment, made it at the Adjutant General request. Friesema Brothers of Detroit printed the history in nineteen o eight. Photographs of all its officers and a map of its field are bound in.

Trowbridge warns that tight space forced him to cut much of worth. Minor matters and details had to be left out of the account. No fit map could be found, so a friend drew one for him. That map shows the regiment active field, save West Tennessee service. That late service fell after the war and would swell the map.
76521-the-hunniwell-boys-and-the-platinu:
L P Wyman wrote The Hunniwell Boys and the Platinum Mystery, a tale put out in New York in 1928. The set bills itself as tales of flight for boys of twelve to sixteen. Wyman had told past tales of the boys in the air. A strange offer starts the plot, by the name of its first part.

Bill Hunniwell drops his paddle and grabs the net as the tale opens. His brother Gordon fights a great fish on a light rod, sixty feet from the boat. The fish breaks the top of the stream as Gordon holds a taut line. By a hut on a hill rests a plane named Albatross, in a tight space. That plane, the text hints, is no plain craft at all. Flight and a rare white metal drive the tale from there.
76583-the-public-library:
The Public Library is a survey of the library movement by Ernest Baker, published in London in 1922. An epigraph from Ruskin's Sesame and Lilies opens it. Ruskin asks why nations buy terror instead of knowledge, in libraries, galleries, and museums.

Six chapters give a historical sketch and ask what a library service is. Library extension, rural libraries, and a national library service follow. Training in librarianship closes the book. Photographs show the King's Library and the British Museum reading room. Other plates show Nottingham's central library, the Guildhall Library, and Stepney's reading room. Baker's preface says the libraries had been saved by the Act of 1919. They stood, he warns, at the critical period of their history.
76664-ballads-of-american-bravery:
Ballads of American Bravery holds verse of brave deeds, picked by Clinton Scollard. Notes by the picker aid school use of the text in class. The book stands in a silver set of home and school classics. Rights date the work to the year nineteen hundred.

A front cut shows the fight in Manila Bay in eighteen ninety eight. The picker says most songs mark a brave act that true lore backs. A few looser picks were let in to widen the field of the set. Songs span wars and seas, from old forts to new fleets in line. The book aims at school youth first, but hopes for all hearts too.
76708-raquel-of-the-ranch-country:
Raquel of the Ranch Country, by Alida Sims Malkus, was copyright in 1927, with a fifth printing in 1937. Pictures are by George F Avison. Sunset brings Raquel to The Towers, a smart girls school whose towers look on the Hudson. Three days of travel from Texas lie behind her.

Raquel comes from Los Ranchos, where her grandparents crossed the plains by wagon. At school she feels stiff, dowdy, and far from home, then keen to join the glad groups within. Twenty chapters take her home again to hunts, a blizzard, and a wild horse. Drouth, a flight across the border, and a drive home with the herd follow. Girls get a warm tale of two worlds in one brave girl.
76795-the-origin-and-development-of-the-:
The Origin and Development of the Atomic Theory is a short book by Maynard Shipley. Haldeman-Julius issued it in 1924 as Little Blue Book number 608. Shipley calls the atom's story the most romantic in the history of science. Five chapters trace it from Greek thinkers to modern times. The Pythagorean atomists open the account. Leucippus and Democritus, the materialistic atomists, come next.

The Eleatic view gets a chapter of objection and reply. Epicurus and Lucretius then revive the doctrine in verse and prose. Post classical atomism closes the survey. Shipley quotes Millikan on Leucippus, whose principles might almost pass today. Osler is quoted too, on knowing Democritus to grasp the theory. Lucretius supplies the happiest illustrations, Osler held. The little book packs two thousand years of thought into a pamphlet.
76893-artistic-embroidery:
Artistic Embroidery is a needlework manual by Ella Rodman Church. Adams and Bishop published the book at New York in 1880. The title promises practical teaching in the fancy branches of needlework. Near two hundred pictures and diagrams explain the stitches and designs.

Church opens by drawing a sharp line between art needlework and mere fancy work. Fancy work, she says, copies a bright pattern with no self in it. True embroidery should carry the same stamp as a painting. The choice of stuff, the drawing of the pattern, and the work itself should rest with one pair of hands. She grants that design is less hard than beginners fear. In art needlework, extra detail is shunned by rule. Old patterns can be adapted to present needs, she adds.
77066-the-evolution-of-the-oil-industry:
Victor Ross wrote The Evolution of the Oil Industry, issued by Doubleday, Page and Company at Garden City, New York, in nineteen twenty. Photos fill the book. A front plate shows the first oil well drilled near Titusville, Pennsylvania, on August twenty seventh, eighteen fifty nine, by Colonel Edwin L Drake. Dr Van H Manning of the American Petroleum Institute wrote a note in praise of the book.

Manning says the chapter heads show a brief survey of a vast change in trade and work. Petroleum, he notes, has spread into all trades, on farm and in factory, on land and sea, in war and peace. That spread took just six decades, with the United States in the lead. Ross sticks close to records and plain facts. Readers get a short, clear tale of oil from the Drake well to world power.
77221-two-girls-and-a-mystery:
Two Girls and a Mystery; or, The Old House in the Glen is a girls' novel by May Hollis Barton. Cupples and Leon published it in New York, copyrighted 1928. Barton had written Three Girl Chums at Laurel Hall. An illustration shows a girl thinking a fortune is hidden here. Twenty-five chapters carry Barbara Winters's adventure. All About Money opens the plot.

Barbara, called Bab, is an orphan raised by her grandparents. She falls asleep over a school book in the window seat. Waking, she overhears Gran and Grandmother talking. The talk was not meant for her ears, and her misery begins. The contents unfold the machinery of a legacy mystery. Lights and noises haunt the old house in the glen, and a secret stairway hides its secret. Bab regains her inheritance by chapter twenty-four.
77412-some-famous-buildings-and-their-st:
Alfred W Clapham and Walter H Godfrey wrote Some Famous Buildings and Their Story. Technical Journals Limited issued it at Westminster. One hundred eight photos and plans aid the text. The papers report fresh research in London and beyond. Godfrey had written a history of London building. The Parish of Chelsea bears his name too.

Fresh inquiry opens new chapters of our past, the preface says. Ancestors' character shows in their buildings, it claims. Learned treatises hide such work too often, it warns. Loose words and sloppy facts mar popular tries, it adds. Short papers can still serve the common reader, they hold. Each paper here makes one firm gift to knowledge. That is the pair's stated aim in print. Careful building history for lay readers stands as an early plea for rigor in popular heritage writing.
77413-my-life-in-poetry:
Stanton A Coblentz looks back on a life spent writing and editing verse, in a memoir issued at New York in 1959. Bookman Associates published it. His own list of books fills a full page first.

The list runs to sixteen verse books, from The Pageant of Man to Senator Goose. Five prose works on poetry follow, plus four anthologies. The memoir opens with a scene of reading. A mild, bespectacled woman of thirty-four reads to a boy of eight in an old San Francisco house. He follows her near-sighted gaze with rapt eyes. Chapters then trace paths of stones and thorns, lucky shots, and poets he has known. Coblentz spent decades in small magazines and little presses. His memoir is a plain record of that half-hidden world.
77549-rhymes-for-the-nursery:
Rhymes for the Nursery, by the authors of Original Poems, is kept here in its twenty-third edition, printed for Harvey and Darton of Gracechurch Street, London, in 1831. The frontispiece, The Dunce of a Kitten, was drawn and engraved by Moses. A preface explains the volume's pretensions: the rhymes are designed to circulate in the nursery, and claim shelter there from the eye of criticism.

Some forty-seven rhymes follow, on the nursery round: the cow, good night, getting up, mamma and the baby, the sparrows, and learning to go alone. Lessons sit lightly on them: the little girl that beat her sister, no breakfast for Growler, and the cruel boy and the kittens. The writers own their doubt, raised by authority, whether ideas fitted to infancy can bear the restrictions of rhyme and metre. The attempt rests on plainness rather than ornament.
77595-the-great-airport-mystery:
Dixon wrote The Great Airport Mystery, a Hardy Boys tale with rights held from nineteen thirty. A cover line quotes Ollie Jacobs saying that, though it is robbery, he will sell the plane. Frank and Joe Hardy drive out of Bayport on the Shore Road in their new roadster. They are bound for the new airport by Barmet Bay on a spring day.

The brothers talk of flying, of school, and of the college their mother wants for them both. Chapter heads promise peril from the sky, a crash, and missing mail. A cabin in the woods, an arrest, and a hearing follow, with the boys held on loose proof. The trail of Ollie Jacobs leads to a capture west of Bacon Hill, and the close is named vindication.
77806-the-oriental-tale-in-england-in-th:
Martha Pike Conant wrote The Oriental Tale in England in the Eighteenth Century. The Columbia University Press issued it in 1908. Comparative literature studies form its series. J B Fletcher vouched for the book up front. Five chapters sort the tales by kind. The Imaginative Group opens the study.

The Moralistic Group follows at page seventy-three. The Philosophic Group takes the third chapter. The Satiric Group fills the fourth at 155. A literary estimate closes the argument. Dated tables and book lists fill the back. The mysterious East charms the wandering mind, Conant opens. No wide land holds a more perennial charm, she says. The Arabian Nights came early in that century, she notes. Its English coming woke the taste, she argues. A scholar's map of England's eastern dream tales traces how Baghdad entered the British nursery and novel.
7790-captain-january:
Laura E Richards's Captain January follows a lighthouse keeper who sells fine lobsters from his red dory. He washes her out with care before sailing home. On the wharf Captain Nazro hails him in a blue coat with brass buttons, asking after the little girl in his charge.

Contents list Star Bright, the story itself, Imogen and Bob, a visit, the captain's star, and a signal. Through seaside talk and tender care, the book tells how a rough old sailor raises a child found by the sea. Love, duty, and a light on the shore shape both their lives.
78060-a-young-man-s-story:
A Young Man's Story, by Sarah Doudney, appeared in the Girl's Own Annual for 1886, in its feathery flakes Christmas part. A young man confesses to his friends that he has known something fairly called a supernatural experience. He would not talk of it in the smoking room the night before. Now, sitting quietly with them at dusk, he will tell it, and bids them not ring for the lamp till he has done.

You have never heard much about my engagement to May Newton, he begins. It was the oft told tale of two people thrown together in a narrow sphere, gliding into close friendship. He met her in an out of the way village on the sea coast. They were not rich enough to think of a speedy marriage.
78085-the-catholic-church-and-history:
Hilaire Belloc examines one charge drawn from history against the Catholic Church in an essay issued in 1926. The essay belongs to the Calvert Series, which Belloc edited, with companion volumes by Chesterton and others. In his preface Belloc says the wider topic could be treated from a hundred sides, so he narrows his aim.

Inside, Belloc sets aside the question of whether the Church has done good, calling it second to the question of truth. His chosen task is to answer the claim that an early pure message was spoiled over the centuries. Readers get a tight, brisk piece of argument from a Catholic writer who treats history as the chief ground of attack in his day.
78114-miniatures-of-french-history:
Hilaire Belloc tells the long story of France in short, sharp scenes. The contents begin with the founding of Marseilles and the fall of the Veneti. They pass through the death of Saint Martin, the baptism of Clovis, and the breaking of Islam. They run on to the Templars, Louis XI, and two men of the Marne.

The first miniature opens in 599 B C with the Phocean Greeks sailing west under the priestess Aristarché, who carried a statue of Artemis at the prow. Belloc credits women with bringing writing, wine, and stone building to the new land. Readers get a swift, opinionated tour of French history, one vignette at a time.
7836-jewish-history-an-essay-in-the-phil:
S. M. Dubnow's Jewish History, an Essay in the Philosophy of History, opens with praise for its author as a leading voice in Russian-Jewish letters. His work on Polish-Russian Jews and on Hasidism, the preface says, broke new ground, joining scientific care with ardent temper and vivid form.

Dubnow refuses the notion that fine form means thin thought, and his essay seeks the inner law of Jewish survival across exile, faith, and communal life. Through history and philosophy, it asks what holds a people together without a state, and why their story matters to all history.
78544-charles-chapin-s-story:
Charles Chapin wrote his own story in Sing Sing Prison, and Putnam published it in New York in 1920. Basil King supplied an introduction. Chapin had been city editor of the New York Evening World for years. In September 1918 he was indicted for murder in the first degree. He had shot his wife Nellie after thirty-nine years of marriage. The testimony called their relations singularly devoted.

The publishers print the report of a commission on Chapin's sanity. Chapin himself wrote that he had felt a nervous breakdown coming on, with pains in his head growing more acute. He was sixty at the time of the killing and received a life sentence. The book is a condemned man's own account, written from his cell: part confession, part explanation, and a strange document of the newspaper world he once ruled.
7863-the-avalanche-a-mystery-story:
Gertrude Atherton's The Avalanche, a mystery story from 1919, opens with Price Ruyler wondering whether his wife's secret was buried by San Francisco's earthquake and fire. Born in a city of odd, whispered pasts, Helene shows subtle changes after a year and a half of uncommon happiness.

Her devotion never wavers, yet her spirits shift, and a silent mother-in-law hints at a past of her own. Ruyler, sure for six months that some gray cloud hangs over his marriage, begins to dig. Through society, money, and old San Francisco, the novel unearths a secret long held.
78704-the-bungalow-mystery:
The Bungalow Mystery is a Nancy Drew mystery by Carolyn Keene, published in New York by Grosset and Dunlap in 1930. Russell H Tandy illustrated it. The title page names Keene as author of The Secret of the Old Clock and The Hidden Staircase. Nancy's third case begins on a lake under black clouds.

Nancy urges her chum Helen to turn back before the storm breaks. A desperate struggle and a new friend follow in the contents. Laura's guardian and Laura's story bring the mystery's human stakes. Nancy's plan leads to the mysterious bungalow, where she is ordered away. A narrow escape, startling revelations, and a familiar face build the middle. Left to starve and in pursuit promise the climax. The early Drew books set the formula: a brave girl, a hidden wrong, and gratitude at the end.
78717-the-silver-bar-mystery:
The Silver Bar Mystery is a west tale by Tuttle, first run in parts past the name The Trail of Deceit. Its rights date is nineteen thirty. The front list names past twenty parts, set in a town on the line past Mexico. Gun play, a ranch, a hold up, and a feast fill that list.

The tale opens at a card game in the town of Silver Bar. Two mates, an old hand and a young one, have rode in for the night on their way to a far range. The old hand wins a pot and stacks his chips with calm. A ranch chief at the table marks whose deal it was. That small chill note starts the web of strife the parts unwind.
78747-the-blacker-the-berry:
Wallace Thurman wrote The Blacker the Berry, a novel of Negro life. The Macaulay Company issued the book in New York in nineteen hundred twenty nine. Its title quotes the old folk saw: the blacker the berry, the sweeter the juice. Countee Cullen lends a verse line to its front.

Emma Lou, a girl of deep black skin, stands at the tale’s heart. Her kin are fair: mother, grandam, and uncle all light of hue. Her black father’s blood set her apart in her own home’s eyes. Bleach, scour, and powder failed to lift her fast black tint. A black boy can get along, her mother says, a black girl not. At Boise’s school feast she sits in white, the one dark face in row. Pyrrhic Victory, a win that costs too much, names its close.
78823-the-french-powder-mystery:
The French Powder Mystery, by Ellery Queen, came out in 1930. Stokes published the problem in deduction at New York. The Roman Hat Mystery stands as Queen's earlier case. Thirty eight chapters stand in five episodes. Nursery rhymes title the first episode's chapters. The queens were in the parlor; Humpty Dumpty had a great fall. Testimony, the corpse, and the watchers follow. The second episode walks the apartment room by room. Bedroom, lavatory, cardroom, and library are searched in turn. Alibis get chapters of their own near the end. Marion, Marchbanks, Carmody, Trask, and Gray are each weighed. A note from Queen opens the cast list.

Study the persons before the story, he urges the reader. Winifred French is dead before it starts. Her murder's hidden cesspool is the question.
78844-west-african-forests-and-forestry:
West African Forests and Forestry, by Harold Unwin, was first published in 1920 at London. Unwin had served as senior conservator of forests in Nigeria. His book carries 110 illustrations made by the author himself. A front plate shows mixed evergreen forest on the edge of Barombo Lake, with cotton trees in front.

Thanks in the front matter name the chief conservator of Nigeria and other forest officers. Two chapters on the forests of the Northern Provinces of Nigeria came from Dr Dalziel. Help with proof reading and with facts came from men across the West African forest service. The work sums up the trees, growth, and care of forests in that region for officials and students. It stands as a record of colonial forestry in its era.
78951-women-in-the-factory:
Women in the Factory, subtitled An Administrative Adventure, is a memoir by Adelaide Anderson of factory inspection. Anderson was the chief lady inspector of factories under the Home Office. Dutton published the New York edition in nineteen twenty two. The story runs from eighteen ninety three to nineteen twenty one.

Anderson wrote at the wish of friends while memory of the work was fresh. She tells what women inspectors did for women and girl workers in Britain. Their tools were the Factory Acts and the Truck Acts of the day. Reports, debates, and press notices supply most of her matter in the book. The inspectors were few, above all in the years before nineteen fourteen. A woman's cry over eight shillings a week for heavy toil drove them on.
7897-the-gray-goose-s-story:
Amy Prentice's The Gray Goose's Story, in Aunt Amy's Animal Stories with thirty-two pictures and a color frontispiece by J. Watson Davis, opens by a pond beyond an apple orchard. Aunt Amy loves to wander there and meet bird and animal friends ready to tell tales.

Mr. Frisky Squirrel, old Mr. Plodding Turtle, and Mr. Bunny Rabbit greet her, but only yesterday, through Master Teddy's mischief, did she meet the gray goose. An angry hiss startles her, mistaken for a snake, and a new friendship begins. It is a gentle farm tale for small children.
7898-mouser-cat-s-story:
Amy Prentice's Mouser Cat's Story, with thirty-five pictures and a color frontispiece by J. Watson Davis, opens on a hard stormy day when Aunt Amy feels lonely, her human friends busy and no animal likely out. Watching rain streams run down the window glass, she expects no story telling.

Then Mrs. Mouser Cat speaks from the doorway, joking about pickles, an animal Aunt Amy knew well but never heard talk before. Surprised and pleased, Aunt Amy listens as the cat begins her tale. It is a cozy companion to the Gray Goose's story, for small readers who love farm animals.
79063-designs-on-prehistoric-hopi-potter:
Designs on Prehistoric Hopi Pottery, by Jesse Walter Fewkes. It was reprinted from the thirty third annual report of the Bureau of American Ethnology and printed at Washington in 1919. An introduction and a chronology of Hopi pottery symbols open the study, centred on the ruin called Sikyatki.

The contents sort the designs by subject. Human figures come first, then quadrupeds, reptiles, and winged figures, with birds shown from above and from the side. Feather designs fill several sections, feathers plain, feathered strings, and feathers joined to the sky band. Geometrical designs, rain clouds, stars, and sun emblems follow, with rectangular figures read as shrines. Later sections trace symbols introduced by incoming groups: from the San Juan River settlements, by the Snake people, by the Badger and Kachina clans, and from Awatobi. Ninety plates and dozens of text figures illustrate the argument.
79181-chemistry:
John Howard Appleton, professor of chemistry at Brown University, wrote this textbook, printed at Providence in 1884. Appleton had written The Young Chemist and manuals of qualitative and quantitative analysis. A chemist's work bench fronts the book. His plan stands in the title: chemistry developed by facts and principles drawn chiefly from the non-metals.

Ads for his other works fill the front: a book of experiments for beginners with simple tools, a brief laboratory manual of analysis with full equations. A yearly laboratory handbook of tables kept abreast of new finds completes the list. The text teaches by experiment first, letting facts lead the student to the laws that bind them, in the Brown classroom manner.
79203-key-to-palmistry:
Key to Palmistry, by Louis Williams, bears a copyright of 1902 and was issued at Seattle. Williams wrote as a teacher of the art, and the book is a short course in reading hands. A verse at the front gives the book to the reader as a gift.

The hand of man comes first: Williams calls the hand the symbol of the mind. Fear, hate, love, and warm feeling show in the fingers, he says, even when the face stays calm. The palm and each finger then get a short part of their own. The lines of the hand follow, with the life line, the heart line, and the line of thought. Symbols, bracelets, and nails close the course, with charts of the head at the end.
79205-discovery:
Discovery is a short story by Helen R Hull, printed in The Touchstone, volume three, in August 1918. It opens on a bridge over a little stream. Richard steps over the low hand rail and sits on a plank, dangling long legs over water yellow with spring turmoil. Cynthia follows, freeing her skirt where a nail has caught it.

Richard tells her she wishes she wore trousers, so that she could do as she pleases. Society, he says, gives her one fate: to fall in love and marry. Cynthia answers that she does not have to. He takes her hand and turns it, saying she has not a lady's hand and could really do things with those fingers. When she closes her fingers in her lap, she shuts in the warm magic of his touch.
79217-the-corporal-s-story:
Ernest Haycox tells a border tale through an old soldier's voice in the hosted story. When Pancho Villa raided Columbus, the narrator's regiment shipped to San Diego and marched toward the border. His company camped opposite the old fort at Tia Juana, near a small village.

Officially the men waited to repel an invasion the old hands knew would never come. The young recruits, fresh at the president's call, found it all thrilling and saw foes in every shadow. Farmers digging a barn became an advance guard, and grazing cows set sentries gripping their rifles. Dale Hawkins, the cleanest and most eager of the boys, stands out in the corporal's memory. Readers get a wry tale of romance meeting routine on border duty.
79224-practical-podiatry:
Practical Podiatry is a textbook of foot medicine by Alfred Joseph, Burnett, and Gross, three professors of the subject. Maurice Lewi, president of the First Institute of Podiatry, edited it. The Institute itself published the book in New York in 1918. It is dedicated to two men named as founders of the modern field.

The introduction opens with the foot's strange standing in science. The ancient Greeks glorified the foot in song and in art, it notes. Yet medically the foot has been a neglected factor, despite its burdens. The book belongs to a movement to raise chiropody into a governed profession. New York took the first steps toward a law for its practice in 1895. Three editors of podiatry journals stand among its authors and sponsors. The work presents the institute's teaching as the standard for practitioners.
7929-parisians-in-the-country:
Honore de Balzac's Parisians in the Country joins The Illustrious Gaudissart with The Muse of the Department, early and late work in one volume. Gaudissart, from 1832 at the height of Balzac's fancy, sketches a traveling salesman in the physiologie manner, with a beginning the introduction calls excellent.

The Muse, ten years later, draws on stores already dipped into, yet still rich. Villagers rolling the great Gaudissart amuse Balzac's Tourangeau pride, though the tale's ending lags its start. Together the pair show a master at flood and at ebb, both vivid with provincial France.
7930-the-advance-of-english-poetry-in-th:
William Lyon Phelps, Lampson Professor of English Literature at Yale, wrote this survey of the new poetry of his own time. He quotes generously, with permission, from publishers of Thomas Hardy, William Butler Yeats, Robert Frost, Vachel Lindsay, Amy Lowell, Edgar Lee Masters, Sara Teasdale, and many others. The book moves poet by poet, judging each voice on its own terms.

Phelps writes as an enthusiastic teacher rather than a theorist, and his aim is to help readers hear what is fresh in verse written after the Victorians. He pairs short critical essays with well-chosen passages, so the poems do much of the persuading. As a snapshot of how English poetry looked while it was still being made, it remains lively and readable.
79553-drift-and-mastery:
Walter Lippmann set out in 1914 to name the causes of the unrest he saw in American life. His book, Drift and Mastery, first looks at the muckrakers and why the public so gladly took up charges of graft. It then asks what has changed in business, work, and wealth.

Chapters take up the weak place of the small shareholder, the buyer who knows too little, and the labor movement as a fight for a share of control. Lippmann also asks how a nation can pay for progress and which kinds of income are not earned. The prose is plain and close to daily life. It gives a sharp young writer's map of a country in the middle of deep change.
7960-early-european-history:
Hutton Webster, Ph. D. , wrote this school textbook as a concise, connected account of human progress in ancient, medieval, and early modern times. It was designed for high schools and preparatory schools where a separate ancient history course was giving way to a broader survey leading into recent times. The preface quotes Samuel Johnson on history as the story of the human mind: its learning, arts, and revolutions.

Webster keeps the narrative clear and continuous, so students can follow Europe from its ancient roots through the Middle Ages to the modern threshold. Maps, structure, and plain exposition suit classroom use. The book still works as a brisk one-volume outline for readers who want the shape of European history before tackling specialist works.
79620-tama-of-the-light-country:
Ray Cummings, author of The Fire People, wrote this serial for Argosy All-Story Weekly across December 13, 20, and 27, 1930. A headnote warns: all New England was frightened by midnight raids on girls' camps and lonely homes, and the kidnapers were suspected of being not of this world.

The tale is set in the summer of 1950 and told by Jack Dean, a newsgatherer for the Broadcasters' Press Association. The first raid struck a girls' camp on Moose Head Lake in Maine, on the night of August 10 and 11. Ten girls were missing, two more dead. The principal was wounded, and two teachers and a matron killed. The news was kept quiet. Jack's friend Jimmy Turk is a flyer with the Interstate Flying Patrol. He summons Jack by telephone from Boston to meet at Bangor and fly in, calling it the biggest piece of news of the year.
79655-connie-morgan-in-the-cattle-countr:
Connie Morgan in the Cattle Country is a boys' novel by James Hendryx, published in 1923. Hendryx also wrote Connie Morgan in Alaska. Putnam's Sons issued the book in New York and London. Frank Schoonover painted the illustrations for it. The contents list twenty three chapters of ranch life. Waseche Bill tells a story in the opening chapter. Connie learns the ropes at the Round Seven ranch.

Later chapters bring left handed branding irons and rolling wagons. A sage brush corral, a fire, and the bad lands follow in turn. Connie meets an outlaw and calls a bluff near the close. The frontispiece shows the remuda sweeping into a valley. The pictures show a cow town street and a rough wagon ride. The series sent its young hero from Alaska to cattle country. Young readers get work, risk, and humour on the range.
79730-the-national-gallery:
The National Gallery is a guide to the London gallery for young folk by Alice Corkran. Wells Gardner, Darton published it in the Treasure-House Series. A van Eyck portrait of Arnolfini and his wife illustrates the front. An introductory note records the author's gratitude to many writers. Vasari, Crowe, Waagen, and the Goncourt brothers helped her compile it. Official guides to the gallery were also consulted throughout. Cook's handbook was a store of inspiration, she says. Ruskin was her unfailing guide as a critic, she adds.

She sometimes ventured to differ from Ruskin, she confides. She never differed from the noble spirit of his teaching. Photographs taken for the volume supply its illustrations. Corkran also wrote Down the Snow Stairs for children. The guide walks young readers through a national collection. It teaches looking by way of famous pictures.
8148-youth-and-egolatry:
Pío Baroja wrote Youth and Egolatry, translated from the Spanish by Jacob S. Fassett Jr. and Frances L. Phillips, with an introduction by H. L. Mencken. Its contents open with a prologue on intellectual love, then essays on egotism: fundamental ideas, the bad man of Itzea. Dogmatophagy, materialism, religion, Dionysus and Apollo, evil, Rousseau, music as a sedative, Wagner, and folk song. A second part turns to Baroja himself, the writer, and his youthful writings.

Baroja, a leading Spanish novelist of the Generation of 1898, writes here as philosopher and provocateur, aphoristic and contrarian. The essays suit readers who enjoy strong opinions and literary argument. They offer a sharp, personal introduction to a mind that distrusted systems and prized individual vision.
8161-fragments-of-ancient-poetry:
James Macpherson's Fragments of Ancient Poetry, presented as translations of old Gaelic verse, launched the Ossian controversy that divided eighteenth-century letters. This Augustan Reprint Society edition, with an introduction by John J. Dunn, presents the fragments that first made Macpherson famous. Readers at the time debated whether the poems were genuine ancient remains or Macpherson's own inventions dressed in antique style.

The fragments matter whatever their origin: they inspired Romantic poetry, fed interest in Celtic antiquity, and raised lasting questions about authenticity and translation. Their misty, heroic tone influenced writers across Europe. For students of literary history, this short volume is the starting point of Ossian, and of the modern cult of the ancient bard.
8221-a-study-of-poetry:
Bliss Perry, professor of English literature at Harvard University, wrote A Study of Poetry following the method he had sketched in his chapter on poetry in Counsel Upon the Reading of Books. His confidence in the genetic method, approaching poetry through impression, transforming imagination, and expression, was shared by many lovers of poetry. Though he hopes his insistence on that threefold process has not hardened into a set formula, since formulas have a dangerous usefulness.

Perry's study guides readers through how poems are made and felt, rather than through rules alone. His Harvard lectures give the book clarity and warmth. For students of poetry, it remains a classic introduction, and a wise warning against letting method replace the poem itself.
8407-the-christian-a-story:
Hall Caine's novel The Christian follows its story across about eighteen months, six months to each of its first three books, with an interval after. Caine, author of The Manxman, sets the tale in the last quarter of the nineteenth century, without fixing particular years. He follows characters tested by faith, love, and the claims of the church.

Caine was among the best-selling novelists of his day, and The Christian was a huge popular success, later staged and filmed. Readers get a Victorian religious novel at full stretch: earnest, emotional, and concerned with what a Christian life should cost. The book's scale and sincerity explain its fame, even where modern tastes differ.
8554-why-worry:
George Lincoln Walton, a neurologist at Massachusetts General Hospital, asks Why Worry? and answers with an old Chinese image: the legs of the stork are long, the legs of the duck are short, and you cannot make one like the other. Why worry, asks Chwang Tsze, quoted at the head, and Walton builds a small book of advice on accepting what cannot be changed.

Walton dedicates the book to his long-suffering family and circle of friends, who heard his advice often. Readers get an early self-help book by a doctor, plain and humane, on worry as a habit to be broken. The book's charm lies in its brevity and its humor, and it anticipates later books on anxiety by decades.
8665-a-strange-discovery:
Charles Romyn Dake published this 1889 novel as a supposed sequel to Edgar Allan Poe's tale of Arthur Gordon Pym, centred on the sailor Dirk Peters. The narrator claims he helped make a discovery of real literary importance, shared by only three men. Kept quiet for nearly twenty-five years because none of them had written for print before. One companion is quiet and retiring, the other erratic and forgetful, which helps explain the long silence.

From that frame, the book follows the search for Peters and the strange facts said to lie behind Poe's unfinished story. Dake plays a double game: part adventure, part literary detective work for Poe's readers. Fans of Pym will enjoy seeing its loose ends picked up. New readers get a brisk Victorian adventure that treats a famous mystery as if it had a real-world answer.
8691-the-american-judiciary:
Simeon E. Baldwin, a Connecticut jurist, examines the American judiciary in this scholarly volume, from its English origins to its practical working.
