Part one covers the nature and scope of judicial power in the United States, the organization of American courts. The separation of judicial power from legislative and executive power in American constitutions. Relations with the political departments, the force of precedents, and the courts' power to develop unwritten and written law follow.

Baldwin writes for lawyers, students, and citizens who want to understand how judges actually work, not merely what constitutions say. His account balances history, doctrine, and courtroom practice. The book remains a classic introduction to the American court system at the start of the twentieth century. A useful background to modern debates about judicial power, precedent, and the courts' place in a democracy.
8699-woman-and-her-saviour-in-persia-by-:
A returned missionary tells the story of woman's life in Persia and of Miss Fiske's fifteen years of labour there. Fine illustrations and a map of Nestorian country. The preface explains that many who knew Fiske's work wanted her to publish the facts. That the writer took up the task only when she could not, so that these records of grace might not be lost. Materials come from letters and firsthand reports, gathered up, in the Saviour's phrase, that nothing be lost.

The book describes Persian women's secluded lives, their sorrows and faith, and the schools and mission work that sought to reach them. It is a missionary document through and through, warm toward its subjects and confident in its message, and it must be read as such.
8823-dutch-life-in-town-and-country:
P. M. Hough describes Dutch life in town and country in this illustrated survey, with thirty-two pictures including the Delft Gate at Rotterdam. Chapters move from national characteristics, court and society. The professional classes, through the position of women and the workman of the towns. To canals and their population, a Dutch village, the peasant at home, and rural customs. Kermis and St Nicholas, amusements, music, theatre, schools, universities, and art and letters follow.

Later chapters cover the Dutch as readers, political life, justice, religion, army and navy, and Holland overseas. Hough writes for English readers curious about a neighbour often reduced to windmills and tulips, and he gives institutions their due. The book offers a thorough, sympathetic portrait of the Netherlands around 1900, useful for travellers then and for historians now. Still readable as a guided tour of a whole society.
8861-the-works-of-lord-byron-vol-1-poetr:
Ernest Hartley Coleridge edits this 1898 first volume of Lord Byron's poetry, in a new, revised, and enlarged edition with illustrations. The preface explains that the text rests on John Murray's 1831 Works in six volumes. Which followed the successive issues of plays and poems published in Byron's lifetime, revised by Byron himself or by Gifford and other accredited readers. Collation with manuscripts at Moore's disposal yielded variorum readings that appear in the notes.

The volume gathers Byron's early and middle poetry, from Hours of Idleness through the satires and tales that made him famous, with the apparatus of a scholarly edition. Readers can trace Byron's growth from a lordling poet to the voice of Childe Harold and Don Juan. In texts closer to his own revisions than many popular reprints. It serves students first, but any Byron reader gains from its careful, documented text.
8883-a-love-story:
A Bushman, writing in 1841, dedicates this love story to Lady Gipps, respectfully inscribed by a grateful friend. His preface explains at length why the work exists: as a solitary, companionless bushman, he found pleasure in lone evenings in creating. In creating living a being more intense. He expatiates on love for his adopted country, Australia, which greatly influenced the book's composition. His opening verse sends thoughts like swallows skimming the main, bearing his spirit back over earth and air, a wild bird and a wanderer.

Volume one follows that wandering spirit into a romance shaped by exile, landscape, and longing, written by a man who lived far from literary society. The author's very pseudonym, A Bushman, marks the book's claim: Australian experience told from inside the bush.
8906-mary-slessor-of-calabar-pioneer-mis:
W. P. Livingstone tells the life of Mary Slessor of Calabar, pioneer missionary, opening with a reflection on people who depart from normal procedure, follow ideals rather than rules. Use irregular, often unwise-seeming methods, yet accomplish important ends. Such a one was Mary Slessor, he says, poor or frail and of no account in her own estimation. Toward the end of her days she was urged to write her story, and this biography draws on her letters and on those who knew her.

Slessor, a Dundee mill girl turned missionary in Nigeria, lived among the Efik and Ibibio peoples, fought twin-killing, built schools, and became a trusted mediator and magistrate. Livingstone presents her as a saint of practical Christianity, and modern readers should weigh his admiration against colonial context. The life remains a classic missionary biography, and a portrait of a formidable woman who made Calabar her home.
9079-the-man-shakespeare-and-his-tragic-:
Frank Harris wrote this bold life of Shakespeare, arguing that the plays paint the poet himself. Harris dedicates it to Ernest Beckett, praised for practical genius and love of high endeavor. Book One reads Hamlet, Romeo, and Falstaff as self-portraits in turn. Book Two traces Shakespeare's love story through the Sonnets.

Harris claims that Shakespeare's tragic heroes voice his own griefs, loves, and pride. Scholars now dispute much of his case, yet his verve still grips. The book remains a lively, if daring, attempt to find the man behind the greatest plays in English.
9094-wild-flowers-or-pastoral-and-local-:
Robert Bloomfield published these pastoral and local poems in London in 1806. They follow his Farmer's Boy and Rural Tales, and keep close to village life. Contents include Abner and the Widow Jones, a familiar ballad, The Horkey, and The Broken Crutch. Shooter's Hill and Barnham Water add local color.

Bloomfield sings of old oak tables, harvest customs, and love of country in a plain, musical voice. His verse never strains for grandeur. The book still gives a warm, true picture of English country folk at the start of the nineteenth century.
9192-the-channings-a-story:
Mrs. Henry Wood, author of East Lynne, wrote this long story of the Channing family, in its two hundred and tenth thousand printing by 1901. Chapters open with an inked surplice, bad news, and Constance Channing, then no holiday today and Roland Yorke. Lady Augusta Yorke at home, Mr. Ketch, and an assistant organist follow.

Hamish's candles, a false alarm, and the cloister keys deepen a tale of church, family, and reputation. Wood keeps Victorian domestic suspense at full stretch. The novel remains a beloved example of her popular art, earnest, intricate, and warm.
9311-hetty-s-strange-history:
Published without a name, but by the author of Mercy Philbrick's Choice, this novel of 1877 tells Hetty's strange history. It opens with a sonnet on love: words are cheap, gifts cheaper still, and one thing remains unnamed on earth. That thing is giving one's own life up for love, not in a martyr's death, but in daily life's wearing groove.

Hetty's story tests that hard doctrine through years of quiet sacrifice. The novel asks what great love returns to such a giver. It remains a moving Victorian tale of devotion, praised for its moral seriousness and its tender, unsparing eye.
9399-a-roman-lawyer-in-jerusalem-first-c:
W. W. Story wrote this verse tale as a letter from Marcus, a Roman lawyer in Jerusalem, to Caius, his best friend in Rome. Marcus greets his friend, and his bearer Lucius, wearied with the East, longs for Rome again. Lucius calls the East hateful, blazing, barren, and bleak, and pants for the circus, its games, and its roaring crowds.

Story sets Roman grandeur against Jerusalem's strangeness, in blank verse rich with marble porticoes and sunlit awnings. The poem is a dramatic monologue of exile and homesickness. It remains a fine Victorian classical piece, vivid and melancholy.
972-the-devil-s-dictionary:
Ambrose Bierce wrote this dictionary of satirical definitions, begun in a weekly paper in 1881 and continued at long intervals until 1906. In that year much of it appeared as The Cynic's Word Book, a name the author had not the power to reject or the happiness to approve. The Devil's Dictionary is its final form.

Bierce defines love, law, politics, and religion with a sting, turning each word into a small essay on human folly. His wit is dark, precise, and unsparing, and his entries reward dipping in at random. The book remains a classic of American satire, quoted wherever cynics gather.
9746-the-ashiel-mystery:
Mrs. Charles Bryce wrote The Ashiel Mystery, a detective story of illness, houses, and hidden deeds. Sir Arthur Byrne, ill after three summers at a Black Sea consulate, takes sick leave and hurries home to Harley Street doctors. He blames drains and Eastern towns, yet fears his health may fail for good. The tale then turns to Ashiel, where a mystery waits.

Bryce, praised by Stevenson for police romance craft, builds suspense from character and place, not mere clues. Doctors, consuls, and country houses cross the plot. A reader gets a classic Edwardian mystery, urbane and tense, with a sick man's dread as its dark opening note.
9795-the-four-faces-a-mystery:
William Le Queux wrote The Four Faces, a mystery of angel faces, snares, and a glittering underworld. Chapters open with curiosity aroused in Linden Gardens, then a Hampstead mystery and a house in Grafton Street. Hugheson Gastrell, Osborne, and Mrs. Stapleton cross the plot, with a baron, a thin-faced stranger, and a channel mystery. Secrets of dusky fowl and modern vice darken the trail.

Later chapters unmask the four faces, as confessions and papers close the snare. Le Queux writes with brisk, Edwardian suspense. A reader gets a lively mystery of faces and disguises, from a master of the spy and crime tale.
9808-the-loudwater-mystery:
Edgar Jepson wrote The Loudwater Mystery in 1920, a tale of a lord, a lady, and a cat named Melchisidec. Lord Loudwater, buried in a Times leader, tugs his red-brown beard and snorts disgust through his nose. Lady Loudwater eats in thoughtful silence, brow faintly frowned. Melchisidec, excited by grilled sole, pricks his lordship's thigh and earns a futile kick at empty air.

From this comic breakfast, a country-house mystery grows, with marriage, money, and murder in its shadow. Jepson writes with dry, observant wit. A reader gets a wry Edwardian mystery, where a cat's prick opens a tale of dark deeds.
9897-introductory-american-history:
Henry Eldridge Bourne and Elbert Jay Benton, professors at Western Reserve University, wrote this school history in 1912. Instead of starting at Plymouth Rock, they begin far earlier, with the peoples of Europe and the ancient world who shaped the ideas America inherited.

Chapters follow Greeks and Romans, early Christians, medieval towns, traders, and explorers, before reaching English self-government and the Atlantic world. The aim is to show young readers why American institutions look as they do. It is a clear, old-style textbook, useful for its long view of the past.
a-court-of-inquiry: Grace Smith Richmond writes a novel of inquiry into the condition of friends. Its parts are named for flowers: Althea, Camellia, Dahlia, Rhodora, Azalea, and Hepatica. Later chapters pair each woman with a professor, a judge, a cashier, and a promoter. Richmond builds a gentle story of friendship, courtship, and character.
a-double-barrelled-detective-story:
Mark Twain opens in Virginia in 1880, as he states, with a wedding between Jacob Fuller, a handsome young man of slender means, and a rich, proud girl of Cavalier blood. Her widowed father opposed the match bitterly. The marriage turns cruel, and the wronged husband swears a revenge that will take years to ripen.

Part two brings the case west. A boy with a miraculous sense of smell tracks men as a bloodhound tracks game. Sherlock Holmes himself appears there, to reason grandly and wrongly. Twain loads both barrels: one for the revenge melodrama, one for the detective story and its master. The result is part tragedy, part burlesque, and wholly his.
a-double-story:
A Double Story, by George MacDonald, is a fairy tale that opens in a country where nothing can be counted on. MacDonald warns that no one there can say whether it will rain or hail. The milk may sour or not. A week old baby may wake sweet tempered or cross, and nobody can tell beforehand. Fourteen chapters carry the disorder into two households at once, one rich and one poor.

The tale pairs a spoiled princess, Rosamond, with a shepherd's daughter, Agnes, whose lives the Wise Woman draws together. Pride in the palace and contentment in the cottage are weighed against each other, and the princess must learn what her nurses and parents never taught her. MacDonald, a minister turned storyteller, writes doctrine as wonder: selfishness shown from inside, and kindness practiced until it becomes strength.
a-fascinating-traitor-an-anglo-indian-st: Colonel Richard Henry Savage's Anglo-Indian novel opens with Major Alan Hawke brooding at Geneva over a past that reaches back to Delhi. Alliances, a veiled rosebud of Delhi and a diplomatic tiffin give way to a mysterious bungalow, a captivated viceroy and Prince Djiddin's visit to England. Daggers, councils at Granville and a French fishing boat carry an intrigue across India, Jersey and the Channel.
a-forgotten-empire-vijayanagar-a-contrib:
Robert Sewell reconstructs the great South Indian empire of Vijayanagar, a contribution, as his subtitle says, to the history of India. The empire held the Deccan against northern invaders for over two centuries, then fell in a single catastrophe. Sewell builds his account from chronicles, inscriptions, and the reports of Portuguese travelers who saw the capital in its glory.

Forty-one chapters trace the city's founding, its kings, its armies, its temples and markets, and the great battle that destroyed it. He prints the foreign visitors' descriptions at length, so the reader sees the bazaars and festivals through their eyes. The book revived interest in a lost capital whose ruins still cover miles of ground.
a-handbook-of-ethical-theory:
George Stuart Fullerton wrote his handbook, by his preface, to help students of ethics reach a clearer view of what morals mean and what ethical study aims at. He makes no apology for a clear, untechnical style. Part one examines the accepted content of morals: the codes of communities, justice, truth-telling, and the common good, then the codes of the moralists from Epicureans and Stoics onward.

Part two treats ethics as a science, its methods and materials. Part three studies man and his environment, bodily, mental, and social. Later parts take up theories of the good, duty, and the virtues. Fullerton writes fairly about every school, and the book served as a college text for students meeting moral philosophy in earnest.
a-history-of-english-romanticism-in-the-: Henry Augustin Beers writes a history of English romanticism in the eighteenth century. His chapters define the subject, then treat Augustans, Spenserians, landscape poets, and the Miltonic group. The school of Warton, the Gothic revival, Percy, Ossian, and Chatterton follow. Beers shows romantic feeling growing within an age of reason.

Henry Augustin Beers continues his history of English romanticism into the nineteenth century. The volume opens with a romance of a northern land, a grey tower, and a forest by the sea. Beers follows romantic poetry and prose through its full flowering. The book completes his survey of the romantic movement in England.
a-kentucky-cardinal-a-story: James Lane Allen tells a Kentucky cardinal story opening on New Year's Day of 1850. Sun shines cloudless over snow buried cedars without thaw, and a lean hare limps across the lawn. Night falls bitter cold, with porches cracking as they freeze tighter. Allen's story follows a cardinal and its human neighbors through a Kentucky winter.
a-knight-of-the-nineteenth-century:
Edward Payson Roe states his theme in verse in his preface: he best deserves a knightly crest who slays the evils that infest his soul within. The contents begin with Bad Training for a Knight and Both Apologize, then Chained to an Iceberg and Passion's Clamor. His young knight, Haldane, is a college man of strong impulses and weak guides.

Chapter titles chart the fall and recovery: birds of prey, their victim, Haldane arrested, our knight in jail, the world's verdict — a criminal — and the world's best offer, a prison. Roe, a minister whose novels outsold nearly everyone's, builds a tale of temptation, crime, and reform meant to arm young men for modern life.
a-love-story: William Harvey Christie writes a love story from his life as a solitary bushman. In lone evenings he created, and in creating lived, a being more intense than himself. The preface explains his motives at length for composing the work. Christie, inscribed to Lady Gipps, writes of love borne in isolation.
a-maker-of-history:
A Maker of History is a 1905 novel by E Phillips Oppenheim, the English writer who became one of the most successful thriller authors of his age. Oppenheim worked in his father's leather business for almost twenty years before writing made him famous. By the time of this book he was building the career that would make him a pioneer of modern spy and intrigue fiction.

The novel belongs to his early run of suspense stories, the genre on which his reputation rests. Its title promises a tale in which private action shapes public events, told in the brisk, plot-driven style that won him a mass readership. Readers meet Oppenheim near the start of his long reign as a self-styled prince of storytellers.
a-review-of-uncle-tom-s-cabin-or-an-essa: A. Woodward answers Uncle Tom's Cabin with this essay on slavery, published at Cincinnati in 1853. The preface tells how a still small voice urged him to write for two years while he pleaded incapacity, poverty, and want of time. Disease in the autumn of 1852 forced him from medical practice. He then commenced the work, turning a physician's enforced leisure into a sustained review of Stowe's novel.
a-roman-lawyer-in-jerusalem-first-centur: William Wetmore Story writes a verse narrative set in first-century Jerusalem, opening as a letter from Marcus to his friend Caius in Rome. The bearer, Lucius, is wearied with the East, which he finds blazing, barren, and bleak, and longs again for Rome's streets, villas, banquets, and games. Against the vast circus alive with heads and roaring crowds, Jerusalem life seems blank and flat to a Roman lawyer far from home.
a-source-book-of-australian-history: Gwendolen Swinburne gathers this source book of Australian history, issued in London in 1919. The first part takes up finding and mapping new lands: Tasmania, Western Australia, the eastern coast, Bass Strait, the Investigator, the crossing of the mountains, and trips across the land. The second part turns to general history, from first landing and Phillip's exit through the Bligh mutiny, the wool trade, and the start of South Australia and Victoria.
a-strange-discovery: Charles Romyn Dake recounts a strange discovery in this narrative subtitled How We Found Dirk Peters, first published in 1889. The narrator once assisted in a discovery of importance to lovers of literature. He explains a silence of nearly a quarter of a century: none of the three participants had written for publication, one was quiet and retiring, another erratic and forgetful. Doctors Castleton and Bainbridge move through the search that follows.
a-strange-story:
Edward Bulwer-Lytton, a star of the Victorian book world, wrote this occult romance in 1862. Its hero is a young doctor drawn to a wise, dark man of great wealth and strange powers. Bulwer-Lytton had a deep taste for the lore of the hidden world.

The tale turns on mesmerism, alchemy, and the search for a drink that grants long life. Love, pride, and dread grow as the young man trades his soul's rest for dark lore. The book was the great public hit of its kind in its age, and it still grips.
a-study-of-poetry: Bliss Perry, professor of English literature at Harvard, studies poetry by what he calls the genetic method in this volume. His threefold process runs from impression through transforming imagination to expression, a formula he refuses to let harden into mere rule. Little space goes to epic and drama, already treated in many books, while the lyric forms that attract his own generation receive especial attention in two parts.
a-summer-in-a-canyon-a-california-story:
Kate Douglas Wiggin pitches camp in Las Flores Cañon in California, in this popular edition of 1914, and lists her campers like a playbill: Dr. Paul Winship as mine host, his wife as guardian angel, small Dicky the scamp, Bell the camp poetess, Polly Oliver, Margery Noble, and Hop Yet, the Chinese cook. Eleven chapters cover preparation, the journey, and life in the cañon.

A lost heir apparent, rhymes and reasons, Queen Elsie's visit, Polly's birthday in two halves, and camp-fire stories fill the summer. The young people climb, ride, and act plays among the live oaks. Wiggin wrote the tale for young readers, and its sunshine and good humor made it a favorite California story.
a-tramp-through-the-bret-harte-country:
Thomas Dykes Beasley wrote A Tramp Through the Bret Harte Country as a walking tour of Gold Rush California. Beasley, author of The Coming of Portolá, follows the mining country Bret Harte made famous. Charles A. Murdock supplies a foreword. The chapters move town by town through the Sierra foothills.

From Stockton the tramp reaches Angel's Camp, Tuttletown, Sonora, and Mokelumne Hill. Ruins of Coloma recall Marshall, who found the first gold and died poor. Placerville, Grass Valley, and Nevada City yield pioneers' recollections. Old-timers explain the origin of mining laws and remember Harte himself. Beasley mixes memoir, gossip, and scenery with obvious affection. His book preserves the glamour of the old mining towns as their generation passed, photographs and all.
a-young-girl-s-diary:
An anonymous girl of the upper middle class kept this diary from age eleven to fourteen and a half, and the contents divide it by her school years. The edition is translated by Eden and Cedar Paul, as the title page states, and prefaced by a letter from Sigmund Freud dated April 27, 1915. Freud calls the diary a gem: nothing before it, he writes, lets readers see so clearly into the soul of a growing girl.

The editor states that nothing was toned down, added, or suppressed, apart from changed names to protect the writer. The entries follow friendships made and broken, family relations deepening, first love, and the dawning of sexual knowledge and the burden of keeping it secret. Freud commends the book to educators and psychologists.
acton-s-feud-a-public-school-story: Frederick Swainson tells Acton's feud, a public school story published by George Newnes in 1901 with twelve illustrations. The contents run from a foul and a penalty through the regeneration of Biffen's house to Cotton and the Jackal, the last cap, and thanks to Acton. Biffen's concert, the end of term, a young brother, and Todd paying a bill follow. Raffles at Rotherhithe and the easy downward road lead to Hodgson's quietus, Acton's trump card, and the end of the feud.
added-upon-a-story: Nephi Anderson writes Added Upon, published by the Deseret News Press at Salt Lake City in its ninth edition, copyrighted in 1898 and 1912. Under an epigraph that those who keep their first estate shall be added upon, the preface to the third edition asks what religion must answer. What am I, whence came I, what is the object of life, and what is my destiny? The book outlines the scheme of things and the ways of God to men as taught by the Gospel and believed by Latter-day Saints.
adventures-in-southern-seas-a-tale-of-th: George Forbes sets a sixteenth-century tale of captivity and escape across the southern seas, where a young captive faces hostile shores and strange peoples. Chapters on New Holland and the wider Pacific carry the hero from capture toward freedom through peril, cunning, and luck. The story blends sea adventure with period colour, giving young readers a fast-moving romance of the age of sail.
aesthetic-poetry:
Walter Pater's essay Aesthetic Poetry defines the school of English verse that took art itself for its country. The aesthetic poetry, he writes, is neither a copy of Greek or medieval work nor a simple idealizing of modern life. It builds, above the transfigured worlds of older poetry, a still fainter and more spectral world, literally an artificial earthly paradise. Its secret is a kind of inverted homesickness, a thirst for escape that no actual life satisfies. Rossetti's ballads and William Morris's earthly paradise stand behind his account.

The essay first served as part of his Renaissance studies, and it reads as that book's manifesto in small. Sensation, strangeness, and beauty added to beauty are its tests. Readers get Pater's criticism at its most concentrated here, a whole movement explained from inside by its finest prose stylist.
all-he-knew-a-story: John Habberton, author of Helen's Babies, tells a story called All He Knew, of a man whose knowledge and judgment are tested by the world around him. The novel moves through domestic and social scenes with Habberton's plain, good-humoured style. Its interest lies less in grand events than in character, conduct, and the lessons of ordinary life.
all-roads-lead-to-calvary:
Jerome K. Jerome opens in an old London church, in the 1919 Hutchinson edition used here, where a young woman journalist slips in during a service. She had meant only to gather copy about old churches and their famous dead. Instead something in the service catches her, and the visit starts a change in her life.

Eighteen chapters follow Joan among editors, reformers, soldiers, and seekers in the years around the Great War. Talk of faith, feminism, and the price of public work fills the novel, as Joan tests what she owes herself against what she owes others. Jerome, famous for comedy, writes here in earnest, and the title states his theme: every road of sacrifice leads one way.
all-sorts-and-conditions-of-men-an-impos:
All Sorts and Conditions of Men, subtitled An Impossible Story, is a novel by Walter Besant about rich and poor meeting in London's East End. Angela Messenger, an idealistic Cambridge graduate with inherited wealth, resolves to use her money for good. She changes her name and takes lodgings in a Stepney boarding-house, determined to understand the East End and its people from inside.

At the same time, the young aristocrat Harry Le Breton haunts the same streets, discovering his own origins and a new sense of kinship with the poor. The novel works at once as a condition-of-England story and as New Woman fiction. It became one of Besant's best-known books, famous for imagining what goodwill and money might do in the slums.
an-antarctic-mystery: Jules Verne writes An Antarctic Mystery, translated by Mrs. Cashel Hoey, as a sequel in spirit to Poe's tale of the southern seas. The story sails toward the Antarctic in search of lost voyagers, through ice, fog, and strange sights. Verne's blend of adventure and speculation carries readers to the edge of the known world.
an-elementary-course-in-synthetic-projec: Derrick Norman Lehmer offers an elementary course in synthetic projective geometry, published in Berkeley, California. Opening with one-to-one correspondence, the book builds the subject by pure reasoning about points, lines, and figures. It served students as a clear entry to a field usually taught by algebra. Worked figures help the reader follow each step.
an-essay-on-the-trial-by-jury:
Lysander Spooner argues his case across twelve chapters and an appendix on taxation. Juries, he says, have the right and duty to judge the justice of the law itself. They are not limited to the facts of a case. His first chapter states the claim outright. He grounds it in Magna Carta, whose history and language fill the second chapter.

Further chapters pile up proofs from the old common law, jurors' oaths, and judges' oaths, then handle objections and civil suits. Spooner calls modern juries and judges illegal where they deny this right. The essay, by an abolitionist lawyer, became a classic statement of the jury's power to refuse unjust laws.
an-expository-outline-of-the-vestiges-of: Samuel Laing outlines the Vestiges of the Natural History of Creation, with a notice of the author's Explanations as a sequel to that work. Laing sets out the book's extraordinary hypotheses on the growth of life and the cosmos, and weighs how far they are supported. The outline helps readers grasp a controversial book that stirred Victorian science.
an-historical-mystery-the-gondreville-my:
Honoré de Balzac opens in the autumn of 1803, under the Consulate, in Katharine Prescott Wormeley's translation. A senator, Gondreville, is seized by masked men, and a young nobleman has vanished. Royalist plotters, secret police, and old families of the Aube all hold pieces of the truth.

Two parts follow Laurence de Cinq-Cygne, a brave young royalist, through hiding, arrest, and trial, while agents of Fouché hunt the conspirators. Balzac based his plot on a real unsolved kidnapping of the period. The novel mixes detective work, court scenes, and the politics of a France not yet settled under Napoleon. Its tension comes from secrets kept under threat of the scaffold.
an-introduction-to-the-study-of-robert-b:
Hiram Corson's study guide introduces readers to the poetry of Robert Browning. The title page names Corson, a professor of English literature at Cornell, as the author. This printing is the third edition, first published in 1886. It opens with a personal letter from Browning himself, dated December 1886, thanking Corson and approving the notes.

Corson writes for students who find Browning hard going. He explains Browning's aims and methods, then works through major poems with commentary meant to open their dramatic monologues and dense thought to a first reader. The book reflects how Browning's reputation was being built in American universities during his lifetime, with the poet's blessing on the enterprise.
andy-at-yale-or-the-great-quadrangle-mys: Roy Eliot Stokes sends Andy to Yale in the Great Quadrangle Mystery, published by the World Syndicate in Cleveland and New York. The college story follows Andy through Yale life, friendship, and a mystery centred on the quadrangle. Stokes writes in the brisk school-story manner, full of sport, pranks, and pluck.
aristotle-on-the-art-of-poetry:
Aristotle's treatise on poetry appears here in Ingram Bywater's translation, first published at Oxford in 1920, with a preface by Gilbert Murray. Murray opens in Plato's Republic, where Plato, having denounced poetry as a false siren, offers her champions a chance to defend her in prose. Aristotle, he suggests, took up that chance.

The treatise itself takes poetry apart: imitation, the kinds of poem, and above all tragedy, with its plot, character, thought, and diction. Aristotle ranks plot first, explains the unity of action, and names the purging of pity and fear. No short book has governed storytelling longer; dramatists and critics still argue in its terms.
autobiography-of-sir-george-biddell-airy:
George Biddell Airy wrote this account of his life, edited after his death by his son Wilfrid Airy in 1896. Airy was Astronomer Royal from 1836 to 1881, and the preface insists his life was that of a hard-working man of business. The quality and variety of the work alone set it apart. He kept all his correspondence, leaving rich material behind.

Forty-six years at Greenwich make the Observatory's history double as his own. Yet the pages stay practical: a telescope mirror reset, screws loosened at night, stars near the zenith sharp again, Saturn greatly improved. Airy records instruments, staff, and state business with an engineer's calm. Readers meet the administrator who standardised British astronomy, time signals, and magnetic and tidal work for two generations.
beyond-the-rocks-a-love-story:
Elinor Glyn's love story appears here in the photoplay edition from the Macaulay Company, illustrated from the Paramount film with Gloria Swanson and Rodolph Valentino. Valentino poses as Lord Bracondale beside Glyn herself in the frontispiece. Theodora, the novel's heroine, spends her engagement to the rich, dull Mr. Brown in hours of dull or rebellious moments, having taken the situation for her family's sake.

Married, she meets Hector, Lord Bracondale, and the rocks of the title — duty and reputation — rise between them. At the theatre, Miss Winmarleigh raises her glasses at a woman in black velvet with splendid pearls, asking Lady Bracondale who she can be. Hector slips from the box rather than hear his darling priced by gossips. Glyn's tale of renunciation became a silent-film classic, and this edition preserves its stills.
black-caesar-s-clan-a-florida-mystery-st:
Albert Payson Terhune sets Black Caesar's Clan among the Florida Keys, and his foreword builds the islands from scratch. A coral worm piles the reef upward, a mangrove bud takes root in salt water, and soil gathers in the tangle. On such a key, generations later, stands the hidden world of the tale.

Chapters follow a hidden path, a man in the dark, and a stranger from nowhere. Traps and a trapper, a siege, and a figure in white raise the mystery. The clan descends from Black Caesar, the pirate whose name haunts these waters. Terhune, famous for dog stories, here writes a treasure-and-smuggling mystery of the mangrove coast. Mockingbirds, ghost trees, and battle in the day carry a Florida adventure steeped in local colour.
britannica-1911-abbon-of-fleury:
Abbon of Fleury receives a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Abbon, a learned Frenchman born near Orleans about 945, shone in the schools of Paris and Reims. Two years in England helped Archbishop Oswald of York restore monastic life, and Romsey took him as abbot.

Fleury on the Loire made him abbot in 988. Twice King Robert the Pious sent him to Rome, in 986 and 996, and twice he turned aside a papal interdict. A monkish revolt at La Réole killed him in 1004 as he sought to quell it. His Epitome of the popes' lives and his letters survive, and his pupil Aimoin wrote his life. That life, the entry notes, serves as a key source for Robert's reign and the papacy.
britannica-1911-abertillery: Abertillery is the subject of a short town entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, read here inside a shared chunk of text. The entry names an urban district in Monmouthshire's western division, north-west of Newport on the Great Western railway. Its people near doubled in ten years, from 10,846 in 1891 to 21,945 in 1901. The town lies in the Ebbw Fach valley amid mountainous mining ground. Coal mines, ironworks, and tinplate works employ most hands. Nantyglo and Blaina, mining townships up the valley, form their own urban district near by.
britannica-1911-accessory:
Accessory names a person guilty of a felony not as the main offender but by taking part through advice, command, aid, or concealment. The 1911 Britannica entry divides accessories into two kinds. An accessory before the fact orders or procures a felony without being present, since presence would make him a principal. An accessory after the fact receives, harbours, assists, or comforts a known felon.

Punishment differs sharply between the two. The accessory before the fact is liable to the same punishment as the principal, and in practice is indicted and tried the same way. The accessory after the fact generally faces at most two years' imprisonment, though sheltering a murderer can bring penal servitude for life.
britannica-1911-acerra-pottery:
Acerra, in Roman antiquity, was a small box or pot for holding incense. The 1911 Britannica entry separates it carefully from the turibulum, or thurible, the censer in which incense was actually burned. One vessel stored the grains, the other burned them, and Roman ritual needed both.

Funerals gave the word a second use. Romans also called acerra the little altar set near a dead person, on which incense was offered every day until the burial. The term lived on in church Latin, where acerra still names the incense boats used in Roman Catholic ritual, the small vessels that carry incense to the thurible.
britannica-1911-actuary:
Actuary began as a Roman clerk's title. Actuarii recorded the public acts of the senate. They also kept the military accounts. Others enforced contracts for military supplies. The English word narrowed by slow stages. First it denoted any clerk or registrar. Then it meant a company's secretary and adviser. Insurance companies used it most of all. Now it names a specialist in life calculations.

Modern actuaries compute probabilities of human life. Life assurance practice rests on their figures. So do annuities and reversionary interests. Statutes first used the word loosely in 1819. The Institute of Actuaries was founded in 1848. Precision of usage dates from that body. Its journal and charter set membership requirements. Convocation's registrar still bears the title too.
britannica-1911-adams-henry:
Henry Adams (born 1838) is an American historian. He was born in Boston in February 1838. Charles Francis Adams was his father. John Quincy Adams was his grandfather. Harvard graduated him in 1858. He served as his father's private secretary in London. That service ran from 1861 to 1868. Harvard made him assistant professor of history in 1870. He edited the North American Review for six years. His seminary method pioneered American historical training.

One work towers over the rest. His History of the United States covers 1801 to 1817. Nine volumes appeared between 1889 and 1891. The entry calls it incomparably the best on Jefferson and Madison. Its diplomatic account wins special praise. Essential impartiality marks the whole work. Biographies of Gallatin and Randolph stand beside it.
britannica-1911-agriculture-implements-a:
Implements and Machinery, within the Agriculture article of the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, surveys the farm tools then winning notice in Britain. Its evidence is the prize competitions held at the yearly shows of the Royal Agricultural Society of England. Those trials, repeated most years, showed the public how mechanical aids to farming kept changing.

Awards are listed from Taunton in 1875 onward, year by year and town by town. Early prizes went to mowing machines, hay-making machines, horse-rakes, and guards for threshing drums. Later lists add self-binding harvesters, sheep-shearing machines, fixed and portable oil engines, spraying machines, sheep-dipping gear, and churns. Read in order, the lists trace farming's shift from horse-drawn tools toward powered machinery.
britannica-1911-ainsworth-henry:
Ainsworth, Henry, an English Nonconformist divine and scholar of 1571 to 1622, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born of yeoman stock at Swanton Morley in Norfolk, he spent four years as a scholar of Caius College, Cambridge. He moved from the Puritan party toward the Separatists, those who broke fully with the national church. Persecution drove him abroad about 1593.

At Amsterdam he worked as porter to a scholarly bookseller, who discovered his skill in Hebrew and made him known. When part of the exiled London church gathered there, Ainsworth was chosen as its doctor, or teacher. He led in drawing up its confession of faith in 1596 and reissued it in Latin for Europe's universities. With Francis Johnson he wrote an apology for Christians commonly called Brownists. His ablest hard work was a reply to John Smyth on Scripture, worship, and ministry.
britannica-1911-air-country:
Air, or Asben, a country of West Africa, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It lies inside the Sahara between fifteen and nineteen degrees north, yet counts among that desert's most fertile regions. The northern part is mountainous, with peaks rising to 5,000 feet. Wooded hollows and wide plains lie between the hills.

Mimosa, dum palm, and date palm grow in abundance there. Some plains give good pasturage for camels, asses, goats, and cattle, while others are waterless desert tablelands. No river runs all year, but rains from August to October flood the mountain water-courses, and wells serve the people and their herds. Lions and gazelles haunt the quieter districts. Salt caravans cross the region toward the Hausa states, and the sultan of Air depends heavily on the Tuareg chiefs to the northwest.
britannica-1911-airay-henry:
Henry Airay (about 1560–1616), an English Puritan churchman, reached Oxford as a servant boy and left it as a ruler of the place. Born at Kentmere in Westmorland, he was William Airay's son. His father served Bernard Gilpin, famed as the North's apostle. Gilpin's gifts sent Henry and his brother to the school Gilpin had endowed, and from there the boy went up to Oxford.

At Oxford Airay passed from St Edmund Hall to Queen's College, where he waited on the fellows as a poor scholar. Degrees followed, up to a doctorate in divinity, and he took holy orders. He preached often and with zeal. His commentary on Paul's letter to the Philippians shows his hot attacks on popery and his bold Calvinist faith. Queen's made him its provost in 1598, and in 1606 he rose to vice-chancellor of the whole university.
britannica-1911-albury:
Albury, a town in New South Wales, Australia, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands in Goulburn county near the Victorian border, 386 miles by rail west-south-west of Sydney, and held 5,821 people in 1901. The town sits on the right bank of the Murray river. Two bridges cross there, one wooden for the road and one iron for the railway.

From Albury the Murray is navigable by small steamers all the way to its mouth, some 1,800 miles. The town centres a sheep-rearing and farming district where grapes, cereals, and tobacco grow widely. Its wine was held in high repute throughout Australia. A tree under which the first explorers camped in November 1824 still stood in an enclosed space when the entry was written. Albury became a municipality in 1859.
britannica-1911-aldrich-henry:
Aldrich, Henry, an English theologian and philosopher of 1647 to 1710, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Westminster and educated at its collegiate school under Dr Busby, he entered Christ Church, Oxford, in 1662. In 1689 he became dean there, succeeding a Roman Catholic dean who had fled abroad. He served as vice-chancellor of the university in 1692.

Aldrich is best known for a little book on logic, the Compendium Artis Logicae, used at Oxford in revised form well past 1850. The entry judges the book itself of little value, which makes its long classroom life the more striking. His gifts were unusually varied. He composed anthems and church services of high merit and adapted Palestrina and Carissimi to English words with skill. His catch Hark, the bonny Christ Church bells is still quoted. As an architect he designed All Saints church in Oxford and three sides of Christ Church's Peckwater Quadrangle.
britannica-1911-alice-maud-mary:
Queen Victoria's second daughter, Alice Maud Mary (1843–1878), became Grand-Duchess of Hesse-Darmstadt by marriage. Born at Buckingham Palace in April 1843, she was the third of the royal children. As a girl she was pretty and fine-featured, gay and full of mischief. She loved gymnastics, skated well, and rode with skill, and all who knew her liked her.

Lessons at home sent the royal children out to visit the poor, and Alice kept that habit for life. Once her elder sister married in 1858, Alice, now the oldest daughter still at home, took up fresh duties and drew nearer to her father. Her many letters home paint her daily life with her husband in full. By her own wish she came back to England each year. When she died, her husband, acting on her request, placed an English flag on her coffin.
britannica-1911-allegory:
Allegory, from Greek words for other and for speaking, is a figure that carries a meaning beyond the plain one, and this 1911 Britannica entry defines it. It is often treated as a figure of speech, but the vehicle need not be words. An allegory can speak to the eye through painting, carving, or acting. The root sense of the word is wider than its use in practice.

The entry sets allegory apart from its neighbours. It differs from metaphor by running longer and being worked out in fuller detail. It differs from analogy in that one speaks to the fancy and the other to reason. The fable or parable is a short allegory with one clear moral. Nearly every nation's writing uses the form with favour. The Hebrew scriptures hold many cases, among them the tale of Israel as a vine in the eightieth psalm.
britannica-1911-allon-henry:
Henry Allon is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Allon was an English Nonconformist minister, born near Hull in 1818. Methodist influence first turned him toward the ministry. Congregational ideas then shaped his training at Cheshunt College.

In 1844 he became co-pastor of Union Chapel in Islington. On his partner's death in 1852 he took sole charge and kept it until 1892. Under him the chapel became firmly Congregational and its influence kept growing. The entry names his chief service to Nonconformity: raising the standard of congregational worship. He gave special care to the service of praise, the singing life of the church. A psalmody class and a fine organist supported that work. Readers meet a pastor whose fame rested less on books than on how his people worshipped.
britannica-1911-almery:
Almery, also spelled aumery, aumbrie, or ambry, is an architectural term for a recess in the wall of a church. The word comes from a medieval form linked to the Latin armarium, a place for keeping tools. Such a recess is sometimes square-headed and sometimes arched over, and it closes with a door like a cupboard.

Priests used the almery to keep the vessels of the service: chalices, basins, and cruets are named. Many examples have stone shelves inside. They often stand near the piscina, the drain for washing vessels, though more often they sit on the opposite side of the chancel. In medieval usage the word also widened beyond churches, coming to mean any closed cupboard, and even a bookcase.
britannica-1911-almonry:
Giving alms needed a set place, and in churches that place was the almonry, the room or spot where gifts reached the poor. The term traces to Latin eleemosynarium, with kin in French and German. At Bishopstone church in Wiltshire it survives as a covered porch on the south transept, oddly cut off from the church interior.

Practice varied with the size of the house. Worcester Cathedral reportedly used stone tables inside its great porch, one on each side. Great monasteries such as Westminster built the almonry as its own building near the gatehouse, a choice meant to keep crowds of alms-seekers from disturbing the house.
britannica-1911-angary:
Two Hague articles of 1899 frame the law of angary. Article 53 lets railway plant, telegraphs, telephones, and ships of companies or private owners be used for war work. They must be handed back at the peace, with payments made. Article 54 sends railway plant from neutral states home as soon as may be. On that footing, the right of use may stretch as far as war's need can be made to cover.

Angary itself is a belligerent's right to take and use property for war, or to keep the enemy from using it. It reaches any property on belligerent ground, even goods owned by citizens of a neutral state. The word comes down through Latin and French forms from a Greek term for a courier's office.
britannica-1911-anglo-israelite-theory:
Scholars gave the Anglo-Israelite theory no quarter. Its premises were judged utterly unsound by students of both religion and mankind, and no case for it is argued at length. Philo-Israel is named as the book that states the claim in full. What survives here is a record of a popular nineteenth-century belief, and of how firmly the reference writing of the day turned it down.

The claim itself holds that the British people descend by race from the ten tribes of Israel. It sweeps in the United Kingdom, its colonies, and the United States. Its starting point is a real event: Sargon, king of Assyria, deported large numbers of those tribes after Samaria fell in 721 B.C. British descent is then built on that deportation.
britannica-1911-anthropometry:
Anthropometry is the name for a system that picks out a man by his frame. The 1911 Britannica entry credits the French scholar Alphonse Bertillon with the name. His plan rests on set measures of parts of the human body. Those measures, he found, stay near fixed through adult life in full. Logged in a set way, they mark each man apart from all others.

Police forces took up the scheme with great speed and zeal. It let them fix a man's true name and past with new trust. False claims of name could be caught, and old crimes traced home. France took the system in 1883 with strong early results there. The name Bertillonage spread with the method round the world fast.
britannica-1911-antiquary:
Antiquary is an article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. An antiquary is a person who gives himself to the study of ancient learning. His field covers old objects of art and science as well. The entry turns quickly to the societies that joined such students together.

The London Society of Antiquaries was formed in the eighteenth century for this study. A first society had been founded in 1572 by Bishop Parker, Cotton, Camden, and others. It worked to preserve the nation's antiquities until James the First shut it down in 1604. Its papers survived in the Cottonian library and were printed in 1720. Meetings began again in 1707, and the society was refounded in 1717. A royal charter followed in 1751. The article traces how a private hobby became a chartered national body.
britannica-1911-apothecary:
Apothecary is a word and trade article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a name that has changed its sense over time. The word comes from a Latin term for the keeper of a store. Galen used it for the room where his medicines were kept. An apothecary once made, sold, and prescribed drugs himself.

That work has since split apart. The making and selling of drugs now falls to trained chemists and druggists. The apothecary, by modern law, has become a general medical man. The article notes the Apothecaries' Society of London, a city corporation with the power to grant licences to practise medicine. Its members never held a sole right to sell drugs. Till 1868, in fact, any person at all could open a drug shop. The entry traces a trade as it turns into a profession.
britannica-1911-augustan-history:
Augustan History is the name of a set of lives of Roman emperors, from Hadrian to Carinus. The lives span the years from 117 to 284. The 1911 Britannica article says the work claims to come from the age of Diocletian and Constantine. Six authors are named as its writers. They are known as the Scriptores Historiae Augustae, the writers of the Augustan history.

Critics doubt much of that claim. The article says many parts were added later, in the age of Theodosius. The papers quoted in the lives are near all forgeries. A stricter school holds that the six author names are made up as well. The piece then sorts the lives by named author, from Hadrian down to Carinus. It grants the work great worth as a store of facts, but rates its style as poor.
britannica-1911-auxiliary:
Auxiliary means that which gives aid or support. The word comes from Latin auxilium, help. Grammar uses it of certain verbs specifically. An auxiliary verb completes another verb's tense. It also completes mood or voice. Engineering uses it of supplementary steam power. Such power supplemented sail-power in ships. Yachts, sealers, and whalers still use it occasionally. Military use covers allied or foreign troops.

More properly it covers troops not permanently maintained. Such troops are not kept under arms constantly. The British army used Auxiliary Forces as a category formerly. That category included the Militia. The Imperial Yeomanry belonged to it. The Volunteers belonged to it as well. The entry is a compact multi-field definition.
britannica-1911-avebury:
Avebury describes a Wiltshire village on the river Kennet, in the Devizes division, eight miles by road from Marlborough. Its church of St James holds an early font with Norman carving, a rich Norman doorway, and an old roodstone. Avebury House is Elizabethan, with a curious stone dovecot.

The village stands inside a huge stone circle ringed by ditch and earth rampart, once reached by two avenues of standing stones. At about 1,200 feet across, it is the largest such monument in Britain, built of unhewn local sarsen stones. Two smaller double circles stood within it. Writers debated its purpose: Druid temple, Arthurian grave site, or, as most antiquaries held, a Bronze Age burial place. Barrows, Silbury Hill, and a Roman road fill the nearby downs.
britannica-1911-aylesbury:
Aylesbury is a market town of Buckinghamshire, England, north-west of London, standing on a slight rise in the fertile Vale of Aylesbury below the Chiltern Hills. Its urban district held 9,243 people in 1901. Narrow, crooked streets give it a picturesque air, the entry says.

St Mary's church, a large cross-shaped building mainly Early English, keeps a transitional Norman font and a small pre-Norman crypt. County hall and town hall face the broad market place, and the grammar school dates from 1611. Work runs to farm trade, duck rearing, for which the vale is noted, straw-plaiting, and condensed milk. Nearby Hartwell house sheltered the exiled French king Louis XVIII from 1810 to 1814.
britannica-1911-baker-henry:
Baker, Henry (1698-1774), was an English naturalist born in London. A bookseller's apprenticeship came first for him. He then devised a teaching system. It served deaf and dumb pupils. The method made him a considerable fortune.

That work brought Baker to Defoe's notice. He married Defoe's youngest daughter Sophia in 1729. A year earlier they started a weekly journal together. It was the Universal Spectator. In 1740 two learned societies elected him. They were the Antiquaries and the Royal Society. His microscope work won the Copley medal in 1744. The prize marked observations on salt crystals. Baker helped found the Society of Arts in 1754. He served as its secretary for a time. His Microscope made Easy appeared in 1743. The Bakerian lecture still bears his name. His will left £100 to found it.
britannica-1911-balfour-sir-james-bart-a:
Sir James Balfour of Denmylne and Kinnaird (about 1600–1657) was a Scottish annalist and antiquary, a writer on old records and remains. He knew Sir William Segar and William Dugdale, and he gave material to Dugdale's Monasticon, a great work on monasteries.

Charles I knighted Balfour in 1630 and made him Lyon king-at-arms, the chief herald of Scotland, the same year. In 1633 he became a baronet of Kinnaird. Cromwell later removed him from his herald's office, and he died in 1657. The 1911 Britannica entry notes that many of his works rest in the Advocates' Library at Edinburgh, and that Haig printed his Annales of Scotland from them in four volumes.
britannica-1911-balnaves-henry:
Henry Balnaves (about 1512–1579) was a Scottish politician and reformer, born at Kirkcaldy. Schooled at St Andrews and on the continent, where he took Protestant views, he came home to study law and in 1538 became a lord of session. The estate of Halhill in Fife, granted in 1539, gave him his usual style.

Balnaves sat on James V's privy council and backed both the English alliance and church reform. Under the infant Queen Mary he served as secretary from January 1543. He pushed the act letting people read the Scriptures in their own tongue, and he helped treat for Mary's marriage to the future Edward VI. The 1911 Britannica entry follows his fall when the regent Arran changed sides.
britannica-1911-banbury:
Banbury is a market town and municipal borough in Oxfordshire, England, on the river Cherwell and the Oxford canal, 86 miles north-west of London by rail. Its population in 1901 was 12,968. The canal links northward to the Grand Junction and Warwick canals, and branch rail lines tie the town to larger systems.

The town serves a rich farming district and makes farm implements, rope, leather, and beer. Banbury cakes, pastry cases filled with currants, had held their fame for three centuries. The 1911 Britannica entry recalls losses too: a fine Gothic parish church burned in 1790, and the ancient Banbury Cross, famed in a nursery rhyme, was pulled down by Puritans in 1610. The townsfolk long had a name as zealous Puritans.
britannica-1911-baneberry:
Baneberry, or herb Christopher, is the common name for Actaea spicata, a plant of the buttercup family. It is a poisonous herb with long-stalked compound leaves, small white flowers, and black berries. In England it grows wild in copses, in limestone districts in the north of the country.

Beyond England, the plant ranges widely across the north temperate zone. The 1911 Britannica entry is very short: it gives the plant's Latin name and family, its look, its poison, and where it is found, and it stops there. Readers get a field identification in brief, covering leaf, flower, berry, and habitat, rather than any account of uses or lore.
britannica-1911-baptistery:
A baptistery is a hall or chapel set apart for baptism. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica ties it to the early Christian church. New converts were taught there before the rite. The true baptistery was most often round, though some had eight or twelve sides. An outer room heard the converts' confession of faith. An inner room held the font itself. Steps led down into that font, where converts were dipped three times.

A gold or silver dove hung over the water. Scenes from the life of John the Baptist lined the walls. Fonts were first of stone, later often of metal. Such halls belong to an age of mass adult baptism. Few traces predate the fourth century, when the faith won state backing. By the sixth century the font had moved into the church porch. Great late cases stand at Pisa and Florence.
britannica-1911-barker-edmund-henry:
Edmund Henry Barker (1788–1839) was an English classical scholar, born at Hollym in Yorkshire. He entered Trinity College, Cambridge, as a scholar in 1807 but left without a degree, kept by religious scruples from taking the oath then required. He had already won the Browne medal in 1809 for Greek and Latin epigrams.

Barker worked as amanuensis, a secretary who writes from dictation, to the famous Samuel Parr, then settled at Thetford in Norfolk for some twenty-five years, marking his books with the initials O.T.N., of Thetford, Norfolk. A lawsuit over a will ruined him, and he spent 1837–1838 as a debtor prisoner. The 1911 Britannica entry notes his school editions of classical authors and his early use of English, not Latin, in commentary notes.
britannica-1911-barnard-henry:
Henry Barnard (1811–1900) was an American educationalist, born at Hartford, Connecticut, on 24 January 1811. He graduated at Yale in 1830 and was admitted to the Connecticut bar in 1835. In the state legislature from 1837 he framed and passed the bill of 1838 for better supervision of the common schools, setting up a board of commissioners.

As that board's secretary Barnard worked without rest to rebuild Connecticut's common school system, winning a national name as a school reformer. Rhode Island then called him to examine its schools, and he served as its first commissioner of public schools from 1845 to 1849. The 1911 Britannica entry follows his return to Connecticut as superintendent and head of the State Normal School at New Britain.
britannica-1911-barratry:
Barratry is a legal term given a three-part treatment in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. In English criminal law it means habitually stirring up quarrels and lawsuits, an offence at common law and by statute, punished by fine and prison. A lawyer guilty of it could be barred from practice under a law of 1726, and at least three acts had to be proved.

Separate meanings fill the rest of the entry. In marine insurance, barratry is fraud by a ship's master against owner or insurers. Writers abroad used the word more widely for wilful acts by master or crew. In Scotland it meant a different crime again: a judge taking a bribe to give judgment. Readers also get a rare modern case from Guildford assizes in 1889 and a list of legal authorities.
britannica-1911-barrowe-henry:
Henry Barrowe (about 1550–1593), an English Puritan and Separatist born at Shipdam in Norfolk, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He studied at Clare Hall, Cambridge, followed the court for a time, and spent a few years at Gray's Inn without being called to the bar. A sermon heard around 1580 turned him toward the strictest Puritanism, and he soon joined John Greenwood and the London Separatists.

Prison took up Barrowe's last six years. Arrested while visiting Greenwood in 1586, he refused the ex officio oath, stayed in the Fleet, and defended separation in examinations and in treatises printed mostly in Holland. A True Description, A Plain Refutation, and A Brief Discovery of the False Church are named as his chief works. Tried for seditious books, Barrowe was twice respited at the gallows before being hanged on 6 April 1593.
britannica-1911-barry:
Barry, an urban district and seaport in Glamorganshire, Wales, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica as a new town on the Bristol Channel, eight miles south-west of Cardiff. Railways tied it to the Rhondda, Aberdare, and Merthyr coalfields and to Cardiff. Growth was startling: the whole district held only about 500 people in 1881, yet by 1901 its population had reached 27,030.

Place and past fill out the entry. Barry Island, now joined to the mainland, was linked with Baruch, a Welsh saint said to have had a cell there, and a medieval castle left only a gateway standing. The district took in Cadoxton, Merthyr-Dovan, and part of Sully. Churches, some thirty chapels, many with Welsh services, a free library, and a county school for 250 pupils show the town that coal and the sea had built.
britannica-1911-bates-harry:
Harry Bates (1850–1899), a British sculptor born at Stevenage, is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica biography. He began as a carver's helper and served a long apprenticeship in carved building work. In 1879 he came to London and entered the Lambeth School of Art, studying under Jules Dalou and Rodin. At the Royal Academy schools he won the gold medal in 1883 with a relief of Socrates teaching in the Agora, the market place of Athens.

Work in Paris and London built his name. His Aeneas, Homer, and Psyche panels showed growing form and dignity. In 1892 his Hounds in Leash won him election as an associate of the Royal Academy. His Pandora, in marble and ivory, was bought that year for the Chantrey Bequest and sits in the Tate Gallery. A huge horse statue of Lord Roberts for Calcutta and a Queen Victoria for Dundee are also named.
britannica-1911-battery:
Battery, from a French word tied to beating, is a term with a legal head and a long military and electrical body in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. In law, battery is the unlawful wounding of another person. From the gear of battering, the word passed to guns. A battery is a unit of mobile artillery, four to eight guns with their men and wagons. In sieges and forts it also names the built place such guns fire from.

Electric battery takes up the bulk of the article. Old electricians used the word for a set of Leyden jars, jars that store electric charge. By 1911 it meant a device that makes electricity by chemical action, or a set of such devices joined together. Primary batteries use up the stuff in their cells as current flows, and need fresh stuff to work again. Secondary batteries, or accumulators, can be charged back.
britannica-1911-beaufort-henry:
Henry Beaufort, who lived from about 1377 to 1447, was an English cardinal. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica follows his power beside three kings. He was a son of John of Gaunt by a mistress. A king act of 1397 made the children of that union lawful.

Church posts came fast, and Lincoln made him bishop in 1398. When his half brother took the throne he rose in state. He became chancellor in 1403, then bishop of Winchester in 1404. That rich see he took from William of Wykeham. He backed the prince of Wales in court struggles that followed. A push to make the old king abdicate backfired in 1411. Under Henry the Fifth he rose to chancellor again. At Constance his work helped end the church split.
britannica-1911-belfry:
Belfry comes from a Teutonic word built on bergen, to protect, and frida, safety or peace. The l in the modern word crept in by a wrong link with “bell.” In medieval siege-craft a belfry was a movable wooden tower of several stages, covered with raw hides, used to attack walls.

The word also meant a watch-tower, above all one fitted with an alarm bell. From there it passed to any detached tower or campanile holding bells, such as the one at Evesham. Most often today it names the ringing room or loft in a church tower where the bells hang.
britannica-1911-bell-henry:
Henry Bell (1767–1830) was a Scottish engineer born at Torphichen in Linlithgowshire. Apprenticed to a millwright uncle, he learned ship modelling at Bo’ness and worked under John Rennie in London. Back in Scotland from 1790, he settled at Helensburgh on the Clyde and chased his own mechanical schemes.

In January 1812 Bell put the Comet on the Clyde, a steamboat of about twenty-five tons driven by a three-horsepower engine at seven miles an hour. Robert Fulton is granted first place in steamboats, but Bell’s help reached him from Britain. Glasgow citizens raised a sum for Bell, and the Clyde trustees gave him a pension.
britannica-1911-bellary:
Bellary, or Ballari, is a city and district of British India in the Madras presidency, 305 miles by rail from Madras. The city counted 58,247 people in 1901. Its fort crowns a huge granite rock that juts 450 feet above the plain, ringed by two lines of works.

The upper fort, once thought beyond attack, holds only a small guard and prisoners now, while the lower fort holds barracks, church and stores. The district covers 5,714 square miles and held 947,214 people in 1901. Its past runs through Vijayanagar, Bijapur and Mysore hands before Britain took the “Ceded Districts” in 1800.
britannica-1911-bence-jones-henry:
Henry Bence-Jones (1814–1873) was an English physician and chemist born at Thorington Hall in Suffolk, son of a dragoon guards officer. Harrow and Trinity College, Cambridge, schooled him, then St George’s hospital for medicine and University College for chemistry. In 1841 he went to Giessen to work under Liebig.

Bence-Jones became a fellow of the Royal Society. He long served as secretary to the Royal Institution, and in 1846 St George’s hospital elected him its physician. He was counted an authority on diseases of the stomach and kidneys. He wrote several scientific books and many papers. He also produced The Life and Letters of Faraday in 1870, three years before his death in London.
britannica-1911-beneficiary:
Beneficiary, from the Latin beneficium, a benefit, is a legal word with two linked senses. In church law it means one who holds a benefice, a church living. In the law of property it means one who is entitled to property for his own benefit.

That second sense sets the beneficiary apart from an executor or trustee. Such men may hold property in their hands, but they hold it for others, not for themselves. The word is nearly the same as the older French term cestui que trust, and modern law is slowly letting beneficiary take its place. The entry is a brief definition, giving both uses and the contrast that defines the second.
britannica-1911-bessemer-sir-henry:
Sir Henry Bessemer (1813–1898) was an English engineer, born at Charlton in Hertfordshire. He invented all his life, but one process made his name world famous. That is the Bessemer process for making steel. The 1911 Britannica entry says it cheapened steel hugely when it appeared. Steel then replaced weaker materials in many uses. Bessemer came to the problem while trying to improve guns for artillery.

He set up a small ironworks in St Pancras, London. Two years of trials led to his key idea. Air blown through molten cast iron burns out the carbon. The entry also covers his later schemes, such as a ship saloon swung level by hydraulics. The Channel boat built on that plan in 1875 failed in practice. His Autobiography appeared in 1905.
britannica-1911-biddery: Biddery, also spelled Bidri, is an Indian alloy used for articles and ornaments inlaid with gold and silver. The whole 1911 Britannica entry is a single sentence. It states that the name is an Indian word taken from Bedar, or Bidar, a town in the Nizam's Dominions, and it gives the alloy's makeup exactly: copper, lead, tin, and zinc. Nothing is said about how the inlay work is done, where the wares are sold, or how the craft began.
britannica-1911-bilberry:
Bilberry, also called blaeberry or whortleberry, is a low shrub of the heath family. Its botanical name is Vaccinium myrtillus, in the order Ericaceae. It grows in woods, copses, and heaths, chiefly in hilly districts. Stiff stems run from half a foot to two feet long. Small oval leaves with toothed edges grow on those stems. Its flowers are small, round, and rosy, tinged with green.

The berries are dark blue with a waxy bloom, about a third of an inch across. People use them for tarts and preserves, the 1911 Britannica entry notes. The plant ranges across the north temperate zone and into the arctic. A close cousin, the cowberry, is named for contrast. Cowberry keeps evergreen leaves and bears a red, acid berry instead. It shares the same sorts of ground, except in south-east England.
britannica-1911-blunt-john-henry:
Blunt, John Henry is a life story from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about an English churchman and writer. He was born at Chelsea in 1823 and died in 1884. Before he went to the university of Durham in 1850, he worked for some years as a manufacturing chemist. He was ordained in 1852 and took his master's degree in 1855.

That same year he printed a work on the Atonement. He held a string of church posts, among them the living of Kennington near Oxford. In 1873 he moved to Beverston in Gloucestershire. His fame rests on steady, useful books. They include an annotated Prayer Book, a history of the English Reformation, and a book of church law. His dictionary of theology and his dictionary of sects and heresies followed. A doctor's degree in 1882 marked the worth of that labour.
britannica-1911-bone-henry:
Henry Bone (1755–1834) was an English painter in enamel who worked at sizes no one in England had tried before. Born at Truro, he was long employed by London jewellers on small enamel designs before the public knew his worth. The Royal Academy took notice in 1800 and made him an associate, then an academician in 1811.

Up to 1831 he made many enamel pieces far larger than the usual miniature scale. His eighty-five portraits of Elizabethan figures, running from 5 by 4 inches to 13 by 8, are the most admired, and they were sold off after his death. His Bacchus and Ariadne, copied from Titian on a plate, fetched the huge price of 2200 guineas, the entry records.
britannica-1911-bottomry:
Bottomry is a sea contract in which a ship, her bottom, is pledged to secure money borrowed for the costs of her voyage. The bargain turns on the ship's fate. If she reaches her port, ship and borrower owe the loan back with an agreed premium. If she is lost, the lender loses all claim, for sum and premium alike.

Freight can be pledged with the ship, and in need the cargo too, with the master's own bond sometimes added. Borrowing on cargo alone is called respondentia, and a master may rarely pledge cargo except under a general bottomry covering ship and freight. Because the lender takes the sea risk, the premium, called maritime interest, runs high. The long entry then sets out the contract's form, the master's powers, and the case law.
britannica-1911-boughton-george-henry:
George Henry Boughton (1834–1905) was an Anglo-American painter whose gentle subject pictures won crowds in America. Born in England, he was taken to the United States in 1839 and raised at Albany, New York. He studied art in Paris in 1861–62 and afterwards lived mainly in London. Frederick Walker's influence marked his work.

Delicacy and grace soon made his reputation. London made him an associate of the Royal Academy in 1879 and a full academician in 1896, and New York's National Academy of Design had elected him in 1871. His pictures of Dutch life and scenery are called especially characteristic. Two subject pictures are singled out as very popular in America, the Return of the Mayflower and The Scarlet Letter.
britannica-1911-brederode-henry:
Henry, Count of Brederode (1531–1568), came from an old Dutch family long active in war and public life, and he was born at Brussels in 1531. He converted to the Reformed faith and stood with the Prince of Orange and Count Egmont against the Spanish Inquisition and Spanish rule in the Netherlands.

In 1566 he helped found the confederacy of nobles bound by the pledge called the Compromise. That April he led 250 confederates to the palace and spoke for them as they handed the regent, Margaret of Parma, their petition of grievances, the Request. Days later, at a banquet he chaired, the mocking name les Gueux, the Beggars, was first fixed on the rebels. Banished by Alva, he died in exile at thirty-six.
britannica-1911-bribery:
Bribery is the public wrong of giving or offering pay, in any shape, so that pay rather than duty moves a person in office. The word came through French and Latin roots tied first to bread given to beggars, then to alms, blackmail and extortion. When hope of gain replaces a clean sense of duty, the office holder is said to be corrupted.

Two broad classes divide the offence: bending a person who holds power to use it badly, and buying the votes that hand power out. Bribery among judges is treated as a stubborn vice of weak states, hard for law alone to cure, since both sides in the deal get what they want and neither complains. Slow cleansing of the bench in most European lands forms the thread the long entry then follows.
britannica-1911-briggs-henry:
Henry Briggs (1556–1630) was an English mathematician born at Warley Wood near Halifax in Yorkshire. He graduated at St John's College, Cambridge, in 1581, took a fellowship in 1588, read the physical lecture founded by Dr Thomas Linacre from 1592. In 1596 became the first professor of geometry at Gresham House in London.

At Gresham he proposed reshaping John Napier's logarithms so that the logarithm of the ratio of ten to one would be one, the base-ten system still in use. He wrote to Napier, then visited him at Edinburgh in 1616 and again in 1617 to settle the change. On his return printed the first thousand of his new logarithms. In 1619 he became Savilian professor of geometry at Oxford, giving up Gresham in July 1620, and in 1624 his Arithmetica Logarithmica carried the work forward.
britannica-1911-briton-ferry:
Briton Ferry is a seaport in Glamorganshire, Wales, on the eastern bank of the Neath river estuary in Swansea Bay, 174 miles by rail from London. Its urban district held 6973 people in 1901. A tram line links it to Neath, 2 miles away, and the Vale of Neath Canal, made in 1797, ends at its wharves.

Scenery once famed has been much marred by factories. Growth took off after 1861, when a dock of 13 acres was built. The South Wales mineral railway then opened the coal districts of Glyncorrwg and Maesteg. Their coal fed the dock as its chief export. Steel and tinplate are made on a large scale, with iron works and a foundry beside them. Norman settlers of the 12th century named the ferry La Brittone; Welsh speakers have called the town Llansawel since at least the 16th century.
britannica-1911-brooke-henry:
Henry Brooke was an Irish author who lived from about seventeen o three to seventeen eighty three. His life entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Rantavan in county Cavan, the son of a rector, he studied law. He was entered at Trinity College, Dublin, in seventeen twenty.

Brooke wed his cousin and ward Catherine Meares before she turned fourteen. His poem Universal Beauty came out in seventeen thirty five in London. He joined the prince of Wales party and lived near Pope at Twickenham. His play Gustavus Vasa was banned at the last hour in seventeen thirty nine. The ban was blamed on a likeness to Walpole in one part.
britannica-1911-brunner-henry:
Henry Brunner (born 1840) was a German historian born at Wels in Upper Austria on 22 June 1840. After study at the universities of Vienna, Gottingen and Berlin he became professor at Lemberg in 1866, then in quick succession held posts at Prague, Strassburg and Berlin. Law and institutions, not narrative politics, made his reputation among scholars of the early middle ages.

From 1872 he devoted himself above all to the early laws and institutions of the Franks and kindred peoples of western Europe. On those subjects his researches are judged of supreme value; he also became a leading authority on modern German law. Member of the Berlin Academy of Sciences from 1884, he took over supervision of the Leges section of the Monumenta Germaniae historica in 1886 after Waitz's death. Chief works named include a study of the origin of jury courts, works on witness and inquisition proof in Carolingian times.
britannica-1911-brunton-mary:
Mary Brunton (1778–1818) was a Scottish novelist born on 1 November 1778 in the island of Varra in Orkney. She was the daughter of Captain Thomas Balfour of Elwick. At twenty she married Alexander Brunton, minister of Bolton in Haddingtonshire and afterwards professor of oriental languages at Edinburgh, a marriage that set her adult life in clerical and scholarly circles.

Fiction made her name: she wrote two novels popular in their day, Self-control in 1810 and Discipline in 1814, the latter reissued in an 1832 edition with a memoir of its author. A third work, Emmeline, came out as a posthumous fragment in 1819, the year after her death on 19 December 1818. The short entry gives birth, marriage, the two finished novels with their dates and the unfinished third, the complete shape of a brief writing life.
britannica-1911-buller-sir-redvers-henry:
Buller, Sir Redvers Henry is a life story from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a British general. Redvers Henry Buller was born in 1839 and died in 1908, a son of a member of parliament from Crediton in Devon. He was schooled at Eton and joined the army in 1858.
