He served with the King's Royal Rifles in the China campaign of 1860. On the Red River expedition of 1870 he first worked with Colonel Wolseley. He went with Wolseley to the Ashantee campaign as head of the intelligence branch and was slightly hurt at Ordabai. The wars in South Africa in 1878 and 1879 then made his name. The article calls him a brave and dogged leader, much liked by his men. It singles out his conduct of the retreat at Inhlobane in March 1879.
britannica-1911-burghersh-henry:
Burghersh, Henry is a life story from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about an English bishop and royal officer. Henry Burghersh lived from 1292 to 1340. He was a younger son of Robert, Baron Burghersh, and a nephew of Bartholomew, Lord Badlesmere. He was schooled in France. Through his uncle's sway, Pope John the Twenty-second named him bishop of Lincoln in 1320.

The chapter there had in fact already picked its own man, yet Burghersh took the post at once. When Badlesmere was put to death in 1322, the king seized the bishop's lands. Near 1326 his lands were given back. That did not stop him from joining Queen Isabella in the move that brought down King Edward the Second. Under Edward the Third he rose to chancellor of England in 1328. He lost that post and was jailed when Isabella fell in 1330.
britannica-1911-burglary:
Burglary is a crime in English law, set out here in a 1911 Britannica entry on law. At common law it meant to break and enter the home of another man by night. The aim had to be to commit a grave crime once inside. In England the Larceny Act of 1861 set the rules for the charge and its cost.

Four points shape the charge: time, place, manner, and intent. Time came to count most, though at first it counted least. The old test asked if it was true night or still light. A man could not be charged if light still let a face be seen. The Act of 1861 then fixed a new plain test for courts.
britannica-1911-bury:
Bury is a market town in Lancashire in England, on a stream north west of London. Its count of folk in nineteen one was past fifty-eight thousand. A church of old root, a town hall, and halls for art and books mark the town. A free school from an old gift still serves its youth.

Cotton work leads its trades, with print, dye, and bleach works, gear and iron shops, and wool mills. Coal pits and stone pits lie near by. A famed statesman was born near the town, and his fathers print works fed its growth. A stone to that man stands in the market place.
britannica-1911-buss-frances-mary:
Frances Mary Buss (1827-1894), an English schoolmistress, is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in London, she was the daughter of a painter who helped draw the first pictures for Pickwick. She learned at a school in Camden Town and stayed on there as a teacher. Soon she joined her mother in keeping a school in Kentish Town.

The article traces how her school moved in 1850 and took the name North London Collegiate School for Ladies. It grew fast in numbers and in good name. In 1864 she gave proof before a royal inquiry into schools, and its report praised her school in strong terms. Trade guilds then gave funds to rehouse her school and to found a second school for girls, with her still at the head.
britannica-1911-calderwood-henry:
Henry Calderwood (1830–1897) was a Scottish philosopher and divine. This 1911 Britannica entry gives his life and thought. He was born at Peebles on 10 May 1830. He studied at the Royal High school and at Edinburgh university. In 1856 he was ordained pastor of Greyfriars church, Glasgow. He also taught moral philosophy at Glasgow. In 1868 he became professor of moral philosophy at Edinburgh.

His first and most famous book was The Philosophy of the Infinite. It appeared in 1854, against Sir William Hamilton. Hamilton had said we can know nothing of the Infinite. Calderwood held that such knowledge is real, though imperfect. Faith, he argued, implies knowledge. His moral philosophy opposed Hegelian doctrine directly. It sought to uphold a divine sanction for right and wrong. He also worked hard for schools in Edinburgh. As first chairman of its school board, he put the Education Act to work.
britannica-1911-calgary:
Calgary is a city in the province of Alberta, Canada. The entry calls it the oldest city in the province. Its population was 4091 in 1901. By 1907 it had jumped to 21,112. This 1911 Britannica entry describes its site and growth. Calgary stands on the Bow river. That river flows from a pass in the Rocky Mountains. The Canadian Pacific railway crosses the range by that pass.

The city's streets are wide and laid out in rectangles. Its buildings are largely of local stone. The stone is a brown sandstone from the Bow valley. Calgary is a key point on the Canadian Pacific line. It is also a wholesale and industrial centre. The entry looks back to earlier posts near the site. The French founded Fort La Jonquière there in 1752. The present city dates from the railway's coming, about 1883.
britannica-1911-canterbury:
Canterbury is a city in Kent, England, and seat of an archdiocese. Its city entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It lies on the river Stour, sixty two miles east south east of London. The city wraps round the grounds of its great cathedral church.

Augustine and his fellow missionaries came to Canterbury in five ninety seven. Aethelberht, king of Kent, gave them a church in his capital city. That gift made Canterbury the head seat of the Church of England. Augustine, a Benedictine, set up a monastery joined to the cathedral. Archbishop Lanfranc put that house on firm ground after the Conquest.
britannica-1911-capitulary:
A capitulary was a law issued by the Frankish kings. The name covers acts of the Merovingian and Carolingian rulers. This 1911 Britannica article studies these texts. They were called capitularies because they split into chapters. The Latin word for a chapter is capitulum. Two questions guide the article. First, how have the texts come down to us? Second, what was their true character and scope?

No capitulary survives in its original form today. Copies went out to archbishops, bishops and counts. The chancellor kept one copy in the palace archives. Later copies survive inside mixed manuscripts of mixed matter. Some of those books date from the 9th or 10th centuries. The rulings cover a great range of subjects. Early on, men began to sort them by topic. In 827 Ansegisus, abbot of St Wandrille, made such a collection. His four books split church rulings from secular ones.
britannica-1911-carey-henry:
Henry Carey (d. 1743) was an English poet and musician. He was reputed to be an illegitimate son of the marquess of Halifax. This 1911 Britannica entry gives his career on the stage. He was born toward the end of the 17th century. His mother is supposed to have been a schoolmistress. Carey himself taught music at various schools. Roseingrave and Geminiani were among his later teachers.

He wrote words and music for The Contrivances, a farce of 1715. His Hanging and Marriage played at Lincoln's Inn Fields in 1722. Chrononhotonthologos, in 1734, burlesqued the bombast of the stage. It called itself the most tragical tragedy ever tragedized. The Dragon of Wantley, a burlesque opera, followed in 1737. His Namby-Pamby parodied Ambrose Philips' verses to an infant. Carey is best remembered by his songs, though. “Sally in our Alley” is the famous example named.
britannica-1911-carpenter-mary:
Mary Carpenter (1807–1877) is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on an English educational and social reformer born at Exeter. Her father, Dr Lant Carpenter, was the Unitarian minister there, and the family moved to Bristol in 1817. She was educated in her father's school for boys, learning Latin, Greek, and mathematics, subjects then rarely taught to girls. She taught in the Sunday school early and later helped her father with his pupils.

Two visits shaped her life's work. The raja Rammohun Roy's visit to Bristol in 1833 stirred her lasting interest in India, and Dr Joseph Tuckerman of Boston turned her thoughts to destitute children. In 1835 she helped organise a Working and Visiting Society and served as its secretary for twenty years. The entry then follows her turn toward ragged schools and the schooling of poor children, work that private effort had to carry after a national education bill failed in 1843.
britannica-1911-carpentry:
Carpentry is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on the art of the carpenter, a workman in wood who builds the frame of a structure. The word comes from the Latin carpentum, a carriage. The entry first covers the sawyer, whose pit-saw once split logs into planks, and notes that saw-mills with powered circular saws had taken over that work in modern practice.

Carpenters' work is divided into three branches. The descriptive branch sets out forms by geometry, the constructive branch shapes and joins the timbers, and the mechanical branch deals with strength and strain. The entry then sticks to practical building detail. It draws a clear line between the carpenter, whose work gives a building its stability, and the joiner, whose work finishes it. Readers get both the trade's theory and its bench practice as the period knew them.
britannica-1911-castelnaudary:
Castelnaudary is a town of south-western France in the department of Aude, 22 miles from Carcassonne on the railway toward Toulouse. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives it 6,650 people in 1906 and a fine seat on a rise amid a rich plain. The Canal du Midi widens beside it into a basin ringed with wharves and stores.

Flour mills, tile and blanket works, and canal boat building support the town, which trades in grain, wine, wool, and cattle. The site is thought to be the old town of Sostomagus, taken by the Visigoths in the 400s. In the Albigensian wars it saw hard fighting between the men of Montfort and Toulouse. The Black Prince burned it in 1355, and in 1632 the rebel duke of Montmorency was beaten and taken in a cavalry fight there.
britannica-1911-casuistry:
The 1911 Britannica article on casuistry defines its subject plainly. Casuistry is the art of bringing general moral principles to bear on single actions. In short, it is applied morality. Anyone who weighs his duties against a moral standard is a casuist. The method takes different shapes in different ages.

The article traces the history of the art across cultures. It begins with the strict legal casuistry of early man. That casuistry was bound up with taboo and sacred law. It moves to casuistry built on sacred books. The rabbis drew many rules from the Jewish law. The article then turns to conscience and common sense. These serve later ages as guides of another kind.
britannica-1911-catenary:
Catenary, the curve of a chain hung free, is set out in a math entry in the 1911 Britannica. The word comes from a Latin word for a chain. A chain of like weight hung from two posts takes this curve by its own weight. Galileo took the curve for a parabola at first in his work. Jungius showed that call to be wrong in time.

The true form was set out in sixteen ninety one by James Bernoulli. Kin curves for chains of mixed weight drew much ink as well. Great names of math took part in that long probe of the curve. Word on its pull and push traits is sent to the Mechanics entry. A spun form of the curve makes the least face for its span, the text notes.
britannica-1911-cauvery:
Cauvery is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a river of southern India, also spelled Kaveri. It rises in Coorg, high in the Western Ghats, and flows south east across the plateau of Mysore. It reaches the Bay of Bengal through two main mouths in Tanjore district. Its total length is 472 miles, and its basin covers an estimated 27,700 square miles.

In Coorg the course twists sharply, with a rocky bed and high, thickly grown banks. In Mysore the river widens to 300 or 400 yards but stays too rocky for navigation. Twelve dams, or anicuts, interrupt it for irrigation, and the ancient system watered 669,000 acres against a modern million. The falls of the Cauvery drive an electric plant that powers the Kolar gold mines and lights Mysore. Devout Hindus know the river as Dakshini Ganga, the Ganges of the south, and hold its whole course holy.
britannica-1911-cavalry:
Cavalry is a long 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on mounted troops, from the French cavalerie, rooted in the late Latin caballus, horse. The word came into military writing about the middle of the sixteenth century. It then covered mounted men of all kinds used in war. Usage has since narrowed it. It now means horsemen trained to achieve their commander's purpose by the combined action of man and horse.

A full history follows the definition. The entry argues that cavalry never grew in the same way everywhere at once. Local conditions shaped it. The first condition is the horse itself, its numbers and fitness for its land. The early horses of Europe and Asia were very small. So their first war use was as draught animals for chariots. Chariot building itself implies level ground and real mechanical skill. The entry builds its long survey on that starting point.
britannica-1911-cavendish-henry:
Henry Cavendish (1731–1810) is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on an English chemist and physicist born at Nice. He was the elder son of Lord Charles Cavendish. He went to school at Hackney in 1742 and entered Peterhouse, Cambridge, in 1749. He left in 1753 without a degree. Until he was about forty he lived on a modest allowance. Later a fortune made him one of the richest men of his time.

The entry dwells on his extreme shyness. He lived mainly at Clapham Common and kept his library in Dean Street, Soho. There he lent books on set days to properly vouched readers. So methodical was he that he entered his own borrowings in the loan book. He attended the Royal Society, a fellow from 1760, and its Thursday club dinners. Otherwise he shunned society. He died at Clapham in February 1810.
britannica-1911-celery:
Celery is a two year plant grown for its mild stalks as salad food. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives its Latin name as Apium graveolens. Wild celery grows by ditches and in marsh ground near the sea in England. In the wild it tastes coarse and rank, with a strong smell.

Farming and blanching turn that harsh plant into a sweet salad crop. Seedlings are moved to deep trenches and earthed up to block light. White kinds are rated best in flavor and crisp bite, it says. Stalks serve stewed and in soups, and seeds flavor dishes as well. A root form called celeriac is grown in north Europe.
britannica-1911-cemetery:
Cemetery is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on burial grounds. The word comes from a Greek term for a sleeping place. The early Christians used it for the places set apart for their dead. These grounds usually stood outside the city walls. They had no link with churches. Burial in churches or churchyards was unknown in the first centuries.

From 1840 to 1855 the press and parliament turned to the state of London's churchyards. Chadwick's report of 1843 led the way. Vaults under church floors were crammed with coffins. The air in many churches was tainted and a direct source of disease. In the churchyards, coffins lay tier above tier, close to the surface. Sextons secretly removed bones to make room for fresh burials. The entry presents the modern cemetery as the reform answer to that scandal.
britannica-1911-centaury:
Centaury is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a plant, Erythraea Centaurium, of the natural order Gentianaceae. It is an annual herb. Its stem is erect and smooth, and it usually branches above. At the top it carries an inflorescence of many small flowers. The flowers are regular, red or pink, with a funnel shaped corolla. The plant grows in dry pastures and on sandy coasts in Britain.

The entry notes how much the plant varies. Specimens differ in the length of the stem. They differ in the degree of branching. They differ in the width and shape of the leaves. They differ too in how loose or close the flower head stands. Several other species of the genus are grown as rock plants. That horticultural note closes the short account. The entry gives the plant's family, form, habitat, and range of variation in a single compact paragraph of fact.
britannica-1911-centenary:
Centenary is a short 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry defining a word for a span of a hundred years. It comes from the Latin centenarius, of or belonging to a hundred. That in turn comes from centeni, the distributive form of centum, hundred. A centenary is a space of a hundred years. In particular, it is the celebration of an event on the lapse of a hundred years, a centennial anniversary.

The entry also settles the near twin word “centennial.” It comes from the Latin centennis, from centum and annus, a year. The word is usually an adjective. The entry gives the case of “the Centennial State.” That name went to Colorado on its admission to statehood in 1876. But centennial is also used as a noun, as a direct synonym of centenary. The whole entry is a brief lesson in two Latin roots and their English use.
britannica-1911-chambery:
Chambery is a city of France and capital of the department of Savoie. The 1911 Britannica entry sets it in a rich district between two hills. The rivers Leysse and Albane flow through the town there. It lies 79 miles by rail south west of Geneva in Switzerland. Its count in 1906 was 16,852 in town and 23,027 in the commune.

The town is built in an irregular plan with two good streets. One is the Place Saint-Leger, the other the Rue de Boigne. That street bears the name of General Benoit Boigne of India fame. Boigne left the town a vast fortune made in India in service. The cathedral there dates from the 1300s and the 1400s in part.
britannica-1911-channing-william-ellery:
William Ellery Channing (1780–1842) was an American churchman and giver to good causes. He was born in Newport, Rhode Island, on 7 April 1780. His grandfather was William Ellery, a signer of the Declaration of Independence. His father was a noted Newport lawyer, and his mother was a woman of strong moral sense. As a child, Channing had fine features and a gentle nature.

The article traces his mix of traits to both parents: plain tastes and warm feeling from his father, and clear moral sight from his mother. He loved the beauty of Newport from his first years and prized its effect on his spirit. His father was a strict Calvinist, and Dr Samuel Hopkins, a head of that school, was a guest in the house. Channing said that even as a child he would argue points of logic with his elders.
britannica-1911-charles-i-king-of-hungar:
Charles the First, king of Hungary, who lived from 1288 to 1342, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the son of Charles Martel of Naples and was known as Charles Robert before his crowning. He claimed the Hungarian crown through his grandfather Stephen the Fifth. He sailed from Naples in 1300 to press that claim.

His path to the throne was long and contested. A rival from Bohemia held the crown, then passed his rights to a duke of Bavaria. Charles was enthroned at Buda in 1309, but the rite counted only after a crowning with the sacred crown in 1310. Three years of revolt followed. A great win at Rozgony in 1312 made him true master of his land. His pact with Poland against Habsburg and Czech foes is praised as his best foreign work.
britannica-1911-chateau-thierry:
Château-Thierry is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a town of northern France, capital of an arrondissement in the department of Aisne. It stands 59 miles east north east of Paris, on rising ground on the right bank of the Marne. Its population in 1906 was 6872. A marble statue on the quay honours La Fontaine, who was born in the town in 1621. His house is still preserved in the street that bears his name.

Above the town stand the ruins of a castle. Tradition says Charles Martel built it for the Frankish king Thierry IV, and it gave the town its name. The chief relic is a gateway with massive round towers, the Porte Saint Pierre. The town's own industry is the making of mathematical and musical instruments. It trades in the local white wine, sheep, and cattle. Its hard history includes capture by the English in 1421.
britannica-1911-cherry:
Cherry, as a cultivated fruit tree, is generally supposed to be of Asiatic origin, brought to Italy by Lucullus after his defeat of Mithradates in 68 B.C., according to Pliny. Cultivated kinds are traced to two species, Prunus Cerasus and Prunus Avium. The first gives morello, duke and Kentish cherries, and the second gives geans, hearts and bigarreaus. Both grow wild through Europe and western Asia to the Himalayas.

Fruit, drink and wood fill much of the entry, from dessert fruit and pies to cherry brandy and liqueurs such as kirschwasser, ratafia and maraschino. Cabinet makers value the wood, and the American wild cherry takes a bright polish for fine work. Long closing sections cover budding on stocks, soil, spacing, pruning and wall training. Forcing needs only mild heat, since the cherry will not bear a close, hot air.
britannica-1911-chicheley-henry:
Chicheley, Henry (1364–1443) was an English archbishop and founder of All Souls College, Oxford, born at Higham Ferrers in Northamptonshire. He was the youngest son of Thomas Chicheley, a mayor of that town, and his mother Agnes Pincheon was said to be of gentle birth. The entry firmly rejects a tale that William of Wykeham found him as a poor ploughboy. Records place him at New College, Oxford, from Winchester College.

At Oxford he took his degree, was ordained sub-deacon, and held a living in Wales while still young. He left for London to practise as an advocate in the court of arches, the main church court. Preferments followed fast, among them archdeacon posts in Dorset and Salisbury and many prebends. In July 1405 he began a diplomatic career with a mission to Pope Innocent VII in Rome.
britannica-1911-chivalry:
Chivalry names the knightly class of feudal times and the code of rules, moral and social, that bound it. The 1911 Britannica entry traces the word from old French and late Latin roots tied to horse troops. Its first sense was knights as a body: men fully armed and mounted for war.

The entry then follows the word as its sense grew. It came to mean brave deeds in battle and a high sense of honor in all things. To do chivalry was to act the knight. At last it took its broad modern sense of plain courtesy. The piece also notes its use in English law for land held by knight service, and the old Court of Chivalry, which judged arms and rank.
britannica-1911-church-history:
Church History, in the portion hosted here, traces the Christian Church through its later medieval crisis into the modern age. Renaissance popes such as Nicholas V, from 1447 to 1455, turned the papacy toward an Italian princedom, the account argues. Savonarola was executed at Florence on 23 May 1498, a loyal son of the medieval Church killed before the Palazzo Vecchio. Twenty years later Luther published his theses against indulgences, and the Reformation began.

That struggle drove the papacy back to its church duties, and the council of Trent fixed medieval dogma as modern Catholic doctrine against Protestantism. The canons of Trent, issued in 1564, open the modern church section as a clear epoch in the story. Long lists of authorities close the medieval part, naming Schaff, Moeller and Milman among general writers. National church histories for England, Scotland, Ireland, Germany, France and Spain are also listed.
britannica-1911-clerestory:
Clerestory, or clearstory, in architecture, is the upper storey of the nave of a church, whose walls rise above the aisles and are pierced with windows. The word clere is simply clear, in the sense of lighted, and names in several tongues are given. Sometimes those windows are very small, mere quatrefoils or spherical triangles in the wall. In large buildings they are important objects, for beauty and for lighting the nave.

Norman clerestory windows, even in large churches, matter less than those of later styles in the sequence traced. Early English windows grew larger, and Decorated ones lengthened as the triforium shrank. Perpendicular work often loses the triforium altogether in this account. Churches at Taunton and across Norfolk and Suffolk show close ranges of windows instead. Egyptian temples and Roman baths lit great halls the same way.
britannica-1911-clinton-sir-henry:
Henry Clinton, born about 1738 and dead in 1795, was a British general and son of an admiral. The 1911 Britannica entry follows him from New York militia service to the Coldstream Guards. By 1760 he served as aide to Ferdinand of Brunswick in the Seven Years War. High praise there brought him colonel rank in 1762 at a young age.

Family sway won him a seat in parliament from 1772 to 1784 in two boroughs. Most of that span he spent on active service in America at war. He fought at Bunker Hill and Long Island in the war for independence. The entry opens the career of the man who later led British forces there.
britannica-1911-close-maxwell-henry:
Close, Maxwell Henry (1822–1903) was an Irish geologist, born in Dublin in 1822 and educated at Weymouth and at Trinity College, Dublin, graduating in 1846. Two years later he entered holy orders and served as curate and rector in Northampton, Leicestershire and Waltham-on-the-Wolds. In 1861, on his father's death, he returned to Dublin. While serving various city churches he devoted himself almost wholly to literary and scientific pursuits.

Glacial geology of Ireland made his name, and he became an acknowledged authority on that subject in the entry's judgment. His 1866 paper on the General Glaciation of Ireland is called a masterly description of glaciation's effects and of the evidence for land ice. Later he argued that shell-bearing gravels near Dublin were laid down by floating ice in a time of submergence. He presided over the Royal Geological Society of Ireland in 1878 and died on 12 September 1903.
britannica-1911-cloudberry:
Cloudberry, Rubus Chamaemorus, is a low growing creeping herbaceous plant, with an unprickly stem and simple, obtusely lobed leaves. Its solitary white flowers resemble those of the blackberry but are larger, at one inch across the bloom. Stamens and pistils sit on different plants in this species, a separation the entry notes. The orange-yellow fruit is about half an inch long, a compact berry in form.

That fruit consists of a few large drupes, the small stony parts that make up such berries, and it has a pleasant flavour. The plant occurs in the mountainous parts of Great Britain, in the entry's home record. It is widely distributed through the more northerly portions of both hemispheres beyond Britain. In northern Denmark and Sweden the fruit is gathered in large quantities and sold in the markets, a trade use that closes the notice.
britannica-1911-cockton-henry: Henry Cockton, an English humorous novelist who lived from 1807 to 1853, is covered in a brief life entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in London on the seventh of December 1807, he issued a number of volumes in his lifetime. He is best known for two of them. The first is Valentine Vox, the Ventriloquist, from 1840. The second is Sylvester Sound, the Somnambulist, from 1844. Cockton died at Bury Saint Edmunds on the twenty sixth of June 1853.
britannica-1911-cole-sir-henry:
Sir Henry Cole (1808–1882) was an English civil servant, and a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry follows his rise. He was born at Bath on the fifteenth of July 1808, the son of an army officer. At fifteen he became a clerk in the record office, under Sir Francis Palgrave. With help from Charles Buller, he worked his way up to assistant keeper.

Cole helped build public support for Sir Rowland Hill and his post office reforms. A link with the Society of Arts drew him out of the record office in time. He was a lead member of the team that ran the Great Exhibition of 1851. After it closed, he became secretary to the School of Design. That office grew into the Department of Science and Art in 1853. Under it the South Kensington Museum was founded in 1855.
britannica-1911-commandery: A commandery was a part of the landed wealth in Europe of the Knights Hospitallers, the order of St John of Jerusalem. The word comes through French from a medieval Latin term for a trust or charge. The order's lands were split into priorates. Priorates split into bailiwicks, and bailiwicks split in turn into commanderies. Each commandery was placed in the charge of a commendator, or commander. The word also names the pay and perks granted to a commander of a military order of knights.
britannica-1911-commentry: Commentry is a town of central France in the department of Allier, in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It lies forty two miles south west of Moulins by the Orléans railway. The town held 7581 people in 1906 at the count. Commentry gives its name to a coalfield of more than 5000 acres in extent round the town. Large foundries and forges at work there form the chief marks of the place and its trade.
britannica-1911-confectionery:
Confectionery is a broad term for food made with sugar as its base or chief part. Sweetmeats and pastry fall under it at once. Fruit kept by means of sugar counts as well. Jams, jellies, fruit syrups and pastes all sit in its range. Ices and sweet drinks join the list too. The word comes from a Latin term for a compound.

In old days the making of sweetmeats was a druggist's work. In the first half of the 1800s it grew into a trade of its own in England. The International Exhibition of 1851 spread it to other lands. France and Germany now lead in fine goods and bon-bons. The candy trade in America has grown to a huge scale. Lozenges form the plainest kind of sugar sweet. Ground sugar, mixed and shaped, makes them up. The entry goes on to shop methods in detail.
britannica-1911-constable-henry:
Henry Constable, an English poet who lived from 1562 to 1613, is profiled in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. His father was a knight who wrote a work on the ordering of a camp. The poet went to Cambridge and took his degree in 1580. He was, or then became, a Roman Catholic.

Next he is heard of in Paris, writing letters to Walsingham in 1584 and 1585. Those letters prove he was in the secret service of the English government, the entry says. A later set of letters to Essex protests his loyalty. In the autumn of 1592 a London publisher issued his Diana, a set of sweet sonnets in praise of his mistress. A larger reissue in 1594 mixed in poems that were certainly by Philip Sidney.
britannica-1911-cooke-rose-terry:
Rose Terry Cooke (1827–1892) was an American writer born at West Hartford, Connecticut, on 17 February 1827. She issued a volume of Poems in 1860, before her marriage. In 1873 she wed Rollin H. Cooke. From then her fresh and humorous stories made her name. More verse came in 1888, in her Complete Poems.

Her fiction deals mainly with New England country life. Happy Dodd came in 1878 and Somebody's Neighbors in 1881. Root-bound followed in 1885 and The Sphinx's Children in 1886. Steadfast appeared in 1889 and Huckleberries in 1891. She died at Pittsfield, Massachusetts, on 18 July 1892. The entry is a short, plain record. Birth, marriage, two verse volumes and six story books form its whole matter.
britannica-1911-cooper-charles-henry:
Charles Henry Cooper (1808–1866) was an English antiquary born at Great Marlow on 20 March 1808. His family had once been settled at Bray in Berkshire. He was schooled in private at Reading. In 1826 he settled at Cambridge, and in 1836 he became coroner of the borough. Four years later he qualified as a solicitor and built a wide practice.

Taste drew him away from law toward research. He gave most of his time to the history of Cambridge university in the end. In 1849 he traded the coroner's post for the town clerkship. He held that post until his death on 21 March 1866. His first book, a guide to the university and town, came out unnamed in 1831. The Annals of Cambridge ran from 1842 to 1853. His chief work, the Athenae Cantabrigienses, followed in 1858 and 1861.
britannica-1911-coparcenary:
Coparcenary, in law, is the descent of inherited land from an ancestor to two or more persons with equal title. The word joins roots for with and for a sharer. It arises in two ways. Common law gives one path, when a man dies without a will and leaves two or more daughters as co-heirs. Set custom gives the other, as with gavelkind lands.

Those lands pass to all sons in equal degree, or to all daughters if no sons live. Co-heirs of this kind are called parceners. Littleton gives the reason for the name. By writ the law can force them to make a partition among themselves. Coparcenary looks much like joint tenancy in its unity of title and holding. One split is key, though. Joint tenants claim by purchase, while parceners claim by descent. No right of survival runs between parceners.
britannica-1911-coppee-henry:
Henry Coppée (1821–1895) was an American educationalist and author born in Savannah, Georgia, on 13 October 1821. His French family had once been settled in Haiti. He studied at Yale for two years and worked as a civil engineer. In 1845 he graduated at West Point. He served in the Mexican War as a lieutenant and won a brevet for gallantry.

From 1850 to 1855 he taught English at West Point, then left the army. He taught English literature and history at the University of Pennsylvania until 1866. On 1 April 1866 Lehigh University chose him as its first president. In 1875 he stepped back to teach history and English there. He served as acting president again in his last years. He died at Bethlehem on 22 March 1895. Textbooks of logic, rhetoric and literature bear his name. Lives of Grant and Thomas stand among his books.
britannica-1911-corry:
Corry is a city of Erie county in Pennsylvania, in the north west part of the state. It stands thirty seven miles south east of Erie, at a height of about fourteen hundred feet. Its people numbered five thousand nine hundred ninety one in nineteen ten. Two rail lines, the Erie and the Pennsylvania, serve the town. Corry sits amid fine farm land rich in oil and natural gas.

The town is widely known for its mineral springs. A state fish hatchery lies one mile west of the city. Fine trout streams run in the country round it. Its works make steel, engines, locomotives, and radiators. Shovels, bricks, flour, furniture, and leather are also made there. Corry was settled in eighteen sixty. It became a borough in eighteen sixty three and a city three years later.
britannica-1911-coventry:
Coventry is a borough of Warwickshire in England, 94 miles north-west of London by rail. Its people numbered 69,978 in 1901. The Coventry canal links it to the Trent and Mersey and Birmingham canals and to the midland system at large. The town stands on a gentle rise, with higher ground to the west. Two small streams, feeders of the Avon, meet within it.

Two gates and parts of the old wall still stand from its ancient defences. Half-timbered houses lean over the footways in the older streets. Churches head the list of sights. Saint Michael's is one of the finest Perpendicular churches in England. Its spire rises 303 feet in height. Holy Trinity church is cross-shaped, with a tall spire at its crossing. Saint John's, or Bablake church, takes a near-square plan on the ground. The entry goes on to trade and civic growth.
britannica-1911-coventry-thomas-coventry:
Thomas Coventry, first Baron Coventry (1578–1640), was lord keeper of England. He was the eldest son of Sir Thomas Coventry, a judge of the common pleas. His line ran back to John Coventry, lord mayor of London under Henry VI. Thomas entered Balliol College, Oxford, in 1592 and the Inner Temple in 1594. He became bencher in 1614 and reader in 1616.

His rare legal gifts won early promotion in office. On 16 November 1616 he became recorder of London. Bacon fought that rise, though he granted that Coventry was well trained and honest. Bacon's grudge was that Coke had bred him in his ways. On 14 March 1617 Coventry became solicitor-general and gained a knighthood. He sat for Droitwich in the parliament of 1621. That January he rose to attorney-general. He took part in the case against Bacon for corruption.
britannica-1911-cowry:
Cowry is the common name for the shells of the Cypraeida, a family of mollusks. More than 100 species are known to science. They spread wide over the world in shallow water along the sea-shore. The best known of them is the money cowry, a small shell about half an inch long. It is white and straw-coloured outside and blue within.

That shell takes its name from its use as a kind of money in many lands. In Africa some tribes set no money value on the shells at all. They prize them as fashionable ornaments in that case. In Germany men used them to trim horse harness in like fashion. German folk names for the shells grew from that use. One shell of the family marks chiefs among the Friendly Islands. A second is a favourite with the islanders of Asia.
britannica-1911-cromwell-henry:
Henry Cromwell (1628–1674) was the fourth son of Oliver Cromwell, born at Huntingdon on 20 January 1628. He served under his father late in the Civil War. His active life was spent mainly in Ireland, where he took troops early in 1650. In 1655 he became major-general of the forces there and joined the Irish council of state. When Fleetwood left for England, Henry ruled Ireland in practice.

As ruler he softened the policy of deporting the Irish and guarded the interests of English settlers. He held the balance evenly between the Protestant sects and, Clarendon attests, was much liked. In November 1657 he became lord-deputy himself, having refused a gift of property worth 1,500 pounds a year on grounds of the country's poverty. He welcomed his brother Richard's succession, yet was recalled in June 1659. His last years passed quietly at Spinney Abbey in Cambridgeshire, and he died on 23 March 1674.
britannica-1911-curry:
Curry, as a verb for grooming and for leather work, is the subject of a word entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. The entry traces the word through Old French to a Latin term meaning to make ready. To curry a horse means to rub it down and groom it with a comb. To curry leather means to dress tanned hides.

The currier pares off rough spots and makes the leather soft and pliant. He also gives it the finish and colour it needs. The entry notes that the word currier has a distinct root tied to hide. The phrase to curry favour is explained as a later twist on an older phrase.
britannica-1911-cutlery:
Cutlery is the trade of making tools that cut, a branch of work whose name comes from a Latin word for a small knife. At first it took in the making of all edge tools of any form or stuff. As trade grew, some of those crafts split off as trades of their own.

Saws and like tools now count as a trade apart, the 1911 Britannica entry says. On the flip side, new cutlery takes in wares that do not cut at all. A steel fork for the table is a prime case: no edge tool, yet classed with knives for ease of trade. The entry then goes back to the first cut tools of man, chips of flint and glass stone flaked to an edge, of which a mass of finds still stand.
britannica-1911-dallmeyer-john-henry:
John Henry Dallmeyer, an Anglo-German optician who lived from 1830 to 1883, is profiled in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. Born at Loxten in Westphalia in September 1830, he was a landowner's son. At sixteen he was apprenticed to an optician at Osnabrück. In 1851 he came to London and found work with an optician, Hewitt.

Hewitt's men soon entered the service of Andrew Ross, the lens and telescope maker. Dallmeyer's place there proved unhappy, and he left for a year as a foreign correspondent. Ross then re-engaged him as scientific adviser, testing and finishing the finest optical work. He married Ross's second daughter and, at Ross's death in 1859, inherited a third of his fortune. He also took over the telescope-making part of the business. He then improved portrait and landscape lenses, microscope lenses, and lantern condensers. He built photo-heliographs for the Wilna and Harvard observatories.
britannica-1911-dalry:
Dalry is a mining and manufacturing town of Ayrshire, Scotland, and an entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica describes its trades and buildings. It stands on the river Garnock, about twenty-three miles south-west of Glasgow, with 5,316 people in 1901. Its name in Gaelic means the field of the king.

The entry lists a library and reading room, assembly rooms, a hospital, and a public park among its buildings. Woollen mills, worsted spinning, box and brick making, and soft drinks lead its industries, with coal and iron found near by. It also notes a stalactite cave called Elf House and the iron works of Blair and Glengarnock close at hand.
britannica-1911-danbury:
Danbury is a city of Connecticut and one of the county-seats of Fairfield county, on the Still river in the south-west of the state. Its people rose from 16,552 in 1890 to 20,234 in 1910. Railways and electric lines tie it to New York and to Bethel. A state normal school opened there in 1904. The city's leading trade is the making of felt hats, begun in 1780.

In 1905 some thirty hat factories worked in Danbury, and hats made up nearly three-quarters of all its factory output. No city in the country matched its share of the trade that year. Silver-plated ware is its other chief product, and the Danbury Fair is a noted yearly show. Settled in 1684 and named in 1687, the town held a store of army supplies in the war of independence. Governor Tryon raided and burned those stores in April 1777, and General Wooster died fighting the retreat at Ridgefield.
britannica-1911-emery:
Emery, in German Smirgel, is an impure variety of corundum, much used as a grinding and polishing agent. The Greeks knew it under a name defined by Dioscorides as a stone used in gem-engraving. The entry treats emery as a rock rather than a fixed mineral species.

Emery occurs as a dark, dense, granular mass much like an iron ore, and under the microscope it proves a mix of corundum grains with magnetite and other iron oxides. Its hardness is about 8, against 9 for pure corundum. The entry gives Dr J. Lawrence Smith's tests of emery from Samos, Naxos, and Gumach against sapphire at 100. Emery has been worked from very early times on the Isle of Naxos. Ground and bound into wheels, cloth, and paper, it serves dentists, lapidaries, and steel workshops.
britannica-1911-epic-poetry:
Epic poetry, or Epos, from Greek words for a story and for what pertains to a story, names the most dignified and elaborate forms of narrative poetry. The entry turns to Greece for its definition, since the earliest literary monuments we hold are epical in character. Their matter, it warns, was never confined to verse tales of warlike deeds.

When the epos is first found, hexameter verse has already been chosen as its vehicle. In that form epic poems served more than war and personal romance. They carried a teaching purpose, or they celebrated the mysteries of religion. Those three strands carry the names, more or less mythical, of Homer, Hesiod, and Orpheus. The entry cautions that even the oldest surviving pieces are not primitive. Unwritten epics, likely in hexameters, ran long before any fragment we have.
britannica-1911-equerry: Equerry is a short term entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It explains a post in a royal household in charge of the stables. The word comes from the French word for a stable, by way of an older form. Its modern spelling wrongly hints at the Latin word for a horse. At the British court such officers serve under the master of the horse. The first of them holds the title of chief equerry.
britannica-1911-erskine-henry:
Erskine, Henry (1746–1817), lord advocate of Scotland, was the second son of Henry David, 10th earl of Buchan, and brother of the lord chancellor Erskine. He was born in Edinburgh on 1 November 1746 and educated at St Andrews, Glasgow, and Edinburgh. Admitted to the faculty of advocates in 1768, he first made his name as a clever, fluent speaker in the debates of the general assembly.

In 1783 Erskine became lord advocate under the coalition ministry of Fox and North. In 1785 he was elected dean of the faculty of advocates and re-elected yearly until 1796. Under Grenville in 1806 he became lord advocate again and entered parliament. He gave up practice in 1811 and died at Almondel on 8 October 1817. The entry remembers him as the finest orator of his day at the Scottish bar, with a wit that, in Jeffrey's words, was all argument.
britannica-1911-escombe-harry:
Harry Escombe, a South African statesman, was born at Notting Hill in London in eighteen thirty eight. He came of a Somersetshire family and was schooled at Saint Paul's. After four years in a stockbroker's office he sailed for the Cape in eighteen fifty nine. The next year he moved to Natal and trained as an attorney. He won a name as the ablest pleader in that colony.

In eighteen seventy two Escombe was elected for Durban to the law council. He later joined the executive council of the colony as well. In eighteen eighty he won a harbour board for Natal and chaired it himself. The change of Durban port into a harbour fit for ocean liners was his work. In eighteen eighty eight he defended Zulu chiefs on a charge of high treason. He later served as premier of Natal.
britannica-1911-estuary:
Estuary, the tidal mouth where a river meets the sea, is defined in a science entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word comes from a Latin term for a place reached by the tide. In form, an estuary may be cut by river and tide in a narrow channel. It may also be the drowned lower part of a river valley.

Most of the entry deals with how salt and fresh water mix. In the Severn and the Thames the change in salt is slow and smooth. Fresh water flows over salt water while tides stir the two. Where a river pours much fresh water through a narrow mouth, the shift is sharp. In a wide inlet like the Firth of Forth, only the upper half acts as a true estuary. The lower half is mixed through and close to sea salt.
britannica-1911-fairy:
Fairy is the common name for a supposed race of magic beings who meddle in human affairs. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica traces the word through French back to Latin fatum, or fate. Fairies are called the most lovely and most storied of minor myth beings. Their roots, the entry argues, grew over long time in many lands.

Belief in them lasted longest and strongest in Ireland, it says. There they live in old earth forts and act as an ordered people. Tales tell of children stolen and changelings left in their place. Dust whirls, lost travelers, and strange stones are all laid at their door.
britannica-1911-falconry:
Falconry, the art of using falcons and hawks in the chase, is the subject of this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. The sport is often called hawking. For many ages it was a chief sport of the richer classes. Since better means of taking game existed, the article argues, it was always carried on as pure sport. Its antiquity is very great.

Falconry seems to have been practised in Asia at a remote period. It was known in China some 2,000 years before Christ, and a king of 689 is recorded as a keen follower. Japan knew it by at least 600 years before Christ. India, Arabia, Persia, and Syria knew it early as well. A relief from Khorsabad may show a falconer with a hawk on his wrist.
britannica-1911-fauntleroy-henry:
Henry Fauntleroy (1785-1824), English banker and forger, spent seven years as a clerk in the London bank of Marsh, Sibbald and Co., which his father had helped found. Taken into partnership, he was left in charge of the whole business. In 1824 the bank suspended payment, and Fauntleroy was arrested for taking trust funds by forging trustees' signatures. Rumour put the sum taken at 250,000 pounds, squandered in debauchery.

At the Old Bailey the case was proved, and Fauntleroy admitted guilt while pleading that he used the money to pay his firm's debts. Seventeen merchants and bankers spoke for his past integrity, his case was argued twice on points of law, and one Italian offered to take his place on the scaffold. All efforts failed. He was executed on 30 November 1824.
britannica-1911-fawcett-henry:
Henry Fawcett (1833-1884), English politician and economist, was born at Salisbury on 25 August 1833. Educated at King's College School and Cambridge, he was seventh wrangler in 1856 and won a fellowship. He had planned a path to parliament through the bar. In September 1858 two stray pellets from his father's gun passed through his glasses and blinded him for life. Within ten minutes, the entry says, he resolved to stick to his old pursuits.

Fawcett kept that resolve across a public career. He became a leading speaker at the Cambridge Union before the accident and a noted economist after it. He sat in parliament for Brighton through the parliament of 1868-1874, lost that seat in February 1874, and later served as postmaster-general, though without a seat in the cabinet. The long entry follows his family background, his Cambridge years, and his work in politics and economics in detail.
britannica-1911-fielding-henry:
Henry Fielding, an English novelist and playwright who lived from 1707 to 1754, is profiled at length in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Sharpham Park in Somerset on the twenty second of April 1707. His father was an army officer of the Denbigh family line. His mother was the daughter of a judge of the kings bench.

The family moved to East Stour in Dorset about 1710, where more children were born. His sister Sarah grew up to write David Simple and other works. A local clergyman gave Henry his first schooling after his mothers death in 1718. That same year he went to Eton, most likely as a day boy. Little is known of his school days there. His first biographer claims he left well versed in Greek and Latin classics. Fielding himself gave a more modest account of his learning in later years.
britannica-1911-foley-john-henry:
John Henry Foley (1818-1874), Irish sculptor, was born at Dublin on 24 May 1818. At thirteen he began studying drawing and modelling at the schools of the Royal Dublin Society, winning several first-class prizes. In 1835 he entered the schools of the Royal Academy in London. He first exhibited in 1839, with a Death of Abel and Innocence. Ino and Bacchus, shown in 1840, gave him instant reputation and was later cut in marble for the earl of Ellesmere.

More works followed fast: Lear and Cordelia, Venus rescuing Aeneas, Prospero and Miranda. In 1844 his Youth at a Stream, shown at Westminster Hall, won him a share in the sculpture for the new Houses of Parliament. Statues of John Hampden and other public men came from his studio. The entry follows his career work by work, building the picture of the leading Irish sculptor of his generation in Britain, honoured in Dublin and London alike.
britannica-1911-frederick-henry:
Frederick Henry (1584-1647), prince of Orange, was the youngest child of William the Silent, born at Delft on 29 January 1584, months before his father murder. His mother was Louise de Coligny, daughter of the Huguenot admiral. His elder brother Maurice trained him to arms, and on Maurice death in 1625 he took the stadtholderates of five provinces and command of the Union forces.

His twenty-two years at the head of the United Provinces are called the golden age of the republic, with wide trade, sea power, and a flowering of art and letters. His siege craft took Hertogenbosch in 1629, Maastricht in 1632, Breda in 1637, Sas van Ghent in 1644, and Hulst in 1645. France was his ally against Spain until, near the end, he sought a separate peace. He died in March 1647, a year before the treaty of Münster closed the long war.
britannica-1911-fuseli-henry:
Fuseli, Henry (1741–1825), an English painter and writer on art, was born at Zürich on the 7th of February 1741. His father, a painter of portraits and landscapes, meant him for the church, and he took orders in 1761. He left Switzerland after helping Lavater expose an unjust magistrate, and in 1765 he reached England. Reynolds advised him to give himself to art, and from 1770 to 1778 he studied in Italy, changing his name from Füssli to Fuseli.

Back in England he painted for Boydell's Shakespeare gallery and later formed a Milton gallery of forty-seven pictures, shown in 1799 without profit. He became an associate of the Royal Academy in 1788 and an Academician two years later, professor of painting in 1799 and keeper in 1803. He painted more than 200 pictures, the Nightmare of 1782 being the first to draw notice, and he left some 800 designs. He died at Putney Hill on the 16th of April 1825.
britannica-1911-garnet-henry:
Henry Garnet, an English Jesuit, is the subject of a life story in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in fifteen fifty five, he was the son of a schoolmaster at Nottingham. He was taught at Winchester and then studied law in London. After he became a Roman Catholic, he went to Italy.

He joined the Society of Jesus in fifteen seventy five and won praise for wide learning. Teachers such as Bellarmine shaped his training there. In fifteen eighty six he joined the mission in England. The next year he became head of the province when its leader was jailed. The entry follows his part in the sharp dispute between Jesuits and secular clergy in the fifteen nineties.
britannica-1911-geometry:
Geometry, in the 1911 Britannica, is a very long article on the branch of mathematics that studies the properties of space. It opens by defining its ground: space is described by axioms that cannot be proved, and from those axioms, with point, line, curve, surface and solid defined, the geometer draws conclusions.

The opening stresses that axioms are conventions. Built from experience, a geometry is a branch of physical science; built by pure logic, it is pure mathematics. The familiar geometry of three-dimensional space is Euclidean, named for its famous expositor. But other systems of axioms give other geometries, and the article sets out to treat the subject on that wide footing. Readers get both the foundations of the science and its later, non-Euclidean branches, set out at full technical length.
britannica-1911-gervase-of-canterbury:
Gervase of Canterbury, an English monk and chronicler who died about 1210, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He entered the house of Christchurch, Canterbury, while still young. He made his profession and took holy orders in 1163. Almost his whole life was spent within that one house.

The only office known for Gervase is that of sacrist, held in the 1190s. He followed the quarrels of the Canterbury monks with their archbishops keenly. His first writings were tracts in those disputes. From 1188 he turned his mind to history in earnest. His Chronica was meant for the private reading of his brethren. It runs from the accession of Stephen to the death of Richard the First. For the years before 1188 he leans on older sources. After that date he stands as an independent authority. A second history traces Britain from Brutus to the year 1209.
britannica-1911-gervase-of-tilbury:
Gervase of Tilbury, an Anglo-Latin writer active about 1211, is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was a kinsman and schoolfellow of an earl of Salisbury. The entry calls him a scholarly wanderer, moving from land to land in search of patrons. Before 1177 he studied and taught law at Bologna.

The article traces his search for great employers. He saw the meeting of emperor and pope at Venice in 1177, but the emperor passed him by. His first royal master was the young king of England, for whom he wrote a jest book now lost. He then served as clerk to a cardinal archbishop at Reims. There, by his own account, he falsely charged a girl who had refused him with heresy, and she was burned to death. Later he won the favour of the king of Sicily.
britannica-1911-gilbert-sir-joseph-henry:
Sir Joseph Henry Gilbert (1817-1901) was an English chemist, born at Hull on 1 August 1817. The 1911 Britannica entry traces a fine training: Glasgow, University College London, and Giessen under Liebig. In 1843 he took charge of the chemical laboratory at Lawes's experimental station at Rothamsted.

He held that post for fifty-eight years, until his death on 23 December 1901. With Lawes he applied chemistry, weather study, botany and physiology to farming, and the entry says the work improved farming practice across the civilized world. Honours came steadily: fellow of the Royal Society in 1860, a royal medal shared with Lawes in 1867, the Sibthorpian chair at Oxford from 1884, and a knighthood in 1893. That year Rothamsted celebrated the jubilee of its experiments.
britannica-1911-glapthorne-henry:
Henry Glapthorne (flourished 1635-1642) was an English poet and dramatist who wrote under Charles I. The 1911 Britannica entry warns that all known of him comes from his own work. His Poems of 1639 praise an unidentified Lucinda, and his Whitehall of 1642 reviews the past glories of the English court.

His plays fill the rest of the entry. Argalus and Parthenia of 1639 is a pastoral tragedy from Sidney's Arcadia. Albertus Wallenstein, his only historical tragedy, makes Wallenstein a monster of pride and cruelty. The Hollander, Wit in a Constable and The Ladies Priviledge complete the list, with The Lady Mother ascribed to him by later editors. The verdict is measured: the plays hardly rise above their age's level, but they hold many happy isolated passages.
britannica-1911-glastonbury:
Glastonbury, a market town in Somersetshire, England, is described in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. It stands on the main road from London to Exeter. Orchards and water meadows ring the town. Those fields were won back from fens round Glastonbury Tor, a cone shaped height that was once an isle.

The town is famed for its abbey, now in ruins. The wreck is so deep that the full plan can no longer be traced. Of the monks' vast buildings, little stands but the abbot's kitchen and a barn. A chapel at the west end is the finest part left. It is work of the twelve hundreds, with a crypt below from a later age.
britannica-1911-glory: Glory is a word article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Coming through Old French from Latin gloria, the word means fame, renown and honour. In the phrase glory of God it means the honour due to the Creator and his majesty. The article lists the church uses: Gloria Patri, Gloria tibi, and Gloria in excelsis. It closes by noting that a glory is also the ring of light round a sacred figure.
britannica-1911-gnome-and-gnomic-poetry:
Gnomes were wise sayings put into verse by the Greeks to aid the memory. The Greek word behind the term means an opinion in plain sense. An Elizabethan critic defines a gnome as a saying on the manners of men. It declares, with apt brevity, what in life ought to be done or not done. The gnomic poets of Greece flourished in the sixth century before Christ.

Those poets arranged strings of such wise sayings in verse for readers. Their works were gathered in the fourth century by Lobon of Argos. That gathering has disappeared, and most of the poets survive only in fragments. The chief names are Theognis, Solon, Phocylides, and Simonides, among others listed. The work of Theognis alone was saved whole, by a schoolmaster's care. Sayings like know thyself were tied to the Seven Wise Men of Greece.
britannica-1911-godfrey-sir-edmund-berry:
Sir Edmund Berry Godfrey, an English magistrate and politician who lived from 1621 to 1678, is profiled in a 1911 Britannica article. He was the younger son of Thomas Godfrey, of an old Kentish family. He was born in December 1621. He was educated at Westminster school and at Christ Church, Oxford.

After entering Gray's Inn, he became a dealer in wood. His business prospered. He was made a justice of the peace for Westminster. In September 1666 he was knighted for his services during the great plague in London. In 1669 he was held in prison for a few days. He had ordered the arrest of the king's physician, who owed him money. The tragic events of his life began in September 1678. The article opens the path to a death that shook the nation. His name still marks the panic of the Popish Plot years.
britannica-1911-gooseberry:
Gooseberry is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a well known fruit bush. Its Latin name is given as Ribes Grossularia. It grows across northern and central Europe in the wild. It sits in the same genus as the currants. Gooseberries form a distinct section of that genus. They differ from true currants in two main ways.

Their stems are spinous, which currant stems are not. Their flowers grow on short footstalks, singly or in small groups. Currant flowers grow in racemes by contrast. The wild gooseberry is a small, straggling bush. It closely resembles the cultivated plant in form. Its branches are thickly set with sharp spines. Those spines stand singly or in tufts of two or three. Bell shaped flowers open from groups of rounded leaves. The fruit is smaller than in garden kinds. It is often of good flavour all the same.
britannica-1911-gosse-philip-henry:
Philip Henry Gosse was an English man of wild life lore who lived from eighteen ten to eighteen eighty-eight. He was born at Worcester, the son of a small scale painter. At Poole his bent for wild lore was seen and urged on by an aunt. Chance to grow it came late.

A clerks post in Newfoundland let him watch life through a lens in dull hours. Farm work in Canada failed, and he taught in the south states for a time. Home in eighteen thirty-nine, he wrote books that sold wide. A trip to pick finds in Jamaica gave him fresh ground.
britannica-1911-goulburn-henry:
Henry Goulburn (1784-1856) was an English statesman schooled at Trinity College, Cambridge. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica traces his rise from a seat for Horsham in 1808. He held posts for home affairs and for war and the colonies. From 1821 he served as chief secretary for Ireland for six years.

He became chancellor of the exchequer under Wellington in 1828. There he cut the rate on part of the national debt. He also let any person sell beer for a small yearly fee. He held the finance post again under Peel and backed the repeal of the corn laws.
britannica-1911-grand-canary:
Grand Canary, or Gran Canaria, is an island in the Atlantic Ocean. It forms part of the Spanish group of the Canary Islands. It had 127,471 people in 1900 and covers 523 square miles. Grand Canary is the most fertile isle of the group. It is near round in shape, with a width of twenty-four miles. A mass of hills fills the inner part, with ravines that run out to the shore.

The highest peak, Los Pexos, rises 6,400 feet. Large tracts carry the native Canary pine. The island has several mineral springs. Las Palmas, the capital, had 44,517 people and is treated in its own article. Telde, the second town, stands on a plain ringed by palm trees. At Atalaya, near Las Palmas, some hundreds of people make clay pots. They live in holes dug in the soft rock.
britannica-1911-grattan-henry:
Henry Grattan, an Irish statesman who lived from 1746 to 1820, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica life story. He was born in Dublin on July 3, 1746, the son of a city recorder. At Trinity College he began a life long love of the classics. He was called to the Irish bar in 1772 but never took law work in earnest.

Grattan honed his gift for speech on great models, among them Bolingbroke and Junius. Brought into the Irish parliament in 1775, he soon passed his friend Flood as head of the national party. His speech powers were ranked first among men of his day. The piece notes his packed epigrams and rich store of deep sayings on rule. He lacked Pitt's dignity and Fox's close logic, though.
britannica-1911-greathead-james-henry:
James Henry Greathead, a British engineer, is the subject of a life story in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Grahamstown, Cape Colony, in eighteen forty four, he moved to England as a teen. In eighteen sixty four he became a pupil of the engineer Barlow. From Barlow he learned the shield method of tunnelling.

That shield method is the core of the entry and of his fame. Barlow had backed the shield and planned tube railways under London built with its help. A subway under the Thames near the Tower was chosen to prove what the method could do. The entry then follows the troubles met on that work and what came of them.
britannica-1911-green-william-henry:
William Henry Green (1825-1900) was an American Hebrew scholar, born at Groveville, New Jersey, on 27 January 1825. The 1911 Britannica entry traces his descent from Jonathan Dickinson, first president of the College of New Jersey. He graduated at Lafayette College in 1840 and at Princeton Theological Seminary in 1846.

From August 1851 until his death he was professor of Biblical and Oriental literature at Princeton Seminary. He refused the presidency of Princeton College in 1868 and long acted as the seminary's head. The entry calls him a great Hebrew teacher. His Grammar of the Hebrew Language of 1861, revised in 1888, improved in method on Gesenius and Ewald. All his Semitic learning served a conservative higher criticism, defended in works on the Pentateuch and beyond. He died at Princeton on 10 February 1900.
britannica-1911-harriman-edward-henry:
Edward Henry Harriman, an American financier and railroad magnate who lived from 1848 to 1909, is profiled in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. Born at Hempstead in February 1848, he was the son of an Episcopal rector. He became a broker's clerk in New York at an early age. In 1870 he bought a seat on the New York Stock Exchange on his own account.

For many years Harriman's success was quiet but steady. His friend Stuyvesant Fish brought him onto the board of the Illinois Central in 1883, and by 1887 he was its vice-president. His career as a great railway organizer began only in 1898. With bankers' aid he formed a syndicate to acquire the Union Pacific line. That road was then in receivership and widely seen as a hopeless failure. Its rescue announced a new power in the railway world.
britannica-1911-havelock-sir-henry:
Sir Henry Havelock (1795–1857) was a British soldier. He became one of the Indian Mutiny's heroes. He was born at Bishop-Wearmouth on 5 April 1795. His father was a wealthy Sunderland shipbuilder. Charterhouse schooled him for seven years. His dead mother's wish sent him to the Middle Temple in 1813. A quarrel with his father cut short his legal studies. In 1815 he took a second lieutenancy in the Rifle Brigade.

India received him in 1823 with the 13th Light Infantry. He had learned Hindustani under Dr Gilchrist first. Staff posts in Burma used his languages and skill. Promotion crawled: captain only in 1838. Twenty-three years' service had passed by then. He published his early campaigns at Serampore in 1828. The Mutiny made his name in 1857. Parliament voted pensions after his death that year.
britannica-1911-hawkins-caesar-henry:
Caesar Henry Hawkins (1798–1884) was a British surgeon. He was born at Bisley, Gloucestershire, on 19 September 1798. His grandfather was serjeant-surgeon to two kings. Christ's Hospital and St George's Hospital trained him. He was surgeon to St George's from 1829 to 1861. In 1862 he became serjeant-surgeon to Queen Victoria. He twice presided over the College of Surgeons. His Hunterian oration came in 1849.

Complex surgical cases built his great reputation. For long he was London's only successful ovariotomy operator in hospital. That operation succeeded in 1846, before anaesthetics existed. He did much to popularise colotomy. Yet he loved conservative surgery above operating. He taught pupils to save limbs rather than remove them. His collected papers appeared in two volumes in 1874. Tumours, hydrophobia and snake-bites were among his subjects. He died on 20 July 1884.
britannica-1911-hawley-henry:
Henry Hawley (c. 1679–1759) was a British lieutenant-general. He entered the army, it is said, in 1694. He served as a captain in the War of Spanish Succession. Almanza sent him home to England. The 19th foot made him its lieutenant-colonel soon after. He was wounded with that regiment at Sheriffmuir in 1715. Major-general rank came to him in 1739.

He accompanied George II to Germany in 1743. Dettingen and Fontenoy saw him command cavalry. In December 1745 he became commander-in-chief in Scotland. Falkirk gave him a severe defeat within a month. The command stayed his despite that disaster. Under Cumberland his dragoons butchered fugitives at Culloden ruthlessly. Lauffeld in the Low Countries closed his active service. James Wolfe, his brigade-major, despised his severity and his skill. Royal favour, however, never left him.
britannica-1911-hawtrey-charles-henry:
Charles Henry Hawtrey (1858– ) was an English actor. He was born at Eton, where his father taught. Rugby and Oxford educated him. He took to the stage in 1881. In 1883 he adapted von Moser's Bibliothekar. The result was The Private Secretary. That adaptation had an enormous success. London then saw him in many modern plays.

He made his name as a comedian of a special kind. Cool, imperturbable lying was his leading stage characteristic. No one could match him in such parts. A Message from Mars was a later popular success. It played well in London and in America. The entry is a short theatrical notice. It rests on the one adaptation and the one manner. His birth year is given as 1858, with no death date.
britannica-1911-henry:
Henry is a name borne by many European sovereigns: Henri in French, Enrique in Spanish and Heinrich in German. It comes from the Old High German Haimirih, from heim, home, and rih, a ruler, so its sense is prince or chief of the house. The Latin rex and the Sanskrit raj, rule, and raja, king, stand beside it as kin.

With so many rulers of one name, a strict order is fixed for the lives that follow. Emperors and German kings come first, then kings of England. Other kings follow in the alphabetical order of their states, and other reigning princes come next in the same order. Non-reigning princes stand fifth. Bishops, nobles and chroniclers named Henry close the list, so a reader can find one man among the many Henrys.
britannica-1911-hicks-henry:
Henry Hicks (1837–1899) was a British physician and geologist, born at St David's in Pembrokeshire on the 26th of May 1837. His father was a surgeon there. Hicks studied at Guy's Hospital, qualified in 1862, and practised at St David's until 1871, then at Hendon. At Hendon he gave special care to mental diseases and took his M.D. at St Andrews in 1878.

Geology claimed his spare time, under the lead of J. W. Salter. With Salter he set up the Menevian group of the Middle Cambrian in 1865, marked by the trilobite Paradoxides. He wrote many papers on Cambrian and Lower Silurian rocks and named new fossils. On the Pre-Cambrian rocks of St David's he described the Dimetian and Pebidian series, and his views won acceptance. He was elected F.R.S. in 1885 and led the Geological Society from 1896 to 1898. He died at Hendon in 1899.
britannica-1911-himmel-frederick-henry:
Frederick Henry Himmel (1765-1814) was a German composer born on 20 November 1765 at Treuenbrietzen in Brandenburg. He first read theology at Halle. On a short stay at Potsdam he had the chance to show his skill at the piano before King Frederick William II. The king gave him a yearly grant so that he could finish his studies in music. He did so under Naumann, a composer of the Italian school.

Himmel took up the style of that school in his serious operas. The first of them, a pastoral opera, was staged at Venice in 1794 to great success. In 1792 he went to Berlin, where his oratorio Isaaco was staged. On the strength of that work he was made court music director to the king of Prussia. In that post he wrote a great deal of state music, cantatas among it.
britannica-1911-history:
History is a word used in two senses in English, the entry opens by warning. It may mean the record of events, or it may mean the events themselves. At first it was limited to inquiry and to statement of findings. Only in fairly modern times was its meaning stretched to cover the things studied. That stretch came by a somewhat careless transfer of ideas, it is said.

Now the wider meaning is indeed the commoner of the two in use. We speak of the history of England with no book in mind at all. We call kings and statesmen the makers of history in that sense. History in the wider sense is all that has happened in the world. It holds not just human life but the natural world as well. All that changes has its history, down to the whole universe.
britannica-1911-hobart-john-henry:
John Henry Hobart, an American Episcopal bishop who lived from 1775 to 1830, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in Philadelphia, he studied at Princeton and graduated in 1793. He trained for the ministry under Bishop William White. He was ordained deacon in 1798 and priest two years later.

Hobart was chosen assistant bishop of New York in 1811, with the right to succeed. He led the diocese in fact from that year, due to the ill health of Bishop Moore. He formally succeeded in 1816. He helped found the General Theological Seminary and taught pastoral theology there. His zeal for the historic office of bishop drove much of his writing. He fought plans for a rival seminary in Ohio at first, then backed a revised plan. He also urged his flock not to join the American Bible Society.
britannica-1911-holland-sir-henry:
Sir Henry Holland (1788–1873) was an English physician and author, born at Knutsford, Cheshire, in 1788. His kin included Josiah Wedgwood's family and Mrs Gaskell's. After schooling at Newcastle and near Bristol, he was articled to a Liverpool merchant firm, but won release and began medicine at Edinburgh in 1806. He graduated in 1811, travelled abroad for some years, and set up in London practice in 1816.

Holland's success was speedily fulfilled, helped by four seasons at Spa and, more, by his happy temper and gifts in conversation. He was elected F.R.S. in 1816 and F.R.C.S. in 1828. He became physician in ordinary to Prince Albert in 1840 and to the queen in 1852, and a baronet in 1853. He was also a D.C.L. of Oxford and a member of Europe's chief learned societies.
britannica-1911-horne-richard-henry:
Richard Henry Horne, also called Hengist (1803–1884), was an English poet and critic, born in London on New Year's Day 1803. Meant for the army, he entered Sandhurst, but no commission came, so he left England and joined the Mexican navy. He served in the war against Spain and went through many adventures. Home again, he turned journalist and edited The Monthly Repository in 1836–1837.

In 1837 Horne published two tragedies, Cosmo de Medici and The Death of Marlowe, and in 1841 a History of Napoleon. The book he lives by is his epic Orion (1843), first sold at a farthing, widely read and often reprinted. In 1844 came his critical essays, A New Spirit of the Age, helped by Elizabeth Barrett, with whom he kept up a huge correspondence from 1839 to her marriage in 1846. In 1852 he sailed for Australia with William Howitt, returning only in 1869. A Civil List pension came in 1874.
britannica-1911-hosiery:
Hosiery names all textile fabrics built on the principle of looping, or loop structure. The word comes from hose, or stocking, one of the first garments made by knitting. Stockings remain a staple of the trade, but only one item in a wide range. The elastic build of knitting suits it to body wear of every kind. Hardly a textile article exists that cannot be remade on the loop principle.

Beside weaving, the art of knitting is very modern. No sure mention of it occurs before the start of the 15th century. An act of Henry VII in 1488 names knitted woollen caps. The art is thought to have begun in Scotland and passed into England, caps being knitted for some time before other goods followed. The long article then follows the trade's growth: hand frames, machine knitting, the chief centres of production, and the goods that fill its modern output.
britannica-1911-hudson-henry:
Henry Hudson is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Hudson was an English navigator and explorer. Almost nothing is known of his life outside four famous voyages. Each voyage sought new trade and a short route to China through the northern seas.

The article takes the voyages in order. In 1607, sailing for the Muscovy Company, he coasted Greenland and reached far north past Spitzbergen. His reports helped start the English whale fishery there. In 1608 he tried the north-east route past Novaya Zemlya and found the ice closed. The entry then turns to his third voyage, made for the Dutch East India Company in the Half-Moon. Readers get a careful record of early Arctic exploration and its hard limits.
britannica-1911-hue-and-cry:
Hue and cry is a phrase of English law for the old process of chasing a criminal with horn and voice, and this 1911 Britannica entry explains it. Any person wronged, or finding a felony done, had the duty to raise the cry. His neighbours were bound to turn out with him and help hunt the offender down. All who joined the chase could arrest the man they pursued, even if he turned out to be innocent.

A swift fate met a man caught by hue and cry with signs of guilt still on him. If he fought back he could be cut down. If he gave himself up he was brought before a court but could say nothing in his own defence, and no formal charge was needed. The statutes on it were repealed in 1827.
britannica-1911-hungary:
Hungary is the subject of a long country entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. The entry places it in the south east of central Europe, with Austria and Rumania on its borders. Serbia, Bosnia, and Dalmatia are named to the south. Its total area is given and set beside that of Great Britain and Ireland.

Hungary formed one of the two states of the Austria Hungary monarchy, the entry explains. It made up just over half of that monarchy's total area. The entry is split into large parts on land, people, and history. Readers get maps of borders, counts of people, and a full account of the kingdom as it stood at that time.
britannica-1911-inman-henry:
Henry Inman, an American artist who lived from 1801 to 1846, is the subject of a short life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in Utica, New York, he was apprenticed at age fourteen to the painter John Jarvis. After seven years he set up on his own, painting portraits, genre scenes, and landscapes.

The entry notes that Inman helped organise the National Academy of Design in New York and served as its first vice president from 1826 to 1832. As a portrait painter he did well in New York and Philadelphia. A trip to England in 1844 brought him sitters such as the poet Wordsworth and Lord Macaulay. His American sitters included President Van Buren and Chief Justice Marshall.
