britannica-1911-ireton-henry:
Henry Ireton is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica life of an English parliamentary general. He lived from 1611 to 1651. He was the eldest son of German Ireton of Attenborough. He was baptized in November 1611 at his home parish. In 1626 he went to Trinity College, Oxford. He took his degree there in 1629. That same year he entered the Middle Temple in London.

When the Civil War broke out, he joined Parliament's army. He fought at Edgehill and at Gainsborough in 1643. Cromwell made him deputy governor of the Isle of Ely. Next year he served under Manchester in Yorkshire. He also fought at the second battle of Newbury. He backed Cromwell in charges against that general. On the night before Naseby, he surprised the Royalist army. He took many prisoners in that night stroke. Next day Cromwell made him commissary general of the army.
britannica-1911-ismay-thomas-henry:
Thomas Henry Ismay, who lived from 1837 to 1899, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica as a British ship owner. Born at Maryport in Cumberland, he trained with a Liverpool shipping firm as a young man. He then worked on his own and later took over the White Star line of ships to Australia. With William Imrie he set up a new steam ship firm in 1868.

That firm, soon known as the White Star Line, moved into trade with America. Its first large steam ship, Oceanic, was launched in 1870 and marked a new stage in Atlantic travel. Ismay also helped plan for fast merchant ships to serve the state in war. The entry notes his charity work for sailors and his gift to a pension fund for Liverpool men.
britannica-1911-jerry: Jerry is a very short word entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It explains a short form of the name Jeremiah and its use for plain, common things. One use names a machine for finishing cloth. A second use lives on in a phrase for houses built fast with poor stuff by builders who cut corners. The entry says there is no proof for a tale that the phrase came from a firm of builders with that name.
britannica-1911-jones-henry:
Henry Jones (1831-1899) was an English doctor who became famed as Cavendish, a writer on whist. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica notes he was born in London, son of a doctor. He followed his father into medicine and practiced for sixteen years. His father loved whist, and the son learned the game well early.

His Principles of Whist in 1862 set the standard for play. Later works covered the laws of piquet and écarté as well. He also wrote on billiards, lawn tennis, and croquet for wide readership. The entry stresses that he ordered and explained old laws rather than making new ones.
britannica-1911-jones-owen-antiquary:
Owen Jones (1741-1814) was a Welsh collector of old Welsh writing, and his life fills an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in Denbighshire, he went to London in 1760 to work for a firm of furriers, whose business he later took over. From boyhood he had studied Welsh books and verse.

The entry tells how he spent more than a thousand pounds to publish the Myvyrian Archaiology of Wales in 1801-1807, a set of works from the sixth to the fourteenth century. His gathered manuscripts went to the British Museum, with much unused verse and prose besides. He also founded the Gwyneddigion Society in London in 1772 to back Welsh studies.
britannica-1911-kater-henry:
Henry Kater (1777–1835) was an English physicist of German descent, born at Bristol on the 16th of April 1777. He first meant to study law, but gave that up on his father's death in 1794 and entered the army. He took a commission in the 12th regiment of foot, then in India, where he gave valued help to the great trigonometrical survey.

Failing health forced him home to England. In 1808, by then a lieutenant, he began a fine student career in the senior department of the Royal Military College at Sandhurst, and rose soon after to captain. In 1814 he retired on half pay and gave the rest of his life to research in science. He died in London on the 26th of April 1835. His first weighty work compared the Cassegrainian and Gregorian telescopes. Papers of 1813 and 1814 drew from them the finding that the first gathers more light.
britannica-1911-keppel-sir-henry:
Sir Henry Keppel (1809–1904) was a British admiral, son of the 4th earl of Albemarle. He was born on the 14th of June 1809 and entered the navy from the old naval academy at Portsmouth in 1822. His family ties won him swift promotion, at a time when less lucky officers rose very slowly. He became lieutenant in 1829 and commander in 1833.

His first command, the brig Childers, was spent largely on the coast of Spain, then in the throes of the Carlist war. Keppel had already made his name as a good seaman. He served with the squadron on the west coast of Africa set to crush the slave trade. In 1837 he was made post captain, and in 1841 he was posted to the Dido for service in China. The long entry follows one of the most active small ship careers of the Victorian navy, from the China seas to high command.
britannica-1911-killigrew-sir-henry:
Sir Henry Killigrew (died 1603) was an English diplomatist, and a short life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica lists his missions. He came of an old Cornish family and sat in parliament for Launceston in 1553. He lived abroad through all or part of the reign of Mary. When Elizabeth came to the throne, he returned at once.

The new queen set Killigrew to work as a diplomat from the start. He was sent on a mission to Germany. He also conducted talks in Scotland, where he met Mary Queen of Scots more than once. He was knighted in 1591, after years of such service. More missions across Europe followed before his death in early 1603. Many of his letters on public matters rest in the Record Office and the British Museum.
britannica-1911-king-henry:
Henry King (1591-1669), an English bishop and poet, is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the eldest son of John King, later bishop of London. He went from Westminster School to Christ Church at Oxford, entering in January 1609 with his younger brother John. He took holy orders and rose through a string of church posts.

The article says he was made bishop of Chichester in 1642, with a rich living in Sussex at the same time. When Chichester fell to the Parliament army that year, he was among the prisoners. After his release he found shelter with kin. He knew Charles the First in person and held the Eikon Basilike to be the king's own work. Restored at the Restoration, he died at Chichester in 1669.
britannica-1911-knighthood-and-chivalry:
Knighthood and chivalry form the subject of one of the longest articles in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The two words name a single field, seen in three ways. It can be a form of feudal land tenure. It can be a personal rank or honour. It can also be a code of manners. Tenure is left to the articles on feudalism and knight-service. This article takes up rank and manners, and traces the words from the Old English cniht, first a boy, then a servant, at last a mounted fighting man.

From origins the article admits are obscure, the text moves through the growth of knighthood in Europe and England. It then turns to the great orders, treated in depth. Their stars, badges, ribbons and collars are shown in plates. The Order of St Patrick, founded by George III in 1788, is one of many orders described officer by officer.
britannica-1911-lacrymatory: A lacrymatory, from the Latin lacrima, a tear, is one of a class of small vessels of terra-cotta, or more often glass, found in Roman and late Greek tombs. They were long supposed to be bottles into which mourners dropped their tears. In fact they held unguents, and their numbers in tombs come from the use of unguents in funeral rites. They are shaped like a spindle, or a flask with a long small neck and a bulbous body.
britannica-1911-landseer-sir-edwin-henry:
Sir Edwin Henry Landseer, who lived from 1802 to 1873, was an English painter born in London. The 1911 Britannica article says he was the third son of John Landseer, a known engraver. He was born on the seventh of March 1802. His father taught him art from the start. At five he drew well, with a keen eye for beasts. At eight his drawing was skilled work, and at ten it showed wit as well.

At thirteen Landseer drew a Saint Bernard dog, which his brother Thomas engraved and sold. That same year, 1815, he sent two pictures to the Royal Academy. Youth kept him an honorary guest in the show list. On advice, he studied the Elgin Marbles and the beasts in the Tower menagerie. He cut up beasts to learn their build. By 1816 he was an Academy student, with more work than he could do.
britannica-1911-lane-james-henry:
Lane, James Henry is a life article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about an American soldier and politician. Lane was the son of Amos Lane, a Democratic leader who sat in Congress. The son studied law and was admitted to the bar in 1840.

The article centres on his Kansas career. His vote for the Kansas-Nebraska Bill ruined him in Indiana, so in 1855 he emigrated to Kansas Territory. There he joined the Free State forces, wrote the platform of their first convention, and presided over the Topeka constitutional convention. Indicted for treason in 1856, he escaped, toured the northern cities, and returned with John Brown. Elected to the Senate as a Republican in 1861, he raised a brigade and later served as recruiting commissioner.
britannica-1911-laurens-henry:
Henry Laurens, an American statesman, is followed in a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Charleston in 1724, he was of Huguenot stock. At sixteen he clerked in a London counting house for trade. Back home, he made a fortune in trade at Charleston. He quit the counting house in 1771, rich and at ease.

Laurens spent three years in Europe watching his sons at school. Though fond of England, he joined a plea against harsh laws. Home by 1774, he led the council of safety in his state. In 1777 he took the chair of the continental congress at Philadelphia. Sent to seek a Dutch loan, he was seized at sea. The British shut him in the Tower of London for his papers.
britannica-1911-layard-sir-austen-henry:
Austen Henry Layard, who lived from 1817 to 1894, was a British writer, envoy, and digger of Nineveh. The 1911 Britannica entry follows a youth spent in part in Italy and in schools in three lands. He worked six years in a law office and then set out overland for Ceylon in 1839. The trip turned into long travel in Persia and a post in Constantinople.

There the British envoy Stratford Canning used him on quiet missions in Turkish lands. In 1845, with help from Canning, he began the digs that made his name. The entry shows how a love of art and travel led to famed finds. Readers get both the early life and the start of that work.
britannica-1911-lazarus-henry:
Henry Lazarus, an English clarinet master, fills a short music life in the 1911 Britannica. Born in London on the first day of eighteen fifteen, he learned from band chiefs of the guards. His first lone show came at a star show in April of eighteen thirty eight. That year he took a second clarinet post with a choir band. From eighteen forty he led the clarinet desk at the opera house.

His sweet tone, clean phrase, and true hand won praise on all sides. He taught the clarinet at the Royal School of Music from eighteen fifty four. A post at the army music school came to him in eighteen fifty eight. His last show was a gain show for him in eighteen ninety two. He died in March of eighteen ninety five at age eighty.
britannica-1911-lection-lectionary:
Lection and lectionary, the set readings of worship, are traced in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Reading the books of Moses in synagogue on the Sabbath was an ancient Jewish custom. Readings from the prophets were added later, before the time of Christ. The Gospel of Luke is cited for proof of that practice.

The Christian service took the custom over from the synagogue. To the older readings it added the writings of apostles and evangelists. Traces of such additions show within the New Testament itself. From the second century onward, mentions of the practice multiply fast. Yet those early mentions do not prove a fixed lectionary, the article warns. They point rather to free choice in the readings used. Justin Martyr describes a Sunday gathering in his day. There the memoirs of the apostles or the prophets were read as long as time allowed.
britannica-1911-ledbury:
The 1911 Britannica article on Ledbury describes a market town in Herefordshire, England. It stands on the south-western slope of the Malvern Hills. Its population was 3,259 in 1901. Cider and farm produce are its chief trade. Limestone is quarried in the hills nearby.

The account points out the town's timbered houses. The finest is the Market House of 1633. It is raised on oak pillars. The church of Saint Michael has a Norman chancel. The article then traces the town's history. An early camp stands nearby. The manor passed to the see of Hereford. Fairs, markets, and a wool trade followed. The town also played a part in the Civil Wars.
britannica-1911-leland-john-antiquary:
John Leland, an English antiquary born near 1506, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica life story. He was born in London on September 13 and schooled at Saint Paul's. A patron's help sent him to Cambridge and later to Oxford and Paris. On his return he took holy orders and tutored two young lords.

His learning brought Leland to the eye of Henry the Eighth. In 1533 the king gave him a new post as king's antiquary. He could search all church houses of England for records and old books. From 1536 to 1542 he toured England and Wales on that quest. He sought to save the books cast loose when the abbeys were shut.
britannica-1911-lime-chemistry:
Lime in chemistry is the plain name for calcium oxide, CaO. Men used it from very old times in mortar and cement. Burning limestone in kilns makes it, a craft Pliny and Dioscorides both set down. Stone purity rules the yield. Pure stone gives a fat lime that slakes with ease. Stone laced with magnesia gives a poor lime that slakes hard.

Pure quick-lime is a white loose solid. Heat in the electric furnace can melt and boil it. Water makes it burst with heat and fall apart. That act is slaking, and the yield is slaked lime. Lime-water is its weak wash in water, used to test for carbonic acid gas. Milk of lime is a cream of the same. Lime-water serves in care of burns and sores. Taken by mouth, it calms acid in the stomach.
britannica-1911-lugard-sir-frederick-joh:
Sir Frederick John Dealtry Lugard (1858– ) was a British soldier and administrator in Africa, born on the 22nd of January 1858. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica follows him from the Norfolk regiment into the Afghan, Sudan, and Burma campaigns. In 1888 he led Nyasaland settlers against Arab slave traders on Lake Nyasa and was badly wounded.

For the Imperial British East Africa Company he went to Uganda in 1890, won mastery there, and mapped the Ruwenzori country. Back in England he fought the plan to abandon Uganda and kept it British. In 1894 he outran French and German rivals in Borgu and won treaties for the Royal Niger Company. He raised the West African Frontier Force in 1897, then became high commissioner of Northern Nigeria. Campaigns against Kano and Sokoto in 1903 let him govern the land in peace before leaving in 1906 for Hong Kong.
britannica-1911-lyrical-poetry:
Lyrical poetry gets a long essay in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The term covers verse that is sung, or that could be sung, with an instrument. In the first times, the text says, all verse was of this kind. Old hymns, charms, and rites joined tune and metre in one act.

Much of the essay sorts out where lyric ends and epic or drama begins. Homer and Hesiod are set apart from true lyric poets such as Pindar. Hegel is quoted for the view that lyric verse shows inner life and feeling. The piece then tests that view against Wordsworth, Tennyson, Racine, and Shakespeare, and warns that form counts as well as feeling.
britannica-1911-mackenzie-henry:
Henry Mackenzie was a Scots writer of tales who lived from seventeen forty-five to eighteen thirty-one. He was born at Edinburgh, the son of a famed healer. He was schooled there and then bound to a Crown law man. A span in London for law study came next, then a post as Crown law man at home.

His first tale, of a man of deep feel, came out with no name in seventeen seventy-one. It was a hit at once, and a false claim to it forced his name out. Two more tales came, then plays that fared less well. He ran two week sheets of essays and notes.
britannica-1911-manuvres-military:
Military manoeuvres are the higher training of troops of all arms in large bodies for war. Most lands have held them since the first standing armies arose. England held no such camps until the start of the 1800s. Then Sir John Moore trained the famed Light Brigade at Shorncliffe camp. France, by contrast, held large camps of training under Louis XIV. The first on record held 18,000 troops at Compiegne in 1666.

Much time at those French camps went to display, and the moves drilled were plain ones. Still, their effect on training for war ran deep. It bore fruit in the wars of the early 1700s. The camps also served as trials for new plans of battle and new gear. One such trial set two schools of foot tactics against each other from 1785 to 1790.
britannica-1911-maritime-territory:
Maritime territory is a term in law between nations. It names coastal waters that touch the open sea but are not classed as territorial waters. In territorial waters the rule of the state next to them has a limit set on it. Over maritime territory that rule has no such limit. The state may close those waters as it sees fit.

The article gives clear cases of such waters. A strait where the state can bar foreign ships from passing counts as maritime territory. The Solent and the Inland Sea of Japan are named as cases in point. Bays that are so shut in by land that they form no part of an ocean highway count too. The short piece works by contrast with the entry on territorial waters.
britannica-1911-marquetry:
Marquetry is an inlay of fine woods, ivory, bone, brass, and other rich materials. Shell and mother of pearl are also used in the craft. Shaped pieces of different stuffs or tints are joined to form a design. It grew out of an older inlay craft of Italy called intarsia. In true intarsia, pieces are sunk into a ground of darker or lighter wood.

In marquetry, by contrast, thin pieces of equal depth are laid on a base with glue. Old work at Ferrara shows that this method was used even in intarsia days. Makers sought more relief by shading and tinting the wood in their designs. Shading was most often made by scorching, with a hot iron or hot sand. Tinting was done by washes of chemicals or by true colour laid on.
britannica-1911-marten-henry:
Henry Marten (1602-1680), an English regicide, is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The elder son of a knight, he was educated at University College in Oxford. He first stood out in 1639, when he refused to pay a general loan. In 1640 he entered Parliament as a member for Berkshire.

The article shows a bold and unruly figure. In the Commons he joined the popular party and spoke for the bill against Strafford. His speech about the king was so frank that Charles demanded his arrest for high treason. He did not fight in the war, but he was busy in Parliament. Once his zeal led him to open a lord's letter to his wife, for which the lord beat him. In 1643 words about wiping out the royal family got him expelled and jailed for a few days.
britannica-1911-martyn-henry:
Henry Martyn was an English missionary to India in the early nineteenth century. He lived from seventeen eighty one to eighteen twelve. His life entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Truro in Cornwall, the son of a mine agent, he studied at Cambridge.

Martyn was senior wrangler and first Smith prizeman in eighteen o one. He had planned a life at the bar before a sharp change came. Talk of William Carey work in India turned his mind to missions. Reading the life of David Brainerd deepened that new resolve in him. He took orders in eighteen o three and sailed for India in eighteen o five.
britannica-1911-mayhew-henry:
Henry Mayhew is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Mayhew was an English author and journalist born in 1812. He was a son of a London solicitor. He was sent to Westminster school, but ran away to sea. He sailed to India, and on his return read law for a short time under his father.

The article tells how he founded a weekly paper in 1831 with a partner. In 1841 he helped found the magazine Punch and edited it jointly for two years. He wrote on all kinds of subjects after that. His lasting fame rests on work about the poor of London. With helpers he published London Labour and London Poor in 1851. The text calls him the first to write up London poverty from a caring point of view. He died in London in 1887.
britannica-1911-mercenary: Mercenary, from a Latin word for reward or gain, is defined in this short 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. A mercenary is one who serves or acts solely for personal gain. The term applies above all to a soldier who offers himself to any army that will hire him. The name is sometimes used as a reproach. Nations that raise armies by conscription aim it at armies raised by voluntary enlistment, whose members are paid a living wage.
britannica-1911-middlebury:
Middlebury is the subject of a village entry in the 1911 Britannica. The village lies in Vermont in the United States. It is the county seat of Addison county there. It stands on Otter Creek north of Rutland. Counts for the village span three census years. The count in 1910 was just under nineteen hundred souls. A rail line of the Rutland road serves the village. It sits in fair view near the Green Mountains.

A college chartered in 1800 stands in the village. That college has taken women since the year 1883. Class types, staff counts, and book counts are given. An art museum and a public book room serve the place. Court house and opera house are its chief halls. Marble works, iron works, and mills give it trade. A state horse breeding farm lies just north of it.
britannica-1911-milne-edwards-henry:
Henry Milne Edwards, a French student of animal life, is the subject of a life story in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in Bruges in eighteen hundred to an English father, he spent most of his life in France. He first trained in medicine and took his degree at Paris. Love of natural history soon drew him away from that path.

He turned to study of the lower forms of animal life, the entry explains. An early paper on crabs and their kin was laid before the Academy of Sciences. Cuvier praised that work in a long report the next year. It grew from two dredging trips off the French coast with his friend Audouin.
britannica-1911-montfleury:
Montfleury, a French stage name of weight, is kept in a brief life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. His true name was Zacharie Jacob, born in Anjou in France. He served as a page to the duke of Guise in youth. Then he ran off to join a band of roving players. Under his stage name he rose at the Hôtel de Bourgogne.

By 1635 Montfleury was a prized man of that Paris company. He played in the first cast of The Cid in 1636. He played in Horace too, four years on from that hit. Richelieu held him high and graced his wedding in 1638. That wedding was held at the great man's own country house. He died on stage in 1667, burst while playing Orestes.
britannica-1911-moore-henry:
Henry Moore, an English painter of the sea, gets a life in the 1911 Britannica. Born at York in eighteen thirty one, he was the ninth son of a painter. His father taught him most of his early art at home. He showed first at the Royal Academy in eighteen fifty three. Land views and beast works in fine point filled his first years of work.

A trip to the west of England in eighteen fifty seven turned him to the sea. That turn brought fast fame and held his brush from then on. Named works span pilot boats, lifeboats, and bays from Kent to Scotland. Paris gave him a gold prize and a knight rank in eighteen eighty seven. Critics in the text call him near peerless as a sea painter.
britannica-1911-more-henry:
Henry More, an English philosopher of the Cambridge Platonist school who lived from 1614 to 1687, is profiled in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. Born at Grantham in 1614, he was the son of earnest Calvinists. He tells us he could never swallow that hard doctrine himself. In 1631 he entered Christ's College, Cambridge, about the time Milton was leaving it. He plunged deep into the study of philosophy.

More fell for a time into scepticism, from which study of the Platonic writers freed him. Neoplatonism held him for life. He took his degrees in 1635 and 1639 and was chosen fellow of his college. He refused almost all other preferment, even the mastership of his college. He drew many thoughtful young men around him as pupils. The article presents him as the mystical side of the Cambridge movement.
britannica-1911-mortuary:
Mortuary, a word tied to the dead and to burial, is explained in a 1911 Britannica article. Its chief modern use names a building where dead bodies are kept for a short time. Bodies may wait there for checks, for naming, or for a post mortem exam.

Older uses fill much of the piece. In abbeys, a notice of a death was sent to other houses to ask for prayers. The notice and its roll were both called a mortuary. In the English Church, the word also named a set gift paid from a dead person's estate. An act of 1529 capped how much could be charged.
britannica-1911-mossop-henry: Mossop, Henry, is the subject of a short 1911 Britannica life of an Irish actor. Born in Dublin in 1729, he first trod the stage there in 1749. His first role was Zanga in a tragedy called The Revenge. In 1751 he made his first London bow as Richard the Third, under Garrick. He went back to Ireland in 1759 and won fresh praise. A bid at running a house himself ruined him. He died poor in 1774.
britannica-1911-notary:
Notary, or Notary Public, is the subject of a law entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. In Roman law the notarius was at first a slave or freedman who took shorthand notes of court work. The modern notary matches more closely the Roman tabellio. In canon law, his word was said to be worth that of two unskilled witnesses.

The office in England is very old, named in a statute of Edward the Third. Since the 1530s the archbishop of Canterbury has named notaries through the master of the faculties. Their main work is secular, not church work. A notary takes acts and contracts that need an authentic form, fixes their date, and keeps the originals. He also gives true copies, and the act of certifying is called a notarial act.
britannica-1911-observatory:
Observatory, for most of its past, was a place for star watching alone. Its science entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Rough weather notes were oft kept there, but stars were the chief work. Growth in earth magnetism and weather science later added new duties there.

Before about three hundred before Christ, no true observatory can be said to stand. Early sky notes were made by lone men at gaps, with crude tools. Strabo tells that Eudoxus kept an observatory at Cnidus in old times. The first true house of that kind rose at Alexandria in Egypt. It worked for about four hundred years of sky study and record.
britannica-1911-offertory: Offertory names the gifts of cash or goods brought by a flock in church. The 1911 Britannica note traces the word to church Latin for a place where gifts were brought. In a broad sense it means the alms raised at a church rite. In a tight sense it names a set part of the Mass rite. That part is said or sung while gifts are raised, before the bread and wine are blessed. In song craft the word names music played at that time.
britannica-1911-oldbury: Oldbury is an urban district in Worcestershire, England, five miles west of Birmingham. The short 1911 Britannica note sets it on two rail lines and on the Birmingham canal. Its count in 1901 was 25,191 people. Coal, iron, and limestone abound in the ground round the town. Works there make alkali and chemicals, rail carriages, iron, edge tools, nails, and steel, with maltings, corn mills, and brick and tile kilns as well.
britannica-1911-ordinary:
Ordinary is a law article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. In canon law, an ordinary is a church superior who holds regular jurisdiction. That power flows from the normal order of the church, not from a special grant. The term is used most often for the bishop of a diocese.

The entry explains how far the word reaches. It covers those who act in the bishop's name or by his delegation. In Germany, the related term named the whole body of diocesan officials. English law narrows the word to the bishop and the chancellor of his court. The pope is described as ordinary of the whole Roman Catholic Church. The article also notes a civil law use, for a judge with regular jurisdiction. It is a compact guide to a term readers meet in old legal texts.
britannica-1911-ossory: Ossory is a short 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on an ancient kingdom of Ireland. Its old name, Osraighe, is given in the text. The kingdom lay in the south west of Leinster. Its name is preserved by church dioceses to this day. Both the Church of Ireland and the Roman Catholic Church keep it. The kingdom was founded in the second century. Its kings held their position until the year 1100.
britannica-1911-outlawry:
Outlawry is the subject of a 1911 Britannica entry on an old process in English law. It put a man outside the shield of the law for good. The cause was a scornful refusal to come to court when called. Flight from justice could bring the same hard fate.

In Saxon times an outlaw lost his rank and his pledge of peace. He was called friendless, since aid to him drew the same pain. He was once said to bear a wolf's head, free for any man to strike. By Bracton's time he could be slain only if he fought or fled. His goods were lost in all cases, and his land in grave ones. In law he was counted as dead.
britannica-1911-palladium-chemistry:
Palladium is a metallic element of the platinum group, and this 1911 Britannica entry deals with how it is won from its ores. It is found in platinum ores, and also native, mixed with gold and silver in the gold-bearing sands of Brazil. Many methods have been devised to part it from platinum ore. The entry gives Bunsen's method of 1868 in detail.

In that method most of the platinum is first taken out as a compound with ammonium chloride. Iron then throws down the remaining metals of the group. The deposit is heated with ammonium chloride and treated with strong nitric acid. The palladium is then brought down as a potassium compound and cleaned by careful dissolving and filtering. Heated in a stream of hydrogen, that compound leaves the pure metal behind.
britannica-1911-palmer-edward-henry:
Edward Henry Palmer (1840–1882) was an English orientalist, and the bent of his mind shows early in a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Cambridge on the seventh of August 1840. His father kept a private school there. At the Perse School, the boy picked up the Romany tongue on his own.

He also made himself at home in the life of the gipsies. From school he was sent to London as a clerk in the city. Palmer disliked that life and varied it by learning French and Italian. He taught himself by seeking out the society of foreigners. In 1859 he came back to Cambridge, seemingly dying of consumption. He made a near miraculous recovery from that illness. New plans then opened, through a teacher of Hindustani he met.
britannica-1911-palmistry:
Palmistry, the reading of the hand, is treated in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is also called chiromancy, from Greek words for hand and divination. The system reads the folds and marks of the palm for character. It also claims to foretell the course of a person's life.

The article sets palmistry among the many fortune-telling systems of mankind. The wish to know the future is nearly as old as duty itself. Palmistry is one of the oldest of that whole family. In China it is said to reach back three thousand years before Christ. Greek literature treats it as a well-known belief from the earliest writings. Homer shows traces of it, gathered by a modern scholar named Blackwell. Greek and Roman medical writers dealt with the hand's signs too.
britannica-1911-pantry:
Pantry is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a household room and office. The word comes from French and Latin terms for bread. At first a pantry was a room for storing bread. From that came pantler, the officer in charge of bread. In the royal household of England, that office merged with butler. At coronations a set lord held the office of panneter. His duty was to carry the salt cellar to the royal table.

He kept those items as his fee for service. The last holder served at Elizabeth's coronation. At his death the manor went back to the Crown. The word pantry soon grew in meaning over time. It came to name a room for storing all kinds of food. Now it names the butler's room for plate and glass. There the gear for table service is kept ready.
britannica-1911-parker-john-henry:
English writer on buildings John Henry Parker, born in London in eighteen oh six, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. His father was a merchant of that city. He was schooled at Chiswick and went into book selling in eighteen twenty one.

In eighteen thirty two he took over his uncle's book shop at Oxford. The firm did well, with a set of pocket classics among its books. His glossary of building terms came out in eighteen thirty six. It helped spread the Gothic revival then under way. He later edited a work on Gothic building and wrote a handbook of his own. He also backed the repair of old churches and dug into the past of Rome.
britannica-1911-parkes-sir-henry:
Parkes, Sir Henry is a life article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about an Australian statesman. Born at Stoneleigh on the twenty-seventh of May 1815, he had only basic schooling. Failing to get on in England, he emigrated to Australia in 1839 and settled in Sydney as an ivory turner. His poems won praise from Tennyson himself.

He campaigned against convict transport and founded the Empire newspaper in 1849. He fought for responsible government and passed a Public Schools Act in 1866. In 1872 he became prime minister, threw the colony open to free trade, and held office until 1875.
britannica-1911-peacham-henry:
Henry Peacham, who lived from about 1576 to about 1643, was an English writer. The 1911 Britannica article says he was the son of a curate who wrote a famed book on rhetoric. The son took degrees at Trinity College, Cambridge. He taught school at Wymondham in Norfolk for a time. In 1612 he settled in London, earning his bread as tutor to young men bound for the universities. His first book, on pen and water-colour drawing, came out in 1606.

From 1613 Peacham spent two years abroad, part as tutor to the sons of the earl of Arundel. He saw Italy, France, and the Low Countries. Back in London he was charged with libel on the king, on papers that were not his. His chief work, the Compleat Gentleman, came out in 1622. Larger forms came out in 1626 and 1627.
britannica-1911-pearson-charles-henry:
Charles Henry Pearson, a historian who turned statesman, is tracked in a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in London in 1830, he shone at Rugby and Oxford. At Oriel College he won a fellowship in 1854. Weak health and poor eyes killed his plan to heal men. In 1855 he took a post in English letters at King's College.

Pearson soon held the chair of modern history at that college. Long trips fed his pen, to Russia first in 1858. He rode through Poland in its rising of 1863 as well. A trip to America in 1868 stocked his later big book. His first tome on early England drew fierce fire from Freeman. He wrote for the great reviews and ran one of his own.
britannica-1911-pelham-henry:
Henry Pelham is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Britannica. He was prime minister of England from 1696 to 1754. He was the younger brother of the duke of Newcastle. He was born in 1696, a younger son of a baron. He was taught at home and at Oxford. As a youth he served as a volunteer at Preston. That fight took place in the year 1715.

He spent time abroad and then entered parliament in 1717. Family pull and Walpole favour raised him fast in posts. In 1724 he became secretary for war in the ministry. In 1730 he moved to a richer post as paymaster. He backed Walpole on the excise tax clash of the day. In 1743 he became prime minister with the purse post. His brother held great sway in the cabinet as well.
britannica-1911-percy-sir-henry:
Sir Henry Percy, called Hotspur, lived from 1364 to 1403. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica makes him the eldest son of the earl of Northumberland. He saw war at fourteen at the siege of Berwick. Border war against the Scots won him his fiery name. His foes gave it for his zeal in the field. In 1386 he was sent to Calais to raid French lands.

Ballad and story know him best from Otterburn. In 1388 the Scots took his pennon before the walls of Newcastle. Douglas swore to fix that flag on his own castle walls. Percy chased the Scots to Otterburn to win it back. Douglas fell in the night fight there. Percy and his brother were both taken prisoner. A heavy ransom, aided by the king, freed him. In 1399 he and his father joined Henry of Lancaster.
britannica-1911-perfumery:
Perfumery is the art of making scents that please the nose. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica splits perfumes into two classes. The first class holds simple scented bodies from plants and beasts. Made chemical scents join that class too. The second class holds blends of the first, mixed in set shares. Toilet powders, tooth powders, and sachets fall in that group.

Animal scents head the list of simple kinds. Ambergris, castor, civet, and musk are the four named. Next come the essential oils drawn from stems, leaves, and blooms. Scented fats, charged by soaking in flowers, form a third kind. Gums and balsams that ooze from trees form a fourth. Lab made copies of natural scents form a fifth. Most goods on sale are blends, the entry notes. Fancy names on those blends may hide what is inside them.
britannica-1911-perjury:
Perjury is a law article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about the crime of a false oath. A false oath is a sworn claim of fact, made in a court case, that the speaker does not hold to be true. The claim must touch a point that bears on the case.

The article traces how the crime was viewed in past ages. At first a false oath counted as a sin more than a crime. Its harm was held to fall on God, in whose name the oath was sworn. In Roman law the perjurer faced the wrath of heaven, not the courts. In England church courts held the matter at first. The old common law dealt long only with false oaths by jurors. In time the plain courts took the whole field.
britannica-1911-perkin-sir-william-henry:
Sir William Henry Perkin (1838–1907) was an English chemist born in London on the 12th of March 1838. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica follows him from the Royal College of Chemistry, where he rose to assist Hofmann, into business on his own. Seeking to make quinine by art in a rough home laboratory, he turned instead to work on aniline.

In 1856 that work gave him the colouring stuff soon known as mauve, and he patented the process at once. At eighteen he left the college and, with his father and brother, built works at Greenford Green that were running by the end of 1857. That year marks the start of the coal-tar colour industry. He later found a workable way to make alizarin, the red dye of madder, and kept a hold on its trade for years.
britannica-1911-phillpotts-henry:
Henry Phillpotts was an English bishop born at Bridgwater, schooled at a college school and at Oxford. He was made a fellow of an Oxford college while still in his teens, took orders, and was picked as a preacher for the whole college body. Church posts in the north then came to him in a steady stream.

For twenty years he served as chaplain to a bishop of Durham, the 1911 Britannica entry says. Rich livings, a canon post, and a dean post followed in turn. At last he was made bishop of Exeter, and held with that see a canon post at Durham. His writ works are a host of speeches and tracts. Among them stand those tied to his famed clash with a writer on the rights of Catholics in the realm.
britannica-1911-phylactery:
Phylactery is a Greek word for a guard against harm. This 1911 Britannica entry explains how the name came to be used for the tefillin worn by observant Jews at morning prayer. These are two small leather cases held by straps, one bound on the left arm and one on the head. Each case holds short passages from the Law, written in Hebrew on parchment. The texts come from Exodus and from Deuteronomy.

The entry traces the custom back to the Pharisees and notes that it was not shared by the Sadducees or by the Samaritan community. In time it became a mark of strict Jewish practice. The entry also links the tefillin with two kindred signs, the fringes on a garment and the parchment case fixed to a doorpost. All three serve as daily reminders of duty to God.
britannica-1911-pike-zebulon-montgomery:
Zebulon Montgomery Pike, an American explorer and soldier who lived from 1779 to 1813, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born in New Jersey, the son of an army officer. He joined his father's company as a cadet about 1794. By 1799 he held the rank of first lieutenant.

In August 1805 Pike set out from Saint Louis with twenty men to find the headwaters of the Mississippi. He met Chippewa chiefs, urged them to expel whisky traders, and bought land for a fort near the Saint Croix river. He reached Leech Lake in February 1806 and took it for the main source of the river. In 1806 a new task sent him west with a party of Osages to return to their homes. That march took him across Kansas to a grand council with the Pawnees.
britannica-1911-pitlochry: Pitlochry is a village of Perthshire in Scotland, on the Highland railway line north west of Perth. The short 1911 Britannica note gives its count in 1901 as 1,541 people. It lies on the left bank of the river Tummel, 350 feet above the sea. The spot is a loved health resort and tourist centre. Sights near by span the pass of Killiecrankie, the falls of the Tummel, a famed Queen's View, and Loch Tummel to the west.
britannica-1911-polyandry:
Polyandry, from Greek words for many and man, is a system of marriage described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. In it one woman is wed to several men who are her husbands alone. Thinkers have traced the custom to poverty and to life in poor lands. There a check on births was held to be a plain need for survival.

Others link it to the killing of girl infants in such lands. Two scholars named in the entry hold it as a stage all human progress had to pass. It must not be mixed up with communal marriage, where a woman is held as the property of the whole tribe. Two kinds of the custom are set apart in the text. In one the husbands are not kin to each other, as among the Nairs of India. In the Tibetan kind a woman weds all the brothers of one house.
britannica-1911-porter-henry:
Henry Porter flourished from 1596 to 1599 and was an English dramatist. The 1911 Britannica life knows him as author of The Two Angry Women of Abingdon. He may be the Henry Porter who entered Brasenose College, Oxford, in 1589. That Porter was sixteen then and the son of a London gentleman. From 1596 Porter wrote plays for Henslowe and the admiral's men.

His closest partner in that work seems to have been Henry Chettle. Early notes in Henslowe's Diary speak of him with respect and care. Large sums paid to Mister Porter prove his plays drew crowds in town. In February 1599 Henslowe bought sole rights in any play Porter touched. The price was an advance of forty shillings on the deal.
britannica-1911-prebendary:
Prebendary is the title of a churchman who holds a prebend, explained in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. A prebend is a grant of land or a pension of money for the keep of a priest. It is tied to a cathedral or a great church. The word at first meant the daily rations dealt out to soldiers.

In the early Church the grant meant a daily share of food and drink. Later, church funds were split into set parts, and each part kept its old name. The clergy who held such parts were canons, and the two titles are often used as one. A simple prebendary has no cure of souls, just his pay. One who is also a dignitary holds rule over others. No man may hold two prebends in the same church.
britannica-1911-queensferry:
Queensferry, a small burgh on the Firth of Forth, is placed in a town entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on the south shore, north-west of Edinburgh. Fewer than two thousand people lived there in 1901. Old use set it apart, for its ferry crossed to Dunfermline and the north shore. Queen Margaret, wife of Malcolm Canmore, used that crossing and gave it its name.

The Hawes Inn there shows in Scott's tale The Antiquary. The burgh won royal rank in stages from the fourteenth century on. Sights near by take in Dalmeny church, a pure Norman work. Dalmeny House, seat of the earl of Rosebery, stands in wooded grounds east of town. Barnbougle Castle looks out on Drum Sands in the park.
britannica-1911-robbery:
Robbery in law is theft from a person by force or threat of force. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica draws it from an old French word for stealing. It counts as larceny with violence added in English law. Terms of penal servitude up to fourteen years could follow a finding.

In Scotland the same crime bears the old name stouthrief, it notes. In the United States each state sets its own law on the crime. Grades of the offense and wide views of force mark that system. Train robbery draws special laws in states where it ran rife. Robbery at sea by pirates is a federal crime with death as penalty.
britannica-1911-rosary:
Rosary is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a Catholic devotion. The Latin name for it is given as rosarium. The devotion is made up of set prayers told on beads. It holds fifteen Paternosters and Glorias in full. It also holds one hundred fifty Aves in full. The whole is split into three parts of five decades. Each decade holds one Pater, ten Aves, and a Gloria.

Each decade also has a subject for meditation. Those subjects come from the mysteries of Christ's life. Some come from the life of the Blessed Virgin. The habit of repeating prayers runs back to early times. One hermit of the fourth century used pebbles to count. He cast one away for each of three hundred prayers. Lay brothers in many orders said Paternosters in place of books. The Ave Maria joined the practice in later centuries.
britannica-1911-rosny-joseph-henry:
Rosny is a pen name shared by two French novelist brothers. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sorts their joint and solo work. Both Boex brothers were born at Brussels in the 1850s. The elder wrote the earliest novels under the name alone.

Science fills their tales, from stars to the study of man. Society, not the lone soul, is their point of view. Yet their figures stand out as real and sharply drawn. Early books show London reform and Paris anarchist parties. Peasant tales of brutal force stand beside those city works. In 1891 a tale of prehistoric man won them wide note. They had joined a public protest against Zola in 1887. Goncourt named them among the first of his new academy. Later novels treat sacrifice, charity, and lost souls in Paris.
britannica-1911-saint-johnsbury:
Saint Johnsbury is a township and county seat in Vermont, set on the Passumpsic river about 34 miles from Montpelier. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives the township 8,098 people in 1910, up from 6,567 in 1890. Two railways serve it, and its farms lean heavily on dairying.

The village holds the Saint Johnsbury Academy of 1842 and an Athenaeum of 1871 with a library and art gallery. The Fairbanks Museum of Natural Science opened in 1891, and the great scales works of the Fairbanks company anchors its trade. Other works turn out farm tools, steam hammers, granite, furniture, and carriages. The township was granted in 1786 and named for Jean Hector Saint John de Crèvecœur, whose Letters of an American Farmer drew many settlers to America.
britannica-1911-sayce-archibald-henry:
Archibald Henry Sayce was a British scholar of the ancient East and its tongues. He was born at Shirehampton on the twenty fifth of September eighteen forty six. His life entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the son of a vicar and was educated at Bath and Oxford.

Sayce became a fellow of Queen College, Oxford, in eighteen sixty nine. In eighteen ninety one he was elected teacher of Assyriology at Oxford. He poured his force into Bible and Eastern studies all his life. Later scholars changed some of his dates and readings in their work. Still, the entry rates his service to Eastern learning as beyond measure.
britannica-1911-scudery:
Scudery is the family name at the heart of an entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. The family was said to be of noble Italian stock that moved to Provence in France. Yet it is known chiefly through a brother and sister of the seventeen hundreds. Georges de Scudery, the elder, was born at Havre in sixteen hundred one.

The entry tells how Georges served in the army before he turned to writing before age thirty. He became a marked figure in Paris in the middle of the century. He won the favour of Richelieu by his attack on Corneille. His letter against the play the Cid is noted as a key act in that feud.
britannica-1911-scullery: Scullery is the back kitchen where dishes and kettles are washed. A short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica traces the word through old tongues. It comes from a Latin term for the keeper of dishes. That term passed through Old French forms into English. The entry also parts scullery from scullion, a kitchen helper word. That second word comes from a French term for a dish cloth. The rough work of a house, as well as the washing, belonged to the scullery room.
britannica-1911-sherry: Sherry first named wine from Xeres, now Jerez de la Frontera near Cadiz in Spain, in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The name now covers the strong white wines of the south of Spain, the lower grades aside. An early English form was sherris, short for sherris wine or sherris sack. That form was taken for a plural by mistake. Sherry was then formed from it as a singular, and the new form stuck in common use across the English speaking world.
britannica-1911-shorthouse-joseph-henry:
Joseph Henry Shorthouse (1834-1903) was an English novelist from Birmingham. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica notes he spent his life in his father chemical works. School at Tottenham and a local essay club fed his taste for books. No book bore his name until he neared fifty years of age.

His novel John Inglesant waited three years for a publisher in vain. He printed one hundred copies himself, and one reached Mrs Humphry Ward. Macmillan took it up, and Gladstone praise made its fame at once. Later novels never matched that first great success in public eyes. A Quaker turned Anglican, he wrote of faith and bigotry in rich prose.
britannica-1911-shrewsbury:
Shrewsbury is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a town in Shropshire, England. It is a borough, a market town, and the county town. A count from 1901 gives it 28,395 people. It is situated on both banks of the river Severn. Most of it lies on a peninsula formed by the river. That peninsula sits on the left bank of the Severn. Two railway companies serve the town with a joint station.

Water communication runs eastward by the Shrewsbury canal. The English bridge crosses the river eastward from the peninsula. The Welsh bridge crosses it in the westward direction. Kingsland and Greyfriars bridges cross to the south. The joint railway station is reached by a massive iron bridge. The streets are hilly and irregular in their layout. Many retain ancient names, curiously corrupted over time.
britannica-1911-sidgwick-henry:
Henry Sidgwick (1838–1900) was an English thinker, born at Skipton in Yorkshire on 31 May 1838. His father was head of the grammar school there. Sidgwick was schooled at Rugby and at Trinity College, Cambridge, where his course was a bright one. In 1859 he was senior classic, a medallist, and a Craven scholar. That year he was made a fellow of Trinity and soon a teacher of classics there.

Sidgwick held that post for ten years, but in 1869 he swapped it for a post in moral thought. That field had drawn more and more of his mind. That same year he found he could no longer call himself a member of the Church of England, and he gave up his fellowship. He kept his teaching post, and in 1881 he was made an honorary fellow.
britannica-1911-sidney-sir-henry:
Sir Henry Sidney (1520-1586) was lord deputy of Ireland, and this 1911 Britannica entry opens with his years at court. He was the eldest son of Sir William Sidney, a leading courtier under Henry the Eighth and Edward the Sixth. His father gained wide grants of land, including Penshurst in Kent, which became the family's chief home. Henry was raised at court as the companion of Prince Edward.

In 1556 he went to Ireland with the lord deputy, the earl of Sussex, who had married his sister. He helped in the military measures meant to bring the native Irish chiefs under the English Crown. In 1557 he ravaged the island of Rathlin, and in the next year, with Sussex away in England, he governed Ireland alone with marked skill.
britannica-1911-sleeman-sir-william-henr:
Sir William Henry Sleeman (1788-1856) was an Indian soldier and administrator famed for breaking the Thugs, and this 1911 Britannica entry gives his career. He was born at Stratton in Cornwall, the son of a yeoman and excise supervisor. In 1809 he joined the Bengal army and served in the Nepal War. In 1820 he became an assistant to the governor-general's agent in the Saugor and Nerbudda territories.

His name rests on the fight against the Thugs, the religious murderers of India. He became superintendent of the work against them in 1835 and commissioner for stamping out Thuggi and Dacoity in 1839. More than 1,400 Thugs were hanged or transported for life, caught only through informers, who were guarded in a special gaol. Sleeman later served as resident at Gwalior and at Lucknow, where he opposed the annexation of Oudh in vain.
britannica-1911-smart-henry:
Henry Smart was an English organist and composer who lived from eighteen thirteen to eighteen seventy nine. Born in London, he was a nephew of Sir George Smart. He first studied for the law, then gave it up for music. In eighteen thirty one he became organist of Blackburn parish church. Later posts took him to churches in London, and last to Saint Pancras in eighteen sixty four.

Smart is now known most for his organ music, which the entry calls full and sweet in tone, if not bold in new ideas. He also wrote vocal works and some of the best part songs of his time. His cantatas include The Bride of Dunkerron and Jacob. His opera Bertha was staged at the Haymarket in eighteen fifty five. He was blind for the last fifteen years of his life.
britannica-1911-spelman-sir-henry:
Sir Henry Spelman, who lived from about 1564 to 1641, was an English student of old records. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica opens with his birth in Norfolk. He took his degree at Trinity College, Cambridge, in 1583. His father's death left him the family estates. He joined Lincoln's Inn, then went home to Norfolk in 1590. There he wrote on the history and relics of his county. He sat in the Society of Antiquaries with Cotton and Camden.

Long court fights over abbey leases shaped his later work. He later stood among those who charged Bacon with graft. His tract against the misuse of churches moved many lay owners. They gave back church goods they had taken. His History and Fate of Sacrilege grew out of that tract. The king blocked his bid to revive the antiquaries' society in 1614.
britannica-1911-stationery:
Stationery, the goods of the desk, is set out in a trade entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word first named all that stationers sold in their shops. Those men were booksellers with set stands by churches and markets. Their guild was formed as far back as the year 1403. The full livery company was not chartered till the year 1556.

At Stationers' Hall in London a book logs new works for rights. A state office of the same name serves the government desks. It feeds paper goods to parliament and the great departments. It steers the state printing work of the realm as well. The name now wraps all writing gear and desk tools. Pens, ink, paper, and bindery work each get their own heads.
britannica-1911-stevens-henry:
Henry Stevens lived from 1819 to 1886 and was an American bibliographer. The 1911 Britannica life opens in Barnet, Vermont, where he was born. He studied at Middlebury College in 1838 and at Yale after that. He took his Yale degree in 1843 and read law at Cambridge. In 1845 he crossed to London, where most of his life was spent.

In London he gathered Americana for the British Museum with great zeal. Panizzi, the chief librarian there, set him to that vast task. He bought for the Smithsonian and for the Library of Congress too. For James Lenox of New York he secured rare books of high worth. He did the same for the John Carter Brown library at Providence.
britannica-1911-stichometry:
Stichometry is the measure of old texts by lines of a fixed length. The Greek word for such a line means a row. Greeks and Romans used this count to gauge the length of their works. In verse, the count was of the verse lines themselves. In prose, a standard line had to be set, since no two scribes wrote lines of the same length.

On the word of Galen, the Greek unit was the mean Homeric line. It held about thirty-six letters, or sixteen syllables. The count of lines in a roll was noted at the end of the work. For a work spread over more than one roll, a grand total was given too. The aim of the count was a trade one, the article notes. The count can be traced back to the fourth century before Christ.
britannica-1911-stoddard-richard-henry:
Richard Henry Stoddard is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was an American author born in Massachusetts in eighteen twenty five. He spent most of his boyhood in New York City streets. There he learned the trades of smith and iron founder as a youth.

The entry tells how he quit the forge to write for a living at last. A famed tale writer helped him win a port post in the city. Clerk, book man, and review posts filled his long years of work. He cut and shaped sets of verse by old English poets for new readers. His own books of song and his long press work fill the tale.
britannica-1911-stoichiometry:
Stoichiometry is the subject of a chemistry entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. The Greek roots of the word mean basic parts and measure. Benjamin Richter coined the term for the study of how much acid and base cancel each other out. That sense was later widened to cover any chemical change.

In its wide sense it covers the masses that take part in a reaction. The entry narrows its own focus to one branch of that field. That branch deals with the weights of elements and of compounds. Readers are sent to other entries for the work of Richter and for the broader treatment of elements and atoms.
britannica-1911-strawberry:
Strawberry is a dessert fruit with an odd build. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica explains its true form and breeding. The genus holds about eight kinds across the north temperate zone. One kind grows wild as far south as Chile.

The plant creeps by long thin runners that root at the tip. Its leaves most often bear three leaflets in a fan. What looks like the fruit is a swollen flower stalk. The true fruits are the small pips set in its flesh. A rose hip shows the same parts turned the other way. Wild kinds from Britain, Virginia, and Chile were crossed for years. Garden sorts now blend those lines past all tracing.
britannica-1911-style-literary:
Style, in literature, is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The entry defines it as language seen from the side of the traits it reveals. By likeness, in other arts it names a way of working marked by its own clear features. The word comes from the stilus, the tool of metal, wood, or ivory that pressed words into wax tablets in classic times.

By a shift of thought, the name passed from the tool that makes the mark to the sentences marked by it. To turn the stylus was to correct what had been written with its blunt end. That act answers, the article says, to the discipline and self-criticism on which fine writing depends. A writer of force would press a firm and full mark. A scribe of quick and fleeting habit would press unevenly and leave a less steady text.
britannica-1911-surgery:
Surgery is a profession article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about the art of healing by hand and by tools. The word comes through French from a Greek term for handwork. The article defines surgery as the cure of disease or injury by operation. Its history, it says, is as old as human need in all lands.

The oldest skills were plain ones. Men learned to stop blood, to pull out arrows, and to bind up wounds. They learned to hold broken limbs firm with splints. From such roots the art grew into a trained profession with schools and rules. The entry traces that growth across ages and countries. For a reader it gives both a working picture of what a surgeon does and a long view of how the craft rose from first aid to a science.
britannica-1911-swinton-and-pendlebury:
Swinton and Pendlebury is a town article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a district in Lancashire, England. It stands five miles north-west of Manchester, on the Lancashire and Yorkshire railway. The count of 1901 gave it 27,005 people. The article treats it as a cotton and coal town with deep roots.

Its church of Saint Peter is a fine stone building with a tall west tower. Sir Gilbert Scott designed it, and it was built in 1869. The Swinton industrial schools, opened in February 1846, form a range of brick buildings in twenty acres of grounds. Cotton making and coal mining are the chief trades of the district. In old times a large part of Swinton belonged to the Knights Hospitallers of Saint John of Jerusalem. That early holding gives the town a past far older than its mills.
britannica-1911-tacheometry:
Tacheometry is a 1911 Britannica article on a system of rapid surveying. The word joins two Greek roots, one for quick and one for a measure. By this system, the positions of points on the earth are fixed fast. Both their horizontal and vertical places are found. No chain or tape is used, and no separate levelling instrument.

The ordinary methods use a theodolite, a chain, and a levelling tool. They serve fairly well when the ground is clear of obstacles. They also serve when the ground is not very steep. But the work grows extremely cumbrous in rough country. Bush cover and ravines make it so. Chain measures are then both slow and open to large error. Levelling, too, goes forward at great disadvantage in speed. The article sets out a quicker way to map broken ground. Survey readers get the case for speed in the field.
britannica-1911-tate-sir-henry:
Sir Henry Tate (1819–1899) was an English merchant and the founder of the National Gallery of British Art. He was born at Chorley in Lancashire in 1819. His father, a minister of religion, put him into trade in Liverpool. He grew rich as a sugar broker. About 1874 he moved to London, where he grew his firm by much. He made the name of Tate's Cube Sugar known all over the world.

From early in his career, Tate gave large sums to good causes and to schools. He gave £42,000 to the University College at Liverpool, set up in 1881. He gave a still larger sum to the hospitals of Liverpool. In London he gave four free public libraries to the parish of Lambeth. His love of art came in later years.
britannica-1911-taylor-sir-henry:
Sir Henry Taylor, an English poet and official, was born in Durham in eighteen hundred. His family had been small landowners there for some generations past. His mother died while he was still an infant in arms. His father, a man of studious tastes, schooled him at home in the main. Finding him slower than his brothers, his father let him join the navy.

Taylor spent only eight months at sea, finding the life uncongenial to him. He then took a clerkship in a stores office in London. Typhus fever struck him soon after, and carried off both his brothers. In a few years his office was abolished while he served in the West Indies. Through his stepmother he met the friend and neighbour of Wordsworth. That link brought him to Wordsworth and Southey, and his powers grew fast.
britannica-1911-taylor-zachary:
Zachary Taylor (1784-1850), the twelfth president of the United States, is the subject of this long 1911 Britannica life story. He was born in Orange county, Virginia, but his father, a veteran of the War of Independence, moved the family to Kentucky while Zachary was a baby. He grew up on the frontier near Louisville, hardy and bold but with little formal schooling. In 1808 he joined the army as a first lieutenant in the infantry.

The entry follows his slow rise through frontier posts and wars. He won praise for holding Fort Harrison against attack in the war of 1812 and was made a major. He later served in the Black Hawk War, where Black Hawk gave himself up to him. In 1836 he was sent to fight the Seminoles in Florida. There he won a hard fight on Christmas Day 1837.
britannica-1911-tellicherry:
Tellicherry is a seaport of British India described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It lies in the Malabar district of Madras, between Cannanore and the French post of Mahe. Its people numbered 27,883 in 1901. The town is held a healthy and fair place. It is built on a knot of wooded hills that run down to the sea, and a reef of rock guards it.

The town and its suburbs spread over about five square miles and were once walled in mud. The old fort still stands north of the town. The East India Company set up a factory here in 1683 for the trade in pepper and cardamoms. For two years, from 1780, the town held out in a siege by the general of Hyder. In the wars with Mysore it was the base for the climb of the Ghats.
britannica-1911-thayer-joseph-henry:
Joseph Henry Thayer is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was an American scholar of the Bible born in Boston in eighteen twenty eight. He was schooled in Boston and took his first degree at Harvard. He then trained for the ministry at two schools of divinity.

The entry notes his years as a preacher and as a war chaplain in the field. He taught sacred texts at one school for close to twenty years. He then took a top chair of New Testament study at Harvard. His chief work is a Greek word book of the New Testament in English. He also served on the team that revised the English Bible.
britannica-1911-tracery:
Tracery is an architecture term explained in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word is a late coinage from trace, drawn from a Latin verb meaning to draw. It names the crossing rib-work in the upper part of a Gothic window. The term also covers like work in vaults, on walls, and in screens.

Window tracery falls into two kinds, plate tracery and bar tracery. The second grew out of the first and at last replaced it wholly. Early English windows were narrow slits, often grouped under one wide arch. Piercing the head of that arch with a round light made plate tracery. In France that round opening filled the full width and was rich with cusping. Moulded bars then gave the chief lights more depth and force. From that change, the article shows, bar tracery rose to its full designs.
britannica-1911-treasury:
Treasury is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a place and a department. The word first names a place for storing treasure. Its roots run through French and Latin words for a hoard. It also names the government department that manages public revenue. The head of that department was a key early official. He managed the king's hoard or treasury in England. 

In those days the main object of government seemed plain. He received the title of lord high treasurer in time. He ranked as the third great officer of state. In time the English treasury split into two departments. Since 1714 that high office has been held in commission. A board administers its duties in place of one man. That board holds a first lord and a chancellor. Four or more junior lords sit on it as well.
britannica-1911-trescot-william-henry:
William Henry Trescot is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Trescot was an American diplomat born in Charleston in 1822. He studied at Charleston College and read law at Harvard. He was called to the bar in 1843 and served at the London legation in the eighteen fifties.

The article follows his work as assistant secretary of state in 1860. He held a key place as a South Carolina man close to President Buchanan. He worked to stop a clash over Fort Sumter before the state voted on leaving the Union. Later he served his state, then acted for the nation in fishery, treaty, and trade talks. He died in 1898. His books on early American foreign policy are also named.
britannica-1911-triangle-geometry:
Triangle, in geometry, is a figure shut in by three lines. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sums the plane form chief rules. Straight lines make a plane triangle of the common kind. Lines on a sphere make a ball surface form instead.

Any corner can be taken as the top, or vertex. The side across from it is called the base. Three sides and three angles make the six elements. Kinds take names from their sides or their angles. Equal sided, two equal, and all unequal sorts are named. Right, blunt, and sharp angled kinds fill the second list. Euclid first book proves the core facts about them. Base angles of a two equal triangle are themselves equal. All three inner angles sum to two right angles. Rules also tell when two triangles match in every part.
britannica-1911-tutbury:
Tutbury is a town article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a town in Staffordshire, England. It stands on the river Dove, a stream that forms the border with Derbyshire. The town lies four and a half miles north west of Burton-upon-Trent. Its count in 1901 was 1,971.

The article names a fine church with rich Norman work in its nave. Ruins of a large castle stand high above the valley. A gateway of the 1300s and a broad tilt yard are among the remains. Glass making is the chief trade, and alabaster is dug near by. The early tale of the town is dark, the text allows. It is said to have been a seat of the Mercian kings. The castle later held Mary Queen of Scots for a time.
britannica-1911-usury:
Usury is set out in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica as an old term that held more than one sense. The Latin word at its root means use, or the gain from use. Till a late date the one term hid in it more than one kind of gain on a loan. The text quotes the old law of the Jews on the point.

That law bans loan gain from a brother in full. It bans it on coin, on food, and on a thing of any kind. To a man from past the tribe, the same law lets gain be charged. In that one ban, all kinds of loan gain are mixed as one. The law of faith thus ran flat against the pull of trade. The entry starts the long tale of how that sense was cut down.
britannica-1911-venn-henry:
Henry Venn, an English evangelical clergyman, is the subject of a life story in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Barnes in Surrey in seventeen twenty five, he was educated at Cambridge. He took orders in seventeen forty seven and became a fellow of Queens' College two years later. He then held curacies in Cambridgeshire and London.

He served at Clapham and was chosen as a lecturer at a London church. From seventeen fifty nine he was vicar of Huddersfield for more than a decade. He then exchanged to a living in Huntingdonshire. Besides leading the evangelical revival, he was known as the author of a famed devotional work.
britannica-1911-walsh-john-henry:
Walsh, John Henry is a life article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about an English writer on sport who wrote under the name Stonehenge. Born at Hackney, London, on the twenty-first of October 1810, Walsh trained in medicine and became a fellow of the Royal College of Surgeons in 1844. He moved from the country to London in 1852.

His first big book, The Greyhound, came out in 1853 from papers he had placed in Bell's Life, and his Manual of British Rural Sports of 1856 ran through many editions. That year he joined the staff of The Field and became its editor at the close of 1857. As editor he ran years of trials of guns, rifles, and powders that did much to improve sporting firearms. He died at Putney in 1888.
britannica-1911-walter-of-coventry:
Walter of Coventry, who flourished about twelve ninety, was an English monk and chronicler. He seems to have been tied to a religious house in the province of York. He is known only through the history book that bears his name, the Memoriale. That word is usually taken to mean a commonplace book of notes. Some critics hold that Walter merely gave the book, not wrote it.

The weight of opinion is against that view, the entry states plainly. The author lived in the reign of Edward the First of England. His main tale runs only to the year twelve twenty five. For the years from twelve o one on, it copies a chronicle of the time. That source was the work of a canon of Barnwell in Cambridgeshire. He was well placed to watch the barons war of King John's reign.
britannica-1911-wardlaw-henry:
Henry Wardlaw died in 1440 and was a Scottish church leader of rank. The 1911 Britannica life makes him son of Sir Andrew Wardlaw. His uncle Walter was bishop of Glasgow and, some said, a cardinal. Henry was schooled at Oxford and at Paris in his youth. He came home to Scotland about the year 1385 in time.

Rich church posts came to him through his strong family ties. Time at the papal court at Avignon shaped his early career too. While there he was chosen bishop of St Andrews in 1403. Back home he taught the young prince who became James the First. He helped win that king's release from English hands in time. In May 1424 he crowned James with his own hands at last.
britannica-1911-westbury:
Westbury is an urban district in Wiltshire in England, as the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets out. It stands on the river Biss, a small branch of the Lower Avon. Its count in 1901 was 3,305 souls in the district. It lies within 3 miles of the Somerset border, sheltered on the east by the high tableland of Salisbury Plain.

All Saints church is Norman and later work, with a magnificent nave in its build. In its south transept stands a monument to Sir James Ley, earl of Marlborough. A chained black letter copy of the Paraphrase of Erasmus is preserved in its south chapel. In the suburb of Westbury Leigh is the Palace Garden, a moated site said to have been a royal residence in Saxon times. Westbury figures in Domesday as a manor held by the king, and it was granted away by Henry the Second in 1172.
britannica-1911-whale-fishery:
Whale-fishery, or whaling, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica article. It is the pursuit and capture of the larger species of whales. Man most likely first learned the value of whale products from stranded animals. When he first ventured to hunt them in the open ocean, no one can now tell.

From King Alfred's account of Ohthere's voyage to the White Sea, one fact is clear. The Norwegians were expert whalers at least a thousand years ago. From the tenth to the sixteenth centuries, the Basques carried on the trade. Their ports were Bayonne, Biarritz, and St Jean-de-Luz. San Sebastian and other French and Spanish ports joined in. The trade in whale products was a lucrative one. The article traces an old sea craft from beach salvage to ocean hunting. Its history runs from Norse sailors to Basque fleets.
britannica-1911-wharton-henry:
Henry Wharton is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica life of an English writer. He lived from 1664 to 1695. He was a son of the Reverend Edmund Wharton of Worstead. He was born at Worstead in Norfolk in November 1664. His father schooled him at home in his youth. He then went to Gonville and Caius College, Cambridge. His university career there was a brilliant one.

In 1686 he entered the service of William Cave. Cave was a historian of the church of his day. Wharton helped him in his literary work for a time. He left, feeling his help was not prized enough. In 1687 he was ordained a deacon of the church. In 1688 he met Archbishop William Sancroft of Canterbury. The archbishop thought highly of his character and gifts. He made Wharton one of his chaplains in reply.
britannica-1911-whig-and-tory:
Whig and Tory are the names of two opposed political parties in England, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica opens its entry by quarrelling over where the words came from. Whig has been tied to a Scots word for whey, as a taunt at sour faced Lowlanders. It has also been read as the initials of a Covenanter motto, or tied to a word for driving horses.

The entry settles on a Scots Gaelic term for cattle and horse thieves, passed to the backers of the Presbyterian cause in Scotland. Tory comes from an Irish phrase meaning come, oh king, tied to the native levies who fought for the loyalist cause in the civil wars. Parliamentary parties as such arose, the entry says, as soon as Parliament aimed at the lead in the state. In 1641 the Long Parliament split over church reform, and then into Cavaliers and Roundheads.
britannica-1911-wilson-henry:
Henry Wilson, vice president of the United States from eighteen seventy three, was born in New Hampshire in eighteen twelve. His birth name was Jeremiah Colbaith, changed later by law. His father was a day labourer and very poor in means. At ten the boy went to work as a farm labourer for hire. He was fond of reading and read more than a thousand books.

At twenty one Wilson had his name changed by act of the legislature. He walked to Natick in Massachusetts and learned the trade of shoemaker there. In his free hours he studied much and read with hunger. For short spells he studied at academies in three New Hampshire towns. He then set up with success as a maker of shoes. Public speaking for a presidential bid in eighteen forty drew notice to him.
britannica-1911-wotton-sir-henry:
