His Spicilegium of 1655 to 1677, a harvest of texts hidden in French libraries, above all Benedictine ones, remains his chief monument, with editions of Barnabas, Lanfranc, and Guibert beside it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-malmesbury:
Malmesbury was a small, decayed market town in Wiltshire, ninety-five miles west of London. It once held a mitred parliamentary abbey of Benedictine monks. Its origin lay with Maildubh, an Irish monk and teacher who settled there about the mid-seventh century. The place was then a border town between Welsh and English, and between Wessex and Mercia.

Maildubh's school drew many pupils, chief among them Aldhelm, kin to King Ina of Wessex. Later, under King John, a raider named Robert slew monks who failed to flee in 1140. John then gave the abbey the castle site and pulled the castle down to widen its forty-five-acre enclosure. A walled town with four gates, a Knights' preceptory, three churches, a mint, and a merchants' guild marked its prosperity, crowned by a vast abbey church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-manila-observ:
Manila Observatory was founded by the Jesuit Frederic Faura in 1865. Its work grew from one man's long study of typhoons, known in the Philippines as baguio, among the islands' worst foes.

Faura, a professor at Ateneo College, hoped to foretell storms and limit their damage. On 7 July 1879 he predicted a baguio over northern Luzon, and events proved him right. It was the first forecast in the Far East of a typhoon's existence, length, and course. A second correct warning for Manila followed that November. City merchants then funded wider work, and Hong Kong merchants asked for his forecasts once a cable linked the cities in 1880. His Faura barometer of 1886 soon served navigators across Philippine and China seas. Under Father Algue the service grew into a telegraph network, with reports cabled twice daily from Japan, Formosa, China, and Indo-China.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-margaret-haug:
Margaret Haughery, called the mother of the orphans, was born in Cavan, Ireland, about 1814 and died at New Orleans on 9 February 1882. Her parents died at Baltimore in 1822, leaving her untaught in reading and writing. She married Charles Haughery in 1835 and moved to New Orleans, where husband and infant died within a year.

The Female Orphan Asylum of 1840 was largely her work, and she cleared it of debt. In yellow fever years she nursed victims house to house, regardless of race or creed, promising dying mothers to care for their children. She ran a dairy, then a bakery, the South's first steam bakery, driving her own rounds. She braved General Butler in the Civil War to carry flour across lines for her orphans. New Orleans mourned her death as a public calamity, and a monument rose in Margaret Place in 1884.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-masonry-freem:
Masonry, or Freemasonry, is treated in this vast article under name and definition, origin and early history, fundamental principles and spirit, and propagation and evolution. It also covers organisation and statistics, inner work of symbolism and oaths, outer work of achievements and methods, and action of state and Church authorities. 

Modern speculative Masonry dates from England's Grand Lodge constitution of 24 June 1717, uniting four old lodges, though Anderson's 1723 Constitutions history is called little more than fables. Its first Old Charge article sets an unsectarian religion in which all men agree, a principle the article judges anti-Catholic and anti-Christian in character. Grand Lodge statistics count some 262,651 members in Britain and colonies, 60,728 in Canada, and 1,203,159 in the United States. Papal pronouncements from Clement XII's In Eminenti of 1738 onward forbid Catholics, under excommunication, to join.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-matthieu-ory:
Dominican inquisitor Matthieu Ory (1492-1557) entered his order at eighteen, studied at St-Jacques in Paris and the Sorbonne, and took his theology licence in 1527. His learning and eloquence won him the post of grand inquisitor for France in 1534, which he held until death. He preached tirelessly, held several offices in his order, and fought false teaching and wrongdoing.

Asked to judge false charges against Ignatius of Loyola and his Spiritual Exercises, Ory saw through the accusers. Instead of condemning the saint, he praised and assisted him, and kept a copy of the Exercises for himself. Some writers wrongly call him a Spaniard named Ortiz. His only fully proven printed work is the Alexipharmacum of 1544, which turns five words of St. Paul, grace, justification, sin, liberty, and law, against heretics.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-memory:
Memory, from Latin memoria, is the mind's power to store conscious processes and bring them back later with some fidelity. Strictly, a revived process counts as remembered only when it is also recognized as something that happened before. Memory thus involves recognition. Voluntary recall of mental processes is often called recollection, and involuntary recall is called recall.

St. Thomas splits memory into sensory and intellectual kinds. He excludes mere storage of mental images from sensory memory and assigns it to imagination. Sensory memory keeps what the special senses cannot take in yet stays individual. Examples are an object's use and its place in past time, meaning only the sensory lesson that certain things help or harm. It sits in the bodily organism. Intellectual memory takes in and stores the abstract and universal, seated in the passive intellect's division, or perhaps only an aspect of understanding, paired with the active intellect.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-missionaries-:
Blessed Louis-Marie Grignion de Montfort established the Company of Mary in 1713. Montfort had already dreamed of a missionary society by 1700. Five months after his ordination in November 1700 he wrote of praying continually for a poor and small company of good priests. They would preach missions and retreats under the standard and protection of the Blessed Virgin.

For years he prayed, fasted, and had others pray for his project. In 1713 he went to Paris to recruit members, and the director of the St-Esprit seminary promised to send him young priests. Montfort died in 1716, but his company, the Montfortians, lived on, preaching parish missions and spreading devotion to Mary, especially through the rosary and total consecration.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mount-calvary:
Mount Calvary is the place of Christ's Crucifixion, a name from Latin calvaria, meaning a skull. That matches Greek kranion and the original Golgotha. The Gospels call it merely a place. The Pilgrim of Bordeaux joined the diminutive monticulus, little mount, to it in 333. Rufinus spoke of the rock of Golgotha near the fifth century's start. Since the sixth century usage has treated Calvary as a mountain.

Why it bears the name is debated. It may have been a public execution ground strewn with skulls, or named from a cemetery nearby. That would also explain the thin population of the district and Joseph's tomb standing there. The entry weighs the theories, traces the site's identification and the churches raised over it, and sets out the topography pilgrims and scholars have argued over.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mystery:
Mystery, from Greek mysterion, rooted in a verb meaning to shut or close, signifies in general what is unknowable or valuable knowledge kept secret. In pagan antiquity it named esoteric doctrines such as Pythagoreanism and private rites like the Eleusinian ceremonies, known only to the initiated. Early Christians used it for teachings carefully guarded from the profane.

Scripture's versions render Hebrew sod, secret, by mysterion. The New Testament applies the word chiefly to the Gospel's sublime revelation, the Incarnation and life of the Saviour proclaimed by the apostles. Theologians therefore call mysteries revealed truths surpassing natural reason, not merely the incomprehensible, since all knowledge is partly beyond full grasp. The entry sorts mysteries of faith from those of nature and grace.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-northern-terr:
The Northern Territory of Australia, a prefecture apostolic larger than many nations, lay almost empty in the early twentieth century. Bounded by ocean, South Australia, Queensland, and Western Australia, it spans 523,620 square miles, mostly within the tropics.

Some 25,000 to 30,000 people lived there, under a thousand Europeans, about 4,000 Asiatics, and the rest Aboriginal peoples. Palmerston at Port Darwin and Southport were its only towns, linked to Adelaide by a telegraph of over 2,000 miles but by rail for just 146. Droughts, cattle disease, and the 1891 financial crisis slowed the country’s growth. Port Darwin probably ranks second only to Sydney Harbour as a deep-water port.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-odo-of-canter:
Odo of Canterbury, abbot of Battle who died in 1200, served Thomas Becket and Christ Church through the Becket quarrel. A monk of Christ Church and subprior by 1163, he carried Becket's appeal to Pope Alexander III against the archbishop of York's carrying his cross in the south.

Prior by 1167, Odo wavered between king and archbishop until Becket's murder fixed him for church authority. Monks put him forward for Canterbury in 1172, Henry stalled, and Richard of Dover won the see, with Odo writing in his support. In 1173 a great fire struck Christ Church, and Odo later attended the Council of Woodstock in 1175.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-offertory:
The Offertory, in the Mass, presents bread and wine to God before consecration, with prayers and chant to match. Justin Martyr already describes bread and a cup brought to the president, and soon a prayer asked God to accept, bless, and change the gifts into Christ's Body and Blood.

Eastern rites prepare the gifts before the liturgy in the proskomide, elaborately in Byzantine use, while Rome keeps the offering within the Mass. The entry traces that split, the offertory chant, and the prayers of priest and people across ancient and medieval rites.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-oratory:
An oratory, from Latin for prayer, is technically a place set aside by church authority for prayer and Mass, other than a parish church. Early oratories rose over martyrs' tombs and in country districts where churches proper stayed in cathedral cities, then spread to bishops' houses, convents, and noble homes.

Canon law sorts them as public, semipublic, and private. Public oratories, erected by the bishop with a street entrance, serve divine worship perpetually, while semipublic and private ones carry narrower rights for Mass, reservation, and indulgences. A public oratory needs an entrance and an exit onto the public road.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ordinary:
An ordinary, in church language, holds jurisdiction joined stably to an office, whether by divine law, as with popes and bishops, or by church law. Ordinary jurisdiction stands against delegated jurisdiction, a temporary grant from a superior to an inferior for particular acts.

Full and real in the external forum, an ordinary's power covers legislating, judging, and governing, while jurisdiction in the internal forum alone does not make an ordinary. Parish priests, therefore, though they guide consciences, are not ordinaries, and the entry sorts the classes of ordinaries. A person may be an ordinary in his own sphere while holding delegated powers for special acts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ossory:
Ossory is an Irish diocese in Leinster, bounded by the Suir in the south, the Barrow in the east, and Tipperary, King's County, and Queen's County on the other sides. It spans 600,000 acres and matches the old Kingdom of Ossory, whose first king, Aengus Osrithe, flourished in the second century. His heirs widened its bounds into Tipperary, lost South Ossory to the Deisi for a century, and won much of it back in the seventh century.

Saint Kieran, apostle and patron of the diocese, was born near Cape Clear in the fourth century and, by tradition, was ordained at Rome. Saint Patrick gave him a bell and told him to found a monastery where it first rang. The entry follows the diocese through Danish wars, Norman changes, and later bishops, schools, and religious houses down to its modern shape.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-papal-consist:
A papal consistory is the senate of the Roman pontiff, the gathering of cardinals in council round the pope. The word comes from the imperial consistorium, the emperor's sacred council, and Innocent III used it in 1212 for the cardinals' assembly. Its roots lie in the old Roman presbytery, the city's clergy of deacons, priests of titular churches, and nearby bishops.

Today's cardinals, in the same three orders, inherit that presbytery's offices and, above all, its task of aiding the pope in church government. From the earliest Christian times popes consulted the presbytery on church affairs, as a letter of Pope Cornelius to Cyprian in 254 shows. Later pages trace the consistory's forms, public, secret, and semi-public, and its role in creating cardinals and settling great causes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-patrick-barry:
Patrick Barry was a horticulturist born near Belfast in May 1816 and dead at Rochester, New York, on 23 June 1890. After teaching in Ireland he emigrated to America in 1836 and worked for a Flushing, Long Island, nurseryman. In 1849 he partnered with George Ellwanger at Rochester, and their firm led in importing or breeding improved flowers, fruits, and hardy exotics, and in bringing wild shade trees into cultivation.

Their nurseries grew into the country's largest. Barry wrote widely on fruit and flower gardening, editing the Genesee Farmer from 1844 to 1852 and the Horticulturalist from 1852 to 1854. His books include a Treatise on the Fruit Garden, printed in 1851 and reissued in 1872, and a catalogue of the American Pomological Society.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paul-de-barry:
Paul de Barry was a French Jesuit born at Leucate in 1587 and dead at Avignon on 28 July 1661. He served as rector of Jesuit colleges at Aix, Nimes, and Avignon, and as provincial of Lyons. He wrote many devout works on the Blessed Virgin, Saint Joseph, and the saints. Above all stands his Pensez-y-bien, or Think Well On It, which circulated widely and was translated into several tongues.

Only three of his works reached English. They are Pious Remarks upon the Life of Saint Joseph, printed in 1600, the Glories of Saint Joseph of Dublin 1835, and Devotions to Saint Joseph, edited by Tickell in London. His Pensez-y-bien travelled farther than his larger works, reaching readers in several tongues.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-perjury:
Perjury is the crime of swearing falsely, and this Catholic Encyclopedia entry weighs it as both sin and crime. A proper oath counts as worship, since it calls on God as all-knowing witness to truth. Invoking that witness for a lie therefore joins the guilt of lying to an offence against religion, and, apart from ignorance or rashness, the sin is always mortal.

The entry works through hard cases with care. Doubt bars swearing to a thing as certain, while a lawful mental reservation may still be confirmed by oath for good cause. Demanding an oath from someone known to lie is grievous, except where justice or necessity requires sworn testimony, as a judge may require it. Canon law classes perjury as a mixed crime, open to church or civil courts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pluscarden-pr:
Pluscarden Priory is a Scottish monastery founded in 1230 by King Alexander III six miles from Elgin for monks of the Valliscaulian Order. That order's mother-house stood at Val-des-Choux in Burgundy. It was the first of three Scottish houses of the order, whose observance blended Carthusian and Cistercian rule.

In 1454 the two surviving monks of Urquhart's Benedictine priory joined the six of Pluscarden, which then took Benedictine rule and became a dependency of Dunfermline Abbey. The last prior died in 1560, yet the monks were never dispersed. The buildings, partly restored by the Marquess of Bute, still show an aisleless choir and transepts. They also keep a chapter-house and cloister garth amid lovely surroundings.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pondicherry:
Pondicherry, an archdiocese of India on the Bay of Bengal, spans French holdings plus nearby British districts. Beyond the town itself it takes in Karikal, Yanaon, and Mahe, two on the east coast and one on the west, plus Chandernagore in Bengal. Catholics there number 143,125, with 78 churches, 210 chapels, and 102 priests.

The archbishop lives at Pondicherry, where the cathedral and seminaries stand, and Paris Foreign Missions priests direct the diocese alongside four sisterhoods. The town stayed a mere village until Francis Martin's shipwrecked Frenchmen made their home there in 1674. Capuchins came first, then Jesuits, and the Carnatic mission spread outward from Pondicherry until the Paris seminary assumed the whole territory in 1773.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pontefract-pr:
Pontefract Priory was a Cluniac monastery in Yorkshire dedicated to Saint John the Evangelist. It was founded about 1090 by Robert de Lacy as a dependency of La Charité-sur-Loire, which supplied the first monks. A bull of Pope Celestine confirmed its gifts and privileges.

Visitations counted sixteen monks in 1262 and twenty-seven in 1279, under a prior who cut the house's debts from 3,200 marks to 350 in twelve years. The priory church held the body of Thomas, Earl of Lancaster, beheaded at Pontefract in 1322 and rumoured a worker of miracles. The last prior surrendered the house to Henry VIII in 1540, and church and buildings are now wholly destroyed, the site marked only by Monk-hill.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-st-zacha:
Zachary, also called Zacharias, reigned from 741 to 752 and died in March 752. He sprang from a Greek family in Calabria, son of Polichronius. Probably a deacon, he signed the Roman council's decrees of 732. After Gregory III's burial on 29 November 741, he was elected at once and unanimously, then consecrated and enthroned on 5 December. His biographer calls him gentle, conciliatory, and charitable to clergy and people.

Soon after his elevation he notified Constantinople, addressing his letter to the church there rather than the iconoclast patriarch Anastasius. His envoys found Artabasdus ruling after revolting against Constantine V in 742, and papal letters dated by Artabasdus's reign in 744. In 743 he held a Roman synod of sixty bishops issuing fourteen canons on discipline. He kept close correspondence with Boniface, who organized Germany's church in touch with Rome. In 749 Ratchis abdicated with wife and daughter to take monastic vows before the pope.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-presbytery:
The presbytery is the part of the church set aside for the higher clergy. In antiquity it bore many names, since priests attached to a church stood there in a half circle round the bishop during liturgical functions. It was called apsis, exedra, and concha, from its shape. It was called bema, since it stood raised above the nave and was reached by a few steps. It was called tribuna, from its place and likeness to the tribunal in civil basilicas, where magistrates gave justice.

In the Middle Ages these names mostly gave way to choir, which in turn gave way to the modern word sanctuary. Rails, cancelli, cut the presbytery off from the rest of the church. Eusebius, in his dedication speech at Tyre, tells how the Holy of Holies, the altar, was ringed with wooden lattice, finely carved, to bar the multitude.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-priory:
A priory is a monastery whose superior is a prior. Dominicans, Augustinian Hermits, Carthusians, Carmelites, Servites, and Brothers of Mercy name every house a priory. Benedictines and their offshoots, Premonstratensians, and military orders mark two kinds: conventual priories and simple, or obedientiary, ones. Conventual priories are self ruling houses with no abbots, either since twelve monks, the canonical number, are not yet reached, or for some other cause.

Cluny's congregation held many conventual priories. In England all houses tied to cathedral churches were called cathedral priories. Nearly all houses of the famed Maurist Congregation in France, in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, were called priories. Today the Benedictine Order counts twenty-seven conventual priories. The simple, or obedientiary, kind stands as abbeys' dependencies, and their superior, subject to the abbot in all things, is called a simple or obedientiary prior.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-purgatory:
Purgatory, from the Latin purgare, to make clean, is treated here under the heads of doctrine, errors, proofs, duration, nature, aid for the dead, indulgences and invocation. Catholic teaching calls it a place or condition of temporal punishment. It holds those who die in God's grace yet still carry venial faults, or owe satisfaction still unpaid for their wrongs. The Council of Florence stated the faith in its Decree of Union, and the Council of Trent defined it in its twenty-fifth session.

Passages quoted against purgatory, it argues, either miss the question or lack the clarity to outweigh the open testimony of the very writers cited. Purgatory passes, since its pains cleanse rather than condemn. Prayers, Masses and indulgences offered by the living form the practical heart of the entry, closing with a meditation on the unfailing lamp of ancient piety before the tombs.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-reform-of-the:
Reform of the Roman Breviary came by the Apostolic Constitution Divino Afflatu of Pius the Tenth, dated 1 November 1911, changing the psalter of the Roman Breviary. This encyclopedia entry explains the new shape. Portions needing rubrics, such as the invitatory, seasonal hymns, blessings, absolutions, chapters, suffrages, dominical prayers, Benedictus, Magnificat and Te Deum, are now printed together under the title Ordinary. The psalms stand together under the title Psaltery.

They are arranged so the whole psalter may be chanted or recited each week. They are distributed or, when too long, divided, so that each day's Office holds roughly the same number of verses. The change aims to restore the liturgy's original use, the weekly recitation of the entire psalter. Feasts with proper lessons keep them, responsories come from the Common or Proper, and precedence turns on rite, classification, personal dignity, external solemnity and local importance, with provision for transferring displaced feasts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-religious-of-:
The Religious of Jesus Mary were founded at Lyons in France in October 1818 by Claudine Thevenet, known in religion as Mother Saint Ignatius. Their constitutions won approval from Pius the Ninth on 31 December 1847. Their aim is a Christian education suited to young ladies' social position, given through boarding schools and academies, and, in large cities, through residences for ladies of the literary profession.

Before the expulsion of 1901 their French houses stood at Lyons, Le Puy, Rodez, and Remiremont. Persecution then moved the mother-house to Rome in September 1901, to the Via Flaminia, with a college called Stella Viae. In New York they kept a house on Fourteenth Street, an academy at Kingsbridge, and a day school for poor Italian children. The Fourteenth Street house, Our Lady of Peace, sheltered literary ladies.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-richard-de-bu:
A fourteenth-century English bishop remembered above all as a lover of books is the subject of this encyclopedia entry. Richard de Bury, born near Bury St Edmund's in 1286, studied at Oxford, became a Benedictine, and tutored the future Edward III. Once his pupil took the throne, he rose swiftly to Bishop of Durham and to high offices of state. He travelled on embassies to Avignon, where he met the poet Petrarch.

Book collecting shaped his lasting fame far more than court service. He gathered manuscripts through a lifetime of searching and founded Durham College at Oxford. He left most of his volumes to its library. They were scattered when Henry VIII closed the college. His own treatise on the love of books, the Philobiblon, praises learning, defends his spending on manuscripts, and urges clergy to cherish reading. First printed in 1473, it has appeared in many editions and translations since.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-richard-mcshe:
Richard McSherry was a Maryland physician who served as a surgeon in both the army and the navy before settling into Baltimore practice. Born at Martinsburg in 1817, the son of a doctor, he studied at Georgetown College and the University of Maryland. He took his medical degree at the University of Pennsylvania in 1841, after already joining the army medical corps.

His service took him to the Seminole War under General Taylor, and later to thirteen years as a navy assistant surgeon. From 1856 he practised in Baltimore until 1883. He helped found the Baltimore Academy of Medicine and served as its first president. He also wrote for medical journals and published books, including a Mexican travel sketch called El Puchero and a popular health guide, Health and How to Promote It. He died at Baltimore in 1885.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rohault-de-fl:
Rohault de Fleury was a nineteenth-century family of French architects and archaeologists. Its most distinguished member was Charles Rohault de Fleury, born at Paris in 1801 and died there in 1875. After a scientific course at the Ecole Polytechnique, he studied sculpture, then turned to architecture in 1825. He designed public and private buildings in one of the most artistic parts of Paris. He wrote the first edition of the Manuel des lois du batiment for the Central Society of Architects in 1862.

His last years went to religious archaeology. These included Les instruments de la Passion in 1870, L'evangile in 1874, and La Sainte Vierge in 1878. A study of a fifth-century Christian tabernacle followed in 1880, and La Messe in 1883-98. Some appeared after his death through his son George, himself a noted writer on Italian art, whose works cover Pisa, Tuscany, and the Lateran in the Middle Ages.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-salisbury:
Salisbury, anciently Sarum, is an English diocese whose roots reach back to Birinus, who set his see at Dorchester in Oxfordshire in 634 and preached to Wessex. From that start sprang Winchester, Sherborne, Ramsbury, and Salisbury itself. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia unwinds a tangle of moves and divisions across four centuries.

Under Headda the see moved to Winchester, then split in 705 into Winchester and Sherborne, where Aldhelm became first bishop. Ten successors later, Wiltshire and Berkshire broke away as Ramsbury in 909, until Herman reunited Sherborne and Ramsbury in 1058 and shifted his chair to Old Sarum in 1075. His successor Osmund built a cathedral there and drew up the Sarum ordinal of services that shaped English worship.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sanctuary:
Sanctuary means the space in a church set aside for the high altar and the clergy. It has borne many names: apse or concha, from its shell-like half-dome, choir since the Middle Ages, from the singers stationed there, and presbyterium, tribuna, hagion, and sanctum. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia traces how that space changed shape across Christian antiquity and the Middle Ages.

Early sanctuaries centred on the apse, where stone benches for clergy ringed the wall like an amphitheatre and the bishop's chair rose in the middle. Yet the apse was not always semicircular: digs, above all in the East, have found over a dozen shapes. In Syria the curve barely projects from the outer wall, flanked by two side rooms with their own uses, and the entry maps those variations.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-savary:
Savary names a noble French family of the seventeenth century devoted to trade and to commercial writings of lasting authority. Its brightest member, Jacques Savary, was born at Doué in Anjou on 22 September 1622 and died on 7 October 1690. His entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia follows a merchant turned lawmaker.

Destined for trade, Jacques studied law in Paris with a procureur, then joined the wholesale haberdashers and made his fortune by 1658. Ties with Superintendent Fouquet brought him the contract for crown-land revenues. After Fouquet's fall he won Chancellor Séguier's favour, and arbitrations in commercial disputes built his standing daily. In 1670 he joined the commission revising trade laws, work that made his name a byword in French commerce.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-school-of-der:
The School of Derry was Columba's first foundation, raised by the great apostle of Scotland and one of Ireland's three patron saints. When the Yellow Plague of 544 scattered Glasnevin's monks, Columba turned homeward to his own kin, intent on founding a monastery among them. His entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia tells how an oak grove became a school.

His princely cousin Aedh, son of Ainmire, offered 200 acres, and his master Mobhi Clarainech gave leave with his dying breath. A few miles from Ailech, the stone fortress of the Hy-Neill, stood a fair oak wood that gave the place its name, Doire Colgaigh, Colgagh's oak wood. Beside it Columba built a church and cells for his first monks. The Annals of Ulster date it to 545, corrected to 546, and students clerical and lay soon flocked there.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-shrewsbury:
Shrewsbury, one of thirteen English dioceses created by Pius IX on 27 September 1850, first covered Shropshire and Cheshire plus seven Welsh counties. When Leo XIII formed the Vicariate of Wales in 1895, the Welsh counties were separated, leaving only Shropshire and Cheshire under the bishop of Shrewsbury. Before the Reformation, Cheshire and northern Shropshire fell under Coventry and Lichfield, and the rest of Shropshire under Hereford.

Henry VIII's creation of Chester took Cheshire from Coventry and Lichfield. Innocent XI's four vicariates of 1688 put Shropshire in the Midland district and Cheshire in the Northern, and Gregory XVI's eight vicariates of 1840 split them between the Central and Lancashire districts. The diocese takes its name from Shrewsbury, county town of Shropshire, under the patronage of Our Lady Help of Christians and Saint Winefride, whose body was translated to Shrewsbury in 1138.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-simon-of-sudb:
Simon of Sudbury, Archbishop of Canterbury, was born at Sudbury in Suffolk of middle-class parents and died at London on 14 June 1381. After a law degree at Paris, he went to Rome and became chaplain to Innocent VI. Sent to England as nuncio in 1356, he became Bishop of London in 1361. He worked with John of Gaunt on French negotiations in 1372 and 1373, and enriched his native town with a collegiate church on his father's old house site.

Sudbury succeeded Langham as Archbishop of Canterbury in 1375. Friendship with John of Gaunt set him against Courtenay of London and William of Wykeham. Amiable but not strong, he shrank from proceeding against Wyclif, whom Gaunt backed, though Courtenay forced a summons in 1377 that ended without condemnation. Made lord chancellor in 1380, he paid for the office with his life in the peasants' rising a year later, when rebels seized and beheaded him.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sir-thomas-ma:
Thomas Malory's life is almost wholly conjecture. We know he was a knight, his book was finished in the ninth year of Edward IV's reign, and Caxton first printed it in 1485. Long taken for a Welshman on an unsound derivation of Bale's, gratified by matching the romancer's birthplace to Arthurian scenes. He is now more probably judged a gentleman of an ancient Warwickshire house. He served young in France with Richard Beauchamp, Earl of Warwick.

The author's obscurity contrasts dramatically with four centuries of unfailing appreciation for his Morte Arthure. Though a compilation, a mosaic of French romances of Merlin, Lancelot, and Tristan and the English Morte Arthure from Geoffrey of Monmouth. Malory turned episodic matter and clashing racial viewpoints into steady ideals of conduct in epic conflict with fate.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sisters-of-ch:
The Sisters of Charity of Jesus and Mary were founded in 1803 by Canon Triest, called the Saint Vincent de Paul of Belgium. He also founded the Brothers of Saint John of God and the Sisters of the Infant Jesus. As curé of Lovendeghem he laid the congregation's foundations and gave up his living to train members. He won first papal recognition in 1806 and final approbation on 9 September 1816 after going to Rome.

The mother-house stands at Ghent, with forty branch houses, and the congregation ranks among Belgium's largest, counting over a thousand members. In 1889 sisters went to the Congo missions and founded several houses there. In 1895 they went to India, opening schools in the Punjab and Ceylon. Their chief work is teaching in training colleges, schools, and orphanages, plus nursing the infirm. They are enclosed, with no lay sisters, in a spirit of simplicity, devotion, and zeal.

The Sisters of Charity of the Blessed Virgin Mary began with five young women in Dublin on 8 December 1831, devoted to teaching children. Their first Dublin school opened in North Ann Street on 19 March 1832. Mary Frances Clarke became first superior, with Margaret Mann as assistant and mistress of novices. On 1 November 1833 they received their present title.

In 1843 the congregation accepted Bishop Loras of Dubuque's invitation and moved to Iowa for pioneer work. The mother-house has stood at Dubuque ever since. Their rules won approval in 1877, confirmed by Leo XIII on 26 April 1885. Education is their only work, and by September 1907 they counted one thousand members teaching 25,000 children.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sisters-of-th:
The Sisters of the Holy Childhood of Jesus and Mary cover two congregations described in this entry. The first began in 1835 in the Diocese of Fréjus for educating girls and caring for the sick, with its mother-house at Draguignan and government authorization in 1853. The second began at Sens in 1838 for teaching and nursing the sick in their homes.

In the fuller account, the religious divide into choir sisters, who staff higher schools, industrial schools, and orphanages, and lay sisters, who handle domestic care. Vows run annually for ten years before final vows. Papal approval came in 1888, with statutes approved in 1899. A Boston diocese branch taught 2,400 pupils, with a novitiate at Salem, Massachusetts, and the congregation counts about 1,400 sisters.

Founded at Dommartin-sous-Amance, France, in 1855 by John Joseph Begel, pastor of Laitre and Dommartin, the Sisters of the Holy Humility of Mary teach poor children in country districts and small towns. Three women offered their services in 1854, and Begel drew up a rule approved by the Bishop of Nancy in 1858. The congregation also trained orphans, nursed the sick, and decorated parish altars.

Begel's open condemnation of Napoleon III's policy toward the Church brought official disfavour, and the sisters were refused diplomas and barred from opening schools. In 1862 Father Louis Hoffer of Louisville, Ohio, asked for four sisters, and Bishop Rappe of Cleveland invited the whole community to his diocese. They sailed on 30 May 1864 and settled on a 250-acre farm near New Bedford, Pennsylvania, named Villa Maria. By 1909 they counted about 200 members running 15 parish schools, 2 academies, and an orphan asylum.

Founded at Longueuil, Quebec, on 8 December 1844 under Bishop Bourget of Montreal, the Sisters of the Holy Names of Jesus and Mary teach young girls. Three Canadian aspirants trained under John Allard after the Marseilles institute of Eugene de Mazenod, then took simple vows as Sisters Marie-Rose, Marie-Madeline, and Marie-Agnes. Bourget gave diocesan approval and named Mother Marie-Rose general superior for life.

Marseilles supplied the title, habit, and rule, with modifications, and under Mother Marie-Rose the congregation grew fast. A course of study served English and French pupils alike, and missionary need later brought boys' teaching under temporary Holy See permission. By 1910 the institute counted 1,257 professed sisters, 110 novices, and 81 postulants, running 99 schools with 24,208 pupils, 48 of them in the United States.

Founded in England in 1877, the Sisters of the Little Company of Mary honour the Blessed Virgin's maternal heart, above all in the mystery of Calvary. The sisters consecrate themselves wholly to her and imitate her virtues. Their chief outward work is nursing the sick and dying, at home and in hospitals and nursing homes linked to their convents.

They serve every class, nationality, and creed alike, and charge nothing, accepting only free offerings. Besides nursing, they pray continually for the dying, keeping watch before the Blessed Sacrament day and night in the novitiate. Leo XIII gave final approbation to their rules in 1893. Houses stand in Italy, England, Ireland, Malta, Chicago, Australia, and South Africa, with a black habit and blue veil.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-adrian-of-:
St. Adrian of Canterbury was an African by birth who died in 710, and this entry tells how humility rerouted his career. Made abbot of Nerida, a Benedictine house near Naples. While very young, he was Pope Vitalian's first choice to succeed Deusdedit as Archbishop of Canterbury. But judged himself unworthy and begged the pope to name the Greek monk Theodore instead.

Vitalian agreed on one condition, that Adrian travel with Theodore to England as his adviser in running Canterbury. They left Rome in 668, but Ebroin, Mayor of the Palace in France, detained Adrian for two years on suspicion of a secret mission from Emperor Constans II. Cleared at last, he reached England, where Theodore made him abbot of St. Peter's, the monastery founded by St. Augustine.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-augustine-:
St. Augustine of Canterbury was the first archbishop of Canterbury and apostle of the English. His date of birth is unknown, and he died on 26 May 604. This entry follows a man probably Roman of the better class, who early in life became a monk in the famous monastery of St. Andrew. Gregory had erected that monastery out of his own patrimony on the Caelian Hill.

It was in the close religious life of the Benedictine rule, and the bracing air of a recent foundation, that the future missionary's character was formed. Chance is said to have furnished the opportunity for the enterprise that would join his name forever with his friend and patron, St. Gregory. Augustine became the true founder of one of Christendom's most important churches, and the channel by which Roman authority was established over the English.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-elizabeth-:
Elizabeth of Hungary, married at fourteen and dead at twenty-four, became one of the Middle Ages' most beloved saints. Daughter of King Andrew II, she was sent to Thuringia as a child bride in a political alliance against Emperor Otto IV. In 1221 she married Ludwig IV, a capable ruler who protected her charities, vigils, and penances. The Catholic Encyclopedia article of 1913 dates her death at Marburg to 17 November 1231.

When flood, famine, and plague struck Thuringia in 1226 while Ludwig served the emperor in Italy, Elizabeth took charge and distributed alms on a grand scale. Widowed soon after, she bore a third child after her husband's death. Her family web runs through the age: her brother became Bela IV, her aunt was Hedwig of Silesia, and her great-niece was Elizabeth of Portugal.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-eucherius-:
Eucherius, bishop of Lyons until about 449, chose the hermit's island before the Church chose him for a see. Born late in the fourth century, he withdrew after his wife's death to Lérins, where his sons Veranius and Salonius lived, then to neighbouring Lerona, now Sainte-Marguerite, for study and mortification. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 follows his correspondence with John Cassian about Egypt's desert hermits.

Cassian answered with his Collationes on the Thebaid's daily life, and Eucherius wrote his letter De laude Eremi to Hilary of Arles about 428. He kept touch with learned and pious friends, including Honoratus and Valerian, while imitating Egyptian solitaries. Fame across southeastern Gaul carried him to Lyons, probably in 434. The entry joins desert longing to episcopal duty.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-gery:
Gery, bishop of Cambrai-Arras, shepherded a diocese still recovering from barbarian invasion. Born of Roman parents Gaudentius and Austadiola at Eposium, now Carignan, about the middle of the sixth century, he led a pious youth that prepared him for zeal and devotion. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death to 11 August, between 623 and 626.

His see was young beside ancient Tongres, and the invasion of 406 had wrecked church organization across Belgium. Under Merovingian recovery, Vaast restored Arras early in the sixth century, and Gery ranked among his earliest successors. The entry sets one bishop's career inside a larger rebuilding: Christians scattered, bishops displaced to Reims, then dioceses slowly knit together again under men like Vaast and Gery.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-lawrence-o:
Lawrence of Canterbury, second archbishop after Augustine, carried news of Kent's conversion to Rome and back. He died on 2 February 619. For his life and rule the entry relies on Bede, with medieval additions lacking proof, though possibly preserving old tradition. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 follows Bede's account closely.

Lawrence was among the original missionaries who left Rome with Augustine in 595 and landed at Thanet in 597. After Augustine's consecration, he was sent back to Rome as a priest, distinct from Peter the monk. He bore news of Ethelbert's conversion, announced the consecration, and asked direction on questions. Gregory decided those questions, and Lawrence returned bearing replies, remaining with Augustine thereafter. Whether he was a parish priest or monk remains disputed by later writers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-patrick-s-:
St Patrick's Purgatory, the celebrated sanctuary on Lough Derg in Donegal, draws pilgrims to Station Island still. The lake covers about 2200 acres, thirteen miles round, with eleven islands, chiefly Saints Island and Station Island. Tradition ties the place to Patrick himself, a link the Bollandists accept on historical evidence.

Canons Regular of St Augustine took charge about 1130 or 1134, making it a dependent priory of Armagh. Its fame turned European after the knight Owen's visit in 1150, and accounts of foreign pilgrimages fill the thirteenth, fourteenth, and fifteenth centuries. The entry traces sanctuary lands, stewards, and pilgrim rites, offering a compact history of Ireland's sternest place of penance.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-stephen-josep:
Stephen Joseph Perry, a Jesuit astronomer, directed Stonyhurst Observatory and led eclipse expeditions. Born in London in August 1833 to a well known Catholic family, he was schooled at Gifford Hall and Douai's Benedictine college, then went to Rome for the priesthood. Resolving to join the Jesuits, he entered the novitiate in 1853 to 1855 at Hodder and Beaumont Lodge, studying later at St Acheul near Amiens and at Stonyhurst.

His bent for mathematics sent him to De Morgan's lectures in London and to Bertrand, Liouville, Delaunay, Cauchy, and Serret in Paris. Recalled to Stonyhurst in autumn 1860, he taught physics and mathematics and took charge of the observatory. Ordained in 1866 after theology at St Beuno's, he resumed those duties for life, save for scientific engagements. With Sidgreaves he surveyed magnetism in France and Belgium, and led government eclipse parties. He died on 27 December 1889.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-stephen-russe:
Stephen Russell Mallory was born in Trinidad in 1813. He grew into a Florida lawyer, then a United States senator, then the man who built the Confederate navy from nothing. This entry traces that rise, from his schooling at a Jesuit college in Mobile to his Florida judgeship and customs post at Key West.

Davis named him navy secretary in February 1861. He took over a department with no ships and no stores, yet he pieced a fleet together from raw materials. After Richmond fell in April 1865, he fled with Davis, was jailed ten months at Fort Lafayette, and won parole in 1866. He then practised law at Pensacola until his death in 1873.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-syon-monaster:
Syon Monastery in Middlesex was founded in 1415 by Henry V at his Isleworth manor. Dedicated to St Saviour and St Bridget of Syon, it was England's only house of Bridget's reformed Augustinian order, counting thirteen priests, four deacons, eight lay brothers, and sixty nuns. Its land ran half a mile along the Thames, and prayer for the founder's soul was its chief duty.

Martin V confirmed the house in 1418, novices were professed in 1420, and the chapel's first stone was laid six years later. Income grew to an estimated 1,730 pounds a year, and even Henry VIII's commissioners found little fault with its observance. Expelled in 1539, the nuns wandered through Flanders, France, Spain, and Lisbon, returning to England in 1861, while Northumberland's descendants still hold Isleworth.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tapestry:
Tapestry, a French word, names a fabric where weaving and embroidery join. Instead of throwing the woof by shuttle, the worker adds it to the warp with a needle. The needle carries a short coloured thread, producing a mosaic of dyed threads rich in colour and shading. Such cloth serves for wall hangings and for floor and furniture coverings.

Egyptians used it first, and the art passed through western Asia to Europe. It reached perfection in the later Middle Ages and Renaissance, above all at Arras. Arras gave its name to all tapestry, wherever made. In pre-Reformation England, monastic houses made it for reredoses, altar frontals, hearse cloths, and choir hangings. It pictured Bible scenes, saints' lives, historic events, and points of faith in symbol.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-aberdeen-:
The Aberdeen Breviary is the Sarum Office in Scottish form. The Salisbury use was adopted in Scotland and Ireland during the Middle Ages, for Mass and hours. Its Scottish introduction is sometimes wrongly credited to Edward I in 1292, but evidence puts it earlier. Herbert, Bishop of Glasgow from 1147 to 1164, adopted Sarum for his church with papal sanction. Father Innes, who died in Paris in 1744, asserted that every Scots missal or breviary he saw followed Sarum use.

Moray's bishop, dean, and chapter received and approved Salisbury's Ordo in 1242, and Moray bordered Aberdeen. Scots preference for Sarum reflected resistance to York's jurisdictional claims over Scotland, which adopting York use might have seemed to justify. The Aberdeen Breviary was the work of William Elphinstone, Bishop of Aberdeen from 1483 to his death in 1514. He gathered the materials and composed lessons, notably for Scottish saints, whose festivals devote all nine Matins lessons to their lives.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-alexandri:
The Great Library of Alexandria, distinct from the smaller Serapeum library, was a foundation of the Ptolemies to sustain Greek civilization in Egypt. If Demetrius of Phalerum's move to Alexandria in 296-295 BC concerned the library, its plan formed under Ptolemy Soter, who died about 284 BC. Completion and its Museum link belonged to his successor, Ptolemy Philadelphus. Since Strabo omits the library from his harbour buildings, it stood elsewhere, likely in Brucheion.

Books came strikingly. Ships entering harbour surrendered manuscripts. Athens' copy of the three tragedians was kept by forfeiting a 15-talent deposit for return. Rivalry with Pergamon grew keen that papyrus export was banned to cripple it, driving the perfection of skins, charta pergamena, our parchment. Rivalry bred spurious works, false antiquing, and hasty copying. Roll counts vary by period: Demetrius counted 200,000 rolls and hoped for more. The entry weighs the library's destructions, including the preposterous fuel tale.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-annunciat:
Luke's Gospel, chapter 1, verses 26 to 38, supplies the event at the centre of this entry: the angel Gabriel's visit to Mary at Nazareth. Six months after Elizabeth conceived John the Baptist, Gabriel came to a young woman of David's house, espoused to Joseph but still living in her mother's home. His greeting, Hail, full of grace, troubled her, since she did not know the visitor or his errand.

Gabriel told her not to fear, for she had found grace with God, and that she would bear a son. Mary's questions and her consent follow, with notes on the words of the greeting and on early art and devotion. Readers find both the Gospel narrative retold with care and the Church's reading of what the moment meant.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-blessed-v:
Mary, mother of Jesus Christ and mother of God, is the subject of this vast entry, which follows theology and history through their sources in order. Old Testament prophecies and types open the account, above all Genesis chapter 3, verse 15, where the woman and her seed face the serpent. Hebrew wording, Septuagint renderings, and later translations are weighed with care.

New Testament narratives follow, from Annunciation to Calvary and beyond, then early Christian and Jewish witnesses, councils, liturgy, art, and devotion. Apparitions, feasts, and doctrines such as the Immaculate Conception receive their own sections. Few entries in the encyclopedia range so widely across Scripture, history, and popular piety.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-monk-of-m:
A phantom author dissolves under scrutiny in this short entry. A chronicle among the Cottonian manuscripts in the British Museum, Vespasian D IV 73, bears the name Godfridus de Malmesbury. Tanner judged it a mere copy of Alfred of Beverley's twelfth-century chronicle, while Sir Thomas Hardy traced it almost wholly to Geoffrey of Monmouth.

Worthless as history, it runs from the Saxon invasion to 1129. Godfrey of Malmesbury, a Jumièges native who became abbot in 1081 and founded the abbey library, once seemed its author. His death by 1107, when Edulf succeeded him, disproves the guess. The signature likely marks ownership, not authorship, a warning against trusting a name on a page.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-name-of-m:
Mary's name, in Scripture and Catholic use, is the puzzle at the heart of this entry. New Testament texts give Mariam and sometimes Maria, and scholars cannot yet say whether Evangelists reserved Mariam for Christ's Mother and Maria for others of the name. Mariam surely renders Hebrew MRYM, borne by Moses and Aaron's sister.

Chronicles chapter 4, verse 17, may even give it to a man, though the Septuagint reads Maron there. Two roots compete for Miriam's sense: MRH, to rebel, tied by some to Moses's sister murmuring against him, and MRA, to be fat, which Semitic minds linked to beauty. Lady, the reading most Fathers favoured, closes the debate.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-rosary:
Fifteen decades of Hail Marys, each ten framed by an Our Father and a mystery of redemption held in meditation, make up the Rosary as the Roman Breviary defines it. When Albigensian heresy ravaged Toulouse, Dominic besought Our Lady's help and, so tradition asserts, was told to preach the Rosary as an antidote to heresy and sin.

From that hour the prayer spread wonderfully, published abroad and developed by Dominic, whom popes in many ages called its institutor and author. History, mysteries joyful, sorrowful, and glorious, indulgences, and confraternities follow. For readers new to the devotion, the entry joins legend, liturgy, and practice in a single thread.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-theodore-arch:
Canterbury's seventh archbishop, Theodore of Tarsus, gave the English Church order after years of drift. Born at Tarsus in Cilicia about 602, he died at Canterbury on 19 September 690. A monk at Rome in 667, he was picked by Pope Vitalian for Canterbury when Wighard died before he could be consecrated.

The pope himself consecrated Theodore on 26 March 668, and he reached Canterbury in May 669. He found sees too large, many with no bishop, and old bitterness from the Easter date row still rankling. He toured the whole island, filled empty sees, put Chad's rank in order, and curbed abuses, giving English faith a shape it had lacked.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tomb-of-the-b:
The Tomb of the Blessed Virgin Mary is venerated in the Valley of Cedron, near Jerusalem, yet many modern writers hold that Mary died and was buried at Ephesus. The entry sets the two traditions side by side. Apocryphal works of the second to fourth centuries favour Jerusalem, placing her tomb at Gethsemane. Pilgrims from the fifth century onward visited a basilica in the Valley of Josaphat holding her sepulchre.

Writers from Gregory of Tours to Sophronius and Germanus of Constantinople repeat the Jerusalem tradition. The Ephesus claim rests on later reasoning about John's residence there, and on the silence of early Ephesian sources. Since 1187 the tomb has belonged to the Muslim government, which still allows Christians to officiate there, and the church keeps frescoes and marble slabs from its long history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tynemouth-pri:
Tynemouth Priory stands on the Northumberland coast of England, on Saxon church ground. That church was built first in wood and then in stone in the seventh century. It won fame as the burial place of St Oswin, king and martyr, before Danish raiders plundered and burned the site again and again. In 1074 the place passed to Benedictine monks from Yarrow, and with them it joined Durham Abbey. Later it became a cell of St Albans under Earl Robert de Mowbray.

The entry traces the priory's buildings as they grew: a Norman church raised about 1100, a choir lengthened some 120 years later, and a Lady chapel added around 1320. It notes the monks' life, the priory's lands and troubles, and its end at the Dissolution, when monastic life there ceased. Ruins and memory remain the theme of a coastal house battered by raiders and rebuilt by Normans.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-usury:
Usury is the taking of interest on money lent, and this long entry asks when, if ever, it is lawful. It begins with usury as condemned by all honest men. Plato and Aristotle held interest contrary to nature, Aristophanes mocked it, and Cato likened it to homicide, as did Seneca and Plutarch. Greek and Roman writers knew little economics, yet ruinous lending rates explain their severity.

Roman and Greek law still allowed the loan for consumption, and the entry follows the church's teaching from Scripture and the fathers through medieval schoolmen to modern moralists. It distinguishes interest that pays for loss or risk from sheer gain on a loan, and weighs modern banking against old bans. Readers get a full history of a moral question that shaped finance for centuries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-vatican-obser:
The Vatican Observatory now bears the official title Specola Astronomica Vaticana. Its name needs a note: osservatorio or specola can mean any high place for watching sky phenomena, not only a star observatory. From that view the Specola Vaticana passed through four stages. The first began when Gregory XIII ordered a tower raised in a handy part of the Vatican and fitted with the finest instruments of the day.

There Gregory held meetings of the learned men charged with reforming the calendar, and the tower still stands as witness to his generosity. Later stages brought the observatory's refounding under Leo XIII, its new instruments, and its work in star mapping and meteorology. The entry traces the Specola from a calendar tower to a modern observatory.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-robert-dr:
Robert Drury was a martyr of 1567 to 1607, born of a good Buckinghamshire family, taken into the English College at Reims on 1 April 1588. On 17 September 1590 he went to the new college at Valladolid, where he finished his studies, was ordained priest, and returned to England in 1593. He worked chiefly in London, where his learning and virtue won him much respect among his brethren.

He joined the appellants against the archpriest Blackwell, and his name stands on the appeal of 17 November 1600, dated from the prison at Wisbech. A government invitation asking these priests to acknowledge allegiance and duty to the queen, dated 5 November 1602, produced the famous loyal address of 31 January 1603. Dr William Bishop drew it up, and thirteen leading priests signed it, including Drury. The entry follows Drury to his execution in 1607.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-vincent-houdr:
Vincent Houdry was a French Jesuit preacher and writer on the spiritual life who lived from 1631 to 1729. Entering the Society at Paris in 1647, he studied philosophy for three years and theology for four, then taught classics for six years, rhetoric for one. Philosophy for four, before becoming a celebrated pulpit orator preaching for twenty-five years in France's chief cities.

His remaining years were given to writing sermons, and his obituary praised his tireless industry as speaker and writer and his faithful observance of the rules even into his ninety-ninth year. He left two major homiletic works: collected sermons on every subject of Christian morality, five parts in twenty-two volumes published at Paris between 1696 and 1702 and reprinted several times. A library of materials for preachers, supplemented by a scrupulously compiled index volume.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-visitation-of:
The Visitation is Mary's journey from Nazareth to her cousin Elizabeth at Hebron, south of Jerusalem, related in Luke 1:39-57. Assuming Annunciation and Incarnation fell about the spring equinox, Mary left at March's end and crossed the mountains, because her presence. Still more the divine Child in her womb, was to bring great graces to John, Christ's forerunner.

At Mary's arrival John leaped in Elizabeth's womb, was cleansed from original sin, and filled with God's grace. Mary first exercised the office of Mother of God made man, that he might sanctify and glorify us through her mediation. Joseph probably accompanied her, returned to Nazareth, and came again after three months to take her home. The angel's appearance in Matthew 1 may have ended his tormenting doubts about her maternity. As a feast it was adopted by the Franciscan chapter in 1263 on Bonaventure's advice.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-voluntary:
Voluntary, or wilful, describes what proceeds from the will following actual knowledge, formal or virtual, in a rational agent. It is not quite the same as free, since a free act supposes self-determination, an agent able at the time to determine himself or not as he chooses. Moralists commonly use the terms interchangeably, because nearly every specific voluntary act in this life is also free.

A thing may be voluntary in itself, falling directly under the agent's efficacious determination, or voluntary in its cause. Requiring at least virtual foreknowledge of the effect and production by the will's efficiency in willing the cause. The moralist distinguishes effects a cause is naturally destined to produce, for which it is the sole adequate cause. From effects it is not so destined to produce, a distinction that decides how far responsibility for unforeseen consequences extends.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-walsingham-pr:
Walsingham Priory stood a few miles from the sea in northern Norfolk. Its chapel of Our Lady founded in Edward the Confessor's time, confirmed to Augustinian Canons a century later, and enclosed within the priory. From the first it was a famous pilgrimage shrine, drawing the faithful from all England and the continent until Henry VIII destroyed the priory in 1538. The pilgrims' main road through Newmarket, Brandon, and Fakenham is still called Palmers' Way.

Gifts of lands, rents, and churches flowed to its canons, and many miracles were reported at the shrine. Kings came on pilgrimage: Henry III in 1241, Edward I in 1280 and 1296, Edward II in 1315, Henry VI in 1455, Henry VII in 1487. Henry VIII in 1513, while Erasmus, fulfilling a vow, came from Cambridge in 1511 and left Greek verses, later writing a colloquy rationalizing some reputed miracles.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-whithorn-prio:
Whithorn Priory stood in Wigtownshire, Scotland, founded about the mid-twelfth century in David I's reign by Fergus, Lord of Galloway, for Premonstratensian, or White, Canons. Its canons formed the chapter of Galloway diocese, re-established about the same time also by Fergus, the old episcopal succession having died out about 796. The prior ranked next to the bishop, as an early thirteenth-century charter's signatories show, and his community held the right of electing the bishop.

York's archbishop, to whom Galloway was long suffragan, sometimes overruled it for secular clergy. The full prior list is lost, but among them were Maurice, who swore fealty to Edward I in 1296, Gavin Dunbar, later Archbishop of Glasgow in 1514. James Beaton, successively archbishop of Glasgow and St Andrews and chancellor of the kingdom. Whithorn long drew pilgrims through St Ninian's venerated memory, Scottish sovereigns Margaret, queen of James III, James IV.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-of-ma:
William of Malmesbury was a twelfth-century monk historian whose works remain the backbone of early English history. Born about 1090, he died about 1143. Schooled at Malmesbury, he became a monk there and bent early toward history, writing, in his own words, because old writings left him unsatisfied. By 1125 he had finished Gesta Regum and Gesta Pontificum, then spent ten years gathering materials now at the Bodleian and writing on Glastonbury and its saints.

Though he might more than once have become abbot, he stayed content as librarian. About 1140 he revised both great works and began Historia Novella, a sequel for 1125 to 1142, left as a first draft rather than a finished book. His record of Stephen's reign is priceless, his Norman kings rest on knowledge or direct hearsay, and his cause-and-effect method, learned from Bede, advanced history beyond his predecessors.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-of-st:
William of Saint-Thierry was a theologian and mystic, abbot of the house that gave him his name. Born at Liège about 1085, he died at Signy about 1148. Of noble stock, he studied with brother Simon at Saint Nicaise, Reims, where both took religious life; Simon led Saint Nicolas-aux-Bois and William led Saint-Thierry near Reims from 1119. He knew Bernard closely and longed for Clairvaux, but Bernard bade him stay with his charges.

William later withdrew to the Cistercian abbey at Signy, dividing suffering days between prayer and study. His writings span the solitary life, contemplation of God after Augustine, and the nature and dignity of love. Mirrors and enigmas of faith, the Eucharist against Rupert, commentaries on the Song of Songs and Romans, and a life of Bernard complete the list. He first exposed Abelard's errors and spurred Bernard against him, with tracts later condemned at Sens.
character-writings-of-the-seventeenth-ce:
Henry Morley, professor of English at University College, London, edited a 1891 anthology of character sketches. Greeks came first in his plan. Theophrastus opens the book, and Thomas Harman's rogue portrait follows. Ben Jonson's stage characters close the prelude. The main body then gives the seventeenth century its own voice.

Sir Thomas Overbury supplies dozens of types. A good woman, a dissembler, a courtier, and a flatterer march past. A pedant, a puritan, a tinker, and a chambermaid get equal care. Joseph Hall adds virtues and vices in pairs. John Earle and others follow. These short prose portraits, half essay and half satire, taught later writers how to sum up a person in a page.
characters-and-events-of-roman-history:
Guglielmo Ferrero delivered the Lowell Lectures of 1908 on Roman history, and Frances Lance Ferrero translated them for the Chautauqua Press. Eight lectures run from Caesar to Nero. Ferrero told a Paris colleague that he had not remade Roman history. He had only returned to Livy's old standpoint, gathering events around corruption of customs.

Antony and Cleopatra get a lecture on history versus legend. Gaul's growth under Rome follows. Nero is judged half insane and truly criminal, yet Ferrero still protests against legends piled on his memory. Julia and Tiberius, wine in Roman life, and the empire's social growth fill later lectures. A final lecture asks how Roman history should be taught today.
civilization-and-beyond-learning-from-hi:
Civilization and Beyond: Learning from History, by Scott Nearing, was issued from the Social Science Institute at Harborside, Maine, in August 1975. Nineteen chapters in four parts survey what Nearing calls the pageant of experiments with civilization. Egypt, Eurasia, and Rome open the account, and the life cycle of Western civilization follows.

A social analysis then takes civilization apart by politics, economics, sociology, and ideologies. Part III argues that civilization is becoming obsolete, torn by world wide revolution and by the West's own wars. Part IV turns constructive: ten building blocks for a new world, world federation, a joined world economy, and care for the natural environment close the book.
confession-or-the-blind-heart-a-domestic:
Confession, or The Blind Heart, a domestic story by W Gilmore Simms, opens under a motto from Goethe's Faust about those who knew and felt, and were crucified or burnt for telling. Simms begins by repeating the quotation and turning it into an essay. The pains and penalties of folly, he argues, are not necessarily death. The old texts threatened as much, but life is subtler. The blind heart of his title is the organ that refuses its own knowledge.

From that somber porch the tale enters Southern domestic life, where a confession withheld or mistimed poisons a household. Simms works here in the domestic vein: marriage, conscience, family honor. What one person knows about another comes out slowly. The Faust epigraph is a warning the characters will spend the book fulfilling, that knowledge shared blindly and knowledge buried can ruin in equal measure.
contrary-mary:
Contrary Mary, by Temple Bailey, was copyrighted in 1914 by the Penn Publishing Company and reached seven printings within its first year. Illustrations by Charles S. Corson include a frontispiece of a quick glance flashed across a room. Its chapter titles are small stories in themselves, in the old manner: In Which Silken Ladies Ascend One Stairway, and a Lonely Wayfarer Ascends Another.

Mary is the contrary heroine, sweet and twenty and speaking a new and modern language. She rents a gentleman's library, and brings Christmas to the Tower Rooms. Roger remembers a face, Delilah remembers a voice, and Porter pleads for a privilege Roger declines. Aunt Frances defends matrimony as a fixed institution and meets flaming arguments. A first-person letter in the later pages measures happiness by those same Tower Rooms.
cow-country:
B M Bower follows Buddy in Cow-Country from ambitious man-child through trail herds and Indian lore to manhood as Bud. The chapter list promises the Muleshoe ranch, a lost boy at Little Lost, the Sinks, the Catrock gang, and Bud meeting the woman. Buddy gives warning and runs true to type before the young eagle must fly.

Bud rides through Catrock and loses Marian, picks his footing in a horse race where Jeff is accused of taking a boy's money unfairly, and faces rustlers with guardian angels riding point. Bower's own Montana years supply the brands, ranges, and talk. The novel is a Western bildungsroman, its hero educated by cattle, horses, and one honest girl.
criticisms-on-the-origin-of-species-from:
Thomas Henry Huxley published this long review essay in the Natural History Review in 1864, five years into the Darwinian controversy. Its occasion is foreign commentary on Darwin's Origin of Species. Huxley notes the support of the linguist Schleicher and of Haeckel, then turns to two substantial attacks, by the Wurzburg anatomist Kolliker and by Flourens of the French Academy.

Kolliker's rival Theory of Heterogeneous Generation gets the closer handling, first in its objections and then in its construction. Huxley charges him with mistaking Darwin for a teleologist, a thinker who builds purpose into nature. Varieties, Huxley insists, arise by general laws whether useful, hurtful, or indifferent. The essay is Darwin's bulldog at work in print: part summary, part cross-examination, part counter-attack.
danny-s-own-story:
Don Marquis lets Danny tell Danny's Own Story in his own unlettered voice, starting with why he has no last name. Found in a basket on the Walters family's steps, he grows up between a drunken Hank and a quarrelsome Elmira. The comedy of his telling softens a hard childhood.

Danny runs away, works farms and lumber yards, falls in with tramps and small-town sharpers, and keeps his shrewd good humor through every beating and betrayal. Marquis, later famous for archy the cockroach, here masters American vernacular storytelling. The novel follows its hero toward the Klondike and manhood, and readers hear Danny thinking in every misspelled, perfectly chosen sentence.
delsarte-system-of-oratory:
A full course in voice and gesture fills the Delsarte System of Oratory, in its fourth edition from Edgar S. Werner of New York, 1893. The book joins four works: the Abbé Delaumosne on Delsarte, Mme Angélique Arnaud, and all the literary remains of François Delsarte in his own words. Lectures by his daughter, Mme Marie Géraldy, given in America, stand fourth.

Voice comes first: vowels, strength of sound, pace, breath, silence, and inflection. Gesture fills the second part, as the direct agent of the heart and the interpreter of speech. Laws of gesture treat the torso, the limbs, and the reason of each motion. Berlioz and others add articles. The system trained actors and speakers across two lands.
discourses-on-satire-and-on-epic-poetry:
John Dryden wrote his Discourses on Satire and on Epic Poetry in his last years, and this 1888 Cassell edition reprints both with an introduction. Dryden's discourse on satire, inscribed to the Earl of Dorset, traces the form from Horace and Juvenal and settles what makes a fine satire: not mere railing, but art. The epic discourse weighs Homer against Virgil and asks how a heroic poem should be built, judged, and translated.

The introduction contrasts these mature essays with his youthful Essay of Dramatic Poesie, written as Dutch guns sounded in 1667. Dryden reasons from wide reading in the French and classical critics yet trusts his own judgment. English criticism begins in earnest here, in prose as masculine and quotable as his verse.
divine-comedy-cary-s-translation-purgato:
Dante Alighieri's Purgatory, the Purgatorio, forms the second canticle of the Divine Comedy in H F Cary's translation. Its first canto lifts the sail of Dante's genius over better waves, glad to leave hell's cruel sea behind. A mountain island rises from the southern ocean, where souls climb toward heaven.

Virgil leads Dante up seven terraces, one for each deadly sin. The proud bend under stones there. The envious, who hoped a neighbor's fall would raise them, have their eyes sewn shut. Statius joins the climb, and the Earthly Paradise crowns the mountain. Cary's blank verse keeps the middle canticle's mood, harsher than paradise, gentler than hell, full of music and morning light.
doctor-claudius-a-true-story:
A German scholar in search of a life fills F. Marion Crawford's novel of 1883. Macmillan and Company of London issued it, and Crawford, author of Mr Isaacs, inscribes it to his dear friends the Countess Margaret and Claudius. The title calls the tale a true story.

Doctor Claudius sits among his books and tells himself he is old, and has told himself so for many long months. Yet his flaxen hair is thick, his hand steady, and his shoulders broad and square. The gap between his life and his companions' lives is his secret theme. A lady hopes to find in him what she never found before, and her words, always, always, ring in his ears. Crawford writes a grave romance of friendship turning to love.
doe-osti-17120798-enhanced-efficiency-in:
Alexander Weberg and Amanda Salazar of Los Alamos tackle a sample saving problem in nuclear forensics, in a report issued 1 October 2026. After a nuclear detonation, debris holds activation products, atoms made radioactive inside device structural materials. These traces tell experts what the device was built from, which aids attribution. They are scarce and hide under intense fission product background.

Standard practice purifies one product at a time and eats large sample shares. In low activity samples, there may not be enough debris to go around. The project develops one sequential separation procedure that pulls several activation products, derived from stainless steel, from a single small aliquot. Preserving the rest of the sample leaves material for other key forensic measurements.
doe-osti-2575661-expedition-ut-gom2-2-su:
An expedition summary by Peter B. Flemings, Carla Thomas, Stephen C. Phillips, and the UT-GOM2-2 science party reports a 2023 drilling campaign in the deepwater Gulf of Mexico. Working from the Helix Q4000 in the Terrebonne Basin, the team drilled at Site H, Walker Ridge Block 313. Their target was gas hydrate, ice-like methane deposits, from the seafloor down to the base of the hydrate stability zone.

Coring ran continuously to 155.1 meters below the seafloor, then periodically through hydrate-bearing sands and their mud boundaries to 861.3 meters total depth. Recovery totaled 162.6 meters of conventional core and 54.8 meters of pressure core, which keeps samples at seabed pressure. Twelve temperature readings between 27.1 and 144.5 meters fixed the geothermal gradient. The samples and logs now feed biological, geochemical, and mechanical models of how hydrates fit the carbon cycle and whether they could serve as an energy resource.
doe-osti-2589620-bayesian-attack-model-b:
The user story of the Bayesian Attack Model, a tool for defenders of industrial control systems, is told in Sandia report SAND2025-11801R. Authors Lee Maccarone, Romuald Valme, and Ted Anaya describe software funded through the Department's cybersecurity office by way of Idaho National Laboratory. Control systems in power and water plants face attacks that unfold across many small clues.

The tool gathers attack observables, the traces an intruder leaves, from many sources into one analyst view. Bayesian reasoning, which updates odds as evidence arrives, helps rank what the traces mean. Analysts can then characterize an attack while it is still under way and interrupt it before damage lands. The document is written as a user story, showing the defender's workflow rather than the code.
doe-osti-3013576-sitka-energy-inventory:
Pacific Northwest National Laboratory's Sitka Energy Inventory, baseline year 2023, counts the energy use and emissions of the City and Borough of Sitka, Alaska. Sitka joined the Energy Technology Innovation Partnership Project in fall 2023, and its Sustainability Commission asked for a repeatable method to track reliance on imported fuel. As an island community, Sitka barges in fuel at prices above national averages, while two hydropower dams keep its electricity near average cost.

Across all three emission scopes, Sitka produced about 84,346 metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent in 2023. The inventory covers electricity, ground transport, fishing and charter boats, heating, waste, air travel, cruise ships, and shipping, sector by sector. Each estimate comes with a method the community can rerun in later years to watch its footprint change.
doe-osti-3022277-advanced-test-reactor-n:
INL report INL/RPT-25-88792, by Michael Reichenberger, Kelly McCary, and Dani Ottaway, presents neutron dosimetry results for Advanced Test Reactor cycle 175A-1. Experimenters who irradiate materials in the reactor need to know the neutron exposure their samples received, position by position, and dosimetry wires are the physical record of that exposure.

A single set of cobalt and nickel wires rode in numerous irradiation locations for the whole cycle. Their measured specific activity, combined with the cycle's power history given in the report, lets users compute thermal and fast neutron fluence rates for each position. Standard test methods do the math. The bulk of the document is the resulting data tables, organized by experiment position so each irradiation team can pull the values for its own spot.
doe-osti-3023845-strategic-energy-plan-t:
Amanda Wachtel and Andrea Mammoli of Sandia National Laboratories, with Kate Klibansky of the Island Institute, wrote a strategic energy plan for the Town of Cranberry Isles, report SAND2026-18496, printed March 2026. Cranberry Isles is a small Maine island community served by Versant, where power options are narrow and outages bite hard. The plan takes stock of past energy work and sets goals and focus areas.

Storage gets close attention. Solar paired with batteries still stops when the grid stops, unless the system adds an islanding breaker and a grid-forming inverter. Cost has long blocked larger battery installs, so grants and loans matter. Versant cannot own generation, and whether it may own and run storage was still under review by the Public Utilities Commission.
doe-osti-3028186-shot-2s-1289-summary:
John Lang of Los Alamos National Laboratory sums up one experiment, shot 2s-1289, in this short record dated April 24, 2025, from Chamber 9 at TA-40. A PTFE-bronze impactor flying at 2.23 kilometers per second struck a PTFE-bronze sample backed by a lithium fluoride window. Photon Doppler velocimetry watched the impact. Staff from Tektronix and Newark joined eight LANL participants for the shot.

Most of the record is the diagnostic setup. Four oscilloscope channels each ran at 0.050 volts per division with 20 gigahertz bandwidth. Record length was set to twenty million points, the horizontal scale to 40 microseconds per division, and the sample rate to 50 gigasamples per second. The full SCPI configuration string is preserved, so another operator could rebuild the exact instrument state from this summary alone.
doe-osti-3097331-autonomous-ion-mass-spe:
Los Alamos National Laboratory offers a space instrument in technology snapshot LA-UR-26-23247, issued April 22, 2026, under Dharmesh N. Patel. AIMSS, the Autonomous Ion Mass Spectrometer Sentry, measures the plasma around Earth from low orbit, with flight operations on the International Space Station. Plasma density and temperature swings help forecast geomagnetic storms, but good forecasts also need plasma composition, which older orbital spectrometers measure poorly.

Inside AIMSS, ions bend by energy and mass as they cross the device, lighter ions curving more before they strike an imaging anode. Knowing the mix matters because density swings can charge spacecraft surfaces, spark discharges, foul optics and solar panels, and disrupt communications. Two patent filings cover the analyzer design and its reconfigurable high-voltage supply.
doe-osti-3367497-resource-the-carbon-neg:
